TO DR. JOHN ELLIOTSON

My dear Doctor,

Thirteen months ago—when this little tale seemed to have reached its last course and the cloth was being drawn, as it were, from my own bedside—a kind friend brought you to me. I lay there listening to the household sounds as a man listens from the far side of a door: the careful footfalls that try not to wake the sick, the hush of whispered messages, the small clink of a spoon against a cup when someone stirs broth in the next room. Those homely noises, so modest and so human, were then as momentous as church bells.

Had you not come—had you not kept your steady watch with the exactness of a cook who will not leave a pot at the wrong simmer, nor let a sauce scorch for want of a glance—I should, in all likelihood, never have risen again. Your skill was not a flourish for spectators, but the quiet, continual practice of a man who understands that life is maintained by attentions: the right draught at the right hour, the proper measure and patience, the vigilance that hears in a breath what others might not perceive. And your kindness—plain, nourishing, unadvertised kindness—was like good bread in a house where the appetite has nearly gone: not showy, not sweetened for sale, but saving.

I like to recall, too, the great goodness and gentleness that met me then from more hands than I had ever suspected were stretched toward me. It was a surprising friendship and sympathy—surprising, because one learns in illness how many voices one has been living among without truly hearing them, and how some voices, though fashionable in the daylight, fall away at night, while others, spoken in quieter dialects, keep their meaning when meaning is most needed. There are phrases of comfort that cannot be translated into any grand, dominant vocabulary; they belong to the private tongue of the hearth, to the idiom of those who know how to be still and present. The world outside may blare and clatter with its modern din—its bustling, self-asserting noises that would sell even compassion like a ticketed performance—but in that chamber, what sustained me was the better music: the low talk, the careful silence, the merciful discretion of people who did not make a spectacle of care.

And as you would take no other fee but thanks, let me set them down here—set them down, as one lays by a family receipt written in an old hand, so it may not be lost when fashions change and memory thins—for me and mine. I subscribe myself,

Yours most sincerely and gratefully,

W. M. THACKERAY.

If this sort of book—stirred with a busy spoon for two full years and now set down before you like a steaming dish on the table—fails in what clever people call Art (as it regularly does, and must, when the cook keeps leaning out of the kitchen to gossip with the guests), it has at least the plain advantage of being honest fare. A more elaborate banquet might be daintier in ornament, more symmetrical in courses, and yet lose the true savour in the over-handling.

For in this continual passing of plates and words between writer and reader, a man is forced into a kind of domestic frankness. He cannot keep his face powdered and his hands gloved the whole time: the talk grows familiar; the apron gets stained; he blurts his mind as it rises—like a pot that will boil over when it has a mind to. Looking back, he sees many a slip of pen and printer, many a seasoning flung in too hastily, many a word that, once served, he would gladly call back to the kitchen and scrape off. But it is a confidential meal, and like most long meals it must sometimes be dull, must sometimes flag. The perpetual speaker—puffing, perspiring, carving, apologising, insisting you take another slice—must, by sheer length of service, betray his own weaknesses, vanities, and peculiarities, as inevitably as a parish baker betrays, by the end of winter, whether he is generous with crusts or stingy with crumbs.

And as we judge a man, after long frequenting his table and his talk, not by one toast, or one temper, or one day’s cheerful hospitality, but by the steady tenor of his conversation and bearing; so, of a writer who gives himself up to you unreservedly, you will ask—Is he honest? Does he tell the truth in the main? Does he seem driven by a desire to find it and speak it? Or is he a quack, who sells sugared sentiment as if it were nourishing bread, and mouths for effect? Does he seek popularity by claptraps—those theatrical dishes made mostly of noise—or any other arts?

I cannot pretend I have been unlucky. I have found many thousands more readers than I ever expected to have sitting at my board, listening to the clink of my plates and the scratch of my knife. I have no right to say to them, You shall not find fault with my cookery, or yawn between courses, or fall asleep with your napkin over your face. But I ask you to believe that the person serving you, however ill he may truss a sentence or overbrown a paragraph, strives to tell the truth. If there is not that, there is nothing—no broth beneath the garnish, no honest grain beneath the icing.

Perhaps the lovers of “excitement”—those who cannot dine unless the dishes come in with a drum and a trumpet—may care to know that this book began with a very precise plan, which was entirely put aside. Ladies and gentlemen, you were to have been treated (and the writer’s and publisher’s pockets comfortably benefited) by a recital of the most active horrors, served up hot and perpetually. What more “piquant” than a ruffian—seasoned with many admirable virtues, as these people always are in the shops—lodging in St. Giles’s, and visited constantly by a young lady from Belgravia, who would rustle in like a white soufflé among frying onions? What more stirring than the contrast of societies? the mixture of slang and fashionable language, like pepper dashed into custard? the escapes, the battles, the murders—those great joints of melodrama brought in at every remove?

Nay, up to nine o’clock this very morning, my poor friend Colonel Altamont was doomed to execution, and the author only relented when his victim was actually at the window—hanging there, as it were, between the street and the noose, between the public appetite and the private conscience, while the whole scene clattered like a badly-managed kitchen at dinner-hour.

But the “exciting” plan was laid aside (with a very honourable forbearance on the part of the publishers), because, on attempting it, I found I failed from sheer want of experience of my subject. Never having been intimate with any convict in my life—never having sat down to supper with a gaol-bird, nor learned his dialect as one learns the cherished names of herbs from an old countrywoman—those manners being quite unfamiliar to me, the idea of entering into competition with M. Eugène Sue was abandoned. To describe a real rascal, you must make him so horrible that he would be too hideous to show; and unless the painter paints him fairly, I hold he has no right to show him at all. The worst thing is not the ugliness, but the falseness: the counterfeit coin of language that passes too easily, and buys applause it does not deserve.

Even the gentlemen of our age—this being an attempt to describe one of them, no better nor worse than most educated men—even these we cannot show as they are, with the notorious foibles and selfishness of their lives and their education. Since the author of *Tom Jones* was buried, no writer of fiction among us has been permitted to depict to his utmost power a MAN. We must drape him, and give him a certain conventional simper, as if truth itself must be muffled and spoken in drawing-room phrases. Society will not tolerate the Natural in our Art. A cry is raised if you let the thing speak in its own tongue, if you let a passion call itself by the word it uses in the club, the college, the mess-room. The very vocabulary is policed: certain honest names are forbidden, and we are forced to substitute genteel counters, as if one could change the taste of garlic by calling it “a foreign perfume.”

Many ladies have remonstrated and subscribers left me, because, in the course of the story, I described a young man resisting and affected by temptation. My object was to say that he had the passions to feel, and the manliness and generosity to overcome them. But you will not hear—it is best to know it—what moves in the real world; what passes in society; what is said and done where your sons sit and eat and laugh, where their talk makes its own rough music, sometimes pleasant as a country fair, sometimes harsh as a steam-mill grinding all day and night. A little more frankness than is customary has been attempted in this story; with no bad desire on the writer’s part, it is hoped, and with no ill consequence to any reader.

If truth is not always pleasant, at any rate truth is best—from whatever chair: from those whence graver writers or thinkers argue, or from that at which the story-teller sits when the last dish is gone, the room grows quieter, the clatter of the world outside still thumps and rattles, and he concludes his labour, and bids his kind reader farewell.

KENSINGTON, Nov. 26th, 1850.

PENDENNIS

One bright morning in the full London season—when the sparrows in Pall Mall must learn to chirp in the key of carriages, and even the wind sounds as if it wore kid gloves—Major Arthur Pendennis came from his lodgings, as punctually as a kettle that has been threatened, to breakfast at his Club.

The Club, being a sort of domestic establishment for men who prefer their homes public and their servants invisible, received him as it always did: with that soft, cushioned hush of feet on thick carpet, of silver laid down without clink, of doors closing as though afraid to disturb important digestion. The waiters bowed before him with the reverence usually reserved for Dukes, Field-Marshals, and persons who can detect a bad bottle at twenty paces.

At a quarter past ten—never at ten, never at half-past, because the Major was the kind of man who believed Time itself ought to keep appointments—he appeared in boots so superbly blacked that they might have been roasted, glazed, and served. His morning cravat sat in crisp checks like a well-pressed napkin that would not consent to be rumpled until dinner. His buff waistcoat carried the crown on its buttons as if the sovereign’s head had taken up residence there; and his linen was so spotless you could almost smell the starch, a clean, dry, papery perfume that suggested both virtue and a very expensive laundress. His whiskers were trimmed as accurately as a border of herbs; his cane looked as if it had been polished with the same devotion one gives to a prized copper saucepan.

From behind, you might have taken him for thirty. From the front, the illusion required more charity: the hair was rich brown with that particular richness which comes from art rather than Providence, and there were crow’s-feet about eyes that had once been brighter, and now looked slightly faded—as if too many chandeliers had shone on them. His nose had the Wellington air of having won battles on principle. His hands were long, pale, and confident, and his wristbands fastened with handsome gold buttons, a gift from the Duke of York—proof that Royalty, like good butter, improves anything it touches. Rings glittered on his fingers, the chief one engraved with the arms of Pendennis, as though the family crest needed constant reminding not to slip off.

He always took possession of the same table in the same corner—by the fire, yet near the window; a station chosen with the strategic genius of a man who had never besieged anything more perilous than a decanter. No one thought now of ousting him. In former days, one or two mad wags had tried it—young fellows who imagined courage consisted in sitting where another man had always sat. But there was a quiet dignity in the Major’s way of taking the next table and simply looking at them—an unspoken, steady gaze like cold gravy setting—that made it impossible to swallow toast under his eye. The interlopers fled; the corner belonged to him by right of long use, polished boots, and social terror.

His letters were already laid out there, as if the post had been trained to obey his habits. Many a young gentleman about town stared, half envious, half hungry, at the number of notes, at the seals and franks—the very wax seeming to exhale perfume and privilege. If you had a question about etiquette, society, who was married to whom, how old a duke really was in private, Major Pendennis was the oracle to consult. Marchionesses drove up and left notes for him, or fetched him out, as one might send for a physician—only that the Major’s remedies were smiles, introductions, and a touch of the hat at precisely the proper angle.

He seated himself, and while the waiters went to bring his toast and his hot newspaper (hot enough to warm the hands and the conscience), he surveyed his correspondence through a gold double eye-glass. He flourished it so jauntily you might not have known it was spectacles in disguise; he examined one pretty note after another, and laid them aside in order, as if arranging courses for a dinner.

There were large, solemn dinner cards suggestive of heavy soups, heavier conversation, and men who talk as if they are chewing. There were neat little confidential notes, with feminine entreaties folded into them like secrets inside a pastry. There was an invitation on thick official paper from the Marquis of Steyne—come to Richmond, to a little party at the Star and Garter, and speak French; the Major spoke French as neatly as he tied a neckcloth, and with as much satisfaction to himself. There was another from the Bishop of Ealing and Mrs. Trail, requesting the honour of Major Pendennis’s company at Ealing House—an engagement he liked, though bishop’s dinners were apt to proceed with the cautious tread of a sermon. He read them all gracefully, and with added relish because Mr. Glowry, the Scotch surgeon, sat opposite eating his breakfast and hating him.

Glowry’s hatred was of the quiet, nutritious kind: it sustained itself on small daily portions. He watched the seals and franks, watched the Major’s easy air of being wanted everywhere, and chewed in the gloom of a man who receives no notes except bills.

The Major, having tasted his importance, took out his pocket-book and began to decide—like a steward planning a week’s provisions—where to expend his presence. He threw over Cutler, the East India Director in Baker Street, in order to dine with Lord Steyne and the French party at the Star and Garter. He accepted the Bishop because—though the dinner might be slow—he liked to dine with bishops. So he went through his list, accepting and declining as fancy and interest dictated, and then turned to breakfast in earnest: toast properly done, not burned into bitterness nor left pale and flabby; butter that spread without sulking; coffee whose aroma rose in a dark, comforting cloud, mingling with the room’s gentle soundscape—murmured greetings, the soft scrape of chair legs, the discreet clatter of crockery carefully trained not to clatter.

Outside, London roared in its usual iron-and-leather way; inside, the Club subdued noise into a kind of gentlemanly purr. It was a refuge from the city’s grinding wheels—a place where even news arrived “hot” but never loud. The Major unfolded the paper, glanced at the gazette, the births and deaths, the fashionable intelligence—making sure his name was present where it should be, like a seasoning that must appear in every respectable dish.

Among all the notes in his morning budget there remained only one unread: it lay solitary and apart, as if it had walked in from muddy lanes and felt shy among all these crested envelopes. It had a country postmark and a homely seal. The superscription was in a delicate female hand; it was marked “Immediate” with a strong dash of anxiety under the word—an underline like a knife-score on a chopping board.

Yet the Major, for reasons of his own, had left this humble rural petitioner to the last. In the antechamber under the slop-bason, as it were, the country letter waited while the grandees of London were admitted and dismissed.

At last it came to be its turn. He broke the seal—“Fairoaks” engraved upon it; “Clavering St. Mary’s” for a postmark—and, being a man who could prolong pleasure or postponement as he pleased, he began by perusing the envelope before he attacked the inner epistle.

“Is it a letter from another Jook?” growled Mr. Glowry inwardly. “Pendennis would not be leaving that to the last, I’m thinking.”

“My dear Major Pendennis,” the letter ran, “I beg and implore you to come to me immediately—”

Very likely, thought Pendennis; and Steyne’s dinner to-day.

“I am in the very greatest grief and perplexity. My dearest boy, who has been hitherto everything the fondest mother could wish, is grieving me dreadfully. He has formed—I can hardly write it—a passion, an infatuation—”

The Major’s mouth twitched into a grin at the words, as if “infatuation” were an over-sweet pudding served by a sentimental cook.

“—for an actress who has been performing here. She is at least twelve years older than Arthur—who will not be eighteen till next February—and the wretched boy insists upon marrying her.”

Whatever sound the Major made at that moment was not one the Club encouraged. Rage and astonishment gathered in his open mouth so visibly that Glowry, alarmed by the look of a man about to burst, felt in his pocket for the lancet he always carried in his card-case. Pendennis’s face had the expression of a person who has bitten unexpectedly on grit in a dish he ordered expensive.

“Hay! What’s making Pendennis swear now?” Glowry asked himself, with the secret hope that it was something irreparable.

“Do, my dear friend,” the grief-stricken lady went on, “come to me instantly on the receipt of this; and, as Arthur’s guardian, entreat, command, the wretched child to give up this most deplorable resolution.”

More entreaties followed, poured out with the helpless urgency of a mother who has discovered that love, like yeast, rises best when you least want it to. The writer ended by signing herself his “unhappy affectionate sister, Helen Pendennis.”

“Fairoaks, Tuesday,” the Major muttered as he read the last words, as if the date itself were an insult. “A d——d pretty business at Fairoaks, Tuesday. Now let us see what the boy has to say.”

He took up the other letter. It was written in a great floundering boy’s hand, sealed with the large signet of the Pendennises—larger even than the Major’s own—and with supplementary wax sputtered all round, like sauce spilled in excitement: unmistakable signs of tremulousness and agitation.

It ran:

“FAIROAKS, Monday, Midnight.

“MY DEAR UNCLE, In informing you of my engagement with Miss Costigan, daughter of J. Chesterfield Costigan, Esq., of Costiganstown, but, perhaps, better known to you under her professional name of Miss Fotheringay, of the Theatres Royal Drury Lane and Crow Street, and of the Norwich and Welsh Circuit, I am aware that I make an announcement which cannot, according to the present prejudices of society at least, be welcome to my family.

“My dearest mother, on whom, God knows, I would wish to inflict no needless pain, is deeply moved and grieved, I am sorry to say, by the intelligence which I have this night conveyed to her. I beseech you, my dear Sir, to come down and reason with her and console her.

“Although obliged by poverty to earn an honourable maintenance by the exercise of her splendid talents, Miss Costigan’s family is as ancient and noble as our own. When our ancestor, Ralph Pendennis, landed with Richard II. in Ireland, my Emily’s forefathers were kings of that country. I have the information from Mr. Costigan, who, like yourself, is a military man.

“It is in vain I have attempted to argue with my dear mother, and prove to her that a young lady of irreproachable character and lineage, endowed with the most splendid gifts of beauty and genius, who devotes herself to the exercise of one of the noblest professions, for the sacred purpose of maintaining her family, is a being whom we should all love and reverence, rather than avoid;—my poor mother has prejudices which it is impossible for my logic to overcome, and refuses to welcome to her arms one who is disposed to be her most affectionate daughter through life.

“Although Miss Costigan is some years older than myself, that circumstance does not operate as a barrier to my affection, and I am sure will not influence its duration. A love like mine, Sir, I feel, is contracted once and for ever. As I never had dreamed of love until I saw her—I feel now that I shall die without ever knowing another passion. It is the fate of my life. It was Miss C.’s own delicacy which suggested that the difference of age, which I never felt, might operate as a bar to our union. But having loved once, I should despise myself, and be unworthy of my name as a gentleman, if I hesitated to abide by my passion: if I did not give all where I felt all, and endow the woman who loves me fondly with my whole heart and my whole fortune.

“I press for a speedy marriage with my Emily—for why, in truth, should it be delayed? A delay implies a doubt, which I cast from me as unworthy. It is impossible that my sentiments can change towards Emily—that at any age she can be anything but the sole object of my love. Why, then, wait?

“I entreat you, my dear Uncle, to come down and reconcile my dear mother to our union, and I address you as a man of the world, qui mores hominum multorum vidit et urbes, who will not feel any of the weak scruples and fears which agitate a lady who has scarcely ever left her village.

“Pray, come down to us immediately. I am quite confident that—apart from considerations of fortune—you will admire and approve of my Emily.

“Your affectionate Nephew,

“ARTHUR PENDENNIS, JR.”

When the Major came to the end, his face took on such a look of outrage and horror that Glowry, still fingering his lancet, believed for a moment that Fashion itself had struck Pendennis down. The intelligence was enough to agitate any guardian who lived by the favourable opinion of other men: the head of the Pendennises going to marry an actress; a headstrong boy plunging into matrimony with the rashness of someone who thinks passion is a permanent income.

“The mother has spoiled the young rascal,” groaned the Major inwardly, with that special bitterness one reserves for other people’s parenting. “With her cursed sentimentality and romantic rubbish. My nephew marry a tragedy queen! Gracious mercy, people will laugh at me so that I shall not dare show my head!”

And in the midst of his moral indignation—like pepper in a dish whose principal ingredient is self—there stung him an inexpressible pang: Lord Steyne’s dinner at Richmond would be lost. The Star and Garter, the French talk, the select society, the agreeable evening he had promised himself—gone. In their place: a night without rest, wedged into an abominable tight mail-coach, rattling through darkness as if the road were determined to saw him into pieces.

Worse yet, this single foolish romance at Fairoaks might swallow not only one dinner, but a whole menu of engagements. Who knew how long it would detain him? Love, in provincial households, had a way of boiling over and sticking to everything.

He quitted his breakfast-table for the adjoining writing-room, and there, with the rueful air of a man canceling a feast because someone at home has upset the larder, he wrote refusals to the Marquis, the Earl, the Bishop, and all his entertainers. The very scratch of his pen seemed louder in that quieter room, a thin, resentful sound—like the last crisp edge of toast being broken in two.

Then he ordered his servant to take places in the mail-coach for that evening—charging, of course, the sum he disbursed to the account of the widow and the young scapegrace of whom he was guardian; for if Romance must be paid for, the Major intended it should never come out of the portion reserved for his own comfort.

Early in the Regency—when George the Magnificent was still being magnificent in public and short of small change in private—there lived in a west-country town called Clavering a gentleman who insisted, with a persistence worthy of a better cause, that he was a gentleman. His name was Pendennis.

There were people in Clavering, and more in Bath, with memories as sharp as vinegar, who could still see (with the inward eye, and sometimes with the outward) a certain board once painted with the word PENDENNIS in honest letters, and crowned—not with a coat-of-arms, mind you, but with a gilt pestle and mortar. It hung above a humble shop-door in Bath, where Mr. John Pendennis had pounded roots and seeds, rolled pills, mixed draughts, and, when the world was particularly unkind, sold a farmer’s wife a pennyworth of salts across the counter as if he had been born to it. If a lady wanted a plaster, he would cut it, fold it, and wrap it in brown paper with a neatness that felt almost like a compliment; if a gentleman wanted sal-volatile, he would pour it with a bow; and if anybody wanted tooth-brushes, hair-powder, or a cake of Windsor soap with a smell of London about it, he would condescend (oh, the condescension!) to supply those too.

Now, it was one of Mr. Pendennis’s private tragedies that he had excellent reasons—on paper—for despising the very counter he stood behind. He possessed a Cornish pedigree that trotted the Pendennises back through Normans and Druids and heaven knew what misty forefathers who probably ate acorns with a good deal of dignity. The family had, at a late period of its existence, intermarried with Normans as if doing a favour to the Conquest. There were shadowy connections, too, with Wales and Brittany; and Mr. Pendennis, if you gave him time and a quiet room, could make you related to almost anybody of consequence.

He had even begun a university career. At Cambridge, in his second year—at that very age when a young man should be learning Latin particles and the art of running up harmless bills—his father died insolvent, leaving the pedigree intact and everything else knocked into a hat. Necessity, that vulgar tyrant who never reads coats-of-arms, drove John Pendennis into apprenticeship under his mother’s brother, a London apothecary of low family. It was a bitter dose. He detested the trade; and detested, with an elegance all his own, the coarse-minded relative who had offered him shelter at the cost of self-respect.

As soon as he was able, he escaped to Bath and set up for himself with a modest medical ensign: the gilded pestle and mortar, the pink bottles, the clean window, the little interior smelling of camphor, cinnamon, spirits of lavender, and that indefinable sharp sweetness which belongs to fresh-mixed draughts. He struggled for a time; he kept his shop and its gilt ornaments decent by sheer scrubbing and thrift; he kept his bed-ridden mother in comfort by denying himself almost everything but the consolations of gentility.

And then—because history is made as often by collisions as by coronations—Lady Ribstone happened to be passing to the Rooms in a chair managed by an intoxicated Irish chairman. The man bumped her ladyship into Mr. Pendennis’s very door-post with a gusto as if he had been paid by the bruised inch, and the chair-pole went clean through the handsomest pink bottle in the surgeon’s window. There was a crash of glass, a flash of coloured liquid like some sacrificial cordial, and a scream that could have been heard in the Pump Room had the Pump Room not been busy making its own noises.

Lady Ribstone alighted in hysterics. Mr. Pendennis, with the coolness of a man who has long practised composure as an ingredient, placed her in a chair inside his shop. He revived her with cinnamon and sal-volatile—warm spice and sharp spirit, domestic comfort and medicinal sting—while the world outside stared at the wrecked bottle as if it were a fallen idol.

His manners were so soothing, so uncommonly gentlemanlike, that Lady Ribstone immediately appointed her “preserver” apothecary to her person and family—an enormous family, like a small parish with better linen. Sir Pepin Ribstone, of Codlingbury, Bart., had the sense to let his wife be grateful. Master Ribstone, home from Eton for Christmas, over-ate himself with the heroic appetite of a boy who considers digestion a superstition, and fell into a fever. Mr. Pendennis treated him with skill and tenderness; and from that day fortune stopped being quite so rude.

Bath patronised him—especially the ladies. His little shop became a smart one; then, step by gentlemanly step, he dropped the sale of tooth-brushes and perfumery, as unworthy of ancient lineage; then he shut up the shop altogether and kept only a surgery, attended by a genteel young man; then he acquired a gig, and a man to drive him; and at last, before she left this world of draughts and drafts, his mother had the happiness of seeing her beloved John step into a close carriage of his own—only one horse, true, but with the arms of Pendennis handsomely emblazoned on the panels, as if paint could undo the past.

“What would Arthur say now?” she asked, with the sharp triumph of a woman who can congratulate and reproach in a single breath. She meant a younger son of hers, a soldier. “Who never so much as once came to see my dearest Johnny through all the time of his poverty and struggles!”

“Captain Pendennis is with his regiment in India, mother,” Mr. Pendennis said, patiently, “and, if you please, I wish you would not call me Johnny before the young man—before Mr. Parkins.”

Presently the day came when she ceased to call him Johnny or anything at all. The house, which had always been half filled with her querulous kindness, went suddenly hollow. Mr. Pendennis altered the night-bell and placed it in the room where she had grumbled for years; he slept in the great bed there, as if to keep watch over the ghost of duty. He was past forty when this happened—before the war was over; before George the Magnificent came to the throne; before this history, indeed. But what is a gentleman without his pedigree? He had it handsomely framed and glazed, hanging between pictures of Codlingbury House and St. Boniface’s College, Cambridge, where he had once lived like a young man with a future. He had taken the pedigree out of a trunk—like Sterne’s officer calling for his sword—now that he was a gentleman and could show it.

About the time of Mrs. Pendennis’s death, another of his patients died too: old Lady Pontypool, daughter of Reginald twelfth Earl of Bareacres, and therefore great-grand-aunt to the present Earl; widow of John second Lord Pontypool, and likewise of the Reverend Jonas Wales of the Armageddon Chapel, Clifton—an accumulation of titles and bereavements like layers of heavy pastry. For the last five years of her life, Lady Pontypool had been attended by Miss Helen Thistlewood, a very distant relative of Bareacres, and daughter of Lieutenant R. Thistlewood, R.N., killed at Copenhagen.

Miss Thistlewood had, under Lady Pontypool’s roof, boarding and lodging and tyranny: the comfortable crust and the daily scourge. It was a particular, domestic kind of despotism—one of those infernal arrangements by which a woman who cannot command an army commands a companion. Mr. Pendennis, who visited at least twice a day, could not help remarking the angelical sweetness with which Miss Helen bore insults that would have made a saint cough. He observed her pale face, her quiet hands, her voice kept low as if loudness were a sin. He watched her serve tea to the old lady—tea brewed to Lady Pontypool’s exacting taste, strong enough to float a spoon yet clear enough to shame muddy water—while the elder criticised the very angle at which the cup was offered.

Then Lady Pontypool died. The Pontypool family descended upon the property like a flight of crows on a field, and everything was nailed into boxes, packed into hampers, swaddled with haybands, buried in straw, locked under three keys in green baize plate-chests, and carted away under Miss Helen’s eyes. Mr. Pendennis sat with her in the fourth mourning coach going to Bath Abbey, where her ladyship’s venerated remains were to be deposited, and as the wheels creaked and the horses’ hooves beat their melancholy measure, he looked at Miss Helen’s sweet pale face and made up his mind to ask a question which made his own pulse gallop up to ninety—at least.

He was more than twenty years older than she, and at no time the most ardent of men. Perhaps he had strangled a love affair in youth; perhaps, indeed, early love affairs should be drowned like blind kittens—painful, but tidy, and done before anyone gives them names. At three-and-forty he was a collected quiet little gentleman in black stockings, with a bald head and careful manners. A few days after the funeral he called to see Miss Helen; and while he felt her pulse he kept hold of her hand a moment longer than the pulse required. (Doctors have their indulgences too; only theirs are counted in seconds.)

He asked her where she was going to live, now that the Pontypools had carried off the plate and the very air of the house. Her eyes filled with tears. She said she did not know. She had a little money—Lady Pontypool had left her a thousand pounds—and she might go into a boarding-house, or into a school, or into any of those respectable limbos where gentlewomen wait for life to happen. In short, she did not know.

Then Mr. Pendennis, still holding the cold little hand, asked if she would come and live with him.

He spoke of his age as though it were an injury done to her; spoke of his birth, his principles, his temper; spoke of his prospects improving daily, and his loneliness, and his need of a kind and constant companion whom it would be his life’s study to make happy. In truth, he recited a small speech which he had composed that morning in bed and rehearsed in his carriage on the way to her—polite, proper, and phrased like a prescription: take one husband, twice daily, against melancholy.

Perhaps Miss Helen too had once imagined another fate—something warmer than being asked to marry a man who rapped his teeth and smiled artificially, who was laboriously polite to the butler as he slid upstairs and profusely civil to the lady’s-maid waiting at the bed-room door; a man whom Lady Pontypool used to ring for as she rang for a servant, and who came with even more eagerness. Yet she knew how worthy he was; how prudent, how honourable; how good he had been to his mother, and constant in his care. And so the upshot was that she blushed very much, made him an extremely low curtsey, and asked leave—to consider his very kind proposal.

They were married in the dull Bath season, which is the height of the season in London (so that Providence, with its usual humour, contrived that the very moment Mrs. Pendennis might have been exhibited to the world, the world was elsewhere). Through a professional friend, M.R.C.S., Mr. Pendennis secured lodgings in Holles Street, Cavendish Square, and carried his wife to town in a chaise and pair. He showed her the theatres, the Parks, the Chapel Royal; he showed her people going to drawing-rooms as if they were an educational exhibit; and gave her all the pleasures of the town which can be enjoyed by two persons who are still a little shy of each other and too well bred to confess it.

He left cards upon Lord Pontypool, upon the Right Honourable the Earl of Bareacres, and upon Sir Pepin and Lady Ribstone. Bareacres took no notice. Pontypool called, admired Mrs. Pendennis, and said Lady Pontypool would come and see her—an achievement accomplished by proxy, in the person of John the footman, who brought a card and an invitation to a concert five weeks off. By that time Mr. Pendennis was back in his one-horse carriage, dispensing pills and draughts again. But the Ribstones asked him and Mrs. Pendennis to an entertainment, and Mr. Pendennis bragged of it to the last day of his life, as a man will brag of a dish he once cooked for royalty, though he has boiled mutton ever since.

For the secret ambition of Mr. Pendennis had always been to be a gentleman. It takes much time and careful saving for a provincial doctor—not rich, only respectable—to lay by enough to purchase house and land; but besides his own prudence, fortune helped. He bought, very advantageously, a house and small estate close upon the village of Clavering. Words cannot describe his pride when he found himself a landed proprietor, and could walk over acres that belonged to him and not to an apothecary’s ledger. A lucky purchase of shares in a copper-mine increased his wealth, and he realised with uncommon prudence while the mine was still in vogue. Finally, he sold his business at Bath to Mr. Parkins for a handsome ready sum and an annuity to be paid for a certain number of years after he retired for ever from the handling of mortar and pestle.

Arthur Pendennis, his son, was eight years old at the time; so it is no wonder the boy, leaving Bath so young, almost forgot that such a place existed, and that his father’s hands had once been dirtied by compounding odious pills or spreading filthy plasters. The old man never spoke of the shop; never alluded to it; called in the medical practitioner of Clavering to attend his family when occasion required; sank black breeches and stockings altogether; attended market and sessions, and wore bottle-green coat and brass buttons with drab gaiters, precisely as if he had been born in a park and nursed on rent-rolls.

He stood at his lodge-gate and watched the coaches come in, bowing gravely as guards and coachmen touched their hats and drove by. He founded the Clavering Book Club and set up the Samaritan Soup and Blanket Society. He brought the mail, which used to run through Cacklefield, away from that village and through Clavering—an act of public spirit which Clavering praised as if the mail had been a family heirloom. At church he was active as vestryman and worshipper. At market every Thursday he went from pen to stall, looked at samples of oats, munched corn, felt beasts, punched geese in the breast, and weighed them with the air of a man who understood both providence and poultry. He did business with farmers at the Clavering Arms as knowing as any old frequenter. It became his shame, as it had once been his pride, to be called Doctor; those who wished to please him called him Squire.

Heaven knows where they came from, but a whole range of Pendennis portraits soon hung round his oak dining-room: Lelys and Vandykes, he vowed—every one of them—and when asked the history of the originals he would say vaguely that they were “ancestors of his.” You could see by Mrs. Pendennis’s looks that she disbelieved these genealogical miracles; she generally tried to turn the conversation when he commenced them. But little Arthur believed with all his might. Roger Pendennis of Agincourt, Arthur Pendennis of Crécy, General Pendennis of Blenheim and Oudenarde became as real to him as Robinson Crusoe or the Seven Champions of Christendom.

Mr. Pendennis’s fortune—at best not above eight hundred a year—did not permit the great people of the county to clasp him to their bosoms; but it provided a decent comfortable society of the second-best sort. They were not roses, perhaps, but they lived near roses and had a good deal of the odour of genteel life. They brought out their plate and dined each other round in moonlight twice a year, driving a dozen miles for the ceremony and eating as if distance gave appetite a moral character.

Besides the county society, there was Clavering town itself—more of it than the Pendennises desired. Mrs. Pybus was always poking about Helen’s conservatories, interfering with soup-tickets and coal-clubs as if charity were a public road. Captain Glanders (H.P., 50th Dragoon Guards) swaggered about the Squire’s stables and gardens, trying to enlist him in quarrels with the Vicar, the Postmaster, the Reverend F. Wapshot of Clavering Grammar School (for overflogging his son Anglesea), and, in short, with the entire parish. Mr. and Mrs. Pendennis often blessed themselves that Fairoaks was nearly a mile out of Clavering; otherwise their threshold would never have been free from prying eyes and practising tongues.

The lawn of Fairoaks came down to the little river Brawl. Across it lay the plantations and woods—what was left of them—belonging to Clavering Park and Sir Francis Clavering, Bart. When the Pendennises first came, the park was let out in pasture and fed down by sheep and cattle; the great house stood with shutters up, a splendid freestone palace with stairs, statues, and porticos, the kind you may admire in a book called Beauties of England and Wales, where ruins look very comfortable and cost nothing. Sir Richard Clavering, Sir Francis’s grandfather, began the family’s ruin by building the palace; his successor achieved it by living in it. Sir Francis himself was abroad somewhere; no one could be found rich enough to rent that enormous mansion with its deserted rooms, mouldy clanking halls, and dismal galleries. Arthur Pendennis, as a boy, walked there trembling many a time, frightened less by ghosts than by the echo of his own small feet.

At sunset from the lawn there was a sight which made even Clavering’s gossip pause: Fairoaks and the opposite park put on a rich golden tinge; the upper windows of the great house flamed so that your eyes winked; the little river ran off noisily westward and was lost in a sombre wood; behind which the towers of the old abbey church of Clavering rose in purple splendour. Little Arthur and his mother cast long blue shadows over the grass; and he would repeat in a low voice—because beauty made him hushed—certain lines beginning, “These are thy glorious works, Parent of Good; Almighty! thine this universal frame,” to Mrs. Pendennis’s great delight. Such walks ended commonly in a profusion of filial and maternal embraces, for to love and to pray were the main occupations of this dear woman’s life; and Arthur, in later wildness, used to declare that he felt sure of going to heaven because his mother never could be happy there without him.

John Pendennis did not much care for the view, nor did he share in poetry and caresses. At six o’clock, to the minute, dinner occurred; after it he had a nap with the Globe newspaper on his knee and a yellow bandanna handkerchief on his face—yellow handkerchiefs sent from India by Major Pendennis, his brother, who had helped in the purchase of the majority and was now restored to favour. Thus, when sunset softened the world at half-past seven, Mr. Pendennis was generally engaged in the serious contemplation of printed columns and his own digestion.

The tenderness between mother and child seldom took place in his presence. However frisky they were before, Mrs. Pendennis and Arthur grew hushed when Mr. Pendennis walked into the drawing-room with his newspaper under his arm. There, while the boy, buried in a great chair, devoured whatever books he could lay hands on, the Squire perused his articles in the Gardener’s Gazette, or took a solemn hand at picquet with Mrs. Pendennis or an occasional friend from the village. Even the sounds of the house had to respect him: the clock ticked as if keeping step, the fire cracked softly in orderly intervals, and servants moved with a caution that suggested not awe but punctuality.

Mr. Pendennis usually contrived that at least one of his grand dinners should take place when his brother visited: “My brother, Major Pendennis,” was a constant theme of his conversation, rolled out with as much relish as any well-basted joint. The Major came biennially to Fairoaks on the return of his regiment from India and New South Wales, having sold out and gone upon half-pay. He was the link binding the family to London and fashion, and every link was made to rattle. He brought down the latest news of nobility, and was in the constant habit of dining with lords and great folks. He spoke of them with soldierlike respect and decorum: “My Lord Bareacres has been good enough to invite me to Bareacres for the pheasant-shooting,” or “My Lord Steyne is so kind as to wish for my presence at Stillbrook for the Easter holidays.” Mr. Pendennis made sure the whereabouts of “my brother the Major” were known at the Reading-room, at justice-meetings, and in the county-town, as if the Major were a particularly valuable shipment.

Carriages came from ten miles round to call upon Major Pendennis when he was at Fairoaks. His fame as a man about town was established throughout the county. There had been talk of his marrying Miss Hunkle of Lilybank—old Hunkle the attorney’s daughter, with at least fifteen hundred a year. But the Major refused the negotiation, advantageous as it seemed to those who think matrimony a financial instrument. “As a bachelor,” he said, “nobody cares how poor I am. I have the happiness to live with people so highly placed that a few hundreds more or less make no difference in the estimation they are pleased to hold me. Miss Hunkle, though most respectable, is not in possession of either the birth or the manners which would entitle her to be received into the sphere in which I have the honour to move. I shall live and die an old bachelor, John; and your worthy friend, Miss Hunkle, will find some more worthy object of her affection than a worn-out old soldier on half-pay.” Time proved his worldly wisdom: Miss Hunkle married a young French nobleman and now lived at Lilybank under the title of Baroness de Carambole, separated from her wild young scapegrace of a Baron shortly after their union—so that she gained a title, lost a husband, and kept the income, which is a very French ending for a Clavering beginning.

The Major was a favourite with almost all the little establishment at Fairoaks. He was good-natured as well as well-bred, and had sincere liking and regard for his sister-in-law, whom he pronounced—with perfect truth—to be as fine a lady as any in England and an honour to the family. Mrs. Pendennis’s tranquil beauty, natural sweetness, simplicity, and the dignity which perfect purity bestows, made the praise seem not flattery but fact. She moved through the world regardless of comment. She did not seem to know she was admired or hated for being so perfect; she carried on calmly, saying her prayers, loving her family, helping her neighbours, and doing her duty, with a quietness that made other women—noisier in speech and silk—feel somehow rebuked.

Yet rebuked they were. Miss Pybus said she was cold and haughty. Miss Pierce declared she was too proud for her station. Mrs. Wapshot, as a doctor of divinity’s lady, demanded the pas of one who was only the wife of a medical practitioner. Mr. Pendennis, when he drove his wife into the county-town to assize balls or concerts, stepped into the assembly with her on his arm and looked the great folks in the face as much as to say: Look at that, my lord—can any of you show me a woman like that?

Arthur Pendennis, for his part, believed in his mother as he believed in light: not as a thing to be proved, but as a thing by which all other things were seen. During his childhood the boy thought of her as little less than an angel—wisdom, love, and beauty in one. And in that household—where a man could change his name from Doctor to Squire as easily as changing his coat, where portraits appeared from nowhere to people the walls with invented ancestors, where the mail-coach’s rumble was treated like music because it chose the “right” road—Mrs. Pendennis preserved, in her own gentle way, something older than pedigrees and more delicate than fashion: the private language of affection, spoken softly, often misunderstood by the world, and, like all true dialects, impossible to translate into mere titles.

Arthur Pendennis was about sixteen when Providence, with the easy carelessness it shows in such matters, handed him the sceptre of Fairoaks and said, “There: reign.” He reigned, as young kings do, chiefly by being looked at.

In figure he was what his friends, in their brutal candour, called dumpy, and what his mamma, in her maternal jurisprudence, registered as “a neat little figure.” Nature had given him hair of that wholesome brown which turns to gold whenever the sun condescends to be civil; a round, rosy, freckled face, set in an expression of such ready good-humour that people forgave him his freckles as they forgive pepper in a sauce, because it gives the whole dish a better relish. His honest blue eyes laughed first and asked questions afterwards. When, later, those whiskers for which he sighed (as if they were a degree at Oxford) at last arrived, they were found to be decidedly red, as if they had been lightly toasted. Between sixteen and eighteen he shot up from five feet six to five feet eight, and then stopped with the obstinacy of a pudding that will not rise another inch though you coax it with more fire. His mother stared at that extra altitude as if it were an act of filial rebellion: three inches taller than Mr. Pendennis! Was there ever such an outrage upon established measures?

Of course he never went back to school. Greyfriars’ discipline did not suit him; it was like being forced to swallow physic through a funnel. At home there were hedges to jump, books to skim, and a mother to adore him at leisure. The question was debated, solemnly, like a matter of State. His uncle wanted him sent back. The Doctor wrote that Arthur’s future depended upon knowing a Greek play thoroughly, as if a man might be saved or damned by Euripides. But Pen, with the dexterity of youth, dropped a few artless hints about the dangers of Greyfriars—what wild chaps there were, what tempests of vice blew through dormitories—and his mother’s timid heart took alarm as readily as a soufflé takes air. The boy remained at home; and the whole Greek drama was spared the indignity of being learned.

Then Major Pendennis offered to procure him a commission in the Foot Guards, being himself acquainted with His Royal Highness the Commander-in-Chief, and having that great man’s kindness in his pocket like a visiting card. Pen’s heart leaped. He had heard the band at St. James’s on a Sunday—trumpets blaring, cymbals clashing, drums beating as if to drown thought itself—and he had seen, in the middle of that glittering racket, Tom Ricketts, once the butt and cockshy of the fourth form, the same Tom whose tight jacket and trousers had made him look like a boiled sausage and invited the lash of older wit. Pen had once cut him over the back with a hockey-stick; and now there he was—crimson and gold, bear-skin cap, staggering under the colours, nodding patronisingly as though he had invented Waterloo, talking familiarly to enormous men with tufts on their chins and medals on their breasts. What would not Pen have given to wear such epaulettes, to be swallowed up in that scarlet splendour, and to be deafened daily by music and martial uproar?

But Mrs. Pendennis, when her son ventured to propose it, put on a face as if he had suggested becoming a highwayman. She did not quarrel with those who thought otherwise (she was always charitable to the brink of being terrible), but in her opinion a Christian had no right to make the army a profession. Mr. Pendennis never, never would have permitted it. She should be very unhappy if Arthur thought of it.

Now, Pen would sooner have cut off his own nose and ears—deliberately, and of aforethought malice—than cause his mother one hour’s unhappiness. He was of that generous order which gives away its own best toys to keep peace in the nursery. So he made her an immediate present of his red coat, his epaulettes, his bear-skin cap, and the whole boiling stew of military glory. Mrs. Pendennis, naturally, thought him the noblest creature alive. Major Pendennis, when the commission was acknowledged and refused, wrote back curtly, with a certain angry dryness, and privately entered “spooney” against his nephew’s name.

Still, the Major was mollified at Christmas, when he came down to Fairoaks and saw the boy out hunting. Pen had a very good mare and rode her with uncommon pluck and grace; he took his fences coolly, yet with judgment, and without that bragging flourish which is the horsemanship of asses. He wrote to the chaps at school about his top-boots and his feats across country, as a young gentleman will write about boots and feats when he has nobody at hand to admire them daily. He began to think seriously of a scarlet coat again—one is always thinking seriously of scarlet at sixteen—and his mother owned, with a sigh and an inward prayer, that it would become him remarkably well, though she passed whole hours in anguish during his absence and daily expected to see him brought home on a shutter, like a joint of mutton.

With so many pleasures, it must not be supposed he neglected study altogether. His appetite for reading was excellent—only it was an appetite that refused the school’s bill of fare. It was when people tried to force his head into the waters of knowledge that he declined to drink. Left to himself, he devoured everything in the house, from Inchbald’s Theatre to White’s Farriery, and ransacked neighbouring book-cases like a boy robbing orchards. At Clavering he found a cargo of old French novels and read them with all his might, as if each volume were a secret pie cooling under somebody else’s window. He would perch for hours on the topmost bar of Doctor Portman’s library steps with a folio on his knees—Hakluyt’s Travels, Hobbes’s Leviathan, Augustini Opera, Chaucer’s Poems—turning pages with the pleased absorption of a young animal gnawing whatever is put before it.

He and the Vicar were excellent friends; and from his Reverence Pen learned that honest taste for port wine which distinguished him through life—a lesson taught as many great lessons are, not by precept but by practice, with the decanter making a soft, persuasive music against the glass. The house had its own acoustic ecology: the hush of the library broken by the crisp rasp of paper, the tender clink of glasses, the distant Sunday bells floating over fields as if the air itself were being stirred in a great invisible bowl. It was the sort of sound-world in which a boy’s hopes ripen quietly, like fruit in a warm pantry. Mrs. Portman, that dear good woman, was not jealous though her Doctor avowed himself in love with Mrs. Pendennis and pronounced her by far the finest lady in the county. Mrs. Portman’s only grief, as she looked up fondly at Pen on the book-ladder, was that her daughter Minny was too old for him—as indeed she was—Miss Myra Portman being only two years younger than Pen’s mother, and weighing as much as Pen and Mrs. Pendennis together.

If these details seem insipid, remember your own youth and ask whether it was made of fireworks or of bread-and-butter. There is a particular sweetness in the well-nurtured boy—brave and gentle, warm-hearted and loving—who looks the world in the face with kind honest eyes, as if it were a table laid for him, full of bright colours and innocent flavours. One does not know those years while one is eating them; only later, when the plate is cleared, does one remember how good they were.

To keep Mr. Pen from that idleness of which his friend the Doctor of the Cistercians had prophesied such dreadful consequences, Mr. Smirke, Dr. Portman’s curate, was engaged at a liberal salary to walk or ride over from Clavering and pass several hours daily with the young gentleman. Smirke was perfectly faultless at a tea-table; he wore a curl on his fair forehead as carefully as a garnish on a dish, and tied his neck-cloth with a melancholy grace, as if each fold were a line of elegy. He was a decent scholar and mathematician, and taught Pen as much as Pen was ever disposed to learn, which was not much. Pen soon took the measure of his tutor, and as the lad possessed a sense of humour, he found it impossible to respect a man who rode into the court-yard at Fairoaks on a pony turning out his toes so absurdly and leaving such a gap between his knees and the saddle that the creature seemed to be riding with an invisible barrel between his legs.

Pen nearly killed him with terror by putting him on his mare, Rebecca—named after Pen’s favourite heroine, the daughter of Isaac of York—and taking him for a ride over a common where the county fox-hounds (then hunted by that staunch old sportsman, Mr. Hardhead of Dumplingbeare) happened to meet. Mr. Smirke, on Rebecca, astonished the hounds as much as he disgusted the huntsman, laming one of the former by persisting in riding amongst the pack and receiving from the latter a speech more remarkable for energy of language than any oration he had ever heard since he left the bargemen on the banks of Isis. The whole scene was a symphony of rural sound—the horn, the yelp of hounds, the thud of hooves, the huntsman’s thunder—into which poor Smirke’s terrified little squeaks fell like cracked notes from a cheap fiddle.

Smirke confided his poems, Latin and English, to his pupil and presented Mrs. Pendennis with a volume of the latter, printed at Clapham, his native place. They read the ancient poets together and rattled through them at a pleasant canter, very different from the steady grubbing pace of the Cistercians, who scented out each word as they went like truffle-pigs, digging up every root in the way. Pen hated halting; if he was at fault he made his tutor construe and so galloped through the Iliad and Odyssey, the tragic writers, and the charming wicked Aristophanes (whom he vowed to be the greatest poet of all). He went at such a pace that, though he certainly traversed a great extent of the ancient country, he forgot it afterwards, retaining only that vague memory which some men in the House of Commons keep—two or three quotations for decency’s sake—or which a reviewer hints at, to show he has once heard of Greek. We are the most prosaic people in the world and the most faithful; and with a curious reverence we transmit, from generation to generation, the superstition of what we call the education of a gentleman.

Besides the ancients, Pen read the English with gusto. Smirke sighed and shook his head sadly about Byron and Moore; but Pen was a sworn fire-worshipper and a Corsair. He had them by heart and used to take little Laura into the window and say, “Zuleika, I am not thy brother,” in tones so tragical that the solemn child opened her great eyes wider, and stitched on, and understood not one word of what he read. He read Shakespeare to his mother (which she said she liked, but didn’t), and Byron, and Pope, and his favourite Lalla Rookh, which pleased her indifferently. But Bishop Heber—and Mrs. Hemans above all—melted her away. She was absorbed into her pocket-handkerchief when Pen read them in his kind boyish voice, as if each sentimental verse were a warm broth poured directly into her heart.

The Christian Year appeared about this time. Mother and son whispered it to each other with awe; faint—very faint—and seldom in after-life did Pendennis hear that solemn church-music, but he always loved the remembrance of it, and of the times when it struck on his heart and he walked over the fields full of hope and void of doubt, while the Sunday bells rang and rang—bells whose mellow, patient sound belonged to the place like its trees and its bread-ovens, a sound that made even a restless boy keep time inwardly for a moment, as if his life had a rhythm older than his own desires. How unlike the brass-and-cymbal clangour of St. James’s—how clean the country’s music was, before railways and iron shrieks and the modern passion for noise began to trample every delicate silence into the road.

It was at this period he broke out in the Poets’ Corner of the County Chronicle with verses with which he was perfectly satisfied. The pieces signed “NEP.” were his: “To a Tear;” “On the Anniversary of the Battle of Waterloo;” “To Madame Caradori singing at the Assize Meetings;” “On Saint Bartholomew’s Day” (a tremendous denunciation of Popery, and a solemn warning to England against emancipating the Roman Catholics), and so on—masterpieces which Mrs. Pendennis no doubt keeps to this day with his first socks, the first cutting of his hair, his bottle, and other relics of infancy, labelled and cherished as if posterity would one day demand them for a museum. He used to gallop Rebecca over Dumpling Downs or into the county town—call it Chatteris—spouting his own poems, full of Byronic afflatus, and believing, as youth will, that his private emotions were a public event.

His genius then was of a gloomy cast. He brought his mother a tragedy in which he killed sixteen people before the second act; it made her laugh so that, in a pet, he thrust the masterpiece into the fire—thus performing the only execution in the play that gave anybody real satisfaction. He projected an epic in blank verse, Cortez, or the Conqueror of Mexico, and the Inca’s Daughter. He wrote part of Seneca, or the Fatal Bath, and Ariadne in Naxos, with choruses and strophes and antistrophes that puzzled poor Mrs. Pendennis, who could follow a recipe better than a Greek chorus. He began a History of the Jesuits in which he lashed that Order with tremendous severity, warning his Protestant fellow-countrymen against their machinations. His loyalty delighted his mother: he was staunch Church-and-King in those days, and at the election, when Sir Giles Beanfield stood on the Blue interest against Lord Trehawk, Lord Eyrie’s son—a Whig and a friend of Popery—Arthur Pendennis, with an immense bow for himself (made by his mother) and a blue ribbon for Rebecca, rode alongside the Reverend Doctor Portman on his grey mare Dowdy, and at the head of the Clavering voters whom the Doctor brought up to plump for the Protestant Champion.

On that day Pen made his first speech at the Blue Hotel; and also, it appears, for the first time in his life took a little more wine than was good for him. Mercy, what a scene at Fairoaks when he rode back at ever so much o’clock at night! What moving of lanterns in the courtyard and stables though the moon shone bright; what a gathering of servants; what clattering over the bridge and up the stable-yard, with half a score of Clavering voters yelling after him the Blue song of the election—voices thick with patriotism and liquor, stamping their tune into the quiet country night as if to prove that enthusiasm is only another sort of noise.

Pen wanted them all to come in and have some wine—some very good Madeira—some capital Madeira. “John, go and get some Madeira!” he cried, with the lavishness of a young gentleman spending his mother’s cellar as though it were the national treasury. There is no knowing what the farmers might have done had not Madam Pendennis appeared in a white wrapper with a candle, her pale handsome face striking the revel like a sudden bell in church. She frightened those zealous Blues so by mere virtue and candlelight that they touched their hats and rode off, leaving the yard to the moon and the uneasy stamping of Rebecca.

Among these amusements there was one which forms, the poets assure us, the main business and pleasure of youth. Pen, always studying poets, was not likely to escape the passion they prescribe; and his heart, being ardent and his imagination eager, soon began to hunger for Love as naturally as it hungered for praise and poetry. He sighed for it first in secret and, like Ovid’s love-sick swain, opened his breast and said, “Aura, veni.” What generous youth has not courted some such windy mistress? It costs nothing and seems for a time to fill the room.

Yes, Pen began to feel the necessity of a first love—of a consuming passion—of an object upon which to concentrate all those vague floating fancies under which he sweetly suffered. He wanted a young lady to whom he could really make verses, whom he could set up and adore in place of those unsubstantial Ianthes and Zuleikas. He read his favourite poems over and over; he called upon Alma Venus; he translated Anacreon’s odes; he picked out passages suitable to his complaint from Waller, Dryden, Prior. Smirke and he were never weary, in their interviews, of discoursing about love. The faithless tutor entertained him with sentimental conversations instead of algebra and Greek—for Smirke was in love too.

Who could help it, being in daily intercourse with such a woman? Smirke was madly in love—so far as such a mild flame may be called madness—with Mrs. Pendennis. That honest lady, downstairs teaching little Laura the piano, or devising flannel petticoats for the poor, or moving through the calm routine of her modest spotless Christian life, never suspected the storms upstairs in the study—storms which consisted chiefly of sighs, glances, and the occasional misquotation. There sat Pen in his shooting-jacket, elbows on the green study-table, hands clutching his curly brown hair, Homer under his nose; and there sat Smirke reading with him and suffering gently.

They would talk about Helen and Andromache. “Andromache’s like my mother,” Pen would avouch; “but I say, Smirke, by Jove I’d cut off my nose to see Helen,” and he would spout favourite lines. He drew portraits of her—straight noses, enormous eyes—with “Arthur Pendennis delineavit et pinxit” gallantly written underneath, as if Latin could make the thing truer. Smirke naturally preferred Andromache, and in consequence he was uncommonly kind to Pen. He gave him his Elzevir Horace, and his little Greek Testament his own mamma at Clapham had bought for him; he bought him a silver pencil-case; and, in learning, let him do as much or as little as he pleased. Smirke always seemed on the point of unbosoming himself. He confessed he had an attachment—an ardently cherished attachment—about which Pendennis longed to hear.

“Tell us, old chap,” Pen said; “is she handsome? has she got blue eyes or black?”

Mr. Smirke heaved a gentle sigh, cast up his eyes to the ceiling, and faintly begged him to change the conversation.

Poor Smirke! He invited Pen to dine at his lodgings over Madame Fribsby’s, the milliner’s, in Clavering; and once, when it was raining and Mrs. Pendennis had driven in her pony-chaise to Clavering on some arrangement—about leaving off mourning, probably—she was prevailed on to enter the curate’s apartments. Smirke instantly sent out for pound-cakes, as if pastry might express what language dared not. The room smelt of damp great-coats, weak tea, and that faint powdery perfume milliners trade in; and Mrs. Pendennis, drying her gloves, brought with her the clean country air and the mild authority of domestic virtue. The sofa on which she sat became sacred to him from that day; and he kept flowers in the glass from which she drank ever after, as though he could preserve a sip of her presence the way one keeps herbs between paper to remember summer.

As Mrs. Pendennis was never tired of hearing praise of her son, Mr. Smirke neglected no opportunity of conversing with her on that subject. It might bore him to hear stories about Pen’s generosity, bravery in fighting the big naughty boy, his fun and jokes, his prodigious skill in Latin, music, riding, and so forth; but what price would he not pay for the privilege of sitting in her company while she served up these maternal dishes again and again? The widow, after such conversations, thought Mr. Smirke a very pleasing and well-informed man. As for her son, she had not settled whether he was to be Senior Wrangler and Archbishop of Canterbury, or Double First Class at Oxford and Lord Chancellor; but that all England did not possess his peer was a point, in her mind, beyond dispute.

A simple person of inexpensive habits, she began forthwith to save—perhaps to be a little parsimonious—in favour of her boy. There were no entertainments at Fairoaks during the year of her weeds. Nor did the Doctor’s silver dish-covers, of which he was so proud—flourished all over with Pendennis arms and surmounted with the crest—come out of the plate-chests again for long years. The household was diminished; expenses curtailed; the table grew plainer. When Pen dined from home there was a blank anchorite repast. He himself headed a remonstrance from the kitchen regarding the deteriorated quality of the Fairoaks beer. She was becoming miserly for Pen. Indeed, who ever accused women of being just? They are always sacrificing themselves—or somebody—for somebody else.

There happened to be no young woman in the widow’s small circle whom Pendennis could possibly endow with the inestimable treasure of a heart he was longing to give away. Some young fellows in such want bestow their affections upon Dolly the dairymaid or cast tender eyes on Molly the blacksmith’s daughter. Pen thought a Pendennis too grand to stoop so low. He was too high-minded for a vulgar intrigue; and had the notion of seduction ever crossed him, his heart would have revolted as from baseness and dishonour.

Miss Minny Portman was too old, too large, and too fond of reading Rollin’s Ancient History. The Miss Boardbacks, Admiral Boardback’s daughters of St. Vincent’s (or Fourth of June House), disgusted Pen with the London airs they brought into the country from Gloucester Place, where they passed the season; they looked down on Pen as a chit, and a chit feels those things as keenly as a barometer. Captain Glanders’s three girls (H.P., 50th Dragoon Guards) were still in brown-holland pinafores, with the ends of their hair-plaits tied up in dirty pink ribbon. Not having acquired the art of dancing, the youth avoided such chances as he might have had at the Chatteris Assemblies. In fine, he was not in love because there was nobody at hand to fall in love with.

So the young monkey rode out day after day in quest of Dulcinea and peeped into pony-chaises and gentlefolks’ carriages along the broad turnpike roads, with a heart beating within him, a secret tremor and hope that she might be in the yellow postchaise swinging up the hill, or one of the three girls in beaver bonnets in the back seat of the double gig driven at four miles an hour by a fat old gentleman in black. But the postchaise contained a snuffy old dowager of seventy with a maid her contemporary; and the three girls in beaver bonnets were no handsomer than the turnips skirting the roadside. Do as he might, ride where he would, the fairy princess he was to rescue and win had not yet appeared to honest Pen.

Upon these points he did not discourse to his mother. He had a world of his own. What generous ardent imaginative soul has not its secret pleasure-place? Let no clumsy prying try to disturb it in children. Actaeon was a brute for pushing in where Diana was bathing. Leave him occasionally alone, my good madam, if you have a poet for a child. Even your admirable advice may bore sometimes. You may be faultless; it does not follow everybody in your family must think exactly like you. That little child yonder may have thoughts too deep even for your great mind, and fancies so coy they will not bare themselves when your ladyship sits by. And there are feelings—like tastes and smells and the music of bells over fields—which cannot be translated into another person’s language without losing half their savour; the heart keeps its own dialect for such matters, and is shy of the dominant lexicon even at home.

Helen Pendennis, by sheer love, divined a great number of her son’s secrets. But she kept them in her heart and did not speak of them. Besides, she had made up her mind that he was to marry little Laura, who would be eighteen when Pen was six-and-twenty—after he had finished college, made his grand tour, and settled either in London astonishing the metropolis with his learning and eloquence at the bar, or, better still, in a sweet country parsonage surrounded with hollyhocks and roses, close to a delightful romantic ivy-covered church, from whose pulpit Pen would utter the most beautiful sermons ever preached.

While these natural sentiments waged their pleasant war in Pen’s bosom, it chanced one day he rode into Chatteris carrying to the County Chronicle a tremendous thrilling poem for next week’s paper. He put up his horse, as usual, at the stables of the George Hotel, and stood talking with the hostler about Rebecca—her coat, her temper, her feed, the whole sacred ritual by which horseflesh becomes companionship—when a grand black tandem with scarlet wheels came rattling into the inn-yard. The driver’s voice called out, loud and patronising, “Hallo, Pendennis, is that you?”

Pen had difficulty recognising, under the broad-brimmed hat and vast great-coats and neckcloths, the person and figure of his quondam schoolfellow, Mr. Foker.

Back at the George, Mr. Foker conducted his guest to the coffee-room with the air of a man bringing a foreign ambassador to view the national treasure-chests. Mr. Rincer, the waiter, entered as solemnly as if he bore the Great Seal upon a salver; he bowed over the dishes with a gravity that would have sat well upon a judge pronouncing sentence, and yet the sentence was only dinner.

Dinner, however, at the George was a thing with a pedigree. The turtle came on first—dark as old mahogany, glossy as a minister’s promise, breathing a warm vapour of Madeira and pepper that climbed straight into a young man’s brain. Then the venison followed, as if the forest itself had been persuaded—by fee and argument—to send one of its best haunches to be carved in an inn parlour. The knife went through it with that yielding resistance which tells you the beast was properly hung and not bullied into tenderness by heat. The gravy ran rich and brown, and the fat had that clean, nutty sweetness which makes you forgive all the crimes of man against deer.

Foker fell to with a gusto that would have done credit to an hereditary alderman, and with a knowledge which proved he had not lived last year wholly upon smuggled polonies and ginger-beer without acquiring, at least, courage. He sniffed, sipped, frowned like a Chancellor, and pronounced the champagne “condemned gooseberry,” as if it were a prisoner at the bar. He winked at the port with one eye, tried it again, and then nodded—an approving nod that passed from his palate to his whole person.

“This,” said he, “is the right sort. There’s no humbuggin’ me.”

He addressed the waiters by their Christian names, inquired after their families with the tenderness of a parish clergyman who knows the christenings and the scandals, and declared one man’s child had “a cough last week,” and another’s wife was “as well as ever.” All this philanthropy was performed between mouthfuls, while he cracked nuts and despatched fruit with the businesslike cheerfulness of one making up accounts.

Outside, the old London coaches—those lumbering, cheerful monsters of the road—rumbled to the door in the early dusk. Their ironwork clinked; the horses stamped and snorted, shaking the frost of the evening from their manes; the ostler’s whip snapped like a pistol-shot; and through it all came that rich acoustic stew of travel—horns tooting, guards calling, harness jingling, wheel-tires grating on stone. Foker flung open the coffee-room window as if he could not bear to have so much good sound shut out.

“Hi, Tom! How’s your missus?—Bill! how’s the little un?” he bawled, and then, to Pen’s amazement, imitated the horns with such liveliness and accuracy that one might have fancied the very coach-guards had crawled into his throat. Jem the ostler whipped off the horses’ cloths; the coaches rolled away with their lanterns bobbing like fireflies; and Foker, shutting the window, turned back to the table with the air of a man who has conducted an orchestra and now resumes supper.

“A bottle o’ sherry, a bottle o’ sham, a bottle o’ port, and a shass caffy,” he said, very well satisfied with the world and his own share of it. “It ain’t so bad, hay, Pen?”

When the last nut had been cracked and the last grape reduced to a stalk, he declared it was time “to toddle.” Pen sprang up with eyes too bright for mere digestion, cheeks warmed by wine and youth, and a heart beating to a rhythm it did not yet recognise as its own.

They made for the theatre and paid their money to a wheezy old lady asleep in the money-taker’s box—so asleep that she might have been a relic exhibited for the edification of playgoers, had she not presently awoke to take the coins with a mechanical snuffle.

“Mrs. Dropsicum,” Foker whispered, “Bingley’s mother-in-law. Great in Lady Macbeth.”

Of course he knew her too.

The house was thin—country theatres commonly resemble a family dinner where half the invited guests have remembered other engagements—despite the bills promising “universal bursts of attraction” and “galvanic thrills,” as if the audience were to be shocked into rapture by a battery. A score of people dotted the pit benches; the gallery contributed a continual undercurrent of kicking, whistling, and conversation, like sparrows disputing on a roof; and in the boxes lounged a dozen more who had drifted in on free admissions.

Lieutenants Rodgers and Podgers, with young Cornet Tidmus of the Dragoons, occupied a private box opposite. Their very boots seemed to applaud; they called actors by name as if addressing troops on parade; and between the dialogue they carried on friendly debates with the stage, as though the curtain were merely a piece of bunting hung to separate two clubs.

Bingley the manager—who took every chief tragic and comic part except when he modestly withdrew to make room for the occasional London star—appeared as the Stranger. He wore the legendary tight pantaloons and Hessian boots; a huge cloak; a beaver with a hearse-feather drooping over a face so raddled that it looked as if it had been basted nightly in lamp-smoke. A great buckled brown wig perched upon him, and upon his fingers he displayed the stage jewellery, selecting the largest rings for his own use with the impartial justice of a man dividing plunder. His favourite ornament was a sham diamond of such size that, when he let his little finger quiver out from the cloak, it seemed to wag at the pit like an argument.

He made a favour of wearing it in light comedy; the younger men in his company flattered him by asking its history. It had belonged, he declared, to George Frederick Cooke, who had had it from Mr. Quin, who might have purchased it for a shilling. Bingley’s belief in its splendour was as touching as any religion: he fancied the world enthralled by its glitter.

He held the stage-book—rouged, tawdry, and unbound in that peculiar fashion which no honest volume ever wears—pointed at lines, wagged his head, rolled his eyes at the ceiling as if literature and heaven were partners in the same concern. And when he saw the young gentlemen in the box, he did what managers always do when they scent money: he acted at them.

He lay upon the stage-bank so that his hand, his ring, and his Hessians were all presented as carefully as cold meat on a sideboard. Over the gilt volume he shot solemn glances, calculating the effect of each ornament on his victims. He was determined to fascinate; they had paid their money, and he could already see their families—actual or imagined—filling the cane chairs behind them in his boxes.

As he brooded, his servant Francis made remarks upon him in that theatrical dialect which no man ever uses in a kitchen.
