“Again reading,” said Francis, “thus it is, from morn to night. To him nature has no beauty—life no charm. For three years I have never seen him smile.”

Bingley’s gloom at this point was of such professional blackness that it seemed to drink up the footlights.

“Nothing diverts him,” continued Francis. “O, if he would but attach himself to any living thing, were it an animal—for something man must love.”

Enter Tobias, from a hut—Goll performing him—giving thanks with caps between hands and eyes lifted to the flies as if the rafters contained Providence. The Stranger watched him as a cat watches a mouse with pretensions to poetry.

“This old man’s share of earthly happiness can be but little,” Francis said. “Yet mark how grateful he is for his portion of it.”

“Because though old, he is but a child in the leading-string of hope,” Bingley moaned, looking steadily—steadily—at Foker, who sucked the top of his stick with the unconcern of a young gentleman examining a bootlace.

“Hope is the nurse of life,” said Francis.

“And her cradle—is the grave,” replied the Stranger, with a sound like a bassoon in agony; and at that moment he fixed his eyes on Pendennis so unwaveringly that Pen felt the whole house must be staring at him too. He cast down his eyes in confusion; when he raised them, the Stranger’s were upon him again. Throughout the scene Bingley played in Pen’s direction, bent upon subjugating him; even when he sent off Francis with the book, he marked the page carefully, as if the stage-life of the volume mattered more than the moral purity of his benevolence.

Pen was never so relieved as when the scene ended and Foker, tapping with his cane, bellowed, “Bravo, Bingley!”

“Give him a hand, Pendennis,” Foker said. “You know every chap likes a hand.”

So Pen laughed, and clapped; and the dragoons clapped; and the thin house made noise enough for a coronation. Wintersen Castle shut like a trap over Tobias’s hut and the Stranger’s boots. Servants bustled on with chairs and tables.

“That’s Hicks and Miss Thackthwaite,” Foker whispered. “Pretty girl, ain’t she, Pendennis? But stop—hurray—bravo! here’s the Fotheringay!”

The pit thumped umbrellas; the gallery fired a volley of applause; the dragoons clapped till you’d have thought the theatre packed to the ceiling. Pen, still warmed with wine and dinner and the coach-horns’ jollity, felt something leap in him at that name, as if an old story—told long before he was born—had been suddenly remembered by his blood.

From the side-scene peered a red face with ragged whiskers: Mr. Costigan. Pen’s eyes opened wider, brighter, as Mrs. Haller entered.

She came on with a downcast look; then rallied at the sound, swept the house with a grateful glance, and folded her hands across her breast before sinking into a curtsey so magnificent that it seemed to bless the whole shabby theatre at once. Umbrellas thumped again. Pen clapped and cried “bravo” louder than all, in a heat that belonged as much to his youth as to his liquor.

Old Mr. Bows, the little first fiddler—perched at his desk with his crutch beside him, and reinforced tonight by a detachment of the Dragoons’ band (by permission of Colonel Swallowtail)—looked up and smiled at the lad’s enthusiasm.

Those who have only seen Miss Fotheringay in later days have little idea what a creature she was at that time. The pencil can draw an ugly face and be content; but beauty puts it out of countenance. She was tall—commandingly so—and in the full prime and splendour of it. Her forehead was broad; her black hair waved over it with a natural ripple that later beauties attempt with hot irons and patience; it was gathered into shining braids at the back of a neck like a statue’s—one of those antique necks that make you think even the air should be filtered before it touches them.

When she lifted her eyes they shone with a tenderness and a mystery that seemed to withdraw the instant you noticed it, as if Love and Genius had looked out from a window and then, ashamed of being seen, drawn the curtain. She seldom laughed—her teeth, indeed, were not good—but a smile of endless sweetness played about her lips, her dimples, her chin, making even stillness expressive. Her nose in those days defied description. Her ears, like little pearl shells, were insulted by the theatre earrings, though they were the handsomest properties available.

She wore long flowing black robes, and managed them with such grace that the folds seemed to obey her mood. Now and then you caught sight of her sandals—rather large, perhaps; but Pen, in his new intoxication, found them as ravishing as Cinderella’s slippers. Above all, her hand and arm—those superb instruments—seemed to frame her whole being. When she folded them over her breast, dropped them in mute agony, raised them in command, or fluttered them in sportive gaiety, it was as if she conducted the entire house with her gestures. She beckoned, repelled, entreated, embraced—not one admirer only, for she carried her virtue like armour, and her father’s valour stood ready at the side-scene—but the whole audience; and the whole audience rose to her, as the phrase was, when she bowed and curtseyed again.

Pen stared as if the lights had been lit for her alone.

“I say, Pen, isn’t she a stunner?” Foker whispered.

“Hush,” Pen said, scarcely knowing he spoke. “She’s speaking.”

Her voice was deep and sweet. The play itself—those who know it will confess—was stuffed with fine words that no sane person would use in a parlour or a field; the dialogue was as sham as the Stranger’s book and wig and ring. Yet, running through the balderdash, there is that reality which never grows old: love, children, forgiveness. However absurdly dressed, that truth will always get itself listened to, like good broth served in a cracked cup.

With what smothered sorrow, with what gushing pathos, did she utter her part! When, as housekeeper preparing for Count Wintersen’s arrival, she gave orders about beds and furniture and dinner, she did it with the calm agony of despair—speaking of domestic arrangements as if each chair placed were a nail driven in. Then, when the stupid servants were gone and she could pour out her grief to pit and boxes, she overflowed to each person as if he were her only confidant, as if the whole theatre were one private kitchen where she might confess her heart while the world’s kettles boiled.

Little Bows in the orchestra—whom she did not seem to watch, though he followed her ceaselessly with his bow and his whole twitching body—nodded, pointed, twisted like a man physically moved by music. When she came to the favourite passage—“I have a William too, if he be still alive—Ah, yes, if he be still alive. His little sisters, too! Why, Fancy, dost thou rack me so? Why dost thou image my poor children fainting in sickness, and crying to—to—their mum—um—other”—the little fiddler cried “Bravo!” and then buried his face in a blue cotton handkerchief.

All the house was affected. Foker took out a large yellow bandanna and wept piteously, the tears running down over the remains of turtle and venison as if supper and sorrow had agreed to share the same tablecloth. Pen was past tears. When she was off the stage, the stage and the world went blank; the red officers and the lamps reeled before him like objects seen through heat.

He watched her at the side-scene, where she waited to go on and where her father took off her shawl with the grave care of a man handling something precious that the public thinks it has bought for a shilling. When the reconciliation arrived and she flung herself upon Bingley’s shoulders—children clinging, Countess (Mrs. Bingley) and Baron Steinforth (Garbetts, lively and spirited) grouping themselves about—Pen saw only Fotheringay. The curtain fell upon him like a pall.

He did not hear Bingley’s announcement for the next night. He was hardly aware the house called for Miss Fotheringay. Bingley, of course, received the applause as usual as if it were his private income. At last even he understood, stepped back with a grin, and presently returned with Mrs. Haller upon his arm.

How beautiful she looked then! Her hair had loosened. The officers threw flowers; she clutched them to her heart as if they were a child brought back. She put back her hair, smiled all round; and her eyes met Pen’s. The moment was no longer part of the play: it was a sound in him, a chord struck that would vibrate long after the fiddles stopped.

Down went the curtain again. She was gone.

Not one note could Pen hear of the overture that the Dragoons’ brass blew afterwards with military goodwill. The very instruments, with their bright, brazen voices, seemed suddenly like an industrial intrusion—metal shouting where a human voice had just confessed. The theatre’s soundscape changed: from sobbing strings and murmured feeling to polished noise that filled space without filling the heart.

“She is a crusher, ain’t she now!” Foker asked.

Pen answered vaguely; he scarcely knew what was said to him. He could not tell another mortal what he felt, and indeed did not quite know it himself. It was something overwhelming, delicious, maddening—a fever of wild joy and undefined longing.

Rowkins and Miss Thackthwaite came on to dance the favourite double hornpipe; Foker abandoned himself to it with the same sincerity with which he had wept a few minutes before, applauding rhythm as if it were moral virtue. Pen scarcely saw the dance at all; it was mist before his eyes. He only remembered—dimly—that Mrs. Haller had acted with that woman when she first came in, as one remembers an ingredient in a dish that mattered solely because a beloved hand had touched it.

At the end of the dance, Pen looked at his watch and said it was time for him to go.

“Hang it, stay to see The Bravo of the Battle-Axe,” Foker pleaded. “Bingley’s splendid in it; he wears red tights, and has to carry Mrs. B. over the Pine-bridge of the Cataract, only she’s too heavy. It’s great fun—do stop.”

Pen looked at the bill with a lingering, foolish hope that Miss Fotheringay’s name might be hiding somewhere among the after-piece actors. It was not. Go he must. He had a long ride home.

He squeezed Foker’s hand, choking to speak and unable. He quitted the theatre and walked frantically about the town, not knowing how long—past silent shopfronts, past lanes where the day’s noises had died and only a distant cart creaked like an old memory. Then he mounted at the George and rode homeward through the night air, while the country’s quieter sounds—hedges whispering, hoofbeats dull on the road, the occasional far bark of a dog—worked upon him like a second play, older than any theatre, older than any printed bill.

Clavering clock sang out one as he came into the yard at Fairoaks. The lady of the house might have been awake; if she was, she heard only his step in the passage as he dashed into bed and pulled the clothes over his head.

Pen had not been in the habit of wakeful nights, so he fell into a sound sleep at once. Even later, when men have anxieties and thoughtful matter enough to keep them up, they begin by going to sleep as usual and get a nap in advance of trouble; but Trouble comes after, jogs them, and says, “No more of this laziness. Wake and talk with me.” Pen was not yet at that stage. He slept like a boy who thinks tomorrow belongs to him.

He did not wake until early morning, when the rooks began to caw from the little wood beyond his window; and at that instant—at the first opening of his eyes—the beloved image stood in his mind as if it had been waiting there all night.

“My dear boy,” he heard her say (for Love, when it enters, takes whatever voice it pleases), “you were in a sound sleep and I would not disturb you; but I have been close by your pillow all this while, and I don’t intend that you shall leave me. I am Love! I bring with me fever and passion: wild longing, maddening desire; restless craving and seeking. Many a long day ere this I heard you calling out for me; and behold, now I am come.”

Was Pen frightened? Not he. He did not know what was coming; it was all pleasure and delight as yet.

And as, three years before, when he entered the fifth form at the Cistercians, his father had given him a gold watch which he drew from under his pillow at waking—polishing it, listening to its ticking in corners, hugging it at the first moment of morning—so now he exulted over this new possession; felt for it in his waistcoat as if it were a thing he could lose; wound it up at night; and at waking seized it again with joy.

That first watch, by the way, was a showy ill-made piece; it never went well and was always out of order, until at last he put it in a drawer, forgot it, and swapped it away for something more useful. Love, too, often comes to us first in glittering, ill-manufactured splendour, and makes the strangest time of our lives—yet for the moment we think it the only true clock in the world.

Pen felt ever so many years older than yesterday. There was no mistake now. He was as much in love as the best hero in the best romance he had ever read.

He told John to bring his shaving-water with the utmost confidence, as if confidence were part of the toilette. He dressed in some of his finest clothes—fine pin, beautiful new waistcoat—and came splendidly down to breakfast, patronising his mother and little Laura, who had been strumming her music lesson for hours, creating those domestic noises which, in a quiet house, feel as powerful as machinery: repeated scales, stubborn bars, the metronome of duty.

He read the prayers—of which he did not heed one single syllable—and Laura, observing his grand appearance, wondered and asked him to tell her what the play was about.

Pen laughed and declined to tell Laura what the play was about. In fact it was quite as well she should not know.

Then she asked why he had got on his fine pin and new waistcoat.

Pen blushed, and told his mother that the old schoolfellow with whom he had dined at Chatteris was reading with a tutor at Baymouth—a very learned man; and as he himself was to go to College, and as there were several young men pursuing their studies at Baymouth—he was anxious to ride over and—and just see what the course of their reading was.

Laura made a long face. Helen Pendennis looked hard at her son, troubled more than ever by the vague doubt and terror that had haunted her since Farmer Gurnett brought home the news Pen would not return to dinner. Arthur’s eyes defied her.

She tried to console herself, to drive off her fears. The boy had never told her an untruth.

Pen, meanwhile, conducted himself during breakfast with a haughty, supercilious manner, as if Love had promoted him and he expected the household to salute. Taking leave of the elder and younger lady, he was presently heard riding out of the stablecourt. He went gently at first, but galloped like a madman the moment he thought himself out of hearing—flinging his hoofbeats at the road as if the very earth must be made to hurry.

Smirke the curate, thinking of his own affairs and riding softly with his toes out, on his way to give Pen his three hours’ reading, met his pupil coming like a gust. Pen shot by him like the wind. Smirke’s pony shied at the sudden thunder; the gentle man went over its head among the stinging-nettles in the hedge. Pen laughed as they met, pointed towards the Baymouth road, and was gone half a mile before poor Smirke had picked himself up, nettles stinging him into a most unwelcome wakefulness.

Pen had resolved he must see Foker that morning—must hear about her, know about her, be with someone who knew her. And Smirke, sitting up among the nettles while his pony cropped quietly in the hedge, thought dismally whether he ought to go to Fairoaks now that his pupil was evidently gone for the day.

Yes, he thought he might go too. He might go ask Mrs. Pendennis when Arthur would be back, and hear Miss Laura her Watts’s Catechism. He got upon the little pony—both were used to his slipping off—and advanced upon the house from which his scholar had just rushed away in a whirlwind.

Thus Love makes fools of all of us, big and little: the curate had tumbled head over heels in pursuit of it without knowing, and Pen had started in the first heat of the mad race.

Rebecca the mare, being of a temper which considered all roads as mere suggestions, carried Arthur Pendennis into Baymouth with the insolent ease of an animal born to make young gentlemen feel heroic. Pen put her up at the inn stables, where a stable-boy—who smelt pleasantly of oats and the honest heat of horseflesh—took the reins and, with them, any remaining dignity Pen might have had.

Pen, still tasting the salt in the wind from his ride, ran straight to Mr. Foker’s lodgings, which perched over a chemist’s shop. Down below, commerce did briskly in cigars and sodawater, those two great medicaments of youthful dissipation; above, the young gentlemen were busy ruining their constitutions with the very articles intended to preserve them.

He found not Foker, but Mr. Spavin—Foker’s friend and part-proprietor in the tandem—smoking in the fashion of a man who had made a pact with the air, and teaching a little dog tricks with a bit of biscuit. The dog, at least, had a clean motive.

Pen’s face—fresh, wind-scrubbed, and ruddy with country health—looked absurdly wholesome beside Spavin’s waxy, jaded little countenance, which seemed to have been kept overnight in a drawer with dice, bad brandy, and a moral.

“Who’s that man?” Spavin thought, watching Pen as if he were a rare vegetable. “He looks as fresh as a bean. His hand don’t shake of a morning—I’d bet five to one.”

Mr. Foker had not come home at all. This was not merely disappointing; it was insulting to Pen’s feverish expectation. Spavin could not say when his friend would return—sometimes a day, sometimes a week—according to whatever tide and moon governed Mr. Foker’s pleasures. Would Pen take anything? There was, he hinted, a very fair tap of ale. Pen, who wanted something much hotter than ale—information—laid down his card (for he had a card now, and the possession of a card is a little ceremony by which a young man informs the world he exists), and presently took his leave.

He went down by the rock and walked the sand, biting his nails, while the sea made a great noise at him. The bay was bright, immeasurable; the waves came rolling in with their old hoarse cookery of foam and brine, as if they were perpetually basting the shore. But Pen stared with blank eyes, scarcely tasting the scene. There was a tide in his head more violent than the tide under his feet; and he had no more power to stop it than to stop the Channel by throwing pebbles.

He did throw stones, however—one after another—just to see something strike and vanish; but the sea continued to arrive in perfect good humour, as if it had not noticed his rebellion.

He must see Foker. He would see Foker. And if Foker was not here, perhaps he was—elsewhere. “Suppose I go on—on the Chatteris road—just to see if I can meet him,” Pen thought, as if he were proposing a casual stroll rather than a campaign.

Within half an hour Rebecca was saddled again. She cantered on the grass by the Chatteris road; and about four miles from Baymouth, where the Clavering road branches off (as everybody knows, and as horses remember), the mare naturally made for that turning, as if home were a warm mash and not a mere direction. Pen, with the cruelty of youth and love, cut her over the shoulder and forced her past. He reached the turnpike without seeing any sign of black tandem or red wheels.

But now he was at the turnpike, and that fact, like many facts, demanded further folly. So he rode on to the George. The yard had its orchestra: hoofs striking cobble, a bucket clanged, a stable-door banged, and somewhere a boy whistled tunelessly—those small rural sounds that keep the mind from entirely falling into itself. The hostler, who had the satirical intelligence of his tribe, told Pen that Mr. Foker was there sure enough, and that he’d been “a makin’ a tremendous row the night afore, a drinkin’ and a singin’, and wantin’ to fight Tom the postboy: which I’m thinkin’ he’d have had the worst of it,” the man added with a grin that tasted of stable-wit.

“Have you carried up your master’s ’ot water to shave with?” he called, very jeeringly, to Mr. Foker’s domestic, who appeared bearing his master’s clothes, brushed and arranged as reverently as if they were church vestments.

“Show Mr. Pendennis up to ’un,” said the hostler.

And Pen, at last, was admitted to the chamber where, in the midst of an immense bed, Mr. Harry Foker lay reposing, as a small idol might repose in a temple made of feathers. The bed and bolsters swelled all round him so that his little sallow face and red silk nightcap seemed like an afterthought in upholstery.

“Hullo!” said Pen.

“Who goes there? brother, quickly tell!” sang out a voice from the bed—flippant, musical, and perfectly satisfied with itself. “What! Pendennis again? Is your Mamma acquainted with your absence? Did you sup with us last night? No stop—who supped with us last night, Stoopid?”

“There was the three officers, sir, and Mr. Bingley, sir, and Mr. Costigan, sir,” answered Stoopid, with the gravity of a man describing a funeral.

“Ah yes: the cup and merry jest went round. We chanted—and I remember I wanted to fight a postboy. Did I thrash him, Stoopid?”

“No, sir. Fight didn’t come off, sir,” said Stoopid, still solemn as a ledger.

He was arranging Mr. Foker’s dressing-case, a travelling altar presented by a fond mother. It contained plate enough to feed a bishop: a silver dish, a silver mug, silver boxes and bottles for every imaginable essence, and a choice of razors waiting against the distant day when Mr. Foker’s beard should arrive and demand negotiation.

“Do it some other day,” said the young fellow, yawning and flinging his thin arms up. “No, there was no fight; but there was chanting. Bingley chanted, I chanted, the General chanted—Costigan I mean.—Did you ever hear him sing ‘The Little Pig under the Bed,’ Pen?”

“The man we met yesterday,” Pen said, all in a tremor that had nothing to do with sea-air. “The father of—”

“Of the Fotheringay,—the very man. Ain’t she a Venus, Pen?”

Before Pen could gather his mind out of his mouth, Stoopid announced, “Please sir, Mr. Costigan’s in the sittin-room, sir, and says, sir, you asked him to breakfast, sir. Called five times, sir; but wouldn’t wake you on no account; and has been here since eleven o’clock, sir—”

“How much is it now?”

“One, sir.”

“What would the best of mothers say,” cried Foker, “if she saw me in bed at this hour? She sent me down here with a grinder. She wants me to cultivate my neglected genus—He, be! I say, Pen, this isn’t quite like seven o’clock school,—is it, old boy?” And he burst into a boyish laugh, pleased with his own rebellion. “Go in and talk to the General whilst I dress. And I say, Pendennis, ask him to sing you ‘The Little Pig under the Bed;’ it’s capital.”

Pen went off in a whirl—toward Mr. Costigan, toward the source of that name which had been burning in him since last night.

Of Mr. Foker’s two grandfathers, one, from whom he had his fortune, brewed; the other was an earl, from whom he inherited a mother who worshipped him. The family had marched, generation after generation, through the Cistercian school; and our friend’s name might be read over the playground wall on a public-house sign, where “Foker’s Entire” was painted with cheerful candour. There he had been bullied for his trade, his face, his dirt, his stupidity, his appetite—indeed for everything that he could not help. Those who know what tyranny does to a sensitive boy will understand how, once free, he sprang into a new sort of creature: humorous, sarcastic, showy—still a dunce, but now a splendid one. Learning cannot be acquired by simply leaving school; but scent and linen can, and were. When he joined his guests he was already perfumed and arrayed, his very collar seeming to declare independence.

Captain Costigan—he preferred Captain to General, as men prefer the title that sounds most like action—sat in the window with the newspaper held at arm’s length. His eyes were dim, and he spelled the words with his lips as well as those bloodshot orbs, like a man chewing letters because he cannot swallow them whole. His hat cocked on one ear; one foot lay up in the window-seat; and the boot on that foot, large and shabby, declared that poverty had begun where it generally begins—with a man’s extremities.

Poverty, you will observe, is a polite enemy: it does not seize a gentleman by the throat at first; it nibbles at his gloves, his hat, his boots, and only afterward considers his heart. All these parts of the Captain were rakish and worn. He rose and saluted Pen: first two fingers, half-hidden in a broken black glove, to the hat; then the hat removed altogether in a flourish. He was going bald, but drew lank iron-grey hair across his pate, with two wisps falling down on either side of his face, as if determined not to desert it entirely. Whisky had ruined what complexion he once had; his handsome face now shone with a copper tinge, like a kettle too long on a fire. His stock was very high, scarred and stained; his dress-coat buttoned tightly wherever the buttons had remained loyal.

“The young gentleman to whom I had the honour to be introjuiced yesterday in the Cathadral Yard,” said the Captain with a bow that belonged, by rights, to a drawing-room. “I hope I see you well, sir. I marked ye in the thayatre last night during me daughter’s perfawrumance; and missed ye on my return. I did but conduct her home, sir, for Jack Costigan, though poor, is a gentleman; and when I reintered the house to pay me respects to me joyous young friend, Mr. Foker—ye were gone. We had a jolly night of ut, sir—Mr. Foker, the three gallant young dragoons, and your ’umble servant. Gad, sir, it put me in mind of one of our old nights when I bore His Majesty’s commission in the Foighting Hundtherd and Third.”

He produced an old snuff-box and presented it with a solemn air, as if snuff were a sacrament.

Arthur was too flurried to say much. This shabby, theatrical old buck—this was her father. The Captain’s breath was perfumed with last night’s cigars, and he twisted the tuft on his chin with the jaunty affectation of a man who had once been admired and could not bear to forget it.

“I hope—Miss—Miss Costigan is well, sir,” Pen stammered, crimsoning. “She—she gave me greater pleasure than—than I—I ever enjoyed at a play. I think, sir—I think she’s the finest actress in the world.”

“Your hand, young man! for ye speak from your heart,” cried the Captain, catching it. “Thank ye, sir; an old soldier and a fond father thanks ye. She is the finest actress in the world. I’ve seen the Siddons, sir, and the O’Nale—they were great, but what were they compared to Miss Fotheringay? I do not wish she should ashume her own name while on the stage. Me family, sir, are proud people; and the Costigans of Costiganstown think that an honest man, who has borne Her Majesty’s colours in the Hundred and Third, would demean himself, by permitting his daughter to earn her old father’s bread.”

“There cannot be a more honourable duty, surely,” Pen said, eager to be noble.

“Honourable! Bedad, sir, I’d like to see the man who said Jack Costigan would consent to anything dishonourable. I have a heart, sir, though I am poor; I like a man who has a heart. You have: I read it in your honest face and steady eye. And would you believe it”—and here the Captain’s voice sank into a confidential whisper—“that that Bingley who has made his fortune by me child, gives her but two guineas a week: out of which she finds herself in dresses, and which, added to me own small means, makes our all?”

Now, the Captain’s means were so small they might be said to be invisible; yet like certain herbs that thrive in cracks of pavement, he contrived to exist in places no sensible person would call nourishing. If he had told his history it might have made a moral tale; but he neither would have told it if he could, nor could if he would. He was not merely unaccustomed to tell the truth—he had long ceased to keep it separate in his own mind. Fact and fiction reeled together in his muzzy, whiskified brain like dancers after too much punch.

He began life brightly: a pair of colours, a fine person and legs, and one of the most beautiful voices in the world. To the last he sang Irish ballads with admirable humour and pathos—and cried at his own singing with the generosity of an audience of one. Poor Cos! brave and maudlin, humorous and an idiot; always good-natured, sometimes almost trustworthy. He would drink with any man and back any man’s bill; and his end would be in a spunging-house, where the sheriff’s officer who took him was fond of him.

Before half an hour had passed he extracted two sovereigns from Pen for tickets for his daughter’s benefit. Pen had but two pounds in his purse; he handed them over with a trembling sort of pride, and would have been afraid to offer more lest he should offend the Captain’s delicacy—an organ which, like certain extinct dialects, survived chiefly in ceremonial phrases. Costigan scrawled him an order for a box, slipped the coins into his waistcoat, and slapped his hand over them. They warmed his old sides like a poultice.

“Faith, sir,” said he, “the bullion’s scarcer with me than it used to be, as is the case with many a good fellow. I won six hundthred of ’em in a single night, sir, when me kind friend, His Royal Highness the Duke of Kent, was in Gibralther.”

And he poured out at once a flood of stories—claret drunk, bets made, races ridden by the garrison there—till their host appeared with breakfast.

The breakfast came in with a smell that might have redeemed a worse company: devilled turkey, sharp and peppery; mutton chops hissing with their own fat; toast browned to a proper bitterness; and coffee which, even at an inn, managed to smell like a promise. The crackle of the fire, the clink of plates, the knife sawing through crisped skin—these homely sounds set a kindlier music under the Captain’s talk than any theatre orchestra.

It was good to see Costigan before food, as some old hounds look handsome once they scent meat. His stories gushed without intermission; his spirits rose with every mouthful. When sunshine fell on him—be it the sunshine of a young man’s company or the warm gravy of a devilled dish—the old lazzarone basked like a creature grateful for heat. He prated of his affairs and past splendours, and all the lords, generals, and Lord-Lieutenants he had ever known. He described the death of his darling Bessie, the late Mrs. Costigan, and the challenge he had sent to Captain Shanty Clancy of the Slashers for looking rude at Miss Fotheringay as she sat on her kyar in the Phaynix; and then how Captain Clancy apologised and gave a dinner in Kildare Street, where six of them drank twinty-one bottles of claret, etc. He announced that to sit with two such noble and generous young fellows was the pride and happiness of an old soldier’s existence; and after a second glass of Curacoa grew so happy he began to cry.

Altogether, the Captain was not a man of much strength of mind, nor an eligible companion for youth; but there are worse men in better places—more calculating, more cold—who have never committed half so many rogueries as he. When they left the George he held an arm of each of his dear young friends and walked between them in a maudlin state of contentment. He winked at one or two tradesmen’s shops where, possibly, he owed money, as if to say, “See the company I’m in—sure I’ll pay you, my boy,” and they finally parted with Mr. Foker at a billiard-room, where that young gentleman had an engagement with some officers of Colonel Swallowtail’s regiment.

Pen and the Captain continued together. Costigan, in his sly way, began sounding Pen about Foker’s fortune and station. Pen, candid as bread-and-milk, told him Foker’s father was a celebrated brewer, and his mother Lady Agnes Milton, Lord Rosherville’s daughter. At this the Captain burst into extravagant compliment and panegyric about Mr. Foker’s “native aristocracie,” which could be seen, he said, “with the twinkling of an oi—and only served to adawrun other qualities which he possessed, a foin intellect and a generous heart”; not one word of which the Captain accurately believed, though he pronounced it with the rich confidence of a man who had long since eaten through his own scruples.

Pen walked on, listening, wondering, amused, puzzled. It had not yet entered into his head to disbelieve any statement made to him; being truthful himself, he took what was told him as truth—like a hungry man taking what is put before him, without asking whether it came from an honest kitchen. Costigan had never had a better listener and was flattered by Pen’s attentive modesty.

So pleased was he with this artless young gentleman that he offered an invitation he seldom accorded: would Mr. Pendennis do him the favour to enter his humble abode, near at hand, where the Captain would have the honour of inthrojuicing his young friend to his daughther, Miss Fotheringay?

Pen was so shocked—so exquisitely, deliciously shocked—that he nearly fell from the Captain’s arm. Happiness, when it comes suddenly, has a rude physicality; it makes the knees untrustworthy. He gasped out incoherent words about the high gratification he should have in being presented to the lady for whose talents he had conceived such admiration—such extreme admiration—and followed, scarcely knowing where.

He was going to see her. He was going to see her. Yesterday, before he knew her, seemed a century and a language ago—as if the very words he had used then belonged to another boy.

The Captain led him into Prior’s Lane, a quiet little street in Chatteris, in the ecclesiastical quarter near Dean’s Green and the canons’ houses, overlooked by the enormous towers of the cathedral. The stones seemed to keep the cathedral’s coolness; the air had that faint, ancient smell of damp masonry and old hymn-books. Even the street sounded different: footsteps were softened, voices lowered, as if the place had trained the very sparrows to respect it.

Costigan’s lodging was on the first floor of a low gabled house, on the door of which was a brass plate: “Creed, Tailor and Robe-maker.” Creed was dead, however. His widow was a pew-opener at the cathedral; his eldest son was a little scamp of a choir-boy who played toss-halfpenny, led his brothers into mischief, and had a voice sweet as an angel’s—so that the cathedral got the music and the lane got the trouble.

Two of the smaller boys sat on the door-step that dropped down into the passage. They sprang up eagerly at the Captain and plunged at the swallow-tails of his dress-coat, to Pen’s surprise. The truth was, when the good-natured gentleman was in cash, he often brought them an apple or a bit of gingerbread—an economy of kindness which, as he remarked later with a wink and a finger to his nose, ensured “the widdy never pressed me for rint when not convanient.”

Pen tumbled down the step; and as he followed his companion up the creaking stair his knees trembled so that he feared the whole building would hear. The stairs complained under them with every plank—an honest domestic music, not like the shriek and hammer of modern streets where every sound must be a cruelty. Here even the house spoke in an old dialect: groan, creak, hush—sounds that said, We have held many footsteps; yours are not the first to be foolish.

He entered—her room. He saw something black before him, moving as if making a curtsey; he heard Costigan’s magniloquent voice, indistinct at first through the pounding in his ears, presenting him to “me child,” and describing Mr. Awther Pindinnis as “a young gentleman of property in the neighbourhood, a person of refoined moind and enviable manners, a sincare lover of poethry, and a man possest of a feeling and affectionate heart.”

“It is very fine weather,” Miss Fotheringay said in an Irish accent, with a deep rich melancholy voice which seemed to carry theatre-music even into a modest room.

“Very,” said Mr. Pendennis.

In this romantic way their conversation began. He found himself seated, and at last had leisure to look.

She looked handsomer off the stage than under the lamps. All her attitudes were naturally grand and majestical, as if she had been trained, not by Bows, but by some ancestral queen. If she stood against the mantelpiece, her robe draped itself classically; her chin settled on her hand; the other lines of her form arranged themselves in harmonious undulations—she looked like a Muse waiting for a poet worth her patience. If she sat on a cane-bottomed chair, her arm rounded over the back, her hand seemed to require a sceptre; the folds of her dress fell into order as if they had been taught discipline. In the morning light her hair was blue-black; her complexion dazzling fair, with the faintest blush flickering like a quick flame in her cheek. Her eyes were grey with prodigiously long lashes; and her mouth, Pen would afterward insist, was of a staring red, outshining geraniums, sealing-wax, and guardsmen’s coats.

“And very warm,” continued this empress, as if meteorology were a royal proclamation.

Pen assented again, helplessly, and the conversation rolled on with that solemn triviality by which strangers first approach one another. She asked her father whether he had had a pleasant evening at the George; and he recounted supper and tumblers of punch as lovingly as if he could still taste them. Then he asked her how she had been employing the morning.

“Bows came,” she said, “at ten, and we studied Ophalia. It’s for the twenty-fourth, when I hope, sir, we shall have the honour of seeing ye.”

“Indeed, indeed, you will,” Pen cried; marvelling that she said “Ophalia” and spoke Irishly now, who had not the least Hibernian accent on the stage. It struck him—though he could not have phrased it—that a voice changes its country according to who is listening; and that there are selves which can only be spoken in certain sounds.

“I’ve secured ’um for your benefit, dear,” said the Captain, tapping his waistcoat pocket—wherein lay Pen’s sovereigns—and winking at Pen, who blushed at being both generous and used.

“Mr—-the gentleman’s very obleging,” said Mrs. Haller.

“My name is Pendennis,” said Pen, blushing harder. “I—I—hope you’ll—you’ll remember it.” His heart thumped so at this audacity that he nearly choked.

“Pendennis,” she answered slowly, looking him full in the eyes with a glance so straight, so clear, so bright, so killing, and in a voice so sweet and low and round, that the single word and look seemed to shoot through him and fix him in a blissful pain.

“I never knew the name was so pretty before,” Pen said.

“’Tis a very pretty name,” Ophelia said. “Pentweazle’s not a pretty name. Remember, papa, when we were on the Norwich Circuit, Young Pentweazle, who used to play second old men, and married Miss Rancy, the Columbine; they’re both engaged in London now, at the Queen’s, and get five pounds a week. Pentweazle wasn’t his real name. ’Twas Judkin gave it him, I don’t know why. His name was Harrington; that is, his real name was Potts; fawther a clergyman, very respectable. Harrington was in London, and got in debt. Ye remember; he came out in Falkland, to Mrs. Bunce’s Julia.”

“And a pretty Julia she was,” the Captain interposed; “a woman of fifty, and a mother of ten children. ’Tis you ought to have been Julia, or my name’s not Jack Costigan.”

“I didn’t take the leading business then,” Miss Fotheringay said modestly; “I wasn’t fit for’t till Bows taught me.”

After that business which had lately knocked all the sense out of Arthur Pendennis, Cicero and Euripides might as well have packed their trunks and gone into lodgings elsewhere. Honest Mr. Smirke, who had been engaged to cultivate a young gentleman’s mind, found himself chiefly employed in cultivating an amiable ignorance, and doing it with remarkable success.

The creature that bore the worst of it was Rebecca, the mare. For whenever Arthur could publicly proclaim, with a candour that would have done credit to a tax-gatherer, that he was “only riding over to Chatteris for a fencing-lesson,” he rode; and when he could not proclaim it, he rode all the same, only faster and with more mystery. Prior’s Lane—where a certain set of lodgings lay like a well-buttered trap for youth—became the true university to which he hurried, leaving Greek plays to Smirke and good intentions to Providence.

So, when Rebecca went lame, Arthur took it as a personal affront from Heaven. He raged over her with the tragical air of a monarch whose favourite charger has been slain at Bosworth, and then, like any sensible young man in love, proceeded to do the most practical thing possible: he plunged into the accounts of the hunting-stables, read up “doctoring” as if it were theology, hired another horse at ruinous rates, and paid for nostrums with the solemnity of a man endowing a church.

Once—sometimes twice—each week, under the pretext of reading a Greek play with Smirke, this young reprobate contrived his campaign with military precision: off he set early enough to catch the Competitor down coach, spent a couple of hours in Chatteris, and came back by the Rival which fled homeward at ten at night, as if it too had been compromised. It was nearly all over one day, through the mere innocence of virtue. Mrs. Pendennis, in her soft way, asked Mr. Smirke whether they had “read a great deal the night before.” Smirke, being born to tell the truth and to look painfully surprised by it, opened his mouth to say he had never seen Mr. Pen at all—when Arthur’s boot-heel descended on the curate’s toe under the table with the weight and distinctness of a moral lesson. Smirke’s countenance became that of a martyr; his words became those of a liar; and Greek, naturally, suffered.

They had, of course, those conversations which young men in love must have with somebody, as cooks must have salt. Smirke was the unfortunate cruet. Under vows of secrecy delivered with all the thunder of a miniature Jupiter, Arthur confessed his state. Smirke trembled, and with the air of a man asked to smuggle gunpowder into a nursery, ventured to hope that it was “no unworthy object—no unlawful attachment”—for if so, duty would force him to break his vow and inform Mrs. Pendennis, and then there would be quarrels, and then—most dreadful prospect—he might never again have the privilege of sitting in the same room with what he liked best in the world.

“Unlawful! Unworthy!” Arthur cried, bounding as if the very adjectives had slapped him. “She is as pure as she is beautiful. I would give my heart to no other woman. I keep it secret in my family because—because—there are reasons of a weighty nature which I am not at liberty to disclose. But any man who breathes a word against her purity insults both her honour and mine; and—dammy—I won’t stand it!”

Smirke, who could have fainted with relief at finding himself not compelled to denounce anybody, gave a small, frightened laugh. “Well, well—don’t call me out, Arthur; you know I can’t fight.” But by this compact the curate fell more completely into the boy’s power; and Greek and mathematics went, like untended broth, thin and tasteless.

Had the reverend gentleman possessed a malicious curiosity, and opened the Poet’s Corner of the County Chronicle when it arrived in Wednesday’s bag, he might have found the air thick with ardour: “Mrs. Haller,” “Passion and Genius,” “Lines to Miss Fotheringay of the Theatre Royal,” and other compositions which smelt of midnight ink and theatrically broken hearts. But these verses were no longer signed NEP; the author had changed his apron and styled himself EROS, as if a new signature could disguise the same hand that peppered the paper. Helen, good soul, who clipped every one of her son’s poems as if they were recipes for family preservation, never suspected that Nep and Eros were one and the same boiling pot.

At last Mrs. Pendennis, with that gentle, domestic interest by which mothers track all the world’s romances as if they were household accounts, asked, “Who is the lady whom your rival is always singing in the County Chronicle? He writes something like you, dear Pen, but yours is much the best. Have you seen Miss Fotheringay?”

Arthur said yes: he had seen her—that very night, indeed, in “The Stranger,” where she played Mrs. Haller. And by the way, she was to have a benefit; she was to appear as Ophelia—suppose they were to go? Shakspeare, you know, mother. They could get horses from the Clavering Arms. Little Laura sprang up as if the word Play had been sugar to a child.

Arthur introduced “Shakspeare, you know,” because his dead father—who respected the bard in the abstract with the fidelity of a man who does not read him in the concrete—had often declared there was more poetry in Shakspeare than in all Johnson’s Poets put together, and had promised what happiness it would be, when Pen was of a proper age, to take mother and boy to see some good plays. The widow’s eyes filled at the remembered speeches of the man that was gone. She kissed her son and said she would go. Laura capered with delight.

Was Arthur happy? Yes. Was he ashamed? Also yes: which is one of the common seasonings in youthful stew. As he held his mother to him he longed to tell her all, but kept his counsel, meaning to try her by the play, as Hamlet tried his uncle—only with less murder and more applause.

In her good humour Helen asked Mr. Smirke to join the party. Mr. Smirke, who had been bred at Clapham by a parent who regarded the theatre as a moral kitchen where the devil stirred the pots, had never yet seen a play. But Shakspeare!—and to sit the whole night by Mrs. Pendennis in her carriage! He spoke feebly of temptation and gratitude, and accepted. As he spoke he gave her a look—half longing, half sanctimonious—at which the widow felt more uncomfortable than if she had seen a mouse in her pantry. She had caught that look before lately. It pursued her like a tune one dislikes and cannot stop humming. Mr. Smirke became more positively odious every day in her eyes.

As for Arthur’s courtship, we shall not report a great deal of what he poured out, because the world contains enough nonsense already, and youth can always manufacture more. He sat with Miss Fotheringay hour after hour and emptied his soul upon her with the honest vehemence of a boy who believes eloquence is the same thing as sincerity. Everything he knew, hoped, felt, read, fancied—Byron, Moore, truth, eternity—came tumbling out as if his heart were a pantry door kicked open.

Miss Fotheringay’s part was not to talk, but to look as if she understood; and to look exceedingly handsome while doing it. Indeed, while Arthur was declaiming for twenty minutes at a stretch—delighted with his own thunder—Emily, who could not comprehend a tenth part of it, had leisure to attend to affairs far nearer the centre of her universe: how the cold mutton should be dressed next day (hashed with a sharp little bite of mustard and a respectful onion? or sliced and warmed in gravy, so it might pretend to be new?), how the black satin should be turned, how to coax a bonnet out of a scarf like Miss Thackthwaite’s. Arthur served up passion and poetry; Emily, with her calm fine eyes and rich voice, supplied the proper exclamations—“Oh, ’tis beautiful! Ah, how exquisite! Repeat those lines again”—as one sprinkles sugar over anything to make it go down. Off the boy went again, and she returned serenely to her mutton and millinery.

His passion was no secret from Emily or from her father. On Arthur’s second visit, both saw the hook was in; and when he had galloped away, Captain Costigan remarked, winking over his grog, “Faith, Milly darling, I think ye’ve hooked that chap.”

“Pooh—’tis only a boy, papa dear,” said Milly. “Sure he’s but a child.” Arthur, had he heard that, would have been transported; for on the ride home he shouted her name at hedges and milestones with the confidence of a conqueror.

“Ye’ve hooked ’um any how,” the Captain continued, “and he’s not a bad fish. I asked Tom at the George, and Flint the grocer where his mother dales—fine fortune—drives in her chariot—splendid park and grounds—Fairoaks Park—only son—property all his own at twenty-one—ye might go further and not fare so well, Miss Fotheringay.”

“Them boys are mostly talk,” said Milly, gravely. “Ye know at Dublin how ye went on about young Poldoody, and I’ve a whole desk full of verses he wrote me when he was in Trinity College; but he went abroad, and his mother married him to an Englishwoman.”

“Lord Poldoody was a young nobleman; and in them it’s natural,” said the Captain; “and ye weren’t in the position ye are now. But ye mustn’t encourage this young chap too much—for, bedad, Jack Costigan won’t have any thrifling with his daughter.”

“No more will his daughter, papa—you may be sure of that,” said Milly. “A little sip more of the punch—sure ’tis beautiful. Ye needn’t be afraid about the young chap—I think I’m old enough to take care of myself, Captain Costigan.”

So Arthur came day after day, rushing in and galloping away, growing wilder with each visit. Sometimes the Captain remained, sometimes—having, as he said, perfect confidence—he cocked his hat over his eye, strutted out on an errand, and left them to that most perilous of entertainments, conversation.

The Captain’s drawing-room was low and wainscoted, with a great window looking into the Dean’s garden. There Arthur sat and talked—talked—and Emily sat calm and beautiful at her work, the sunshine laying a warm glaze over her superb face and form like butter over hot bread. And the world, with a quaint mercy, kept interrupting him by sound. The great cathedral bell would begin to boom, and he would pause and smile, and be silent until the last vibration died away into the summer air. Toward sunset the rooks in the elms would quarrel like old women over a market-stall. Sometimes the organ and choristers would come drifting over the close, a soft discipline of harmony that hushed his noisy passion for a moment, as if the very air insisted on a quieter language than his.

It must be said, too, that Miss Fotheringay went to church every Sunday of her life, in a plain shawl and close bonnet and veil, accompanied by her indefatigable father, who gave the responses in a rich brogue, joined psalms and chanting with exemplary fervour, and behaved as if religion were a performance in which he had a respectable part.

Little Bows, the family’s house-friend, was furious at the notion of Emily marrying a stripling seven or eight years younger. Bows—crippled, and even a trifle more deformed than Bingley the manager, so he could not appear on the stage—was a wild singular man, with talent and humour in him like pepper in a stew. Attracted first by Emily’s beauty, he had taken to teaching her acting. He shrieked the parts in his cracked voice; she learned them by rote from his lips and repeated them in full rich tones. He indicated attitudes, set and moved those beautiful arms, drilled her eyes, her pauses, her very tears. Those who remember her afterwards can recall the precision: the same plank of the stage, the same instant of eye-roll, the same degree of weeping over the same syllable—acting as punctual as a kitchen clock.

And then, when she had come out trembling before the audience, looking so exhausted and tearful you fancied she might faint with sensibility, she would be behind the curtain in a moment gathering up her hair, and go home to a mutton-chop and a glass of brown stout; and the day’s harrowing labours over, she went to bed and snored as regularly as a porter. Bows, who had screamed her into greatness, was indignant that she should throw away her chances by marrying a little country squire. A London manager, seeing her, prophesied an engagement and success. The misfortune was: London managers had seen her. Three years before she had played in London and failed from sheer stupidity. Since then Bows had worked and screamed and twisted and repeated lines until he had made a machine of her; and she—patient and dull—let herself be made. She was not grateful or ungrateful, kind or ill-humoured: she was only stupid. And Arthur was madly in love with her.

The post-horses from the Clavering Arms arrived in due time and drew the party to the theatre at Chatteris. Arthur was gratified to see a tolerably large audience. The young gentlemen from Baymouth had a box; in the front sat Mr. Foker and his friend Mr. Spavin, blazing in full evening costume, as if they had been lit for the occasion. They saluted Arthur cordially and examined his party with approval. Little Laura, rosy-cheeked, with a quantity of shining brown ringlets, looked fit for any respectable comedy. Mrs. Pendennis, in black velvet with the diamond cross she wore on great occasions, looked handsome and majestic enough to be a duchess in exile. Behind sat Mr. Arthur and gentle Smirke, curl composed on his fair forehead, white tie in perfect order. He blushed to find himself there—yet was never so happy in his life. He and Mrs. Pendennis had brought books of Hamlet to follow the tragedy, as honest country-folks do when they go to a play in state, lest Shakspeare should slip a word past them unnoticed.

Samuel, coachman, groom, and gardener to Mr. Pendennis, took his place in the pit, where Mr. Foker’s man was also visible. The pit was dotted with non-commissioned officers of the Dragoons; their band, by permission of Colonel Swallowtail, sat in the orchestra; and the corpulent warrior himself, with his Waterloo medal, and a number of his young men, made a handsome show in the boxes.

“Who is that odd-looking person bowing to you, Arthur?” Mrs. Pendennis asked.

Arthur blushed. “His name is Captain Costigan, ma’am—a Peninsular officer.” It was the Captain indeed, in a new “shoot of clothes,” with large white kid gloves; one he waved to Arthur, the other he laid sprawling over his heart and coat-buttons. Arthur said no more. And how was Helen to know that this fine Peninsular officer was the father of the very lady whose praise was humming through the County Chronicle?

Mr. Hornbull, from London, played Hamlet; Mr. Bingley contented himself with Horatio and reserved his chief strength for William in Black-Eyed Susan, which was the second piece.

We have nothing to do with the play, except that Ophelia looked lovely and performed with admirable wild pathos: laughing, weeping, gazing, waving her beautiful white arms, flinging snatches of flowers and songs with charming madness. What a brave use she made of her splendid black hair, tossing it over her shoulders! She made the most charming corpse ever seen; and while Hamlet and Laertes battled in her grave, she was peeping from the back scenes with some curiosity towards Arthur’s box and the family party gathered there.

In that box there was but one voice about her: rapture. Mrs. Pendennis went into ecstasies over her beauty. Little Laura was bewildered by Ghost and murder and play-within-play; during which, as Hamlet lay at Ophelia’s knee, Arthur felt he could gladly strangle Mr. Hornbull for the convenience of the drama. Yet Laura cried praises of that beautiful young creature. Arthur was charmed by the effect Emily produced on his mother; and Smirke, for his part, grew enthusiastic.

When the curtain fell on that heap of slaughtered persons who are dispatched so suddenly at the end of Hamlet—poor Laura being not a little astonished at the quantity of death—there broke out an immense shouting and applause. The intrepid Smirke, violently excited, clapped and cried “Bravo! Bravo!” as loud as the Dragoon officers. The officers were greatly moved, and cheered as if courage were contagious; led by portly Swallowtail, who waved his cap, the non-commissioned officers in the pit following their chiefs as gallantly as if it were a charge. Bravos roared through the house. Arthur bellowed loudest, “Fotheringay! Fotheringay!” Messrs. Spavin and Foker gave the view-halloo from their box. Even Mrs. Pendennis began to wave her pocket-handkerchief; Laura danced, laughed, clapped, and looked up at Arthur with wonder.

Hornbull led the beneficiaire forward amid bursts of enthusiasm. She looked so handsome and radiant, hair still loose over her shoulders, that Arthur could hardly contain himself. He leaned over his mother’s chair and shouted, hurrahed, waved his hat, disguising the desire to cry, “Look—there! That’s the woman!” under a hurricane of applause.

As for Miss Fotheringay’s behaviour, she went through precisely the same business as always: surveyed the house with grateful glances, trembled, almost sank with emotion over her favourite trap-door, seized flowers and pressed them to her swelling heart, and so forth. Mr. Foker discharged a prodigious bouquet at her; even Smirke, blushing dreadfully, made a feeble shy with a rose, which fell into the pit and caused him an agony as if he had thrown it into sin. Twinkling at Emily’s breast, Arthur spied the locket he had bought at Mr. Nathan’s in High Street with the last shilling he was worth and a sovereign borrowed from Smirke.

Black-Eyed Susan followed; and at that sweet story the gentle-hearted party were charmed and affected. Susan in russet gown and pink ribbon looked as lovely as Ophelia, only with more hope of supper. Bingley was great in William. Goll as the Admiral resembled the figure-head of a seventy-four. Garbetts as Captain Boldweather—a miscreant who planned to carry off Susan—waved an immense cocked hat and proclaimed “Come what may, he will be the ruin of her,” with such relish you might have fancied he meant to be the ruin of the audience’s composure as well. It was with sincere regret that the friends saw the curtain fall and end that pretty tender tale.

If Arthur had been alone with his mother in the carriage on the way home, he would have told her all that night. But he sat on the box in the moonshine smoking a cigar by Smirke, who warmed himself with a comforter and the glow of having said “Bravo” in public. Mr. Foker’s tandem and lamps whirled by the sober Clavering posters a couple of miles on the road, and Mr. Spavin saluted Mrs. Pendennis’s carriage with variations of Rule Britannia on the key-bugle, making the night ring with heroic noise enough to scare the hedgerows into patriotism.

Two days after these gaieties, the Dean of Chatteris entertained select clerical friends at dinner at his Deanery. That they drank uncommonly good port, and abused the Bishop over dessert, is likely enough; but it is not our affair. Dr. Portman of Clavering was among the guests; and being a gallant man, and seeing from his place at the mahogany the Dean’s lady walking on the grass with her children sporting and her pink parasol over her head, he stepped out through the French windows into the lawn, leaving the other white neckcloths to gird at my lord Bishop. He offered Mrs. Dean his arm, and they sauntered over the ancient velvet lawn—mowed and rolled for immemorial Deans—in that quiet comfortable manner with which middle-aged good-tempered people walk after a good dinner in a calm golden summer evening, when the sun has just sunk behind the enormous cathedral towers and the sickle-shaped moon grows brighter every minute in the heaven.

Now at the end of the Dean’s garden stood Mrs. Creed’s house; and the windows of the first-floor room were open to admit the pleasant summer air. In that chamber, a young lady of six-and-twenty whose eyes were perfectly wide open sat with a luckless boy of eighteen whose eyes were shut by love. We have seen them there before; the reader will have no difficulty recognising Mr. Arthur Pendennis and Miss Costigan.

The poor boy had taken the plunge. Trembling, heart beating and throbbing, tears forcing themselves out in spite of him, voice choking with feeling, he had at last said the words he could withhold no more; and flung his whole store of love, admiration, ardour—his whole small treasure of life—at the feet of this mature beauty, as savages stake land and possessions for a draught of fire-water, or as civilised youth stakes peace and pride for a pair of fine eyes.

“Does your mother know of this, Arthur?” said Miss Fotheringay slowly.

He seized her hand and kissed it again and again. She did not withdraw it. “Does the old lady know it?” thought Miss Costigan; “well, perhaps she may.” And she remembered the handsome diamond cross Mrs. Pendennis wore at the play, and thought, with a practical tenderness all her own, “Sure ’twill go in the family.”

“Calm yourself, dear Arthur,” she said in her low rich voice, and sniffled sweetly and gravely upon him. With her disengaged hand she put the hair lightly off his throbbing forehead. He was in such a whirl of happiness he could hardly speak. At last he gasped, “My mother has seen you, and admires you beyond measure. She will learn to love you soon—who can do otherwise? She will love you because I do.”

“’Deed then, I think you do,” said Miss Costigan—perhaps with a sort of pity for him.

Think he did? Of course he went off into a rhapsody—love, truth, eternity, and the rest of the household gods of youth. Words were tried and found too small for the tremendous depth of his affection. This speech is no business of ours. It was most likely not very wise; but what right have we to pry into the pantry where a boy empties out his heart? Let him fling it down and be gentle with him. It is best to love wisely, no doubt; but to love foolishly is better than not to be able to love at all. Some of us can’t, and are proud of our impotence too, which is like being proud one cannot taste.

At the end of his speech Arthur again kissed the imperial hand with rapture. And it was at this very moment—while Mrs. Dean and Dr. Portman were talking comfortably together—that young Master Ridley Roset tugged his mother by the back of her capacious dress and said, waggling his innocent head,

“I say, ma! look up there.”

Indeed it was a view from the Dean’s garden such as seldom is seen by Deans—or written in chapters. There was poor Arthur performing a salute upon the rosy fingers of his charmer, who received the embrace with perfect calmness and good humour. Master Ridley looked up and grinned; little Miss Rosa looked at her brother and opened her mouth of astonishment. Mrs. Dean’s face defied expression. And as for Dr. Portman—when he beheld the scene, and saw his prime favourite and dear pupil Arthur—he stood mute with rage and wonder.

Major Arthur Pendennis arrived at Fairoaks in due time, after a night spent in that ancient instrument of torture miscalled a mail-coach; a machine contrived, as it seemed, not so much to convey a Christian gentleman from one place to another, as to rub every joint in his body with a file, to shake every tooth in his head loose, and to fill his ears with a perpetual concert of horn, gate-chain, wheel, whip, and human snore.

A stout fellow-passenger, who had expanded himself into a kind of upholstered fortress by means of great-coats, had wedged the Major into a corner, and kept him awake by producing, from somewhere about his neckcloth, a bass note of snoring which set the window-glass jingling like a saucepan-lid. Opposite sat a widow lady, who not only shut out the little honest night-air by closing every window as if the fresh breeze were an unpaid creditor, but seasoned the interior of the coach with Jamaica rum-and-water, which she drew perpetually from a bottle hidden in her reticule, with the zeal of a housekeeper basting a roast. And whenever the Major contrived, for a blessed minute, to doze, there came—twang!—the horn at a turnpike, or—scrape!—the huge neighbour shifting his fortifications and pushing him another inch nearer suffocation, or—tap-tap-tap—madam’s industrious feet practising upon the Major’s tender toes as if they were a little drum.

Eight miles an hour, for twenty or five-and-twenty hours; a hard seat; a gouty tendency that disliked adventure; coachmen who grumbled for fees as if it were part of the King’s mail to convey their ill-humour; and a fellow-traveller partial to spirits-and-water,—these were the “jolly old times,” which, being happily past, are now praised precisely because they can no longer be endured.

On the roof, next the widow, and close by Mr. Morgan (the Major’s man, who sat there with the resigned grandeur of a steward travelling with plate), were two schoolboys going home for the midsummer holidays; and at Bagshot, when the coach took in passengers and the inn took in profits, the Major watched them sup with a kind of pale amazement. They fell upon ham, eggs, pie, pickles, tea, coffee, and boiled beef, as if they had been two young locusts with a warrant; while he, who had once known dinners that began with a turtle and ended in a coronet, sat sipping a cup of tea so feeble that it might have been brewed from the shadow of a leaf, and thinking with melancholy tenderness that Lord Steyne’s dinner was coming off at that very moment, to the sound of clinking glasses, soft laughter, and those well-bred voices which never shout unless it be at an opera.

The ingenuous ardour of the boys amused him. He grew more interested when he discovered that the one inside the coach was a lord’s son—whose noble father, of course, Major Pendennis must have met in that world where everybody meets everybody, especially when it is convenient afterward to say so. The little lord slept all night through, despite squeezing, horn-blowing, widow, rum, and all; and at the lodge-gate of Fairoaks he looked as fresh as paint—nay, pronounced himself so—while the Major descended with a yellow face, a bristly beard, a wig out of curl, and rheumatic griefs shooting through him like ill-tempered arrows.

At the lodge the porteress and the gardener’s wife greeted him with reverence, and Mr. Morgan with a reverence even more respectful than theirs, because it was professional and knew its duty.

Helen Pendennis saw the expected guest from her window, but did not advance at once. She understood the Major’s religion, which required certain rites before he could appear among the faithful. Pen, when a boy, had once incurred disgrace by carrying off from the Major’s dressing-table a little morocco box; which, it must be confessed, contained the Major’s back teeth—those useful domestics whom he did not choose to take jolting about in a mail-coach, and without which he would not choose to be looked at by his own family. Mr. Morgan, too, made a mystery of the wigs—curling them in private places, introducing them to his master as if they were contraband, and treating hair as though it were state papers. Without that head of hair the Major would as soon have appeared as a chef would serve a great dinner without salt.

So to his room he went, to supply deficiencies. Through his toilet there issued groans, moans, wheezes, and such curses as old bucks emit when rheumatism has been sitting up with them all night and they have a long duty to perform in the morning. And at last, belted, curled, set straight, and furnished with those necessary appendages which make a man presentable in society, he descended upon the drawing-room with a grave majestic air—part man of business, part man of fashion; a person who could negotiate a loan or lead a cotillon, as might be required.

Pen was not there. Only Helen, and little Laura at her knees sewing. To Laura the Major never gave more than a forefinger; and on this occasion, after saluting his sister-in-law, he presented it like a dry twig offered to a frightened bird. Laura took it trembling, dropped it, and fled out of the room.

Major Pendennis did not want to keep her—or indeed to have her in the house at all—and had his private reason for disapproving of her, which may be mentioned on some future occasion. Meanwhile Laura, being expelled by a finger, wandered about the premises in search of Pen, and presently found him in the orchard pacing up and down a walk there in earnest conversation with Mr. Smirke.

It was one of those orchard mornings that smell of bruised grass, bark warmed by early sun, and the tart promise of apples not yet ready; and the place had its own soft music—the far-off scythe whispering in a field, sparrows scolding in a hedge, the slow creak of a cart somewhere beyond the trees. Such honest rural sounds are a kind of nourishment; they settle upon the mind like a good broth, and are more wholesome than all the horns of turnpikes and all the grinding of wheels upon London stones. But Pen did not hear Laura’s clear voice singing out until Smirke pulled him by the coat and pointed towards her as she came running.

She ran up and put her hand into his.

“Come in, Pen,” she said; “there’s somebody come; uncle Arthur’s come.”

“He is, is he?” said Pen; and she felt him grasp her little hand. He looked round at Smirke with an uncommon fierceness, as much as to say, I am ready for him or any man. Mr. Smirke cast up his eyes as usual and heaved his gentle sigh, as if sighing were a profession.

“Lead on, Laura,” Pen said, with a half fierce, half comic air—“lead on, and say I wait upon my uncle.”

But he laughed in order to hide a great anxiety; and was screwing his courage inwardly to face the ordeal which he knew was now before him.

Pen, in the last two days, had taken Smirke into his confidence; and ever since the outbreak attendant on the discovery of Doctor Portman, during every one of those forty-eight hours passed in Smirke’s society, had done little else than talk of Miss Fotheringay—Miss Emily Fotheringay—Emily, and all the rest of it. Smirke listened without difficulty. He was in love himself; he was anxious to propitiate Pen; and he was, moreover, much enraptured by the personal charms of this goddess—whose like, never having been before at a theatrical representation, he had not beheld until now.

Pen’s fire and volubility, his hot eloquence and rich poetical tropes, his manly heart (kind, ardent, hopeful), refusing to see defects in the person he loved or difficulties in their position that he might not overcome—had half convinced Mr. Smirke that the arrangement proposed by Mr. Pen was very feasible and prudent; and that it would be a great comfort to have Emily settled at Fairoaks, Captain Costigan in the yellow room established for life, and Pen married at eighteen.

Indeed, in these two days the boy had almost talked over his mother too; had parried her objections with that indignant good sense which is often the perfection of absurdity; and had brought her almost to acquiesce in the belief that if the marriage were doomed in heaven, why doomed it was; that if the young woman were a good person, it was all she had to ask; and rather to dread the arrival of the guardian uncle, whom she foresaw would regard Mr. Pen’s marriage in a very different manner from that simple, romantic, honest, and utterly absurd way in which the widow was already disposed to look at questions of this sort.

For, as in the old allegory of the gold and silver shield, about which two knights quarrelled, each is right according to the point from which he looks: so about marriage; whether it is foolish or good, wise or otherwise, depends upon the point of view from which you regard it. If it means a snug house in Belgravia, pretty little dinner-parties, a pretty little brougham to drive in the Park, and a decent provision not only for the young people but for the little Belgravians to come; and if these are the necessaries of life (and they are with many honest people), to talk of any other arrangement is absurdity; of love in lodgings, a babyish folly of affection; that can’t pay coach-hire or afford a decent milliner—mere wicked balderdash and childish romance.

If, on the other hand, your opinion is that people, not with an assured subsistence but with a fair chance to obtain it, and with the stimulus of hope, health, and strong affection, may take the chance of Fortune for better or worse and share its good or evil together, the polite theory becomes absurd in its turn—worse than absurd, a blasphemy almost, and a doubt of Providence; and a man who waits to make his chosen woman happy until he can drive her to church in a neat little carriage with a pair of horses is no better than a coward or a trifler, neither worthy of love nor fortune.

Helen Pendennis was country-bred; and the book of life, as she interpreted it, told her a different story from that page read in cities. Like most soft and sentimental women, matchmaking formed a great part of her thoughts; and she had begun to speculate about her son’s falling in love and marrying long before the subject had entered into the brains of the young gentleman. It pleased her—with that dismal pleasure which the idea of sacrificing themselves gives to certain women—to think of the day when she would give up all to Pen; when he should bring his wife home; when she would surrender the keys and the best bedroom; and go and sit at the side of the table and see him happy. What did she want in life but to see the lad prosper? An empress certainly was not too good for him, and would be honoured by becoming Mrs. Pen; and if he selected humble Esther instead of Queen Vashti, she would be content with his lordship’s choice. Never mind how lowly or poor the person might be who was to enjoy that prodigious honour; Mrs. Pendennis was willing to bow before her, welcome her, yield her up the first place.

But an actress—a mature woman, who had long ceased blushing except with rouge as she stood under the eager glances of thousands of eyes—an illiterate and ill-bred person, very likely, who must have lived with light associates and heard doubtful conversation—oh, it was hard that such a one should be chosen, and that the matron should be deposed to give place to such a Sultana.

All these doubts the widow laid before Pen during the two days which had of necessity to elapse before the uncle came down; but he met them with that frankness and ease which a young gentleman exhibits at his time of life, and routed her objections with infinite satisfaction to himself. Miss Costigan was a paragon of virtue and delicacy; as sensitive as the most timid maiden; as pure as unsullied snow; with the finest manners, the most graceful wit and genius, the most charming refinement and justness of appreciation in all matters of taste. She had the most admirable temper and devotion to her father, a good old gentleman of high family and fallen fortunes, who had lived with the best society in Europe. He was in no hurry, and could afford to wait any time till he was one-and-twenty.

But Pen felt—and here his face assumed an awful and harrowing solemnity—that he was engaged in the one only passion of his life, and that DEATH alone could close it.

Helen told him, with a sad smile and a shake of the head, that people survived these passions; and as for long engagements contracted between very young men and old women—she knew an instance in her own family—Laura’s poor father was an instance—how fatal they were. Mr. Pen, however, was resolved that death must be his doom in case of disappointment; and rather than baulk him, his mother would have submitted to any sacrifice or personal pain, and would have gone down on her knees and kissed the feet of a Hottentot daughter-in-law.

Arthur knew his power over the widow, and the young tyrant was touched while he exercised it. In those two days he brought her almost into submission and patronised her very kindly. He passed one evening with the lovely pie-maker at Chatteris, in which he bragged of his influence over his mother; and he spent the other night composing a most flaming and conceited copy of verses to his divinity, vowing, like Montrose, that he would make her famous with his sword and glorious by his pen; and that he would love her as no mortal woman had been adored since the creation of womankind.

It was on that night, long after midnight, that wakeful Helen, passing stealthily by her son’s door, saw a light streaming through the chink into the dark passage and heard Pen tossing, tumbling, and mumbling verses in his bed. She waited outside a while, anxiously listening. In infantile fevers and early boyish illnesses, many a night before, the kind soul had so kept watch. She turned the lock very softly now and went in so gently that Pen for a moment did not see her.

His face was turned away. His papers lay scattered on the desk, and more were strewn on the bed around him. He was biting a pencil and thinking of rhymes, and all sorts of follies and passions. He was Hamlet jumping into Ophelia’s grave; he was the Stranger taking Mrs. Haller to his arms—beautiful Mrs. Haller, with raven ringlets falling over her shoulders. Despair and Byron, Thomas Moore and all the Loves of the Angels, Waller and Herrick, Béranger and every love-song he had ever read, were seething in the young gentleman’s mind; and he was at the very height and paroxysm of imaginative frenzy when his mother found him.

“Arthur,” said the mother’s soft silver voice; and he started up and turned round. He clutched some of the papers and pushed them under the pillow like contraband verses.

“Why don’t you go to sleep, my dear?” she said, with a sweet tender smile; and sate down on the bed and took one of his hot hands.

Pen looked at her wildly for an instant. “I couldn’t sleep,” he said; “I—I was—I was writing.” And hereupon he flung his arms round her neck and said, “O mother! I love her, I love her!”

How could such a kind soul help soothing and pitying him? The gentle creature did her best, and thought with strange wonder and tenderness that it was only yesterday he was a child in that bed; and how she used to come and say her prayers over it before he woke upon holiday mornings.

They were very grand verses, no doubt, though Miss Fotheringay did not understand them; but old Cos, with a wink and a knowing finger on his nose, said, “Put them up with th’ other letthers, Milly darling. Poldoody’s pomes was nothing to this.” So Milly locked up the manuscripts, as one locks up spices—because they are precious, because they are pungent, and because they do not belong to the general table.

When, then, the Major—being dressed and presentable—presented himself to Mrs. Pendennis, he found in the course of ten minutes’ colloquy that the poor widow was not merely distressed at the idea of the marriage contemplated by Pen, but more distressed still at thinking that the boy himself was unhappy about it, and that his uncle and he should have any violent altercation on the subject.

She besought Major Pendennis to be very gentle with Arthur. “He has a very high spirit, and will not brook unkind words,” she hinted. “Dr. Portman spoke to him rather roughly—and I must own unjustly, the other night—for my dearest boy’s honour is as high as any mother can desire—but Pen’s answer quite frightened me, it was so indignant. Recollect he is a man now; and be very—very cautious,” said the widow, laying a fair long hand on the Major’s sleeve.

He took it up, kissed it gallantly, and looked in her alarmed face with wonder—and a scorn which he was too polite to show.
