“Bon Dieu!” thought the old negotiator. “The boy has actually talked the woman round; she’d get him a wife as she would a toy if Master cried for it. Why are there no such things as lettres-de-cachet—and a Bastille for young fellows of family?”

He lived in such good company that he might be excused for feeling like an Earl. He kissed the widow’s timid hand, pressed it in both his, and laid it down on the table with one of his own over it as he smiled and looked her in the face.

“Confess,” said he, “now, that you are thinking how you possibly can make it up to your conscience to let the boy have his own way.”

She blushed, and was moved in the usual manner of females.

“I am thinking that he is very unhappy—and I am too——”

“To contradict him or to let him have his own wish?” asked the other; and added, with great comfort to his inward self, “I’m d——d if he shall.”

“To think that he should have formed so foolish and cruel and fatal an attachment,” the widow said, “which can but end in pain whatever be the issue.”

“The issue shan’t be marriage, my dear sister,” the Major said resolutely. “We’re not going to have a Pendennis, the head of the house, marry a strolling mountebank from a booth. No, no; we won’t marry into Greenwich Fair, ma’am.”

“If the match is broken suddenly off,” the widow interposed, “I don’t know what may be the consequence. I know Arthur’s ardent temper, the intensity of his affections, the agony of his pleasures and disappointments, and I tremble at this one if it must be. Indeed, indeed, it must not come on him too suddenly.”

“My dear madam,” the Major said, with an air of deepest commiseration, “I’ve no doubt Arthur will have to suffer confoundedly before he gets over the little disappointment. But is he, think you, the only person who has been so rendered miserable?”

“No, indeed,” said Helen, holding down her eyes. She was thinking of her own case, and at that moment she was seventeen again—and most miserable.

“I, myself,” whispered her brother-in-law, “have undergone a disappointment in early life. A young woman with fifteen thousand pounds—niece to an Earl—most accomplished creature. A third of her money would have run up my promotion in no time, and I should have been a lieutenant-colonel at thirty. But it might not be. I was but a penniless lieutenant; her parents interfered; and I embarked for India, where I had the honour of being secretary to Lord Buckley, when commander-in-Chief—without her. What happened? We returned our letters, sent back our locks of hair”—and here the Major passed his fingers through his wig—“we suffered—but we recovered. She is now a baronet’s wife with thirteen grown-up children; altered, it is true, in person; but her daughters remind me of what she was, and the third is to be presented early next week.”

Helen did not answer. She was still thinking of old times. There are passages of early life which, if one lives to be a hundred, will always carry one back to youth again; and Helen was thinking of one of these.

“Look at my own brother, my dear creature,” the Major continued gallantly; “he himself, you know, had a little disappointment when he started in the—the medical profession. An eligible opportunity presented itself. Miss Balls, I remember the name—daughter of an apoth—a practitioner in very large practice. My brother had very nearly succeeded in his suit. But difficulties arose; disappointments supervened; and—and I am sure he had no reason to regret the disappointment, which gave him this hand,” said the Major; and he once more politely pressed Helen’s fingers.

“Those marriages between people of such different rank and age,” said Helen, “are sad things. I have known them produce a great deal of unhappiness.—Laura’s father, my cousin, who—who was brought up with me”—she added, in a low voice—“was an instance of that.”

“Most injudicious,” cut in the Major. “I don’t know anything more painful than for a man to marry his superior in age or his inferior in station. Fancy marrying a woman of low rank of life, and having your house filled with her confounded tag-rag-and-bobtail of relations! Fancy your wife attached to a mother who dropped her h’s, or called Maria Marire! How are you to introduce her into society? My dear Mrs. Pendennis, I will name no names, but in the very best circles of London society I have seen men suffering the most excruciating agony. I have known them to be cut—to be lost utterly—from the vulgarity of their wives’ connections.

“What did Lady Snapperton do last year at her dejeune dansant after the Bohemian Ball? She told Lord Brouncker that he might bring his daughters, or send them with a proper chaperon; but that she would not receive Lady Brouncker, who was a druggist’s daughter, or some such thing; and as Tom Wagg remarked of her, never wanted medicine certainly, for she never had an h in her life. Good Ged! what would have been the trifling pang of a separation in the first instance, to the enduring infliction of a constant misalliance and intercourse with low people?”

“What, indeed!” said Helen, dimly disposed towards laughter, but checking the inclination, because she remembered in what prodigious respect her deceased husband held Major Pendennis and his stories of the great world.

“Then this fatal woman is ten years older than that silly young scapegrace of an Arthur. What happens in such cases, my dear creature? I don’t mind telling you, now we are alone, that in the highest state of society, misery—undeviating misery—is the result. Look at Lord Clodworthy come into a room with his wife—why, good Ged, she looks like Clodworthy’s mother. What’s the case between Lord and Lady Willowbank, whose love match was notorious? He has already cut her down twice when she has hanged herself out of jealousy for Mademoiselle de Sainte Cunegonde, the dancer; and mark my words, good Ged, one day he’ll not cut the old woman down.

“No, my dear madam, you are not in the world, but I am. You are a little romantic and sentimental (you know you are—women with those large beautiful eyes always are); you must leave this matter to my experience. Marry this woman! Marry at eighteen an actress of thirty—bah, bah! I would as soon he sent into the kitchen and married the cook.”

“I know the evils of premature engagements,” sighed out Helen.

And as she has made this allusion no less than thrice in the course of the above conversation, and seems so oppressed with the notion of long engagements and unequal marriages, and as the circumstance we have to relate will explain what perhaps some persons are anxious to know—namely who little Laura is, who has appeared more than once before us—it will be as well to clear up these points in another chapter.

It befell, not so very long ago (and yet long enough for a ham to cure twice over in a clean West-country loft), that a young gentleman of Cambridge came down for the Long Vacation to the very village where Helen Thistlewood lived with her mother—the widow of that lieutenant who had been laid low at Copenhagen, as neatly and abruptly as a candle-snuff in a draught.

This gentleman was the Reverend Francis Bell: a Fellow, a Tutor, a terror to idle undergraduates, and—what is rarer—a nephew who could be trusted to lodge under his aunt’s roof without immediately eating her out of house and home. He brought three or four pupils with him, as one might bring hungry goslings to a pond; and the little household, which lived in a small way, suddenly found itself full of Latin, young voices, footsteps in the passage, and the perpetual scratching of pens—an industrious music that, to ears accustomed to village quiet, sounded like a brood of crickets who had all learned the same psalm-tune.

The two ladies discovered, early enough, that Mr. Bell carried an engagement in his pocket along with his watch and his sermons. He was only waiting, they understood, for a college living to make him respectable in a parsonage and solvent at a butcher’s. His intended was Miss Martha Coacher, daughter of another reverend gentleman—Mr. Coacher—who had once been Bell’s private tutor; and it was under that learned roof, when Bell was a raw boy of seventeen or eighteen, that the romance had boiled over.

Picture, if you please, a garden in spring; peas on their sticks; the earth smelling damp and honest; a wicker basket; and Miss Martha, then in what she called her bloom, picking pods with that determined snap which is not the worst qualification in a woman, unless she applies it later to a husband’s comfort. There, with pea-vines for witnesses and a robin for clerk, young Bell flung himself on his knees—actually in the mould—and pledged himself to endless affection. A man who can swear eternal constancy while his stockings are taking the print of a garden-bed is either a hero or a simpleton; and young Bell, like most young men, was a little of both.

Miss Martha was many years his senior; and her heart—poor thing—had been scored and carved upon by previous suitors, like an old chopping-board that has known too many knives. No fewer than three of her father’s pupils had warmed themselves at her fire and walked away whistling. The village apothecary had jilted her as coolly as he might cork a phial. A dragoon officer—one of those bright, jingling persons who borrow hearts as they borrow lodging—had danced her through a season at Bath, shaken his bridle-rein gaily one morning, and galloped off, leaving her to waltz with memory. When a woman has been thus served up and sent back from the table so often, it is not astonishing if she longs at last to be eaten in peace.

So she listened to the honest gawky boy with kindness and a good-humour that had a touch of condescension in it, and said, “Law, Bell, I’m sure you are too young to think of such things;” but hinted that she would revolve the proposal in her own virgin bosom—an apartment in which, it must be owned, there was already a good deal of stored furniture. She could not refer him to her mamma—there was no mamma to be referred to; Mr. Coacher was a widower, and so sunk in books that a woman’s heart might have been simmering on his very hob and he would have asked only whether it were Greek or Latin.

Presently Bell received, tied in a bit of blue ribbon, a lock of Miss Martha’s auburn hair—sent like a slice from the joint, as earnest of the whole feast. She had snipped off and bestowed such ringlets before—thrice, indeed—and the possessors had proved faithless; but the hair had obligingly grown again, as if to supply the market. “Men are deceivers,” Martha had occasion to say; and this time, to do her justice, Number Six was the exception. Francis Bell was faithful.

When the time came that it must be told to Mr. Coacher, that gentleman cried, “God bless my soul, I hadn’t the least idea what was going on!”—which was likely enough, for he had been taken in precisely the same manner already; and Bell went up to the University with his ambition set like yeast: to rise, to swell, to win honours, and to lay them hot and steaming at Martha’s feet.

The young man worked as if he were kneading dough for a famine. Term after term brought news of prizes and triumphs. He sent prize-books for his essays to old Coacher, and a silver declamation cup to Miss Martha—tokens that glittered handsomely on a parlour shelf, though they did not make her temper any the sweeter. He became high among the Wranglers, a Fellow of his college; and all this while letters went and came—tender, constant, dutiful—so that Miss Martha, tasting each line as if it were her portion, could fairly say that her influence had fed his success.

But time, that slow cook, alters every dish. When the Reverend Francis Bell, M.A., Fellow and Tutor, reached six-and-twenty, Miss Martha was four-and-thirty; and though she had been browned and aired by years, she was not improved by them. Her charms, her manners, her temper—none had mellowed, like a good cheese. Having achieved his honours, Bell relaxed; his judgement cooled; and what had looked rosy in the pea-garden began to show, under the clearer light of manhood, as rather coarse, rather sour, and very certainly middle-aged.

And it was after one of those altercations in which Miss Martha’s eloquence shone so fiercely that she often indulged it for pleasure, that Bell refused to take his pupils to Bearleader’s Green (where Mr. Coacher’s living was) for the vacation. He bethought him instead of his aunt’s village, not visited for years—not since little Helen, then a child, used to sit on his knee and listen to stories, as one listens to the crackle of a hearth.

Down he came; and Helen—no longer little—stood grown into a beautiful young woman. The cousins were together nearly four months, from June to October. They walked in summer evenings when the hedges smelt of warm leaf and bruised mint; they met in early mornings when birds stitched the air with their voices and the world’s great machinery had not yet begun to grind. They read out of the same book while the old lady dozed at night over the candles; and the house had its domestic sounds—the ticking clock, the soft clink of a spoon, the sighing of a sleepy fire—into which, little by little, their hearts slipped and fitted like two parts of one old tune.

What Helen knew, Frank taught her. She sang to him; and her voice, coming through the stillness, might have seemed a kind of bread for his spirit—warm, sustaining, impossible to forget once tasted. She gave him her artless heart. She was aware of all his story. Had he made any secret? He had shown her the picture of the woman to whom he was engaged; had shown her too—blushing, and miserable—letters hard, eager, cruel, as if written with a pen dipped in vinegar.

The days went on—happier, closer; with more kindness, more confidence, more pity; until at last an October morning came when Francis went back to college, and Helen felt, as surely as if it had been lifted from her breast, that her tender heart had gone with him.

Frank too awoke from his midsummer dream to the horrible reality of his chain. He tore at it, gnashing like a man who has been tricked into wearing his own handcuffs. Should he confess? Should he give his savings to the woman he was bound to and beg release? There was time—perhaps—yet. He temporised. No living might fall in for years. Meanwhile he and Helen corresponded sadly and fondly; while the betrothed woman, jealous, dissatisfied, harsh as ever, complained—bitterly, and with reason—of his altered tone.

At last the new attachment was discovered. Francis owned it; he cared not to disguise it; rebuked Martha with her violent temper, her imperious anger, and—worst of all—with her inferiority and her age.

Her answer was a threat that made all honour seem a trap. If he did not keep his promise, she would carry his letters into every court in the kingdom—letters in which he had pledged love ten thousand times; she would expose him as perjurer and traitor; and after that—she would kill herself.

He had one more interview with Helen. Her mother was dead then; Helen lived companion with old Lady Pontypool. There, in that last meeting, it was resolved—solemnly, miserably—that he must “do his duty”: that is, redeem his vow; that is, pay a debt cozened from him by a sharper; that is, make two honest people wretched, and call it virtue. They judged it so, and parted.

The living fell in only too soon; yet Frank Bell was quite grey and worn by the time he was inducted. Helen wrote him upon his marriage, beginning “My dear Cousin,” and ending “always truly yours.” She sent back his letters, and the lock of hair—every bit but a small piece. That little remnant lay in her desk years later, when she spoke to the Major.

Bell lived three or four years in his living, then, the Chaplainship of Coventry Island falling vacant, applied privately, obtained it, and announced it to his wife. She objected—as she did to everything. He told her bitterly he did not want her to come; so she went. They sailed out in Governor Crawley’s time; and Bell was intimate with that gentleman in his later years. And it was in Coventry Island—years after his own marriage, and five years after he had heard of the birth of Helen’s boy—that his own daughter was born.

Not by the first Mrs. Bell. That lady died of island fever, very soon after Helen Pendennis and her husband (for Helen had told her husband everything) wrote to inform Bell of the birth of their child. “I was old, was I?” said Mrs. Bell the first. “I was old, and her inferior, was I? but I married you, Mr. Bell, and kept you from marrying her?”—and upon this nourishing reflection she died, as if spite itself were a draught too strong.

Bell married again—a colonial lady—whom he loved fondly. But love, for him, was always served with a side-dish of loss. This second wife died in childbirth; and Bell gave up, as a man gives up music after too much noise. He sent his little girl home to Helen Pendennis and her husband, with a parting prayer that they would befriend her.

The child came to Fairoaks from Bristol—not far, by map, though far enough for a small heart to feel it—dressed in black, in company of a soldier’s wife who had nursed her. At parting from this nurse she wept bitterly; but Helen’s care dried the tears as a warm kitchen dries damp clothes. Around the girl’s neck hung a locket with hair—Helen’s gift of years ago to poor Francis, now dead and buried. This child was all that was left of him; and Helen cherished the legacy with that secret tenderness which lives in women’s cupboards and desk-drawers, among keepsakes and folded papers that have their own smell and silence.

Her father’s dying letter said her name was Helen Laura. But John Pendennis, though he accepted the trust, was always a little jealous of the orphan; and gloomily ordered she should be called by her own mother’s name, and not by that first name her father had given. She was afraid of Mr. Pendennis to the last moment of his life; and only when her husband was gone did Helen dare openly to indulge the full tenderness she felt for the little girl.

Thus Laura Bell became, in all but blood, Mrs. Pendennis’s daughter. Neither her husband nor that gentleman’s brother, the Major, viewed the child with favourable eyes. She reminded the first of circumstances in his wife’s life that he had been forced to accept, but would much have preferred to forget; and as for the second—how should he regard her? She was not related to the Pendennises, nor to any nobleman in the empire; and she had but a couple of thousand pounds.

And now, having kept Mr. Pen waiting on the threshold while we have been stewing this family history down to its essence, let him be admitted.

He had strung up his nerves outside the door like fiddle-strings, and came in determined to face the awful uncle. In his mind the encounter was to be a grand battle; he would be heroic; he would stand for the dignity of his famous family, and for Love, that rash cook who over-salts all youth’s dishes. So he flung open the door with a warlike air, as though he carried a lance and a banner instead of nothing but eighteen years and a hot heart; and he glanced at his adversary as if to say, “Come on. I am ready.”

Major Pendennis, man of the world, surveying this martial entrance, could hardly help grinning at the boy’s pompous simplicity. The Major, too, had measured his ground; he saw the widow was already half conquered by her son’s romantic nonsense, and guessed that threats and tragedy would only make the lad stubborn and solemn. So he laid aside authority at once, stepped forward with the most good-humoured smile in the world, held out his hands, shook Pen’s passive fingers gaily, and said, “Well, Pen, my boy, tell us all about it.”

Mrs. Pendennis was delighted with the Major’s generosity of temper. Pen, on the contrary, was taken aback and disappointed; his tragedy had been robbed of its thunder. His grand entry suddenly felt ridiculous. He blushed; he winced; he was mortified, bewildered, and so near tears that his throat worked like a child swallowing a sob.

“I—I—I didn’t know that you were come till just now,” he said. “Is—is—town very full, I suppose?”

If Pen could hardly gulp the tears down, it was all the Major could do not to laugh them out. He turned and shot a comical glance at Mrs. Pendennis, who felt the scene was ridiculous and sentimental at once; and, having nothing better to do, she went up and kissed Mr. Pen. Thinking of her tenderness and soft obedience to his wishes, the boy melted, as a pat of butter melts at the edge of a pan.

“What a couple of fools they are,” thought the old guardian. “If I hadn’t come down, she would have driven over in state to pay a visit and give her blessing to the young lady’s family.”

“Come, come,” said he, still grinning, “let us have as little sentiment as possible; and, Pen, my good fellow, tell us the whole story.”

Pen rallied into his tragic air again, as if he had picked up the dropped mask. “The story is, sir,” said he, “as I have written it to you before. I have made the acquaintance of a most beautiful and most virtuous lady; of a high family, although in reduced circumstances: I have found the woman in whom I know that the happiness of my life is centred; I feel that I never, never can think about any woman but her. I am aware of the difference of our ages and other difficulties in my way. But my affection was so great that I felt I could surmount all these; that we both could: and she has consented to unite her lot with mine, and to accept my heart and my fortune.”

“How much is that, my boy?” said the Major. “Has anybody left you money? I don’t know that you are worth a shilling in the world.”

“You know what I have is his!” cried Mrs. Pendennis.

“Doubtless, doubtless,” said the Major, swallowing what he was disposed to say. “You would sacrifice anything for him. Everybody knows that. But it is, after all, your fortune which Pen is offering to the young lady; and of which he wishes to take possession at eighteen.”

“I know my mother will give me anything,” Pen said, disturbed.

“Yes, my good fellow; but there is reason in all things. If your mother keeps the house, it is but fair she should select her company. When you give her house over her head, and transfer her banker’s account to yourself for the benefit of Miss What-d’-you-call-’em—Miss Costigan—don’t you think you should at least have consulted my sister, as one of the principal parties in the transaction? I speak without anger or assumption of authority—though the law and your father’s will give it me for three years to come—but as one man of the world to another. Because you can do what you like with your mother, have you a right to do so? As you are her dependent, would it not have been more generous to wait, and at least pay her the courtesy to ask her leave?”

Pen’s head drooped. The romantic heroism began to taste, suddenly, of selfishness—like a rich dish discovered to have been cooked in another person’s fat.

“I did it in a moment of passion,” he said, floundering; “I was not aware what I was going to say or do”—and in this he was perfectly sincere—“but now it is said, and I stand to it. No; I neither can nor will recall it. I’ll die rather than do so. And—I don’t want to burden my mother,” he added. “I’ll work for myself. I’ll go on the stage, and act with her. She says I should do well there.”

“But will she take you on those terms?” the Major interposed. “Mind, I do not say Miss Costigan is not the most disinterested of women; but don’t you suppose, fairly, that your position as a young gentleman of ancient birth and decent expectations forms part of the cause why she finds your addresses welcome?”

“I’ll die, I say, rather than forfeit my pledge,” cried Pen, doubling his fists, red as if the blood itself were affronted.

“Who asks you, my dear friend?” said the Major, imperturbable. “No gentleman breaks his word, of course, when it has been given freely. But you can wait. You owe something to your mother, something to your family—something to me as your father’s representative.”

“Oh, of course,” Pen said—relieved, as if a heavy pot had been lifted from the fire.

“Well; as you have pledged your word to her, give us another, will you, Arthur?”

“What is it?” Arthur asked.

“That you will make no private marriage—that you won’t be taking a trip to Scotland, you understand.”

“That would be a falsehood. Pen never told his mother a falsehood,” Mrs. Pendennis cried.

Pen’s eyes filled with shameful tears. Had not the whole intrigue been a falsehood to that tender creature who would give up all for his sake? He gave his uncle his hand.

“No, sir—on my word of honour, as a gentleman,” he said, “I will never marry without my mother’s consent!” And, giving Helen a bright look of confidence and unchangeable affection, the boy went out into his own study.

“He’s an angel—he’s an angel,” the mother cried, in one of her raptures.

“He comes of a good stock, ma’am,” said the Major—“of a good stock on both sides.” He was greatly pleased with the result of his diplomacy; so much so, that he saluted the tips of Mrs. Pendennis’s glove, and, dropping the curt manly tone he had used with the lad, assumed that particular drawl which always came upon him like a dressing-gown when he felt himself most fine.

“My dear creature,” said he, “I think it certainly as well that I came down; and I flatter myself that last botte was a successful one. I tell you how I came to think of it. Three years ago my kind friend Lady Ferrybridge sent for me in the greatest alarm about her son Gretna, whose affair you remember, and implored me to use my influence with the young gentleman, engaged in an affaire de coeur with a Scotch clergyman’s daughter, Miss MacToddy. I implored, I entreated gentle measures. But Lord Ferrybridge was furious, tried the high hand. Gretna was sulky and silent, and his parents thought they had conquered. But what was the fact, my dear creature? The young people had been married for three months before Lord Ferrybridge knew anything about it. And that is why I extracted the promise from Master Pen.”

“Arthur would never have done so,” Mrs. Pendennis said.

“He hasn’t—that is one comfort,” answered the brother-in-law.

Like a wary man of the world, Major Pendennis did not press Pen farther at the moment. He hoped time would open the boy’s eyes to the absurdity of the scrape. And having found how keen the lad’s point of honour was, he worked upon it kindly after dinner over their wine, discoursing of uprightness and openness, and entreating that communications with the interesting young friend—“Miss Fotheringay,” as the Major politely called Miss Costigan—should be carried on with Mrs. Pendennis’s knowledge, if not her approbation.

“After all, Pen,” the Major said, with a frankness convenient to negotiation, “you must bear in mind you are throwing yourself away. Your mother may submit to your marriage as she would to anything you desire, if you but cry long enough for it; but be sure it can never please her. You take a young woman off the boards of a country theatre and prefer her—such is the case—to one of the finest ladies in England. Your mother will submit, but you can’t suppose she will be happy under it. I have often fancied, entre nous, that my sister had it in her eye to make a marriage between you and that little ward of hers—Flora, Laura—what’s her name? And I always determined to do my small endeavour to prevent any such match. The child has but two thousand pounds. It is only with the utmost economy and care that my sister can provide for the decent maintenance of her house, and for your appearance and education as a gentleman; and I don’t mind owning to you I had other and much higher views for you. With your name and birth, sir—with your talents, which I suppose are respectable—with the friends whom I have the honour to possess, I could have placed you in an excellent position—a remarkable position for a young man of such exceeding small means—and hoped to see you try to restore the honours of our name. Your mother’s softness stopped one prospect, or you might have been a general like our gallant ancestor at Ramillies and Malplaquet. I had another plan: my excellent kind friend Lord Bagwig would, I have little doubt, have attached you to his mission at Pumpernickel, and you might have advanced in diplomacy. But—pardon me—how is a man to serve a young gentleman of eighteen who proposes to marry a lady of thirty, selected from a booth in a fair?—well, not a fair—a barn. That profession at once is closed to you. The public service is closed to you. Society is closed to you. You may get on at the bar, where I am given to understand gentlemen of merit occasionally marry out of their kitchens; but in no other profession. Or you may come and live down here—down here, mon Dieu!—for ever,” said the Major, shrugging, thinking with inexpressible fondness of Pall Mall, “where your mother will receive the Mrs. Arthur that is to be with kindness; where the good people of the county won’t visit you; and where, by Gad, sir, I shall be shy of visiting you myself, for I like to live with gentlemen; where you will have to live with rum-and-water—drinking gentlemen—farmers; and drag through life the young husband of an old woman, who, if she doesn’t quarrel with your mother, will at least cost that lady her position and drag her down into the dubious caste into which you must fall. It is no affair of mine. I am not angry. Your downfall will not hurt me further than that it extinguishes the hopes I had of seeing my family once more taking its place in the world. It is only your mother and yourself that will be ruined; and I pity you both from my soul. Pass the claret: it is some I sent to your poor father; I remember I bought it at poor Lord Levant’s sale. But of course,” added he, smacking the wine, “having engaged yourself, you will do what becomes you as a man of honour, however fatal your promise may be. However, promise us on our side what I set out by entreating you to grant—that there shall be nothing clandestine, that you will pursue your studies, that you will only visit your interesting friend at proper intervals. Do you write to her much?”

Pen blushed, and said—why, yes—he had written.

Major Pendennis came down into the country as conquerors come down into provinces—reluctantly, with the air of a man making history, and with a private conviction that history was making a very poor return.

For consider what he surrendered. London in May: that perfumed season when the town is at its most insolent, when a man’s name may blossom in the Morning Post like a rare hot-house fruit, and his hat be recognised—nay, saluted—in drawing-rooms where the very footmen look as if they have pedigrees. He gave up his newspapers and his mornings; his afternoons, which were a regular campaign from club to club; his confidential visits to certain Great Ladies (confidential, select, and of course strictly whispered); his rides in Rotten Row where a bow from a Duke is as nourishing as a luncheon; his dinners; his stall at the Opera; his brisk raids to Fulham or Richmond on Saturdays and Sundays; his chance of being observed by my Lord Marquis at a great entertainment, and written down afterwards as if it were a public service.

All these delights—these well-seasoned, well-served courses of metropolitan existence—he pushed away from him, with a sigh, and shut himself into a lone little country-house, where the society consisted of a simple widow who did not know how to prize a Court Guide, a greenhorn of a son who did; a mawkish curate; and a little girl of ten years old, who could not be expected to have an opinion about the Peerage at all.

He made the sacrifice; and it was the greater, as nobody, properly speaking, applauded it. His letters still came down franked from town; he exhibited the invitations to Helen with the air of a martyr displaying his wounds. It was beautiful—if you had the taste for such beauty—and tragical to see him refuse one party after another; tragical, at least, to those who could understand the melancholy grandeur of self-denial. Helen did not. Helen smiled at the Major’s awful pathos over the Court Guide, as one smiles at a man who mourns because his soufflé has failed; but young Pen looked with very honest reverence at the great names on the superscriptions, and listened as a hungry boy listens when somebody else’s dinner is described in detail.

For the Major’s memory was a larder of anecdotes, hung round with titles, alliances, scandals, reconciliations, and family feuds, all preserved with the nicest care. He poured them into Pen’s willing ear as they paced the terrace for the Major’s two hours’ constitutional walk, or as they sat together after dinner, the decanter between them, like a third party to the conversation who always agreed.

“My dear boy,” the Major would say, with a mournful earnestness, as if he were recommending prayer, “you cannot begin your genealogical studies too early. I wish to Heaven you would read Debrett every day.”

“Debrett, sir?” Pen asked, delighted to have so manly a lesson.

“Not so much the historical part,” the Major continued—lowering his voice at the word historical, as though it were slightly vulgar—“for between ourselves, the pedigrees are many of them very fabulous; and there are few families that can show such a clear descent as our own. No, no: attend to the alliances. Who is related to whom. I have known a man’s career blasted—blasted, Arthur—by ignorance on this all-important subject.”

And then out came one of those neat little stories of the great world which, like certain sauces, seem harmless until you discover how much fire they contain.

“Why, only last month, at dinner at my Lord Hobanob’s, a young man—young Mr. Suckling—lately received among us—author of a work, I believe—began speaking lightly, in the most audacious manner, of Admiral Bowser’s conduct for ratting to Ministers. Cutting his jokes as if all the world were laughing with him. And who do you suppose sate next and opposite to this young gentleman? Why—why—next to him was Lady Grampound Bowser’s daughter; opposite to him was Lord Grampound Bowser’s son-in-law. Conceive Lady Hobanob’s feelings—Hobanob’s!—and those of every well-bred man as the wretched intru exposed himself. He will never dine again in South Street. I promise you that.”

Pen thrilled. South Street sounded like an enchanted land from which fools are banished.

The Major mourned too, in his way, over the absence of great people from the neighbourhood. Sir Francis Clavering did not come down to live in the Park since his marriage, and so there was no society worth the name—no proper table to be admitted to, no proper table to refuse. Lord Eyrie was not in the country. If Lord Eyrie had been there, the Major would have taken Pen, presented him, and planted him—so to speak—among the Trehawks like a sapling among old trees.

“He has daughters,” the Major said, with that candour by which men sometimes commit the greatest insolences. “Who knows? you might have married Lady Emily or Lady Barbara Trehawk. But all those dreams are over. My poor fellow, you must lie on the bed you have made for yourself.”

Young Pendennis, who was at an age when any bed seems magnificent if it is spoken of as a bed of destiny, listened with serious inclination. In print, these discourses may look like dry bones; but in the Major’s mouth they were living creatures, with eyebrows and waistcoats and coronets. His anecdotes of the great George, the Royal Dukes, statesmen, beauties, fashionable ladies, and the small jests that ruin men for ever, filled young Pen’s soul with longing and wonder. Mrs. Pendennis was sadly bored and perplexed by all this talk of great folks—she, who thought a good roast fowl and quiet gratitude a better thing than the whole Almanack de Gotha; but Pen never found it tedious. It was a new music in the house, a patter of names like a drum, and he marched to it.

We must not pretend that the Major discoursed upon the most elevated subjects, or treated the subjects he chose in the most elevated manner. His morality, such as it was, had the merit of being consistent. It was not, perhaps, a system intended to advance a man’s interest in another world; but it was admirably calculated to forward him in this one. And the Major never doubted for an instant that his views were the only views practicable, and that his conduct was perfectly virtuous and respectable. He was a man of honour—he said so himself—and had his eyes, as he called it, open. He took pity on his young greenhorn of a nephew, and intended to open the boy’s eyes too, without in the least considering whether the operation might be painful.

No man, for example, went more regularly to church, when in the country, than this old bachelor.

“It don’t matter so much in town, Pen,” he said; “for there the women go, and the men are not missed. But when a gentleman is sur ses terres, he must give an example to the country-people. And if I could turn a tune, I even think I should sing. The Duke of Saint David’s, whom I have the honour of knowing, always sings in the country; and, let me tell you, it has a doosed fine effect from the family pew. And you are somebody down here. As long as the Claverings are away you are the first man in the parish: and as good as any. You might represent the town if you played your cards well. Your poor dear father would have done so had he lived; so might you.—Not if you marry a lady, however amiable, whom the country-people won’t meet.—Well, well: it’s a painful subject. Let us change it, my boy.”

But if the Major changed the subject once, he returned to it a score of times a day; and the moral of every discourse was, that Pen was throwing himself away.

Now it does not require much coaxing to make a simple boy believe he is a very fine fellow. Pen drank his uncle’s counsel as eagerly as he drank his uncle’s wine. It began to work in him like strong liquor: he felt warmer, bolder, more certain that he had a destiny which ought not to be marinated in small beer.

And the consequence was, that Captain Costigan’s conversation became by no means pleasant to him; and the idea of that tipsy old father-in-law haunted him like a nightmare that smelt of punch. Pen could not bring himself to associate that man—unshaven, shabby, reeking—with his mother’s clear parlour and gentle hands. Even about Emily—when the pitiless guardian began to question him—Pen faltered in his answers.

“Was she accomplished?” the Major asked.

Pen was obliged to own, no.

“Was she clever?”

Well—she had a very good average intellect; but he could not absolutely say she was clever.

“Come,” said the Major, “let us see some of her letters.”

Pen confessed that he had but those three we have mentioned—trivial invitations or answers; nothing like the eager pages a woman in earnest will send, when her heart boils over into her inkstand.

“She is cautious enough,” the Major said drily. “She is older than you, my poor boy.”

And then he apologised with the utmost frankness and humility; flung himself upon Pen’s good feelings; begged the lad to excuse a fond old uncle who had only his family’s honour in view. For Arthur would flame up whenever Miss Costigan’s honesty was even hinted at, and swore he would never have her name mentioned lightly, and never—never—would part from her.

He repeated these vows to his uncle and friends at home; and, it must be confessed, repeated them with great fervour too to Miss Fotheringay and the amiable family at Chatteris, with whom he still continued to spend some portion of his time.

Miss Emily was alarmed when she heard of the guardian’s arrival, and rightly conceived that the Major came down with hostile intentions towards herself.

“I suppose ye intend to leave me, now your grand relation has come down from town,” she said. “He’ll carry ye off, and you’ll forget your poor Emily, Mr. Arthur!”

Forget her? In her presence; in that of Miss Rouncy the Columbine (Milly’s confidential friend of the company); in the presence of the Captain himself; Pen swore he never could think of any other woman than his beloved Miss Fotheringay. And the Captain, looking up at his foils—hung as a trophy on the wall where Pen and he used to fence—said grimly that he would not advoise any man to meddle rashly with the affections of his darling child; and that he would never believe his gallant young Arthur—whom he treated as his son, whom he called his son—would ever be guilty of conduct so revolting to every idaya of honour and humanity.

He went up and embraced Pen after speaking. He cried, and wiped his eye with one large dirty hand as he clasped Arthur with the other.

Arthur shuddered in that grasp, and thought of his uncle at home.

His father-in-law looked unusually dirty and shabby; the odour of whisky-and-water was more decided even than common. How was he to bring that man and his mother together? He trembled when he remembered he had actually written to Costigan (enclosing a sovereign, the loan of which the worthy gentleman had need), and saying that one day he hoped to sign himself, “your affectionate son, Arthur Pendennis.”

He was glad to get away from Chatteris that day: from Miss Rouncy the confidante; from the old toping father-in-law; from the divine Emily herself. “O, Emily, Emily,” he cried inwardly, as he rattled homewards on Rebecca, “you little know what sacrifices I am making for you!—for you who are always so cold, so cautious, so mistrustful;” and he thought of a character in Pope to whom he had often involuntarily compared her.

Pen never rode over to Chatteris upon that certain errand, but the Major found out on what errand the boy had been. Faithful to his plan, Major Pendennis gave his nephew no let or hindrance; but the constant feeling that the elder’s eye was upon him, the uneasy shame attendant upon that inevitable confession which the evening’s conversation would be sure to elicit in the most natural manner, made Pen go less frequently to sigh away his soul at the feet of his charmer than he had been wont to do before his uncle’s arrival.

There was no use trying to deceive him. No pretext of dining with Smirke, or reading Greek plays with Foker. When Pen returned from his flying visits, he felt everybody knew whence he came; and he sat, looking absurdly guilty, before his mother and guardian—over their books or their game at picquet—like a boy who has been stealing jam and still smells of it.

Once, having walked half a mile to the Fairoaks Inn beyond the Lodge gates, to be in readiness for the Competitor coach (which changed horses there), Pen was saluted by a man on the roof who touched his hat: it was his uncle’s man, Mr. Morgan, going on a message for his master, and “took up at the Lodge,” as he said. Mr. Morgan came back by the Rival too; so Pen had the pleasure of that domestic’s company both ways—an accompaniment, as one may say, to his guilty melody.

Nothing was said at home. The lad seemed to have every decent liberty; and yet he felt himself watched and guarded, and that eyes were upon him even in the presence of his Dulcinea.

In fact, Pen’s suspicions were not unfounded. His guardian had sent forth to gather all possible information regarding the lad and his interesting young friend; and the discreet, ingenious Mr. Morgan—a London confidential valet, whose fidelity could be trusted because it was part of his profession—had been to Chatteris more than once and made inquiry into the past history and present habits of Captain Costigan and his daughter.

He cross-examined the waiters, the ostlers, and all the bar-inmates at the George, with that delicacy which a man uses when he intends to repeat everything afterwards. He got what little they knew of the Captain. The worthy gentleman, it appeared, was not held in very great regard there. The waiters never saw the colour of his money, and were warned not to furnish him with liquor for which some other party was not responsible. He swaggered sadly in the coffee-room; consumed a toothpick with an air as if it were a cigar; looked over the paper; and if any friend asked him to dinner, he stayed.

Morgan heard at the George of Pen’s acquaintance with Mr. Foker, and went over to Baymouth to enter into relations with that gentleman’s man; but the young student was gone to a Coast Regatta, and his servant travelled, of course, in charge of the dressing-case—so that source ran dry, like a tapped bottle.

From the servants of the officers at the barracks, Mr. Morgan learned that the Captain had so frequently and outrageously inebriated himself there that Colonel Swallowtail had forbidden him the mess-room. The indefatigable Morgan then put himself into communication with some of the inferior actors at the theatre and pumped them over cigars and punch; and all agreed that Costigan was poor, shabby, and given to debt and drink.

But—here lay the mischief for the Major’s purposes—not a breath touched Miss Fotheringay’s reputation. Her father’s courage had more than once displayed itself towards persons disposed to treat his daughter with freedom. She never came to the theatre but with her father; and in his most inebriated moments the Captain still kept watch over her. Finally Mr. Morgan, from his own experience, added that he had been to see her act and was uncommon delighted with the performance, besides thinking her a most splendid woman.

Mrs. Creed, the pew-opener, confirmed these statements to Doctor Portman, who examined her personally and threatened her with the terrors of the Church one day after afternoon service. Mrs. Creed had nothing unfavourable to her lodger to divulge.

“She saw nobody; only one or two ladies of the theayter. The Captain did intoxicate himself sometimes, and did not always pay his rent regular; but he did when he had money—or rather Miss Fotheringay did. Since the young gentleman from Clavering had been and took lessons in fencing, one or two more had come from the barracks; Sir Derby Oaks, and his young friend Mr. Foker, which was often together; and which was always driving over from Baymouth in the tandem. But on the occasions of the lessons Miss F. was very seldom present, and generally came downstairs to Mrs. Creed’s own room. And whenever he come, she always have me or one of the children with her. And, Mrs. Creed, marm, says she, if you please, marm, you’ll on no account leave the room when that young gentleman’s here. And many’s the time I’ve seen him a-looking as if he wished I was away, poor young man; and he took to coming in service-time, when I wasn’t at home, of course: but she always had one of the boys up if her Pa wasn’t at home, or old Mr. Bowser with her a teaching of her her lesson, or one of the young ladies of the theayter.”

It was all true. Whatever encouragements might have been given Pen before he avowed his passion, Miss Emily’s prudence was prodigious afterwards; and the poor fellow chafed against her reserve. It maintained his ardour as it excited his anger; he was like a man kept perpetually hungry by the promise of a dinner that is always being covered up and taken away again.

The Major surveyed the state of things with a sigh.

“If it were but a temporary liaison,” the excellent man said, “one could bear it. A young fellow must sow his wild oats, and that sort of thing. But a virtuous attachment is the deuce. It comes of the d——d romantic notions boys get from being brought up by women.”

“Allow me to say, Major,” replied Doctor Portman, with that pious sharpness which is as much a habit as a collar, “that you speak a little too like a man of the world. Nothing can be more desirable for Pen than a virtuous attachment—for a young lady of his own rank and with a corresponding fortune. This present infatuation, of course, I must deplore as sincerely as you do. If I were his guardian, I should command him to give it up.”

“The very means,” cried the Major, “to make him marry to-morrow. We have got time from him—that is all—and we must do our best with that.”

And then, at the end of one of these consultations, the Doctor—who was not, of course, a play-going man, but who could be curious under his conscience—said with hesitation, “I say, Major—suppose—we go and see her?”

The Major laughed. He had been a fortnight at Fairoaks and, strange to say, had not thought of that.

“Well,” he said, “why not? After all, it is not my niece, but Miss Fotheringay the actress; and we have as good a right as any other of the public to see her if we pay our money.”

So upon a day when it was arranged that Pen was to dine at home and pass the evening with his mother, the two elderly gentlemen drove over to Chatteris in the Doctor’s chaise; and there—like a couple of jolly bachelors on an escapade carefully disguised as duty—they dined at the George Inn before proceeding to the play.

Only two other guests were in the room: an officer of the regiment quartered at Chatteris, and a young gentleman whom the Doctor thought he had somewhere seen. They left these two to their meal, however, and hastened to the theatre.

It was Hamlet over again. Shakespeare was Article XL. of stout old Doctor Portman’s creed, to which he made a point of testifying publicly at least once a year. The play was as it had been before; and those who saw Miss Fotheringay perform Ophelia saw precisely the same thing on one night as on another—each gesture in its place like a well-learnt recipe, each sigh measured, each tear ready at the proper moment, as if kept in a little bottle behind the scenes.

Both the elderly gentlemen looked at her with extraordinary interest, thinking how very much young Pen was charmed with her.

“Gad,” said the Major between his teeth, surveying her as she was called forward and swept her curtsies to the scanty audience, “the young rascal has not made a bad choice.”

The Doctor applauded her loudly and loyally. “Upon my word,” he said, “she is a very clever actress; and I must say, Major, she is endowed with very considerable personal attractions.”

“So that young officer thinks in the stage-box,” Major Pendennis answered; and he pointed out to the Doctor’s attention the young dragoon from the George coffee-room, who sat there applauding with immense enthusiasm. She looked extremely sweet upon him too, thought the Major; but that was their way; and he snapped up his natty opera-glass and pocketed it, as if he wished to see no more that night.

Nor did Doctor Portman propose to stay for the after-piece. So they rose and left the theatre: the Doctor returning to Mrs. Portman, who was on a visit at the Deanery; and the Major walking home, full of thought, towards the George, where he had bespoken a bed.

Major Pendennis, having sauntered homeward with the steady courage of a man who has dined well and intends to make other people indigested, reached the George at last. The inn was settling into its nightly domestic hush: the tap-room’s last laugh dying like a cork popped and forgotten, the stairboards giving their accustomed old cough under a boot, the wind making a thin flute in the keyhole—country music, at least, and not the iron bawling of London streets.

Mr. Morgan, his valet—faithful as a ladle, and just as apt to dip into any pot—stood waiting at the door with that air of respectful omniscience which says, “I know more than you, sir, and I shall tell you as though you had guessed it yourself.”

As the Major was about to take his candle and retire, Morgan stopped him with a little cough that might have been learned in a drawing-room.

“I think, sir, if you would step into the coffee-room, there’s a young gentleman there as you would like to see.”

“What, is Mr. Arthur here?” cried the Major, with the sudden heat of a man who fears he shall find love served up again at midnight.

“No, sir—but his great friend, Mr. Foker, sir. Lady Hagnes Foker’s son, sir. He’s been asleep in the coffee-room since he took his dinner, and has just rung for his coffee, sir. And I think, p’raps, you might like to git into conversation with him,” Morgan added, opening the door as neatly as one uncovers a dish, confident the aroma will do the rest.

Major Pendennis entered; and there indeed sat Mr. Harry Foker, the only occupant of the apartment, placed at a table which looked as though a small siege had been raised and provision-trains captured. Empty decanters stood like slain glass soldiers; crumbs and nut-shells and peelings lay about like the relics of a dessert that had died honourably. The coffee—when it came—sent up its homely brown breath, that bitter, comforting steam which can make even a scandal smell respectable.

Foker was rubbing his eyes, his cheeks still wearing that faint, prosperous flush which wine paints upon youth as a cook paints glaze upon a ham. He had meant, it seemed, to go to the play; but a copious meal had conquered tragedy and comedy alike. He had thrown up his legs on the bench, and napped like a man practising for Parliament.

The Major was turning over, as carefully as a maître d’hôtel considers his sauces, the best mode of address; but Mr. Foker, who was always affable and ready to press his acquaintance as a waiter presses hot rolls, spared him the trouble.

“Like to look at the evening paper, sir?” said Foker, taking up the Globe and offering it with the easy sociability of a gentleman who would offer you his last macaroon if it gave him an excuse to talk.

“I am very much obliged to you,” said the Major, bowing with gratitude as though the paper were a coronet. “If I don’t mistake the family likeness, I have the pleasure of speaking to Mr. Henry Foker—Lady Agnes Foker’s son. I have the happiness to name her ladyship among my acquaintances—and you bear, sir, a Rosherville face.”

“Hullo! I beg your pardon,” said Mr. Foker, who had been going to say, “I took you for a commercial gent,” but swallowed that phrase as a man swallows a fish-bone when a lady looks at him. “To whom have I the pleasure of speaking?”

“To a relative of a friend and schoolfellow of yours—Arthur Pendennis, my nephew, who has often spoken to me of you in terms of great regard. I am Major Pendennis, of whom you may have heard him speak. May I take my soda-water at your table? I have had the pleasure of sitting at your grandfather’s.”

“Sir, you do me proud,” said Foker, moving with alacrity to make room, as though the table were an omnibus and the Major a fare. “And so you are Arthur Pendennis’s uncle, are you?”

“And guardian,” added the Major, dropping that word as one drops a bay-leaf into broth—quietly, but for effect.

“He’s as good a fellow as ever stepped, sir,” said Foker, with the generous warmth of youth, and perhaps with the additional warmth of claret still glowing in him.

“I am glad you think so.”

“And clever, too—I was always a stupid chap, I was—but you see, sir, I know ’em when they are clever, and like ’em of that sort.”

“You show your taste and your modesty, too,” said the Major, smiling as suavely as if he were tasting a well-made sauce. “I have heard Arthur repeatedly speak of you, and he said your talents were very good.”

“I’m not good at the books,” said Mr. Foker, wagging his head—“never could manage that—Pendennis could—he used to do half the chaps’ verses—and yet”—here the candid young gentleman broke out, like a bottle that has been shaken—“you are his guardian; and I hope you will pardon me for saying that I think he’s what we call flat.”

The Major’s heart gave a pleased little leap. A young man fresh from dinner is a natural historian of other people’s secrets.

“And how is Arthur a flat?” asked the Major, with a smile that invited confidence as a warm kitchen invites loitering.

“You know,” answered Foker, winking—he would have winked at the Duke of Wellington with just as little scruple, being in that frank, fearless, foggy state which two bottles of wine sometimes confer—“you know Arthur’s a flat,—about women I mean.”

“He is not the first of us, my dear Mr. Harry,” replied the Major, with a fine air of veteran indulgence. “I have heard something of this—but pray tell me more.”

“Why, sir, you see—it’s partly my fault. He went to the play one night—for you see I’m down here readin’ for my little go during the Long, only I come over from Baymouth pretty often in my drag—well, sir, we went to the play, and Pen was struck all of a heap with Miss Fotheringay—Costigan her real name is—an uncommon fine gal she is too; and the next morning I introduced him to the General, as we call her father—a regular old scamp and such a boy for the whisky-and-water!—and he’s gone on being intimate there. And he’s fallen in love with her—and I’m blessed if he hasn’t proposed to her,” cried Foker, slapping the table until the remnants of dessert jingled like little bells, as if the very raisins were laughing.

“What! you know it too?” asked the Major.

“Know it! don’t I? and many more too. We were talking about it at mess, yesterday, and chaffing Derby Oaks—until he was as mad as a hatter. Know Sir Derby Oaks? We dined together, and he went to the play: we were standing at the door smoking, I remember, when you passed in to dinner.”

“I remember Sir Thomas Oaks, his father, before he was a Baronet or a Knight; he lived in Cavendish-square, and was physician to Queen Charlotte,” said the Major, who could season any modern dish with an antique reference, like a cook dusting an old spice over new meat.

“The young one is making the money spin, I can tell you,” said Mr. Foker.

“And is Sir Derby Oaks,” asked the Major, very softly and very eagerly, “another soupirant?”

“Another what?”

“Another admirer of Miss Fotheringay?”

“Lord bless you! we call him Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, and Pen Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. But mind you, nothing wrong! No, no! Miss F. is a deal too wide-awake for that, Major Pendennis. She plays one off against the other. What you call two strings to her bow.”

“I think you seem tolerably wide-awake, too, Mr. Foker,” said the Major, laughing.

“Pretty well, thank you, sir—how are you?” replied Foker, imperturbable, as if their talk were merely a polite exchange about the weather and the roast. “I’m not clever, p’raps: but I am rather downy; and partial friends say I know what’s o’clock tolerably well. Can I tell you the time of day in any way?”

“Upon my word,” said the Major, delighted—delighted as a man is when he finds a sharp knife for a difficult carving—“I think you may be of very great service to me. You are a young man of the world, and with such one likes to deal. And as such I need not inform you that our family is by no means delighted at this absurd intrigue in which Arthur is engaged.”

“I should rather think not,” said Mr. Foker. “Connexion not eligible. Too much beer drunk on the premises. No Irish need apply. That I take to be your meaning.”

The Major declared it was exactly his meaning—though he did not quite know what half those phrases might be in the original tongue; but he caught their flavour, as one catches the flavour of a foreign dish by the look of its grease. He set himself, with patient curiosity, to question his new acquaintance regarding the Costigan household; and Mr. Foker, who had no more notion of locking his tongue than of corking his thoughts, gave him particulars enough to stock a pantry.

To do him justice, the young man spoke favourably of the Costigans’ moral character.

“You see,” said he, “I think the General is fond of the jovial bowl, and if I wanted to be very certain of my money, it isn’t in his pocket I’d invest it—but he has always kept a watchful eye on his daughter, and neither he nor she will stand anything but what’s honourable. Pen’s attentions to her are talked about in the whole Company, and I hear all about them from a young lady who used to be very intimate with her, and with whose family I sometimes take tea in a friendly way. Miss Rouncy says, Sir Derby Oaks has been hanging about Miss Fotheringay ever since his regiment has been down here; but Pen has come in and cut him out lately, which has made the Baronet so mad, that he has been very near on the point of proposing too. Wish he would; and you’d see which of the two Miss Fotheringay would jump at.”

“I thought as much,” said the Major, tasting this intelligence as if it were a particularly promising relish. “You give me a great deal of pleasure, Mr. Foker. I wish I could have seen you before.”

“Didn’t like to put in my oar,” replied the other. “Don’t speak till I’m asked, when, if there’s no objections, I speak pretty freely. Heard your man had been hankering about my servant—didn’t know myself what was going on until Miss Fotheringay and Miss Rouncy had the row about the ostrich feathers, when Miss R. told me everything.”

“Miss Rouncy, I gather, was the confidante of the other.”

“Confidant? I believe you. Why, she’s twice as clever a girl as Fotheringay, and literary and that, while Miss Foth can’t do much more than read.”

“She can write,” said the Major, remembering, with a little internal rattle like a spoon tapping a glass, the letter he had surprised in his nephew’s breast-pocket.

Foker gave a sardonic “He, he!”

“Rouncy writes her letters,” said he; “every one of ’em; and since they’ve quarrelled, she don’t know how the deuce to get on. Miss Rouncy is an uncommon pretty hand, whereas the old one makes dreadful work of the writing and spelling when Bows ain’t by. Rouncy’s been settin’ her copies lately—she writes a beautiful hand, Rouncy does.”

“I suppose you know it pretty well,” said the Major archly.

Mr. Foker winked again, as if winks were the punctuation of his conversation.

“I would give a great deal to have a specimen of her hand-writing,” continued Major Pendennis. “I dare say you could give me one.”

“No, no, that would be too bad,” replied Foker. “Perhaps I oughtn’t to have said as much as I have. Miss F.’s writin’ ain’t so very bad, I dare say; only she got Miss R. to write the first letter, and has gone on ever since. But you mark my word, that till they are friends again the letters will stop.”

“I hope they will never be reconciled,” said the Major, with the sincerity of a man who hopes the cook will never make up with the butcher. “And I can’t tell you how delighted I am to have had the good fortune of making your acquaintance. You must feel, my dear sir, as a man of the world, how fatal to my nephew’s prospects in life is this step which he contemplates, and how eager we all must be to free him from this absurd engagement.”

“He has come out uncommon strong,” said Mr. Foker. “I have seen his verses; Rouncy copied ’em. And I said to myself when I saw ’em, ‘Catch me writin’ verses to a woman,—that’s all.’”

“He has made a fool of himself, as many a good fellow has before him,” said the Major, setting his glass down as carefully as if it were a piece of evidence. “How can we make him see his folly, and cure it? I am sure you will give us what aid you can in extricating a generous young man from such a pair of schemers as this father and daughter seem to be. Love on the lady’s side is out of the question.”

“Love, indeed!” cried Foker. “If Pen hadn’t two thousand a year when he came of age——”

“If Pen hadn’t what?” shouted the Major, starting as if a hot drop of coffee had splashed him.

“Two thousand a year: hasn’t he got two thousand a year?—the General says he has.”

“My dear friend,” cried the Major—shrieked, indeed, with an eagerness which he commonly kept corked down—“thank you! thank you! I begin to see now.—Two thousand a year! Why, his mother has but five hundred a year in the world.—She is likely to live to eighty, and Arthur has not a shilling but what she can allow him.”

“What! he ain’t rich then?” asked Foker, his candour sobering a little, as men sober when the joint they thought was beef proves to be mutton.

“Upon my honour he has no more than what I say.”

“And you ain’t going to leave him anything?”

The Major, who had sunk every shilling he could scrape into an annuity, and was going to leave his nephew nothing but his example and perhaps his shirts, did not choose to put that dish upon the table.

“How much do you think a Major on half-pay can save?” he asked, with a sigh that sounded like a purse-string drawn tight.

“If these people have been looking at him as a fortune,” he continued, “they are utterly mistaken—and—and you have made me the happiest man in the world.”

“Sir to you,” said Mr. Foker, politely, rising; and when they parted for the night they shook hands with the greatest cordiality. The younger gentleman promised not to leave Chatteris without a further conversation in the morning.

So the Major went upstairs to his room with his mind bustling like a kitchen at noon; and Mr. Foker stood and smoked his cigar against the door-pillars of the George, sending out little clouds that melted into the night air as softly as secrets into gossip.

And Pen, very likely, ten miles off, lay in bed kissing a letter from his Emily—pressing paper to his lips as devoutly as a hungry man presses his face to the steam of a newly lifted pie.

In the morning, before Mr. Foker drove off in his drag, the insinuating Major had actually got a letter of Miss Rouncy’s in his own pocket-book. Let it be a lesson to women how they write; for ink, though it seems as innocent as gravy, will leave stains that no hot water of denial can wash out.

With this prize secured, Major Pendennis, in very high spirits, went to call upon Doctor Portman at the Deanery, and related his discoveries with the relish of a man carving up a scandal before a friend who likes the breast. In the Dean’s oak breakfast-parlour they sat in confidential talk, with the solid old wood about them smelling faintly of age, toast, and respectability; and they could look across the lawn and see Captain Costigan’s window, at which poor Pen had been only too visible some three weeks since—like an imprudent moth against a lighted pane.

The Doctor was vehement against Mrs. Creed, the landlady, for her duplicity in concealing Sir Derby Oaks’s constant visits to her lodgers, and threatened to excommunicate her out of the Cathedral, as though ecclesiastical thunder could frighten a woman who made money by shutting doors and opening mouths. But the wary Major thought all things were for the best; and having taken counsel with himself overnight, felt himself strong enough to face Captain Costigan.

“I’m going to fight the dragon,” he said, laughing, to Doctor Portman.

“And I shrive you, sir, and bid good fortune go with you,” answered the Doctor.

Perhaps he and Mrs. Portman and Miss Myra, as they sat with their friend the Dean’s lady in her drawing-room, looked up more than once at the enemy’s window to see if any signs of combat were visible—some flutter of curtain, some retreating shadow, some domestic omen. The house itself had its own soundscape: a distant clink of a spoon, the rustle of a gown, the mild ticking of a clock that seemed to say, in the language of old houses, that time remembers even when people forget.

The Major walked round, found Mrs. Creed’s little door as directed, passed it, and began to ascend to Captain Costigan’s apartment. Before he reached the landing, he heard stamping of feet and a great shouting of “Ha, ha!” within—noise of a very different kind from the Deanery’s measured hush; more like the brutal cheer of a fairground than the clean ring of a chapel bell.

“It’s Sir Derby Oaks taking his fencing lesson,” said the child who piloted Major Pendennis. “He takes it Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays.”

So there was the regimen, even in gallantry: days assigned like joints on a menu.

The Major knocked; and at length the door opened, and a tall gentleman came forth with a foil and mask in one hand and a fencing glove on the other—equipped for honour, and looking as if he might be about to carve reputation into slices.

Major Pendennis made him a deferential bow.

“I believe I have the honour of speaking to Captain Costigan—My name is Major Pendennis.”

The Captain brought his weapon up to the salute, and cried, in his rich brogue, as hearty as a dram poured without measure, “Major, the honer is moine; I’m deloighted to see ye.”

Major Pendennis and Captain Costigan had both smelt powder in their time, and neither man’s nerves were likely to be undone by the mere sight of an unexpected enemy. The rest of the company, however—collected in Cos’s sitting-room like ingredients that hadn’t yet agreed to become a dish—were plainly put out when Pen’s uncle appeared in the doorway as if he’d been served up without warning.

Miss Fotheringay’s steady Irish blood ran a shade quicker; her cheek warmed to a good, wholesome flush, the kind you see rise when a hearth is newly stoked or when a young woman has climbed a stair too fast and pretends she hasn’t. Sir Derby Oaks, in the act of looking handsome, looked chiefly savage: he cast her a scowl that might have curdled milk at twenty paces.

In the window-seat, the little crooked old music-copyist—who had been trying to set down theatre airs until the stamping and lunging of the fencing lesson made the ink tremble on the paper—popped up his head like a startled wren. The room, small and low, had that particular lodging-house atmosphere of stale coal-smoke, boot-leather, cheap pomatum, and the faint ghost of yesterday’s onions. Into this domestic vapour came Major Pendennis, boots gleaming as if they’d been glazed with black treacle, distributing bows with the grace of a man ladling sauce: to each person a measured portion, no waste, no stinginess.

“Me daughter—me friend, Mr. Bows—me gallant young pupil and friend, I may call ’um, Sir Derby Oaks,” cried Costigan, sweeping his hand as if presenting courses at table. “In one moment, Meejor, I’m your humble servant,” and he darted into his little sleeping closet.

What happened there was as brisk as the whisking of eggs. With an ancient hair-brush—heroic relic of campaigns and pawnbrokers—he gave his lank hair a twist; tore off an old stock and replaced it with a new one stitched by Emily’s own fingers; clapped on a clean collar; and assumed the new coat ordered for the benefit night, as though by putting it on he also put on respectability. Sir Derby followed him into the same cupboard of a room and presently emerged cased in his tight shell-jacket, which made the large young man look as if he’d been packed for travel and nailed down.

Meanwhile, Miss Fotheringay and the Major made their first passes of conversation—weather, the inevitable seasoning—and had barely finished exchanging those polite, tasteless wafers before Costigan reappeared in his “Shoot,” as he called his new attire, radiating the satisfaction of a man who has found a clean napkin.

“I needn’t apologoise to ye, Meejor,” he said, rich as port, “for receiving ye in me shirt-sleeves.”

“An old soldier can’t be better employed than in teaching a young one the use of his sword,” the Major replied, as gallant as if the room had been a drawing-room and the foils silver. “I remember in old times hearing that you could use yours pretty well, Captain Costigan.”

“What, ye’ve heard of Jack Costigan, Major,” cried the Captain, swelling.

The Major said—very civilly, very firmly—that he perfectly recollected meeting Mr. Costigan and hearing him sing at Sir Richard Strachan’s table at Walcheren. Mr. Bows, who knew exactly which songs were sung at which tables when because he’d been paid to copy them, stared as if someone had claimed to remember a dinner they’d never attended. But the Major, never minding the puzzled look, turned his attention to the most important dish on the board.

“It is to Miss Fotheringay that I came to pay my respects to-day,” he said, and gave her a bow so finished it might have been polished like his boots.

He went on, with a seasoned tongue, to praise her performance: how his nephew raved; how nephews were boys and given to extravagant seasoning; how he himself, being older and less easily intoxicated, had wanted to judge. He declared himself delighted and astonished; he compared her to Siddons and O’Neill and Jordan with the easy generosity of a man handing out compliments like sugared almonds at a christening.

“Faith, I always said so,” Costigan put in, winking at his daughter. “Major, take a chair.”

Milly rose, lifted an unripped satin garment—some theatrical finery that had been draped over the only vacant seat like a sauce-cloth over a pot—and offered the chair with one of her finest curtseys.

“And your manner reminded me of Mars,” the Major continued, enjoying himself.

“There was two Mahers in Crow Street,” Miss Emily said briskly, proud of knowing a fact. “Fanny was well enough, but Biddy was no great things.”

“Sure, the Major means the god of war, Milly, my dear,” said her father, rescuing the compliment from the pit it was falling into.

“It is not that Mars I meant,” the Major replied, smiling, and sent the smile full at Sir Derby Oaks, who had re-entered like a sulky pudding forced back to table. Miss Fotheringay did not understand the words; Sir Derby likely understood even less, and in any case received them with stiffness, his brow knitted as if every syllable were an insult to his digestion.

Major Pendennis, who had lived long enough to relish the sour note in a room’s music, was not at all put out by Sir Derby’s ill-humour. It delighted him. A rival, then, was simmering in the same pot. He hoped—devoutly—that the rival would bubble up and boil over, and perhaps carry the whole foolish stew off the fire.

“I fear I interrupted your fencing lesson; but my stay in Chatteris is very short,” he said, “and I was anxious to make myself known to my old fellow-campaigner Captain Costigan, and to see a lady nearer who had charmed me so much from the stage.”

He spoke of last night’s theatre: a reverend friend who went home in raptures with Ophelia; Sir Derby’s bouquet; how he himself would have brought flowers had he known. Were not those the very flowers in a glass of water on the mantelpiece?

“I am very fond of flowers,” said Miss Fotheringay, with a languishing look at Sir Derby.

Sir Derby responded by looking as if flowers were a personal affront.

“Sweets to the sweet—isn’t that the expression of the play?” asked the Major, bent on amiability.

“’Pon my life, I don’t know,” Sir Derby answered. “Very likely it is. I ain’t much of a literary man.”

The Major widened his eyes—politely astonished. “You don’t inherit your father’s love of letters, then, Sir Derby? He was a remarkably fine scholar, and I had the honour of knowing him very well.”

“Indeed,” said Sir Derby, with a wag of his head which conveyed that learning was a family eccentricity he was glad to have avoided.

“He saved my life,” the Major continued.

“Did he now?” Miss Fotheringay cried, rolling her eyes first at the Major with surprise and then at Sir Derby with gratitude—an expression like a warmed-up compliment, offered again. Sir Derby, however, appeared less grateful than annoyed, as if the notion of his apothecary father’s having saved an officer’s life were an impertinent advertisement.

“My father, I believe, was a very good doctor,” he said. “I’m not in that line myself. I wish you good morning, sir. I’ve got an appointment—Cos, bye-bye—Miss Fotheringay, good morning.”

And out he went, stiff as a carving-knife, down the creaking stairs, his sabre clattering in the passage like a pan-lid in a scullery. Little Tom Creed, playing in the corridor, yelped as the Baronet kicked his peg-top—sent it spinning into the street with an oath, adding to the town’s noise as though Chatteris weren’t already plagued enough by horses, wheels, and men who thought loudness was a proof of breeding.

The Major didn’t smile—at least not visibly. His attention, in those moments, was very much like a skilled cook’s: absorbed in the state of the flame rather than the theatrics of the diners.

“Monstrous handsome young man that,” he remarked. “As fine a looking soldier as ever I saw.”

“A credit to the army and to human nature in general,” Costigan agreed, with the solemnity of a man praising a roast. “A young man of refoined manners, polite affabilitee, and princely fortune. His table is sumptuous: he’s adawr’d in the regiment: and he rides sixteen stone.”

“A perfect champion,” said the Major, laughing. “I have no doubt all the ladies admire him.”

“He’s very well, in spite of his weight, now he’s young,” said Milly, with the calm judgment of someone assessing a joint of meat, “but he’s no conversation.”

“He’s best on horseback,” Mr. Bows offered; and Milly, eager to prove her knowledge, replied that Sir Derby had ridden third in the steeple-chase on his horse Tareaways. The Major, listening to this dullest of menus delivered with confidence, began to comprehend that the young lady who could act tragedy so grandly could also talk like an empty pot.

Costigan, with the hospitality of a man who believes good feeling must be watered, pressed refreshment. The Major, who could no more have been hungry than a man after a Lord Mayor’s dinner, declared he should like a biscuit and a glass of wine above all things, as he felt quite faint from long fasting. He knew—like a food historian who understands the old laws of the hearth—that accepting small kindnesses makes the giver kinder still: a shared cup is a softening of the tongue.

“Some of the old Madara, Milly, love,” Costigan said, winking.

Milly understood at once with that domestic intelligence which often outruns her theatrical one. She slipped out, down the stair, and softly summoned her small emissary, Master Tommy Creed. Into his hand she put money and instructions: a pint of Madeira at the Grapes, and sixpennyworth of sorted biscuits at the baker’s, and hurry back—two biscuits for himself if he ran like a hare.

While Tommy was off, the house below filled with a different kind of murmur—Mrs. Creed’s talk, the scrape of crockery, the soft thud of feet, the little acoustic ecology of a lodging-house: noises that can soothe or fret a mind as much as any music. Milly sat with Mrs. Creed and told her, in confidence and excitement, that Mr. Arthur Pendennis’s uncle—the Major—was upstairs; such a nice, soft-spoken old gentleman, butter wouldn’t melt in his mouth; and how Sir Derby had stalked out in jealous rage. Milly, thinking of two men at once as one thinks of two sauces that cannot be poured into the same dish without curdling, wondered what must be done to pacify both.

Upstairs, Costigan watched the door with pride. “She keeps the keys of the cellar, Major,” he said, as if this were an office of state.

“Upon my word you have a very beautiful butler,” the Major answered, gallantly. “And I don’t wonder at the young fellows raving about her. When we were of their age, Captain Costigan, I think plainer women would have done our business.”

“Faith, and ye may say that,” said Costigan. “Ask me friend Bob Bows here whether Miss Fotheringay’s moind is not even shuparior to her person, and whether she does not possess a cultiveated intellect, a refoined understanding, and an emiable disposition?”

“O of course,” said Bows, drily—the tone of a man who has copied too many love-songs to believe in any of them.

Milly returned, cheeks bright from the cellar air and the stair’s exertion, and Mr. Bows, catching her eye, chose the moment to declare it was time for rehearsal, that she’d be fined if late. His look said plainly: leave the old men to their business; do not stand between them and their knives.
