“Must you go?” the Major asked, and pressed her hand at the door with a paternal warmth that nevertheless had the unmistakable firmness of purpose in it, like a cook testing a joint and finding it ready.

Miss Fotheringay curtseyed; Bows hobbled away with his papers. The door closed. The room’s soundscape changed at once—less rustle, more silence; and in that silence the men’s real talk began to simmer.

“Now for it,” thought Major Pendennis.

Costigan, profiting instantaneously by his daughter’s absence, drank up what remained of the Madeira with the eager speed of a man afraid it might be taken from him. His hand shook slightly as he poured, as if the bottle were a promise and he meant to drain it before it vanished.

The Major went to the table and drained his own glass with a hearty smack. He made public-house Cape taste, by sheer performance, like Lord Steyne’s private bin.

“Capital Madeira, Captain Costigan,” he said. “Where do you get it? I drink the health of that charming creature in a bumper. Faith, Captain, I don’t wonder that the men are wild about her. I never saw such eyes in my life, or such a grand manner. I am sure she is as intellectual as she is beautiful; and I have no doubt she’s as good as she is clever.”

“A good girl, sir,—a good girl, sir,” Costigan cried, delighted. “And I pledge a toast to her with all my heart. Shall I send to the—to the cellar for another pint? It’s handy by. No? Well, indeed sir, ye may say she is a good girl, and the pride and glory of her father—honest old Jack Costigan. The man who gets her will have a jew’l to a wife, sir; and I drink his health, sir, and ye know who I mean, Major.”

“I am not surprised at young or old falling in love with her,” said the Major, “and frankly must tell you, that though I was very angry with my poor nephew Arthur, when I heard of the boy’s passion—now I have seen the lady I can pardon him any extent of it. By George, I should like to enter for the race myself, if I weren’t an old fellow and a poor one.”

“And no better man, Major, I’m sure,” Costigan burst out, transported. Tears gathered in his bloodshot eyes—those honest, drink-bright eyes—like moisture on a glass in a warm room. “Your friendship, sir, delights me. Your admiration for my girl brings tears to me eyes—tears, sir—manlee tears—and when she leaves me humble home for your own more splendid mansion, I hope she’ll keep a place for her poor old father, poor old Jack Costigan.”

“Your sentiments do you honour,” the Major said. “But, Captain Costigan, I can’t help smiling at one thing you have just said.”

“And what’s that, sir?” asked Costigan, still mounted on his high horse of emotion.

“You were speaking about our splendid mansion—my sister’s house, I mean.”

“I mane the park and mansion of Arthur Pendennis, Esquire, of Fairoaks Park,” Costigan cried, stiffening, “whom I hope to see a Mimber of Parliament for his native town of Clavering, when he is of ege to take that responsible stetion.”

The Major smiled again, recognising his own earlier talk—his own seasoning—coming back to him as brag. So the boy had been boasting here, had he? Or had the father been cooking castles out of rumour?

“Fairoaks Park, my dear sir,” said Major Pendennis. “Do you know our history? We are of excessively ancient family certainly, but I began life with scarce enough money to purchase my commission, and my eldest brother was a country apothecary: who made every shilling he died possessed of out of his pestle and mortar.”

“I have consented to waive that objection, sir,” Costigan replied, lofty, “in consideration of the known respectability of your family.”

The Major’s inward thought was unprintable; outwardly he smiled and bowed, as if the insult were merely an ill-chosen spice.

“The Costigans, too, have met with misfortunes; and our house of Castle Costigan is by no manes what it was. I have known very honest men apothecaries, sir, and there’s some in Dublin that has had the honour of dining at the Lord Leftenant’s teeble.”

“You are very kind to give us the benefit of your charity,” the Major said. “But permit me to say that is not the question. You spoke just now of my little nephew as heir of Fairoaks Park and I don’t know what besides.”

“Funded property, I’ve no doubt, Meejor, and something handsome eventually from yourself.”

“My good sir, I tell you the boy is the son of a country apothecary,” cried Major Pendennis, the temper beginning to rise like a pot neglected, “and that when he comes of age he won’t have a shilling.”

“Pooh, Major, you’re laughing at me,” said Costigan. “Me young friend, I make no doubt, is heir to two thousand pounds a year.”

“Two thousand fiddlesticks!—Has the boy been humbugging you? Upon my word and honour, as a gentleman and an executor to my brother’s will too, he left little more than five hundred a year behind him.”

“And with aconomy, a handsome sum of money too, sir,” Costigan answered, undaunted. “Faith, I’ve known a man drink his clar’t, and drive his coach-and-four on five hundred a year and strict aconomy, in Ireland, sir. We’ll manage on it, sir—trust Jack Costigan for that.”

“My dear Captain Costigan—I give you my word that my brother did not leave a shilling to his son Arthur.”

Then the Captain’s face changed as if the last sweetness had been burned. The Madeira, the praise, the imagined mansion—all turned suddenly bitter on his tongue.

“Are ye joking with me, Meejor Pendennis?” he cried. “Are ye thrifling with the feelings of a father and a gentleman?”

“I am telling you the honest truth,” said the Major. “Every shilling my brother had, he left to his widow: with a partial reversion, it is true, to the boy. But she is a young woman, and may marry if he offends her—or she may outlive him, for she comes of an uncommonly long-lived family. And I ask you, as a gentleman and a man of the world, what allowance can my sister, Mrs. Pendennis, make to her son out of five hundred a year— which is all her fortune,—that shall enable him to maintain himself and your daughter in the rank befitting such an accomplished young lady?”

The Captain’s indignation blew up like a sudden draught through a kitchen-door.

“Am I to understand, sir, that the young gentleman, your nephew, and whom I have fosthered and cherished as the son of me bosom, is an imposther who has been thrifling with the affections of me beloved child?” he shouted. “Have you yourself been working upon the feelings of the young man’s susceptible nature to injuice him to break off an engagement, and with it me adored Emily’s heart? Have a care, sir, how you thrifle with the honour of John Costigan. If I thought any mortal man meant to do so, be heavens I’d have his blood, sir—were he old or young.”

“Mr. Costigan!” the Major cried.

“Mr. Costigan can protect his own and his daughter’s honour, and will, sir,” Costigan thundered. He pointed to a chest of drawers, as if it were a larder full of evidence. “Look at that chest of dthrawers, it contains heaps of letthers that that viper has addressed to that innocent child. There’s promises there, sir, enough to fill a bandbox with; and when I have dragged the scoundthrel before the Courts of Law, and shown up his perjury and his dishonour, I have another remedy in yondther mahogany case, sir, which shall set me right, sir, with any individual—ye mark me words, Major Pendennis—with any individual who has counselled your nephew to insult a soldier and a gentleman.”

“I am to understand then,” said the Major, perfectly cool, “that you threaten in the first place to publish the letters of a boy of eighteen to a woman of eight-and-twenty: and afterwards to do me the honour of calling me out.”

“You have described my intentions with perfect accuracy, Meejor Pendennis,” Costigan answered, dragging his ragged whiskers over his chin, as though smoothing them could smooth his fury.

“Well, well; these shall be the subjects of future arrangements,” the Major replied, as calmly as if discussing tomorrow’s dinner. “But before we come to powder and ball, my good sir,—do have the kindness to think with yourself in what earthly way I have injured you? I have told you that my nephew is dependent upon his mother, who has scarcely more than five hundred a year.”

“I have my own opinion of the correctness of that assertion,” Costigan said, with a troubled flicker behind the bravado—like a man who suddenly hears, under the room’s words, another sound: the low, ominous hum of reality.

“Will you go to my sister’s lawyers, Messrs. Tatham here, and satisfy yourself?”

“I decline to meet those gentlemen,” Costigan said, disturbed now in earnest, as if lawyers were a louder, uglier machinery than any sabre-clatter. “If it be as you say, I have been athrociously deceived by some one, and on that person I’ll be revenged.”

“Is it my nephew?” cried the Major, starting up and putting on his hat. “Did he ever tell you that his property was two thousand a year? If he did, I’m mistaken in the boy. To tell lies has not been a habit in our family, Mr. Costigan, and I don’t think my brother’s son has learned it as yet. Try and consider whether you have not deceived yourself; or adopted extravagant reports from hearsay.

“As for me, sir, you are at liberty to understand that I am not afraid of all the Costigans in Ireland, and know quite well how to defend myself against any threats from any quarter. I come here as the boy’s guardian to protest against a marriage, most absurd and unequal, that cannot but bring poverty and misery with it: and in preventing it I conceive I am quite as much your daughter’s friend (who I have no doubt is an honourable young lady) as the friend of my own family: and prevent the marriage I will, sir, by every means in my power. There, I have said my say, sir.”

“But I have not said mine, Major Pendennis—and ye shall hear more from me,” Costigan answered, with a severity that tried to be magnificent though it wobbled on drink and wounded pride.

“’Sdeath, sir, what do you mean?” the Major asked, turning on the threshold, meeting him full in the face.

“Ye said, in the coorse of conversation, that ye were at the George Hotel, I think,” Costigan replied, stately as a man serving a challenge on a salver. “A friend shall wait upon ye there before ye leave town, sir.”

“Let him make haste, Mr. Costigan,” cried the Major, rage finally cracking through his polish. “I wish you a good morning, sir.”

And Captain Costigan, standing high on the landing as if it were a battlement, bowed a magnificent bow of defiance over the stairwell, while the Major went down into the noisy street below—where tops spun, sabres clattered, and men made threats in the common language of pride, which always sounds grand in the mouth and always tastes, afterward, like ashes.

Early in the town’s memory—back when the Magpie Hotel’s parlour still smelled of spilled porter, damp greatcoats, and that indefinable perfume which rises from a table where men have argued themselves thirsty—there was Mr. Garbetts, principal tragedian, a large-limbed performer with a voice that could frighten pigeons off a roof and legs that the whole company admired as if they were a public monument. He and Captain Costigan were intimate in the particular way two men become intimate when they have, between them, a generous assortment of bills coming due, and only one respectable signature each left to lend.

Garbetts, to do him justice, was jovial, athletic, and capable of snapping a poker across his arm to amuse the room—an accomplishment which, like juggling knives, is valued far more highly by those who watch than by those who keep pokers in their households. He did not often visit the Costigans’ lodging; Miss Fotheringay disliked him, and Mrs. Garbetts disliked Miss Fotheringay, and the truth of that triangle was old gossip: Garbetts had once paid his court to Emily and been refused, before he offered his hand to Mrs. G. The theatre forgets nothing, except its lines.

Still, when Arthur Pendennis and Mr. Bows had scarcely got down the stairs, and the Captain’s injured honour began to boil like a pot set too close to the fire, it was to Garbetts that Costigan flew, as men do, not for wisdom, but for noise and muscle.

“Run, Tommy,” cried the Captain to the small errand-boy, “and fetch Mr. Garbetts from his lodgings over the tripe-shop—ye know—and tell ’em to send two glasses of whisky-and-water, hot, from the Grapes.”

The mention of the tripe-shop is not idle. All that lane had its own domestic mythology of smells: the pale, vinegary steam of boiled offal; the sharp tang of pickled onions; the sweet, dirty breath of wet straw from the costermonger’s cart. Even the street had a soundtrack: knives tapping on boards, women calling prices, cart-wheels grumbling in ruts. In that honest market-noise there was more health than in any salon’s hush; but Captain Costigan, at this moment, preferred the particular music of whisky being poured into a glass.

Tommy went; and presently Mr. Garbetts arrived with the steaming tumblers, which sent up an aroma of spirits cut with hot water—an odour that, once in a room, takes possession like a bold actor who has mistaken the play for his own benefit-night.

Captain Costigan did not, to his friend, narrate the entire chain of his humiliations, for there are events a man tells in full only to himself at midnight; but with a pen in one hand and a hot glass in the other, he composed a letter to Major Pendennis—threatening, elegant in its own eyes, and sealed with elaborate care by the great silver seal of the Costigans, the only piece of family plate the Captain could call up as a witness to his gentility.

In this epistle he commanded Major Pendennis to offer no hindrance to the marriage which Captain Costigan had now proclaimed as projected between Mr. Arthur Pendennis and his daughter Miss Fotheringay, and to fix an early day for the ceremony; or else, failing the altar, to afford the satisfaction usual among gentlemen of honour. If the Major should dislike even that, the Captain hinted that he could be persuaded by a horsewhip applied to his person. One regrets to be unable to provide the exact phraseology; but the misfortune is unavoidable, for the letter never reached the stage of being read by the Major at all.

Garbetts was dispatched as ambassador. Costigan squeezed his hand with that theatrical benediction which men give when they have been drinking hot spirits and feel themselves both wronged and heroic.

As soon as Garbetts was gone, the Captain took down his venerable duelling-pistols, flint-locks, that had done the business of “many a pretty fellow in Dublin,” as he loved to say, and examined them with a tenderness more suited to polishing a family christening-spoon. Then he drew out from a drawer all Pen’s letters and poems—those documents which he kept like a miser keeps bank-notes, reading them himself before permitting Emily their perusal, as though he were tasting the dish before allowing his daughter to sit to dinner.

In twenty minutes Mr. Garbetts returned. His face, made for Roman despair, wore now a look more domestic—anxious, crestfallen, and very much inclined to keep out of trouble.

“Ye’ve seen ’um?” cried Costigan.

“Why—yes,” said Garbetts.

“And when is it for?” asked the Captain, trying the lock of one of the pistols and bringing it level with his oi—that bloodshot orb he so affectionately mispronounced, as if the eye, too, were Irish.

“When is what for?” Garbetts asked, already suspecting that this conversation had pistols at its end.

“The meeting, my dear fellow.”

“You don’t mean to say you mean mortal combat, Captain?” Garbetts cried, aghast.

“What the devil else do I mean, Garbetts? I want to shoot that man that has trajuiced me honor, or meself dthrop a victim on the sod.”

Mr. Garbetts recoiled as a family man recoils from another man’s romance. “D—— if I carry challenges,” he said. “I’m a family man, Captain, and will have nothing to do with pistols—take back your letter.” And, to Captain Costigan’s surprise and indignation, Garbetts flung the letter down upon the table, with its great sprawling superscription and the blotched seal as ostentatious as a cheap pudding’s glaze.

“Ye don’t mean to say ye saw ’um and didn’t give ’um the letter?” Costigan roared, as if a messenger could keep a challenge in his pocket the way a child keeps a sweet.

“I saw him,” said Garbetts, “but I could not have speech with him, Captain.”

“And why the devil not?”

“There was one there I cared not to meet—nor would you,” the tragedian answered, dropping his voice into the sepulchral tone he reserved for ghosts and creditors. “The minion Tatham was there, Captain.”

“The cowardly scoundthrel!” bellowed Costigan. “He’s frightened, and already going to swear the peace against me.”

“I’ll have nothing to do with the fighting, mark that,” Garbetts said doggedly. “And I wish I’d not seen Tatham neither, nor that bit of—”

“Hold your tongue, Bob Acres. It’s my belief ye’re no better than a coward,” cried Costigan, quoting Sir Lucius O’Trigger with that pious satisfaction actors feel when life supplies them a line.

After more parley—condensed here, for it was chiefly a duet of pride and prudence—they separated not in very good humour. Garbetts departed with the air of a man who has been asked to carry a live coal in his hands and has, sensibly, declined.

And thus it happens that the Captain’s letter, though composed with heat, sealed with dignity, and perfumed by whisky vapour, was never opened by Major Pendennis, never weighed in his cool fingers, never read with that Pall Mall politeness which can make an insult feel like a compliment. It lay, unread, like an unserved pie cooling on a window-sill.

When Miss Costigan came home from rehearsal that evening—she returned with faithful Mr. Bows—she found her father pacing the small sitting-room in a storm. The air was thick with hot spirits-and-water; the table was littered with Pen’s papers surrounding empty goblets and the now useless teaspoon that had stirred the Captain’s courage into solution. If the room had any music, it was the wrong sort: the scrape of boots on boards, the rattle of a pistol-case touched too often, the loud breathing of a man who thinks himself tragic. In such domestic acoustics there is no comfort; it is a noise that makes even silence nervous.

Costigan caught Emily as she entered and clasped her with tears in his eyes. “Prepare yourself, me child, me blessed child,” he cried in a voice of agony, as though she were about to be served up as a sacrifice.

“Ye’re tipsy again, Papa,” Miss Fotheringay said, pushing him back with the calm of a woman who has seen men perform. “Ye promised me ye wouldn’t take spirits before dinner.”

“It’s to forget me sorrows, me poor girl, that I’ve taken just a drop,” sobbed the bereaved father. “It’s to drown me care that I drain the bowl.”

“Your care takes a deal of drowning, Captain dear,” said Bows, mimicking his friend’s accent with a fiddler’s irreverence. “What has happened? Has that soft-spoken gentleman in the wig been vexing you?”

“The oily miscreant! I’ll have his blood!” roared Cos.

Emily, who had slipped out of his reach into her own room, came back presently looking as healthy and unconcerned as a well-made loaf sitting cool on the board while other things burn. She carried in a pair of ex-white satin shoes, and—because the theatre’s gods demand cleanliness—meant to rub them as near to virgin brightness as possible with bread-crumb, intending on next Tuesday evening to go mad in them as Ophelia.

She looked at the papers on the table, seemed about to ask something, and thought better of it. Then, going to the cupboard with practical ceremony, she selected a promising piece of bread—firm enough to crumble, not so stale as to scratch—like a cook choosing the right crust to thicken a stew. Returning, she sat down comfortably with the shoes in her lap and began her careful rubbing, raising a faint floury smell that, against the whisky, was almost wholesome.

“What have ye got them letthers, and pothry, and stuff, of Master Arthur’s out for, Pa?” she asked in her honest Irish brogue. “Sure ye don’t want to be reading over that nonsense.”

“O Emilee!” cried the Captain. “That boy whom I loved as the boy of mee bosom is only a scoundthrel, and a deceiver, mee poor girl.” He cast a tragical look at Mr. Bows; Bows, in his turn, watched Emily with the anxious attention of a man who hears, in the smallest domestic phrase, the beginning of a storm.

“He! pooh!” she said, unruffled, rubbing at the satin. “Sure the poor lad’s as simple as a schoolboy. All them children write verses and nonsense.”

“He’s been acting the part of a viper to this fireside, and a traitor in this familee!” cried the Captain. “I tell ye he’s no better than an impostor.”

“What has the poor fellow done, Papa?” Emily asked, not lifting her eyes from the shoe, as if a clean slipper were the more urgent business.

“Done? He has deceived us in the most athrocious manner. He has thrifled with your affections, and outraged my own fine feelings. He has represented himself as a man of property, and it turruns out that he is no betther than a beggar. Haven’t I often told ye he had two thousand a year? He’s a pauper, I tell ye, Miss Costigan; a depindent upon the bountee of his mother; a good woman, who may marry again, who’s likely to live for ever, and who has but five hundred a year. How dar he ask ye to marry into a family which has not the means of providing for ye? Ye’ve been grossly deceived and put upon, Milly, and it’s my belief his old ruffian of an uncle in a wig is in the plot against us.”

“That soft old gentleman?” said Emily, still imperturbable. “What has he been doing, Papa?”

Costigan recounted the Major’s statement: that young Pendennis had no fortune; that Costigan was urged to go to the lawyers and inspect the father’s will—“wherein he knew the scoundthrels have a bill of mine, and I can’t meet them,” he inserted, as if even honour must take notice of outstanding accounts. Finally, the Captain declared an infernal swindle had been practised upon him by uncle and nephew, and that he was resolved upon marriage or blood.

All the while Emily rubbed. The bread-crumbs fell like little pale flakes of snow; the satin, under her fingers, slowly regained its innocent shine.

“Sure, if he’s no money, there’s no use marrying him, Papa,” she said at last, with the cool decisiveness of a housekeeper deciding against an over-priced joint. “Why did the villain say he was a man of prawpertee?”

“The poor fellow always said he was poor,” Emily answered. “’Twas you would have it he was rich, Papa—and made me agree to take him.”

“He should have been explicit and told us his income, Milly,” the Captain insisted. “A young fellow who rides a blood mare, and makes presents of shawls and bracelets, is an impostor if he has no money;—and as for his uncle, bedad I’ll pull off his wig whenever I see ’um. Bows, here, shall take a message to him and tell him so. Either it’s a marriage, or he meets me in the field like a man, or I tweak ’um on the nose in front of his hotel or in the gravel walks of Fairoaks Park before all the county, bedad.”

“Bedad, you may send somebody else with the message,” said Bows, laughing. “I’m a fiddler, not a fighting man.”

“Pooh, you’ve no spirit, sir,” roared the General. “I’ll be my own second, if no one will stand by and see me injured. And I’ll take my case of pistols and shoot ’um in the Coffee-room of the George.”

“And so poor Arthur has no money?” Emily sighed, the first softening in her tone. “Poor lad, he was a good lad too: wild and talking nonsense, with his verses and pothry and that, but a brave, generous boy, and indeed I liked him—and he liked me too,” she added, rather softly, and rubbed on.

“Why don’t you marry him if you like him so?” Bows burst out, with a sudden sourness. “He is not more than ten years younger than you are. His mother may relent, and you might go and live and have enough at Fairoaks Park. Why not go and be a lady? I could go on with the fiddle, and the General live on his half-pay. Why don’t you marry him? You know he likes you.”

“There’s others that likes me as well, Bows, that has no money and that’s old enough,” Miss Milly said, with the same practical gravity she might have used in discussing the price of meat.

“Yes—d—— it,” Bows answered, with a bitter curse, “that are old enough and poor enough and fools enough for anything.”

“There’s old fools, and young fools too,” she returned, with an imperious glance that dismissed his anger as if it were smoke. “You’ve often said so, you silly man. If Pendennis has not enough money to live upon, it’s folly to talk about marrying him: and that’s the long and short of it.”

“And the boy?” said Bows. “By Jove! you throw a man away like an old glove, Miss Costigan.”

“I don’t know what you mean, Bows,” she replied placidly, taking up the second shoe. “If he had had half of the two thousand a year that Papa gave him, or the half of that, I would marry him. But what is the good of taking on with a beggar? We’re poor enough already. There’s no use in my going to live with an old lady that’s testy and cross, maybe, and would grudge me every morsel of meat.”

(The truth was, it was near dinner time, and Suky had not laid the cloth yet; and in households like theirs hunger and economy are always waiting in the passage, listening.)

“And then,” she added quite simply, “suppose there was a family?—why, Papa, we shouldn’t be as well off as we are now.”

“’Deed, then, you would not, Milly dear,” Costigan said, soothed by her good sense as men are soothed by a warm dish set before them.

“And there’s an end to all the fine talk about Mrs. Arthur Pendennis of Fairoaks Park—the member of Parliament’s lady,” Milly laughed. “Pretty carriages and horses we should have to ride!—that you were always talking about, Papa! But it’s always the same. If a man looked at me, you fancied he was going to marry me; and if he had a good coat, you fancied he was as rich as Crazes.”

“—As Croesus,” said Bows.

“Well, call ’um what ye like. But it’s a fact now that Papa has married me these eight years a score of times. Wasn’t I to be my Lady Poldoody of Oystherstown Castle? Then there was the Navy Captain at Portsmouth, and the old surgeon at Norwich, and the Methodist preacher here last year, and who knows how many more? Well, I bet a penny, with all your scheming, I shall die Milly Costigan at last. So poor little Arthur has no money? Stop and take dinner, Bows; we’ve a beautiful beef-steak pudding.”

At that word the whole room changed key, as if some invisible hand had shifted a tune from minor to major. The promised pudding rose in everyone’s imagination: suet crust steamed and swelling; beef cut small so it would surrender properly; onions softened to sweetness; pepper and salt measured by a practised hand; and, above all, the smell—rich, brown, domestic—capable of calming revolutions. Even Captain Costigan’s pistols, hearing of beef-steak pudding, seemed less eager for blood.

“I wonder whether she is on with Sir Derby Oaks,” thought Bows, whose eyes and thoughts were always watching her. “The dodges of women beat all comprehension; and I am sure she wouldn’t let the lad off so easily, if she had not some other scheme on hand.”

It may be seen that Miss Fotheringay, though often silent and by no means brilliant where poetry, literature, or the fine arts were concerned, spoke freely and sensibly in her own circle. She was not romantic; she had no appetite for reading Shakespeare once she left the stage (and, indeed, had not truly understood him while she adorned it). But give her a pudding to judge, a piece of needle-work to finish, a household crisis to settle, and she was as steady as a cook who knows precisely when to take a dish off the fire. Strong imagination and passionate temper did not mislead her; she kept her judgment cool, and her hands busy.

Over dinner—where the beef-steak pudding proved indeed beautiful, the crust cut with a spoon and letting out a savoury steam that fogged the windows a little—Captain Costigan tried to convince himself, and the company, that Major Pendennis’s account of Pen’s finances must be a trick: a ruse by the old hypocrite to make them break the match on their side. But Milly would not, for a moment, entertain the notion of deceit in the adversary. In her plain way she showed it was her father who had deceived himself; poor little Pen had never tried to take them in.

“As for that poor lad,” she said, “I pity him with all my heart.”

And she ate an exceedingly good dinner—an act which filled Mr. Bows with that odd mixture of admiration and contempt she constantly inspired in him, as though her appetite were both a virtue and an insult.

During and after the meal—while the room settled into the softer, safer sounds of domesticity: knives laid down, plates shifted, the kettle singing for tea—the three devised the best means of bringing this love-matter to an end. Costigan’s idea of tweaking the Major’s nose faded with his supply of after-dinner whisky-and-water; the liquor, which before had made him roar, now made him pliant. He became submissive to his daughter, ready for any plan she chose, as a blustering cook submits to the one sensible person in the kitchen when the sauce begins to split.

The Captain, who had been eager enough to face and demolish both Pen and his uncle while he believed himself wronged, perhaps shrank a little from the thought of meeting the young man, and asked, with sudden practicality, “what the juice they were to say to the lad if he remained steady to his engagement, and they broke from theirs?”

“What? don’t you know how to throw a man over?” said Bows. “Ask a woman to tell you?”

Miss Fotheringay, without malice and without flourish, explained how it was done—simply enough; nothing more easy.

“Papa writes to Arthur to know what settlements he proposes to make in event of a marriage; and asks what his means are. Arthur writes back and says what he’s got, and you’ll find it’s as the Major says, I’ll go bail. Then papa writes, and says it’s not enough, and the match had best be at an end.”

“And, of course, you enclose a parting line,” Bows put in, eyeing her with scorn, “in which you say you will always regard him as a brother.”

“Of course, and so I shall,” Emily answered. “He’s a most worthy young man, I’m sure. I’ll thank ye hand me the salt. Them filberts is beautiful.”

“There will be no noses pulled, Cos, my boy? I’m sorry you’re baulked,” Bows said.

“Dad, I suppose not,” Costigan replied, rubbing his own nose as if to console it for the loss of another. “What’ll ye do about them letters, and verses, and pomes, Milly darling?—Ye must send ’em back.”

“Wigsby would give a hundred pound for ’em,” Bows said with a sneer, for in the theatre there are always men ready to trade in other people’s feelings as if they were old playbills.

“’Deed, then, he would,” Captain Costigan cried, easily tempted as a child is by the thought of sweets.

“Papa!” said Miss Milly, with sudden firmness. “Ye wouldn’t be for not sending the poor boy his letters back? Them letters and pomes is mine. They were very long, and full of all sorts of nonsense, and Latin, and things I couldn’t understand the half of; indeed I’ve not read ’em all; but we’ll send ’em back to him when the proper time comes.”

And going to a drawer, she took out a number of the County Chronicle and Chatteris Champion in which Pen had written flaming verses celebrating her appearance as Imogen. Like ladies of her profession, she kept favourable notices the way thrifty wives keep good recipes—folded, saved, and ready for future proof. She put by the leaf on which the poem appeared, then wrapped up Pen’s letters, poems, passions, and fancies, and tied them with a piece of string neatly, as she would a parcel of sugar.

Nor was she in the least moved in doing it. The papers, that had cost the boy so many hours—his watchful nights, his hungry hopes, his feverish faith—became, in her hands, a tidy bundle, squared at the corners, trussed for return like groceries.

Afterwards she sat down and made tea with a perfectly placid and contented heart, while ten miles off Pen was yearning after her, and hugging her image to his soul.

At Fairoaks, the household began to take the Major’s absence personally, as if Chatteris had kidnapped him for ransom and was sending back only vague excuses. Dr. Portman and his lady, rattling homeward to Clavering with the tidy regularity of people who never mislay a sermon, stopped at Helen’s lodge-gate and delivered a note from Major Pendennis.

He would remain at Chatteris another day. He was anxious to have a talk with Messrs. Tatham, the lawyers. He would meet them that afternoon. He added nothing—nothing at all—about the delicate little explosion he had spent the morning arranging, as though the less said about a fire, the quicker it might go out.

Pen, meanwhile, contrived to be wonderfully busy at doing nothing in particular that might take him into the town. He could not endure the idea of walking past that odious Dean’s grass-plat with the polished boots potentially planted there—his guardian’s boots—shining like moral surveillance. How was a man to sigh properly, or to look meaningfully at a young lady, while an uncle might be within spying distance? Pen’s love, like a shy dish sent up too soon, turned watery in public. It could only show itself by his eyes, which—poor boy—did all the hard labour, rolling and gazing in a way that must have given them muscle-ache; but his tongue, before witnesses, became as useless as a fork in soup.

And indeed, for those not engaged in the cookery of it, lovers’ talk is much like a recipe written in a dead dialect: plenty of words, no key; quantities, no taste. People keep old love-letters the way they keep stale cake in a tin—out of sentiment—and when they open it later, the thing is dry, crumbly, and astonishing that it ever nourished anyone. Six absurd lines once fed you for a week. Then you were famished again until the next batch of folly arrived, hot from the oven of delusion. For this reason—pure tenderness for Pen’s future complexion—we decline to serve up his verses from this period. Young ladies should not be asked to eat such rich spoon-meat cold. We will keep the papers tied up in newspapers with Miss Fotheringay’s string, and sealed with Captain Costigan’s great silver seal, like a ham wrapped for winter and best left hanging.

The Major, for his part, emerged from his morning’s interview with Captain Costigan in a condition of fury so concentrated you might have lit a candle from it. The “impudent bog-trotting scamp” had dared to threaten him; had dared to speak as if a Costigan might be permitted to marry into the Pendennises; had even, with the swagger of a man who thinks himself a whole regiment, hinted at a challenge. The Major’s mind performed its usual swift arithmetic: if the fellow could find any person resembling a gentleman to carry such a message, the Major felt a violent temptation not to balk him—then immediately recoiled from the picture of himself going out to fight a tipsy mountebank over an actress in a barn. The Major loved honour, but he loved the right sort of honour, properly laundered, scented, and spoken of discreetly.

When he met Dr. Portman, who inquired anxiously—like a parson testing the temperature of a moral fever—how the battle with the dragon had gone, Major Pendennis would not repeat the General’s insolences. He said only that the affair was very ugly, very disagreeable, and by no means finished. He begged Dr. and Mrs. Portman to say nothing at Fairoaks, and contented himself with sending Helen the note already mentioned.

Then he returned to the George, where he relieved his feelings upon Morgan his valet with a series of explosions which were heard upstairs and downstairs, and were afterwards described by Morgan, over his own dinner in the servants’ room, to Mr. Foker’s man, with professional pride. That news, like smoke, went where smoke always goes: into other people’s rooms.

Mr. Foker had finished his breakfast—at two o’clock in the afternoon, which was his notion of early—and remembered he wished to know what had happened between his two friends. So, wrapped in a brocade dressing-gown and wearing an embroidered skull-cap that had been stitched with maternal devotion, he skipped to the Major’s sitting-room and knocked.

Major Pendennis was indeed engaged: papers, red tape, and the solemn machinery of money and land lay spread out before him. Old Mr. Tatham, the lawyer—white-headed, composed, smelling faintly of parchment and caution—sat opposite, like a crow who had learned to read.

Foker, seeing business, began to retreat with a modest “Oh, you’re busy—call another time.” But the Major, who wanted an audience and whose anger had been longing for somewhere safe to rest, begged him to enter. Foker removed his fez with an air as if he were saluting royalty, advanced, bowed, and installed himself in an arm-chair, spreading his crimson skirts as though he meant to be framed and hung in a gallery.

“You seem to like my dressing-gown, sir,” he said to Mr. Tatham, with a bland smile. “Pretty thing, isn’t it? Neat, but not in the least gaudy.”

Mr. Tatham stared as a countryman stares at a foreign fruit—uncertain whether it is edible or merely ornamental.

“And how do you do, Major Pendennis, sir, and how does the world treat you?”

“There,” said the Major, glad to speak, “I have had an interview with that Irishman—you may speak before my friend Mr. Tatham, who knows all the affairs of the family—and it has not been satisfactory. He won’t believe that my nephew is poor. He says we are liars. He did me the honour to hint that I was a coward as I took leave. And when you knocked I thought you might be the gentleman I expect with a challenge from Mr. Costigan. That is how the world treats me, Mr. Foker.”

“You don’t mean that Irishman—the actress’s father?” cried Mr. Tatham, who, being a dissenter, did not patronise the drama and spoke of it as of an infection.

“The very man. Have not you heard what a fool my nephew has made of himself about the girl?”

Mr. Tatham had heard nothing—he never went within a theatre wall, as if painted scenery might stain his conscience—so the Major was obliged to recount his nephew’s loves from the beginning, with Mr. Foker chiming in, in his familiar idiom, as though narrating a farce at a club.

Mr. Tatham listened in increasing astonishment. Why had not Mrs. Pendennis married a serious man, he wondered—Mr. Tatham was a widower, and saw serious men everywhere, like useful vegetables—who might have kept the boy from perdition? As for the daughter, he said nothing: her profession was enough.

Mr. Foker, always ready to be generous where it amused him, declared he had known excellent people in the booths—by which he meant the Temple of the Muses.

“Perhaps,” Mr. Tatham allowed, with a sigh, “perhaps. But the father, Major—I know him. A man of the worst character. A wine-bibber. An idler in taverns and billiard-rooms. A notorious insolvent.”

And then, with a sort of grim relish, the lawyer related that his office had a writ out against Costigan and another disreputable fellow—one of the play-actors—for a bill given to Mr. Skinner of the city, a respectable grocer and wine and spirit merchant and a Member of the Society of Friends.

“This Costigan came crying to Mr. Skinner,” said Mr. Tatham, offended at the memory, “crying in the shop, sir—and we have not proceeded, as neither was worth powder and shot.”

It was while he spoke that a third knock came—heavier, like a fist trained to applaud tragedians and to threaten creditors. An athletic gentleman entered in a shabby braided frock, holding a letter sealed with a large blotched red seal. He cleared his throat as if about to deliver doom.

“Can I have the honour of speaking with Major Pendennis in private?” he began. “I have a few words for your ear, sir. I am the bearer of a mission from my friend Captain Costigan—”

But his voice faltered. His face went pale. His eyes fixed upon Mr. Tatham’s red and well-remembered countenance, and his courage, which had been marching bravely, suddenly remembered it had no shoes.

“Hullo, Garbetts, speak up!” cried Mr. Foker, delighted, like a boy hearing the first crack of a squib.

“Bless my soul,” said Mr. Tatham. “It is the other party to the bill!”

“I say, sir; stop, I say—” began the lawyer, rising.

But Garbetts, with a face as blank as a man who has seen a ghost in a bailiff’s hat, gasped something unintelligible and fled out of the room.

The Major’s gravity collapsed. He burst into laughter—sharp, relieved, almost musical. Mr. Foker laughed too, rocking in his brocade like a delighted ornament. Even Mr. Tatham, though professionally serious, smiled.

“By Jove, it was a good ’un,” said Foker. “I don’t think there’ll be any fight, Major.” And he began mimicking the tragedian’s stricken look, to their renewed entertainment. “If there is, the old gentleman—your name Tatham? very happy—may send the bailiffs to separate the men.”

Mr. Tatham promised he would.

The Major, though he disliked vulgarity, was not sorry to see the quarrel end in such a ridiculous puff of smoke.

“It seems to me, sir,” he said to Mr. Foker, “that you always arrive to put me into good-humour.”

And Mr. Foker, by one of those idle impulses which in his case sometimes fell accidentally into usefulness, went later in the afternoon to Captain Costigan’s lodgings to hear what had passed in the morning. Costigan was not at home. His daughter had permitted—indeed encouraged—him to go to the convivial club at the Magpie Hotel, where, no doubt, he was at that very moment giving his courage an airing, like a horse pranced before friends, bragging of his intention to murder a ruffian, and enjoying the sound of his own heroism over beer.

But Miss Fotheringay was at home, washing the tea-cups, while Mr. Bows sat opposite—hands in pockets, eyes observant, as fiddlers’ eyes often are, taking the measure of a room as if it were a tune.

“Just done breakfast, I see—how do?” said Mr. Foker, popping in his little head.

“Get out, you funny little man,” cried Miss Fotheringay.

“You mean come in,” said he, and came in at once. He folded his arms and began twirling his head with immense rapidity like Harlequin on a stage the instant he breaks out of his cocoon. Miss Fotheringay laughed with all her heart. A wink of Foker’s could set her off, where the bitterest joke of Bows’s would not win so much as a smile, and the finest speeches poor Pen delivered only puzzled her, like French cookery described to a person who has never tasted butter.

When the harlequinade ended, Foker sank on one knee and kissed her hand. She called him “the drollest little man,” and gave him a great good-humoured slap. Pen used to tremble when he kissed that hand. Pen would have died of a slap. Different temperaments, different sauces.

They talked. Foker, delighted with his own story, recounted Garbetts’s discomfiture, and thus they learned for the first time how far the General had carried his wrath. Foker spoke sturdily in favour of the Major’s honour and veracity, describing him as a tip-top swell, moving in the upper circle, and incapable of deceit—especially incapable of deceiving such a charming young woman as Miss Foth. He touched, with all the delicacy he could command, upon the delicate marriage question; yet he could not help letting it be seen that he held Pen rather cheap. Pen’s sentimentality was a flavour Foker never cared for—too sweet, too frothy, too easily upset by the slightest draught.

“I knew it wouldn’t do, Miss Foth,” said he, nodding. “Couldn’t do. Didn’t like to put my hand into the bag, but knew it couldn’t do. He’s too young for you: too green: a deal too green: and he turns out to be poor as Job. Can’t have him at no price, can she, Mr. Bo?”

“Indeed he’s a nice poor boy,” said Miss Fotheringay rather sadly.

“Poor little beggar,” said Bows, with a queer look at her, as if wondering how women pat a man’s head and then send him out into the rain.

Bows had no objection to declare that Miss Fotheringay was perfectly right in giving up Arthur Pendennis, and that the match had always been absurd. She owned she thought so herself; only she couldn’t send away two thousand a year.

“It all comes of believing Papa’s silly stories,” she said. “Faith I’ll choose for meself another time.” And very likely Lieutenant Sir Derby Oaks—large as life, large as income—strode across her mind at that instant.

After praising Major Pendennis—“a proper gentleman entirely,” she declared, “smelling of lavender, and as neat as a pin”—and after Bows pronounced him the right sort of fellow, though rather too much of an old buck, Mr. Foker suddenly proposed a stroke of reconciliation.

“Come and meet the Major this very evening at dinner at my apartment at the George. He agreed to dine with me—and after the—after the little shindy this morning, in which I must say the General was wrong—it would look kind, you know. I know the Major fell in love with you, Miss Foth: he said so.”

“So she may be Mrs. Pendennis still,” said Bows with a sneer. “No, thank you, Mr. F. I’ve dined.”

“Sure, that was at three o’clock,” said Miss Costigan, who had an honest appetite, “and I can’t go without you.”

“We’ll have lobster-salad and champagne,” said the little monster, who could not construe a line of Latin nor do a sum beyond the Rule of Three, but could always summon a feast like a conjurer pulling ribbons from his mouth.

For lobster-salad and champagne in an honourable manner, Miss Costigan would have gone anywhere. And so it happened that at seven o’clock Major Pendennis found himself seated at dinner with Mr. Bows, a professional fiddler, and Miss Costigan—whose father had wanted to blow his brains out a few hours before.

To complete the comedy, Mr. Foker, who knew Costigan’s haunts as a cook knows the nearest market, sent Stoopid—his man—to the Magpie club, where the General was in the act of singing a pathetic song, and brought him off to supper.

Captain Costigan arrived flushed with drink and sentiment, as if he had been marinated in both. To find his daughter and Bows at the board struck him into a sort of astonished delight. Major Pendennis laughed and held out his hand cordially. The General grasped it avec effusion, and called him his dearest friend. He burst into tears more than once—tears already started by his own song before he joined them—and toasted everybody with reckless tenderness. The champagne went off with an agreeable hiss, the lobster-salad with that sharp sea-sweetness which makes even peace taste possible, and the room at the George rang with voices and laughter, the very clink of glasses sounding like a treaty.

Stoopid and Mr. Foker walked home with the General afterwards, while the Major gallantly gave his arm to Miss Costigan. When he called the next day he was received with friendliness; civilities passed between the gentlemen like coins exchanged at a counter. On taking leave, the Major expressed his anxious desire to serve Miss Costigan whenever useful; and he shook hands with Mr. Foker most cordially, saying the young gentleman had done him the very greatest service.

“All right,” said Mr. Foker; and they parted with mutual esteem.

Major Pendennis returned to Fairoaks next day and said nothing of the previous night—no mention of lobster-salad, no mention of champagne, no mention of the company in which he had eaten and laughed. Yet he asked Mr. Smirke to stop to dinner, and any person accustomed to watch him might have noticed something constrained in his hilarity—an unusual watchfulness in his kindness to his nephew. He gave Pen an emphatic God-bless-you at bedtime; and when he and Mrs. Pendennis were about to part for the night, he seemed on the point of saying something, but checked himself, fearing to spoil her rest, and let her sleep.

Next morning he was down earlier than usual, greeting everyone with marked cordiality. The post generally arrived toward the end of breakfast. When old John entered and discharged the bag of letters and papers, Major Pendennis looked hard at Pen as the lad took his own. Arthur blushed and put a letter down. He knew the handwriting; it was Costigan’s. He did not want to read it before the table.

Major Pendennis knew it too. He had posted it himself in Chatteris the day before.

He told little Laura to go away. The child, who had a thorough dislike to him, went gladly enough. When the door closed, the Major took Mrs. Pendennis’s hand, gave her a look full of meaning, and pointed to the letter lying under the newspaper Pen was pretending to read.

“Will you come into the drawing-room?” he said. “I want to speak to you.”

Helen followed, wondering and nervous.

“What is it?” she asked.

“The affair is at an end,” Major Pendennis said. “He has a letter there giving him his dismissal. I dictated it myself yesterday. There are a few lines from the lady too, bidding him farewell. It is all over.”

Helen ran back to the dining-room with her brother close behind. Pen had seized the letter the instant they were gone. He read it with a stupefied face, as if the paper were written in an unfamiliar tongue and yet somehow cut him like a knife.

Costigan wrote that he was most gratified by Arthur’s kindness to his daughter, but that he had only now been made aware of Mr. Pendennis’s—spelled in Costigan’s manner—peecupiary circumstances. They were such that marriage was out of the question at present; and considering the disparity of age, future union impossible. Under these circumstances, and with deepest regret and esteem, Captain Costigan bade Arthur farewell and suggested he cease visiting, for some time at least, at his house.

A few lines from Miss Costigan were enclosed. She acquiesced in Papa’s decision. She pointed out she was many years older than Arthur and that an engagement was not to be thought of. She would always be grateful for his kindness and hoped to keep his friendship, but until the pain of separation was over, she entreated they should not meet.

Pen read mechanically, as though his eyes had become mere instruments. Then he looked up wildly and saw his mother and uncle watching him. Helen’s face was all tender anxiety.

“What—what is this?” Pen cried. “It’s some joke. This is not her writing. This is some servant’s writing. Who’s playing tricks upon me?”

“It comes under her father’s envelope,” said the Major. “Those letters you had before were not in her hand: that is hers.”

“How do you know?” Arthur asked fiercely.

“I saw her write it,” said the uncle, as the boy started up.

Helen moved forward and took Pen’s hand. He shook her off.

“How came you to see her? How came you between me and her? What have I ever done to you that you should—Oh, it’s not true! it’s not true!” Pen broke out with a wild execration. “She can’t have done it of her own accord. She can’t mean it. She’s pledged to me. Who has told her lies to break her from me?”

“Lies are not told in the family, Arthur,” Major Pendennis replied coldly. “I told her the truth—that you have no money to maintain her, for her foolish father had represented you to be rich. And when she knew how poor you were, she withdrew at once, and without persuasion of mine. She was quite right. She is ten years older than you are. She is perfectly unfitted to be your wife, and knows it. Look at that handwriting, and ask yourself, is such a woman fitted to be the companion of your mother?”

“I will know from herself if it is true,” Arthur said, crumpling the paper. “I’ll hear it from herself.”

The Major, with the faintest possible sneer, drew out a billet. “Her letters were written by a confidant of hers, who writes better than she can. Look here—here’s one from the lady to your friend Mr. Foker. You have seen her with Miss Costigan, as whose amanuensis she acted.”

“It’s not that,” Pen said, burning with shame and rage. “I suppose what you say is true, sir—but I’ll hear it from herself.”

“Arthur!” his mother pleaded.

“I will see her,” Arthur insisted. “I’ll ask her to marry me once more. I will. No one shall prevent me.”

“What, a woman who spells affection with one f?” said the Major. “Nonsense, sir. Be a man, and remember that your mother is a lady. She was never made to associate with that tipsy old swindler or his daughter. Be a man and forget her, as she does you.”

“Be a man and comfort your mother, my Arthur,” Helen said, and embraced him. Seeing both were deeply moved, Major Pendennis went out and shut the door, judging wisely that they were best alone.

He had won a complete victory. He had even brought away Pen’s letters in his portmanteau from Chatteris. When he returned them to Costigan, he complimented the Captain by giving him the little promissory note that had disquieted Garbetts; and the Major settled it with Mr. Tatham.

Pen rushed off wildly to Chatteris that day, but could not see Miss Fotheringay. He left a letter for her enclosed to her father. The enclosure came back, returned by Costigan, who begged that all correspondence might end. After one or two further attempts, the indignant General desired their acquaintance to cease altogether. He cut Pen in the street.

One day, as Arthur and Foker paced the Castle walk, they met Emily on her father’s arm. She passed without nod or sign, as if Pen were a stranger on the pavement. Foker felt the boy trembling on his arm.

The uncle wished Pen to travel, to quit the country awhile; his mother urged him too, for he was growing ill and suffered severely. But he refused, point-blank. He would not go. He would not obey in this instance; and his mother was too fond, his uncle too wise, to force him.

Whenever Miss Fotheringay acted, he rode over to the Chatteris Theatre and saw her. One night there were so few people that the manager returned the money. Pen came home, went to bed at eight, and had a fever. If this continues, his mother will be going over and fetching the girl, the Major thought in despair. As for Pen, he thought he should die.

We are not going to set down a dreary journal of his despair and passion. Other gentlemen besides Mr. Pen have been baulked in love—yes, indeed—and few die of it, however convincingly they insist upon the point.

Mr. Bingley was that night dying heroically as Rolla in Pizarro to an audience so thin you might have used it to strain soup. The pit held a cough, a boot, and a disappointed echo; the boxes looked like so many respectable pews waiting for a sermon that had been postponed.

Arthur Pendennis sat almost alone—an island of misery in plush upholstery—with eyes reddened as if he had been slicing onions for the whole county. He leaned over the ledge and stared at the stage as a starving man stares at a window where a pie has been cooling for an hour. The pie, to him, was Miss Fotheringay.

Spaniards and Peruvians marched and declaimed; priests threatened; virgins of the sun looked chilly in their properties; battles happened with the mild inconvenience of people moving furniture in a lodging-house. Pen saw none of it. When Miss Fotheringay was off the stage, the world went out like a snuffed candle. When she entered, it blazed again—white raiment, leopard-skin, a brazen sun on her breast, and tawdry bracelets that glittered like cheap sugar on a fairing. She had only a handful of words to say, but she said them as if each syllable were a cherry to be displayed before it was eaten. She looked still better than she spoke; and her eyes—those famous eyes—rolled and gleamed, bright as polished chestnuts. Only, that evening, they were not ladled in Pen’s direction.

He did not even notice that two gentlemen had taken the next box—nor, indeed, anything human in the theatre besides Cora. He did not see that her glances kept flying, like well-trained birds, towards box No. 3; nor did he observe the sudden miracle that followed the arrival of those two men: the stage, which had been lounging through the first act as if it had been asked to work overtime, sprang up into an unnatural bustle of virtue.

For the play had begun in a manner to make an honest manager consider returning the money on principle. Actors yawned through noble sentiments; they spoke to one another too loud in the pauses, as if they were trading recipes for punch. Even Bingley was slack; even Mrs. Bingley, as Elvira, economised her voice as though it were coal. But then—pop!—up went their energy, as if someone had thrown open the kitchen door and announced that the Marquis himself was coming to dine.

Mrs. Bingley began to raise her voice and bellow like a pious cow; Bingley darted and yelled with a sudden conviction that the fate of Peru depended on his lungs; Garbetts, Rowkins, and Miss Rouncy all began to act, swagger, scowl, and spout as if each had been promised a crown roast for doing it loud enough. And all this zeal was directed—not at the empty benches—but at the two gentlemen in the neighbouring box.

One of these was a quiet little man in black, grey-headed, with a shrewd, comfortable face: the sort of person you would trust to choose anchovies. The other was a spectacle—tall, portly, hooked-nosed, and decorated in a manner that suggested his wardrobe had been designed by a committee of jewellers. His coat flashed with frogs and velvet; rings and pins glittered; chains looped and winked. When he drew out a yellow pocket-handkerchief with a hand cased in white kid, a wave of musk and bergamot floated through the theatre—so that even the stale air seemed to have been suddenly garnished.

This splendid presence was no other than Mr. Dolphin, manager from London, attended—as faithfully as a sauce follows a roast—by his friend and secretary, Mr. William Minns, without whom Dolphin rarely travelled, and never, if he could help it, thought.

The effect of Mr. Dolphin’s appearance was immediate. Bingley and company, who had been acting as men do when only their creditors are listening, now performed as if the public consisted entirely of dukes. Even Miss Fotheringay’s dull heart, which was usually stirred by nothing more delicate than admiration and dinner, felt a flutter at the sight of this London Sultan of playhouses. She had little to do but look handsome and stand in attitudes, encircling her stage-child; she executed this task with the perfection of a cook laying parsley round a dish she means to be praised for.

In vain the various actors strained and poured themselves out. Pizarro got not a hand from Dolphin; Bingley roared; Mrs. Bingley thundered; the Manager took snuff from his great gold box with the unconcern of a man tasting soup he knows is too salty and refuses to be impressed by the cook’s feelings.

It was only at the last scene—when Rolla came in staggering with the infant (and Bingley, not being as strong as he was, and Master Talma Bingley being a monstrous large child for his age, made the staggering look rather like a man carrying home a sack of flour)—it was only then, when Cora rushed forward with a shriek and cried, “O God, there’s blood upon him!” that Mr. Dolphin clapped his hands and broke out with an enthusiastic bravo.

Then he slapped his secretary on the shoulder. “By Jove, Billy, she’ll do!”

“Who taught her that dodge?” said old Billy, with the sour relish of a man who remembers being forced to eat burnt pudding. “I remember her at the Olympic, and hang me if she could say Bo to a goose.”

It was little Mr. Bows of the orchestra who had taught her the “dodge,” as a patient cook teaches an idle girl to whisk till the sauce turns, not till her arm tires. The applause ran through the theatre like sudden warmth through a cold house; and, as the curtain fell, the whole company swarmed round Miss Fotheringay to congratulate and hate her—those twin services of the profession.

Mr. Dolphin’s appearance in remote Chatteris had causes as solid as a loaf. For all his advertised blazes of triumph—his “coruscations of talent,” his “victories of good old English comedy”—his London theatre (which, to spare living feelings and present investments, we shall call the Museum) had been doing no better than a shop that sells nothing but fine sentiments. Great Hubbard had played legitimate drama for twenty nights and paid nobody but himself. Mr. and Mrs. Cawdor had declaimed tragedy and performed their favourite rounds to ungrateful benches. Herr Garbage’s lions and tigers had drawn for a brief season—until one animal took a piece out of Herr Garbage’s shoulder, and the Lord Chamberlain, who does not approve of managers being eaten in public, put a stop to that species of entertainment. The grand Lyrical Drama, with Monsieur Poumons as first tenor and an enormous orchestra, had been brought out with such splendour that it nearly crushed Dolphin beneath its own success. He was dragging on with half salaries, small operas, feeble comedies, and a ballet company; and people were looking, with that tender interest which the world always has in another man’s bankruptcy, for the day he should appear in the Gazette.

Among the patrons of the Museum was the Most Noble the Marquis of Steyne—refined lover of the arts, enlightened friend of music and drama, and not at all above letting the arts know it. His lordship rarely came early, his statesmanlike avocations being remarkably useful whenever he did not wish to be bored; but he occasionally arrived in time for the ballet, and was always received with profound respect. His proscenium-box communicated with the stage. When anything especially pleased him—some new face among the coryphees, a dancer’s leg rising to a height that stirred his patronage—one of his aides-de-camp, Mr. Wenham or Mr. Wagg, was sent behind the scenes to carry messages of approbation, or inquiries prompted by curiosity and interest in the dramatic art.

Lord Steyne sat modestly behind a curtain and looked only toward the stage. Yet you always knew he was there: you could hear it in the changed sound of the house, and see it in the way the ballet’s eyes kept turning, as if their gaze were a kind of silent music they played for him. In one particular ballet—Cook at Otaheite—where one hundred-and-twenty lovely female savages in palm leaves danced round Floridor as Captain Cook, there were, as it were, one hundred-and-twenty pairs of eyes perpetually seasoning their performance with glances at that curtained box. Even Mademoiselle Sauterelle and Mademoiselle de Bondi (called la petite Caoutchoue), when up in the air quivering like shuttlecocks, could still keep their eyes winking at his lordship’s corner, as though the true rhythm of the theatre came not from fiddles but from that hidden seat.

Now, one night, Lord Steyne was in his box with a few friends, making such a noise and laughter that the pit grew scandalised and bawled for silence; and Mr. Wagg wondered the police did not come to take the rascals out—though the police, like everyone else, had an ear for rank. Mr. Wenham was amusing the party by reading extracts from a private letter received from Major Pendennis, whose absence from London during the full season had been remarked and deplored with that sincerity which costs nothing.

“The secret is out,” said Wenham. “There’s a woman in the case.”

“Why, d—— it, Wenham, he’s your age,” growled the gentleman behind the curtain.

“Pour les ames bien nees, l’amour ne compte pas le nombre des annees,” said Wenham, with a gallant air. “For my part, I hope to be a victim till I die, and to break my heart every year of my life.”

Which meant—being translated into the dialect of gentlemen who live by other men’s favour—that his lordship need not be severe, because Wenham was three years younger and twice as well preserved.

“Wenham, you affect me,” said the great man, with one of his oaths. “By —— you do. I like to see a fellow keeping the illusions of youth warm so late. Hang it, it’s a comfort to meet such a generous candid creature. Who’s that gal in the second row, with blue ribbons, third from the stage—fine gal. Yes, you and I are sentimentalists. Wagg, I don’t think so much cares—it’s the stomach rather more than the heart with you, eh, Wagg, my boy?”

“I like everything that’s good,” said Wagg, generously. “Beauty and Burgundy, Venus and Venison. I don’t say that Venus’s turtles are to be despised because they don’t cook them at the London Tavern: but—but tell us about old Pendennis, Mr. Wenham,” he added abruptly, for he saw his patron was not listening. Lord Steyne’s glasses were up; he was examining something on the stage.

“Yes, I’ve heard that joke before—you begin to fail, my poor Wagg. If you don’t mind I shall be obliged to have a new Jester,” said Steyne, setting down his glass. “Go on, Wenham, about old Pendennis.”

Wenham read: “Dear Wenham,—as you have had my character in your hands for the last three weeks, and no doubt have torn me to shreds, I think you can afford to be good-humoured by way of variety, and to do me a service. It is a delicate matter, entre nous, une affaire de coeur. There is a young friend of mine gone wild about a certain Miss Fotheringay, an actress at the theatre here, and I must own to you, as handsome a woman, and, as it appears to me, as good an actress as ever put on rouge. She does Ophelia, Lady Teazle, Mrs. Haller—that sort of thing. Upon my word she is as splendid as Georges in her best days. I want a London engagement for her. Can’t you get Dolphin to come and see her—to engage her—to take her out of this place? A word from a noble friend of ours would be invaluable—if you could get the Gaunt House interest for me—I will promise anything in return. Do this now as a good fellow. Yours truly, A. Pendennis.”

“It’s a clear case,” said Wenham, when he had finished. “Old Pendennis is in love.”

“And wants to get the woman up to London—evidently,” said Wagg.

“I should like to see Pendennis on his knees, with the rheumatism,” Wenham laughed.

“Or offering a lock of his hair,” said Wagg.

“Stuff,” growled Lord Steyne. “He has relations in the country, hasn’t he? A nephew—interest enough to return a member. It’s the nephew’s affair. The young one is in a scrape. I was myself—when I was in the fifth form at Eton—mad about a market-gardener’s daughter—swore I’d marry her. Poor Polly!” He paused; something old, and half-human, flickered up under the curtain like a coal that refuses to die. Then he said, briskly, “But she must be a fine woman from Pendennis’s account. Have in Dolphin; let us hear if he knows anything of her.”

Wenham slipped from the box, passed the servitor at the door communicating with the stage—who bowed as if Wenham were part of the architecture of power—and found Dolphin behind the scenes. The manager was employed, as he often was, in swearing at the ladies of the corps-de-ballet for not doing their duty. The oaths died on his lips the instant Wenham appeared. He drew back a clenched hand from the face of an offending coryphee and seized Wenham’s hand with the warmth of a man suddenly presented with a line of credit.

“How do, Mr. Wenham? How’s his lordship to-night? Looks uncommonly well,” said Dolphin, smiling as if he had never in his life threatened anyone with dismissal, starvation, or the devil. He was delighted to follow Lord Steyne’s ambassador and pay respects in person.

From that conversation came the visit to Chatteris; and from Chatteris came Dolphin’s letter to his lordship: he had seen the lady; he was struck by her talents and appearance; he had made an engagement with Miss Fotheringay; she would soon have the honour of appearing before a London audience—and, in due time, before the noble and enlightened patron, the Marquis of Steyne.

Pen read the announcement in the Chatteris paper—the same columns in which he had so often praised her charms. The editor wrote handsomely of her talent and beauty and prophesied metropolitan triumph, as editors will, being fond of prophecy when it costs no money. Bingley began to advertise “The last night of Miss Fotheringay’s engagement.”

Poor Pen and Sir Derby Oaks became constant as churchgoers—Sir Derby in the stage-box, flinging bouquets and receiving glances, like a man feeding swans with crumbs that have been perfumed. Pen sat in the almost deserted boxes—haggard, wretched, lonely—watching her as if watching would keep her from being packed up and sent away like china.

Nobody cared whether Miss Fotheringay went or stayed except those two—and perhaps one more: Mr. Bows of the orchestra.

One night, Bows climbed out from his place, came into the house, and walked up to Pen’s box. He held out his hand and asked him, quietly, to come and walk. They went down the street together and sat upon Chatteris bridge in the moonlight, where the river made its steady, consoling sound—an old tune, not in fashion, but better for the nerves than any orchestra. The town behind them had its usual clatter—doors, distant laughter, a cart wheel protesting at a rut—but here the water spoke in a language older than playbills, and indifferent to applause.

“We may sit on the same bridge,” said Bows. “We have been in the same boat for a long time. You are not the only man who has made a fool of himself about that woman. And I have less excuse than you, because I am older and know her better. She has no more heart than the stone you are leaning on; and it or you or I might fall into the water, and never come up again, and she wouldn’t care. Yes—she would care for me, because she wants me to teach her: and she won’t be able to get on without me, and will be forced to send for me from London. But she wouldn’t if she didn’t want me. She has no heart and no head, and no sense, and no feelings, and no griefs or cares—whatever. I was going to say no pleasures—but the fact is, she does like her dinner, and she is pleased when people admire her.”

“And you do?” Pen asked, pulled for a moment out of his own torment by the odd, homely bitterness of the little man.

“It’s a habit,” said Bows, “like taking snuff, or drinking drams. I’ve been taking her these five years, and can’t do without her. It was I made her. If she doesn’t send for me, I shall follow her: but I know she’ll send for me. She wants me. Some day she’ll marry, and fling me over, as I do the end of this cigar.”

He flicked the cigar’s little flaming spark; it dropped into the water and vanished at once, swallowed without sound, as if the river had its own way of consuming griefs and leaving no ash. And Pen, riding home that night, actually found himself thinking—if only for a little while—of somebody besides himself.

Until the enemy had quite marched off from before the place—until every last rumour, post-chaise, and petticoat-shadow that might possibly contain Miss Fotheringay had been routed—Major Pendennis was resolved to keep his little garrison shut up at Fairoaks. He made no proclamation, posted no sentries, forbade nothing in terms. He merely did that masterly thing which experienced generals and experienced uncles do: he contrived that his nephew’s steps should always sound somewhere within hearing. If Arthur went out, somebody happened to be coming in; if Arthur rode, somebody had seen him take the turn; if Arthur sighed, the Major had a lozenge ready and a theory for it. Thus the young gentleman enjoyed liberty with a string to it—a very long, very civil string, held by a gloved hand.

There are few men—there are none who read novels—who have not at some hour been balked in love by fate, by circumstance, by that peculiar feminine talent for saying No as if it were a hymn-tune, or by their own folly which is the most punctual of all impediments. If any such person will be good enough to remember the taste of those nights—how the pillow is hot, the sheet too cold, the clock louder than the church-bell, and the future a sort of blank larder—he may season Pen’s anguish with his own recollection and so do justice to the boy.

Ah, what fevers! what thirsts! what hungry fits of longing, like a stomach that will have its supper, dashing itself against the granite of indifference and coming away bruised! If a bill of fare could be made of all the groans of London at two o’clock in the morning—of all the men lying awake counting the strokes as if each were a spoon tapping the rim of an empty basin—what a prodigious catalogue it would be. I never knew a man die of love; but I have known a twelve-stone gentleman reduced to nine-stone five by a disappointment, so that very nearly a quarter of him might be said to have perished—gone off, as it were, in a slow consumption of sighs. He filled out again afterwards; some fresh affection put a comfortable layer over the ribs, like good suet over a joint, and made him as plump as ever. Young Pen too, being a healthy creature with a hearty palate for life (in spite of his present nausea), would console himself one day; and we mention this to prevent tender ladies from ordering mourning too soon.

His mother, however, ordered it all in her heart: the crape, the coffin, the whole melancholy establishment. What will not maternal fondness invent? “Depend on it, my dear creature,” Major Pendennis would say, with that gallantry which is as much a part of his toilette as his neckcloth, “the boy will recover. As soon as we get her out of the country we will take him somewhere—show him a little life. Meantime make yourself easy. Half a fellow’s pangs at losing a woman result from vanity more than affection. To be left by a woman is the deuce and all, to be sure; but look how easily we leave ’em.”

Mrs. Pendennis did not know. Such knowledge had never been served at her table. The subject offended her modesty, as onions do some delicate nostrils; she had had her own little private misadventure once, borne it, cured it, and packed it away like lavender in a drawer; and perhaps she had not much patience with other people’s passions—except, of course, Arthur’s, which she made entirely her own. She watched him now with a jealous, silent tenderness, and suffered more in fancy than he did in fact. Yet he would not talk to her about it; he kept his pain as boys keep contraband sweetmeats—close and sticky and hidden.

The Major must be allowed his merit. For a man whose natural air was London—who lived by dinner-bells, drawing-room chimes, coach-wheels, and the polite clatter of evening talk—Fairoaks was a kind of rural mute. To dine with Doctor Portman or a neighbouring squire now and then; to play a dreary rubber at backgammon with the widow, who tried to sweeten the hours as she sweetened her tea; these were his chief diversions. He longed for the arrival of the bag with the letters as a cook longs for the market-cart; he read every word of the evening paper as if it were a receipt for keeping life fresh.

He doctored himself assiduously too—quiet living, he said, after the London banquets. His medicine-chest stood like a little private pantry of pills and draughts. He dressed himself laboriously every morning and afternoon, tying his cravat with the conscientiousness of a man basting a fowl lest it brown unevenly. He took regular exercise up and down the terrace walk, cane tapping out a measured rhythm as steady as a kitchen clock. Thus with his cane, his toilette, his bottles, his backgammon-box, and his newspaper, this worldly philosopher fenced himself against ennui. If he did not improve each shining hour like the bees by the widow’s garden wall, he at least got through one hour after another, and made his captivity tolerable. It was remarked presently that he grew fond of bringing the conversation round to the American war, the massacre of Wyoming, and the brilliant actions of Saint Lucie—the truth being he had a couple of volumes of the Annual Register in his bedroom, which he studied as a housewife studies a household book when company threatens.

Pen sometimes took the backgammon-box of a night, or listened to his mother’s simple music in the summer evenings; but he was restless and wretched for all. He has been known to be up before the early daylight and down at a carp-pond in Clavering Park: a dreary pool, with whispering rushes and green alders, and that peculiar damp smell of old water and decaying leaves that goes to the heart like memory. A milkmaid had drowned herself there in the Baronet’s grandfather’s time, and her ghost was said to walk still—though whether she walked in pattens or barefoot, and whether she sighed in the Clavering dialect or in some older tongue now lost, nobody could tell with certainty. Pen did not drown himself, as his mother in her terrors may have fancied; he went to fish there, and to think—think and think—while the float quivered in little eddies and the pond made small secret noises to itself, as if whispering gossip like the town.

If he got a bite he was excited enough; and in this way he occasionally brought home carps, tenches, and eels—cold, sleek, and ancient-looking—out of that melancholy water. The Major cooked them in the Continental fashion, with the importance of a man who can turn a provincial grief into a Parisian sauce. He would wipe the fish dry, score it neatly, and lay it to take a relish of herbs; he would speak of butter as if it were diplomacy; he would reduce a glass of white wine with shallots until it smelled sharp and promising, and then slip in the fish as delicately as he slipped a compliment into a widow’s ear. The kitchen at Fairoaks, which had been used to plain roasts and honest puddings, learned foreign accents. Even sorrow, when it comes into an English house, must submit to the discipline of dinner.

By the pond, under a tree which was his favourite resort, Pen composed a number of poems suitable to his circumstances—verses over which he blushed in after-days, wondering how he could ever have invented such rubbish. As for the tree: there was a hollow in it where he used to put his tin-box of ground-bait and other fishing gear; and in that hollow he afterwards—but we are advancing matters. Suffice it that he wrote poems and relieved himself. When a man’s grief is at the rhyming stage—when he cudgels his brain to find any rhyme for sorrow besides borrow and to-morrow—his woes are nearer their end than he thinks. So were Pen’s. He had hot and cold fits; days of sullenness and peevishness; of blank resignation; of despondency; and occasional mad paroxysms of rage and longing. In those fits Rebecca would be saddled and galloped fiercely about the country, or into Chatteris, her rider gesticulating wildly, startling carters and turnpike-men, crying out the name of the false one as if it were a curse that ought to crack the sky.

Mr. Foker became a very frequent and welcome visitor at Fairoaks during this period. His good spirits and oddities amused both the Major and Pendennis and astonished the widow and little Laura not a little. His tandem made a prodigious sensation in Clavering market-place; he upset a market-stall (and made compensation with a magnificence that was half apology and half advertisement), cut Mrs. Pybus’s poodle over the shaven quarters with a whip that was meant for the air, and drank a glass of raspberry bitters at the Clavering Arms with the air of a man founding a club.

All the society in the little place heard who he was and looked out his name in their Peerages. He was so young, and their books so old, that his name did not appear in many of their volumes; his mamma, now quite antiquated, figured among the progeny of the Earl of Rosherville as Lady Agnes Milton still.
