But his name, wealth, and honourable lineage were speedily known in Clavering; and you may be sure that poor Pen’s little transaction with the Chatteris actress was discussed with even greater punctuality than the price of barley.

Looking at Clavering St. Mary from the London road as it runs by the lodge at Fairoaks—seeing the rapid shining Brawl winding down from the town and skirting the woods of Clavering Park; the ancient church tower; the peaked roofs rising among trees and old walls; and behind them the sunshiny hills stretching westwards towards the sea—the place looks so cheery and comfortable that many a traveller’s heart must have yearned towards it from the coach-top, and he must have thought: Here, at the end of the struggle, one might rest; here the kettle would sing without malice; here the air itself would taste like bread.

Tom Smith, who drove the Alacrity coach, would often point to a tree near the river, from which a fine view of the church and town was commanded, and inform his companion on the box that “Artises come and take hoff the Church from that there tree—It was a Habby once, sir.” And indeed it is a pretty view, with the Brawl making its clean talk over stones, and the crows and bells sharing the sky between them.

But like Constantinople seen from the Bosphorus; like Mrs. Rougemont viewed in her box from the opposite side of the house; like many an object pursued in life and admired at a distance—Clavering is rather prettier far off than near. Close acquaintance shows blankness. Except on market days there is nobody in the streets. The clack of a pair of pattens echoes through half the place, and you may hear the creaking of the rusty old ensign at the Clavering Arms without being disturbed by any other noise. The soundscape, which on the road promised water and bells and industry, turns out in the streets to be mostly vacancy—an acoustic emptiness where each little noise makes a great show of itself, as a single spoon in an empty dining-room sounds insolent.

There has not been a ball in the Assembly Rooms since the Clavering Volunteers gave one to their Colonel, the old Sir Francis Clavering; and the stables that once held a great part of that brilliant but defunct regiment are now cheerless and empty, except on Thursdays, when farmers put up there and their tilted carts and gigs make a feeble show of liveliness; or on Petty Sessions, when the magistrates attend in what used to be the old card-room, and the old walls hear law where they once heard laughter.

On the south side of the market rises the church with its great grey towers; the sun illuminates delicate carving, deepens the shadows of huge buttresses, and gilds glittering windows and flaming vanes. The image of the Patroness was wrenched out of the porch centuries ago; such saints as were within reach of stones and hammers were maimed and headless. Of those out of reach, only Doctor Portman knew the names and histories: his curate Smirke was not much of an antiquarian, and Mr. Simcoe—husband of the Honourable Mrs. Simcoe, incumbent and architect of the Chapel of Ease in the lower town—thought them the abomination of desolation. It is a curious thing, how a village will forget its own stone alphabet, how names die even while the figures stand; and how the loudest voices in the present will insist that the past must speak their accent or be silent.

The Rectory is a stout, broad-shouldered brick house of Queen Anne’s reign. It communicates with the church and market by different gates and stands at the opening of Yew-tree Lane, where the Grammar School is (Rev. —— Wapshot); Yew-tree Cottage (Miss Flather); the butchers’ slaughtering-house (an old barn or brew-house of Abbey times); and the Misses Finucane’s establishment for young ladies. The two schools had their pews in the loft on each side of the organ until the Abbey Church grew rather empty—through the falling-off of the congregation, inveigled to the “Heresy-shop” in the lower town. Then the Doctor induced the Misses Finucane to bring their pretty little flock downstairs, and the young ladies’ bonnets made a tolerable show in the rather vacant aisles.

Nobody sat in the great pew of the Clavering family except the statues of defunct baronets and ladies: Sir Poyntz Clavering kneeling in a square beard opposite his wife in a ruff; Dame Rebecca Clavering, very fat in alto-relievo, borne up to Heaven by two little blue-veined angels who seemed to have a severe task—and so forth. How well Pen remembered those effigies afterwards, and how often in youth he scanned them while the Doctor grumbled the sermon from the pulpit and Smirke’s mild brow peered over the prayer-book! Statues and sermons alike spoke a language: the statues in silence, the sermon in a drawl; and Pen, in his anguish, understood both chiefly by their tone.

The Fairoaks folks were constant at the old church; their servants had a pew, so had the Doctor’s, so had Wapshot’s, and those of Misses Finucane’s establishment—three maids and a very nice-looking young man in livery. The Wapshot family were numerous and faithful. Glanders and his children came regularly: so did one of the apothecaries. Mrs. Pybus went turn and turn about to the Low Town church and to the Abbey. The Charity School and their families came of course. Wapshot’s boys made a good cheerful noise, scuffling with their feet as they marched in and up the organ-loft stair, and blowing their noses a good deal during the service. To be brief, the congregation looked as decent as might be in these bad times.

The Abbey Church was furnished with a magnificent screen and many hatchments and heraldic tombstones. Doctor Portman spent a great part of his income in beautifying his darling place; he had endowed it with a superb painted window bought in the Netherlands, and an organ grand enough for a cathedral—so that the very building seemed to insist, by colour and sound, on a kind of remembered splendour.

But in spite of organ and window—or because of the window, very likely, which had come out of a papistical place and was blazoned all over with idolatry—Clavering New Church prospered scandalously in the teeth of Orthodoxy. Many of the Doctor’s congregation deserted to Mr. Simcoe and the Honourable woman his wife. Their efforts had thinned the very Ebenezer hard by, which before Simcoe’s advent used to be so full you could see the backs of the congregation squeezing out of the arched windows. Mr. Simcoe’s tracts fluttered into the doors of all the Doctor’s cottages and were taken as greedily as honest Mrs. Portman’s soup—though the graceless people found fault with the soup, too, as people will, when a good thing comes from the wrong side of their quarrel.

With the folks at the Ribbon Factory by the weir on the Brawl—round which the Low Town had grown—Orthodoxy could make no way at all. Quiet Miss Myra was put out of court by impetuous Mrs. Simcoe and her female aides-de-camp. It was a hard burden for the Doctor’s lady: to see her husband’s congregation dwindle; to give precedence, on the few occasions when they met, to a notorious low-churchman’s wife who was the daughter of an Irish Peer; to know there was a party in Clavering—Clavering, their own town, on which her Doctor spent more than his professional income—who held him up to odium because he played a rubber at whist, and pronounced him a heathen because he went to the play. In her grief she besought him to give up play and rubber—indeed they could scarcely get a table now, the outcry was so dreadful—but the Doctor declared he would do what he thought right and what the great and good George the Third did (whose chaplain he had been). And as for giving up whist because silly folks cried out against it, he would play dummy to the end of his days with his wife and Myra rather than yield to their despicable persecutions.

Of the two families owning the factory (which had spoiled the Brawl as a trout-stream and brought all the mischief into the town), the senior partner, Mr. Rolt, went to Ebenezer; the junior, Mr. Barker, to the New Church. In a word, people quarrelled in this little place more than neighbours do in London; and in the Book Club which the prudent and conciliating Major Pendennis had set up—and which ought to have been neutral territory—they bickered so much that scarcely anybody was seen in the reading-room except Smirke, who though he kept up a faint amity with the Simcoe faction still had a taste for magazines and light worldly literature; and old Glanders, whose white head and grizzly moustache might be seen at the window; and of course little Mrs. Pybus, who looked at everybody’s letters as the post brought them, and read every advertisement in the paper. (The Clavering Reading-room, as every one knows, was held at Baker’s Library, London Street, formerly Hog Lane.)

One may imagine, then, the sensation in this amiable little community when the news reached it of Mr. Pen’s love-passages at Chatteris. It travelled from house to house like a bad smell from a scorched pan—everybody pretending they had not noticed it first, everybody sniffing very hard. It was discussed at high-church, low-church, and no-church tables; canvassed by the Misses Finucane and their teachers; and very likely debated by the young ladies in the dormitories, with much whispering and the peculiar half-hush that makes a dormitory more noisy than a kitchen. Wapshot’s big boys had their version, and eyed Pen curiously as he sat in his pew, or raised the finger of scorn at him as he passed through Chatteris. They hated him always and called him Lord Pendennis, because he did not wear corduroys like they did, rode a horse, and carried himself like a buck.

And if truth must be told, it was Mrs. Portman herself who became the chief narrator of the story. Whatever tales this candid woman heard, she was sure to impart them to her neighbours; and after she had been put into possession of Pen’s secret by the little scandal at Chatteris, poor Doctor Portman knew that next day it would be all over the parish of which he was rector. And so it was: at the news-room, at the milliner’s, at the shoe-shop and the general warehouse at the corner of the market; at Mrs. Pybus’s, at the Glanders’s, at the Honourable Mrs. Simcoe’s soirée, at the factory—nay, through the mill itself the tale was current in a few hours, and young Arthur Pendennis’s “madness” was in every mouth, pronounced in every accent, twisted into every dialect, until the thing itself was scarcely recognisable—so completely can a village translate a private pain into a public entertainment, and lose the original sense in the process.

All Doctor Portman’s acquaintances barked out upon him when he walked the street next day. The poor divine knew his Betsy was author of the rumour and groaned in spirit. Well, well—he consoled himself— it must have come in a day or two; and perhaps it was as well the town should have the real story instead of a worse one, which is always the village’s favourite cookery: take a plain fact, add a pinch of malice, stew it in conjecture, and serve it up cold.

What the Clavering folks thought of Mrs. Pendennis for spoiling her son, and of that precocious young rascal Arthur for daring to propose to a play-actress, need not be told at length. If pride exists among any folks in our country—and assuredly we have enough of it—there is none more deep-seated than that of twopenny old gentlewomen in small towns. “Gracious goodness,” was the cry, “how infatuated the mother is about that pert headstrong boy, who gives himself the airs of a lord on his blood-horse, and for whom our society is not good enough; and who would marry an odious painted actress off a booth, where very likely he wants to rant himself. If dear good Mr. Pendennis had been alive this scandal would never have happened.”

No more it would, very likely; nor should we have been occupied with Pen’s history. It was true he gave himself airs to the Clavering people. Naturally haughty and frank, their cackle and small talk and small dignities bored him; and he showed a contempt he could not conceal. The Doctor and the Curate were the only people he cared for in the place. Even Mrs. Portman shared the general distrust of him and of his mother—the widow—who kept herself aloof from village society and was sneered at accordingly because she tried, forsooth, to keep her head up with the great county families. She indeed! Mrs. Barker at the factory has four times the butcher’s meat that goes up to Fairoaks, with all their fine airs.

Etcetera, etcetera: let the reader fill up the rest according to his acquaintance with village scandal. It will suffice to show how a good woman, occupied solely in doing her duty, and an honest brave lad, impetuous, full of good, and wishing well to every mortal alive, found enemies and detractors among people to whom they were superior and to whom they had never done harm. The Clavering curs were yelping all round the house of Fairoaks and delighted to pull Pen down; and because the village itself was so quiet, each yelp sounded the louder, and echoed longer in the empty streets and in Pen’s already over-resonant heart.

Doctor Portman and Smirke were both cautious of informing the widow of the constant calumny pursuing poor Pen, though Glanders, being a friend of the house, kept the young man au courant. One may imagine Pen’s indignation. Was there any single man in the village he could call to account, and so shut the mouths of the rest? Presently some wags began to chalk “Fotheringay for ever!” and other sarcastic allusions upon the gate at Fairoaks. Another night, some inventive person brought a large playbill from Chatteris and wafered it there, as if the very threshold must be made to smell of grease-paint and candle-smoke.

On one occasion Pen, riding through the Lower Town, fancied he heard the factory boys jeer him; and finally, going through Doctor Portman’s gate into the churchyard where some of Wapshot’s boys were lounging, the biggest of them—a young gentleman of about twenty, son of a neighbouring small squire, living as parlour-boarder with Mr. Wapshot in that doubtful half-gentility which is always loudest—flung himself into a theatrical attitude near a newly made grave and began repeating Hamlet’s lines over Ophelia, with a hideous leer at Pen.

The young fellow was so enraged he rushed at Hobnell Major with a shriek very much resembling an oath, cut him furiously across the face with the riding-whip he carried, flung it away, calling on the cowardly villain to defend himself, and in another minute knocked the bewildered young ruffian into the grave which was waiting for a different lodger.

Then, fists clenched, face quivering with passion and indignation, Pen roared out to Hobnell’s gaping companions to know if any of the blackguards would come on. They held back with a growl and retreated as Doctor Portman came up to his wicket; and Mr. Hobnell, with nose and lip bleeding piteously, emerged from the grave, looking as if he had been badly buried before his time.

Pen, still looking death and defiance at the lads as they retreated towards their side of the churchyard, walked back through the Doctor’s wicket and was interrogated by that gentleman. The boy was so agitated he could scarcely speak; his voice broke into a sob as he answered. “The ——— coward insulted me, sir,” he said; and the Doctor passed over the oath and respected the emotion of the honest suffering young heart.

Major Pendennis, who like a true man of the world had a proper and constant dread of the opinion of his neighbour, was prodigiously annoyed by the absurd little tempest blowing from Chatteris and tossing about Master Pen’s reputation like chaff in a mill-yard. Doctor Portman and Captain Glanders had to support the charges of the whole Clavering society against the young reprobate, who was looked upon as a monster of crime, as if proposing to an actress were the same thing as poisoning the communion wine.

Pen said nothing at home about the churchyard scuffle; but went over to Baymouth and took counsel with his friend Harry Foker, Esq. Harry drove over presently in his drag to the Clavering Arms, whence he sent Stoopid with a note to Thomas Hobnell, Esq., at the Rev. J. Wapshot’s, and a civil message to ask when he should wait upon that gentleman.

Stoopid brought back word that the note had been opened by Mr. Hobnell and read to half a dozen of the big boys, on whom it seemed to make a great impression; and that after consulting together and laughing, Mr. Hobnell said he would send an answer “arter arternoon school,” which the bell was then ringing; and “Mr. Wapshot he came out in his Master’s gownd.” Stoopid, being learned in academical costume from attendance upon Mr. Foker at St. Boniface, delivered this intelligence with gravity, as if it were a message from a university rather than from a country schoolroom where lads’ tongues were sharper than their pens and their mirth noisier than the church organ.

Pen’s escapade—his furious notions of honour, his challenge, his whip-hand heroics—could no more be kept private than the smell of onions in a snug parlour. The whole neighbourhood had it in its nostrils by breakfast. Doctor Portman took the news as if Pen had flung a loaded sauce-boat at the Ten Commandments. Major Pendennis took it as if it were a little after-dinner story—highly improper, certainly, but seasoned and therefore amusing. Mrs. Pendennis took it as if the roof had fallen into the pudding.

To hear that her boy had been “violent,” “unchristian,” “ferocious in intention,” was to poor Helen like hearing that the bread had been dropped in the dirt and then served up with a smile. Every consequence she could imagine—discomfort, disgrace, crime, all the black kitchen-smoke of calamity—seemed to roll out of that one foolish squabble; and, above all things, she hungered (with a mother’s desperate appetite) to have him out of Chatteris, away from the actress who had brought so much fever into their quiet house.

Pen, when remonstrated with—when his mother pleaded and the Doctor stormed—assumed that grave, inflated earnestness which youth wears as solemnly as a new coat.

He was “very sorry,” he said, with the air of a man signing a treaty; but the insult, he protested, had come upon him “without provocation.” He would permit no man to insult him “upon this head” without vindicating his honour; and then, appealing to his uncle, demanded with great dignity whether he could possibly have acted otherwise “as a gentleman” than by resenting the outrage and offering satisfaction.

“Vous allez trop vite, my good sir,” said Major Pendennis, who had been sprinkling the lad with his own old campaigning notions—pistols and punctilio, a little gunpowder in the gravy. The Major was puzzled now to find the dish served back to him, piping hot. “Between men of the world, I don’t say. But between two schoolboys—ridiculous, my dear boy—perfectly ridiculous.”

“It is extremely wicked,” sobbed Mrs. Pendennis, “and unlike my son.” Her eyes filled, and her voice had the bewildered tremble of one who has tasted salt where she expected sugar.

Pen kissed her, and answered with pompous tenderness, “Women, dear mother, don’t understand these matters. I put myself into Foker’s hands. I had no other course.”

Major Pendennis shrugged and grinned as if he had just heard a clever epigram at his club. The young ones were certainly making progress.

Mrs. Pendennis, however, declared Mr. Foker a wicked little wretch, and was sure he would lead her dear boy into mischief if Pen went to the same college with him. She even threatened, in that impulsive maternal fashion, that she had “a great mind” not to let him go at all—until she remembered, like a hand laid on hers, that Pen’s father had always destined the boy for the very college where he himself had once had his brief education. That recollection, like an old family recipe, had authority; and the veto melted.

Go he was to go, at the October term. The authorities who presided over Arthur’s welfare had settled it as firmly as if they were salting down a ham for winter. Foker promised introductions to the right set; and Major Pendennis laid store on those introductions as a careful housekeeper lays store on knowing which butcher supplies the best joints. The Major, who could recite noble names as some men recite sauces, ran them off with relish.

“Mr. Foker knows the very best young men,” he said. “Pen will form acquaintances of the greatest advantage through life. The young Marquis of Plinlimmon is there—eldest son of the Duke of Saint David’s. Lord Magnus Charters is there—Lord Runnymede’s son, and first cousin of Mr. Foker. Lady Runnymede—Lady Agatha Milton—you remember. Lady Agnes will certainly invite him to Logwood. And far from being alarmed at his intimacy with her son—a singular and humorous, but most prudent and amiable young man—to whom we are under every obligation for his admirable conduct in the affair of the Fotheringay marriage—I look upon it as one of the luckiest things possible that Pen should have formed an intimacy with this most amusing young gentleman.”

Helen sighed. She supposed the Major knew best; he spoke of society as if it were a grand dinner at which one must be properly placed. Mr. Foker had been kind in the wretched Miss Costigan business; for that she was grateful. Yet she could not help a dim presentiment of evil, as one hears a far-off cart-wheel on a night road and knows it will soon be at the door. Quarrels, riots, “worldliness”—those harsh sounds, those jangling modern noises of the soul—frightened her for her boy.

Doctor Portman, for his part, was decidedly of opinion that Pen should go. He hoped the lad would read; he allowed a moderate indulgence in the best society too (as if prescribing wine by the glass). He expected Pen would distinguish himself; Smirke spoke very highly of his proficiency. The Doctor had heard him construe, and thought he acquitted himself remarkably well. Anyhow, to get him out of Chatteris was a great point; and Pen, distracted from private grief by public rows, said gloomily that he would obey.

Meanwhile, August and September brought assizes, races, dinners, visits—the whole clatter of county life, with its carriages and its clinking glasses and its perpetual talk, as if talk were the only harvest the gentry reaped. Miss Fotheringay continued to act and to take her farewells at the Chatteris Theatre. Her announced departure moved nobody very much except the few persons already named; and the polite county folks, who had London houses and could admire her there—when Fashion had first told them to—found nothing remarkable in the actress on the little Chatteris boards. Many a genius and many a quack have been chilled by that same provincial draught before and since.

Miss Costigan bore public neglect, and any other crosses, with a comfortable equanimity. She ate, drank, acted, slept, with the regularity of a person whose nature is like a well-managed kitchen range: always warm, always ready, never much disturbed by storms outside. What grief and harmful excitement a healthy dulness and cheerful insensibility save! One does not say Virtue is not Virtue because it was never tempted; only that dulness is a finer gift than we credit, and some are lucky whom Nature has endowed with a good store of that great anodyne.

Pen went drearily in and out of the play according to his fancy. His doings tortured his mother; her anxiety would often have led her to interfere, but Major Pendennis checked and encouraged her by turns, for the wily man fancied he saw a favourable change in the lad’s malady. One symptom pleased him exceedingly: an efflux of versification, violent as a boil-over.

Pen might be heard spouting lines in the shrubbery, or muttering them between his teeth at night among the home party, as if he were chewing rhymes like tough meat. One day, prowling about the house in Pen’s absence, Major Pendennis found a great book full of verses in the lad’s study—English and Latin, quotations set out in scholarly foot-notes, like little garnishes placed with care around the main dish.

He can’t be very bad, thought the Pall-Mall Philosopher; and he made Pen’s mother remark—perhaps not without a secret disappointment, for she loved romance like other soft women—that during the last fortnight the young gentleman came home quite hungry to dinner and showed a very decent appetite at breakfast.

“Gad, I wish I could,” said the Major, thinking ruefully of his dinner pills. “The boy begins to sleep well, depend upon that.” Cruel—true.

Pen had no one to confide in. He could not speak to his mother of his loves and mortifications; his uncle treated such matters with a guarded, worldly scorn that jarred on the lad’s sentiment; Foker was much too coarse for refined secrets. So Pen’s friendship for the Curate redoubled: he was never tired of having Smirke for a listener on that one subject. What is a lover without a confidant? He employed Mr. Smirke as Corydon does the elm-tree—to cut the name upon, to make it echo. He made Smirke ring continually with the name of the beautiful Amaryllis. When men have left off playing the tune, they care little for the pipe; but Pen fancied he had a great friendship for Smirke because he could pour his sighs into the Curate’s ears—and Smirke had his own reasons for being always ready.

Pen’s affection gushed into sonnets to the “friend of his heart.” He plied Smirke with Latin Sapphics and Alcaics—hot little dishes of scholarship, served up with love-sauce. The songs multiplied; Smirke declared them beautiful and believed it too. Pen, in return, expressed boundless gratitude that Heaven had sent him such a friend. He presented his tutor with his best-bound books, with his gold guard-chain, and even wished him to take his double-barrelled gun. He went into Chatteris and got a gold pencil-case on credit—he had no money, and was still in debt to Smirke for some of the Fotheringay presents—and gave it to the Curate with an inscription proclaiming unalterable and eternal regard. Smirke, of course, was pleased.

But Smirke was naturally dismayed at the contemplated departure of his pupil. When Arthur should go, his occupation and delight would go too. What pretext would remain for daily visits to Fairoaks, for a kind word or glance from the lady there—those small mouthfuls of comfort which nourished him better than Madame Fribsby’s frugal dinners? Arthur gone, Smirke could only visit like any other acquaintance; little Laura could not learn the Catechism more than once a week. He had curled himself like ivy round Fairoaks, and now felt the gardener’s hand approaching.

Should he speak his mind to the widow—go down on his knees? He turned over her words and looks as a cook turns over remembered flavours. She had praised his sermons three weeks ago; she had thanked him exceedingly for his present of a melon for a little dinner-party Mrs. Pendennis gave—oh, a melon properly chosen, with its cool scent and honeyed heart, is no mean ambassador. She had said she should always be grateful for his kindness to Arthur; and when he declared there were “no bounds” to his love for that dear boy, she had replied in a romantic manner, indicating her strong gratitude and regard for all her son’s friends. Should he speak out—or delay? If he spoke and she refused him—awful!—the gate of Fairoaks might be shut for ever; and within that door lay all the world for Mr. Smirke.

Thus we see how every soul carries its own private business, more pressing than another’s sorrow. While Mrs. Pendennis fretted at losing her boy—her anxious hold upon him in the mother’s nest whence he was to fly—while the Major’s great soul chafed inwardly, thinking of London parties and dukes and duchesses, and of his being marooned in a country hole by “cursed affairs”—while Pen tossed between passion and another sensation, unacknowledged yet but swaying him: a longing to see the world—Mr. Smirke lay awake with his own care, like a ticking clock in a silent room, hearing every sound of his hope and fear. How lonely we are; how secret. Two people may press the same pillow forty years and still each has a world under their own hat—each hears different music in the same room, each tastes a different taste from the same dish, because experience has its own dialect and no dictionary can translate it cleanly. But let us return to the solitary Smirke.

Smirke had one confidante: that most injudicious woman, Madame Fribsby. How she became “Madame,” nobody knew. She had left Clavering as Miss Fribsby for a London milliner’s; she pretended she acquired her title in Paris. How the French king, were he ever so obliging, could have made her “Madame,” need not detain us. She went away a bouncing young lass; she returned rather elderly, with a Madonna front and melancholy countenance, bought Mrs. Harbottle’s business for a song, took her elderly mother to live with her, was good to the poor, constant at church, and had the best of characters. But no one in Clavering—not even Mrs. Portman—read so many novels. She had time for it (few besides the Rectory and Fairoaks employed her), and perpetual perusal of works not so moral then as now had made her sentimentally absurd. In her eyes life was one immense love-match; she could not see two people together without fancying they were dying for each other.

The day after Mrs. Pendennis’s visit to the Curate—long ago recorded—Madame Fribsby settled it in her mind that Mr. Smirke must be in love with the widow, and she set to encourage the passion on both sides, as if she were basting a roast and keeping the fire up.

Mrs. Pendennis she rarely saw except in public and in her pew. The widow needed little millinery; she made much of her own. But on the rare occasions when Madame Fribsby received a visit from her, or paid respects at Fairoaks, she never failed to praise the Curate: what an angelical man; how gentle, studious, lonely; and she would wonder, with a sigh ready-made from her novels, that no lady took pity on him.

Helen laughed at such remarks and wondered why Madame herself did not pity and console her lodger. Madame Fribsby shook her Madonna front. “Mong cure a boco souffare,” she said, laying her hand where she indicated her “cure.” “It est more en Espang,” she added with a sigh, proud of her French, which flowed more readily than it meant. Mrs. Pendennis had no desire to penetrate the secrets of this wounded heart. Reserved, perhaps proud, she considered her son’s tutor merely an attendant on that young prince—respectable as a clergyman, certainly, but still a dependant. Madame’s constant allusions were not agreeable; yet Madame persisted in the pernicious error that the widow had a secret regard for Mr. Smirke.

Her lodger, however, was much more willing to talk. Every time after Madame praised the Curate to Mrs. Pendennis, she came away with the notion that Mrs. Pendennis had been praising him in return.

“Etre soul au monde est bien ouneeyoung,” she would say, glancing up at a print of a French carbineer in green coat and brass cuirass that decorated her room, like an old label from her Paris fable. “Depend upon it, when Master Pendennis goes to College, his Ma will find herself very lonely. She is quite young yet—you wouldn’t suppose her five-and-twenty. Monsieur le Cury—song cure est touchy—j’ang suis sure—Je conny cela biang—Ally, Monsieur Smirke.”

He blushed softly; sighed; hoped; feared; doubted; sometimes yielded to the delicious idea. His pleasure was to sit in Madame Fribsby’s little apartment and talk it over, while the milliner ran on in French, and her old mother—deaf as an old kettle at the back of the stove—understood not one syllable. This secrecy, made by accident and bad pronunciation, was to Smirke like a hedge around a forbidden garden.

So when Major Pendennis at last announced to the Curate that his nephew would go to college in October, and that Mr. Smirke’s valuable services would no longer be needed—at which the Major, speaking as grandly as a lord, professed himself exceedingly grateful and besought the clergyman to command his interests in any way—Smirke felt the critical moment had come. The thought racked him like toothache in a quiet night.

Madame Fribsby, naturally, had taken the strongest interest in Master Pen’s love affair with Miss Fotheringay. She went to Chatteris, saw the actress perform, and pronounced her old and overrated; and then talked Master Pen’s passion to death in her shop with the half-dozen old maids and old women in male clothes who form the genteel population of little towns. Captain Glanders, H.P., declared Pen was going to be a devil of a fellow and had begun early. Mrs. Glanders bade him check his horrid observations and respect his own wife, if he pleased. She said it would be a lesson to Helen for her pride and absurd infatuation about that boy. Mrs. Pybus observed that many were proud of very small things, and for her part she did not know why an apothecary’s wife should give herself such airs. Mrs. Wapshot called her daughters away from that side of the street one day when Pen, mounted on Rebecca, was stopped at the saddler’s for a new lash to his whip. One and all made visits of curiosity to Fairoaks, tried to condole or to bring the Fotheringay affair on the tapis, and were checked by Mrs. Pendennis’s haughty reserve and the Major’s frigid politeness.

Rebuffs do not put an end to gossip; they only make it louder, like a door slammed on a noisy crowd. Slander increased about the unlucky family at Fairoaks. Glanders—half-pay and a large family—fuddled on brandy-and-water instead of claret since leaving the Dragoons, had occasional entrée at Fairoaks and kept the Major informed of every story in Clavering. Mrs. Pybus took an inside place by the coach to Chatteris and went to the George on purpose to get particulars. Mrs. Speers’s man treated Mr. Foker’s servant to drink at Baymouth for a similar purpose. It was said Pen had hanged himself in despair in the orchard and his uncle had cut him down; or, on the contrary, that Miss Costigan had been jilted and not young Arthur; and that the whole affair had been hushed up by payment of a large sum—the exact amount of which several people could testify, varying beautifully with the imagination and spite of the teller.

Pen shook his mane and raged when these scandals—touching Miss Costigan’s honour and his own—reached him. Why was not Pybus a man (she had whiskers enough), that he might call her out and shoot her? Seeing Simcoe pass by, Pen glared so from Rebecca and clutched his whip so menacingly that the clergyman went home and composed—or thought over, for he delivered oral testimony at great length—a sermon upon Jezebel, theatrical entertainments (a double cut, for Doctor Portman was known to frequent such), and youth going to perdition; and it was clear to every capacity that Pen was meant, and the road alluded to.

After the affair with Hobnell, Pen was pronounced a murderer as well as a profligate; his name became a byword and terror in Clavering. Nor was he the only one talked of. The village began to chatter about his unlucky mother.

“It is all settled,” said Mrs. Pybus to Mrs. Speers; “the boy is to go to college, and then the widow is to console herself.”

“He’s been there every day, in the most open manner, my dear,” continued Mrs. Speers.

“Enough to make poor Mr. Pendennis turn in his grave,” said Mrs. Wapshot.

“She never liked him, that we know,” says one.

“Married him for his money. Everybody knows that: was a penniless hanger-on of Lady Pontypool’s,” says another.

“It’s rather too open, though, to encourage a lover under pretence of having a tutor for your son,” cried a third.

“Hush! here comes Mrs. Portman,” said someone, as the Rector’s wife entered Madame Fribsby’s shop to inspect the monthly book of fashions from London—fresh printed commandments of cap and trimming, which the country obeyed as devoutly as any creed.

And indeed Madame Fribsby could hold out no longer. One day, after she and her lodger had been talking of Pen’s approaching departure and the Curate had gone off to give one of his last lessons, Madame communicated to Mrs. Pybus—who stepped in with Mrs. Speers—her strong suspicion, her certainty almost, that an attachment existed between a certain clerical gentleman and a certain lady whose naughty son was growing quite unmanageable, and that a certain marriage would take place pretty soon.

Mrs. Portman saw it all, of course, the instant it was mentioned. What a sly fox that Curate was! Low-church too; she never liked him. And to think of Mrs. Pendennis taking a fancy to him after being married to such a man as Mr. Pendennis! Mrs. Portman could hardly stay five minutes at Madame Fribsby’s, so eager was she to run to the Rectory and tell Doctor Portman.

When Doctor Portman heard the intelligence, he flew into such a rage that his first movement was to break with his curate and beg him to transfer his services to some other parish.

“That milksop of a creature pretend to be worthy of such a woman as Mrs. Pendennis!” broke out the Doctor. “Where will impudence stop next!”

“She is much too old for Mr. Smirke,” Mrs. Portman remarked. “Why, poor dear Mrs. Pendennis might be his mother almost.”

Mr. Smirke had gone, as he went every day, on his modest pilgrimage to Fairoaks; and there, in Pen’s study upstairs, sat pretending to read with his pupil—pretending, that is, with that conscientious, clerical air with which a man will sometimes disguise to himself that he is watching a clock and counting down his own release.

It was in the early part of that same afternoon—so fine, so bright, so obligingly mild—that Mrs. Portman, having transacted her little pieces of business with Mrs. Pybus, found the weather almost indecently persuasive and extended her walk to Fairoaks to see her dear Mrs. Pendennis. One may call it a call; but when two ladies sit down together, tea between them, and the whole parish politely hushed outside, it is more like a sitting of council.

In the course of their conversation, Mrs. Portman let off a secret with that careful relish with which good people hand round a particularly rich preserve: you are expected to admire it, but not to spill it.

“It is about Mr. Smirke,” she said, lowering her voice as if the very china might repeat her. “He has—my dear—a long attachment. A very old attachment. And he has kept it quite private.”

Mrs. Pendennis drew herself up with a superb composure, as though no curate living could possibly be interesting, and yet felt, somewhere beneath her laces, the small inward alarm which all mothers keep ready folded like a pocket-handkerchief.

“And on whom,” she asked, “has Mr. Smirke bestowed his heart?”

“Why, my dear,” Mrs. Portman answered, “when first he came and used to dine at the Rectory, people said we wanted him for Myra; and we were forced to give up asking him. Then they said he was smitten in another quarter; but I always contradicted it, for my part, and said that you—”

“That I!” cried Mrs. Pendennis. “People are very impertinent. Mr. Smirke came here as Arthur’s tutor; and I am surprised anybody should dare to speak so—”

“’Pon my soul,” said Major Pendennis from his newspaper, dropping his double eye-glass with dignity into his hand, “it is a little too much.”

“I have no patience with that Mrs. Pybus,” Mrs. Pendennis continued, colouring indignantly.

“I told her there was no truth in it,” Mrs. Portman said. “I always said so. And now it comes out that my demure gentleman has been engaged to a young lady—Miss Thompson of Clapham Common—ever so long. I am delighted, for my part; and on Myra’s account too; for an unmarried curate is always objectionable about one’s house. And of course it is strictly private—strictly. But I thought I would tell you, as it might remove unpleasantnesses. Only mind—not a word.”

Mrs. Pendennis, with perfect sincerity, professed herself exceedingly glad. She hoped Mr. Smirke, so kind and amiable a man, would have a deserving wife. When Mrs. Portman departed, Helen and the Major discoursed on the intelligence with great satisfaction—Helen reproaching herself for her late haughty distance to Mr. Smirke, whom she had avoided, when she ought to have been grateful to him for Arthur’s sake.

“Gratitude to that sort of people,” said the Major, “is all very well; but familiarity is out of the question. The gentleman gives lessons and receives money like any other master. You are too humble, my good soul. There must be distinctions of ranks.”

But Helen—who had ranks enough in her heart to keep them from overflowing into her manners—would not hear of this; and now that Arthur was going away, and she remembered how politely Mr. Smirke had run messages, brought books, copied music, taught little Laura a dozen pretty things, and pressed kind little gifts upon her, she felt a sincere pang. So much so, that when Mr. Smirke came down from the study with Pen and lingered in the hall before departure, she actually went out, shook hands with him—with a slight blush that belonged properly to girlhood but suited her widow’s face well enough—and begged him to come into the drawing-room where, she said, they never saw him now.

And as there was to be a rather good dinner that day—good enough to make the house seem, for an hour, like its old self—she invited Mr. Smirke to partake of it. Mr. Smirke accepted with a gratitude so prompt and tender that one might have thought she had offered him not mutton but salvation.

Relieved by Mrs. Portman’s report of all former doubts and misgivings, Helen was exceedingly gracious during dinner; perhaps the more so because the Major was exceedingly reserved to the tutor of his nephew. When the Major asked Smirke to drink wine, he did it as if he were a sovereign bestowing a cup upon a very meritorious footman: so condescending that even Pen, who was ready to be as conceited as young men commonly are, could not help laughing.

Smirke did not care for the Major’s impertinences while he had Helen’s kindness to feed upon. He sat near her and exerted all the powers of his conversation—clerical and worldly in one—to please. He spoke of the Fancy Bazaar as though the very pin-cushions had souls; of the Great Missionary Meeting as though the tea-urn were consecrated; of the last new novel; of the Bishop’s excellent sermon; and of fashionable parties in London, which he knew by reading the newspapers with an industry that would have done honour to the Acts of the Apostles. In fine, he left no art untried by which a college divine with sprightly and serious talents, a taste for the genteel, irreproachable conduct, and a susceptible heart will try to recommend himself to the object of his affections.

Major Pendennis came yawning out of the dining-room very soon after Helen and little Laura had left it.

“What an unsufferable bore that man is,” he said, “and how he did talk!”

“He has been very good to Arthur,” Mrs. Pendennis said. “I wonder who the Miss Thompson is whom he is going to marry.”

“I always thought the fellow was looking in another direction,” said the Major.

“And in what?” asked Mrs. Pendennis, with that innocence which is sometimes the most provoking form of knowledge.

“Towards Helen Pendennis—if you must know.”

“Towards me! impossible!” Helen cried—who knew perfectly well it was not only possible but true. “His marriage will be a very happy thing. I hope Arthur will not take too much wine.”

Now Arthur, flushed with the pride of having the keys of the cellar (which is a kind of temporary coronation for a young gentleman), and remembering that very few more dinners would happen which he and his dear friend Smirke might share, had brought up a liberal supply of claret. When the elders and little Laura left him, he and the Curate began to pass the wine very freely indeed, as if it were a consolation one might ladle like soup.

One bottle very speedily yielded up the ghost; another shed more than half its blood before the two topers had been much more than half an hour together. Pen, with a hollow laugh and a voice that took a tragedy-tone upon it, drank a bumper to the falsehood of women, and said sardonically that wine at any rate was a mistress who never deceived and was always sure to give a man welcome.

Smirke gently protested that he knew women who were all truth and tenderness; and casting his eyes up towards the ceiling with a sigh, as if invoking some dear being who must not be named, drained his glass. The rosy liquor began to suffuse his face; it was as though a sunset had got into his very conscience.

Pen trolled over some verses he had been making that morning—verses which declared, with much noble groaning and a brave supply of capital letters in the mind, that the woman who had slighted his passion could not be worthy to win it; that he was awaking from love’s mad fever and therefore was of course leaving her; that a name once famous might again be heard in the land; and that though he never should be the happy careless boy of a few months ago, and though death was personally as welcome as life, yet for the love of one kind being—his mother—he would live, prove himself worthy of his race, and one day bring the false one to know what treasure and noble heart she had flung away.

He rolled out these verses in his rich sweet voice which trembled with emotion; and he blushed in that excited way of his, while his large honest grey eyes showed such genuine hearty sensibility that—had Miss Costigan owned a heart—she might have softened; and very likely she was, as he said, altogether unworthy of the affection he flung away at her and immediately reclaimed from the wine.

The sentimental Smirke was caught by the feeling as a moth is caught by candlelight. He grasped Pen’s hand across the dessert dishes and the glasses. The verses were beautiful. Pen was a poet—great poet. Heaven permitting, he would run a great career. The grief he endured would cleanse and strengthen him. Smirke had always prophesied the greatest and brightest things—once certain little weaknesses were corrected. “But you will get over these, my boy,” he cried; “you will get over these; and when you are famous and celebrated, as I know you will be, will you remember your old tutor and the happy early days of your youth?”

Pen swore he would, with another shake of the hand across the apricots and stemware. “I shall never forget how kind you have been to me, Smirke. I don’t know what I should have done without you. You are my best friend.”

“Am I—really, Arthur?” said Smirke, peering through his spectacles; and his heart began to beat so violently that, in his own imagination, it made a noise in the room louder than the clink of glass.

“My best friend. My friend for ever,” Pen said. “God bless you, old boy.” And he drank up the last glass of the second bottle of that famous wine which his father had laid in, his uncle had bought, Lord Levant had imported, and which now, like an indifferent slave, ministered pleasure to its present owner.

“We’ll have another bottle, old boy,” Pen cried. “By Jove we will. Hurray—claret goes for nothing. My uncle was telling me he saw Sheridan drink five bottles at Brookes’s besides a bottle of Maraschino. This is some of the finest wine in England, he says. So it is. There’s nothing like it. Nunc vino pellite curas—cras ingens iterabimus aeq—fill your glass, old Smirke, a hogshead of it won’t do you any harm.” And Pen began to sing the drinking-song out of Der Freischütz.

The dining-room windows were open. Outside, in the sweet disciplined hush of the evening—the birds taking their turns as politely as choristers, the lawn giving back a soft footfall instead of a street’s iron clatter—Mrs. Pendennis paced. Little Laura looked at the sunset. The fresh notes of the boy’s voice floated out; and the widow’s kind heart was cheered to hear him sing.

“You—you are taking too much wine, Arthur,” Mr. Smirke said softly. “You are exciting yourself.”

“No,” said Pen, “women give headaches; but this don’t. Fill your glass, old fellow, and let’s drink. I say, Smirke—my boy—let’s drink to her—your her, I mean; not mine, for whom I swear I’ll care no more—not a penny—not a fig—not a glass. Tell us about the lady, Smirke. I’ve often seen you sighing about her.”

“Oh!” said Smirke; and his beautiful cambric shirt-front and glistening studs heaved with the emotion that shook his gentle bosom.

“Oh—what a sigh!” Pen cried, hilariously. “Fill, my boy, and drink the toast. You can’t refuse a toast; no gentleman refuses a toast. Here’s her health—and good luck to you—and may she soon be Mrs. Smirke.”

“Do you say so?” Smirke whispered, trembling all over. “Do you really say so, Arthur?”

“Say so? Of course I say so. Down with it. Here’s Mrs. Smirke’s good health. Hip, hip, hurray!”

Smirke convulsively gulped down his glass. Pen waved his over his head and cheered so that his mother and Laura wondered on the lawn, and his uncle, dozing over the paper in the drawing-room, started and thought, That boy’s drinking too much.

Smirke set down the glass as though it were suddenly heavy with fate.

“I accept the omen,” he gasped, blushing. “Oh, my dear Arthur—you—you know her—”

“What—Myra Portman?” Pen cried. “I wish you joy; she’s got a dev’lish large waist; but I wish you joy, old fellow.”

“Oh, Arthur!” groaned Smirke, and nodded, speechless with misery.

“Beg your pardon—sorry I offended you—but she has got a large waist, you know—devilish large waist,” Pen went on, the third bottle beginning to do the sort of tutoring that is never paid for.

“It’s not Miss Portman,” Smirke said, in a voice of agony.

“Is it anybody at Chatteris or at Clapham? Somebody here? No—it ain’t old Pybus? it can’t be Miss Rolt at the Factory—she’s only fourteen.”

“It’s somebody rather older than I am, Pen,” the Curate cried, looking up and then guiltily down into his plate.

Pen burst out laughing. “It’s Madame Fribsby. By Jove, it’s Madame Fribsby. Madame Frib—by the immortal gods!”

The Curate could contain no more.

“O Pen,” he cried, “how can you suppose that any of those—of those more than ordinary beings you have named could have influence upon this heart, when I have been daily in the habit of contemplating perfection! I may be insane, I may be madly ambitious, I may be presumptuous—but for two years my heart has been filled by one image and known no other idol. Haven’t I loved you as a son, Arthur? Say—hasn’t Charles Smirke loved you as a son?”

“Yes, old boy, you’ve been very good to me,” Pen said; with a liking that was honest enough, though not in the least filial.

“My means,” rushed on Smirke, “are at present limited, I own; and my mother is not so liberal as might be desired. But what she has will be mine at her death. Were she to hear of my marrying a lady of rank and good fortune, my mother would be liberal—I am sure she would be liberal. Whatever I have or subsequently inherit—and it’s five hundred a year at the very least—would be settled upon her, and—and—and you at my death—that is.”

“What the deuce do you mean? and what have I to do with your money?” cried Pen, puzzled.

“Arthur—Arthur!” the other exclaimed wildly. “You say I am your dearest friend—let me be more. Oh, can’t you see that the angelic being I love—the purest, the best of women—is no other than your dear, dear angel of a—mother.”

“My mother!” cried Arthur, jumping up—sober in a minute, as if a bucket of cold water had been poured down his spine. “Pooh! Damn it, Smirke, you must be mad—she’s seven or eight years older than you are.”

“Did you find that any objection?” Smirke cried piteously—meaning, of course, the elderly subject of Pen’s own unlucky passion.

Pen felt the hit and blushed red. “The cases are not similar, Smirke,” he said. “And the allusion might have been spared. A man may forget his own rank and elevate any woman to it; but allow me to say our positions are very different.”

“How do you mean, dear Arthur?” the Curate interposed sadly, cowering as a man does who sees the axe lifted and yet cannot help presenting his neck.

“Mean?” Arthur cried. “I mean what I say. My tutor—yes, my tutor—has no right to ask a lady of my mother’s rank of life to marry him. It’s a breach of confidence. I say it’s a liberty you take, Smirke—it’s a liberty. Mean, indeed!”

“O Arthur!” Mr. Smirke began with clasped hands and a scared face; but Arthur stamped his foot and pulled at the bell.

“Don’t let’s have any more of this. We’ll have some coffee, if you please,” he said, with a majestic air which, if one must be unjust, is at least very soothing to oneself.

The old butler entered. Arthur bade him serve the coffee.

John said he had just carried coffee into the drawing-room, where his uncle was asking for Master Arthur; and the old man cast a glance of wonder at the three empty claret-bottles lined up like slain enemies. Smirke said he thought he’d—he’d rather not go into the drawing-room. Arthur, very high, answered, “As you please,” and called for Mr. Smirke’s horse.

The poor fellow said he knew the way to the stable and would get his pony himself; and he went into the hall and sadly put on coat and hat, as if clothing himself for exile.

Pen followed him out, uncovered. Helen was still walking up and down the lawn in the sunset hush, the day’s sounds thinning to that soft rural music which seems to preserve words as well as leaves. Smirke took off his hat and bowed farewell, then passed to the door leading into the stable-court, by which the pair disappeared.

Smirke fumbled at the girths of the saddle; Pen fastened them, put on the bridle, led the pony into the yard. Pen, touched in spite of himself by the grief on the other’s face, held out his hand; Smirke wrung it silently.

“I say, Smirke,” Pen said in an agitated voice, “forgive me if I have said anything harsh—for you have always been very, very kind to me. But it can’t be, old fellow, it can’t be. Be a man. God bless you.”

Smirke nodded, mounted, and rode out through the lodge-gate. Pen looked after him until he disappeared down the road and the clatter of hoofs died away into the evening’s proper quiet.

Helen was lingering on the lawn, waiting until the boy came back. She put his hair off his forehead and kissed it fondly. She was afraid he had been drinking too much wine. Why had Mr. Smirke gone away without any tea?

Pen looked at her; there was a kind humour beaming in his eyes she had not seen for a long while.

“Smirke is unwell,” he said, with a laugh.

For an hour at least, he was almost light again. He put his arm round her waist and walked her up and down the path in front of the house. Laura drubbed on the drawing-room window and nodded and laughed from it. “Come along, you two people,” cried Major Pendennis; “your coffee is getting quite cold.”

When Laura was gone to bed, Pen—big with his secret—burst out with it and described the dismal but ludicrous scene. Helen listened with many blushes, and a perplexity which Arthur, rogue that he was, enjoyed mightily.

“Confound the fellow’s impudence,” said Major Pendennis, taking his candle. “Where will the assurance of these people stop?”

Pen and his mother had a long talk that night, full of love, confidence, and laughter; and somehow the boy slept more soundly and woke more easily than he had done for many months before—his heart, after all its noisy complaints, finding relief in the one language that needed no translation between them.

Before the great Mr. Dolphin quitted Chatteris, he not only made an advantageous engagement with Miss Fotheringay, but left with her—liberally—a sum of money to pay off any debts the little family might have contracted during their stay; and which, chiefly through the lady’s own economy and management, were not considerable. The small account with the spirit merchant—which Major Pendennis had settled—was the chief of Captain Costigan’s debts; and though the Captain at one time talked about repaying every farthing, it never appears that he executed his menace, nor did the laws of honour in the least call upon him to accomplish that threat.

When Miss Costigan had seen all outstanding bills paid to the uttermost shilling, she handed over the balance to her father—who immediately broke out into hospitalities as if money were a kind of punch that must be drunk before it went flat. He gave the little Creeds more apples and gingerbread than he had ever bestowed upon them, so that Widow Creed ever after held the memory of her lodger in veneration, and the young ones wept bitterly when he went away; and in a word, he managed the money so cleverly that it was entirely expended within a few days, and he was compelled to draw upon Mr. Dolphin for travelling expenses when the time of departure arrived.

There was held at an inn in that county town a weekly meeting—festive, almost riotous—of a society of gentlemen who called themselves the Buccaneers. Some of the choice spirits of Chatteris belonged to this cheerful club: Graves, the apothecary (than whom a better fellow never put a pipe in his mouth and smoked it); Smart, the talented and humorous portrait-painter of High Street; Croker, an excellent auctioneer; and the uncompromising Hicks, able editor for three-and-twenty years of the County Chronicle and Chatteris Champion. Bingley, the manager, liked to join of a Saturday evening too, whenever he had permission from his lady—which was as necessary as a theatre-license and rather harder to obtain.

Costigan had been an occasional Buccaneer; but a want of punctuality of payments had of late somewhat excluded him from the Society, where he was subject to disagreeable remarks from the landlord, who declared that a Buccaneer who didn’t pay his shot was utterly unworthy to be a Marine Bandit. But when it became known to the “Ears” (as the clubbists called themselves) that Miss Fotheringay had made a splendid engagement, a great revolution of feeling took place. Solly, mine host of the Grapes—worthy as any fellow who ever stood behind a bar and heard the world confess itself over ale—told the gents in the Buccaneers’ room one night how noble the Captain had behaved: having been round and paid off all his ticks in Chatteris, including his score of three pound fourteen at the Grapes. Solly pronounced Cos a good feller, a gentleman at bottom; he, Solly, had always said so; and finally worked upon the feelings of the Buccaneers to give the Captain a dinner.

The banquet took place on the last night of Costigan’s stay and was served in Solly’s accustomed manner. Mrs. Solly produced as good a plain dinner of old English fare as ever smoked upon a table—meat honestly roasted, potatoes not ashamed of their skins, gravy that knew its duty and performed it; the whole accompanied by the clatter of plates, the scrape of chairs, and that rising tide of male conversation which, once it sets in, is as hard to dam as a mill-stream.

About eighteen gentlemen sat down. Mr. Jubber, the eminent draper of High Street, was in the chair, with the distinguished guest of the club on his right. The able and consistent Hicks officiated as croupier. Most of the club were present; and H. Foker, Esq., and Spavin, Esq., friends of Captain Costigan, joined too.

The cloth having been drawn, the Chairman said, “Costigan, there is wine, if you like,” but the Captain preferring punch, that liquor was voted by acclamation—as if the company had at last found a language in which his patriotism could be accurately expressed. “Non Nobis” was sung in admirable style by Messrs. Bingley, Hicks, and Bullby (of the Cathedral choir, than whom a more jovial spirit ne’er tossed off a bumper or emptied a bowl). Then the Chairman gave “The King!” which was drunk with the loyalty of Chatteris men; and, without further circumlocution, proposed their friend “Captain Costigan.”

After enthusiastic cheering had rung through old Chatteris and subsided, Captain Costigan rose and made a speech of twenty minutes, in which he was repeatedly overcome by his emotions.

He must be pardoned for incoherence, he said; his heart was too full. He was quitting a city celebrated for its antiquitee, its hospitalitee, the beautee of its women, the manly fidelitee, generositee, and jovialitee of its men. (Cheers.) He was going from that ancient and venerable city—of which, while Mimoree held her sayt, he should never think without fond emotion—to a methrawpolis where the talents of his daughther were about to have full play, and where he would watch over her like a guardian angel. He should never forget it was at Chatteris she had acquired the skill she was about to exercise in another sphere; and in her name and his own Jack Costigan thanked and blessed them.

The gallant officer’s speech was received with tremendous cheers.

Mr. Hicks, in a brilliant and energetic manner, proposed Miss Fotheringay’s health.

Captain Costigan returned thanks in a speech full of feeling and eloquence.

Mr. Jubber proposed the Drama and the Chatteris Theatre; and Mr. Bingley was about to rise, but was prevented by Captain Costigan, who, as long connected with the Chatteris Theatre and on behalf of his daughter, thanked the company. He informed them that he had been in garrison at Gibraltar and at Malta, and had been at the taking of Flushing. The Duke of York was a patron of the Drama; he had the honour of dining with His Royal Highness and the Duke of Kent many times; and the former had justly been named the friend of the soldier. (Cheers.)

Every man who has ever worn a cap too large for his wisdom, and a gown too long for his discretion, carries somewhere about him—like a nutmeg in his pocket, or a remembered smell of toast in a childhood passage—the tenderness of his University days. Youth begins there with a clink of keys and bells: the leading-strings are cut, and a fellow fancies he is a free agent because nobody tells him, this hour, not to put his elbows on the table.

And he drinks his first draught of liberty as if it were new cider—sharp, sparkling, unwholesome in quantity, and delicious beyond all reason. Old epicures, who are reduced by time and circumstance to nibbling poached eggs and pretending that water has a bouquet, can still take a keen pleasure in seeing young jaws work honestly; and I hope there is no age so crabbed, no experience so sour, that a man cannot be amused by the sound of a boy laughing at the world as though it were made for his entertainment.

Only a few weeks ago, coming back from a visit to the old University of Oxbridge (where my friend Mr. Arthur Pendennis once went to be improved), I was packed in a railroad carriage beside a young gentleman now studying at Saint Boniface. He had acquired an exeat by some miracle known only to college authorities and their victims, and was bound for a day’s riot in London. He talked from the first jolt to the last—cracking his jokes like walnuts, spilling his laughter as freely as a cook spills flour—till, when we reached the terminus, nothing would content him but a hansom, that he might be pitched into town the quicker and begin at once to waste his time with the most industrious zeal.

Off he went, whipped away into smoke and hurry, his face lit up as if London were a pie just taken from the oven. As for your humble servant—being encumbered only with a small carpet-bag and no appetite whatever for haste—I climbed to the outside of an omnibus and sat contentedly between a Jew-pedlar smoking a cigar that had clearly been steeped in old boots, and a gentleman’s servant who guarded a poodle as if it were the heir to an earldom. We waited until Fate filled the seats and lashed on the boxes; then the coachman rumbled away at a pace suited to digestion. We were not in a hurry to plunge into that near smoking Babylon. The pedlar did not dream of dining at a club; the servant did not long to dance at a casino. A few years more, and my young railroad companion will be no more eager either; he will have learned that pleasure, like porter, loses something when it is kept too long.

There were no railroads when Arthur Pendennis went up to Oxbridge. He travelled thither in a handsome coach, thick with dons, gownsmen, freshmen, and the guardians who conveyed them like parcels labelled FRAGILE. Major Pendennis sat within beside a fat City gentleman in grey stockings, whose pale-faced son—destined, no doubt, for great things in account-books—looked as if he had already been lectured into an early grave. The old citizen was frightened out of his propriety when he learned that the coach had been driven for a couple of stages by young Mr. Foker of Saint Boniface: a friend of all mankind (coachmen included), able to handle reins with the air of a man who has been born in a box-seat and christened with a whip.

Pen sat on the roof, peering at everything—coach, passengers, hedges, clouds—with the delighted hunger of a boy who has never yet been overfed with sights. When Oxbridge came in view, his heart gave such a jump you might have heard it above the rattle of wheels: venerable towers and pinnacles, tall elms, a shining river laid out like silver sauce beside the old brown city roofs. It looked to him like a dish long promised and at last set upon the table.

He had spent a few days in London first at his uncle’s lodgings in Bury Street. Major Pendennis declared the lad’s wardrobe wanted renewal; and Arthur, who could appreciate a good coat as readily as a good compliment, was by no means averse. The self-denying uncle made sacrifices in the boy’s behalf with that touching heroism which costs the martyr nothing but other people’s money.

London, in those days, was awfully lonely in the season. Pall Mall’s pavement seemed deserted; the very red jackets had migrated; faces in club windows were as scarce as pheasants in a poulterer’s shop on a bad day. The Major took his nephew into one or two of those quiet mansions, wrote down his name in a candidate-book, and thereby caused Pen a thrill of gratification so intense that it might almost have served as a dinner.

There, in cold parchment dignity, he saw himself set down as “Arthur Pendennis, Esquire, of Fairoaks Lodge, ——shire, and Saint Boniface College, Oxbridge; proposed by Major Pendennis; seconded by Viscount Colchicum.” Pen’s imagination instantly furnished the stucco-halls with his own future ease; he walked through libraries as if they were already his larders, and surveyed drawing-rooms with the proprietary eye of a young gentleman who had not yet learned that a door may be shut upon him. The Major laughed slyly at the boy’s strut; vanity in a comely lad always pleases an old man who has spent his life cultivating it as an art.

Pen and Foker drove down in the latter’s cab to Grey Friars to renew acquaintance with old comrades. The boys came crowding to the gates to admire the chestnut horse, the livery, the tights, and the grave countenance of Stoopid the tiger, who sat behind like a small footman nailed to a plank. The afternoon bell rang as they swaggered in the playground. The awful Doctor passed into school, grammar in hand. Foker shrank away, uneasy as a boy caught near a jam-closet; but Pen, blushing, went up and shook the dignitary’s hand, laughing inwardly to remember how that same Latin Grammar had once boxed his ears. He was generous, good-natured, and, like most generous good-natured youths, perfectly satisfied with himself.

Then to the parental brew-house: Foker’s Entire—an empire of vats and brick, with its gilded name shining from innumerable public-house signs like a lord’s arms on his tenants’ doors. The venerable junior partner and manager did honour to the young lord of the mash-tuns and his friend; and served them with silver flagons of brown stout so potent that you would have thought the very horse drank by sympathy. In truth, the animal rushed home westward at a pace which endangered pie-stalls and crossing-sweepers, brought cab-steps into alarming intimacy with corner-posts, and caused Stoopid to swing and clutch like a man clinging to a ship’s yard in a gale.

The Major was delighted to see Pen in such company. He listened to Foker’s artless stories with solemn approval; gave the two boys a fine dinner at a Covent Garden coffee-house—where the smell of hot joints and chopped herbs rose like incense, and the knives made their pleasant music on plates—and then took them to the play. But his chief bliss was obtained when Mr. and Lady Agnes Foker, being in London, requested the pleasure of Major Pendennis and Mr. Arthur Pendennis at dinner in Grosvenor Street.

“Having obtained the entrée into Lady Agnes Foker’s house,” the Major said to Arthur with affectionate solemnity, as if he were presenting him with a sacrament, “it behoves you, my dear boy, to keep it. Never neglect to call in Grosvenor Street when you come to London. Read up carefully, in Debrett, the alliances and genealogy of the Earls of Rosherville; and if you can, make some trifling allusions to the family—something historical, neat, complimentary: the sort of thing you, with a poetic fancy, can manage. Mr. Foker himself is worthy enough, though not of high extraction nor much education. He always makes a point of having some of the family porter served round after dinner; you will on no account refuse it—which I shall drink myself, though all beer disagrees with me confoundedly.”

And the heroic martyr did indeed sacrifice himself, and swallowed the porter with a face arranged for suffering, while old Mr. Foker, at the head of the table, made his time-honoured joke about Foker’s Entire. One would have given a guinea to see Major Pendennis’s grin at that venerable witticism—so sleek, so thankful, so calculated.

Lady Agnes, wrapped up in her son as a joint is wrapped in bacon, received Pen with cordiality, and astonished him by accounts of the severe studies her darling was pursuing, and which she feared might injure his precious health. Mr. Foker the elder burst into a horse-laugh at some of these speeches; and the heir winked knowingly at his friend over the tureen. Then her ladyship, beginning at Harry’s infancy and continuing without drawing breath, related his miraculous sufferings in measles and hooping-cough, his escape from drowning, the shocking tyrannies practised upon him at that horrid school (to which Mr. Foker would send him because he had been brought up there himself), and how she never would forgive that disagreeable Doctor—no, never. For an hour she ladled out maternal narrative as steadily as if she were serving soup.

When pheasants came with the second course—hot, rich, scented with their own wildness and the butter that had kissed them in the pan—the Major praised them as the finest birds he ever saw; and Lady Agnes said they came from Logwood (as the Major knew perfectly well), and begged both gentlemen would visit there—at Christmas, or whenever dear Harry was at home.

“God bless you, my dear boy,” said Major Pendennis to Arthur afterwards in Bury Street, as they lit their candles to go to bed. “You made that little allusion to Agincourt, where one of the Roshervilles distinguished himself, very neatly and well; though Lady Agnes did not quite understand it. Exceedingly well for a beginner—though you ought not to blush so, by the way. And remember through life: with an entrée—with a good entrée, mind—it is just as easy to have good society as bad. It costs a man, when properly introduced, no more trouble to keep his footing in the best houses than to dine with a lawyer in Bedford Square. Mind this at Oxbridge, pursuing your studies; and for Heaven’s sake be very particular in the acquaintances you make. The premier pas in life is the most important of all—did you write to your mother to-day?—No?—well, do, before you go, and call and ask Mr. Foker for a frank—They like it—Good night. God bless you.”

Pen wrote a droll account to his dearest mother: of London’s emptiness, the play, the visit to the old Friars, the brewery stout with its black froth, the Grosvenor Street dinner with its pheasants and its porter. At home, in the lonely house at Fairoaks, his mother said her prayers with a heart full of love that had no words for itself; and she and Laura read that letter, and those which followed, many times, and brooded over them as women do—turning each line as though it were a slice of bread to see where the sweetness lay.

It was Pen’s first step. Ah, what a dangerous journey begins with a first step, and how often the brave stumble where they meant to stride. Brother wayfarer, may you have a kind arm linked in yours; may truth guide, mercy forgive at the end, and love go always with you. Without that lamp, the road is blind indeed, and the night very black.

So the coach drove up to the ancient and comfortable inn called the Trencher, in Main Street, Oxbridge. Pen, with eagerness, remarked for the first time gownsmen going about; chapel bells clinking—for in Oxbridge the bells ring from morning-tide till even-song, a continual silver rain of sound that freshens the spirit if one is not too fashionable to hear it. How different from London’s iron uproar, its cart-rattle and hammer-clang and shouting—noise without meaning, as if the city had forgotten its own language and spoke only in wheels. Here the sound had lineage; it belonged to the place as yeast belongs to old dough, and made the air itself seem alive.

Towers and pinnacles rose calm over gables and antique roofs, above a homely, busy city that smelt of river damp, old stone warmed by sun, ink, leather, and dinners. Communications had passed between Dr. Portman (on Pen’s part) and Mr. Buck, Tutor of Boniface, with whom Pen was entered. As soon as Major Pendennis had arranged his personal appearance into that expression which might convey at once gentility and authority, he and his nephew walked down Main Street, passed Saint George’s great gate and belfry-tower, and came to Saint Boniface.

Again Pen’s heart beat as they entered at the wicket of the venerable ivy-mantled gate. Above it rose an ancient dome almost hidden by creepers; the effigy of the Saint looked down with a stone serenity, while coats-of-arms of royal and noble benefactors told, in painted heraldry, stories that many a modern tongue could no longer pronounce. The porter pointed out a queer old tower at the quadrangle corner by which Mr. Buck’s rooms were approached. They crossed the square, and Pen’s eyes drank in everything with the thirst of first impressions: the little fountain playing in the centre, making its own cool music; the tall chapel windows and buttresses to the right; the hall with its tapering lantern and oriel window; the lodge doors, from which the Master issued with rustling silks; the carved chimneys, grey turrets, quaint gables. The Major surveyed all with calmness, having a gentleman’s indifference to picturesqueness and eyes somewhat dimmed by the perpetual glare of Pall Mall.

Saint George’s, huge and consecrated, with its four vast quadrangles, its beautiful hall and gardens, lay near and gave its men airs. The Georgians wore gowns of a peculiar cut and superiority of a still more peculiar. Little Saint Boniface was but a hermitage beside that great pile; yet, for its size, it kept an excellent name. Its ton was good; the best families of certain counties had time out of mind sent their young men there; the college livings were remarkably comfortable; fellowships easy; Boniface men had a generous share of honours; their boat was third on the river; their chapel-choir not inferior to Saint George’s; and, best point of all, their ale the best in Oxbridge.

In the wainscoted College Hall, and about Roubilliac’s statue of Saint Boniface (who stood in seraphic benediction over uncommonly good cheer), portraits of eminent Bonifacians looked down at dinner with painted gravity. There was learned Doctor Griddle, who suffered in Henry VIII.’s time, and Archbishop Bush who roasted him; Lord Chief Justice Hicks; the Duke of St. David’s, K.G., Chancellor of the University; Sprott the Poet, of whose fame the college was proud; Doctor Blogg, late Master and friend of Doctor Johnson. Their coats-of-arms flashed emerald and ruby, gold and azure in the tall windows; a whole vocabulary of rank and memory—much of it, like forgotten dialects, meaningful only to the initiated, and yet powerful enough to make a freshman sit up straighter as if grammar and genealogy were one.

The venerable cook of the college was one of the best artists in Oxbridge (his son had taken highest honours at Camford), and the wine in the fellows’ room was famed for excellence and abundance. Into this snug arbour among the groves of Academe Pen now found his way, leaning on his uncle’s arm, and they reached Mr. Buck’s rooms.

Mr. Buck, having received previous information from Dr. Portman, was cordial to the young freshman and his guardian. Portman had described Arthur as “a young gentleman of some fortune and landed estate, of one of the most ancient families in the kingdom, and possessing such a character and genius as were sure, under proper guidance, to make him a credit to the college and the university.” Under such recommendations, the tutor invited the Major to dine in hall, that he might see his nephew wear gown and eat commons for the first time; requested them to take wine afterwards; and—upon the strength of Arthur’s reported merits—offered him the best set of rooms in college: a gentleman-pensioner’s set, luckily vacant.

They parted till dinner, which was near at hand. Major Pendennis pronounced Mr. Buck uncommonly civil indeed; and when a college magnate chooses to be polite, no man can be more splendidly courteous. These reverend gentlemen, immersed in books and excluded from the world, have a solemn magnificence of compliment; when they rustle and swell in their state manners, you feel you are being bowed to by the University itself.

On returning into Mr. Buck’s anteroom—handsome, turkey-carpeted, hung with excellent prints and richly framed pictures—they found the tutor’s servant waiting, with a man bearing a bag full of caps and a number of gowns. Pen was in a tremor of pleasure as the bustling tailor tried on a gown and pronounced it an excellent fit. Then Arthur set the pretty college cap on his head with a dandified touch, a little on one side, as he had seen Fiddicombe, the youngest master at Grey Friars, wear it. He inspected himself in one of the great gilt mirrors. Some college divines, it appears, are no more above a looking-glass than ladies are, and consider the set of a gown with an anxiety almost devotional.

The Major smiled to see the boy dandifying. He was not displeased with the comely lad’s appearance. Then Davis, the skip, led the way across the quadrangle, keys jingling like a small bell-chorus, and brought them to the rooms destined for the freshman, vacated by the retreat of the gentleman-pensioner Mr. Spicer.

They were comfortable rooms, with large cross-beams, high wainscots, and small windows sunk in deep embrasures. Mr. Spicer’s furniture remained, to be sold at a valuation. Major Pendennis agreed to take what was available, though he and Pen both laughingly declined six sporting prints and four groups of opera-dancers with gauze draperies that formed the late occupant’s pictorial collection. A man can be a gentleman-pensioner, it seems, without pensioning his taste.

Then they went to hall.
