Pen sat down with his brother freshmen and ate his commons—bread with honest crust, meat properly browned, the steam smelling of pepper and fat and that indefinable comfort which is called dinner when one is young. Above, the Major took his place at high table among dignitaries and other fathers or guardians who had brought their sons up to Oxbridge and now watched them begin to feed as if watching them begin to live.

After hall they went to Mr. Buck’s to take wine; after wine to chapel, where the Major sat with gravity in the upper place, with a fine view of the Master in his carved throne under the organ-loft. Doctor Donne sat magnificent with the great prayer-book before him—statuesque piety in silk and solemnity. The freshmen behaved with decorum; but Pen was shocked to see that atrocious little Foker, arriving very late, and half a dozen comrades in the gentleman-pensioners’ seats giggling and talking as if they were in stalls at the Opera. These things, remember, happened some years back when William the Fourth was king. Young men are much better now—besides, Saint Boniface had the name of being rather fast.

Pen could hardly sleep that night at the Trencher, so eager was he to begin his college life and get into his own apartments. What did he think of as he tossed? His mother at home—pious soul whose life was bound up in his? Yes, let us hope he thought of her a little. Miss Fotheringay and his eternal passion? That passion which had kept him awake so many nights and made him wretched with longing? He had a trick of blushing; and had you been there (the candle not out), you might have seen his face redden more than once as he broke into incoherent exclamations regarding that luckless episode.

His uncle’s lessons had not been thrown away upon him: the mist of passion had lifted, and he saw her as she was. To think he—Pendennis—had been enslaved by such a woman, and then jilted by her! That he should have stooped so low to be trampled in the mire! That there was a time—only months back—when he was willing to take Costigan for his father-in-law! “Poor old Smirke!” Pen presently laughed out. “Well, I’ll write and try to console the poor old boy. He won’t die of his passion—ha, ha!”

The Major, had he been awake, might have heard a score of such ejaculations. Perhaps it would have been better, on the eve of the battle of his life, to have kept a different vigil; but the world had got hold of Pen in the shape of his selfish old Mentor. Those who care for his character must already have seen that he was weak as well as impetuous, vain as well as frank; generous, yet a little selfish amid his profuseness; and fickle too, as eager pursuers of self-gratification often are. Six months’ passion had aged him; there was a gulf between Pen the victim of love and Pen the innocent boy of eighteen sighing after it. He came to Oxbridge with a sense of superiority already, an experience that was not wisdom but had the insolent air of it; and that conceit and imperiousness, which afterwards grew upon him, gave him a kind of command over the young men with whom he now began to live.

In the morning he and his uncle passed hours with great satisfaction making purchases to render the rooms more comfortable. Mr. Spicer’s china and glass were in a dreadfully dismantled condition; his lamps smashed; his bookcases too small for the shelves that would be required to receive the contents of the boxes lying at Fairoaks, addressed to Arthur in the hand of poor Helen.

Those boxes arrived in a few days—packed by his mother with loving care. Pen was touched as he read the superscriptions in that dear well-known hand. He set everything in its place: books—old friends—linen and table-cloths chosen from the family stock; jam-pots which little Laura had bound in straw; a hundred simple gifts of home, smelling faintly of pantry and lavender and the quiet dialect of Fairoaks that no Oxbridge man could ever speak quite right.

Pen had another Alma Mater now.

But it is not all children who take to her kindly.

Pen was not sorry when his Mentor took himself off on the second day after their arrival at Oxbridge; and the Major, for his part, wore the air of a man who has at last set down a weighty dish he never meant to carry farther than the kitchen door. More than three months of his valuable leisure had that heroic martyr bestowed upon his nephew—three months in which the Major might have been improving his complexion at Cheltenham, or improving his acquaintance at great houses where the pheasants were fat and the people fatter. We are all ready enough to risk our heads for “honour,” which is a light thing to pack; but ask a man to give up his morning, his nap, his dinner, his favourite chair, his favourite talk, his favourite sauce—and see how soon his courage falls flat like a soufflé taken too early from the oven.

So Foker and Pen saw the Major off in the coach; and Foker, whose benevolence always expressed itself in the imperative mood, gave the coachman such particular instructions to “take care of that gentleman inside,” that it was wonderful the man did not climb in too and sit on the Major’s knees by way of security. The elder Pendennis was pleased: his boy, he fancied, was in the hands of a young fellow who could usher him into the very best set—like a well-trained waiter who knows which door opens upon the great dining-room. The Major rushed to London and thence to Cheltenham; and from that watering-place—where they give you water with an expression as if it were claret—he descended upon neighbouring mansions not yet migrated abroad, where society and shooting were still in season, and noise in the proper places (a crack of a gun, the crunch of boots on gravel) drowned the improper noises (the clink of small talk, the rattle of vanity).

If I were to tell every step of Pen’s university life at the pace of this chapter, some descendant of mine would have to take up the ladle when I drop it, and keep stirring the pot for the entertainment of a future generation. Besides, the daily life of boys—alas!—does not bear inspection like a well-browned joint. I wish it did. I ask you, does yours? So long as what we call our “honour” looks fair on the outside, we are content to let the inside be—how shall I put it—less wholesome than the cook pretends. Women keep their milk sweet longer than men; we have trained them to self-denial as we train orchards to yield: pruning, tying, and expecting fruit. But you, my good sir, with your whiskers and your opinions, what sum of sacrifices will you truly carry to your credit? There now—let us not poison the soup by talking of such things.

During Pen’s first term he attended classical and mathematical lectures with tolerable assiduity; and then discovered two facts. The first was that the exact sciences were a dish for which he had no appetite, no teeth, and no patience; the second, that one or two very vulgar young men—fellows who wore their trousers without straps, leaving their ankles exposed like raw joints in a butcher’s window above thick coarse shoes and stockings—beat him completely in the lecture-room. Pen could endure a great many things; but he could not endure being outdone by a man who looked as if he had never heard a spoon clink against china in his life. So he gave up mathematics and announced to his fond mother that he would devote himself exclusively to Greek and Roman literature.

Mrs. Pendennis was delighted that her darling should pursue the branch of learning to which he had the greatest inclination, and only besought him not to ruin his health by too much study; for she had heard frightful histories of young men who, by over-fatigue, brought on brain-fevers and died in the very midst of their career—like custards that curdle at the moment of triumph. Pen, whose health had always been handled by his mother as delicately as a thin-stemmed wineglass, promised he would not sit up too late; and in this particular he kept his word with more steadfastness than he showed in some other small vows a young gentleman will make when his conscience is warm and his head cool.

Presently he found, too, that the classical lecture was no better than the mathematical—only in a different manner. In one, his companions were too clever for him; in the other, they were too dull. Mr. Buck, the tutor, could, no doubt, parse and count feet with a humdrum conscientiousness—like a man weighing out flour who has never smelt fresh bread—but of poetry he had no more sense than Mrs. Binge the bed-maker. Pen grew tired of hearing the tutor and the students blunder and stumble through a few lines of a play, when he could read it in a tenth of the time, and taste the flavour at once, without having it chopped and served cold. Private reading, he discovered, was the only study that nourished; and he informed his mamma he should read much more by himself and much less in public. She knew no more about Homer than about Algebra; but she had faith in her boy as devoutly as she had faith in the rector, and was perfectly sure Arthur would earn the place he merited.

He did not come home until after Christmas, to the disappointment of his mother and of Laura, who had been longing for him to build a fine snow-fort as he had done three winters before—a domestic epic of white walls and frozen fingers, with the sound of laughter muffled by falling flakes. But Pen was invited to Logwood, Lady Agnes Foker’s, where there were private theatricals and a gay party of very fine folks—some of whom Major Pendennis would on no account have his nephew neglect. However, he spent the last three weeks of the vacation at home, and Laura could remark what a quantity of fine new clothes he brought, and his mother admired his improved appearance and his manly decided tone, as if a tailor had stitched courage into the seams.

At Easter he did not come home at all; but when he arrived for the long vacation, he brought more smart clothes still: wonderful shooting-jackets in the morning, with buttons that seemed to have been invented solely to catch the sun; and at night velvet waistcoats gorgeous enough to make a modest man blush for his own plain linen, with richly embroidered cravats and curious finery which had the air of being half raiment, half confectionery. His mother, in her gentle prowling about his room (a mother’s feet make no more noise than a cat’s when curiosity is pious), discovered a dressing-case with silver mountings, rings and jewellery, and—crowning insult to the dead—an elegant French watch and gold chain in place of the big old chronometer which had once hung from Dr. John Pendennis’s fob, jingling with seals, and measuring time while that good man measured pulses. It was but a few months since Pen had longed for that very chronometer, deeming it the most august timepiece in the world; and just before he went to college his mother had taken it from her trinket-box—where it had lain unwound since her husband’s death—and given it to him with a solemn little speech about his father’s virtues and the proper use of time. Pen now pronounced it “out of date,” and even compared it to a warming-pan, which Laura, who loved relics as she loved old receipts, thought downright irreverent. He left the watch in a drawer among soiled primrose gloves, abandoned cravats, and that other school watch of his which has already played its part in this history.

Rebecca, the old horse—an honest creature whose hoofbeats were part of the household music—was declared “no longer up to his weight,” and swapped for a more powerful animal at a heavy figure. Mr. Pendennis supplied the money; Laura cried when Rebecca was led away; and the stable yard, which had known her familiar snort and the soft munch of her hay, sounded suddenly emptier, as if a note had been removed from the farm’s daily tune.

Pen also brought down a large box of cigars with names that seemed invented by foreign cooks—Colorados, Afrancesados, Telescopios, Fudson Oxford Street, and the like—and began consuming them about the stables and greenhouses, where the smoke, he declared, was “very good for the plants,” and in his own study, which his mother at first disapproved. But he was at work upon a prize-poem, he said, and could not compose without a cigar; and he quoted Lord Byron in defence of the practice, as a man quotes a recipe by a celebrated chef when asked why he uses so much pepper. Since he smoked “to such good purpose,” Mrs. Pendennis could not refuse permission. Indeed, she came in one day and found him on the sofa in the midst of his labours—his “labours” consisting partly in consulting a novel recently appeared, for the cultivation of light literature had become, in his view, as necessary to genius as butter to toast. Rather than disturb him, she went into his bedroom, fetched the light-box and cigar-case, put the cigar into his mouth with her own hand, and lighted it for him. Pen laughed, kissed her hand as it hovered fondly over the sofa-back, and said, “Dear old mother, if I were to tell you to burn the house down, I think you would do it.” And it is likely he was right; her devotion was that domestic kind which will season any dish, even when the dish itself is questionable.

Along with English “light literature,” this diligent student brought boxes of French light literature too; and when Helen dipped into the leaves, she found things that made her open her eyes as if she had tasted vinegar when expecting cream. Pen explained—very gravely—that he did not write the books; that it was necessary to keep up his French by acquaintance with the most celebrated writers of the day; that it was as clearly his duty to read the eminent Paul de Kock as to study Swift or Molière. Mrs. Pendennis yielded with a sigh of perplexity, feeling that modern learning, like modern cookery, was full of spices she could not name. Miss Laura was warned off those volumes—by her anxious mother, and by that rigid moralist Mr. Arthur Pendennis himself; for, though he might be called upon to sample every dish in the intellectual kitchen in order to form his mind and perfect his style, he would by no means prescribe such tasting to a young lady whose business in life, he said, was “very different.”

In the course of this long vacation Mr. Pen drank up the bin of claret which his father had laid in—a claret of which Pen had once remarked that there was not a headache in a hogshead; and when it was exhausted, he wrote for more to “his wine merchants,” Messrs. Binney and Latham of Mark Lane, London. Old Doctor Portman had recommended that house when Pen first went to college, advising him to get port and sherry from honest London merchants rather than have recourse to Oxbridge tradesmen whose liquor, if memory served, was both dear and deleterious. “You will, no doubt, have to entertain your young friends at Boniface with wine-parties,” the worthy rector had said, remembering the customs of his own time, when young gentlemen thought hospitality began in the cellar and ended in the head.

So Pen ordered a stock for the cellars at Fairoaks, and hinted that Messrs. Binney and Latham might send in his university account for wine at the same time with the Fairoaks bill. Mrs. Pendennis was frightened at the amount; it struck her like the sudden clatter of a factory cart passing a quiet lane—too loud, too heavy, too new for comfort. Pen laughed at her old-fashioned views, said the bill was moderate, that everybody drank claret and champagne now; and finally the widow paid, feeling dimly that the household expenses were swelling like dough left too near the fire, and that her narrow income would scarcely suffice. But the extravagance, she told herself, was only occasional. Pen came home but for weeks at a time. Laura and she could pinch when he was gone. In the brief time he was with them, ought they not to make him happy? So the house, which kept its country quiet all year—the creak of the pantry door, the caw in the elms, the soft rural hush—was for a few weeks invaded by the pop of corks and the bustle of a young gentleman’s pleasures, as if some travelling fair had pitched its tents on the lawn.

Arthur’s own allowances were liberal—indeed, more liberal than those of the sons of far wealthier men. Years before, the thrifty affectionate John Pendennis, whose darling project had been to give his boy a university education denied to himself by his own father’s extravagance, had begun laying by money which he called Arthur’s Education Fund. In his books the executors found sums vested year after year as A. E. F.; and after her husband’s death, before Pen went up, the widow added to it too, so that when he entered Oxbridge it had reached no inconsiderable amount. “Let him be liberally allowanced,” was Major Pendennis’s maxim. “Let him make his first entrée into the world as a gentleman, take his place with men of good rank: after giving him the means, it will be his duty to hold it. There is no such bad policy as stinting a boy—or putting him on a lower allowance than his fellows.” Arthur would have to face the world and fight for himself presently; meanwhile they should procure him good friends, gentlemanly habits, and have him well backed and trained against the time when the real struggle came. These opinions were, no doubt, partly just, and partly convenient; for it is easier to be generous with other people’s money than with one’s own.

Thus young Pen—the only son of an “estated” country gentleman, with a good allowance and a gentlemanlike bearing—looked to be a lad of much more consequence than he truly was; and Oxbridge authorities, tradesmen, and undergraduates treated him as quite a young buck, a sort of aristocracy in embryo, to be handled carefully like a delicate glass and charged accordingly. His manner was frank, brave, and perhaps a little impertinent, as becomes a high-spirited youth. He was generous and free-handed with money that seemed plentiful. He loved joviality, and had a good voice for a song; and though boat-racing had not yet risen to the frenzy it has since attained, riding and tandem-driving were the fashions of ingenuous youth. Pen rode well to hounds, appeared in pink as became a buck, and though not outrageously extravagant in any single amusement, contrived to run up a fine bill at Nile’s livery-stables and in a number of other quarters. It is not one blazing kitchen-fire that burns down a house, but a dozen little candles left unattended.

For this lucky young gentleman had almost every taste to a considerable degree. He loved books of all sorts: Doctor Portman had taught him to relish rare editions, and Pen’s own palate ran to handsome bindings. It was marvellous what tall copies, what gilding, marbling, and blind-tooling, the booksellers and binders contrived to pile upon his shelves. He had a fair taste in art too, and a keen relish for high-school prints—none of your French opera-dancers or tawdry racing prints, such as had delighted the simple eyes of Mr. Spicer before him, but your Stranges and Rembrandt etchings and Wilkies before the letter; and his rooms became furnished with what the university allowed to be “perfect good taste.” He had a partiality for rings, jewellery, and fine raiment; and it must be owned that during his time at Oxbridge Mr. Pen was rather a dressy man and loved to array himself in splendour. He and his polite friends would dress themselves with as much care to dine at each other’s rooms as other folks would use who were going to enslave a mistress. They said he wore rings over his kid gloves—a charge he always denied; but youth will commit follies with admirable gravity. That he took perfumed baths is true; and he used to say he required them after meeting certain men of a very low set in hall—as if the sound of their broad vowels and heavy boots left a smudge upon his ears and skin alike.

In Pen’s second year, when Miss Fotheringay made her chief hit in London, and prints of her were published by the score, Pen hung one of them in his bedroom and confided to the men of his set how awfully, wildly, madly, passionately he had loved that woman. He showed them, in confidence, the verses he had written to her; his brow would darken, his eyes roll, his chest heave as he recalled that “fatal period” and described the woes and agonies he had suffered. The verses were copied out, handed about, sneered at, admired, passed from coterie to coterie like a favourite dish whose recipe everyone steals while pretending disdain. There are few things that elevate a lad in the esteem of other lads more than the reputation of a great romantic passion. Perhaps it is noble at any time; among very young men it is heroic. Pen was pronounced a tremendous fellow. They said he had almost committed suicide; that he had fought a duel with a baronet about her. Freshmen pointed him out. At promenade time, at two o’clock, when he swaggered out of college surrounded by his cronies, he was famous to behold—elaborately attired, ready to ogle the ladies who came to lionise the university, and to give his opinion upon their charms or their toilettes with the gravity of a critic whose experience entitled him to speak. Men said they had been walking with Pendennis, and were as pleased to be seen in his company as some of us would be if we walked with a duke down Pall Mall. He and the Proctor capped each other as they met, like rival powers; and the undergraduates scarcely knew which was the greater authority—law in a gown, or fashion in a velvet waistcoat.

In truth, during his second year Arthur Pendennis became one of the men of fashion in the university. It is curious to watch the easy admiration and simple fidelity of youth: how they cluster round a leader, wonder at him, love him, imitate him. No generous boy ever lived who did not worship another boy a little. Monsieur Pen at Oxbridge had his school, his faithful band, and his rivals. When young men heard at the haberdashers’ that Pendennis of Boniface had ordered a crimson satin cravat, you might see two dozen crimson satin cravats in Main Street within the week; and Simon the jeweller was known to sell no less than two gross of “Pendennis pins,” from a pattern the young gentleman had selected—so that Pen’s taste, like a dominant dialect, spread until everybody spoke it, even those who could not pronounce it properly.

Now any person with an arithmetical turn may calculate what it costs a young man to indulge freely in all these propensities, and it will be seen that, in two or three years, a lad of such tastes must spend or owe a handsome sum. Pen had no calculating turn. No one of his tastes was outrageously extravagant in itself; and certainly Paddington’s tailor’s account, Guttlebury’s cook’s bill for dinners, Dillon Tandy’s score with Finn the print-seller for Raphael-Morghens and Landseer proofs, Wormall’s dealings with Parkton the great bookseller for Aldine editions, black-letter folios, and richly illuminated missals of the sixteenth century, and Snaffle’s or Foker’s score with Nile the horse-dealer—each and all were incomparably greater than any single little bill Pendennis ran up. But Pen had what his friends admired as catholicity: he wanted everything. Whereas Lord Paddington did not care twopence for the most beautiful print unless it had a mirror in it; whereas Guttlebury did not mind how he was dressed and had a terror of horses; whereas Snaffle never read any printed work but the Racing Calendar or Bell’s Life, nor cared for any manuscript save the greasy scrawl of his betting-book—our universal-minded young friend occupied himself in every branch of pleasure and “science” above mentioned, and distinguished himself tolerably in each; and that universality, like a kitchen where every sauce is simmering at once, made the whole establishment dear.

Some little while before Mr. Foker packed up his portmanteau and his cautious conscience and quitted Oxbridge, Boniface College received—after an amount of refusal elsewhere that would have cooled a lesser vanity—a gentleman who came like a late frost upon a tender garden-bed.

His name was Horace Bloundell; and because his family had been ancient long enough to have forgotten what youth looks like, he was, by universal consent of the young wags, “Bloundell-Bloundell, of Bloundell-Bloundell Hall, in Bloundell-Bloundellshire,” as though the very syllables must be paid for by the acre. He had belonged once to Camford, the other university; but had quitted it in consequence of “differences” with tutors and authorities—differences, that is to say, of such a nature that the authorities were of one opinion and Mr. Bloundell of another, and the authorities possessed power.

There was a living in the family; and it was thought important that Mr. Bloundell should hold it. While he wore crimson pantaloons and a sable shako in a dragoon regiment, he was not designed for the pulpit; but when his third brother—who was—to whom the benefice had been as naturally destined as the best goose to the Christmas table—sickened and died, Horace, with the adaptability of a man who can change uniforms without changing habits, resolved to exchange spurs for a white neckcloth. Camford, in its prudish way, would not have him: but Dr. Donne, Master of Boniface, was a Suffolk man; and Suffolk, like a big kitchen, will sometimes take in a questionable joint because the label on it is venerable, and because it once lay in the same larder as the cook’s own.

So Mr. Bloundell came up, and, without the least delay, sat down among the “select” as though he had been born at the High Table.

In Pen’s second year, Major Pendennis paid one of those brisk visits which are meant to admonish youth without interrupting it. He was introduced to Pen’s chosen companions: to gentle Lord Plinlimmon, whose politeness seemed hereditary; to gallant Magnus Charters, open as a door in summer; to sly Harland, who fired off Greek quotations as other men flick crumbs; to intrepid Ringwood—“Rupert” in the Union, because his opinions rode hard and his blunders rode harder; to Broadbent, dubbed “Barebones,” because he was republican and wore his dissenting shoes as if they, too, protested; and to Mr. Bloundell-Bloundell, who managed in five minutes to look as if the whole university had been waiting his arrival in order to become fashionable.

Major Pendennis did not understand Harland’s Greek, nor did he quite approve the grimy sincerity of Broadbent’s hands; but he was delighted with the circle round his nephew, and approved of everybody—except precisely the person who most approved of himself.

The morning after the party in Pen’s rooms, uncle and nephew sat at breakfast. The Major was in that fine humour which follows upon having told old stories to a young audience. In London, anecdotes are like yesterday’s fish—people sniff and push the plate away: at Oxbridge they come on like steaming new rolls, and the lads butter them with laughter. The Major had been listened to with that honest roar, that eager pleasure, that respectful gravity, which is the very music a practiced raconteur lives upon. Only once or twice, while the tale was being carved and handed round, Mr. Bloundell’s face took on a look as if the dish were beneath him and he had dined on it before.

Indeed, he had the audacity to interrupt; to correct a particular; and to give his own version, which, he said, he knew to be right because it had been “talked of openly at the Club” by persons of the vaguest and grandest description—So-and-so and T’other—who were present at the business. The young gentlemen stared. They did not yet understand that melancholy grace with which Major Pendennis could accept correction from a cub and thank him for it, as if receiving a favour instead of an impertinence.

When next they met, Bloundell spoke contemptuously of “old Pen;” said everybody knew old Pen; regular old trencherman at Gaunt House; notorious old bore; regular old fogey.

Major Pendennis, on his side, liked Mr. Bloundell not one whit; and these antipathies, like the smell of certain cheeses or the taste of certain wines, are commonly mutual. You may prove by every rule of logic that a dish is wholesome; but if the stomach turns, it turns. All the reasons in the world will not make us love Dr. Fell; and if we dislike him, we may take it as certain he is not composing sonnets upon our virtues.

So the Major, tapping his egg with that air of judicial delicacy with which he could condemn a man while praising a sauce, said:—

“Pen, my boy, your dinner went off a merveille; you did the honours very nicely; you carved well. I am glad you learned to carve. In most good houses it’s done on the sideboard now, but it remains an important point, and may aid you in middle life. Lord Plinlimmon is a very amiable young man; quite the image of his dear mother, Lady Aquila Brownbill, whom I knew. Lord Magnus’s republicanism will wear off: it sits prettily on a young patrician, though nothing is so loathsome among persons of our rank. Mr. Broadbent seems to have much eloquence and considerable reading. Your friend Foker is always delightful. But your acquaintance, Mr. Bloundell”—and here the Major’s spoon paused, as if it did not choose to travel further in such company—“struck me as in all respects a most ineligible young man.”

“Bless my soul, sir—Bloundell-Bloundell!” cried Pen, laughing, for names that repeat themselves always seemed to him to be twice as good as other names. “Why, he’s the most popular man of the university. We elected him of the Barmecides the first week he came up—had a special meeting on purpose. He’s of an excellent family—Suffolk Bloundells—descended from Richard’s Blondel; bears a harp in chief—and motto O Mong Roy.”

“A man may have a very good coat-of-arms and be a tiger, my boy,” the Major said, chipping his egg with a firmness that suggested he would gladly have chipped the subject of discourse instead. “That man is a tiger. A low man. I will lay a wager he left his regiment, which was a good one (for a more respectable man than my friend Lord Martingale never sat in a saddle), in bad odour. There is the unmistakable look of slang and bad habits about him. He frequents low gambling-houses and billiard-hells—haunts third-rate clubs. I know it by his style. I never was mistaken in my man yet. Did you remark the quantity of rings and jewellery he wore? That person has Scamp written on his countenance, if any man ever had. Mark my words and avoid him. Let us turn the conversation. The dinner was a leetle too fine—but I don’t object to your making a few extra frais when you receive friends. Of course you don’t do it often, and only those whom it is your interest to fêter. The cutlets were excellent; and the soufflé uncommonly light and good. The third bottle of champagne was not necessary; but you have a good income, and as long as you keep within it I shall not quarrel with you, my dear boy.”

Poor Pen! The worthy uncle little knew how often those dinners occurred—how frequently the young Amphitryon, eager to be thought a judge of everything that ever simmered or sparkled, delighted to show hospitality and skill in gourmandise. There is no art (so long to learn, so difficult to acquire, so impossible to practice in perfection without a purse as well as a palate) about which boys are more anxious to wear an air of knowingness. They will sniff a claret as if it were a cousin, and discuss a salmi as if they had raised the bird and written the recipe in their own dialect. The cookery and the wine are to them what a moustache is to a raw ensign—a sign of manhood, whether earned or glued on.

Pen, in his character of Admirable Crichton, felt it necessary to be great in dinners; and the old college-cook (who could talk of capons and gravies with the same tenderness with which an agrarian elder speaks of weather and wheat) respected him for it, and trusted him—blindly, fatally—because Pen praised the crispness of the skin, the perfume of the herbs, the clean crack of the crust, with such honest delight. The kitchen loved a young gentleman who could hear, even through the din of plates, the soft approving murmur a good sauce makes when it is properly finished with butter, and who could smell, in imagination, the thyme on the hill and the cellar’s cool corked darkness in a bottle of wine.

But appetite is a creditor that never signs a receipt. In the third year of the lad’s residence at Oxbridge, his staircase was no longer besieged by dish-covers and desserts and cheerful waiters bearing in triumph hot metal and cold glass. Instead, crowds of different sorts of attendants—messengers with faces sulky or piteous—hung about the outer oak, and assailed the unfortunate lad when he issued from his den, as if he were a rare bird to be plucked for payment.

Nor did his guardian’s advice take any effect, or induce Mr. Pen to avoid the society of the disreputable Mr. Bloundell. Young men love in companions what got Pen himself half his reputation—a real or supposed knowledge of life. A man who can speak of the world with a knowing air; a Lovelace with adventures; a roue with a story ready at the end of his cigar—is sure of an admiring audience among boys. It is hard to confess; but so it is. We are taught early—by books, by banter, by the very language of our praises—to admire that sort of prowess; and the lexicon of a school is often a tyrant, crowning the wrong kings. The thought should make the man tremble who holds the pen, lest untruth, impurity, unjust anger, or unjust praise escape it; for words travel further than men, and outlive them; and a fashionable phrase may do more mischief than a fashionable vice.

One such diseased creature is enough to infect a whole colony. The tutors of Boniface began to find the moral tone of their college lowered and their young men growing unruly—almost ungentlemanlike—soon after Mr. Bloundell’s arrival. The young magnates of neighbouring St. George’s, in whose society Pen lived, were not taken in by Bloundell’s flashy graces and rakish airs of fashion. Broadbent called him Captain Macheath, and said he would live to be hanged. Foker, during his brief stay at the university with Macheath, declined, with characteristic caution, to say anything openly in the Captain’s disfavour; but hinted to Pen that it was better to have him for a partner at whist than play against him, and better to back him at écarté than bet on the other side.

“You see, he plays better than you do, Pen,” was Foker’s astute remark. “He plays uncommon well, the Captain does; and Pen, I wouldn’t take the odds too freely from him, if I was you. I don’t think he’s too flush of money, the Captain ain’t.”

Beyond these dark suggestions and generalities, the cautious Foker could not be got to speak.

Not that his advice would have weighed much with a headstrong young man. Pen’s appetite for pleasure was insatiable; he rushed at it wherever it presented itself with an eagerness that bespoke his fiery constitution and youthful health. He called it “seeing life,” and quoted Terence and Horace and Shakspeare to show that one should do all that might become a man—taking the maxims, as hungry lads take mustard, not because it is nourishing, but because it bites.

One night, after a supper-party in college at which Pen and Macheath had been present, and at which a little quiet vingt-et-un had been played—an amusement much pleasanter to men in their second and third year than the old boisterous custom of singing songs and bringing the proctors thumping to the door, every man having expended his budget of choruses long ago—when the caps were being taken up and the guests were going, after no great losses or winnings, Mr. Bloundell playfully picked up a green wine-glass from the supper-table. It had been destined for iced cup—that innocent, fragrant compromise of lemon-peel and sugar and chill. But into it he inserted something far more pernicious, namely a pair of dice, which he took from his waistcoat-pocket as neatly as if producing a lozenge.

Then, giving the glass a graceful wave that showed his hand was well acquainted with the profession of throwing, he called sevens the main, whisked the ivory cubes gently on the table, swept them up lightly again, and repeated the process two or three times. The other men looked on—Pen among them—who had never rattled dice yet, except in the humdrum domestic piety of backgammon at home, with the fire singing and the kettle keeping time.

Mr. Bloundell, who had a good voice, began to troll out the chorus from Robert the Devil, then in great vogue; many joined, and especially Pen, who was in very high spirits, having won a good handful of shillings and half-crowns at the vingt-et-un. Presently, instead of going home, most of the party were seated round the table playing at dice, the green glass going round from hand to hand—until Pen, after throwing six mains, finally shivered it.

From that night Pen plunged into hazard as eagerly as it was his custom to pursue any new pleasure. Dice can be played in the morning as well as after dinner or supper; sin is not a bird that only sings at dusk. Bloundell would come into Pen’s rooms after breakfast, and it was astonishing how quick the time passed while the bones were rattling, or rather, while they ought to have rattled. For they had little quiet parties with the doors closed, and Bloundell devised a box lined with felt, so that the dice should make no noise and their tell-tale music not bring the sharp-eared tutors padding up the staircase.

Once, indeed, Bloundell, Ringwood, and Pen were very nearly caught by Mr. Buck, who, passing in the quadrangle, thought he heard through Pen’s open window the words “Two to one on the caster.” But when the tutor got into Arthur’s rooms, he found the lads with three Homers before them, and Pen, with great gravity, said he was trying to coach the other two, and asked Mr. Buck what was the present condition of the River Scamander, and whether it was navigable or no. Thus did scholarship become a felt box to smother noise; and the old languages—those precious dialects that carry whole worlds of feeling—were used as a screen for modern folly, the meaning of Homer turned into mere vocabulary for evasion.

Mr. Arthur Pendennis did not win much money in these transactions with Mr. Bloundell, nor indeed gain good of any kind except a knowledge of the odds at hazard, which he might have learned out of books without losing his character into the bargain.

Captain Macheath had other accomplishments which he exercised for Pen’s benefit. His stories had a great and unfortunate charm for Arthur, who was never tired of hearing histories of garrison conquests and feats in country-quarters—tales delivered with that easy club-air by which the cheapened word “world” is made to seem a passport. He had been at Paris, and had plenty of legends about the Palais Royal and the Salon and Frascati’s.

“I went to the Salon one night,” said he, after a dinner at the Café de Paris, “when we were all devilishly cut, by Jove; and on waking in the morning in my own rooms, I found myself with twelve thousand francs under my pillow, and a hundred and forty-nine Napoleons in one of my boots. Wasn’t that a coup, hay?”

Pen’s eyes glistened as he heard. He respected the man who could win such a sum; and sighed that it would set him all right. Macheath laughed, and told him to drink another drop of Maraschino—that syrupy cherry cordial, perfumed and treacherous, which makes virtue seem a little dull and debt a little distant.

“I could tell you stories much more wonderful than that,” he added; and so indeed the Captain could have done, without further trouble than invention, with which portion of the poetic faculty Nature had copiously endowed him.

He laughed to scorn Pen’s love for Miss Fotheringay, when he came to hear of that amour from Arthur—pretty soon, for Pen was not averse to telling the story now to confidential friends, and he and they were rather proud of the transaction. But Macheath took away all Pen’s conceit on this head—not by showing the folly of the lad’s passion for an uneducated woman much his senior, but by exposing, with a sneer, Pen’s absurd desire of gratifying his passion in a legitimate way.

“Marry her?” said he. “You might as well marry ——,” and he named one of the most notorious actresses on the stage.

“She hadn’t a shred of a character.” He knew twenty men openly her admirers; named them; named the sums each had spent.

No kind of calumny is more frightful or frequent than this which takes away the character of women; no men more reckless and mischievous than those who lightly use it; and no cowards more despicable than the people who invent such slanders. They coin a word and pass it; and the world, with its lazy ear, hears the jingle and calls it truth. So the dominant lexicon—those ready-made labels of “pure” and “lost,” so convenient to men—does the work of power without a blow.

Is it, or is it not, a misfortune that a man of candid disposition, disposed like Pen to blurt out the truth, begins life by believing all that is said to him? Would it be better for a lad to be less trustful and so less honest? It requires no small experience to know that a man, without especial reason, is telling you lies. At all events, Pen had a natural credulity which enabled him to accept all statements made to him; and he took every one of Captain Macheath’s figments as if they had been unquestioned history.

So Bloundell’s account about Miss Fotheringay pained and mortified Pen exceedingly. If he had been ashamed of his passion before, what were his feelings now, when the object of so much pure flame and adoration turned out, by this fellow’s easy assertion, to be only a worthless impostor—an impostor detected by all but him? It never occurred to Pen to doubt the fact, or to question whether the stories of a man who never spoke well of any woman were likely to be true.

One Easter vacation, when Pen announced to his mother and uncle his intention not to go down, but stay at Oxbridge and read, Mr. Pen was nevertheless induced to take a brief visit to London in company with his friend Mr. Bloundell. They put up at a hotel in Covent Garden, where Bloundell had a “tick,” as he called it; and took the pleasures of the town very freely after the wont of young university men.

Bloundell still belonged to a military club, whither he took Pen to dine once or twice. The young men would drive thither in a cab, trembling lest they should meet Major Pendennis on his beat in Pall Mall, as if the Major were a moral constable and they were smuggling a barrel of contraband champagne. At the club Pen was introduced to a number of gallant young fellows with spurs and mustachios, who drank pale-ale of mornings and beat the town of nights; and here he saw “life” indeed. The roaring places they frequented—theatres and singing-houses—were of a sort where a guardian with the Major’s sense of decorum was not likely to appear.

One night, nevertheless, they were very near. A plank only separated Pen, who was in the boxes of the Museum Theatre, from the Major, who was in Lord Steyne’s box with that venerated nobleman. On the stage, Miss Fotheringay was in the pride of her glory. She had made a hit: had drawn good houses for nearly a year; had starred the provinces with great éclat; had returned to London with somewhat diminished lustre; and now was acting with “ever increasing attraction,” and “triumph of the good old British drama,” as the play-bills vowed, to houses where there was plenty of room for anybody who wanted to see her.

It was not the first time Pen had seen her since that memorable day at Chatteris when they parted. In the previous year, when the town made much of her and the press lauded her beauty, Pen had found a pretext for coming up in term-time, and rushed to the theatre to see his old flame. He recollected it rather than renewed it. He remembered how ardently he used to watch at Chatteris for the speech before Ophelia’s entrance—how the mere preparation on the actor’s lips used to set his heart listening, as if love were an acoustic creature that lived in the pause before applause.

Now, as the actor spoke, he had but a feeble thrill. As the house thundered, and Ophelia entered with her old bow and sweeping curtsey, Pen felt a slight shock and blushed very much as he looked at her, and could not help thinking the whole house regarded him. He hardly heard her in the first part of the play; he thought with rage of the humiliation she had caused him; and began to fancy he was jealous and in love still.

But that illusion did not last. He ran round to the stage-door, eager to see her if possible, and did not succeed. She passed indeed under his nose with a female companion; but he did not know her—nor did she recognise him. The next night he came in late and stayed quietly for the afterpiece. And on the third and last night of his stay in London—why, Taglioni was to dance at the Opera—Taglioni!—and there was to be Don Giovanni, which he admired of all things in the world: so Mr. Pen went to Don Giovanni and Taglioni.

This time the illusion about her was quite gone. She was not less handsome, but she was not the same, somehow. The light was gone out of her eyes—or else Pen’s no longer were dazzled by it. The rich voice spoke as of old, yet did not make his bosom thrill as formerly. He thought he could recognise the brogue underneath; the accents seemed coarse and false. It annoyed him to hear the same emphasis on the same words, only uttered louder: worse than that, it annoyed him to think he should ever have mistaken loud imitation for genius, or melted at mechanical sobs and sighs. He felt it was another life, another man who had loved her so madly. He was ashamed and bitterly humiliated, and very lonely. Fine dreams are sometimes better than dismal waking; the imagination seasons the plainest fare, and truth can taste stale.

They went and had an uproarious supper that night—hot meats, sharp pickles, the greasy comfort of late-hour dishes, and wine that talked louder and louder as the candles burned down; and Mr. Pen had a fine headache next morning, with which he went back to Oxbridge, having spent all his ready money.

As all this narrative is taken from Pen’s own confessions, the reader may be assured of the truth of every word of it; and as Pen himself never had any accurate notion of the manner in which he spent his money, and plunged into deeper pecuniary difficulties during his luckless residence at the University, it is impossible to give any precise account of his involvements beyond the general notion already sketched.

He does not speak too hardly of the roguery of university tradesmen, or of those in London whom he honoured with his patronage at the outset of his career. Even Finch, the money-lender to whom Bloundell introduced him, and with whom he had various transactions in which the young rascal’s signature appeared upon stamped paper, treated him, according to Pen’s own account, with forbearance, and never mulcted him of more than a hundred per cent. The old college-cook—his fervent admirer—made him a private bill, offered to send him dinners up to the very last, and never would have pressed his account to his dying day. There was a kindness and frankness about Arthur Pendennis which won most people he came near; and which, if it rendered him an easy prey to rogues, got him perhaps more goodwill than he merited from many honest men. It was impossible to resist his good nature; or, even in his worst moments, not to hope for his rescue from utter ruin.

At the very height of his university pleasure, he would leave the gayest party to go sit with a sick friend. He never knew the difference between small and great in the treatment of acquaintances; however much his sumptuous tastes led him to prefer good society, he was only too ready to share his guinea with a poor friend; and when he got money had an irresistible propensity for paying, which he never could conquer through life.

Everybody who has ever peeped into a book of arms—and everybody who has ever peeped into a nursery—knows the famous device of the Pendennises: a mother-pelican in the very act of doing what mothers have been doing since the first small creature discovered it could whistle, cry, or look tragically hungry; namely, feeding her young with herself. Heraldry, which will tell you with a straight face that a lion is “rampant” and a unicorn is “couchant,” insists that the maternal bird offers her own breast, obligingly sanguine, to be pecked by a nest of chirping little wretches. There are people who say the story is natural history; there are people who say it is poetry; there are a few who suspect it is merely a family joke carried on for centuries at the expense of women.

For whether pelicans enjoy the operation or not, women, it is certain, submit to it as if it were part of the day’s domestic marketing. Give them a reckless husband, a scapegrace son, a prodigal brother, and you will see them put the best joint on the table, pour out the best wine of their patience, and carve their own comfort into thin slices, smiling while they do it. They will go without seasoning that others may have it; they will eat the crust that others may have the crumb; and at the first rumour that the sinner is on the road home, down goes the lid of the larder, out comes the fatted calf, and the whole kitchen is in a bustle of mercy and forgiveness, as if the angels themselves were in aprons and had tied up their sleeves. If we had nothing but Justice for breakfast, Heaven help us; most of us would go hungry.

During the latter part of Arthur Pendennis’s residence at Oxbridge, his uncle’s partiality for him had swelled like a well-fed pudding. The Major—an old London bachelor with the morals of a drawing-room and the economy of a desert island—was proud of Pen’s figure, spirits, frank talk, and that air of being born to have people hold doors open for him. It delighted the Major to see his nephew walking with young patricians under college gateways; and though the Major’s thrift had become a proverb at his Club (among gentlemen who envied his constant “engagements” and did not care to discover they were often engagements to dine elsewhere), he actually took to giving snug little dinners in his lodgings: dinners with sound claret, a dish or two whose excellence he would have sworn was accidental, and stories so neatly told that they ought to have been served under glass, never to be touched again. Some of them, if repeated, would lose their flavour; others, if repeated, would poison society.

He paid court to the parents through the sons; he paid court to himself through the sons; he made himself sprightly and juvenile with young lords as if years were a coat to be put off on entering the room. He went down to Oxbridge; was entertained, partly to be honoured and partly to be laughed at; and he laughed too, and told his stories, and accepted breakfasts and fêtes with the air of a man who had always breakfasted and fêted for the good of others. He heard Pen speak at the Union, and crowed and cheered, and rapped his stick as though it had been elected to Parliament. He came away persuaded he possessed a young Pitt in the family—only better dressed. He bragged of him at the Clubs, introduced him into conversation as if he were an improvement on the constitution, and wrote to Helen again and again that Lord Runnymede would certainly take the boy on an embassy, or the Duke bring him into a borough—anything, in short, that could happen to a young gentleman who spoke well and bowed correctly.

Helen, poor soul, was ready to believe any good report of her son with the prompt faith of a mother tasting a sauce she herself has made: she wants it to be perfect, therefore it is. And all this pride and affection—this careful cellaring of hope—had been dashed and spilt by Pen’s extravagance and idleness, as a clumsy foot knocks over a bottle which has been keeping for years.

Pen himself, when he awoke to what he had done, found remorse to be a kind of hunger that eats whatever is left in the house. He had slept, and the tortoise had won. He had spoiled at the beginning what might have been a brilliant career. He had dipped into a generous mother’s purse as if it were a public pantry; he had wasted her little store as if it were mere dripping to be thrown out. And if he felt the wrong done to others (which he did, for he was not without heart), we may be very sure he felt still more sharply the shame done to himself; for wounded self-love groans louder than any conscience, and is harder to quiet. He convinced himself, with that maddening vanity which is the true fever of youth, that all England would remark the absence of his name from the lists, and that boots, bed-makers, tutors, duns, undergraduates—every human creature who had ever seen him—would wag their heads and whisper, “Plucked!”

He rushed to his rooms, shut himself in, and wrote to his tutor a letter full of gratitude, despair, and tragic flourish; he begged that his name might be taken off the college books, and hinted in a manner meant to melt stone that death would probably end the woes of Arthur Pendennis. Then, like a man who has burnt the roast and cannot bear to stay in the kitchen, he slipped out, scarcely knowing where he went, and took the little lanes behind the colleges until he cleared the precincts and came down by the Camisis.

The river lay deserted in a thin January drizzle—no cheering gownsmen now, no racing boats, no holiday racket of oars and laughter. Only the small natural noises were awake: the damp whisper of reeds, the faint click of water against a mooring, the long sigh of wind that goes through winter branches as though the trees were remembering a forgotten language. It was a kinder sound than the university’s loud, polished talk; it asked nothing, it accused nothing. Pen wandered on until he was a few miles from Oxbridge, and was in fact discovered by acquaintances leaving it.

As he went up a hill with the rain beating in his face, his ragged gown streaming behind him—for he had not even taken off his academic dress since morning—a postchaise came rattling towards him, and the road, which a moment before had belonged to drizzle and birds, was suddenly seized by iron hoops, cracking whips, the postboy’s shout, and that furious modern noise by which men announce their importance. A servant sat on the box; within, half out of the window, lounged a young gentleman smoking a cigar and bawling encouragement as if speed were a virtue.

It was Mr. Spavin of Baymouth, degree in pocket at last, driving home in triumph in a yellow postchaise. He caught sight of Pen’s figure gesticulating uphill, and of Pen’s pale face as the chaise whirled by.

“Wo!” roared Mr. Spavin; and the horses stopped as if surprised that any human voice could be louder than their own hooves. The carriage pulled up fifty yards ahead. Pen heard his name shouted, and saw the upper half of Spavin thrust out of the side-window, beckoning as though he were signalling a ship in distress.

Pen stopped, hesitated, nodded fiercely, and pointed onwards, as if ordering fate to drive on and leave him. He did not speak; but his look must have been sufficiently desperate, for Spavin stared with blank alarm, jumped down, ran back, seized Pen’s hand, and cried, “I say—hullo, old boy, where are you going, and what’s the row now?”

“I’m going where I deserve to go,” Pen said, with an oath that had more misery than wickedness in it.

“This ain’t the way,” Spavin answered, grinning. “This is the Fenbury road. I say, Pen, don’t take on because you are plucked. It’s nothing when you are used to it. I’ve been plucked three times, old boy—and after the first time I didn’t care. Glad it’s over, though. You’ll have better luck next time.”

Pen stared at him—at this cheerful survivor who had been rusticated, plucked, and only after repeated misfortunes brought to spell properly; and yet here he was, degree achieved at last, cigar glowing, and a bright yellow chaise behind him like a canary come to life. “This man has passed,” Pen thought, “and I have failed!” It was almost unbearable.

“Good-bye, Spavin,” Pen said. “I’m very glad you are through. Don’t let me keep you; I’m in a hurry—I’m going to town to-night.”

“Gammon,” said Spavin. “This ain’t the way to town; this is the Fenbury road, I tell you.”

“I was just going to turn back,” Pen muttered.

“All the coaches are full with the men going down,” Spavin said.

Pen winced as if he had been struck.

“You’d not get a place for a ten-pound note,” Spavin continued, with the good nature of a man who believes the world is a public-house and all troubles are paid for with a round of drinks. “Get into my yellow; I’ll drop you at Mudford, where you have a chance of the Fenbury mail. I’ll lend you a hat and a coat; I’ve got lots. Come along; jump in, old boy—go it, leathers!”

And thus, by the charity of a man who had been plucked three times and was therefore proof against catastrophes, Pen found himself seated in the yellow postchaise, with a borrowed coat about him and the smell of Spavin’s cigar mixed with wet wool and muddy road—an odd, homely perfume of failure on the move. They rattled as far as the Ram Inn at Mudford, fifteen miles from Oxbridge, where the Fenbury mail changed horses; and there Pen got a place to London.

At Boniface College there was, next day, an immense excitement. Rumour, like an idle cook, had put in too much of the dramatic seasoning. A battered cap—Pen’s name scarcely visible—together with a seal bearing his crest (an eagle looking at a now extinct sun) had been found three miles out on the Fenbury road, near a mill-stream; and for four-and-twenty hours it was believed that Pendennis, frantic at losing his degree, had thrown himself into the water. Tutor and tradesmen grew pale; duns began to imagine they might never be paid even by the respectable machinery of shame. Then letters arrived with the London post-mark, and the stream was allowed to go on murmuring without a corpse.

The mail reached London at the dreary hour of five. Pen hastened to the Covent Garden inn where he commonly put up, and the ever-wakeful porter admitted him and showed him to a bed. Pen looked hard at the man and wondered whether Boots knew he was plucked; whether even the slippers and chamber-candles had heard of it. He lay down, but the bed would not take him in. He tossed until the dismal London daylight crept in—daylight that seemed filtered through soot and old breath—and then sprang up and walked to his uncle’s lodgings in Bury Street.

A maid was scouring the steps. She looked up suspiciously at the sight of him—unshaven, yesterday’s linen, that broken look which is like a stain men imagine visible to all.

“Good ’evens! Mr. Harthur, what as ’appened, sir?” asked Mr. Morgan the valet, who had just arranged well-brushed clothes and shiny boots at the Major’s door, and was carrying in the Major’s wig.

“I want to see my uncle,” Pen cried, and flung himself into a chair with a voice that sounded as if it had been scraped thin.

Morgan backed away from the pale face and went in.

The Major put his head out as soon as his wig was on. “What? examination over? Senior Wrangler, double First Class, hay? I’ll come directly,” he called, in his high cheery tone; and disappeared again.

“They don’t know,” Pen groaned. “What will they say when they know all?”

Pen stood with his back to the window in the dubious light that Bury Street enjoys on a foggy January morning, so his uncle did not at first catch his expression. But when the Major came out neat and radiant—preceded by faint odours from Delcroix’s shop, from which emporium his wig and pocket-handkerchief drew their scented importance—he held out his hand and began to speak; and then he saw Pen’s face.

“Good God! Pen, what’s the matter?” he cried, dropping the hand as if it had touched fever.

“You’ll see it in the papers at breakfast, sir,” Pen answered.

“See what?”

“My name isn’t there, sir.”

“Hang it, why should it be?” the Major asked, bewildered.

“I have lost everything, sir,” Pen groaned. “My honour’s gone; I’m ruined irretrievably; I can’t go back to Oxbridge.”

“Lost your honour?” screamed the Major. “Heaven alive! you don’t mean to say you have shown the white feather?”

Pen laughed bitterly at the word, and repeated it: “Feather.”

“No, it isn’t that, sir. I’m not afraid of being shot; I wish to God anybody would. I have not got my degree. I—I’m plucked, sir.”

The Major had heard of plucking in a vague way and, being a man of old-fashioned discipline, concluded it was some bodily ceremony inflicted publicly on refractory youth.

“I wonder you can look me in the face after such a disgrace, sir,” he said. “I wonder you submitted to it as a gentleman.”

“I couldn’t help it, sir. I did my classical papers well enough: it was those infernal mathematics, which I have always neglected.”

“Was it—was it done in public, sir?” the Major asked, anxiously.

“What?”

“The—the plucking?” said the Major, staring.

Pen understood at last the nature of his uncle’s terror, and in the midst of misery the absurdity brought him a faint smile—as if a cracked bell had tried to ring. He explained that he had gone in for the examination and failed it; and then the Major, relieved that no physical outrage had been committed, declared that there was no dishonour as far as he saw, no great misfortune, and that Pen must try again.

“Me again at Oxbridge,” Pen thought, “after such humiliation?” He felt he could not enter the place, unless it were to burn it.

But when he produced his debts, then the Major’s relief turned to anger. Pen had determined to make a clean breast of it. He had written out a full list—true, complete, and hideous—of bills and liabilities at the university and in London: tailors in both places; horses; haberdashery for shirts and gloves; printseller; jeweller; books; the college cook; binding; Grump for desserts; hairdresser and perfumery; bootmaker; hotel bill; wine merchant; sundries—those dreadful “sundries” which, like scraps in a kitchen, somehow always add up to another meal.

The reader may season the items at pleasure; such accounts have been tasted, to the sourness of soul, by many a parent of university youth. All told, they amounted to about seven hundred pounds; and, worse still, it was calculated that Pen had had more than twice that sum in ready money during his stay at Oxbridge. That, too, was gone. And for it—what remained? Not even a respectable appetite; only the gnawing emptiness of having eaten and not been nourished.

“You need not press a man who is down, sir,” Pen said gloomily. “I know very well how wicked and idle I have been. My mother won’t like to see me dishonoured,” he added, his voice failing. “And I know she will pay these accounts. But I shall ask her for no more money.”

“As you like, sir,” the Major replied, stiffening himself. “You are of age, and my hands are washed of your affairs. But you can’t live without money, and have no means of making it that I see, though you have a fine talent in spending it; and it is my belief you will proceed as you have begun, and ruin your mother before you are five years older. Good morning. It is time for me to go to breakfast. My engagements won’t permit me to see you much during the time you stay in London. I presume you will acquaint your mother with the news which you have conveyed to me.”

And pulling on his hat, trembling a little in his limbs, Major Pendennis walked out before his nephew, and went ruefully off to take his accustomed corner at the Club.

There he saw the Oxbridge examination-lists in the morning papers, and read the names with mournful accuracy, not understanding the business but feeling the blow. He consulted old fogies at his clubs—Wenham, a Dean, various Civilians—took their “opinion,” showed some of them the amount of Pen’s debts dotted on the back of a card, and asked whether such debts were not monstrous, preposterous? What was to be done? There was nothing for it but to pay. Wenham and the rest consoled him with tales of young men who owed twice as much, five times as much, and had no means at all. These comparisons, like watering weak wine, made the Major feel a little better. After all, he was not the one who would pay. Still he thought bitterly of the plans he had formed, the sacrifices he fancied he had made, and the disappointment that sat down at table with him and would not be served away.

He wrote off to Doctor Portman, informing him of the direful events and begging the Doctor to break them to Helen. The Major, orthodox in all his habits, believed bad news ought to be carved and handed round by a proper person, rather than sent straight, like a common joint, by post. Having dispatched this messenger, he went out to dinner one of the saddest men in any London dining-room that day, though he doubtless ate like a gentleman and smiled when it was necessary.

Pen, too, wrote his letter—full of tenderness and remorse—and then skulked about London streets, fancying that every passer-by was looking at him and whispering, “That is Pendennis of Boniface, who was plucked yesterday.” He wept bitter tears over his letter, and the very act of suffering soothed him, as if pain were a kind of penance paid in coin he happened to possess. He saw a party of roaring young blades from Oxbridge in the coffee-room of his hotel and slipped away from them as from a kitchen where old acquaintances were already smelling the smoke. He paced the streets. He remembered, afterwards, the prints at Ackermann’s window hanging in the rain, and a book he read at a stall near the Temple; and at night he went into the pit and saw Miss Fotheringay, but could not even recollect the piece—only that her voice rang out above the crowd like something alive, not bought and sold like so much fashionable applause.

On the second day a letter came from his tutor—kind, grave, appropriate—urging him not to take his name off the university books, and to retrieve a disaster which everybody knew was due to his own carelessness and could be repaired by a month’s application. The tutor added that he had ordered Pen’s skip to pack up some trunks of wardrobe; the trunks arrived duly—and on the top of them, like cold dishes set out to shame a glutton, lay fresh copies of all Pen’s bills.

On the third day a letter came from home. Pen read it in his bedroom; and when he had done, he fell on his knees with his head in the bedclothes and prayed out his heart, humbled, broken, and for once speaking within himself in a language no fashionable world could translate. Then—having emptied himself of pride as one empties a pot—he went downstairs, ate an immense breakfast, and sallied forth; and that evening took his place at the Bull and Mouth, Piccadilly, by the Chatteris coach.

Such a letter as the Major despatched—thin, sharp, and folded with the neat cruelty of a man who likes his bad news to arrive punctually—could not but set Doctor Portman in motion. He went to Fairoaks with the briskness common to worthy people when they have to perform a painful duty upon somebody else. A dentist, if you mark him, will sigh over your jaw, lament the necessity, call the instrument “unpleasant,” and then, with the air of a philanthropist saving your life, will tug as though the tooth were a personal enemy. So the Doctor, having read the epistle aloud to Myra and Mrs. Portman, seasoning every line with pious thunder against the young scapegrace who was “going down, down,” left the ladies to transmit the intelligence through Clavering with that speed and precision for which neighbourhoods are famed, and strode off to Fairoaks to administer his moral lancet to the widow.

He was forestalled. She had the news already.

Helen had read Pen’s own letter; and in some strange domestic arithmetic (which is not taught at universities, and never appears in Portman’s sermons), it had eased her. For months and months she had lived with a shadow in the house, a weight in the air, as if the very curtains listened for a misfortune. Now the thing had a name, a handwriting, a seal. The worst, whatever it was, had spoken. And—this was all her heart needed—her darling boy was coming home, repentant, tender-hearted, her boy again. Did she want a degree, if she had her son? What were these academical laurel-leaves, which sensible men and good divines shook like a rattle over a mother’s cradle? What good would the parchment do Pen, compared with the sight of him at her own table, hearing his own household sounds again—the kettle’s small singing, the clock’s faithful click, the soft fall of a foot on the stair?

The Rector fired his arrows of indignation; they fell upon her gentleness and dropped, blunted, to the carpet. Debts must be paid—certainly: but whose money was it but his? Why send him amongst temptations in the first place? Why not leave him at home, where the very air had known him as a child and would have kept him decent? She had arguments enough to bewilder virtue itself; and the Doctor went on, frowning and instructing, only to find that a mother’s forgiveness is a kind of armour: it does not ring with the blow; it merely closes more softly.

Meanwhile, another change had been growing at Fairoaks—a change more startling, to Mr. Arthur at least, than any examination-paper. There is a practice, ancient as brothers and sisters, by which they express affection with an innocent freedom; and this custom, between Pen and his little sister Laura, had been dropped of late by mutual consent, as quietly as one puts away childish shoes. For when Arthur came home after months of absence, he found that the simple girl he had left had become a tall, slim young lady, who offered him—not her cheek—but a curtsey, a hand, and a blush precisely upon the very spot where, in former days, he had been used to bestow his brotherly salute. It is astonishing how swiftly propriety grows up between two people who have not altered their hearts at all, only their height.

Miss Laura Bell at sixteen was what Clavering called “tall” and what small ladies called “gawky,” which is the revenge of the short upon the long. If she was a maypole, she had roses about her—those quick colourings that come and go like a sudden flame under thin skin. Her eyes, always large, were blamed for shining, as though Nature had committed an indiscretion in providing her with light; and when she lowered them behind their long black lashes, the same critics declared she did it to show the lashes. One would think some people would prefer women to look and see nothing at all. Her voice, low and sweet, had in it that domestic music which makes a room kinder—the very opposite of the hard clatter of the world outside; and though Miss Piminy, whose own appetite would have swallowed a button with difficulty only from sheer reluctance to share it, averred that Laura’s mouth was rather large, everybody allowed that her smile was charming and her teeth as neat as peeled almonds laid out for dessert.

This young lady, now that she had begun to think for herself (and in two years her mind and person had both shot up like a well-tended sapling), had been only half pleased with her brother’s late behaviour. His letters had grown rare and short—like the notes of a miser. Helen excused him: his studies, his engagements, his uncle’s plans. Laura would not have it.

“It would be better he should lose a prize,” she said, “than forget his mother. And I don’t see that he gets many prizes. Why doesn’t he come home and stay with you, instead of passing his vacations at fine houses? Nobody there will love him half so much as—as you do.”

“As I do only, Laura?” Helen sighed; and Laura, stoutly declaring she did not love Pen a bit when he neglected his duty, would not be convinced by any of those maternal arguments which mothers invent and children disbelieve—about men’s “ties” and “calls,” about acquaintance to be cultivated, and the necessity of a way in the world. Perhaps Helen did not quite believe her own excuses; but she tried to believe she believed them, which is a mother’s principal occupation.

And there was more than silence in Pen that vexed Laura. There had been a laxness in his talk, a lightness, an audacity—nothing gross, for he was always polite to women by nature and breeding; but he spoke of women in general with an easy disrespect, and in a dozen little offices of life he was less courteous in action than in phrase. It offended her that he smoked his horrid pipes in the house, turning a clean parlour into a travelling tavern; that he refused to go to church with his mother, or on walks and visits, and lay in his dressing-gown yawning over a novel when the widow returned from duty. The Pen of her childhood—of those evenings when Helen had told story after story of the boy’s virtues, bravery, and tenderness—had been a bright figure indeed; the Pen she now saw could be brilliant, yes, and bold, and sarcastic, and defiant, and seemed to scorn the gentle occupations and devotions of the two women who loved him most, quitting them on any light pretext, as though affection were a chair one rises from when bored.

Then came that Fotheringay affair. Laura heard of it first by Major Pendennis’s sarcastic allusions on a visit, and then by the neighbours, who, being charitable, had a plentiful supply of facts. The notion struck her like smoke in a nursery: Helen’s boy—galloping day after day to fall on his knees to an actress, to drink with her “horrid father,” to dream of bringing such people into his home, setting that woman over his mother! Laura blazed out.

“I would have run away, mamma; I would, if I had had to walk barefoot through the snow!”

“And you would have left me too, then?” Helen answered; at which Laura instantly retreated from her heroism, and the two women fell into one another’s arms with that warmth and foolish tenderness which sober historians pretend not to understand, though they profit by it all their lives.

Where had Laura’s indignation come from? Perhaps from hearing the story dressed in the bitter dialect of Mrs. Portman’s circle; perhaps from that old Mrs. Portman’s especial dislike since Pen had behaved “impertinently” to the Doctor and—crowning crime—had smoked cigars during church-time. Or perhaps, if one must rummage for explanations, it was jealousy; but that is a vice in which ladies, we are told, very seldom indulge. At any rate, against Helen she had no resentment. Her devotion to the widow was complete: passionate, foolish, inexhaustible—the sort of affection women give to the near female heart when their own is unattached elsewhere; the sort of affection that fills a house with whisperings and soft footfalls, and makes the very silence between two rooms feel inhabited.

And yet, the moment she heard that Pen was unfortunate and unhappy, all her wrath vanished like steam from a kettle when the lid is lifted. The Pen of old came back to her imagination at once—frank, generous, affectionate. She took Helen’s side against Doctor Portman with a courage that, in a general, would have earned medals.

Debts? What were debts? A trifle, a mere kitchen account, compared with the bill the world sends young men for being young in expensive company. Disgraced for not getting his degree? He must have been ill. His mind could not attend to “mathematics and stuff” with such worries. The tutors were jealous; examiners had favourites; other people were unfair and cruel: she was certain. So reasoned this young advocate, cheeks flushing, eyes bright with anger. She went up, seized Helen’s hand, kissed it in the Doctor’s presence, and looked at that good man as though to ask by what right he dared to say a syllable against her darling mother’s Pen.

The Doctor departed, discomfited and amazed to find two women obstinate against common sense and antiquity. Laura repeated her arguments tenfold once he was gone; and Helen, who wanted to believe there must be jealousy against Pen, found Laura’s passionate logic extraordinarily convincing. And truly, the calamity vexed them very little. Pen, in London, tortured with shame and remorse, fancying his mother stricken with grief, would have been astonished to see how lightly she bore it. Misfortune is sometimes welcome to women—if it brings the truant heart home again. Reduce a mistress to a crust, and she will eat the smallest bit herself, provided you will eat the rest beside her.

Indeed, directly Portman had gone, Laura flew to practical mercy. Fires were ordered for Mr. Arthur’s rooms; bedding aired; the very curtains seemed to shake out their dust and prepare to receive the prodigal. Helen wrote at once a letter so tender that each line might have been warmed at the grate before being put to paper. When she had finished, Laura, smiling with that fond business-like happiness young women have in doing kind deeds, took her mamma by the hand and led her into Pen’s apartments, where the fires blazed cheerfully. There the two sate down upon the bed and talked of Pen ever so long—of his childhood, his voice, the way he used to laugh, the looks he had when he was good and when he was naughty. Laura added a postscript, calling him her dearest Pen, bidding him come home instantly, and underlining the command with two of the handsomest dashes, as though punctuation could drag a son down the road by the collar.

That night they read their Bibles more than usual, as people do when they are at once frightened and hopeful; and as they passed to their own room they took a look into Pen’s, as if by seeing the empty bed they could summon its occupant.

In the middle of the night, Laura cried suddenly, “Mamma, are you awake?”

“Yes,” Helen answered.

The truth was, though she lay still as death, she had not slept for an instant, but watched the night-lamp in the chimney and listened to the house as if each creak were Pen’s foot upon the stair. Laura, too, had been lying with the hypocrisy of the innocent—motionless, silent, and wide awake, her thoughts as busy as mice in a pantry. Her head not unfrequently chose to occupy that pillow where the late Mr. Pendennis’s nightcap had been wont to press; and now, in the dark, she unfolded a plan, notable, triumphant, and as easy in her telling as making toast.

“You know, mamma,” she began, “I have been living with you for ten years, and you have never taken any of my money, but treated me as if I was a charity girl. This has offended me extremely, because I am proud and do not like to be beholden. If I had gone to school—only I wouldn’t—it must have cost at least fifty pounds a year; so clearly I owe you fifty times ten pounds, which you have put in the bank at Chatteris for me, and which doesn’t belong to me a bit. To-morrow we will go to Chatteris and see that nice old Mr. Rowdy with the bald head and ask him for it—not for his head, but for the five hundred pounds. I dare say he will send you two more, which we will save and pay back. And we will send the money to Pen, and he can pay all his debts without hurting anybody; and then we will live happy ever after.”

What Helen replied was made up of incoherent exclamations, kisses, embraces, and such soft nonsense as women, when they are noble, are apt to indulge in. But after that, the two slept—soundly, sweetly—like people who have put a heavy box down at last.
