When the night-lamp went out with a little splutter and the sun rose over the purple hills, and the birds began their clear January piping among leafless branches and glistening evergreens on the Fairoaks lawn, Helen woke and looked at the sleeping girl beside her. Laura’s lips were parted with a faint smile; her cheeks held those shy roses that come even in dreams; and as the child’s breath rose and fell like a gentle tide, Pen’s mother felt thankful beyond what words can carry—thankful with that kind of gratitude which turns itself, as naturally as a bird turns to light, toward the Giver of love and mercy.

Although it was January and cold, so sincere was Pen’s remorse, and so determined his new economy, that he would not take an inside seat in the coach, but sat up behind with the Guard, who remembered his former liberality and lent him great-coats enough to make a small regiment. Perhaps it was the cold that made his knees tremble when he got down at the lodge-gate; or perhaps it was the thought of the kind creature for whose love he had made so selfish a return. Old John was waiting for the baggage, but appeared in fustian, and no longer wore the drab and blue livery.

“I’se garner and stable man, and lives in the ladge now,” John remarked with a welcoming grin and a blush, as if even his employment had grown shy; and then, as Pen turned the shrubbery corner and the coach was out of sight, Helen herself came, her face beaming with love and forgiveness—for forgiving is, with some women, the dearest feast of all.

She had written already to Pen of Laura’s offer—the noble, magnanimous, magnificent offer—filling her letter with blessings upon both her children; and this knowledge, no doubt, caused Pen to blush when he saw Laura waiting in the hall. On this occasion—on this occasion only—she broke through the little compact of handshakes and curtseys which had been established of late between them; but there has been far too much kissing in this history already, and the reader may supply such embraces as are necessary without further assistance.

So the prodigal came home; the fatted calf was killed (and, to do Fairoaks justice, killed properly, with a respect for soup, roast, and cold collations that would have pleased any serious student of English domestic cookery); and he was made as happy as two simple women could make him. No one alluded to Oxbridge. No one questioned him as to the future. The house, which had listened so long for sorrow, now listened for him: the crackle of the parlour fire, the soft clink of tea-things, the whisper of skirts, the spoon’s small tap against china—sounds that are a kind of music, and far better for the mind than the roar and grinding din of the great world’s streets. Even Pen, moody as he was, could not but feel the relief of it, as one feels relief in stepping out of a factory into a garden.

Yet he debated everything anxiously in his own room. A few days after his return he rode to Chatteris on his horse and came back atop of the coach—a change of dignity which he called economy. He informed his mother he had left the horse to be sold; and when it was sold, handed her the cheque. Helen (and perhaps Pen too) thought this an act of uncommon virtue and self-denial; Laura pronounced it strict justice, which is a colder dish and healthier.

He rarely mentioned the loan Laura had devised, and which Helen had accepted with certain modifications; but once or twice, with hesitation and stammering, he thanked her. It plainly pained his vanity to be beholden to the orphan for succour. He was wild to find some means to repay her—wild, too, to scrape dignity out of the ashes of his failure.

He left off wine, and took to whisky-and-water, but with moderation, as if even his vices were now under tutoring. He gave up cigar-smoking; but it must be confessed he had come to like pipes as well or better, so the sacrifice was not so martyr-like as it sounded. He fell asleep a great deal after dinner when he joined the ladies in the drawing-room; and he was certainly moody, melancholy, and prone to stare at nothing as though nothing were a landscape. He watched the coaches with interest, walked into Clavering to read the papers assiduously, dined with anybody who would ask him (the widow being glad he should have any entertainment in their solitary place), and played much cribbage with Captain Glanders. He avoided Doctor Portman; and the Doctor, whenever Pen passed, gave him severe looks from under his shovel-hat, as though a glare were a sacrament.

Pen went to church with his mother, however, very regularly, and read prayers at home to the diminished household. Diminished it was indeed. Two maids now did the work of the house at Fairoaks; the silver dish-covers never saw daylight. John put on his livery for church on Sundays to assert his dignity, but it was only for form’s sake: he was gardener and outdoor man now, vice Upton resigned. There was little fire in the kitchen; John and the maids drank their evening beer by a single candle, and the house’s old cheerful hum seemed pared down to a thin thread of sound. It was all Pen’s doing—his economy, his penance—and the austerity did not brighten him. A quiet house can be a comfort; but a house made quiet by want can feel, even to the penitent, like being shut up inside one’s own bad conscience.

For a time Pen declared no power on earth could induce him to return to Oxbridge after his failure. Then one day Laura, with many blushes, said she thought that, as a reparation—as a punishment upon himself for his idleness—he ought to go back and get his degree, if he could fetch it by doing so. And so back Mr. Pen went.

A plucked man is a dismal creature in a university. He belongs to no set and is owned by no one. Pen felt himself stripped indeed of all his fine feathers—those brilliant years’ plumage—rarely appearing out of college, going regularly to morning chapel, and shutting himself up of nights away from the noise and suppers of undergraduates. There were no duns at his door now: they were paid. There were scarcely any cards: the men of his year had taken their degrees and were gone. He went in for a second examination and passed with perfect ease; and when he wore his bachelor’s gown, he felt—if not happy—at least less naked.

On his way back he paid a visit to his uncle in London. The old gentleman received him with cold looks and would scarcely give him his forefinger to shake. Pen called a second time; Morgan said his master was from home. So Pen came back to Fairoaks—and to books, and to idleness, and to loneliness and despair.

He commenced several tragedies and wrote many copies of verses of a gloomy cast. He formed plans of reading and broke them. He thought of enlisting—of the Spanish legion—of a profession. He chafed against his captivity and cursed the idleness that had caused it. Helen said he was breaking his heart, and grieved to see his prostration. As soon as they could afford it he should go abroad—he should go to London—he should be freed from the dull society of two poor women.

It was dull—very, certainly. The widow’s habitual melancholy deepened into a sadder gloom; and Laura, listening with a girl’s quick ear to the house’s changing sounds—the fewer footsteps, the softer voices, the longer silences—saw with alarm that her dear friend became every year more languid and weary, and that the pale cheek grew more wan.

While the good people at Fairoaks were nursing their days along as one nurses a weak broth—covered, dutiful, and a little drowsy—the great house beyond the Brawl, that old stone stomach on the hill which had digested two generations of silence, began to growl again with appetite.

It was, in fact, at about the date of Mr. Arthur Pendennis’s private calamity (which, like a burn on one’s own tongue, makes all other people’s dinners seem unimportant), that a notice crept into the provincial journals and set the whole county clattering. It ran from mouth to mouth with the cheerful certainty of a recipe: Clavering Park was to be inhabited again.

They discussed it everywhere that England permits herself a remark. At Clavering Market, among barrows of onions and the wet gleam of mackerel; at Cackleby Fair, where the showman’s drum bullied the fiddler; at Chatteris Sessions, where the lawyers’ voices rasped like knives on pewter. It was repeated at Gooseberry Green, when the squire’s carriage met the vicar’s one-horse contrivance and both parties paused, as if the road itself demanded a bit of gossip. It was whispered at Tinkleton Church gate while the bell tolled in the sunshine, and the smocks and scarlet cloaks came over the grass with that soft shuffling sound—country feet making their old music on the earth. Even the rooks above the elms seemed to take the matter up, and the river, busy as ever, carried it down in a rippling treble: the Park, long shut like a larder nobody had the key to, was to be opened; the great hearth was to be lit; the plates—those ancestral plates, one hoped—would clink again.

Five years earlier, the county papers had recorded, with a delicacy proper to print and a relish proper to a county, the marriage at Florence, at the British Legation, of Francis Clavering, Esquire, only son of Sir Francis Clavering, Baronet, of Clavering Park, to Jemima Augusta—daughter of Samuel Snell, of Calcutta, Esquire—and widow of the late J. Amory, Esquire. At that time the local legend, simmered and skimmed by all the idle tongues, was that young Clavering had been ruined for a good while and had done what ruined young men do: he had taken, with the widow, a portion.

People had caught glimpses of this couple abroad as one catches glimpses of strange dishes through the open door of an inn-kitchen: a waft of perfume, a flash of silver, then the door shuts. The Kickleburys, touring in Italy, had seen them in Florence, where Clavering occupied the Poggi Palace, gave parties, and lived comfortably—comfortably, that is, so long as England remained out of reach. Another year, young Peregrine of Cackleby, doing the Long Vacation grand tour, stumbled upon them at Schloss Schinkenstein by the Mummel See; and thereafter, now at Rome, now at Lucca, now at Nice, now at the baths and gambling places of the Rhine and Belgium, you heard of them at intervals—rumours arriving like gusts from far off, tasting of foreign sauces and bad morals.

Their last kitchen, so to speak, had been Paris; and there, after the news came that Samuel Snell of Calcutta was dead, the widow Amory—now Lady Clavering by a stroke of mortality and law—appears to have boiled up into a very handsome splendour indeed.

As for Sir Francis Clavering’s antecedents, they were not of that kind which a family Bible likes to keep pressed between its leaves. Son of an outlaw who lived goutily and gloomily in a dismal old château near Bruges, this gentleman had made a feeble attempt at respectability with a commission in a dragoon regiment, and had broken down almost before the first polish had taken on his boots. The gaming-table finished what the army began. After a couple of years he sold out, passed some time in Her Majesty’s prison of the Fleet (a sort of national pantry where imprudent gentlemen are stored when they cannot pay for their suppers), and then shipped to Ostend to join his exile father. For years thereafter he might be found, like a fly on a sugar-bowl, wherever there were billiard-rooms and watering-places: punting at gambling-houses, dancing at boarding-house balls, riding steeple-chases on other men’s horses, always hungry for the next mouthful of luck and always chewing the same old disappointment.

It was at a boarding-house at Lausanne that Francis Clavering made what he called his lucky coup: he married the widow Amory, lately returned from Calcutta. His father died soon after, and by that demise the lady acquired her title. Mr. Snell, the father, so delighted to have a baronet in the family stew-pot, doubled his daughter’s allowance; and, dying himself not long after, left a fortune to her and her children which rumour served out in portions of ten, twenty thousand a year—according to the appetite of the teller.

Before this, there had not been scandals of the downright sort about Lady Clavering so much as a general sense—an unpleasant flavour, if you will—that she was not of the finest ingredients. The best English people abroad, those who like their society strained clear and served cold, were shy. Her manners were not the most refined; her origin was lamentably low and doubtful. The retired East Indians, a tribe to be found thick as raisins in continental towns, spoke with scorn of her father as a disreputable old lawyer and indigo-smuggler; and of Amory, her first husband, as the mate of the Indiaman in which Miss Snell came out to Calcutta. Neither father nor daughter had been in society at Calcutta; Government House had never tasted them. Old Sir Jasper Rogers, Chief Justice of Calcutta, had once said to his wife that he could tell a queer story about Lady Clavering’s first husband; but like a cook who promises a wonderful dish and then “can’t be got” to produce it, the old Judge never would reveal the mystery, greatly to Lady Rogers’s disappointment and that of the young ladies his daughters, who loved a secret as other girls love sugar.

Yet Paris is a city that will swallow many flavours if they are rich enough; and when Lady Clavering took the Hotel Bouilli in the Rue Grenelle and blazed out in the polite world in the winter of 183—, the very people who had held their noses before were suddenly willing to take a seat at her table. The Faubourg St. Germain took her up. Viscount Bagwig, our excellent ambassador, paid her marked attention. Princes frequented her salons. Those notable English ladies resident in the French capital—so rigid, so severe, so venerable, so sparkling with moral purity that one fancied they might fizz if shaken—acknowledged and countenanced her: Lady Elderbury, Lady Rockminster, the Countess of Southdown. Ten (some said twenty) thousand a year had a very beneficent influence upon Lady Clavering’s character and reputation; it sweetened her, like sugar in a bitter draught, until all the world declared the draught wholesome.

Her munificence, too, was unbounded. Anybody in society with a scheme of charity found her purse ready, like a pantry-door that opens at a touch for the right kind of hand. French ladies of piety got money for schools and convents; she subscribed indifferently for the Armenian patriarch; for Father Barbarossa collecting for his monastery on Mount Athos; for the Baptist Mission to Quashyboo; for the Orthodox Settlement in Feefawfoo, the largest and most savage of the Cannibal Islands. It is recorded of her that on the same day Madame de Cricri got five Napoleons from her for the persecuted Jesuits, Lady Budelight put her down for the Reverend J. Ramshorn, who had had a vision ordering him to convert the Pope of Rome. And, for the benefit of the worldly, she gave the best dinners and the grandest balls and suppers known at Paris that season; so that while the saints had their alms, the sinners had their soufflés.

During this time, too, the good-natured lady must have arranged matters with her husband’s creditors in England; for Sir Francis reappeared in his native country without fear of arrest, was announced in the Morning Post and the county paper as having taken up his residence at Mivart’s Hotel; and one day the anxious old housekeeper at Clavering House beheld a carriage and four drive up the long avenue and stop before the moss-grown steps of the vast melancholy portico.

Three gentlemen were in the open carriage. On the back seat sat our old acquaintance Mr. Tatham of Chatteris. In the places of honour were a handsome portly gentleman wrapped in moustachios, whiskers, fur collars, and braiding—as if he had dressed himself from the trimmings of an entire cavalry regiment—and by him a pale, languid man who descended feebly when the little lawyer and the furred gentleman jumped out with briskness enough for both.

They mounted the mossy steps to the hall-door. A foreign attendant with earrings and a gold-laced cap tugged strenuously at the great bell-handle. The cracked bell clanged through the vast gloom as if the house itself were surprised at being addressed. Presently steps resounded on the marble pavement within, and the doors opened; and finally appeared Mrs. Blenkinsop the housekeeper, Polly her aide-de-camp, and Smart the keeper, bowing humbly as if the very air in the hall demanded a curtsey.

Smart pulled the wisp of hay-coloured hair that decorated his sunburnt forehead, kicked out his left heel as though a dog snapped at his calves, and brought down his head. Old Mrs. Blenkinsop dropped a curtsey full of tremble. Little Polly made a curtsey and several rapid bows, like a toy wound too tight. And Mrs. Blenkinsop, with emotion enough to salt a whole ham, quavered, “Welcome to Clavering, Sir Francis. It du my poor eyes good to see one of the family once more.”

The greeting was addressed to the grand gentleman in fur and braiding, who wore his hat magnificently on one side and twirled his moustachios with royal leisure. He burst out laughing.

“You’ve saddled the wrong horse, old lady—I’m not Sir Francis Clavering what’s come to revisit the halls of my ancestors. Friends and vassals! behold your rightful lord!” And he pointed towards the pale languid gentleman, who said with faint irritation, “Don’t be an ass, Ned.”

“Yes, Mrs. Blenkinsop,” said the pale one, “I’m Sir Francis Clavering; I recollect you quite well. Forgot me, I suppose?—How dy do?” He took the old lady’s trembling hand and nodded in her astonished face with a not unkind vacancy.

Mrs. Blenkinsop protested upon her conscience she would have known Sir Francis anywhere; that he was the very image of Sir Francis his father and of Sir John before him—those old portraits whose eyes had stared down for so long at dust.

“O yes—thanky—of course—very much obliged—and that sort of thing,” said the Baronet, looking about the hall as though searching for a door out of his own inheritance. “Dismal old place, ain’t it, Ned? Never saw it but once, when my governor quarrelled with gwandfather in the year twenty-thwee.”

“Dismal?—beautiful!—the Castle of Otranto!—the Mysteries of Udolpho, by Jove!” cried Ned, with the delight of a man who smells old stone and imagines romance rising like steam from it. “What a fireplace! You might roast an elephant in it. Splendid carved gallery! Inigo Jones, by Jove! I’d lay five to two it’s Inigo Jones.”

“The upper part by Inigo Jones; the lower was altered by the eminent Dutch architect, Vanderputty, in George the First his time, by Sir Richard, fourth baronet,” said Mrs. Blenkinsop, proud as any cook displaying the pedigree of her sauce.

“O indeed,” said the Baronet. “Gad, Ned, you know everything.”

“I know a few things, Frank,” Ned answered, marching his eyes over the walls as if tasting each panel. “I know that’s not a Snyders over the mantelpiece—bet you three to one it’s a copy. We’ll restore it, my boy. A lick of varnish, and it will come out wonderfully, sir. That old fellow in the red gown, I suppose, is Sir Richard.”

“Sheriff of the county, and sate in parliament in the reign of Queen Anne,” said the housekeeper, astonished at the stranger’s knowledge and eager to serve it up. “That on the right is Theodosia, wife of Harbottle, second baronet, by Lely, represented in the character of Venus, the Goddess of Beauty,—her son Gregory, the third baronet, by her side, as Cupid, God of Love—”

“Thank you—needn’t go on, Mrs. Blenkinsop,” said the Baronet, cutting her catalogue as one cuts a too-long string of sausages. “We’ll walk about the place ourselves. Frosch, give me a cigar. Have a cigar, Mr. Tatham?”

Little Mr. Tatham tried a cigar handed by Sir Francis’s courier and spluttered over it with the frantic distress of a man whose mouth has been invaded by foreign policy. “Needn’t come with us, Mrs. Blenkinsop. What’s—his—name—you—Smart—feed the horses and wash their mouths. Shan’t stay long. Come along, Strong,—I know the way: I was here in twenty-thwee, at the end of my gwandfather’s time.”

And Sir Francis and Captain Strong—for such was the style and title of the furred gentleman—passed out of the hall into the reception-rooms, leaving the discomfited Mrs. Blenkinsop to vanish by a side-door to her quarters, now the only habitable rooms in that long-uninhabited belly of a mansion.

It was a house so large that no tenant could afford to keep it warm; its rooms lay like empty dishes after a banquet: splendid shapes, cold surfaces, a grandeur that made one a little hungry and a little melancholy. Sir Francis and his friend walked through room after room, admiring vastness and dreary deserted state. On one side of the hall were the saloons and drawing-rooms; on the other, the oak room, parlour, grand dining-room, library—where Pen had once found books in old days. Around three sides of the hall ran a gallery, and beyond it passages to bedrooms of stately proportions, still showing marks of splendour as a silver tureen shows tarnish. Above, on the second story, was a labyrinth of little discomfortable garrets meant for servants in the days when my lord and my lady slept under gold canopies and their people lay overhead in quarters not so airy nor so clean as stables are now. The house had its own acoustics too: their footsteps went away from them in long echoes, and the draughts sighed in chimneys that had not tasted fire for years, as if the building remembered old voices but could not translate them into any speech the present could understand.

Up and down they wandered; and the owner of the mansion was silent and resigned about the pleasure of possessing it, as a man might be resigned to inheriting a cold roast when he has no hunger. The Captain, however, examined everything with such eagerness you would have thought him master and Sir Francis a visitor dragged along.

“I see capabilities in it—capabilities in it, sir,” cried Captain Strong, his voice enlivening the halls more than any candle could. “Gad, sir, leave it to me, and I’ll make it the pride of the country, at a small expense. What a theatre we can have in the library here, the curtains between the columns! What a famous room for a galop!—it will hold the whole shire. We’ll hang the morning parlour with the tapestry in your second salon in the Rue de Grenelle, and furnish the oak room with the Moyen-age cabinets and the armour. Armour looks splendid against black oak, and there’s a Venice glass in the Quai Voltaire will suit that high mantelpiece to an inch, sir. The long saloon, white and crimson of course; the drawing-room yellow satin; and the little drawing-room light blue, with lace over—hay?”

“I recollect my old governor caning me in that little room,” Sir Francis said, with the calm of a man recalling a bad dinner from childhood. “He always hated me, my old governor.”

“Chintz is the dodge, I suppose, for my lady’s rooms—the suite in the landing, to the south, the bedroom, the sitting-room, and the dressing-room. We’ll throw a conservatory out, over the balcony. Where will you have your rooms?”

“Put mine in the north wing,” said the Baronet with a yawn, “and out of the reach of Miss Amory’s confounded piano. I can’t bear it. She’s scweeching from morning till night.”

Captain Strong burst out laughing, and settled the whole future of the place as easily as a man laying out a supper-table on paper. When their promenade ended, they went into the steward’s room—now Mrs. Blenkinsop’s domain—where Mr. Tatham sat poring over a plan of the estate, and the old housekeeper had prepared a collation in honour of her lord and master. It was not one of Lady Clavering’s Parisian triumphs; but it smelt honest: cold meats, bread, cheese, and that very English fragrance of strong tea and pride. If the great house had been dumb, this little table spoke in a homely dialect.

They inspected the kitchen and stables, about both of which Sir Francis took some interest—there is a straightforward truth in bricks, straw, and a horse’s breath which even a languid baronet can comprehend. Captain Strong wished to examine gardens; but Sir Francis said, “D—— the gardens, and that sort of thing!” and finally drove away from the house as unconcernedly as he had entered it. That night Clavering learned, with the satisfaction of people who like a new noise in an old silence, that Sir Francis had visited the Park and was coming to live in the county.

When the news reached Chatteris, it set all the little place in commotion: High Church and Low Church, half-pay captains and old maids and dowagers, sporting squireens, farmers, tradesmen, factory people—all buzzing as if a hive had been tapped. The tidings came to Fairoaks too, and were received by the ladies there and by Mr. Pen with some excitement.

“Mrs. Pybus says there is a very pretty girl in the family, Arthur,” Laura said, with the calm cruelty of women who think a romance is as necessary as a pudding. “A Miss Amory, Lady Clavering’s daughter by her first marriage. Of course, you will fall in love with her as soon as she arrives.”

Helen cried out, “Don’t talk nonsense, Laura.” Pen laughed. “Well, there is the young Sir Francis for you.”

“He is but four years old,” Miss Laura replied. “But I shall console myself with that handsome officer, Sir Francis’s friend. He was at church last Sunday, in the Clavering pew, and his mustachios were beautiful.”

Indeed, the number of Sir Francis’s household—every member already paraded by rumour like dishes at a banquet—was soon known in the town; and everything else as nearly as human industry could calculate. In summer evenings the Park avenue and grounds were dotted with townsfolk strolling up to peep and criticise improvements. Loads of furniture arrived in vans from Chatteris and London, and numerous as the vans were, there was not one whose contents Captain Glanders did not know, and escort up to the Park House as if each chair and sideboard were a regiment under his command.

By this time Captain Glanders and Captain Edward Strong had formed an intimate acquaintance. The younger Captain took the lodgings at Clavering once occupied by the peaceful Smirke, and was deep in the good graces of Madame Fribsby his landlady, and of the whole town besides. He was splendid in person and raiment; fresh-coloured, blue-eyed, black-whiskered, broad-chested, athletic—though with a slight tendency to fulness that did not lessen the comeliness of his jolly figure. As he strode down Clavering High Street, hat on one side, cane clanking or wheeling in soldierly flourishes, his jolly laughter ringing through the otherwise quiet place, he was as welcome as sunshine and as noisy as a fair. He brought his own soundscape with him: the click of boot-heels, the tap of cane, the burst of laugh; and you could see townsfolk brighten as if their ears had been hungry.

On the first market-day he knew every pretty girl in the market as quickly as if he had been cataloguing fruit. He joked with the women; he had a word with farmers about stock; and he dined at the Agricultural Ordinary at the Clavering Arms, where he set the gentlemen in top-boots dying with laughter by his fun. “Tu be sure he be a vine veller, tu be sure that he be,” was the universal verdict, given in the local dialect with the local relish—as if the very vowels belonged to the soil. He shook hands with a score of them as they rode out on old nags, and waved his hat to them splendidly, smoking his cigar in the inn-gate. Before evening was done he was free of Madame Fribsby’s bar, knew what rent the landlord paid, how many acres he farmed, how much malt went into the strong beer; and whether a little brandy, unexcised by kings, ever slipped inland from Baymouth or the fishing villages along the coast.

He had tried living at the great house at first, but found it too dull.

“I am a creature born for society,” he told Captain Glanders. “I’m down here to see Clavering’s house set in order; for between ourselves, Frank has no energy, sir, no energy; he’s not the chest for it, sir”—and he threw out his own trunk as he spoke, broad enough for any campaign—“but I must have social intercourse. Old Mrs. Blenkinsop goes to bed at seven, and takes Polly with her. There was nobody but me and the Ghost for the first two nights at the great house, and I own it, sir, I like company. Most old soldiers do.”

Glanders asked where he had served.

Captain Strong curled his moustache and laughed. The other might almost ask where he had not served. “I began, sir, as cadet of Hungarian Uhlans, and when the war of Greek independence broke out, quitted that service in consequence of a quarrel with my governor, and was one of seven who escaped from Missolonghi, and was blown up in one of Botzaris’s fireships, at the age of seventeen. I’ll show you my Cross of the Redeemer, if you’ll come over to my lodgings and take a glass of grog with me this evening. I’ve a few of those baubles in my desk. I’ve the White Eagle of Poland; Skrzynecki gave it me”—he pronounced Skrzynecki with a gusto as if it were something you could taste—“upon the field of Ostrolenka. I was a lieutenant of the fourth regiment, sir, and we marched through Diebitsch’s lines—bang thro’ ’em into Prussia, sir, without firing a shot. Ah, Captain, that was a mismanaged business. I received this wound by the side of the King before Oporto,—where he would have pounded the stock-jobbing Pedroites, had Bourmont followed my advice; and I served in Spain with the King’s troops, until the death of my dear friend, Zumalacarreguy, when I saw the game was over, and hung up my toasting iron, Captain. Alava offered me a regiment, the Queen’s Muleteros; but I couldn’t—damme, I couldn’t—and now, sir, you know Ned Strong—the Chevalier Strong they call me abroad—as well as he knows himself.”

Thus almost everybody in Clavering came to know Ned Strong. He told Madame Fribsby; he told the landlord of the George; he told Baker at the reading-rooms; he told Mrs. Glanders and the young ones at dinner; and finally he told Mr. Arthur Pendennis, who, yawning into Clavering one day, found the Chevalier in company with Captain Glanders and was delighted with his new acquaintance.

Before many days were over, Captain Strong was as much at home in Helen’s drawing-room as in Madame Fribsby’s first floor, and made the lonely house very gay with good-humour and ceaseless talk. The two women had never before seen such a man. He had a thousand stories of battles and dangers; of Greek captives, Polish beauties, Spanish nuns. He could sing scores of songs in half a dozen languages, and would sit down to the piano and troll them off in a rich manly voice. His notes filled the room and pushed back its quiet like a curtain; and yet—when the song ended—the old country hush flowed in again, and you heard the clock and the faint sounds of the night outside, as if the house insisted on its own native tongue.

Both ladies pronounced him delightful—and so he was; though, in truth, they had not had much choice of men’s society, having seen in their lives but few persons besides old Portman, the Major, and Mr. Pen, who was a genius to be sure; but geniuses, like sauces too much reduced, can be intense and somewhat moody at home.

Captain Strong, who never came to a house without bringing a whole baggage-train of information, acquainted his friends at Fairoaks not only with his own biography but with the history of the family now coming to Clavering. It was he, he said, who had made the marriage between his friend Frank and the widow Amory. She wanted rank; he wanted money. What match could be more suitable? He organised it; he made them happy. There was no romance—Lady Clavering was not of an age or a person for romance, and Sir Francis, if he had his billiards and his dinner, cared for little besides. But they were as happy as people could be. Clavering would return to his native place; his wife’s fortune would pay the encumbrances; his son and heir would be one of the first men in the county.

“And Miss Amory?” Laura asked. Laura was uncommonly curious about Miss Amory, as though a new girl were a new spice.

Strong laughed. “Oh, Miss Amory is a muse—Miss Amory is a mystery—Miss Amory is a femme incomprise.”

“What is that?” asked simple Mrs. Pendennis; but the Chevalier gave her no answer—perhaps because the phrase was the kind of foreign condiment one sprinkles on conversation when one has no solid meaning to serve.

“Miss Amory paints, Miss Amory writes poems, Miss Amory composes music, Miss Amory rides like Diana Vernon. Miss Amory is a paragon, in a word.”

“I hate clever women,” said Pen.

“Thank you,” said Laura; and for her part she was quite sure she should be charmed with Miss Amory, and longed for such a friend. With which she looked Pen full in the face, as if every word the little hypocrite spoke were Gospel truth, and as if she could already hear—through the still country air—the first thin approach of that “confounded piano” which Sir Francis dreaded, like a modern noise beginning to creep into an old, quiet world.

Every house, if you listen carefully enough at night when the fires have dropped to a whisper and the boards begin to talk in their old wooden dialect, has something it keeps in a cupboard. It may be an unpaid bill; it may be a portrait with eyes that follow you; it may be an aunt who refuses to die out of mere politeness. At Clavering Park the skeleton wore a ribbon, quoted Lamartine, and could weep on cue with the neatness of a kitchen-maid separating whites from yolks. Blanche Amory—“Missy” at home when people felt brave, “Blanche” when she insisted on being poetry itself—was as pretty as a sugared violet and as soothing, in constant use, as grit in a shoe.

You would have said she must make sunshine in whatever room she entered. And so she did—if you define sunshine as that bright, relentless glare which shows every speck of dust and makes everybody blink.

“I say, Strong,” Sir Francis Clavering drawled one day, after dinner, when the billiard-table had become a confessional and a cigar the priest, “I wish to the doose your wife was dead.”

Captain Strong, who met most of life the way a good cook meets a boiling pot—with a laugh and a towel—blew a calm cloud and answered, “So do I. That’s a cannon, by Jove. But she won’t; she’ll live for ever—you see if she don’t. Why do you wish her off the hooks, Frank, my boy?”

“Because then you might marry Missy. She ain’t bad-looking. She’ll have ten thousand, and that’s a good bit of money for such a poor old devil as you,” said the Baronet, as if proposing a joint of meat at market.

“And gad, Strong,” he added, souring, “I hate her worse and worse every day. I can’t stand her, Strong. By gad, I can’t.”

“I wouldn’t take her at twice the figure,” Strong said, laughing outright. “I never saw such a little devil in my life.”

“I should like to poison her,” Sir Francis observed, with the cool deliberation of a man choosing between port and claret. “By Jove I should.”

“Why, what has she been at now?” asked Strong.

“Nothing particular,” said Clavering; and that “nothing” in a house is commonly the very thing that breaks plates. “Only her old tricks. That girl has such a knack of making everybody miserable that, hang me, it’s quite surprising. Last night she sent the governess crying away from the dinner-table. Afterwards, as I was passing Frank’s room, I heard the poor little beggar howling in the dark, and found his sister had been frightening his soul out of his body, by telling him stories about the ghost that’s in the house. At lunch she gave my lady a turn; and though my wife’s a fool, she’s a good soul—I’m hanged if she ain’t.”

“What did Missy do to her?” Strong asked, still amused, for he was one of those obstinate men whose good-humour has no handle.

“Why, hang me, if she didn’t begin talking about the late Amory—my predecessor,” said Sir Francis with a grin that tried to look manly and came out peevish. “She got some picture out of the Keepsake, and said she was sure it was like her dear father. She wanted to know where her father’s grave was. Hang her father! Whenever Miss Amory talks about him, Lady Clavering always bursts out crying: and the little devil will talk about him in order to spite her mother. Today when she began, I got in a confounded rage; said I was her father; and—and that sort of thing, and then, sir, she took a shy at me.”

“And what did she say about you, Frank?” asked Strong.

“Gad, she said I wasn’t her father; that I wasn’t fit to comprehend her; that her father must have been a man of genius, and fine feelings, and that sort of thing: whereas I had married her mother for money.”

“Well, didn’t you?” Strong inquired, with that blunt honesty which makes the truth sound like a joke told at the wrong time.

“It don’t make it any the pleasanter to hear because it’s true, don’t you know,” Sir Francis said, shifting his cue as if he could rearrange his conscience with it. “I ain’t a literary man and that; but I ain’t such a fool as she makes me out. I don’t know how it is, but she always manages to put me in the hole. She turns all the house round her in her quiet way, and with her confounded sentimental airs. I wish she was dead, Ned.”

“It was my wife whom you wanted dead just now,” Strong reminded him.

“Well; when people bore my life out, I do wish they were dead,” said the Baronet, with his usual candour, “and I wish Missy were down a well, with all my heart.”

Thus, from the frankness of two gentlemen digesting their dinner in smoke, it appears that our little accomplished fairy possessed certain gifts which are not always welcomed in families—especially when they arrive without warning, like a sharp smell from the kitchen at midnight.

Blanche had talent, literary tastes, exquisitely tuned sympathies, and the firm belief that nobody within three counties deserved her. She lived, like many a genius, among relatives who could not comprehend her; and, like many a genius, she took pains that they should never forget it. Her stepfather’s reading—if you may call it that—lay between Bell’s Life and the Racing Calendar; and Lady Clavering wrote in a hand and orthography that suggested her education had been abandoned at thirteen in favour of ribbons. The poor lady would call asparagus “sparrowgrass,” and add an “h” to objects as if trying to give them a little pedigree; and Blanche, who corrected grammar the way a cook corrects seasoning—with a pinch that stings—would smile gently and set her mother trembling into worse mistakes.

If Blanche suffered, as she declared, it was chiefly in her own soul—where the tears were stored, decanted, and poured out at convenience. She had the kind of sorrow that increases with practice; the more she wept, the more accomplished her weeping became, until Mes Larmes would dribble on demand like a well-trained sauce from a ladle. Sentiment, indeed, behaves like certain maladies: indulge it and it grows greedy.

She had begun her “gush” early. Lamartine had been her chosen prophet from the first moment she could feel herself interesting. After that, she nourished her mind—so she said—upon French novels with an appetite that would have done honour to a farm-boy with a loaf. Balzac and George Sand were her daily bread; she devoured them by sixteen, and then, finding her own household too plain, lived with companions in what she called the spirit-world: tender Indiana, passionate Lélia, amiable Trenmor (that angelic convict), fiery Stenio, and all the other high-souled persons who inhabit romances and never have to pay for coal. She had been in love with Prince Rodolph and Prince Djalma while still in pinafores, and had settled the rights of woman with Indiana before she had finished learning to tie her sash. She played at love with heroes as she had once played at maternity with dolls—choosing, neglecting, resuming; to-day the blue-eyed darling, to-morrow the black-eyed one; and sometimes, in a fit of perverse taste, it would be the battered little object with a burnt nose and no eyes at all that received the warmest caresses.

As novelists are expected to know everything—even what a young lady does not know about herself—we may say (with the discretion of people peeping through keyholes in the name of art) that Mademoiselle Betsi, as Blanche had been called in her early Paris days, felt tender emotions at eleven for a Savoyard organ-grinder whom she persisted in believing a prince stolen from his parents; that at twelve an old and hideous drawing-master had “agitated” her heart (for love, like appetite, is not always fastidious); and that at thirteen, at Madame de Caramel’s boarding-school in the Champs Élysées—next door, as everybody knows, to Monsieur Rogron’s pension for young gentlemen—she carried on a correspondence with two youthful pensioners of the College of Charlemagne.

Betsi—yes. For the child had been christened Betsy, and had later, by her own will and fancy, crowned herself Blanche, as if baptism were a hat one could choose in a shop-window. Sir Francis’s one weapon, held always in reserve like a kitchen threat—“I’ll put you on bread and water”—was to call her publicly Betsy. The menace could still bring the Muse to momentary order; no genius enjoys being dragged into the world by its nursery-name.

In her treasure-chest she possessed a little museum of locks of hair, relics of “dear, dear” friendships—some married away, some transferred to other schools, one darling “Leocadie” recovered in horror keeping books in her father’s grocery in the Rue du Bac. Blanche had tasted disappointments, estrangements, and disillusions (always in her pretty French jargon), and felt herself marked for suffering as genius must be. Meanwhile she made her mother as uncomfortable as the day allowed, and drove her stepfather to dreams of wells and poison. Captain Strong alone, by the sheer obstinacy of his cheerfulness, refused to be governed by her tongue.

And while the household at the Park simmered with this delicate domestic acid, the town of Clavering bubbled with curiosity. It was not to be supposed that Madame Fribsby—the milliner, the purveyor of caps and gossip—should remain unmoved. At the first appearance of the Park family in church, she noted every bonnet, ribbon, and brodequin with the attention of a food-historian reading an old recipe: what was trimmed where, what was stitched how, what kind of silk whispered when it moved. Doctor Portman delivered one of his oldest sermons—richly preserved like fruit in brandy—but Madame Fribsby tasted none of it. Her mind was occupied with the rustle of fabrics and the faint squeak of new gloves, and the way modern fashion had begun to sound like commerce.

In a few days she had arranged an interview with Lady Clavering’s confidential attendant in the housekeeper’s room at the Park. Cards in French and English—proclaiming that Madame Fribsby received the newest fashions from Paris through her correspondent Madame Victorine, and that she made court and ball dresses for the nobility and gentry of the shire—were conveyed into the hands of Lady Clavering and Miss Amory, and, to Madame’s satisfaction, received favourably. The first thread had been slipped into the needle; the seam would follow.

Mrs. Bonner, Lady Clavering’s woman, soon became a frequent visitor in Madame Fribsby’s drawing-room, where evenings were stitched together out of green tea, scandal, hot Sally-Lunn cakes, and a little novel-reading. There is a certain kind of talk that rises like yeast when warmed with sugar and a secret. Mrs. Bonner found much time for these entertainments—far more than Miss Amory’s maid, who could seldom be spared; for Blanche worked her attendant harder than any factory.

Blanche loved clothes as some people love language: not for warmth, but for power, for transformation, for the way a new cut could rename a body. With poetic hunger for change, she altered her attire daily. Her maid, Pincott—an English girl apprenticed in Paris, skilled in the whole holy trinity of ripping, remodelling, and making the old look new—was kept at needle and comb from morning until far into night. The girl had respectable parents and a poor home: her father crippled, the family not quite ruined but never quite afloat; if she returned, she would only add weight to the sinking boat. So Pincott stayed where she could support herself and send a little relief back like crumbs from the rich table.

And Blanche, with that candour which is sometimes merely cruelty with good pronunciation, never let her forget it.

“I should send you away, Pincott,” she would say, “for you are a great deal too weak, and your eyes are failing you, and you are always crying and snivelling and wanting the doctor; but I wish that your parents at home should be supported, and I go on enduring you for their sake, mind.” Or: “Pincott, your wretched appearance and slavish manner, and red eyes, positively give me the migraine; I think I shall make you wear rouge, so that you may look a little cheerful.” Or: “Pincott, I can’t bear—even for the sake of your starving parents—that you should tear my hair out of my head in that manner; write to them and say that I dispense with your services.”

And then—after keeping the poor girl an hour trembling over her hair, which Blanche liked combed slowly while she lay reading French novels—she would go to bed at one, and say with royal sweetness, “Pincott, you may kiss me. Good night. I should like you to have the pink dress ready for the morning.” And thus, having dealt out her little blessings like sugared almonds at a funeral, the Muse would turn and sleep.

Blanche could lie abed as long as she chose; Pincott rose early to make the day’s miracle of ribbons and hems. She appeared with the same red eyes and wan face—offending Blanche by the stubborn fact of illness. The servant persisted in being unwell, and the mistress persisted in being surprised by it. Yet Blanche never thought herself harsh. At times she “made quite a friend” of Pincott, wrote pretty verses about the lonely little tiring-maid whose heart was far away, and considered this poetry as payment, or at least as proof of delicacy. She was a superior being and expected service as such. There are tyrannies done with oaths and whips; there are tyrannies done with a soft voice and a well-bred simper. The bruises are quieter in the second case; they are no less real.

But Blanche was a Muse—tremulous with excitability, tearful at the slightest touch, a butterfly who claimed that merely to brush her wing was to crush her. Vulgar people, she implied, did not understand the fine skin of genius.

So Pincott, occupied all day and night with stitching, hemming, ripping, combing, ironing, crimping; reading to her mistress in bed (for the girl knew both languages, and had a sweet voice and manner), took no share in Madame Fribsby’s little entertainments. Nor was she much missed; in society as in kitchens, those who do the hardest work are expected to be invisible.

Another person from the Park, however, became a constant guest of our milliner: the chief of the kitchen, Monsieur Mirobolant, with whom Madame Fribsby soon formed an intimacy.

The rustic inhabitants of Clavering, not being accustomed to Frenchmen except as a word in a war-song, were not so favourably impressed by Monsieur Alcide’s manners and appearance as that gentleman had imagined they must be. On a summer afternoon when his services were not required, he walked down the street in what he considered the easiest, most natural thing in the world: a light green frock or paletot; a crimson velvet waistcoat with blue glass buttons; a pantalon écossais with a check so large and decided it might have been intended as a warning signal; an orange satin neckcloth; jean-boots with shiny leather tips; and, crowning the whole, a gold-embroidered cap and a richly gilt cane. He fancied that, unless the beauty of his person attracted observation, there was nothing remarkable in the ensemble; he believed he showed the air of a gentleman of good Parisian ton. The very street, had it possessed ears educated in acoustic ecology, would have told him otherwise: his cane clicked, his buttons flashed, his colours shouted, and the town’s quiet domestic soundscape—hens, carts, the mild gossip of hedges—received him as it receives a factory whistle.

He went grinning and ogling at every woman he met with glances he meant to be fatal, and peered over railings and into windows at tranquil evening domesticity. Betsy, Mrs. Pybus’s maid, shrank back with a “Lor bless us!” as he ogled her over the laurel-bush. The Miss Bakers and their mamma stared as if an exotic bird had escaped into the lane. Presently children left their dirt-pies to follow him.

For a time Mirobolant believed himself admired, and walked on the more proudly, pleased to think he could confer delight like seasoning scattered with a generous hand. But the small followers were joined by larger ones; lads and girls from the factory, loosed at that hour, swelled the train. Laughter turned sharper. Jeers began to crack like thrown nutshells. “Frenchy! Frenchy!” they cried. “Frogs!” One demanded a lock of his long hair, which fell in rich ringlets. The hooting rose in a harsh chorus, a kind of human machinery, and the poor chef—who understood applause but not this particular music—began to perceive he was being cooked in his own sauce.

At this moment Madame Fribsby spied him with his mob at his heels and heard the scornful shouts. She ran out, crossed the street, held out her hand, and addressed him in his own language—ever so ill spoken, but recognisably home. She invited him into her abode; and when she had housed him within her door, she stood bravely on the threshold, facing the gibing crowd like a small general. She told them they were a pack of cowards to insult a man who could not speak their language and was alone without protection.

The little crowd, with ironical cheers and final hoots, retreated. Madame Fribsby was respected in the place; her oddity and kindness had earned her friends; and even factory girls can recognise a force of character when it speaks plainly.

Poor Mirobolant was grateful to hear French, however battered. Frenchmen, with their national politeness, pardon our faults more readily than we pardon their English; they will endure our blunders through a long conversation without the least propensity to grin. He vowed she was his guardian angel; he declared he had not yet met such suavity among les Anglaises; and he paid her compliments as if she had been the fairest duchess in Europe. Alcide Mirobolant did homage, after his fashion, to all womankind, and never troubled himself with distinctions of rank in the realms of beauty.

Next day one of his aides-de-camp arrived at the milliner’s with a basket, bearing the tributes of the rescued artist: a cream flavoured with pineapple, cool and perfumed as a summer pantry; a mayonnaise of lobster he declared not unworthy of his hand nor of her to whom he offered it; and a box of preserved fruits of Provence, jewel-like and sticky with sun. A gallant note accompanied them to “La respectable Fribsbi.” Her kindness, he wrote, had made “a green place in the desert of his existence”; her suavity would ever contrast in memory with the grossièreté of the rustic population unworthy to possess such a jewel.

Thus sprang up an intimacy of the most confidential nature between the milliner and the chief of the kitchen. Yet Madame did not know whether to receive his friendship with pleasure or mortification; for he persisted in calling her “La respectable Fribsbi,” “La vertueuse Fribsbi,” and in declaring that he should consider her as his mother, while hoping she would regard him as her son. It was not very long ago, she thought, that French words had been addressed to her suggesting another sort of bond. She sighed, and looked up at the picture of her Carabineer. It is astonishing how young some hearts remain when heads have need of a front, or a little hair-dye; and at that moment Madame Fribsby, as she told young Alcide, felt as romantic as a girl of eighteen.

When talk drifted in that direction—and at their first intimacy Madame was rather inclined to steer it there—Alcide always diverged, politely as a man turning a sauce so it shall not catch. It was as his mother he insisted on regarding her. In no other capacity would he recognise her; and with that relationship the gentle lady was forced to content herself, when she found how deeply the artist’s heart was engaged elsewhere.

He was not long before he described to her the subject and origin of his passion.

Sir Francis Clavering had spoken of the lady who had fetched him home with her fortune as though she were a sort of rich parcel misdirected by Providence; and—making all allowances for a baronet’s gratitude when it has to dine at the same table with it—he was not entirely astray. Lady Clavering was not what the world calls instructed. Her education had been a short, sharp one, like a cook’s lesson given to a child who keeps tasting the sugar: a couple of years in Europe, in a London suburb which she steadfastly christened “Ackney,” as if the place had offended her and she would not grant it its proper consonants to its dying day. At fifteen she was shipped off to her father in Calcutta; and it was during that voyage—aboard the Ramchunder East Indiaman, Captain Bragg—that she made the acquaintance of Mr. Amory, third mate, and (as the sequel proved) first-rate nuisance.

We need not unpack all the early seasoning of Lady Clavering’s history. Enough that Captain Bragg, who had undertaken to deliver Miss Snell safely to her father—an attorney, a speculator, a man who owned pieces of ships as other men own slices of cheese—found reason, before they reached the Cape, to clap the rebellious rascal of a mate into irons. The voyage itself was stormy enough to make even a curry go cold; the Ramchunder, her cargo, and the passengers were well shaken, wetted, and terrified. Bragg left Mr. Amory behind at the Cape like a bad smell one can’t carry into polite company, and presented his ward at Calcutta to her father, who no doubt weighed her with his eye as he would have weighed a bag of rupees.

A few months later—because a man like Amory is never properly thrown away—he turned up in Calcutta again, having worked his passage out before the mast. He married the rich attorney’s daughter in spite of the old gentleman, then tried, one after another, to set himself up: indigo-planter and failed; agent and failed; editor of the Sunderbund Pilot and failed. Through each enterprise he quarrelled incessantly with his father-in-law and his wife, as if ill-temper were a kind of capital that might replace cash. At last there came a crash so final it compelled him to bolt the place altogether and go to New South Wales.

It was in the course of those unlucky proceedings that he likely made the acquaintance of Sir Jasper Rogers, the respected Calcutta judge we have already met; and since truth has a way of insisting on being served, even when no one has ordered it, it must be said that Mr. Amory’s ruin was clinched by an improper use of his father-in-law’s name—his father-in-law being perfectly able to write for himself, and having no need of a son-in-law to act as pen, ink, and conscience. Europe, which does not read Calcutta law-reports with the appetite it bestows on French menus, knew little of these particulars; Bengal knew them all, and repeated them with the relish people give to stories not happening to themselves.

Mrs. Amory and her father decided that India was not a comfortable kitchen for her to stew in. She returned to Europe with her little daughter Betsy—Blanche—then four years old. With them came Betsy’s nurse, the same Mrs. Bonner who now, in a higher domestic mythology, figures as Lady Clavering’s confidential maid. Captain Bragg took a house for them near his own in Pocklington Street; and the summer that greeted them was bitter as over-brewed tea. Rain drummed daily on the windows—an incessant, joyless percussion like a bad military band practising next door—so that the very sound of London seemed to Mrs. Amory a scolding.

Bragg, pompous and disagreeable, strutted about as though he had personally invented propriety and must keep it varnished. He was perhaps ashamed of his Indian passenger, perhaps merely anxious to be rid of her. She, poor soul, imagined all London was gossiping over her husband’s disgrace: that the King, the Queen, and the Court of Directors were all whispering over their cutlets about Mrs. Amory. She had an allowance from her father and no reason to be drenched in English rain beneath Captain Bragg’s surveillance. So she resolved—like a sensible woman driven from a noisy street—to go where the air was kinder.

Off she went abroad, glad to slip away from that odious bully. Continental towns received her willingly enough. Boarding-houses adored her; she paid royally, like a lady who believes money is chiefly meant to prevent arguments. She called Hackney “Ackney,” certainly—an act of pronunciation like putting cloves in a pudding whether the recipe allows it or not—and though she spoke English with a little foreign twang, it was curious and not unpleasant, like a spice you can’t name but keep tasting. She dressed amazingly. She loved eating and drinking with the devotion other people reserve for religion, and in every boarding-house she turned the common kitchen into a small Calcutta: curries ground and simmered, pillaws steamed, rice washed and aired, onions fried to a brown so fragrant it would have converted a fasting hermit. You could tell when Mrs. Amory was in the building: the corridors carried cumin and ghee the way churches carry incense; even the staircases seemed to breathe.

Her singularities, far from ruining her, gave her society a zest. She was jovial, good-natured, generous—ready for any party of pleasure, by whomsoever proposed. At picnics she brought three times more champagne and fowl and ham than anyone else, and distributed it with a laugh that made the corks sound cheerful instead of merely loud. She took endless boxes at the play, tickets for masked balls, and flung them about as if gaiety were a household staple. She paid boarding-house people months beforehand; she helped shabby moustachioed bucks and anxious dowagers whose remittances lagged, feeding them from her purse as she fed herself from her saucepans. So she tramped through Europe—Brussels, Paris, Milan, Naples, Rome—following fancy like a spoon following gravy.

At Rome news came to her that Amory was dead; and at Rome, too, Captain Clavering happened to be staying—unable to pay his hotel bill, as indeed was his friend the Chevalier Strong. The widow, who professed no particular grief for a husband she had lost in all but geography long before, married the descendant of the ancient house of Clavering with the same good-humoured practicality with which she would order a supper for unexpected guests. Thus she arrived at the present moment: mistress of Clavering Park, posed while Mr. Pinckney, the celebrated painter, portrayed her with her little boy beside her—Master Francis, the heir and the appetite.

Missy—Blanche—had followed her mamma through most of those peregrinations, and learned a great deal of life, as children do when the world is their schoolroom and boarding-house tables their desks. There had been a governess for a while; then, after the second marriage, the select pension of Madame de Caramel in the Champs Elysees—a place where young ladies were taught accomplishments with the same careful tyranny with which cooks are taught to whip eggs. When the Claverings came to England, Blanche came too.

It was only within a few years—after the death of her grandfather, and after the birth of her little brother—that she began to understand the change in her place at table. Miss Amory, nobody’s daughter, was suddenly a very small personage in a great house compared with Master Francis Clavering, heir to an ancient baronetcy and a noble estate. But for little Frank she would have been an heiress, in spite of her father. She knew, and did not much care about money—she had never known stint. She was a romantic little Muse, full of verse and attitudes. Yet she could not reasonably be grateful to the people who had helped to alter her condition; nor did she fully understand what that condition meant until she had made further progress and acquired more exact knowledge of the world’s dictionary—where certain words are written in larger type than others.

This much, however, was clear to her. Her stepfather was dull and weak; mamma dropped her H’s and was not refined; and little Frank was a spoiled, quarrelsome urchin, always having his way, always treading on Blanche’s feet, always upsetting his dinner on her dresses—as if gravy, like the estate, were meant to flow toward him—and, worst of all in Blanche’s eyes, keeping her out of her inheritance. None of them, she felt, could comprehend her. So her solitary heart pined for other attachments, and she cast about for someone upon whom she might bestow the precious boon of her unoccupied affection.

The consequence was that, from want of sympathy or from surplus of temper, she made herself so disagreeable at home, frightened her mother, and bored her stepfather so much, that they were almost as anxious as she could be that she should settle for herself. Hence Sir Francis Clavering’s wish, expressed to his friend in the last chapter, that Mrs. Strong should die—so that he might take Blanche to himself as a second Mrs. Strong. But as Mrs. Strong persisted in living, any other person was welcome to win Blanche; and a smart young fellow, good-looking and well educated like Arthur Pendennis, might have proposed for her if he had the mind—and would have been received with open arms by Lady Clavering as a son-in-law—had he possessed the courage to come forward.

Mr. Pen, however, was afflicted with that particular vanity which calls itself diffidence. Ashamed of his late failures, his idle and nameless condition, and the poverty he had brought upon his mother by his folly, he nursed doubt and distrust as though they were virtues. How could he ever hope for such a prize as brilliant Blanche Amory—she in a fine park and mansion waited on by a score of grand domestics—while at Fairoaks a maid-servant brought in a meagre meal and his mother pinched and managed and made two ends meet only by sewing them together? Obstacles looked insurmountable which would have melted before a bold advance. He preferred despairing, or dallying with his wishes—or perhaps not quite shaping them—to making a gallant attempt. Many a young man fails through that species of vanity called shyness, who might, for the asking, have his will. We do not even say that Pen had yet ascertained his will, or was doing more than thinking about falling in love.

Miss Amory was charming and lively. She fascinated and cajoled him by a thousand arts—or natural graces, or flatteries. Yet besides shyness and vanity, there were other doubts. Pen’s mother had divined the girl and did not trust her. Mrs. Pendennis saw Blanche light-minded and frivolous; detected wants in her which offended the pure and pious lady—a want of reverence for parents and for things more sacred; worldliness and selfishness lurking beneath pretty words and tender expressions.

Laura and Pen battled these points at first with the widow—Laura still enthusiastic about her new friend, and Pen not far gone enough to hide his feelings. He laughed at his mother’s objections. “Psha, mother! you are jealous about Laura—all women are jealous.”

But when, in the course of a month or two, Helen watched with that anxious attention with which brooding women watch a son’s affection—there is, in the confession of it, a kind of sexual jealousy in the mother, a secret pang—when she saw the intimacy progressing; saw the two young people perpetually finding pretexts to meet; saw Miss Blanche at Fairoaks or Mr. Pen at the Park every day; then the poor widow’s heart began to fail her. Her darling project seemed to vanish. Giving way to her weakness, she told Pen one day what her hopes had been: that she felt herself breaking and not long for this world; and that she prayed before she went, she might see her two children one.

Late events—Pen’s career, his life, his former passion for the actress—had shaken the tender lady’s spirit. She felt he had escaped her; that he was in the maternal nest no more. She clung with a sickening fondness to Laura—Laura left to her by Francis in Heaven. Pen kissed and soothed her with a grand, patronising kindness. He had long suspected his mother’s wish. Did Laura know anything of it? Not she, Mrs. Pendennis said; not for worlds would she have breathed a word to Laura.

“Well, well,” Pen replied, laughing in that way young men do when they are frightened but would rather sound witty than honest. “There is time enough. You won’t die. And as for the Muse—she is too grand a lady to think about poor little me. And as for Laura—who knows she would have me? She would do anything you told her, to be sure. But am I worthy of her?”

“O, Pen, you might be,” the widow answered; and though Mr. Pen never truly doubted his worthiness, a pleasant self-complacency came over him as he thought of the proposal and imaged Laura as he had known her for years: fair and open, kindly and pious, cheerful, tender, and true.

At the end of this talk Laura came in from the garden. Her cheeks were a little flushed; her look frank and smiling; in her hand a basket of roses. She took the finest and brought it to Mrs. Pendennis, refreshed the room with its colour and odour, and hung over her mother with fondness as she gave it.

“And I might have this prize for the asking!” Pen thought, with a thrill of triumph, looking at the kindly girl. “Why, she is as beautiful and as generous as her roses.” The image of the two women remained with him ever after; he never recalled it without tears rising in his eyes.

Before many weeks had passed, however, Laura was obliged to concede that Helen’s judgment of Blanche was right: the Muse was selfish, unkind, inconstant. Of course Blanche confided to her bosom friend the little griefs and domestic annoyances: how the family could not comprehend her; how she moved among them isolated; how poor mamma’s education had been neglected and Blanche was forced to blush for her blunders; how Sir Francis was weak and deplorably unintellectual and only happy when smoking odious cigars; how since the birth of her little brother she had seen her mother’s precious affection estranged from the once darling daughter; how she was alone, alone, alone in the world.

These griefs, however real to a young lady of exquisite sensibility, did not persuade Laura that Blanche’s conduct in small incidents was proper. Little Frank might be provoking; might have deprived Blanche of mamma’s caresses; but this was no reason for Blanche to box the child’s ears because he upset a glass of water over her drawing; nor to call him opprobrious names in English and French. Nor was the preference accorded to little Frank any reason for Blanche to assume imperial airs toward the boy’s governess, and send that young lady on errands to fetch a book or a pocket-handkerchief, as if a governess were a bell-pull.

When a domestic did an errand for Laura, she always thanked them with that warmth which costs nothing and buys comfort; whereas Laura could not help seeing that Blanche gave commands as naturally as she breathed, disturbing anybody’s ease to administer to her own. It was Laura’s first great experiment in friendship; and it pained her generous heart to strip away, one by one, the charms she had dressed her new friend in, and to find the fascinating fairy a mortal—and not a very amiable mortal. What generous person has not been deceived so? And who has not, in turn, deceived somebody else?

After the scene with little Frank—after the French and English compliments, and the box on the ear—Laura, who had plenty of humour, could not help remembering some touching verses Blanche had read from Mes Larmes. They began: “My pretty baby brother, may angels guard thy rest,” and proceeded to compliment the infant upon the station he was about to occupy, contrast it with Blanche’s own lonely condition, and vow that he would never find affection so constant as a sister’s heart.

“It may be,” the forlorn one had sighed, “it may be, you will slight it, my pretty baby sweet,
You will spurn me from your bosom, I’ll cling around your feet!
O let me, let me, love you! the world will prove to you
As false as ’tis to others, but I am ever true.”

And here was the Muse boxing the darling’s ears instead of kneeling at his feet; giving Laura her lesson in cynical philosophy—not quite her first, indeed: she had seen something of the same contrast between poetry and practice at home, in Mr. Pen. But then Pen was different. Pen was a man. It seemed somehow natural that he should be self-willed and have his own way; and under his selfishness there was a kind and generous heart. Hard, thought Laura, that such a diamond should be exchanged for such a false stone.

In a word, Laura began to tire of Blanche. She had assayed her and found her not true. Her former admiration—so frankly expressed—gave way to a feeling we will not call contempt, but which lived next door to it; and Laura adopted toward Blanche a grave, tranquil superiority which was not at all to the Muse’s liking. Nobody enjoys being found out; nobody who has posed as a queen likes being asked to step down and mind the scullery. Blanche’s knowledge that she was slipping in Laura’s esteem did not improve her temper; it made her peevish, dissatisfied with herself, and therefore less agreeable to others.

So there arose, one fatal day, a battle-royal between dearest Blanche and dearest Laura, in which their friendship was all but slain outright.

Blanche had been unusually capricious and wicked. She had been insolent to her mother; savage with little Frank; odiously impertinent to the boy’s governess; intolerably cruel to Pincott, her attendant—menial, confidante, companion, and always slave, according to the weather in Miss Blanche’s mind. The Muse, timid as a cat with claws only for weaker creatures, did not venture to attack Laura outright; so she raked everyone else.

Pincott, driven from the room in tears by her mistress’s cruelty and sent sobbing out with a parting sarcasm like a thrown crust, was too much for Laura. Laura broke out into loud indignation. How could one so young forget the deference owed to elders as well as to inferiors? How could one who talked so much of sensibility torture other people’s feelings wantonly? Laura told Blanche her conduct was wicked—absolutely wicked—and that she ought to ask pardon of Heaven on her knees for it.

Having delivered herself of a hot, voluble speech whose vehemence astonished the speaker almost as much as the auditor, Laura fled for her bonnet and shawl and went home across the park in a great flurry, to Mrs. Pendennis’s surprise, who had not expected her until night.

Alone with Helen, Laura recounted the scene and gave up her friend henceforth. “O Mamma,” she cried, “you were right. Blanche, who seems so soft and kind, is selfish and cruel. She who is always speaking of her affections can have no heart. No honest girl would afflict a mother so, or torture a dependant; and—and I give her up from this day, and I will have no other friend but you.”

The two ladies performed the osculatory ceremony in which they habitually indulged. Mrs. Pendennis derived a secret comfort from the quarrel. It seemed to say, “That girl can never be a wife for Pen. She is light-minded and heartless, unworthy of our noble hero. He will find out her unworthiness, and be saved.”

But Laura did not tell her mother—perhaps did not tell herself—what the real spark had been.

Blanche, in a wicked mood and bent upon mischief as other people are bent upon cookery, had begun her tricks early. Laura had come to pass a long day; and as they sat together in Blanche’s room, Blanche artfully steered the talk toward Mr. Pendennis.

“I am afraid he is sadly fickle,” Miss Blanche observed. “Mrs. Pybus, and many more Clavering people, have told us all about the actress.”

“I was quite a child when it happened,” Laura answered, blushing, “and I don’t know anything about it.”

“He used her very ill,” Blanche said, wagging her little head. “He was false to her.”

“I am sure he was not!” Laura cried. “He acted most generously by her. He wanted to give up everything to marry her. It was she that was false to him. He nearly broke his heart about it. He—”

“I thought you didn’t know anything about the story, dearest,” Blanche interposed sweetly, letting the word dearest do the work of a pin.

“Mamma has said so,” Laura faltered.

“Well, he is very clever,” Blanche continued, as though nothing had happened. “What a sweet poet he is! Have you ever read his poems?”

“Only the ‘Fisherman and the Diver,’ which he translated for us, and his Prize Poem, which didn’t get the prize; and indeed I thought it very pompous and prosy,” Laura said, laughing in spite of herself.

“Has he never written you any poems, then, love?” asked Miss Amory.

“No, my dear,” said Miss Bell.

Blanche ran up, kissed her, called her “my dearest Laura” at least three times, looked archly in her face, nodded, and said, “Promise to tell no-o-body, and I will show you something.”

She tripped to a little mother-of-pearl inlaid desk, opened it with a silver key, and drew out two or three papers crumpled and stained with green—like leaves pressed too roughly in a book. She put them in Laura’s hands.

Laura read them. They were love-verses—something about Undine, a Naiad, a river. She looked long, but the lines were not distinct before her eyes; the room seemed to swim as if the river in the poem had overflowed.

“And you have answered them, Blanche?” she asked at last, putting the papers back.

“O no! not for worlds, dearest,” Blanche replied; and when Laura had finished, Blanche popped the verses back into the pretty desk as one hides a sweetmeat from a hungry child.

Then Blanche went to the piano and sang two or three Rossini songs. Her flexible little voice executed the flourishes to perfection, trilling and running like a bright stream over stones. Laura sat by, vaguely listening as the notes filled the room and made a kind of gaiety in the air; but inside her the sound went oddly, as if it had found some hollow place. What was she thinking? She hardly knew. She sat silent while the songs rolled by.

After the concert they were summoned to luncheon; they went, of course, with arms around each other’s waists. And it could not have been jealousy or anger that had made Laura silent; for as they passed along the corridor, descended the steps, and paused at the door leading into the hall, Laura stopped, looked Blanche kindly and frankly in the face, and kissed her with sisterly warmth.

Then something occurred—Master Frank’s manner of eating, perhaps, or mamma’s blunders, or Sir Francis smelling of cigars—that vexed Blanche. She gave way to that chain of naughtiness: insolence, savagery, cruelty, tyranny; and it ended, as we have seen, with Pincott driven off in tears, Laura’s indignant outburst, and the friendship lying wounded on the floor like a dropped fan nobody thinks to pick up until it is broken.

The difference between the two young ladies—so loud overnight, so fluttering and tragic in the morning—lasted about as long as a dish of hot cakes at a children’s tea. Laura was always too eager to forgive and be forgiven; and as for Miss Blanche, her hostilities were never of that durable sort which keeps well—like smoked bacon. Nobody is seriously injured by being accused of wickedness: it is not a charge that pricks vanity; it only tickles it. Blanche was, in truth, rather pleased than provoked by her friend’s indignation, which never would have risen into flame but for a cause which both perfectly knew, and neither chose to name.

So Laura, with one of those sighs which seem made to be served with a lace handkerchief, was forced to own that the romantic part of her first friendship was ended; and that the object of it—once a heroine in Laura’s private epic—was only fit henceforth for a very ordinary sort of regard.

Blanche, on her side, did not sit down to plain bread like other mortals. She instantly composed touching verses about desertion and disenchantment—love met with coldness, fidelity repaid by neglect; the old recipe, whisked up with fresh rhymes, and sent to table as if it were a new dish. And, as it happened, some new neighbours arrived from London about this time with daughters; and Miss Amory, who could always find a sister as readily as she could find a ribbon, had the advantage of selecting an eternal friend on the spot, to whom she poured out her sorrows in a tone meant to be overheard by Providence.

The tall footmen came but seldom now with notes for sweet Laura; the pony-carriage was rarely despatched to Fairoaks to be at the ladies’ orders. Blanche, when Laura visited, assumed a look of suffering martyrdom, as though she had been roasted—slowly—upon the spit of sensibility. Laura laughed at her, and treated the whole performance with a good humour that was not in the least respectful.

But if Miss Blanche found new female friends to console her, it must also be said—by any faithful historian with a palate for truth—that she discovered acquaintances of the other sex who seemed to administer comfort quite as successfully. If ever this artless young creature met a young man and had ten minutes’ talk with him—whether in a garden walk, a drawing-room window, or between the first and second acts of a waltz—she confided in him, so to speak. She played with her beautiful eyes as a clever cook plays with a spice-box: a little, and then a little more, until the whole air was perfumed. She spoke in a tone of tender interest and simple appeal, and then left him—warm, flattered, and seasoned—for the same pretty drama to be served to his successor.

When the Claverings first came down to the Park there were scarcely any audiences before whom Blanche could perform; hence Pen had all the benefits of her glances and confidences, and the drawing-room window or garden walk entirely to himself. In the town of Clavering there were, it has been said, no young men at all; in the surrounding country only a curate or two, or a rustic young squire with large feet and clothes that looked as if they had been cut with a hedging-bill. To the dragoons quartered at Chatteris the Baronet made no overtures: it was unhappily his own regiment; he had left it on bad terms with certain officers—an ugly business about a horse bargain, a disputed play account, blind-Hookey, a white feather—who need ask? We will not go rummaging in the cold larder of bygones when the present course is still on the table.

But autumn, and the end of Parliament and the London season, brought one or two county families down to their houses; it filled the little watering-place of Baymouth; it opened Mr. Bingley’s Theatre Royal at Chatteris; it collected the usual company at Assizes and Race-balls. Up to this time the old county families had been shy of Clavering Park.
