The Fogeys of Drummington, the Squares of Tozely Park, the Welbores of The Barrow, and their like, had all sorts of stories in circulation; and anyone who says country people have no imagination should only hear them talk of new neighbours. About Sir Francis and his Lady—about her birth and parentage—about Miss Amory, about Captain Strong—there had been endless histories, which we will not reheat.

But at the end of the season the Earl of Trehawk, Lord Lieutenant of the county, coming to Eyrie Castle, and the Countess Dowager of Rockminster (whose son was also a magnate) taking a mansion on the Marine Parade at Baymouth—these great folks called publicly, immediately, and in state upon the family at Clavering Park; and the carriages of the county families rolled promptly after, as if the wheel-ruts of rank were as binding as Scripture.

Then Mirobolant had opportunity to exercise his skill and forget, in the honest occupations of his art, the pangs of love. One could almost hear the kitchen itself revive—knives with their quick, bright whisper on the boards; saucepans answering one another with their metallic chime; spits turning like clockwork; the whole domestic orchestra tuning up to welcome county grandeur. Then the large footmen were too much employed at the Park to linger over cups of small beer with the poor little maids at Fairoaks. Then Blanche found other dear friends than Laura, and other places to walk in besides the river-side where Pen was fishing. He came day after day and whipped the stream; but the “fish, fish!” would not do their duty, nor the Peri appear.

And here—strictly between ourselves, with a request that the matter go no further—we may mention a delicate business, of which hint has already been given. There was a certain hollow tree at which Pen used to take his station in his passion; and whose cavity he afterwards used for purposes beyond baits and fishing-cans. The truth is, he converted that tree into a post-office. Under a piece of moss and a stone he used to put little poems—or letters equally poetical—addressed to an Undine or Naiad of the stream; and once or twice these were replaced by a receipt in the shape of a flower, or by a modest word or two of acknowledgment, written in a delicate hand, in French or English, on pink scented paper. Miss Amory did walk by that stream; and it is a fact she used pink scented paper. But after the great folks had invaded Clavering Park, and the family coach passed out of the lodge-gates evening after evening to other great houses, nobody came for Pen’s letters at the post-office. The white paper lay undisturbed under its stone and moss, while the tree reflected itself in the water and the Brawl went rolling by—its old sound unbought, unadvertised, and all the sweeter for it; for rivers, unlike theatres, do not require a printed bill to make them admirable.

There was not much in the letters, certainly; and in the pink notes scarcely anything—only a word or two half jocular, half sympathetic, such as any young lady might write. But oh, you silly Pendennis—if you wanted this one, why did you not speak? Perhaps neither party was in earnest. You were only playing at being in love, and the sportive little Undine humouring you at the same game.

Yet when a man is baulked at play he often turns suddenly serious, as if the toys were sacred. When nobody came any more for Pen’s poems, he began to look upon those compositions as if they were a tragedy in five acts. He felt romantic again; at any rate, he was bent on an explanation.

One day he went to the Hall, and found a room full of visitors. Another day Miss Amory was not to be seen: she was going to a ball that night, and was lying down to take a little sleep. Pen cursed balls, and cursed also his narrow means and humble position which caused him to be passed over by the givers of these entertainments—cursed them with that bitterness which has, at the bottom, a great deal of wounded appetite. On a third occasion Miss Amory was in the garden, and he ran thither; but she was walking there in state with the Bishop and Bishopess of Chatteris and the episcopal family, who scowled at him and drew up in dignity when he was presented and they heard his name. The Right Reverend Prelate had heard it before—and also of the little transaction in the Dean’s garden.

“The Bishop says you’re a sad young man,” good-natured Lady Clavering whispered to him. “What have you been a doing of? Nothink, I hope, to vex such a dear Mar as yours? How is your dear Mar? Why don’t she come and me? We an’t seen her this ever such a time. We’re a goin about a gaddin, so that we don’t see no neighbours now. Give my love to her and Laurar, and come all to dinner to-morrow.”

Mrs. Pendennis was too unwell to come out; but Laura and Pen came, and there was a great party—voices and giggles, the scrape of chairs, the thin laugh of politeness, and, between it all, the orchestra of the house: doors opening with little sighs, fire crackling, glasses clinking like tiny bells. Pen only got opportunity for a hurried word with Miss Amory.

“You never come to the river now,” he said.

“I can’t,” said Blanche; “the house is full of people.”

“Undine has left the stream,” Mr. Pen went on, choosing to be poetical.

“She never ought to have gone there,” Miss Amory answered. “She won’t go again. It was very foolish: very wrong: it was only play. Besides, you have other consolations at home,” she added, looking him full in the face for an instant, and dropping her eyes.

If he wanted her, why did he not speak then? She might have said yes even then. But when she spoke of other consolations at home, he thought of Laura—so affectionate, so pure—and of his mother, who had bent her fond heart on uniting him with her adopted daughter. “Blanche!” he began in a vexed tone—“Miss Amory!”

“Laura is looking at us, Mr. Pendennis,” the young lady said. “I must go back to the company,” and she ran off, leaving Mr. Pendennis to bite his nails in perplexity and to stare out into the moonlight in the garden, where the night air smelt of damp earth and clipped box, and the distant talk within sounded like a sea of shallow laughter.

Laura indeed was looking at Pen. She was talking with—or appearing to listen to the talk of—Mr. Pynsent, Lord Rockminster’s son, and grandson of the Dowager Lady, who was seated in state in the place of honour, gravely receiving Lady Clavering’s bad grammar, and patronising the vacuous Sir Francis, whose interest in the county she desired to secure. Pynsent and Pen had been at Oxbridge together, where the latter, during his heyday of good fortune and fashion, had been the superior of the young patrician and perhaps rather supercilious. They had met for the first time since the University that day at table, and given each other that exceedingly impertinent demi-nod of recognition practised in England only, and to perfection by University men—the nod which says as plainly as speech: Confound you; what do you do here?

“I knew that man at Oxbridge,” Mr. Pynsent said to Miss Bell—“a Mr. Pendennis, I think.”

“Yes,” said Miss Bell.

“He seems rather sweet upon Miss Amory,” the gentleman went on. Laura looked at them, and perhaps thought so too, but said nothing.

“A man of large property in the county, ain’t he? He used to talk about representing it. He used to speak at the Union. Whereabouts do his estates lie?”

Laura smiled. “His estates lie on the other side of the river, near the lodge-gate. He is my cousin, and I live there.”

“Where?” asked Mr. Pynsent, with a laugh.

“Why, on the other side of the river, at Fairoaks,” answered Miss Bell.

“Many pheasants there? Cover looks rather good,” said the simple gentleman.

Laura smiled again. “We have nine hens and a cock, a pig, and an old pointer.”

“Pendennis don’t preserve, then?” continued Mr. Pynsent.

“You should come and see him,” the girl said, laughing, vastly amused at the notion that her Pen was a great county gentleman and had perhaps given himself out to be such.

“Indeed, I quite long to renew our acquaintance,” Mr. Pynsent said gallantly—and with a look which plainly added, It is you I would like to come and see. Laura vouchsafed a smile and made a little bow.

Here Blanche came stepping up with her most fascinating smile and ogle, and begged dear Laura to come and take the second in a song. Laura, ready for any kindness, went to the piano; and Mr. Pynsent listened as long as the duet lasted, and until Miss Amory began for herself, when he strode away.

“What a nice, frank, amiable, well-bred girl that is, Wagg,” said Mr. Pynsent to a gentleman who had come over with him from Baymouth—“the tall one, I mean, with the ringlets and red lips—monstrous red, ain’t they?”

“What do you think of the girl of the house?” asked Wagg.

“I think she’s a lean, scraggy humbug,” said Mr. Pynsent with great candour. “She drags her shoulders out of her dress, she never lets her eyes alone; and she goes simpering and ogling about like a French waiting-maid.”

“Pynsent, be civil,” cried the other. “Somebody can hear.”

“Oh, it’s Pendennis of Boniface,” Mr. Pynsent said. “Fine evening, Mr. Pendennis; we were just talking of your charming cousin.”

“Any relation to my old friend, Major Pendennis?” asked Mr. Wagg.

“His nephew. Had the pleasure of meeting you at Gaunt House,” Mr. Pen said with his very best air; and the acquaintance was made in an instant.

In the afternoon next day, the two gentlemen staying at Clavering Park were found by Mr. Pen, on his return from a fishing excursion in which he had no sport, seated in his mother’s drawing-room at Fairoaks in comfortable conversation with the widow and her ward. Mr. Pynsent, tall and gaunt, with large red whiskers and an imposing tuft to his chin, was striding over a chair in the intimate neighbourhood of Miss Laura. She was amused by his talk—simple, straightforward, rather humorous and keen—and interspersed with homely expressions sometimes called slang. It was the first specimen of a young London dandy that Laura had seen or heard; for she had been but a chit when Mr. Foker had been introduced at Fairoaks, and that ingenuous gentleman was little more than a boy.

Mr. Wagg, as he entered the premises with his companion, eyed and noted everything, as if his mind were a pantry and he must label every jar. “Old gardener,” he said, seeing Mr. John at the lodge—“old red livery waistcoat—clothes hanging out to dry on the gooseberry-bushes—blue aprons, white ducks—gad, they must be young Pendennis’s white ducks—nobody else wears ’em in the family. Rather a shy place for a sucking county member, ay, Pynsent?”

“Snug little crib,” said Mr. Pynsent; “pretty cosy little lawn.”

“Mr. Pendennis at home, old gentleman?” Mr. Wagg asked. John answered that Master Pendennis was agone out.

“Are the ladies at home?” asked the younger visitor. John said yes; and as the pair walked over the trim gravel and by the neat shrubberies, up the steps to the hall-door which old John opened, Wagg noted everything: the barometer and letter-bag, umbrellas and ladies’ clogs, Pen’s hats and tartan wrapper. Such minutiae attracted Wagg instinctively; he seized them in spite of himself, as a dog seizes a bone.

“Old fellow does all the work,” he whispered to Pynsent. “Caleb Balderstone. Shouldn’t wonder if he’s the housemaid.”

The next minute they were in the presence of the Fairoaks ladies; and Pynsent could not help recognising two perfectly well-bred women. Mr. Wagg made his obeisance with florid bows and extra courtesy, accompanied by an occasional knowing leer at his companion. Mr. Pynsent declined to acknowledge these signals, except by extreme haughtiness towards Wagg and particular deference to the ladies.

If there was one thing laughable in Mr. Wagg’s eyes, it was poverty. He had the soul of a butler brought from his pantry to make sport in the drawing-room. His jokes were plenty and his good-nature genuine; but he did not seem to understand that a gentleman could wear an old coat, or that a lady could be respectable without a carriage or a French milliner.

“Charming place, ma’am,” said he to the widow; “noble prospect—delightful to us Cocknies, who seldom see anything but Pall Mall.” The widow said simply she had never been in London but once in her life—before her son was born.

“Fine village, ma’am, fine village,” said Mr. Wagg, “and increasing every day. It’ll be quite a large town soon. It’s not a bad place to live in for those who can’t get the country, and will repay a visit when you honour it.”

“My brother, Major Pendennis, has often mentioned your name to us,” the widow said, “and we have been very much amused by some of your droll books, sir.” Helen continued, who never could be brought to like Mr. Wagg’s books, and detested their tone most thoroughly.

“He is my very good friend,” Mr. Wagg said with a low bow, “and one of the best known men about town—and where known, ma’am, appreciated; I assure you appreciated. He is with our friend Steyne at Aix-la-Chapelle. Steyne has a touch of the gout, and so—between ourselves—has your brother. I am going to Stillbrook for the pheasant-shooting, and afterwards to Bareacres, where Pendennis and I shall probably meet;” and he poured out a flood of fashionable talk, names of peers and places rattling like coins in a shallow dish, whilst the simple widow listened in silent wonder. What a man, she thought; are all the men of fashion in London like this? I am sure Pen will never like him.

Mr. Pynsent meanwhile was engaged with Miss Laura. He named some houses in the neighbourhood whither he was going, and hoped very much to see her at some of them. He hoped her aunt would give her a season in London. He said that in the next Parliament it was probable he should canvass the county, and he hoped to get Pendennis’s interest. He spoke of Pen’s triumph as an orator at Oxbridge, and asked was he coming into Parliament too? He talked pleasantly, and greatly to Laura’s satisfaction—until Pen appeared, as has been said, and found these gentlemen in his quarters.

Pen behaved courteously to the pair. Though he remembered with a twinge an Oxbridge conversation—after a great Union debate, with supper and champagne-cup inflaming everybody—in which he had announced his intention of coming in for his native county, and had absolutely returned thanks in a fine speech as the future member; yet Pynsent’s manner was so frank and cordial that Pen hoped he might have forgotten the fanfaronnade and any other youthful braggadocio. Pen suited himself to the tone of the visitors and talked about Plinlimmon and Magnus Charters and the old set at Oxbridge with careless familiarity and high-bred ease, as if he lived with marquises every day and a duke were no more to him than a village curate.

But at this juncture—being then six o’clock—Betsy the maid, who did not know of the advent of strangers, walked into the room without any preliminary but flinging the door wide open, bearing in her arms a tray containing three tea-cups, a tea-pot, and a plate of thick bread-and-butter.

It was as though, in the middle of a grand speech about empire, somebody should cough and say, “Soup’s on.” All Pen’s splendour vanished. He faltered, and became quite abashed. What will they think of us? he thought. And indeed Wagg thrust his tongue in his cheek, thought the tea infinitely contemptible, and leered and winked at Pynsent to that effect.

But to Mr. Pynsent the transaction appeared perfectly simple. There was no reason in his mind why people should not drink tea at six if they were minded, as well as at any other hour. When they went away he asked Wagg what the devil he was grinning and winking at, and what amused him.

“Didn’t you see how the cub was ashamed of the thick bread-and-butter?” Mr. Wagg chuckled. “I dare say they’re going to have treacle if they are good. I’ll take an opportunity of telling old Pendennis when we get back to town.”

“Don’t see the fun,” said Mr. Pynsent.

“Never thought you did,” growled Wagg; and they walked home rather sulkily—each offended by a different thing, like two men quarrelling at a dinner-table because one dislikes the salt and the other the silence.

Wagg told the story at dinner very smartly, with wonderful accuracy. He described old John, the clothes drying, the clogs in the hall, the drawing-room and its furniture and pictures: “Old man with a beak and bald head—feu Pendennis I bet two to one; sticking-plaster full-length of a youth in a cap and gown—the present Marquis of Fairoaks, of course; the widow when young in a miniature, Mrs. Mee; she had the gown on when we came, or a dress made the year after, and the tips cut off the fingers of her gloves which she stitches her son’s collars with; and then the sarving maid came in with their teas, so we left the Earl and the Countess to their bread-and-butter.”

Blanche, near whom he sat, and who adored les hommes d’esprit, burst out laughing and called him such an odd, droll creature. But Pynsent, who began to be utterly disgusted with Wagg, broke out loud: “I don’t know, Mr. Wagg, what sort of ladies you are accustomed to meet in your own family, but by gad, as far as a first acquaintance can show, I never met two better-bred women in my life; and I hope, ma’am, you’ll call upon ’em,” he added, addressing Lady Rockminster.

Sir Francis turned to his guest and whispered, “That’s what I call a sticker for Wagg.” And Lady Clavering, giving the young gentleman a delighted tap with her fan, winked her black eyes at him and said, “Mr. Pynsent, you’re a good feller.”

After the affair with Blanche, a difference ever so slight—a tone of melancholy, perhaps a little bitter—might be perceived in Laura’s converse with her cousin. She seemed to weigh him and find him wanting too. The widow saw the girl’s clear honest eyes watching the young man at times, and a look of almost scorn pass over her face as he lounged in the room with the women, or lazily sauntered smoking upon the lawn, or lolled under a tree over a book he was too listless to read. Even the place itself, quiet as it was, had its own soundscape—leaves shifting, a distant cart, the river’s murmur—and Pen, who might have listened and learned contentment from such honest music, seemed deaf to it, as though his ears had been trained only to the loud instruments of town.

“What has happened between you?” eager-sighted Helen asked the girl. “Something has happened. Has that wicked little Blanche been making mischief? Tell me, Laura.”

“Nothing has happened at all,” Laura said.

“Then why do you look at Pen so?” his mother asked quickly.

“Look at him, dear mother!” Laura cried. “We two women are no society for him. We don’t interest him; we are not clever enough for such a genius as Pen. He wastes his life and energies away among us, tied to our apron-strings. He interests himself in nothing: he scarcely cares to go beyond the garden-gate. Even Captain Glanders and Captain Strong pall upon him,” she added with a bitter laugh; “and they are men, you know, and our superiors. He will never be happy while he is here. Why, is he not facing the world, and without a profession?”

“We have got enough, with great economy,” said the widow, her heart beginning to beat violently. “Pen has spent nothing for months. I’m sure he is very good. I am sure he might be very happy with us.”

“Don’t agitate yourself so, dear mother,” the girl answered. “I don’t like to see you so. You should not be sad because Pen is unhappy here. All men are so. They must work. They must make themselves names and a place in the world. Look—the two captains have fought and seen battles; that Mr. Pynsent, who came here, and who will be very rich, is in a public office; he works very hard, he aspires to a name and a reputation. He says Pen was one of the best speakers at Oxbridge, and had as great a character for talent as any of the young gentlemen there. Pen himself laughs at Mr. Wagg’s celebrity (and indeed he is a horrid person), and says he is a dunce, and that anybody could write his books.”

“I am sure they are odious and vulgar,” interposed the widow.

Under the calico draperies of a window that had been meant, no doubt, for moonlight and sighs, Arthur Pendennis established himself like a sulky house-cat—half-hidden, wholly offended with the universe—and set his face to practise that excellent accomplishment of youth, namely, looking as if one has been wronged by everybody, particularly by Providence. From this shaded embrasure he watched Miss Laura Bell go into her first quadrille with Mr. Pynsent.

Mr. Pynsent danced as a conscientious Englishman walks to his pew: straight, grave, and with the air of a man discharging a duty to the constitution. If the fiddle had burst into flame or the floor had opened and swallowed the set, he would have completed the figure before falling in. But Laura—Laura was all June and music. The lamps, the crowd, the scrape and swing of the band put a brightness into her honest rosy face; her brown ringlets shook back with every turn; her white gown spread and gathered as if it too had a heart; and she smiled on partner and neighbour with such open good-humour that half the room, being male, began to admire her for the best of reasons—because she looked as if she enjoyed herself.

Lady Fogey, who kept a London house and carried her fashion down into the country like a travelling bonnet-box, asked Lady Rockminster who the young person might be; compared her to some reigning beauty (as though girls were patterns cut from one expensive paper), and pronounced that she would “do.”

Lady Rockminster, with her eyeglass and her manner of judging the universe as if it were linen on a line, would have been vastly astonished if any protégée of hers did not “do,” and thought Lady Fogey’s presumption in pronouncing on the point a sort of social poaching. She surveyed Laura with majestic approval. The girl’s manner was artless and gay; her tone good; her arms—well, a trifle red; but youth is allowed its own colouring, as kitchens are allowed their own heat.

Opposite Laura in the dance stood Miss Blanche Amory, who smiled at her “dearest friend” with such killing sweetness that one could almost see the little daggers glitter behind the dimples. Blanche’s shoulders were the whitest in the room; and never, for a single instant, were they at rest in their frock. Nor were her eyes, which rolled and searched and flashed like two small mirrors set to catch attention. Her whole little figure seemed to call out, over the heads of the set: Come and look at me—not at that pink, healthy, bouncing country lass. This is the true Parisian manner—this is the prettiest little foot, and the prettiest little chaussure. Look at it, Mr. Pynsent. Look at it, Mr. Pendennis, you behind the curtain. I know you are pining to dance with me.

Laura danced on, yet kept an attentive eye on Pen in his calico confessional. He stayed there through the first quadrille, and would have stayed longer, had not good-natured Lady Clavering beckoned him to the dais, where the dowagers sat in state, like an array of richly dressed casseroles waiting to be served. Up went Pen—blushing, exceedingly awkward, and with that injured vanity most conceited young men wear when summoned from their sulk to society. He performed a haughty salute to Lady Rockminster, who returned it with the smallest possible acknowledgment, such as one gives to a door one must pass through. Then he paid his respects to Mrs. Amory, widow of the late gentleman, who glittered with diamonds, velvet, lace, feathers, and the sort of millinery and goldsmith’s ware that seems designed to warn younger women what marriage may end in.

Young Mr. Fogey—fifth form at Eton, ardently expecting his beard and his commission—was presently honoured with Miss Bell’s hand for the second dance. He regarded her as if she were a revelation. “I like you much better than the French girl,” he said candidly (having danced with Miss Amory before). Laura laughed—laughed the more, because in the midst of it she caught sight of Pen still looking absurdly pompous and sulky, as though he were presiding over a funeral instead of a ball.

The next dance was a waltz. Fogey sighed that he did not know how, and vowed to hire a master in the holidays, as men vow to be saints on Sunday and forget by Monday. Mr. Pynsent claimed Laura again, and Pen, watching her whirl round the room with that gentleman’s arm about her waist, felt a fury as fresh as if jealousy had been invented that evening for his exclusive use.

He had not always been angry at such sights. At Clavering Park, in summer, when chairs and tables were removed, the governess called down to the piano, and Chevalier Strong—who could dance anything from British hornpipe to Spanish fandango with the ease of a man slicing an orange—helped the two girls improvise little balls, Pen had stood twirling and laughing and had thought the world a tolerable place. But now Laura, so animated that she even animated Mr. Pynsent, looked altogether too happy; and happiness, witnessed from behind a curtain, is an offence.

Blanche, who danced beautifully, had drawn for her partner Captain Broadfoot of the Dragoons at Chatteris—a heavy honest man who threw energy at his task but possessed not the smallest ear for music. He moved too slowly and did not know it; he waltzed as if the tune were a government regulation to be consulted. So, in quadrille and in waltz, Blanche saw Laura carrying off the honours with ease, and was not pleased. After a couple of turns with the dragoon, she pleaded fatigue and begged to be led back near her mamma—where Pen was talking—and immediately demanded, with a shrug, why he had not asked her to waltz and had left her to the mercies of that great odious man in spurs and a red coat.

“I thought spurs and scarlet were the most fascinating objects in the world to young ladies,” Pen said. “I should never dare put my black coat in competition with that splendid red jacket.”

“You are very unkind and cruel and sulky and naughty,” said Miss Amory, as if listing his crimes in order of elegance. “You had better go away. Your cousin is looking at us over Mr. Pynsent’s shoulder.”

“Will you waltz with me?” Pen asked.

“Not this waltz. I can’t, having just sent away that good Captain Broadfoot. Look at Mr. Pynsent—did you ever see such a creature? But I will dance the next waltz with you, and the quadrille too. I am promised, but I will tell Mr. Poole I had forgotten my engagement to you.”

“Women forget very readily,” said Pen.

“But they always come back,” Blanche replied, “and are very repentant and sorry for what they’ve done. See—here comes the Poker, and dear Laura leaning on him. How pretty she looks!”

Laura approached and gave Pen her hand with the same frank kindness she had been wearing all evening, as if her heart were a warm loaf to be broken and shared. Mr. Pynsent made a stiff bow—indeed as little graceful as that domestic implement to which Blanche had likened him—while Laura said, delighted, “I am so glad to have come, dear Pen. I can speak to you now. How is mamma? The three dances are over, and I am engaged to you for the next, Pen.”

“I have just engaged myself to Miss Amory,” Pen said; and Blanche nodded, curtseyed, and looked as if she had signed a treaty.

“I don’t intend to give him up, dearest Laura,” Blanche said.

“Well, then, he’ll waltz with me, dear Blanche,” Laura answered, with a quiet firmness that made her good nature look like strength. “Won’t you, Pen?”

“I promised to waltz with Miss Amory.”

“Provoking!” Laura said; and curtseying, she went and placed herself under the ample wing of Lady Rockminster.

Pen was delighted with his own spite. The two prettiest girls in the room were quarrelling about him: he flattered himself he had punished Laura. He leaned against the wall with a dandified elbow, talked to Blanche, and quizzed the men and women with an unmerciful liveliness—the dragoons in tight jackets; country dandies in curious attire; ladies with toilettes that looked as if they had been dressed by imaginative pastrycooks. One had a bird’s nest for a head; another carried what might have been six pounds of grapes in her hair besides her false pearls.

“It’s a coiffure of almonds and raisins,” Pen declared. “It might be served up for dessert.”

He kept this satire up through the quadrille with unflinching bitterness and considerable wit, and Blanche laughed continually—at his wickedness, at his jokes, and because Laura, opposite again as vis-à-vis, could see how merry and confidential they were. Across Cornet Perch’s shell-jacket Blanche whispered to Laura, while Pen drawled through a figure with thumbs in both waistcoat pockets, “Arthur is charming to-night.”

“Who?” Laura asked.

“Arthur,” Blanche answered in French. “Oh, it’s such a pretty name!”

Now the ladies changed places; Cornet Perch performed his own pas seul, hands hanging large and swollen in front of him, since his tight little jacket supplied no convenient pockets for attitude. In the interval before the succeeding waltz, Pen took care to notice Laura only enough to wound her: he asked whether Cornet Perch was amusing, and whether she liked him as well as her other partner, Mr. Pynsent. Having planted these two daggers in her gentle bosom, he returned to his loud jokes with Blanche, good or bad, but always audible.

Laura could not understand her cousin’s sulkiness, and did not know where she had offended him. She was not angry in turn—she was too forgiving; and besides, jealousy in a man is not always displeasing to a woman, being a compliment with teeth. Since Pen would not dance with her, she was glad to take up with the brisk Chevalier Strong, who danced even better than Pen; and when the waltz began, she set off with all her heart, as a young girl should, as naturally as she breathes.

Captain Broadfoot now occupied the floor with a lady of proportions scarcely inferior to his own—Miss Roundle, large and helplessly conspicuous in a strawberry-ice coloured crape dress, daughter of the lady with the grapes. If ever a colour begged to be eaten rather than worn, it was that; and the band scraped on, while the room filled with the soft thunder of feet, the whisper of skirts, the little cries and laughter, the whole cheerful ecology of sound that makes a ballroom bearable. It was only now and then, when a chair scraped harshly or a boot-heel struck too sharply, that one felt how easily pleasure is jarred by clumsy noise, as a delicate sauce is spoiled by a careless hand.

Pen, with Blanche hanging on the arm which encircled her waist, set out upon his waltzing career at last, feeling that they performed brilliantly indeed. Perhaps he looked to see if Miss Bell admired the spectacle; but Laura would not or did not see him, being engaged with Strong and very content. Pen’s triumph was not destined to last long. Blanche was doomed another discomfiture.

For while Pen and Blanche spun rapidly, as light as opera-dancers in their own opinion, Broadfoot and Miss Roundle revolved with majestic leisure, taking time as a principle. They were in everybody’s way—but more particularly in Pendennis’s. Pen and Blanche, executing their brisk gyrations, came bolt up against the heavy dragoon and his strawberry-ice planet with such force that the common centre of gravity deserted them all in terror. Broadfoot and Miss Roundle were fairly upset; Pen, less lucky than Blanche, came down sprawling upon the floor among the general ruin, while Blanche herself was flung upon a bench against the wall.

Captain Broadfoot, heavy but good-natured, burst out first into a loud laugh at his own misfortune; and as nobody can long be angry with a man who laughs at himself, his fall passed almost as an entertainment. But Miss Amory was savage; Miss Roundle, seated again and looking pitifully round, presented an object which very few people could behold without giggling; and Pen, hearing the giggles, turned furious. He was one of those sarcastic young gentlemen who can laugh at the universe but cannot endure the universe laughing back. Of all things he feared ridicule most; and now it hopped and tittered all around him like a chorus.

As he scrambled up, Laura and Strong were laughing; everybody was laughing; Pynsent and his partner were laughing. Pen boiled with wrath against them, and could have stabbed them both on the spot for daring to be amused. He turned away, blundering out apologies to Blanche: it was the other couple’s fault—the woman in pink—the whole calamity had been produced by strawberry-ice and gravity. Was Blanche hurt? Would she not have courage for another turn?

Miss Amory, in a pet, declared she was very much hurt indeed, and would not take another turn. A cavalier in a blue ribbon and a three-pointed star rushed to fetch her a glass of water. She accepted it, drank, smiled graciously on the bringer, and then—turning her white shoulder upon Pen with a marked haughtiness—besought the gentleman with the star to conduct her to her mamma, holding out her hand to take his arm.

The man with the star trembled with delight, bowed over her hand, pressed it fervidly to his coat, and looked round with triumph. He was no other than Mirobolant.

Blanche had never fairly looked into the artist’s face since he had been employed in her mother’s family, and had no idea—none whatever—that the distinguished person to whose arm she clung was the chef. She took the decorations, the dark eyes, the air of foreignness, and made—like many people in society—an instant translation into nobility. Pen, seeing her go, forgot his humiliation in astonishment, and cried out, “By Jove, it’s the cook!”

The moment the words were out he regretted them; for it was Blanche who had invited Mirobolant, and the man could hardly refuse a lady’s command. Blanche in her flutter did not hear; but Mirobolant heard, and cast back over his shoulder a glance so furious it might have roasted Pen where he stood. It amused Pen, who was in that mischievous, sour humour that longs for a quarrel; and besides, the notion that a cook—or any man under a cook’s title—could have feelings of honour did not conveniently enter the mind of this lofty young aristocrat, the apothecary’s son.

But it had never entered poor Mirobolant’s head that he was not equal, as a man, to any other mortal; nor that his position was so degrading it should forbid him to offer his arm to a lady who asked it. In his own country he had seen fine ladies join dances with Blaise or Pierre; and he might even, in his simplicity, have taken Blanche up to Lady Clavering and asked her to dance too—had not Pen’s exclamation struck him as if it had been a shot. It cruelly humiliated him; anger rose hot and fast, like a pot boiling over.

Blanche did not know what made him start and grind a Gascon oath between his teeth. But Chevalier Strong—who, having received interesting information from Madame Fribsby, understood the poor fellow’s state—was luckily near, and spoke rapidly to Mirobolant in Spanish, which the other understood. Strong then begged Miss Amory to come and take an ice before she returned to Lady Clavering. At that, the unhappy Mirobolant relinquished the arm he had held for a minute, bowed most profoundly and piteously, and fell back as if struck out of the scene.

“Don’t you know who it is?” Strong asked Blanche as he led her away. “It is the chef Mirobolant.”

“How should I know?” Blanche said. “He has a croix; he is very distingué; he has beautiful eyes.”

“The poor fellow is mad for your beaux yeux,” Strong replied. “He is a very good cook—but he is not quite right in the head.”

“What did you say to him in the unknown tongue?” Blanche asked.

“He is a Gascon, from the borders of Spain,” Strong answered. “I told him he would lose his place if he walked with you.”

“Poor Monsieur Mirobolant!” said Blanche. “Did you see the look he gave Pendennis?”

Strong, enjoying the mischief, said, “I think he would like to run little Pen through with one of his spits.”

“He is an odious, conceited, clumsy creature, that Mr. Pen,” Blanche said.

“Broadfoot looked as if he would like to kill him too; so did Pynsent,” Strong answered. “What ice will you have—water ice or cream ice?”

“Water ice. Who is that odd man staring at me—he is décoré too.”

“That is my friend Colonel Altamont,” Strong said. “A very queer character, in the service of the Nawaub of Lucknow. Hallo! what’s that noise? I’ll be back in an instant.” And he sprang out, for a scuffle and high voices were heard in the ballroom.

The refreshment-room in which Miss Amory now found herself was the place set apart for supper, which Mr. Rincer the landlord had provided at five shillings a head for those who liked to pay for midnight courage. In this room, too, superior refreshments were ready for the county families; and the commoner sort were kept out by a waiter at the portal who announced, like a doorkeeper to Paradise, that this was a select room for Lady Clavering and Lady Rockminster’s parties, not to be opened to the public until after midnight. The distinction was as carefully preserved as if it were a recipe: some people might taste at once; others must wait until the hour when everybody is hungry and dignity is weak.

Pynsent, who danced with his constituents’ daughters, took them and their mammas in for refreshment there. Strong, manager and master of revels wherever he went, had of course the entrée. And the only person now occupying the room was the gentleman with the black wig and the orders in his buttonhole—the officer in the service of his Highness the Nawaub of Lucknow.

He had established himself early in the evening, declaring himself confoundedly thirsty, and called for a bottle of champagne. The waiter, hearing champagne in a select room, instantly supposed he had to do with a grandee. The Colonel sat down, began to eat his supper and absorb his drink, and entered affably into conversation with anybody who came in, as if hospitality were a uniform. Sir Francis Clavering and Mr. Wagg had found him there when they left the ballroom early—Sir Francis to smoke a cigar and look at the people gathered outside on the shore (which he declared was much better fun than remaining within), Mr. Wagg to hang on a baronet’s arm, as he loved to do with the greatest man in company.

Colonel Altamont had stared at them in so odd a manner that Sir Francis asked the landlord who he was, and hinted a strong opinion that the Nawaub’s officer was drunk. Mr. Pynsent, too, had conversed with the same gentleman; Pynsent’s cue was to speak to everybody (and he did it, to do him justice, in the most ungracious manner), and he took the man in the black wig for some constituent, some merchant captain, or other outlandish local specimen. Coming in with a lady on his arm, Pynsent was asked by the Colonel if he would try a glass of Sham. Pynsent, with great gravity, bowed, tasted, pronounced it excellent, and retreated. This decorum surprised and routed the Colonel more than rudeness would have done: he stared after Pynsent stupidly and told Mr. Rincer over the counter that he was a rum one.

Mr. Rincer blushed, hardly knowing what to say. Mr. Pynsent was a county earl’s grandson, aiming at Parliament. Colonel Altamont wore orders and diamonds, jingled sovereigns in his pocket, and paid like a man. Not knowing how to reconcile pedigree with payment, Mr. Rincer escaped by addressing somebody else: “Yes, Colonel—yes, ma’am—did you say tea? Cup a tea for Mr. Jones, Mrs. R.,” and thus slid away from discussion.

For, in plain truth, Mr. Altamont, having remained at the buffet almost all night and employed himself actively there, had flushed his brain considerably by drinking, and was still going on when Strong ran out and left Blanche alone with her water ice.

She was absorbed in absorbing it—for it was very fresh and good: cold, clean, sharply sweet, the sort of taste that makes the mouth feel newly made. Or perhaps she was not curious about the noise in the next room, though the waiters were, and ran after Strong. So when she looked up from her glass she beheld the strange man with the little red eyes staring at her.

He rose and advanced with a rather unsteady gait, and after gazing said, with a familiarity that smelt of champagne and empire, “And so you’re Betsy Amory. Betsy Amory, by Jove!”

“Who—who speaks to me?” said Betsy, alias Blanche.

But the noise in the ballroom had grown so loud—voices clashing, feet stamping, the bright social music turning suddenly into the rougher racket of a quarrel—that we must rush back thither at once and see what has caused the disturbance.

Civil war, as our ancestors modestly called it, was raging in the corner of the ballroom—high words, hotter faces, and a dense press of shoulders and satin sleeves jammed about an open window as if the night-air were the prize in a raffle. Outside, the street below contributed its own music to the entertainment: a chorus of nasal encouragement—“Pitch into him!” “Where’s the police?”—rising between the fiddlers’ last stifled squeak and the incessant stamping of impatient shoes.

On one side of the ring Madame Fribsby blazed—fan fluttering, eyes shining, bosom heaving with that peculiar compassion which never fails to find a public quarrel irresistibly touching. In the middle, conspicuous as a caper in a blanc-mange, stood Monsieur Alcide Mirobolant—Sir Francis Clavering’s little culinary celebrity—pale, curled, glaring, vibrating with wrath like a kettle beginning to sing. Opposite him, with gentlemen and ladies clinging about him as if he were a mast in a storm, stood Arthur Pendennis, looking as if he could swallow a man whole and complain that the bones were sharp.

Through the crush shouldered the Chevalier Strong, large, noisy, and cheerful, as if he had entered a pantry rather than a battlefield. Madame Fribsby, delighted to see him—delighted, indeed, to see anybody in a uniform of authority—caught at his arm and cried in frantic pathos, “Save him! save him!”

Him, it turned out, was the cook.

For shortly after Strong had quitted the room, and while Mr. Pen—still bleeding inwardly from his waltzing catastrophe, still smarting at Miss Amory’s coolness, and therefore doing what irritated men do when they wish to appear philosophical—had marched to the open window to take the sea-breeze and practice looking indifferent, he had been engaged in the stern domestic task of composing himself.

The sea, sparkling far off, murmured with that calm, old, tireless sound which has never yet been bribed by fashion, or drowned by a county ball; it was saying, in its ancient language, “Hush,” while inside, violins and vanity said, “Look at me.” Pen, for a moment, half owned to himself that he had been absurd—peevish—childish; which confession, like many a good resolution made near salt-water, lasted exactly until a human hand laid itself upon his shoulder.

He wheeled round—and there, to his utter surprise and horror, was Monsieur Mirobolant’s pale face with its fierce eyes, its ringlets, its lips compressed as if he were tasting vinegar. To be tapped on the shoulder by a French cook was, to the blood of Pendennis, like being served soup in a boot. Astonishment and indignation boiled together.

“You speak French?” Mirobolant said, in French, with the clipped certainty of a man presenting a dish he knows to be good.

“What is that to you, pray?” Pen answered, in English, as if the language itself were a rampart.

“At any rate, you understand it?” the other persisted, bowing—oh, with politeness!—as men bow before they strike.

“Yes, sir,” said Pen, stamping; “I understand it pretty well.”

“Vous me comprendrez alors, Monsieur Pendennis,” replied the little Gascon, rolling out his r as if it were a peppercorn to be cracked between the teeth, “quand je vous dis que vous êtes un lâche. Monsieur Pendennis—un lâche, entendez-vous?”

“What?” said Pen, turning in a flash.

“You understand the meaning of the word and its consequences among men of honour?” asked Mirobolant, hand to hip, eyes fastened on Pen with the rigid attention of a man checking whether a sauce has taken.

“The consequences are, that I will fling you out of window, you impudent scoundrel!” bawled Pen; and he darted.

He might very likely have performed the whole operation—window being close, Frenchman being small, and Pendennis being young and vexed—had not Captain Broadfoot and another heavy officer thrust themselves between, like two beefy joints interposed between knife and appetite; had not ladies screamed; had not fiddles stopped mid-scrape; had not the crowd surged up; had not Laura’s frightened face appeared over shoulders; and had not Strong, at that blessed second, come in from the refreshment-room to find Alcide grinding his teeth and spitting oaths in his “Galleon French,” and Pen wearing that wicked calm which, in certain men, is only anger with gloves on.

“What has happened?” Strong asked the chef, in Spanish—choosing a third language, as if to cool the quarrel by changing the air.

“I am Chevalier de Juillet,” cried Mirobolant, slapping his breast, “and he has insulted me.”

“What has he said to you?” Strong inquired.

“Il m’a appelé—Cuisinier,” hissed the little man, as if the word were a cinder.

Strong could hardly help laughing. “Come away with me, poor Chevalier,” he said. “We must not quarrel before ladies. Come away; I will carry your message to Mr. Pendennis.” Then, bending, he murmured to one or two, “The poor fellow is not right in his head.”

Meanwhile others clustered round Pen, and Laura—anxious, imploring—asked what had happened.

Pen himself scarcely knew, the manner in which rage makes a man stupid. “The man was going to give his arm to a young lady, on which I said that he was a cook, and he called me a coward and challenged me to fight. I own I was so surprised and indignant, that if you gentlemen had not stopped me, I should have thrown him out of window.”

“D— him,” said the gentlemen; “serve him right—the impudent foreign scoundrel.”

“I—I’m very sorry if I hurt his feelings, though,” Pen added; and Laura’s face brightened, grateful even for that grain of justice, while some of the young bucks muttered that foreigners wanted thrashing, like under-done meat.

“You will go and shake hands with him before you go to sleep—won’t you, Pen?” Laura said, close to him now. “Foreigners may be more susceptible than we are, and have different manners. If you hurt a poor man’s feelings, I am sure you would be the first to ask his pardon. Wouldn’t you, dear Pen?”

She looked all gentleness and pardon; and Pen—who could be melted by goodness as readily as he could be inflamed by a slight—took both her hands and looked into her kind face and said indeed he would.

“How fond that girl is of me!” he thought. “Shall I speak to her now? No—not now. This absurd business with the Frenchman must be ended first.”

She asked him to stop and dance with her. She was as eager to keep him in the room as he to escape it. “Won’t you stop and waltz with me, Pen? I’m not afraid to waltz with you.”

It was affectionate, and it was unlucky. In an instant Pen saw again his own legs betraying him, Miss Roundle and a dragoon forming a trap, Blanche shot against the wall as if launched by a culinary catapult, and the whole room laughing—Laura and Pynsent amongst them.

“I shall never dance again,” he replied, with a dark face of martyrdom. “Never. I’m surprised you should ask me.”

“Is it because you can’t get Blanche for a partner?” asked Laura, with that little wickedness that sometimes peeps out even in kind souls as a kitten peeps out from a basket.

“Because I don’t wish to make a fool of myself for other people to laugh at me,” Pen answered. “For you to laugh at me, Laura. I saw you and Pynsent. By Jove! no man shall laugh at me.”

“Pen, Pen, don’t be so wicked!” cried the poor girl, hurt at the savage vanity and morbid twist of his mood. He was glaring towards Mr. Pynsent as if he would gladly have had another duel, and another window.

“Who thinks the worse of you for stumbling in a waltz? If Laura does, we don’t. Why are you so sensitive, and ready to think evil?”

At that unlucky moment Mr. Pynsent came up, smooth as a well-buttered roll, and said, “I have it in command from Lady Rockminster to ask whether I may take you in to supper?”

“I—I was going in with my cousin,” Laura said.

“O—pray, no!” said Pen. “You are in such good hands, that I can’t do better than leave you; and I’m going home.”

“Good-night, Mr. Pendennis,” said Pynsent, drily—with that dryness which, translated into plain English, signifies, “Go to the deuce, you jealous boy; I could box your ears with pleasure.” Mr. Pendennis vouchsafed only a bow; and, in spite of Laura’s imploring looks, left the room.

Outside the atmosphere changed at once—music muffled, laughter dimmed, the sound of the sea coming in again like an old tune remembered. Within, Pynsent, offering his arm, remarked, “How beautifully calm and bright the night outside is! and what a murmur the sea is making! It would be pleasanter to be walking on the beach than in this hot room.”

“Very,” said Laura, whose heart was not on beaches or ballrooms.

“What a strange congregation of people,” Pynsent continued. “I have had to go up and perform the agreeable to most of them—the attorney’s daughters—the apothecary’s wife—I scarcely know whom. There was a man in the refreshment-room who insisted upon treating me to champagne—a seafaring-looking man, extraordinarily dressed, and seeming half tipsy. As a public man one is bound to conciliate all these people, but it is a hard task—especially when one would so very much like to be elsewhere”—and he blushed as he spoke, as if he could hear his own voice in the heated air and was ashamed of its vanity.

“I beg your pardon,” said Laura. “I—I was not listening. Indeed—I was frightened about that quarrel between my cousin and that—that—French person.”

“Your cousin has been rather unlucky to-night,” Pynsent said. “There are three or four persons whom he has not succeeded in pleasing—Captain Broadwood; what is his name—the officer—and the young lady in red with whom he danced—and Miss Blanche—and the poor chef—and I don’t think he seemed to be particularly pleased with me.”

“Didn’t he leave me in charge to you?” Laura asked, looking up at him and dropping her eyes instantly, like a guilty little coquette who has told a truth with a twist.

“Indeed, I can forgive him a good deal for that,” Pynsent cried eagerly; and she took his arm, and he led his little prize towards supper.

Supper was served, as the county paper afterwards observed, “in Rincer’s well-known style”—meaning that everything was abundant, varnished with sauces, and arranged to flatter eyes that were already half-tired of looking at each other. There were jellies that trembled at every stomp of a boot; chickens trussed as compactly as secrets; lobsters flaming red as if embarrassed by their own publicity; and wines popping and fizzing with an ambition to drown conversation. The room rang with that particular racket of plates, laughter, and officious waiters which makes a table feel less like a family and more like a factory of chewing.

Laura, however, had no appetite for triumphs of cream and truffle; she tasted little, heard less, and felt only the ache of Pen’s temper. Captious and quarrelsome; jealous and selfish; fickle and violent and unjust when anger led him astray—how could her mother, by a thousand hints, ask her to give her heart to such a man? And if she did—would it make him happy?

At the end of half an hour—a long half-hour, measured not by the clock but by the pounding of her own thoughts—a waiter brought her a small note in pencil. It was from Pen.

“I met Cooky below ready to fight me; and I asked his pardon. I’m glad I did it. I wanted to speak to you to-night, but will keep what I had to say till you come home. God bless you. Dance away all night with Pynsent, and be very happy.—PEN.”

She could almost have cried with gratitude over those scratchy lines. There was forgiveness in him still, and a sort of goodness, stubborn but real—like honest bread under burnt crust.

Pen, after leaving the ballroom, had gone downstairs with his heart reproaching him. Laura’s gentle looks followed him like a quiet melody that won’t be silenced by stamping. He longed to turn back and ask pardon—but he remembered he had left her with that confounded Pynsent. He could not apologize before him; he would compromise by making peace with the Frenchman.

The Chevalier Strong found him in the hall, where Mirobolant paced like a small general awaiting cannon. Strong’s own face was lit with mischief.

“I have got him in the coffee-room,” he said, “with a brace of pistols and a candle. Or would you like swords on the beach? Mirobolant is a dead hand with the foils, and killed four gardes-du-corps with his own point in the barricades of July.”

“Confound it,” Pen burst out, “I can’t fight a cook!”

“He is a Chevalier of July,” Strong returned gravely. “They present arms to him in his own country.”

“And do you ask me, Captain Strong, to go out with a servant?” Pen cried. “I’ll call a policeman on him—but—but—”

“You’ll invite me to hair triggers?” Strong laughed. “Thank you for nothing; I was but joking. I came to settle quarrels, not to fight them. I have been soothing down Mirobolant; I have told him you did not apply the word ‘Cook’ to him in an offensive sense: that it was contrary to all the customs of the country that a hired officer of a household—as I called it—should give his arm to the daughter of the house.” And then Strong, lowering his voice, told Pen the grand secret Madame Fribsby had confided: the violent passion under which the poor artist laboured.

When Arthur heard it, he broke into a hearty laugh, and Strong joined him; and Pen’s rage vanished as swiftly as steam when a lid is lifted. For he had himself been jealous all evening, and hungry for a pretext to insult Pynsent; he remembered old jealousies in older follies, and felt suddenly generous to any man possessed by so ridiculous and human a fever.

So he went into the coffee-room where Mirobolant waited with pistols and pride, and offered his hand outright. He made a speech in French—very solemn, very gentlemanlike—declaring himself “sincèrement fâché d’avoir usé une expression qui avoit pu blesser Monsieur Mirobolant, et qu’il donnoit sa parole comme un gentilhomme qu’il ne l’avoit jamais, jamais—intende,” said Pen, aiming at a French word for “intended,” and privately delighted with his own fluency, as if he had whipped up an omelette without spilling a drop.

“Bravo, bravo!” cried Strong, as pleased as he was amused.

And the Chevalier Mirobolant, of course, withdrew his pistols, withdrew his insult, withdrew his chin.

“Monsieur Pendennis has disproved my words himself,” Alcide said with profound politeness. “He has shown that he is a galant homme.”

Thus hands were shaken, dignity restored, and peace made; Arthur first despatching his pencilled note to Laura, before he and Strong committed themselves to the Butcher Boy.

As they drove along, wheels humming on the road with that steady rural sound no ballroom can imitate, Strong complimented Pen on his conduct and his French. “You’re a good fellow, Pendennis, and you speak French like Chateaubriand, by Jove.”

“I’ve been accustomed to it from my youth upwards,” said Pen; and Strong, with the grace of a man trying not to be rude, held out for five minutes—then exploded into such laughter as might have been heard, had one been listening, above even the far murmur of the sea.

It was daybreak when they got to the Brawl, where they parted. The ball at Baymouth was over too. Madame Fribsby and Mirobolant were on their way home in the Clavering fly; Laura, with an easier heart, slept at Lady Rockminster’s. The Claverings rested at the inn; and shortly after the disturbance Blanche had emerged from the refreshment-room, pale as a lemon-ice, and had told her maid—having no other confidante—that she had met the most romantic adventure: a singular man who had known the author of her being—her persecuted, unhappy, heroic, murdered father; and she began a sonnet to his manes before sleeping, as other people take a posset.

So Pen returned to Fairoaks without having uttered the message he had been so anxious to deliver at Baymouth. He could wait till Laura’s return, which would be the next day. He was not seriously jealous of Pynsent’s progress; and, being young and accustomed to the homage of his small world, he felt pretty certain that, in this as in other arrangements, he had but to ask and have; that Laura, like his mother, could refuse him nothing.

When Helen’s anxious looks questioned him—what had happened, and whether her darling project was fulfilled—Pen told of the waltzing calamity in a gay tone, made light of it, and laughed. “There will be plenty of time for sentiment, dear mother, when Laura comes back,” he said; and he looked in the glass with a killing air. Helen put his hair off his forehead and kissed him, and thought, of course, that no woman could resist him, and was exceedingly happy that day.

When he was not by her sofa, Mr. Pen occupied himself with packing books and portmanteaus, burning and arranging papers, cleaning his gun and putting it into its case—in short, making dispositions for departure. For though he was ready to marry, he was also eager to go to London; at three-and-twenty he considered it high time to begin the serious business of life, and make a fortune as quickly as possible.

His plan was already a banquet in his imagination, every dish served in due order. “I shall take chambers,” he said, “and enter myself at an Inn of Court. With a couple of hundred pounds I shall carry through the first year very well; after that my pen will support me, as it is doing with several Oxbridge men in town. I have a tragedy, a comedy, and a novel, all nearly finished, and for which I can’t fail to get a price. So I shall live pretty well without drawing on my poor mother, until I have made my way at the bar. Then, some day, I will come back and make her dear soul happy by marrying Laura. She is as good and as sweet-tempered a girl as ever lived—besides being really very good-looking—and the engagement will serve to steady me,—won’t it, Ponto?” Thus, smoking his pipe and talking to his dog as he sauntered through the gardens and orchards of Fairoaks, he built castles in the air with the ease of a man spreading butter on warm bread. “Yes, she’ll steady me, won’t she? And you’ll miss me when I’ve gone, won’t you, old boy?” Ponto quivered his tail and thrust his brown nose into his master’s fist; and licked hand and shoe, as they all did in that house, while Mr. Pen received their homage as other folks receive flattery and call it affection.

Laura came home rather late on the second day; and Mr. Pynsent, as ill luck would have it, drove her from Clavering. She could not refuse his offer; but his very appearance brought a dark cloud upon Arthur Pendennis’s brow. Laura saw it and was pained; but Helen—eager widow, matchmaking dove—noticed nothing, and, anxious that the delicate question should be asked at once, would have gone to bed very soon, rising from the sofa where she generally lay and where Laura would sit and work or read beside her. But when Helen rose, Laura—blushing and alarmed—said she too was tired and wanted to go to bed; so the widow’s scheme was thwarted for that night at least, and Mr. Pen was left another day in suspense.

His dignity was offended at being kept in the ante-chamber when he wished for an audience. A sultan like he could not be expected to wait in the corridor. Still, he went to bed, slept comfortably upon his disappointment, and did not wake until early morning, when he opened his eyes and found his mother standing in his room.

“Dear Pen, rouse up,” she said. “Do not be lazy. It is the most beautiful morning in the world. I have not been able to sleep since daybreak; and Laura has been out for an hour. She is in the garden. Everybody ought to be in the garden on such a morning as this.”

Pen laughed at the transparent artifice. He saw what thoughts were uppermost in that simple heart. His laughter cheered her.

“Oh you profound dissembler,” he said, kissing her. “Oh you artful creature! Can nobody escape from your wicked tricks? and will you make your only son your victim?” Helen laughed too, blushed, fluttered—happy as only a tender, plotting mother can be when her dearest project seems within reach.

After knowing looks and hasty words she left him; and Pen rose, decorated his handsome person, shaved his ambrosial chin, and in half an hour issued forth into the garden in quest of Laura.

Yet his reflections while dressing were dismal. “I am going to tie myself for life,” he thought, “to please my mother. Laura is the best of women, and—and she has given me her money. I wish to Heaven I had not received it; I wish I had not this duty to perform just yet. But as both the women have set their hearts on the match, I suppose I must satisfy them—and now for it. A man may do worse than make happy two of the best creatures in the world.” So, now that he was come to the point, he felt grave rather than elated, and thought it a great sacrifice he was about to make—like a man who praises the virtue of fasting while staring at a full table.

It was Miss Laura’s custom, on her garden excursions, to wear a sort of uniform—homely, but not unbecoming. A large straw hat, ribbon streamer flying for show more than use, shaded her face. Over her gown she wore a blouse or pinafore fastened at the waist by a smart belt; and her hands, guarded from rose-thorns by a pair of gauntlets, gave her a resolute, almost martial air—an innocent gardener armed against beauty’s prickles.

She had, somehow, the very same smile with which she had laughed at him the night before; and the recollection of his public tumble offended Pen afresh. Still, when she saw him coming down the walk—gloomy, solemn, full of care—she met him with provoking good humour and held out a gauntleted hand, as if offering him a knightly challenge.

He condescended to shake it; but his face did not lose its tragic expression.

“Excuse my glove,” said Laura, laughing, and pressing his hand kindly through the leather. “We are not angry again, are we, Pen?”

“Why do you laugh at me?” he said. “You did the other night, and made a fool of me to the people at Baymouth.”

“My dear Arthur, I meant you no wrong,” Laura answered. “You and Miss Roundle looked so droll as you—as you met with your little accident, that I could not make a tragedy of it. Dear Pen, it wasn’t a serious fall. And besides, it was Miss Roundle who was most unfortunate.”

“Confound Miss Roundle!” bellowed out Pen.

“I’m sure she looked so,” said Laura, archly. “You were up in an instant; but that poor lady sitting on the ground in her red crape dress, and looking about her with that piteous face—can I ever forget her?” And Laura began to mimic Miss Roundle’s expression—but checked herself, repentant. “Well, we must not laugh at her; but I am sure we ought to laugh at you, Pen, if you were angry about such a trifle.”

“You should not laugh at me, Laura,” he said bitterly. “Not you, of all people.”

“And why not? Are you such a great man?” asked Laura.

“Ah no, Laura—I’m such a poor one,” Pen answered. “Haven’t you baited me enough already?”

“My dear Pen—and how?” she cried. “Indeed, indeed, I didn’t think to vex you by such a trifle. I thought such a clever man as you could bear a harmless little joke from his sister.” And she held out her hand again. “Dear Arthur, if I have hurt you, I beg your pardon.”

“It is your kindness that humiliates me more even than your laughter,” Pen said. “You are always my superior.”

“What! superior to the great Arthur Pendennis? How can it be possible?” said Miss Laura, who had a little wickedness as well as a great deal of kindness in her. “You can’t mean that any woman is your equal?”

“Those who confer benefits should not sneer,” said Pen. “I don’t like my benefactor to laugh at me, Laura; it makes the obligation very hard to bear. You scorn me because I have taken your money, and I am worthy to be scorned; but the blow is hard coming from you.”

Our reader must consent—if only for a few miles—to shut the door upon the west, upon Clavering chatter and Fairoaks quiet, and to be tumbled, like a pat of butter in a churn, into London; that great kitchen of smoke and noise where reputations are stewed down, fortunes are whisked up, and young gentlemen are served, hot, to the public.

Arthur Pendennis took his seat on the “Alacrity,” bound once for all (so he vowed) to face the world and make his fortune. The coach went rattling away from the friendly gates of home, wheels drumming a steady tattoo on the road; and in that travelling music—hoof, harness, horn, and axle—Pen heard the beginning of his campaign. He lay awake in the night, seasoning his future with a hundred plans: prudence sliced thin, ambition laid on thick, repentance sprinkled like salt, and vanity—well, vanity was the sauce he always had within reach.

He had failed once, and the taste of it still lingered sharp on the tongue; yet it had not broken his appetite. He knew, as young men know, that he was better than many who had got the first servings. A year’s thought and mishap had made him feel older than when, twelve months ago, he had travelled this same road to and from Oxbridge, light as a cork and as empty.

His mind went back, with a tenderness that would have softened even a coffee-house chop, to the mother who had blessed him at parting: who trusted him still, loved him still, though he had given her small cause. Blessings on her, he prayed, looking up at the cold, bright stars—those quiet lamps in Heaven’s ceiling, burning without fuss, without smoke, without the clatter of London. O give him strength, he begged, to work, to endure, to be honest, to avoid temptation—to be worthy of that love which asked no questions and kept the hearth warm for him though he strayed.

And Laura’s love? He would have liked, in his best moments, to pack it into his portmanteau like a white handkerchief and carry it always. But she had refused it, because he was not worthy; and he confessed it with shame, and yet—since we are dealing with a young gentleman who can be sincere and selfish in one breath—he was glad to be free. “I am not good enough for such a creature,” he owned; and drew back from her spotless innocence as a prodigal draws back from a church he once entered without fear: not hating it, only feeling he has no right to that clean air.

So, while the coach flew through silent commons and by dark woods under calm skies, Pen vowed, and planned, and reproached himself, and congratulated himself, until the nipping dawn of October found him still awake. He slept at last, and woke with a traveller’s hungry refreshment when they stopped at the old breakfasting place at B——, where he had eaten a score of merry meals in boyhood—meals whose very memory brought back the clink of plates, the steam of coffee, the smell of toasted bread and damp greatcoats drying by the fire.

How a man’s courage rises with a warm room and a hot dish! The sun broke out brightly as they left; the pace was rapid; the horn blew; milestones slipped away like crumbs brushed from a table. Pen smoked, joked with the guard, exchanged merry words with passengers and roadside folk along that familiar ribbon of road. And as the traffic thickened, as the air grew heavier with the breath of the approaching city—coal smoke, wet stone, and that sour-sweet odour of crowds—his spirits rose until the last team of greys came out at H—— and the coach drove into London.

What young fellow has not felt that thrill—half hunger, half fear—on first entering the vast place? Hundreds of other carriages, stuffed with their thousands of men, hurried along as if the whole nation had overslept and was running for its breakfast. “Here is my place,” thought Pen; “here is my battle beginning. I must fight and conquer, or fall. I have been a boy and a dawdler. Oh, I long to show I can be a man!” And from the coach-roof he looked down upon the city with the eager longing of a young soldier hearing the first distant guns.

On the road he had made acquaintance with a cheery fellow-passenger in a shabby cloak, who talked incessantly of men of letters as though he had them all in his pantry and could bring them out at pleasure—Tom Campbell, Tom Hood, Sydney Smith—this one and that—each served up with a flourish, as if the speaker had carved their reputations himself. The gentleman was indeed a reporter for a London newspaper, returning from a great wrestling-match in the west; and his name, set down boldly on a card, was Mr. Doolan of the Star.

As they passed by Brompton, Mr. Doolan pointed out Mr. Hurtle the reviewer, walking with his umbrella. Pen craned over the coach like a boy trying to spy the cook through the kitchen door. He had not yet learned to distrust reviewers, editors, and authors; he believed in them as country people believe in London—thinking all its bread whiter and all its wit sharper. Even Wagg, whose books did not strike him as masterpieces, he secretly revered as a successful writer; and when Doolan told him that Wagg received three hundred pounds a volume, Pen began at once to reckon how quickly five thousand a year might be boiled out of paper and ink.

The very first acquaintance Pen met, as the coach pulled up at the Gloster Coffee-house, was his old friend Harry Foker, prancing down Arlington Street behind an enormous cab-horse. Foker had white kid gloves, white reins, and, as nature had lately taken to decoration, a considerable tuft on his chin. A very small cab-boy (Stoopid being retired from office) swung on behind the vehicle—knock-kneed, and imprisoned in the tightest leather breeches that ever took the joy out of a child.

Foker stared at the dusty coach and its smoking horses as if he were watching the roast come in. “What, Foker!” cried Pendennis.

“Hullo! Pen, my boy!” Foker waved his whip in salutation; and Pen’s heart warmed at the queer, kind face. Mr. Doolan, too, instantly enlarged his respect for Pen upon seeing that he had an acquaintance who commanded so grand a cab-horse. Pen, excited to be free and in London, asked Doolan to dine with him at the Covent Garden Coffee-house, where he put up. Off he rattled in a cab in the highest spirits, delighted to see the bustling waiter again, the polite bowing landlord, missing the old Boots as if he were a kinsman, and wishing to shake hands with the very furniture.

He had a hundred pounds in his pocket; which is an amount that makes a young man feel virtuous in advance. He dressed in his best, dined in the coffee-room with a modest pint of sherry—being determined, he told himself, to be very economical—and went to the theatre adjoining.

The lights, the music, the crowd, the gaiety—London serving up its first course—charmed and intoxicated him. The fiddles scraped, the audience buzzed, the painted scenery smelled faintly of lamp-oil and damp canvas; and beneath it all ran that great urban sound—laughter, coughing, foot-shuffling—like a tide against a sea-wall. Pen laughed at the jokes, applauded the songs with such honest freshness that the dreary old habitues in the boxes—those men who had long ago ceased to taste anything unless it were over-seasoned—looked at him almost with gratitude, as one looks at a young stomach enjoying what one’s own has grown tired of digesting.

At the end of the first piece he strutted about the lobbies, fancying himself in the very centre of fashion. What tired frequenter of London stones cannot remember his early delusions, and would not, if he could, bring them back—those first bright bites of the town, before the palate is blunted?

There was Foker again, ardent votary of pleasure; and with him Grandy Tiptoff of the Household Brigade (Lord Tiptoff’s brother) and Lord Colchicum, Captain Tiptoff’s uncle—a venerable peer who had been a man of pleasure ever since the first French Revolution and seemed resolved to outlive all reforms. Foker rushed upon Pen, insisted he should come into his private box, and there, like the chief dish in a supper-party, sat a lady with the longest ringlets and the fairest shoulders. This was Miss Blenkinsop, the eminent actress of high comedy; and in the back of the box, snoozing in a wig, sat old Blenkinsop, her papa—“the veteran Blenkinsop,” “the useful Blenkinsop,” “that old favourite of the public,”—he who played heavy fathers on the stage and, by all accounts, did not lay the part aside at home.

And while Pen, on his first London night, sat blinking at gaslight and beauty, it was about eleven o’clock at Fairoaks; Mrs. Pendennis had gone to bed, wondering whether her dearest Arthur was at rest after his journey. Laura, too, was awake. Yesterday night, as the coach rolled over silent commons and by cottage windows twinkling like little hearth-fires in the dark, Pen had been vowing to reform. Now the farce was going on very successfully, and Mrs. Leary, in a hussar jacket and braided pantaloons, was enchanting the audience with her archness, her figure, and her ballads—while London’s constant roar outside, wheels and cries and endless human stir, throbbed like a drum under the music, never stopping for anyone’s prayer.

Pen would have liked to listen; but the other people in the box did not care about her song or her pantaloons, and kept up an incessant chattering, as if talk were the only art worth paying for. Tiptoff knew where her maillots came from. Colchicum declared he had seen her when she came out in ’14. Miss Blenkinsop pronounced that she sang out of tune; which pained and astonished Pen, who thought Mrs. Leary as beautiful as an angel and as musical as a nightingale. When Hoppus came on as Sir Harcourt Featherby, the young man of the piece, the gentlemen declared Hoppus was getting stale; and Tiptoff proposed flinging Miss Blenkinsop’s bouquet to him.

“Not for the world,” cried Miss Blenkinsop. “Lord Colchicum gave it to me.”

Pen remembered that nobleman’s name; and, with bow and blush, said he believed he had to thank Lord Colchicum for proposing him at the Megatherium Club, at the request of his uncle Major Pendennis.

“What, you’re Wigsby’s nephew, are you?” said the peer. “I beg your pardon—we always call him Wigsby.” Pen blushed to hear his venerable uncle treated like a nickname. “We balloted you in last week, didn’t we? Yes, last Wednesday night. Your uncle wasn’t there.”

Delightful news! Pen poured out handsome thanks, which Lord Colchicum listened to with his double opera-glass up, as though examining a picture for flaws. Pen’s mind danced at the thought of being a member of that polite club—of belonging, at last, to the city’s inner dining-room.

“Don’t be always looking at that box, you naughty creature,” cried Miss Blenkinsop to one of the gentlemen.

“She’s a dev’lish fine woman, that Mirabel,” said Tiptoff; “though Mirabel was a d——d fool to marry her.”

“A stupid old spooney,” said the peer.

“Mirabel!” cried Pendennis.

“Ha! ha!” laughed Foker. “We’ve heard of her before, haven’t we, Pen?”

It was Pen’s first love. It was Miss Fotheringay—Emily—who, the year before, had been led to the altar by Sir Charles Mirabel, G.C.B., formerly envoy to the Court of Pumpernickel, busy at the Congress of Swammerdam, signer of the Peace of Pultusk, and wearer of a star and other decorations which glitter bravely even when sense does not.

“Emily was always as stupid as an owl,” said Miss Blenkinsop.

“Eh! Eh! pas si bête,” the old peer murmured.

“Oh, for shame!” cried the actress, who did not in the least know what he meant.

Pen looked out, beheld his first love again, and wondered—as a man who once burned his mouth on a foolishly hot pie wonders afterwards—how he ever could have been so eager.

Thus, on the very first night of his arrival in London, Mr. Arthur Pendennis found himself introduced to a club, to an actress of genteel comedy and a heavy father of the stage, and to a dashing society of jovial blades, old and young. For my Lord Colchicum, though bald, enfeebled, and stricken in years, was still indefatigable in the pursuit of enjoyment; and it was his boast that he could drink as much claret as the youngest member of any society he frequented. He lived with youth about town, gave them countless dinners at Richmond and Greenwich, and, being an enlightened patron of the drama in all languages and of the Terpsichorean art, entertained dramatic professors of all nations at his banquets—English from Covent Garden and the Strand, Italians from the Haymarket, French from their own pretty theatre, or from the Opera boards where they danced. And at his villa on the Thames, this pillar of the State gave sumptuous entertainments to scores of young men of fashion, who consorted affably with the greenroom—chiefly with the ladies, for Viscount Colchicum preferred their society as more polished and gay than that of their male brethren.

The next day Pen went and paid his entrance-money at the club—an operation which carried off exactly one-third of his hundred pounds, as neatly as a practised carver removes the choicest slice. He took possession of the edifice, ate luncheon there with immense satisfaction, plunged into an easy-chair in the library and tried to read all the magazines at once—like a glutton attacking a whole sideboard. He wondered whether the members were looking at him; and marvelled that they could dare to keep on their hats in such fine rooms. He sat down and wrote to Fairoaks on club paper, describing what a comfort the place would be after his day’s work was over.

Then, in compliance with his mother’s earnest desire, he went over to his uncle’s lodgings in Bury Street with some tremor. He was relieved to find the Major not yet returned to town. The apartments were blank; brown hollands covered the library-table; bills and letters lay on the mantelpiece, grimly awaiting their master. The Major, the landlady said, was on the Continent, at Badnbadn, with the Marquis of Steyne. Pen left his card upon the shelf with the rest—Fairoaks still written on it, as if he were a boy asking permission to come in.

When Major Pendennis returned to London—coming back in time for the November fogs, after which he proposed to spend Christmas with friends in the country—he found another card of Arthur’s; this one engraved, with an air of business, “Lamb Court, Temple,” and a note from Arthur and from Mrs. Pendennis stating that the young gentleman had come to town, entered a member of the Upper Temple, and was reading hard for the bar.

Lamb Court, Temple—where was it? The Major remembered ladies of fashion talking of dining with Mr. Ayliffe the barrister, who was “in society,” and lived there in the King’s Bench—of which prison there was probably a branch in the Temple; and Ayliffe might very likely be an officer. Mr. Deuceace, Lord Crabs’s son, had also lived there, he recollected. He despatched Morgan to find Lamb Court and report upon the lodging selected by Mr. Arthur. Morgan, who had tracked game much harder to find than a young gentleman with his name on a door, had little difficulty.

“What sort of a place is it, Morgan?” asked the Major next morning from out of the bed-curtains in Bury Street, while the valet arranged his toilette in the thick yellow fog.
