“I should say rayther a shy place,” said Mr. Morgan. “The lawyers lives there and has their names on the doors. Mr. Harthur lives three pair high, sir. Mr. Warrington lives there too, sir.”

“Suffolk Warringtons! I shouldn’t wonder: a good family,” thought the Major. “Cadets of good families follow the robe. Comfortable rooms, eh?”

“Honly saw the outside of the door, sir—Mr. Warrington’s name and Mr. Arthur’s painted up, and a piece of paper with ‘Back at 6;’ but I couldn’t see no servant, sir.”

“Economical at any rate,” said the Major.

“Very, sir. Three pair, sir. Nasty black staircase as ever I see. Wonder how a gentleman can live in such a place.”

“Pray, who taught you where gentlemen should or should not live, Morgan? Mr. Arthur is going to study for the bar,” the Major said with dignity; and closed the subject, as one snaps down a dish-cover.

Left to himself, he mused more kindly. “Boys will be boys. He has written me a devilish good letter. Colchicum says he has dined with him and thinks him a gentlemanlike lad. His mother is one of the best creatures in the world. If he has sown his wild oats and will stick to business, he may do well yet. Think of Charley Mirabel, the old fool, marrying that flame of his! that Fotheringay! Gad, I’ll go and see him—hang me if I don’t.”

So, having learned from Morgan that a city omnibus would put him down at the gate, the Major one day after breakfast at his club—not the Polyanthus, where Mr. Pen had just been elected (the Major was too wise to have a nephew constantly under his own club roof), but another—entered one of those public vehicles and bade the conductor set him down at the Upper Temple.

It was about twelve when Major Pendennis reached that dingy portal. A civil personage with a badge and white apron directed him through dark alleys and under melancholy archways into courts each more dismal than the last, until at length he reached Lamb Court. If Pall Mall was dark, what was Lamb Court? Candles were burning in many rooms: in Mr. Hodgeman the special pleader’s pupil-room, where six pupils scribbled declarations under tallow; in Sir Hokey Walker’s clerk’s room, where the clerk—far more cheerful and gentlemanlike than the celebrated counsel—conversed patronisingly with an attorney’s managing clerk at the door; and in Curling the wigmaker’s melancholy shop, where, behind the feeble glimmer of two lights, large serpents’ wigs and judges’ wigs loomed drearily, blank blocks staring out at the lamp-post in the court as if waiting to be given faces and voices.

Two little clerks were playing toss-halfpenny under that lamp. A laundress in pattens clacked in at one door. A newspaper boy issued from another with a sharp cry that cut the fog like a knife through suet. A porter, his white apron faintly visible, paced up and down. Sound here did not sing; it dripped—muffled footsteps, distant coughs, the scrape of pens—everything smothered by old stone and stale air. The Major, who liked a world where conversation was crisp and claret clear, shuddered. “Good Ged!” he said. “The poor boy mustn’t live on here.”

The filthy oil-lamps that lit the Temple staircases by night were, of course, not lit by day; and the Major, having read with difficulty his nephew’s name under Mr. Warrington’s on the wall of No. 6, found still greater difficulty climbing the abominable black stairs. His gloved hand groped along banisters that contributed damp exudations to his kid. At last he reached the third story. A candle burned in the passage of one of the two sets of rooms; doors stood open; and the names of Mr. Warrington and Mr. A. Pendennis were clearly visible as he went in. An Irish charwoman with pail and broom opened to him.

“Is that the beer?” cried a great voice. “Give us hold of it.”

The gentleman speaking was seated on a table, unshorn and smoking a short pipe; in a farther chair sat Pen with a cigar, his legs near the fire. A little boy who acted as clerk grinned at the Major’s face, delighted at the notion of a gentleman of his appearance being mistaken for beer.

“Pen, my boy—it’s I—it’s your uncle,” the Major said, choking a little with the smoke; but as most young men of fashion used the weed, he pardoned it easily enough.

Mr. Warrington rose from the table; Pen rose too, perturbed from his chair.

“Beg your pardon for mistaking you,” said Warrington in a frank loud voice. “Will you take a cigar, sir? Clear those things off the chair, Pidgeon, and pull it round to the fire.”

Pen flung his cigar into the grate; and was pleased—more pleased than he cared to show—by the cordiality with which his uncle shook his hand. As soon as he could speak for the stairs and the smoke, the Major began to ask Pen kindly after himself and his mother; for blood is blood, and the sight of the boy softened him.

Pen gave his news, and then introduced Mr. Warrington—an old Boniface man—whose chambers he shared.

The Major was quite satisfied to hear that Mr. Warrington was a younger son of Sir Miles Warrington of Suffolk. He had served with an uncle of the Major’s in India and in New South Wales years ago.

“Took a sheep-farm there, sir, made a fortune—better thing than law or soldiering,” Warrington said. “Think I shall go there too.” And here the expected beer arrived in a tankard with a glass bottom; whereupon Warrington, laughing, supposed the Major would have none, and took a long deep draught himself, then wiped his wrist across his beard with immense satisfaction. He wore a ragged old shooting-jacket; his beard was bristly and blue; he drank beer like a coalheaver; and yet you could not but perceive he was a gentleman.

After sitting a minute or two, Warrington went out, leaving uncle and nephew together.

“Rough and ready, your chum seems,” the Major said. “Somewhat different from your dandy friends at Oxbridge.”

“Times are altered,” Arthur replied, blushing. “Warrington is only just called, and has no business, but he knows law pretty well; and until I can afford to read with a pleader, I use his books and get his help.”

“Is that one of the books?” the Major asked with a smile; for a French novel lay at the foot of Pen’s chair.

“This is not a working day, sir,” Pen said. “We were out very late at a party last night—at Lady Whiston’s,” he added, knowing his uncle’s weakness for the seasoning of great names. “Everybody in town was there except you, sir; Counts, Ambassadors, Turks, Stars and Garters—I don’t know who—it’s all in the paper—and my name too,” he said with great glee. “I met an old flame of mine there, sir,” he added with a laugh. “You know whom I mean—Lady Mirabel—to whom I was introduced over again. She shook hands and was gracious enough. I may thank you for being out of that scrape, sir. She presented me to the husband too—an old beau in a star and a blonde wig. He does not seem very wise. She has asked me to call on her, sir: and I may go now without any fear of losing my heart.”

“What, we have had some new loves, have we?” the Major asked in high good-humour.

“Some two or three,” Mr. Pen said, laughing. “But I don’t put on my grand sérieux any more, sir. That goes off after the first flame.”

Colleges, ancient schools, and those venerable Inns where the Law is supposed to be brewed into a livelihood, still keep up a brave show of reverence for antiquity; and, like elderly aunts who will not hear a syllable against last century’s housekeeping, they preserve innumerable customs simply because the dust upon them is respectable. A new prison will give you air, water, light, cleanliness, and a moral text upon the wall in letters you can read without a telescope; but a Foundation School, a College, or an Inn of Court will lodge you lovingly in a cupboard, charge you for it like a villa with lilacs, and then look offended if you inquire, in a low voice, where a man may possibly contrive to wash.

The poorest weaver in Spitalfields may turn a tap and summon a Niagara to his basin. But the gentlemen of the Temple and the Universities—gentlemen who quote the ancients with ease—are served their water like a rare sauce: fetched in jugs, portioned out by laundresses and bedmakers, and doled with the air of administering medicine. Their staircases were built when the national mind had not yet discovered the connection between soap and decency. There are men still alive who call “the people” dirty with a curled lip. Gentlemen, your forefathers were, beyond dispute, the Great Unwashed; and in the Temple, where walls remember the smell of centuries, it is plain that the virtue said to be next to godliness could only have been practised by stratagem and with witnesses.

Old Grump, of the Norfolk Circuit—now well past his half-century, and lodged for more than thirty years in chambers under those occupied by Messrs. Warrington and Pendennis—was nightly roused by the roaring of the shower-baths which those wild innovators had erected overhead. A portion of this audacious waterfall would now and then condescend to trickle through his ceiling, to the great injury of his temper and the slight moistening of his plaster. Grump declared the whole practice an absurd, dandified, newfangled folly; and daily anathematised the laundress who slopped the stairs with a deluge meant, no doubt, for civilization. The old gentleman had lived very handsomely without water, and so had the fathers before him. He could not see why a man should seek out damp on purpose.

One looks up, in the famous hall of the Upper Temple, at the painted escutcheons of knights and baronets, lords and gentlemen bearing arms, and cannot help wondering whether not one among them—some charitable soul with imagination enough to see beyond the next dinner—ever devised a set of baths, a Hummums of the Law, for the benefit of his learned successors. The Temple historian is silent. There is Pump Court, there is Fountain Court, there is hydraulic apparatus enough to suggest refreshment; but no one has heard of a bencher disporting in the fountain, and one can only mourn how many a counsel in the old days might have been improved in argument by the honest pump.

Yet for all its dinginess and its jugs of water, the place has an attraction, a rough freedom, a comfort of ancient irresponsibility, which men remember as they remember the smell of a childhood kitchen—smoky, perhaps, and rather questionable for the lungs, but dear for the sake of what was cooked there. I cannot say whether the student of law permits himself much enthusiasm as he passes historical doors and murmurs, “Here Eldon lived; on this site Coke wrestled with Littleton; here Chitty toiled; here Barnewall and Alderson laboured; here Byles wrote upon bills, and Smith compiled his immortal cases; here Gustavus still toils, with Solomon to aid him.” But the man of letters must love a place inhabited by so many of his brethren, or peopled by creations as real to us as their authors: Sir Roger de Coverley in the Temple Garden discoursing with Mr. Spectator upon the beauties in hoops and patches; Samuel Johnson rolling through the fog with the Scotchman behind him towards Goldsmith’s chambers in Brick Court; Harry Fielding, with inked ruffles and a wet towel round his head, battering out copy at midnight while the printer’s boy snores in the passage. If some Temple Asmodeus would but lift roofs for us and give the history of one day in one of those four-storied houses in the dingy courts, he might furnish a queer volume—full of dinners, debts, vows, cigar-ashes, and the small tragedies that are made of unpaid bills and overboiled chops.

On the ground floor you may have a great parliamentary counsel, who drives off to Belgravia at dinner-time, and whose clerk, the moment his master’s carriage wheels are gone, becomes a gentleman also, and goes away to play the gentleman in his own cheaper key. A short time since, that counsel was hungry and briefless in a garret of the Inn; lived by stealthy literature; waited, hoped, sickened; saw no clients come; spent his own means and his friends’ kindness; implored the patience of creditors with the humility of a man apologising for being poor. Ruin stared; then the wheel of fortune turned, and the lucky wretch drew one of those prodigious prizes which the Bar sometimes throws up as if to prove it is not wholly unjust. Many a better lawyer than he cannot make a fifth of his income; and his clerk, who not long ago could hardly get credit for blacking his master’s unpaid boots, now dines like a Christian.

On the first floor, perhaps, lives a venerable name: a man famous, solitary, and rich; fifty years in the Inn; shelves full of classical and legal lore; brains packed with books as a larder is packed with jars. He comes home at night from his club, where he has dined freely, to lonely chambers where he lives a godless old recluse. When he dies, the Inn will erect a tablet to his honour; his heirs will burn part of his library. Would you like such an old age—money and learning stored like winter provisions, and no one to share the meal? But we must not stay long at Mr. Doomsday’s door.

Worthy Mr. Grump lives over him; another ancient inhabitant; and when Doomsday comes home to read Catullus, Grump is sitting down with three steady seniors of his standing to a steady rubber at whist, after a dinner at which they have consumed their three steady bottles of port. You may see the old boys asleep in the Temple Church of a Sunday, their heads nodding to the organ as if the music were an argument they had heard too often. Attorneys seldom trouble them; they have small fortunes of their own; they are as fixed in their habits as old cheese in a pantry.

On the other side of the third landing, where Pen and Warrington were to lodge till long after midnight, sits Mr. Paley: first in honours, fellow of his college, a man who reads and notes cases until two in the morning; rises at seven; is at the pleader’s chambers as soon as they open; works until an hour before dinner; comes home from Hall and reads and notes cases again until dawn—when perhaps Arthur Pendennis and his friend Mr. Warrington are returning from some wild expedition, with London’s late noises still in their ears.

How differently employed has Mr. Paley been! He has not been throwing himself away; only bringing a great intellect down, laboriously, to the comprehension of a mean subject; and in his fierce grasp of that, shutting out from his mind all higher thoughts, all better things—philosophy, history, poetry, wit, fancy, reflection, art, love, truth; everything, in short, that makes a man human instead of a walking index. Outside his reading-lamp all is dark. Love, Nature, and Art—the expression of our praise for the beautiful world—are barred like thieves from his room. When he turns off his lonely lamp at night, he thinks he has spent the day profitably, and goes to sleep thankless and remorseless. Yet he shudders when he meets Warrington on the stairs and shuns him as one doomed.

Warrington and Paley had once been competitors for university honours and had run each other hard; and now everybody said Warrington was wasting his time and energies, while all praised Paley for his industry. There may be doubts as to which used his time best. One could afford to think; the other never could. One could have sympathies and do kindnesses; the other must needs be always selfish—not by choice perhaps, but by discipline. He could not cultivate a friendship, do a charity, admire genius, kindle at beauty or at the sound of a sweet song—he had no time, no ears for anything but his law-books. In the Temple, where sounds carry oddly through old brick and along stone passages—voices, footsteps, the scrape of chairs, the nightly quarrel of a fiddle with an amateur—Paley heard none of it as music, but only as interruption.

It may have been that sight of cadaverous ambition and self-complacent meanness, twinkling in Paley’s narrow eyes and showing in his yellow face; or it may have been a natural appetite for pleasure and joviality (and it must be confessed Mr. Pen had a hearty one); but something deterred that luckless youth from pursuing the Bench or Woolsack with the steady ardour required for those lofty seats. He enjoyed the Temple life with great relish. His worthy relatives believed he was reading as became a regular student; his uncle wrote congratulatory letters to the kind widow at Fairoaks, announcing that the lad had sown his wild oats and was becoming quite steady. The truth was, the life was new excitement; and Pen, having given up some dandified pretensions and fine-gentleman airs contracted among aristocratic college acquaintances (whom he now saw little), found the rough pleasures of a London bachelor novel and agreeable, and tasted them all.

There was a time he would have envied dandies their horses in Rotten Row; but now he was content to walk in the Park and look at them—as a sensible man looks at game in a poulterer’s window when he has only money for a chop. He was too young to succeed in London society without a better name and larger fortune, and too lazy to get on without such helpful seasoning. Old Pendennis, seeing that the boy neglected certain social advantages, fondly inferred it was because he was immersed in law; and because Pen had tried half a dozen balls and evening parties and retreated before their dulness and sameness, the Major concluded scholarship had conquered pleasure. Whenever anybody asked after his nephew, the old gentleman declared the young rascal reformed, and that he could not be got away from his books.

The Major would have been almost as horrified as Mr. Paley, had he known how much pleasure entered into Mr. Pen’s studies. A long morning’s reading; a walk in the Park; a pull upon the river; a stretch up to Hampstead (where the wind, at least, had not yet been entirely bribed by the city); and then a modest tavern dinner, honest and smoking, with its clatter of plates, its warm fog of roasted meat, its smell of ale and browned gravy—those domestic incenses which make even a dreary day seem briefly hospitable. A bachelor night passed here or there, in joviality, not vice (for Arthur Pendennis admired women so heartily that he could not bear the society of any whom, in his fancy at least, were not good and pure). A quiet evening at home with a friend and a pipe or two; a humble potation of British spirits, the quality of which Mrs. Flanagan, the laundress, invariably tested with conscientious severity—these were the pursuits of our young gentleman; and it must be owned his life was not unpleasant.

In term-time, Mr. Pen showed most praiseworthy regularity in performing one part of a law-student’s duty: he ate his dinners in Hall. The Hall of the Upper Temple is no uninteresting sight; and save for trifling improvements and anachronisms, a man may sit there and fancy he joins in a meal of the seventeenth century. The bar have their messes; the students their tables apart; the benchers sit aloft at the high table on a raised platform, surrounded by pictures of judges and portraits of royal personages who have honoured the place with their patronage—faces looking down as if to say they have seen many a man carve his hopes as clumsily as his beef.

Pen, on his first introduction, looked about not a little amused. Among the student class were gentlemen of all ages, from sixty to seventeen: stout grey-headed attorneys proceeding to take the superior dignity; dandies and men about town who wished for some reason to be barristers of seven years’ standing; swarthy black-eyed natives of the Colonies who came to be called here before they practised in their own islands; many gentlemen of the Irish nation, who make a sojourn in Middle Temple Lane before returning to the green country of their birth. There were little squads of reading students who talked law all dinner-time—an almost unknown and quite uninteresting language to Pen; there were rowing men whose discourse was of sculling matches, the Red House, Vauxhall, and the Opera; there were others great in politics, and orators of debating clubs; and with all these sets, except the legal linguists, Mr. Pen made gradual acquaintance and found points of sympathy.

The ancient and liberal Inn provides in its Hall, and for a very moderate price, an excellent wholesome dinner: soup, meat, tarts, and port wine or sherry. The parties are arranged in messes of four; each quartet has its piece of beef or leg of mutton, its sufficient apple-pie, its bottle of wine. But the honest habitués of the Hall among the lower rank of students, who have a taste for good living, possess many harmless arts by which they improve their banquet—innocent dodges by which they aspire to more delicate food than the common roast meat of the students’ tables. These contrivances were as much a part of the Inn’s tradition as its portraits: handed down, improved, whispered over, as receipts are whispered in families.

“Wait a bit,” said Mr. Lowton, one of these Temple gourmands. “Wait a bit,” he repeated, tugging at Pen’s gown with the tenderness of a man who feels he is saving another from ignorance. “The side-tables are very full, and there’s only three benchers to eat ten dishes—if we wait, perhaps we shall get something from their table.”

Pen looked with amusement, as did Lowton with eyes of fond desire, towards the high table, where three old gentlemen stood before a dozen silver dish-covers while the clerk quavered out a grace. Even the grace had its acoustics: it rose thinly, wavered, and sank into the great wooden roof where centuries of speeches had lodged like smoke. The lid-covers shone; the odours floated down in teasing little messages—something rich and sea-sweet that might be fish; something dark and dignified that might be turtle; something buttery that made a man suddenly remember he was alive.

Lowton was great in the conduct of dinner. His aim was to manage so as to be first—a captain of the mess—and to secure for himself the thirteenth glass of the bottle of port. Thus he commanded the joint on which he operated favourite cuts, making rapid, dexterous appropriations of gravy, which amused Pen infinitely. Poor Jack Lowton! Thy pleasures were harmless; an eager epicure, thy desires did not go beyond eighteen pence, and thy heroism was exercised upon potatoes.

Pen was somewhat older than many fellow-students, and there was about his style and appearance—haughty and impertinent, if you will—that stamped him as a man of ton; unlike pale students murmuring law to one another, and unlike ferocious dandies in rowing shirts with astonishing pins and waistcoats, representing the idle part of the community. The humble good-natured Lowton felt attracted by Pen’s superior looks and presence, and opened acquaintance at the mess by beginning, gravely, with the great subject.

“This is boiled-beef day, I believe, sir,” said Lowton to Pen.

“Upon my word, sir, I’m not aware,” said Pen, hardly able to contain his laughter; but added, “I’m a stranger; this is my first term.”

On which Lowton began to point out notabilities in the Hall.

“That’s Boosey the bencher,” he said, “the bald one sitting under the picture and aving soup. I wonder whether it’s turtle? They often ave turtle. Next is Balls, the King’s Counsel, and Swettenham—Hodge and Swettenham, you know. That’s old Grump, the senior of the bar; they say he’s dined here forty years. They often send ’em down their fish from the benchers to the senior table. Do you see those four fellows opposite us? Those are regular swells—tip-top fellows, I can tell you—Mr. Trail, the Bishop of Ealing’s son; Honourable Fred Ringwood, Lord Cinqbar’s brother, you know. He’ll have a good place, I bet any money; and Bob Suckling, who’s always with him—a high fellow too. Ha! ha!”

Here Lowton burst into a laugh.

“What is it?” asked Pen.

“I say, I like to mess with those chaps,” Lowton said, winking knowingly and pouring out his glass.

“And why?” asked Pen, still amused.

“Why! they don’t come down here to dine, you know; they only make believe to dine. They dine here! Law bless you! They go to some swell club, or else to some grand dinner-party. You see their names in the Morning Post at all the fine parties in London. Why, I bet anything Ringwood has his cab, or Trail his Brougham—he’s a devil of a fellow, and makes the bishop’s money spin—I bet it’s at the corner of Essex Street at this minute. They dine! They won’t dine these two hours, I dare say.”

“But why should you like to mess with them, if they don’t eat any dinner?” Pen asked, still puzzled. “There’s plenty, isn’t there?”

“How green you are,” said Lowton. “Excuse me, but you are green. They don’t drink any wine, don’t you see; and a fellow gets the bottle to himself if he likes it when he messes with those three chaps. That’s why Corkoran got in with ’em.”

“Ah, Mr. Lowton, I see you are a sly fellow,” Pen said, delighted with his acquaintance.

Lowton modestly replied that he had lived in London the better part of his life and of course had his eyes about him; and he went on with his catalogue.

“There’s a lot of Irish here,” he said; “that Corkoran’s one, and I can’t say I like him. You see that handsome chap with the blue neck-cloth and pink shirt and yellow waistcoat—that’s another; that’s Molloy Maloney of Ballymaloney, and nephew to Major-General Sir Hector O’Dowd, he, he,” Lowton added, trying to imitate the Hibernian accent. “He’s always bragging about his uncle; and came into Hall in silver-striped trousers the day he had been presented. That other near him, with the long black hair, is a tremendous rebel. By Jove, to hear him at the Forum it makes your blood freeze; and the next is an Irishman too—Jack Finucane, reporter of a newspaper. They all stick together, those Irish. It’s your turn to fill your glass. What? you won’t have any port? Don’t like port with your dinner? Here’s your health.”

This worthy man grew no less attached to Pendennis because the latter professed dislike of port at dinner; some men can forgive any failing except abstinence from their own favourite relish, and Lowton was generous enough to forgive even that.

It was while Pen was taking his share of one of these dinners, with Lowton as captain of the mess, that there came to join them a gentleman in a barrister’s gown who could not find a seat among persons of his own degree. He strode over and took his place on the bench where Pen sat. He wore old clothes and a faded gown hanging behind him; his shirt, though clean, was extremely ragged—very different from the magnificent pink raiment of Mr. Molloy Maloney, who in the next mess shone like a tropical bird among sparrows.

To notify their appearance at dinner, it is the custom for gentlemen eating in the Hall to write their names upon slips of paper provided for the purpose, with a pencil for each mess. Lowton wrote first; then Arthur Pendennis; and next came the name of the gentleman in old clothes. He smiled when he saw Pen’s name and looked at him.

“We ought to know each other,” he said. “We’re both Boniface men; my name’s Warrington.”

“Are you St— Warrington?” Pen cried, delighted, as if a storybook had stepped down into the Hall.

Warrington laughed. “Stunning Warrington—yes,” he said. “I recollect you in your freshman’s term. But you appear to have quite cut me out.”

“The college talks about you still,” said Pen, who had generous admiration for talent and pluck. “The bargeman you thrashed, Bill Simes, wants you up again at Oxbridge. The Miss Notleys, the haberdashers—”

“Hush!” said Warrington quickly, with a grin that made the prohibition friendly. “Glad to make your acquaintance, Pendennis. Heard a good deal about you.”

They were friends immediately, deep at once in college-talk—the sort that makes two men who have eaten the same bad dinners feel as though they were brothers. And Pen, who had been acting rather the fine gentleman on a previous day when he pretended to Lowton he could not drink port at dinner, seeing Warrington take his share with gusto, did not scruple about helping himself any more—rather to the disappointment of honest Lowton, whose whole philosophy of life included a private bottle.

When dinner was over, Warrington asked Arthur where he was going.

“I thought of going home to dress, and hear Grisi in Norma,” Pen said.

“Are you going to meet anybody there?” Warrington asked.

Pen said no—only to hear the music, of which he was fond.

“You had much better come home and smoke a pipe with me,” said Warrington, “a very short one. Come; I live close by in Lamb Court, and we’ll talk over Boniface and old times.”

They went away; Lowton sighed after them. He knew Warrington was a baronet’s son, and he looked up with simple reverence to all the aristocracy, as some men look up at high tables as if gravy descended more nobly there.

From that night Pen and Warrington were sworn friends. Warrington’s cheerfulness and jovial temper, his good sense, his rough welcome, and his never-failing pipe of tobacco charmed Pen. It was pleasanter to dive into shilling taverns with him—where the air was full of clinking glasses, rasped laughter, and the homely music of knives on plates—than to dine in solitary state among the silent, polite frequenters of the Polyanthus. Ere long Pen gave up the lodgings in St. James’s, to which he had migrated on quitting his hotel, and found it much more economical to take up his abode with Warrington in Lamb Court, furnishing and occupying his friend’s vacant room there. For it must be said of Pen, no man was more easily led to do a thing when it was a novelty, or when he had a mind to it. And Pidgeon the youth, and Flanagan the laundress, divided their allegiance now between Warrington and Pen, as impartial publicans divide their smiles between two customers who both pay.

Pen, having once caught the London fever, must needs taste the whole city as a greedy boy tastes a fair—one stall after another, one sweetmeat after another, vowing each last mouthful the finest he ever knew, and instantly forgetting it for the next. He prowled into a hundred queer haunts with the air of a young gentleman who had read of “Life” in books and was resolved to have it served up hot, with sauce. Coalheavers he visited in their tap-rooms, where the beer was brown as the river at low tide and the talk rolled heavy as casks. Boxers he watched in inn-parlours, where the walls were smoky with old oaths and newer pipe-fumes. Honest citizens he observed in suburban gardens, taking their pleasure as if it were a Sunday joint—cut carefully, praised loudly, and meant to last. And had Fate but offered him a celebrated pickpocket in a convenient corner, Pen would willingly have clinked pewter with him, merely for the novelty, as a child will eat a strange berry to boast he has eaten it.

The merriest part of this expeditionary cookery of experience was Warrington, who went through these houses as a man goes through his own pantry: knowing what shelf held the best relish, which drawer the sharpest mustard, and which landlord could be trusted not to water the gin. Pen delighted to see the gravity with which Warrington listened to the Tutbury Pet or the Brighton Stunner at the Champion’s Arms, and the downright affection he showed the coalheaving company at the Fox-under-the-Hill. His acquaintance with public-houses was not so much wide as intimate; he was greeted at the bar as at a club, and nodded to by tapsters with the respectful ease with which cooks salute a man who tips well and never complains of his steak.

“In society,” Warrington would say—sanding his words as the floor was sanded—“everybody is the same: same coat, same grin, same talk, same everything. One young dandy at the club looks and chatters just like another; one Miss at a ball resembles the next, like loaves turned out of the same tin. But here there’s flavour. I like to talk with the strongest man in England, or the man who can drink the most beer in England, or with that tremendous republican hatter who thinks Thistlewood the greatest character in history. I like better gin-and-water than claret. I like a sanded floor in Carnaby Market better than a chalked one in Mayfair. I prefer Snobs, I own it.”

And indeed he was a sort of social republican; it never entered his head, while talking with Jack and Tom, that he was in any respect their better—though, to do him justice, the deference they paid him might have been as pleasant to his vanity as a warm roll to a hungry man.

Pen followed him with immense glee and enormous assiduity; yet Pen, being younger, wore his humility as young men wear their first dress-coat—stiffly, and as if it proved nobility. He moved among these fellows like a young prince in disguise visiting the poor of his father’s kingdom; and they received him accordingly, as a high chap, a fine fellow, a swell with good humour. He had an imperious frankness, a kind of royal condescension; though, in strict revenue, he was heir-apparent to twopence-halfpenny, and but one in descent from a gallypot. But if the world lays a cushion for us to sit higher, we drop onto it readily enough; and there is nothing so touching and so ridiculous as the conceit of a clever generous lad—so frank, so certain, so wrong.

They read pretty hard of a morning—Pen, I fear, not law alone, but politics and history and literature and, above all, the newspaper, that great steaming dish in which the whole town is boiled daily and served to whoever can swallow it. Then, when dinner drew nigh and appetite with it, they sallied out upon the town with spirits sharpened like knives, bent upon a merry night as they had passed a busy forenoon. There is a season—four-and-twenty—when the world is new bread and you believe it will never go stale. Afterwards you may fancy yourself young again with the comrades of that time; the tunes you hum in old age are the tunes you learned then. Yet the same pleasure-garden, revisited, looks dingy: garlands tattered, company thin, and half the lamps out. Grey hairs come on like daylight streaming in—daylight and a headache with it. Pleasure goes to bed with the rouge still on her cheeks. Well: let us walk through the day, sober if we must, but friendly.

Laura and Helen—had they chanced to be up in London—might sometimes, at very early morning when the bridges blushed in sunrise and the city streets shone clean in the dawn, have seen Mr. Pen and Mr. Warrington rattling over the echoing flags toward the Temple after one of their wild nights. Wild—but not so wicked as such nights often are. Warrington hated women; and Pen, lofty even in his faults, was too proud to stoop to a vulgar intrigue. He could not speak to a woman but with instinctive courtesy, and shrank from a coarse word as from a sour smell in a clean room. If he fell in love with a fool—as wiser men have done—he still, for the time of the delusion, set her up as a goddess and waited upon her. Men serve women kneeling; when they get on their feet, they go away.

That hard homely aphorism was delivered to Pen, not by a philosopher in a book, but by an old acquaintance met again in London—honest Mr. Bows of the Chatteris Theatre—now reduced (or promoted, according to how you rate the dignity of labour) to be pianoforte player to the eminent lyrical talent which nightly delighted the public at the Fielding’s Head in Covent Garden; where, behind the scenes and beyond the decencies, flourished the little club called the Back Kitchen.

A number of Pen’s friends frequented this merry meeting. The Fielding’s Head had been a house of entertainment almost since the days when the famous author of Tom Jones sat as magistrate hard by in Bow Street. Fielding’s place was pointed out; Fielding’s chair was said to survive, and in it sat nightly the president of the revels. Most often that president was Cutts, the landlord: a jolly man with a voice like a well-corked bottle—strong, cheerful, and certain to go off with a pop. He sang profusely; his songs belonged to the British Brandy-and-Water School—“The Good Old English Gentleman,” “Dear Tom, this Brown Jug,” and others of that comfortable tribe wherein hospitality and pathos are kneaded together and baked in a baritone.

Often have I marvelled, in my youth, at Cutts’s double capacity: how he would work a room to patriotism by singing of brave Abercrombie receiving his wound, or melt us with the autumn leaf proclaiming the old man must die—Cutts shedding tears liberally, voice faltering, fists thumping approval on the tables—when, before the applause had ended, he would become instantly Cutts the landlord, and call out, brisk as a cook at service: “Now, gentlemen, give your orders; the waiter’s in the room—John, a champagne cup for Mr. Green. Sausages and mashed potatoes? John, attend on the gentleman.”

“And I’ll thank ye give me a glass of punch too, John, and take care the wather boils,” would cry, not unfrequently, a voice Pen knew too well; a voice that made him blush and start when he heard it first. It was the venerable Captain Costigan—now established in London, and one of the great pillars of the harmonic meetings at the Fielding’s Head.

Costigan’s very ruin had a kind of gusto to it. He was never merely drunk; he was steeped. He would insist on punch as if it were a medicinal broth, and on the water boiling as if the kettle were the last outpost of discipline in a besieged life. His manners and his talk brought many young men to the Back Kitchen, for he was a character, and fame has a way of making even folly sound like entertainment when it is delivered loudly enough. He talked to the friend of the moment—his neighbour drinking by his side—about “me daughther”; about her marriage; about the grandeur before and after it; about the carriages she kept; about Mirabel’s adoration for her and for him; about the hundred pounds he was at liberty to draw from his son-in-law whenever necessity urged him.

Then—having sworn, with the solemnity of a man blessing a joint, that he would “dthraw next Sathurday—the fourteenth—at Coutts’s—the very instant I present the cheque”—he would as solemnly ask to borrow a half-crown until that day of Greek Calends, pledging on the honour of an officer and gentleman to “repee the thrifling obligetion.”

Sir Charles Mirabel did not in truth adore his father-in-law as Costigan sometimes boasted, though in other moods Costigan would weep over his daughter’s ingratitude and the wealthy old man’s stinginess. Yet the Mirabels had not been unkind: they had settled a small pension on him, paid with regularity, and forestalled with still greater regularity by poor Cos. The period of payment was always known at the Fielding’s Head; where the Captain, bank-notes in hand, would demand change at the top of his voice amid the songs and suppers, as if money were a trumpet meant to be blown. “I think ye’ll find that note won’t be refused at the Bank of England, Cutts, my boy,” he would say. “Bows, have a glass? Ye needn’t stint yourself to-night, anyhow; and a glass of punch will make ye play con spirito.” He was lavish when he had money—buttons were not invented for his pocket until the coin was gone; and sometimes, indeed, not even then, unless a creditor approached within smelling distance.

It was in one of these moments of exultation that Pen found the old man swaggering at the singers’ table in the Back Kitchen, ordering brandy-and-water for any acquaintance who appeared. Warrington, who was on confidential terms with the bass singer, made his way up to that quarter; Pen followed close.

Pen started and blushed to see Costigan. He had just come from Lady Whiston’s party, where he had met and spoken with the Captain’s daughter again for the first time since very old days; and the sight of the father brought back, with the suddenness of a taste on the tongue, a whole remembered season. He came up with outstretched hand, kindly and warmly; for though Pen might be capricious in his attachments, he always respected the place where Love had dwelt, and—like the Sultan who has once flung the royal handkerchief—desired honours paid to the lady he had once chosen.

The Captain, tipsy, returned the clasp with all the strength of a palm made shaky by constant lifting of tumblers. He looked hard at Pen, as if trying to focus him out of a double world, and cried, “Grecious Heavens, is it possible? Me dear boy, me dear fellow, me dear friend!” Then, with a look of muddled curiosity, he fairly broke down: “I know your face, me dear dear friend, but, bedad, I’ve forgot your name.”

Five years of constant punch had passed since Pen and Costigan met; Arthur was changed, and when a man at that actual moment sees things double, we can pardon his past being muzzy.

Pen laughed, though perhaps a little mortified. “Don’t you remember me, Captain? I am Pendennis—Arthur Pendennis, of Chatteris.”

The sound of the young man’s voice steadied the old remembrance as a spoon steadies a spinning cup. “Pendennis!” cried Costigan, and now the floodgates opened. Pen was his dearest boy, his gallant young friend, his noble collagian, held in his inmost heart ever since they had parted. How was his fawther—no, his mother—and his guardian, the General, the Major? “I preshoom, from your apparance, you’ve come into your prawpertee; and, bedad, yee’ll spend it like a man of spirit—I’ll go bail for that. No? not yet come into your estete? If ye want any thrifle, heark ye, there’s poor old Jack Costigan has got a guinea or two in his pocket—and, be heavens! you shall never want, Awthur, me dear boy. What’ll ye have? John, come hither, and look aloive; give this gentleman a glass of punch, and I’ll pay for’t.—Your friend? I’ve seen him before. Permit me to have the honour of making meself known to ye, sir, and requesting ye’ll take a glass of punch.”

“I don’t envy Sir Charles Mirabel his father-in-law,” thought Pen; for Costigan’s affection, like his punch, came in quantities that might drown discretion. Aloud, he asked after another old friend. “And how is my old friend, Mr. Bows, Captain? Have you any news of him, and do you see him still?”

“No doubt he’s very well,” said Costigan, jingling his money and whistling “The Little Doodeen,” for which ditty he was celebrated at the Fielding’s Head. Then, with that treacherous loop of his memory, he blinked and said, “Me dear boy—I’ve forgot your name again—but my name’s Costigan, Jack Costigan, and I’d loike ye to take as many tumblers of punch in my name as ever ye loike. Ye know my name; I’m not ashamed of it.” And he maundered on, proud as a drunken rooster.

“It’s pay-day with the General,” said Mr. Hodgen, the bass singer, to whom Warrington was listening; “and he’s a precious deal more than half seas over. He’s already tried that ‘Little Doodeen’ of his, and broke it, too, just before I sang ‘King Death.’ Have you heard my new song, ‘The Body Snatcher,’ Mr. Warrington?—angcored at Saint Bartholomew’s the other night—composed expressly for me. Per’aps you or your friend would like a copy of the song, sir? John, just ’ave the kyndness to ’and over a ‘Body Snatcher’ ’ere, will yer?—There’s a portrait of me, sir, as I sing it—as the Snatcher—considered rather like.”

“Thank you,” said Warrington. “Heard it nine times—know it by heart, Hodgen.”

At this moment the gentleman at the pianoforte began to play, and Pen, turning toward the sound, beheld the very Mr. Bows for whom he had been inquiring, and whose existence Costigan had mislaid. There sat the little old man before the battered piano—an instrument that had injured its constitution by sitting up so many nights, and now spoke in a voice at once hoarse and faint, like a kettle that has boiled too often and been scoured too little. Bows accompanied the singers, or played with taste and grace between songs, coaxing music out of that weary box as a frugal housewife coaxes flavour from bones.

Bows had seen and remembered Pen the moment he entered, and had marked the young man’s eager warmth toward Costigan. Now he played an air Pen instantly knew—one sung by the village chorus in The Stranger, just before Mrs. Haller came in. The tune struck Pen like a remembered smell: dusty boards, lamp-oil, cheap oranges, and a heart beating too fast for a boy’s ribs. Nobody else heeded Bows’s playing; the air was scarcely heard amid the clatter of knives and forks, calls for poached eggs and kidneys, the tramp of guests and waiters, the hiss of ale drawn, the scrape of pewter. In that room, music had to fight not only tobacco-smoke but the whole harsh orchestra of appetite.

Pen went up and shook the player’s hand at the end, kindly. Bows greeted him with respectful cordiality. “What, you haven’t forgot the old tune, Mr. Pendennis?” he said. “I thought you’d remember it. I take it, it was the first tune of that sort you ever heard played—wasn’t it, sir? You were quite a young chap then. I fear the Captain’s very bad to-night. He breaks out on a pay-day; and I shall have the deuce’s own trouble in getting home. We live together. We still hang on, sir, in partnership, though Miss Em—though my lady Mirabel has left the firm.—And so you remember old times, do you? Wasn’t she a beauty, sir?—Your health and my service to you,”—and he took a sip from the pewter measure of porter at his side, as naturally as another man might wet a finger to turn a page.

Pen, after this, had many opportunities of seeing the old musician again, and renewing acquaintance with Costigan; for London is wide, but it is stitched together by certain tables and certain tunes, and a man may wander the whole town and still come back to the same battered piano.

As Pen and Bows sat thus in friendly colloquy, men of all sorts drifted in and out of the Back Kitchen: healthy country tradesmen and farmers in London on business, refreshing themselves with song and supper; squads of young apprentices and assistants, the shutters closed over their day’s labour, coming for “fresh air,” which they took chiefly through pipes; rakish young medical students, loudly dressed and (must it be owned) somewhat dirty, applauding with vociferous hands; young university bucks with that genteel simper learned at Alma Mater’s knees; handsome young guardsmen; florid clubmen from St. James’s Street; nay, senators English and Irish; and even members of the House of Peers—who, after all, must eat and drink like the rest of us, though they may pretend their appetites are hereditary.

Mr. Hodgen had made an immense hit with “The Body Snatcher,” and the town rushed to hear it, as the town rushes to any noise that promises a thrill. The curtain drew aside; Hodgen appeared as the Snatcher, seated on a coffin, a flask of gin before him, a spade at hand, and a candle stuck in a skull. The song was sung with an admirable terrific humour: his voice went down so low it seemed to rumble under the floorboards into the listener’s soul; and in the chorus he clamped with his spade and gave a demoniac “Ha! ha!” that made the glasses quiver on the tables, as if the sound itself had struck them. One could scarce tell whether the shiver came from fear or from that gross pleasure by which men pay themselves for imagining horrors at a safe distance. The louder the song, the better London liked it; the more it imitated a graveyard’s racket, the more the Back Kitchen rang with applause—so that you might have thought the city could not bear silence, nor let the dead lie quietly even in music.

None of the other singers, not even Cutts (as that high-minded man owned), could stand up before the Snatcher; Cutts commonly retired to Mrs. Cutts’s private apartments, or into the bar, before that fatal song extinguished him. Poor Cos’s ditty, “The Little Doodeen,” which Bows accompanied charmingly, was sung to but a few admirers who chose to remain after the tremendous resurrectionist chant. The room was commonly emptied after “The Body Snatcher,” or left to a small stubborn remnant of pleasure’s votaries, who sat over cooling plates and thinning punch, as if unwilling to let even the night’s last noise die out.

It was while Pen and Warrington sat there one night—or rather one morning—that two habitues entered almost together.

“Mr. Hoolan and Mr. Doolan,” whispered Warrington to Pen, saluting them; and in the latter Pen recognized the gentleman of the Alacrity coach, who had declined dining with Pen on that former day, being compelled, by professional duties, to decline dinner engagements on Fridays.

Doolan’s paper, the Dawn, lay on the table, much bestained by porter and pressed cheek-by-jowl with Hoolan’s journal, which we shall call the Day. The Dawn was Liberal; the Day ultra-Conservative. Many of our journals are officered by Irish gentlemen; and their gallant brigade does the penning among us as their ancestors did the fighting in Europe—engaging under many a flag, and being good friends again when the battle is over. In their mouths, even the same English word could mean a different insult, according to the paper that paid for it; and there are tones and turns of phrase—native dialect, half-suppressed, half-performed—that carry more power than any argument, because they tell you at once who commands the language and who must borrow it.

“Kidneys, John, and a glass of stout,” said Hoolan. “How are you, Morgan? how’s Mrs. Doolan?”

“Doing pretty well, thank ye, Mick, my boy—faith she’s accustomed to it,” said Doolan. “How’s the lady that owns ye? Maybe I’ll step down Sunday, and have a glass of punch, Kilburn way.”

“Don’t bring Patsey with you, Mick, for our Georgy’s got the measles,” said the friendly Morgan; and straightway, without ceremony, the two fell to talk of their trade: foreign mails, correspondents at Paris and Madrid, the expense of couriers, the circulation of rival sheets—news handled like meat in a market, weighed, wrapped, and shouted over.

Warrington, laughing, took up the Dawn and pointed to a leading article, beginning thus:

“As rogues of note in former days who had some wicked work to perform,—an enemy to be put out of the way, a quantity of false coin to be passed, a lie to be told or a murder to be done—employed a professional perjurer or assassin to do the work, which they were themselves too notorious or too cowardly to execute: our notorious contemporary, the Day, engages smashers out of doors to utter forgeries against individuals, and calls in auxiliary cut-throats to murder the reputation of those who offend him. A black-vizarded ruffian (whom we will unmask), who signs the forged name of Trefoil, is at present one of the chief bravoes and bullies in our contemporary’s establishment. He is the eunuch who brings the bowstring, and strangles at the order of the Day. We can convict this cowardly slave, and propose to do so. The charge which he has brought against Lord Bangbanagher, because he is a Liberal Irish peer, and against the Board of Poor Law Guardians of the Bangbanagher Union, is—”

“How did they like the article at your place, Mick?” asked Morgan. “When the Captain puts his hand to it he’s a tremendous hand at a smasher. He wrote the article in two hours—in—whew—you know where, while the boy was waiting.”

“Our governor thinks the public don’t mind a straw about these newspaper rows, and has told the Docthor to stop answering,” said the other. “Them two talked it out together in my room. The Docthor would have liked a turn, for he says it’s such easy writing, and requires no reading up of a subject: but the governor put a stopper on him.”

“The taste for eloquence is going out, Mick,” said Morgan.

“’Deed then it is, Morgan,” said Mick. “That was fine writing when the Docthor wrote in the Phaynix, and he and Condy Roony blazed away at each other day after day.”

“And with powder and shot, too, as well as paper,” said Morgan. “Faith, the Docthor was out twice, and Condy Roony winged his man.”

“They are talking about Doctor Boyne and Captain Shandon,” Warrington said to Pen, “the two Irish controversialists of the Dawn and the Day—Boyne the Protestant champion, Shandon the Liberal orator. Best friends in the world, I believe, in spite of their rows; and though they cry out against the English for abusing their country, by Jove they abuse it themselves more in a single article than we should take pains to do in a dozen volumes. How are you, Doolan?”

“Your servant, Mr. Warrington—Mr. Pendennis, I am delighted to have the honour of seeing ye again,” said Doolan; and instantly the man’s whole accent shifted, like a cook changing sauce for company. “The night’s journey on the top of the Alacrity was one of the most agreeable I ever enjoyed in my life, and it was your liveliness and urbanity that made the trip so charming. I have often thought over that happy night, sir, and talked over it to Mrs. Doolan. I have seen your elegant young friend, Mr. Foker, too, here, sir, not unfrequently. He is an occasional frequenter of this hostelry, and a right good one it is. Mr. Pendennis, when I saw you I was on the Tom and Jerry Weekly Paper; I have now the honour to be sub-editor of the Dawn, one of the best-written papers of the empire”—and he bowed very slightly to Mr. Warrington.

His speech was unctuous and measured, his courtesy almost oriental; and his tone, when talking to the two Englishmen, differed as much from his talk with his comrade as a parlour dish differs from a kitchen one. Yet the same man sat in the same room, with the same stout and kidneys before him, under the same din of knives and laughter and song; and Pen, watching him, could not but feel—though he might not have put it into words—that in London, as in Ireland, a man’s very language may be a livery he puts on, and that power often lies not in what is said, but in who is allowed to say it, and how.

Pen, in the very middle of his small, noisy pleasures—his chop from the cook-shop, his pint of porter that hissed as it was drawn, his nightly laughter that rang along Lamb Court and was answered by the thin clack of boots on Temple flags—felt all the while as if a knife hung by a thread above his plate.

It was not a poetic knife either, hung in some antique legend over a king’s banquet. It was a plain, London knife: blunt from too much carving of other people’s joints, and certain, sooner or later, to come down upon his own.

His money was going. Not in a grand catastrophe, but in the most humiliating manner—by subscriptions, by tips he could not help giving, by little civilities to beggars whose children looked as if they had never heard a wholesome kitchen sound in their lives, and by those fatal cabs that rattle you into extravagance as surely as a drum encourages marching. He had furnished his little bedroom with the grave air of a young nobleman establishing himself—bed, table, a few proud conveniences. He had still his gold chain and his dressing-case that smelt faintly of past gentilities; and now, at last, he had come down to one solitary five-pound note, lying in his pocket-book like the last slice of cold beef at the bottom of a dish: respectable, melancholy, and already imagined as gone.

Warrington, for his part, had never asked, and could not guess. An only son, a mother somewhere in the country, an uncle who dined daily with a great man and had the air of knowing the whole bill of fare of the kingdom—why should not Pen have a private larder of bank-notes, and a cellar of sovereigns, for anything the other knew? Pen had the look of a man whose boots might be brushed by fate itself. Not that he was an epicure in the vulgar meaning: he could attack a plate of beef from the cook’s shop with a gratitude as honest as a ploughman’s, and set to with the relish of a healthy youth. But he had never been trained to those penny-wise domestic arts by which men keep a dinner safe for to-morrow. He could not do the delicate arithmetic of refusing twopence to a waiter; he could not walk when it rained; and when he did take a cab, the jingling, splashing, wheel-grinding thing had him at its mercy, and he overpaid it as naturally as he breathed. He had a kind of disdain for cleaned gloves—those little economies which smell of soap and self-denial. And if a poor devil with a sorrowful tale came whining at him, or two children with faces as pale as flour offered for sale in a cellar, Pen’s hand went into his pocket as if his fingers had been born to do it.

Perhaps it was generosity; perhaps vanity; perhaps merely that he could not bear to be thought stingy by cabmen and waiters, those harsh critics who can praise you with a “Thank ye, sir” more intoxicating than claret. Who knows? We are all cooks of our own motives, and the dish we boast of most may be found, on examination, flavoured with the cheapest spice.

At length Pen, seated with Warrington, fell into a stare at that last note’s change upon the public-house tray—those small coins clinking like a warning bell among the pewter and stale beer-scent.

“It is the last rose of summer,” Pen said, with a tragical countenance, as if he were about to be buried with military honours; and then, in a rush—because there is a relief in getting the confession over, like gulping a bitter draught—he told Warrington the whole story: his mother’s narrow means, his own old follies, Laura’s generosity.

Warrington smoked and listened without interrupting, the pipe making a steady domestic sound in the pauses—puff, draw, tap—like a kitchen clock that will not stop for anybody’s romance.

When Pen had done, Warrington knocked the ashes out with the composure of a man who has seen many dinners end.

“Impecuniosity will do you good,” he said. “For an honest man—mind you. For rogues it’s like water to a duck. But for a man who means to keep his hands clean, there is nothing so wholesome as being in a state of tick. It’s an alterative and a tonic. It braces you, as when you’re riding at a fence and must take it, or when a man’s single-stick is up before you and you must meet it. Necessity brings out the pluck, if there’s any in you. You’ll discover how many things you can do without when you’ve no money to buy them. New gloves, varnished boots, eau de Cologne, cabs—poof! You’ve been nursed like a molly-coddle, Pen; spoilt by the women. A single man with health and brains who can’t find a livelihood doesn’t deserve to stay in the world. Let him pay his last halfpenny and jump over Waterloo Bridge. Or let him steal a leg of mutton, get transported, and at least have the decency to quit the country. Dixi. I have spoken. Give us another pull at the pale ale.”

“You have spoken enough for three pamphlets,” Pen said. “But how is one to live? Beef and bread are plentiful in England, but you must pay for them with work or money. Who will take my work? What work can I do?”

Warrington laughed. “We’ll advertise in the Times for an usher’s place at a classical and commercial academy. ‘A gentleman, B.A. of St. Boniface College, and plucked for his degree—’”

“Confound you,” cried Pen.

“‘—wishes to give lessons in classics and mathematics, and the rudiments of the French language; he can cut hair, attend to the younger pupils, and play a second on the piano with the daughters of the principal. Address A. P., Lamb Court, Temple.’”

“Go on,” Pen said, growling, though his mouth twitched.

“Men take to all sorts of trades. Bloundell-Bloundell is a professional blackleg, and lives on young gentlemen as other men live on mutton. Bob O’Toole drives the Ballynafad mail, and carries honest Jack Finucane’s letters. I knew a doctor’s son—don’t look savage, I meant nothing—who came to his last five-pound note, let his moustachios grow, went down to a provincial town, and set up as Professor Spineto, chiropodist to the Emperor of All the Russians. By a happy operation on the editor of the local paper he established himself in practice, lived three years, and is now reconciled, and has succeeded to his father’s gallypots.”

“Hang gallypots!” Pen cried. “I can’t drive a coach, cut corns, or cheat at cards. Is that all your wisdom?”

“No,” Warrington said. “There’s our own correspondent. Every man has his secrets, look you. Before this confession, with your airs and look, any one would suppose you had a bank behind you as long as the Strand. But with what you tell me of your mother’s income, you must not touch it. You can’t go on spunging on the women. You must pay off that trump of a girl—Laura, is it? Here’s your health, Laura!—and carry a hod sooner than ask for a shilling from home.”

“But how earn one?” Pen persisted.

“How do I live?” Warrington asked, and for a moment the jest fell away from him like smoke blown aside by a wind. “On my younger brother’s allowance, do you think? I made away with that five years ago. If I had made away with myself a little sooner, it might have been better.” He said it lightly, but his face did not consent to the lightness. “I’ve played off my own bat ever since. I don’t want much. When my purse is empty, I work and fill it; and then I lie idle like a serpent or an Indian till I’ve digested the mass.” He held out a long, lean purse with a few sovereigns huddled at one end like last potatoes in a sack. “Look. I begin to feel empty.”

“But how do you fill it?” Pen asked.

“I write,” Warrington said; and, absurdly, blushed as if he had confessed to stealing. “I don’t proclaim it. Perhaps I’m an ass and don’t want it said that George Warrington writes for bread. But I do. I write in the Law Reviews—here, these are mine.” He turned over some sheets. The pages had that sober look which suggests ink that smells of midnight, and thoughts boiled down as carefully as stock. “And now and then I do a bit for a newspaper—an editor’s friend. Come to the club.”

They went; and Warrington called for a file of the Dawn, and, with no speech, touched two articles with his finger. Pen read, and his spirits rose as if he had tasted something strong after thin fare: the sense, the satire, the scholarship, the curt, clean strokes—like a knife that knows its trade.

“I’m not up to this,” Pen said honestly. “I know very little of politics or history. I’ve only a smattering. I can’t fly on such a wing as yours.”

“But you can on your own,” Warrington said, good-humouredly. “Lighter wings sometimes go higher. Those little scraps and verses you’ve shown me—there’s a natural gift in them. Rare enough. Don’t blush, you conceited young jackanapes. You’ve thought so yourself any time these ten years. You’ve got the sacred flame—a little real poetical fire. All our oil-lamps are nothing to it, though ever so well trimmed. You are a poet, Pen, my boy.” And he clapped him on the shoulder with a hand that might have flattened a joint of meat.

Arthur was so pleased that his eyes smarted. “How kind you are,” he said.

“I like you,” Warrington answered. “I was devilish lonely in chambers. Wanted somebody. The sight of your honest face pleased me somehow. I liked the way you laughed at Lowton—that poor good little snob. And—well, I don’t know why—so it is. I’m alone in the world, sir; and I wanted some one to keep me company.” There was a quick kindness and a melancholy in his dark eyes that would have been understood by any man who had ever listened to an empty room after a door shuts.

Pen, however, was too full of his own delicious vanity to notice. “Thank you,” he said; “and—what you say about me. I have often thought I was a poet. I will be one—if the world won’t, I will. Is it the Ariadne in Naxos you liked? I was only eighteen. Or the Prize Poem?”

Warrington broke into a roar. “Why, you young goose! Of all the weak rubbish I ever tried, Ariadne in Naxos is the most mawkish and disgusting. And the Prize Poem is so pompous and feeble that I’m surprised it didn’t get the medal. You don’t suppose you’re going to cut out Milton and Æschylus? Setting up for Pindar, you absurd little tom-tit, and fancying you’ve the Theban eagle’s pinion? No. I think you can write a magazine article and turn a pretty copy of verses. That’s what I think.”

“By Jove!” Pen cried, bouncing up, his pride as quick as a match. “I’ll show you I’m a better man than you think!”

Warrington only laughed the more, and answered with twenty-four puffs out of his pipe—rapid, dry, provoking as a boy drumming on a table.

An occasion for Pen’s trial came sooner than he expected.

Mr. Bacon, that eminent publisher of Paternoster Row—formerly Bacon and Bungay—proprietor of the legal Review where Warrington laboured, and of other grave periodicals that smelt of paste and authority, had also a yearly gaudy blossom: a gilt volume called the Spring Annual, edited by the Lady Violet Lebas, and stuffed with fashionable verse. In it young lords first lisped their rhymes; honourable gentlemen practised chivalry on paper; Eastern “Ghazuls” blossomed like forced fruit; and the whole book, like many vernal blossoms, has since perished out of the world, though it was born in gold.

It was illustrated with prints of reigning beauties and tender subjects, prepared long in advance—because engraving, like pickling, takes its own time; so it was not the painter who illustrated the poet, but the poet who was ordered to garnish the plate, as a cook is handed some absurd mould and told to make a dinner look handsome in it.

Just when the Annual was on the eve of publication, Warrington went to Paternoster Row to see Mr. Hack—Bacon’s reader and manager, a professional gentleman employed because Mr. Bacon had the good sense to know he had no taste. Warrington found Hack with proof-plates and sheets spread before him, and glanced at them.

One plate was called The Church Porch. A Spanish damsel, prayer-book in hand, hurried to church; a youth in a cloak lurked in a niche, watching her. The picture had a pretty sentiment. Unfortunately, the verses supplied by the Honourable Percy Popjoy were of that peculiar kind which can only be written by a young nobleman who has never been refused anything—not even praise.

Warrington laughed aloud as he read. Hack laughed too, but with the face of a man hearing the cook announce that the joint is burnt and the company already seated.

“It won’t do,” Hack said. “The public won’t stand it. Bungay’s people are bringing out a very good book and have set up Miss Bunyan against Lady Violet. We’ve the names, to be sure—but the stuff is too bad. Lady Violet herself owns it. She’s busy with her own poem. What’s to be done? We can’t lose the plate. The governor gave sixty pounds for it.”

“I know a fellow who’ll do the verses,” Warrington said. “Give me the plate; I’ll take it home in my pocket. Send to my chambers in the morning.”

“You’ll pay well, of course,” he added.

“Of course,” said Hack, with a sigh of relief; and Warrington, pocketing the Church Porch as coolly as if it were a handkerchief, went back to the Temple.

He flung the plate before Pen.

“Now, boy. Here’s a chance. Turn me off a copy of verses to this.”

Pen looked. “A Church Porch. A lady going in, and a youth out of—what?—a wine-shop window ogling her. What the deuce am I to do with it?”

“Try,” said Warrington. “Earn your livelihood for once, you who long so to do it.”

Pen set his jaw, as if he had been given a tough bit of meat and was resolved to make something of it. “Well. I will try.”

“And I’ll go out to dinner,” Warrington said, and left him.

Pen sat alone. The Temple had its own soundscape: distant wheels grinding on Fleet Street; clerks’ voices thinning away; a bell somewhere counting the hour; then quieter, the whisper of paper, the scratch of a pen, and the private little groan a man makes when he cannot find the right word. Outside, London never stopped humming—an iron, commercial hum—yet in that room Pen tried to listen for another music: the remembered toll of a minster bell above a city’s rout, the hush of a porch, the soft footfall of a girl with downcast eyes. He had never been to Spain; he had, however, been to supper, which is sometimes more instructive.

Warrington came home late. The air he brought in with him was full of tavern warmth and street damp; the candles smelt a little of grease; and Pen, pale and triumphant, pushed the pages over as if offering a dish that had taken him hours to reduce and season.

“There they are,” he said. “I’ve screwed ’em out at last. I think they’ll do.”

Warrington read; and as he went on, the mockery in his face subsided into a professional approval, the way a stern man nods at a well-made loaf. When he finished, he said, simply, “I think they will.”

Pen’s verses ran thus:

Although I enter not,  
Yet round about the spot  
Sometimes I hover,  
And at the sacred gate,  
With longing eyes I wait,  
Expectant of her.

The Minster bell tolls out  
Above the city’s rout  
And noise and humming  
They’ve stopp’d the chiming bell,  
I hear the organ’s swell  
She’s coming, she’s coming!

My lady comes at last,  
Timid and stepping fast,  
And hastening hither,  
With modest eyes downcast.  
She comes—she’s here—she’s past.  
May Heaven go with her!

Kneel undisturb’d, fair saint,  
Pour out your praise or plaint  
Meekly and duly.  
I will not enter there,  
To sully your pure prayer  
With thoughts unruly.

But suffer me to pace  
Round the forbidden place,  
Lingering a minute,  
Like outcast spirits, who wait  
And see through Heaven’s gate  
Angels within it.

“Have you any more?” Warrington asked. “We must make them give you a couple of guineas a page. If the stuff’s liked, you’ll get an entrée into Bacon’s magazines, and may turn a decent penny.”

Pen rummaged in his portfolio and found another ballad—one of those pieces that had been lying like a dried herb, waiting for boiling water. He thought it might do for the Annual too. Then, with Warrington as ambassador and agent, they walked from the Temple to Paternoster Row.

Bacon’s shop stood there, ancient and low-browed, with a few books displayed under a bust of my Lord of Verulam; the brass name on the private door had the polished air of prosperity. Opposite, Bungay’s house showed off in fresh paint and an elaborate seventeenth-century style, as if Mr. Pepys might step in to sniff at the bindings and note down the prices. The Row itself had its own peculiar chorus: the faint toll from Saint Paul’s overhead; the murmur of trade; the rustle of paper; the ding of a shop bell; the constant small shuffling of messengers—printer’s boys and men with parcels—each footstep part of the enormous machinery that grinds thought into print.

Warrington went in. Pen stayed out, pacing like a man waiting for a tooth to be pulled. He looked into the windows as if they were the consoling books on the dentist’s table. Here were black-letter volumes; there the pale neat types of Aldus and Elzevir. Next, the Penny Horrific Register, Halfpenny Annals of Crime, histories of celebrated murderers; Raff’s Magazine; The Larky Swell—ink boiled to a cheap, acrid broth for the multitude. In the next window stern portraits of dissenting divines stared out, with fac-similes of reverend signatures and sermons for mental pabulum. Hard by was a little casement hung with rosaries, medals, paltry prints of saints gilt and painted, and penny controversial books for faithful distribution; and close beside that, a sermon called Come out of Rome, preached at the opening of Shepherd’s Bush College by John Thomas, Lord Bishop of Ealing. Scarce an opinion but had its stall and its cry there, each with its own vocabulary—dominant words elbowing lesser dialects, each trying to drown the other out in print, while the bells of Saint Paul tolled on, indifferent and ancient.

Pen walked, waited, listened to the iron city-noise, and fancied he could hear, through it all, the tender hush he had written—minster bell, organ swell—like a remembered flavour in a room that smells of coal.

Warrington was long inside; he was pleading, bargaining, playing upon the small vanities and large appetites that govern publishers. Pen did not hear the speech—worse luck for his modesty—but it was delivered.

It happened that Mr. Bacon himself came downstairs into Mr. Hack’s room while Warrington was there. Warrington, knowing Bacon’s weaknesses, served up his friend as deftly as a cook humours a capricious palate. He put on his hat to address Bacon, seated himself on the table with the comfortable insolence of a gentleman, and spoke as if doing Bacon a favour by permitting him to buy genius.

“What! not know Mr. Pendennis, Mr. Bacon?” Warrington said. “You can’t live much in the world, or you would know him. A man of property in the West, of one of the most ancient families in England, related to half the nobility in the empire—cousin to Lord Pontypool—one of the most distinguished men at Oxbridge; dines at Gaunt House every week.”

“Law bless me,” said Mr. Bacon, swelling like a man who feels he is entertaining quality without having paid for it. “You don’t say so, sir. Well—really—Law bless me now.”

“I’ve just shown Mr. Hack some verses he sat up last night to write at my request; and Hack talks of paying him with a copy of the—what-d’-you-call-’em.”

“Law bless me now, does he? The what-d’-you-call-’em. Indeed!”

“‘The Spring Annual,’” Warrington snapped. “As payment. You don’t suppose such a man as Mr. Arthur Pendennis gives up a dinner at Gaunt House for nothing? The men of fashion want to be paid.”

“That they do, Mr. Warrington, sir,” Bacon said, with an approving groan.

“He’s a star,” Warrington continued. “He’ll make a name. He’s a new man.”

“They’ve said that of so many of those young swells,” Bacon sighed. “Lord Viscount Dodo now—I gave his lordship a good bit of money, and only sold eighty copies. Popjoy’s Hadgincourt fell dead.”

“Well then,” Warrington said, rising as if the whole conversation were beneath him, “I’ll take my man over to Bungay.”

The threat was like a knife at Bacon’s throat. He gave in at once; asked Hack, in a hurry, what the terms were; and when he heard it was only two ballads for the Annual, he cried, “Law bless you, give him a check directly.”

With this precious paper Warrington emerged at last, and put it into Pen’s hand with a grin.

Pen stared at it as if it were a hot pie placed before a starving man. He was elated as though someone had left him a fortune. The street seemed brighter; the bells friendlier; even the carts’ rattling less insulting.

He offered Warrington a dinner at Richmond on the spot. “And what shall I buy for Laura? For my mother? I must buy something.”

“They’ll like the book better than any trinket,” Warrington said. “With the young one’s name among the swells.”

“Thank God! thank God!” Pen cried. “I needn’t be a charge on the old mother. I can pay off Laura now. I can get my own living. I can make my own way.”

“I can marry the Grand Vizier’s daughter,” Warrington said dryly. “I can purchase a house in Belgrave Square. I can build a fine castle in the air! Well, you may get bread and cheese, Pen; and I own it tastes well—the bread you earn yourself.”

At dinner in the club that day Pen insisted on a magnum of claret—an extravagance he had not seen for many a day. Warrington would not baulk him. The cork came out with a report like a small gun; the wine smelt of dark fruit and old wood, like a memory of country dinners in rooms that did not echo with borrowed laughter; and they drank to the health of the Spring Annual as if it were a living benefactor.

And, because Fortune likes to make a joke of her own—first starving you, then flinging loaves at your head—another chance came quickly.

One day Warrington tossed a letter across the table. It had been brought by a printer’s boy—one of those small emissaries who carry other men’s hopes under their arm, and lie down to sleep in passages as if they were part of the furniture. The boy announced it “from Captain Shandon, sir,” and then, having done his duty, curled himself on Warrington’s accustomed bench outside, where his subsequent visits would become as regular as the knocking of type.

The letter ran:

F. P. Tuesday Morning.

“MY DEAR SIR,—Bungay will be here to-day, about the Pall Mall Gazette. You would be the very man to help us with a genuine West-end article,—you understand—dashing, trenchant, and d—— aristocratic. Lady Hipshaw will write; but she’s not much you know, and we’ve two lords; but the less they do the better. We must have you. We’ll give you your own terms, and we’ll make a hit with the Gazette.

“Shall B. come and see you, or can you look in upon me here?—Ever yours,

“C. S.”

Captain Shandon, being for the present lodged at Her Majesty’s expense within those brick bowels near Ludgate Hill where the air tastes faintly of wet rope and yesterday’s porter, announced—through a prospectus written with such a crack of the whip in every line—that the hour had struck for the Gentlemen of England to shoulder their rights like ancestral hams and defend the whole pantry of the Constitution from hungry new doctrines.

Foreign revolutions, he declared, were boiling up like a foreign soup of suspicious colour. Intestine radicalism (a phrase with a medical sound, as if the nation had eaten unripe fruit) was grumbling below decks. Mill-owners and cotton-lords were slandering the aristocratic roast, and the masses—those same masses whom, with a perfectly straight face, he accused the Gentlemen of having “gulled and led”—were, in his picture, a kind of perpetual, ill-trained dinner-party that would overturn the table the moment the footman looked away.

“The ancient monarchy,” he wrote and now read aloud with a theatrical toss of paper, “is insulted by a ferocious republican rabble. The Church is deserted by envious dissent, undermined by stealthy infidelity. The good institutions which made our country glorious, and the name of English Gentleman the proudest in the world, are left without defence—”

And here the Captain, as if carving a joint, laid down the knife-edge of one clause and took up the next with a flourish.

“It was because the kings of France mistrusted their gentlemen,” Mr. Shandon went on, “that the monarchy of Saint Louis went down: it was because the people of England still believed in their gentlemen that this country encountered and overcame the greatest enemy a nation ever met: it was because we were headed by gentlemen that the Eagles retreated before us from the Donro to the Garonne: it was a gentleman who broke the line at Trafalgar, and swept the plain of Waterloo.”

Mr. Bungay, the publisher—who sat planted like a dumpling in a chair too small for him, his stick upright between his knees—nodded in the knowing rhythm of a man who hears “Waterloo” as other men hear “pudding.” He even winked at that name, as if Wellington were a private joke between tradesmen. Mr. Warrington, who had been leaning back with that air of lazy judgment he cultivated as carefully as a moustache, burst out laughing.

“You see how our venerable friend Bungay is affected,” Shandon said, looking up slyly from his sheet. “That’s your true sort of test. I have used the Duke of Wellington and the battle of Waterloo a hundred times, and I never knew the Duke to fail.”

He proceeded—modest as a man can be while declaring war upon half the kingdom—to confess that gentlemen had hitherto left their political interests, like their estates and lawsuits, to paid persons; and that the day for such delegation was over. Gentlemen must become their own champions; their enemies were brave, numerous, uncompromising; and, above all, they must not be represented in the press by hireling advocates.

“They must not have Grub Street publishing Gazettes from Whitehall—” he cried, with a side glance. “That’s a dig at Bacon’s people, Mr. Bungay.”
