Bungay clapped his stick on the floor as if it were a mallet bringing down the price of pork. “Hang him—pitch into him, Capting!” he said, beaming; and then, turning his heavy head to Warrington, wagged it with solemn relish. “For a slashing article, sir, there’s nobody like the Capting—no-obody like him.”

Some gentlemen, Shandon announced next—names withheld for reasons too “obvious” to be printed—had determined to bring out a journal of impregnable principles.

At “obvious reasons,” Warrington began to laugh again; and the Captain, enjoying the laugh as a cook enjoys the hiss when his pan hits the fire, flourished his paper.

“These men are proud of their order, anxious to uphold it. They are loyal to their Sovereign by faithful conviction and ancestral allegiance; they love their Church, where they would have their children worship, and for which their forefathers bled; they love their country, and would keep it what the gentlemen of England—yes, the gentlemen of England,” he insisted, turning upon Bungay with the familiarity of a man ordering a compositor, “we’ll have that in large caps, Bungay, my boy—have made it—the greatest and freest in the world: and as the names of some of them are appended to the deed which secured our liberties at Runnymede—”

“What’s that?” asked Bungay, who could smell printer’s ink at a mile but would have mistaken Magna Charta for a new brand of cheese.

“An ancestor of mine sealed it with his sword-hilt,” Pen said gravely, while the little girl—Mary Shandon—stood staring at these men as if they were all performing tricks.

“It’s the Habeas Corpus, Mr. Bungay,” Warrington said.

“All right, I dare say,” Bungay yawned, and, as if history were a long sermon, added: “Go on, Capting.”

“—at Runnymede; they are ready to defend that freedom to-day with sword and pen, and now, as then, to rally round the old laws and liberties of England.”

“Bravo!” cried Warrington.

The child, not understanding England or Runnymede, understood hands and faces. Warrington beckoned her with a large paw of a hand and patted her curls; but she shrank as if his touch were too rough a towel. She sidled away, climbed up on Pen’s knee, and began to play gravely with his watch-chain, as if its cool links had more sense than all this patriotic thunder. Pen—who had a soft heart that he tried to cover with a shy pompousness, like a tender dish concealed beneath a too-loud garnish—was pleased by her preference.

“You were laughing,” Shandon said to Warrington, enjoying his own phrase again. “About the ‘obvious reasons.’ Now I’ll show ye what they are, ye unbelieving heathen.”

And he read on, offering the audience a vision of invisible grandees and secret wires, of “influential friends in both Houses of the Senate,” allies in “every diplomatic circle in Europe,” and sources of intelligence so exquisitely confidential that no other journal—no other journal!—could possibly acquire them.

But while his words were all high corridors and velvet doors, the place they were spoken in had its own loud, uninvited commentary: the scrape of prison shoes in the passage; a distant cough; the clink of a tin mug; a hoarse laugh from some unseen room; a key turning somewhere with the finality of a guillotine. The very building kept time with his rhetoric, a kind of acoustic reminder that “gentlemen” here were measured by bolts and bars.

Nevertheless, Shandon did not miss a syllable of his music.

“The very earliest information connected with the movement of English and Continental politics,” he declaimed, “will be found only in the columns of the Pall Mall Gazette. The Statesman and the Capitalist, the Country Gentleman and the Divine, will be amongst our readers, because our writers are amongst them. We address ourselves to the higher circles of society: we care not to disown it—the Pall Mall Gazette is written by gentlemen for gentlemen; its conductors speak to the classes in which they live and were born. The field-preacher has his journal; the radical free-thinker has his journal: why should the Gentlemen of England be unrepresented in the Press?”

He then, with much modesty (the kind that manages to praise itself without seeming to look), sketched the literary and fashionable departments of the paper, to be conducted by gentlemen of acknowledged reputation—men famous at the Universities, known at the Clubs, and intimate with the very Society they would describe.

At “famous at the Universities,” Pen could not help laughing and blushing; the phrase struck him like a spoon tapped on a glass, calling attention to him in a room of strangers.

Shandon turned, as delicately as a cook suggesting sauce, to the advertisers: there would be no medium like the Pall Mall Gazette for giving publicity to their sales. He called upon the nobility, the baronetage, the revered clergy, the bar, the matrons, the daughters, the homes and hearths of England to rally. Bungay, who had fallen into a second snooze during these rolling appeals, woke at the conclusion and pronounced it all right.

Then came the practical talk—the politics, the management, the habits of the journal—where Bungay sat nodding, his approvals ready-made and indiscriminate. His opinions were plain as boiled potatoes. He wanted Bacon’s opposition house smashed; he believed Shandon could smash it. If the Captain had copied out the Church Catechism or written Junius on a sheet, Bungay would have smacked his lips at the “slashing article” all the same. He pocketed the papers with the satisfaction of a man securing a pie; and having paid for the manuscript, he called little Mary and gave her a penny as he went away—an action that sat oddly beside all the talk of ancient liberties, and yet somehow was the only coin in the room that looked like actual kindness.

With the prospectus read and pocketed, Shandon grew jaunty, putting on that second-hand fashionable air he wore in compliment to his guests, as if his tattered dressing-gown were merely an eccentric morning wrapper in St. James’s. He spoke of the great world with easy familiarity and jocular allusions: he told anecdotes of great personages, private sayings, entertainments at which this or that occurred; and Pen was amused to hear this shabby prisoner, in slippers, talking glibly of the great of the land as if he had them all in his pocket next to Bungay’s note.

Mrs. Shandon sat quietly at her work, her needle going in and out like a patient little clock. She listened with fond admiration. The great Society was the right place for her Charles; he shone in it; he was respected in it. Indeed, once, an Earl of X had asked him to dinner; and she treasured the invitation-card in her workbox still, as if it were a relic and not merely pasteboard.

At last Bungay had enough of fashionable talk and rose to take leave. Warrington and Pen rose too, to depart with him, though Pen would gladly have stayed: the poor little household, for all its imprisonment and tatters, interested and touched him. He murmured something about hoping for leave to repeat his visit.

Shandon, with a rueful grin that showed his teeth like a man pretending at cheer over cold victuals, said he was always to be found at home, and would be delighted to see Mr. Pennington.

“I’ll see you to my park-gate, gentlemen,” said Captain Shandon, clapping on his hat in spite of a deprecatory look and a faint “Charles” from his wife.

And so, in shabby slippers, he shuffled out before them, leading the way through dismal passages where the very echoes sounded poor. As he took leave of the three gentlemen at the wicket, his hand was already fiddling with the waistcoat pocket where Bungay’s five-pound note lay—warm, new, and doomed. Pen, when he found himself again on the flags of Farringdon Street, drew a freer breath, as if the air outside—though full of carts and street cries—were cleaner than those locked-in sounds behind him.

Mrs. Shandon, left at the window that looked into the court, went on with her work. She saw her husband with a couple of men at his heels run rapidly in the direction of the prison tavern. She had hoped to have had him to dinner. There was a piece of meat—poor fare, but honestly meant—and some salad in a basin on the ledge outside the window, where the cool air could keep it a little while: she had expected she and little Mary would share it with the child’s father.

But there was no chance now. The tavern would have him until closing; then there would be cards or drink in some other man’s room; then he would come back silent, glazed-eyed, reeling a little, to be nursed by the woman who had been waiting with the meat and the salad.

She went to the cupboard and, in lieu of dinner, made herself some tea.

If there is a domestic sound more sorrowful than the soft settling of tea-leaves under boiling water, it has not yet been invented. The prison had its coarse clangours—keys, bolts, footsteps—yet in their room the gentler noises were the ones that pierced: the lid of the teapot set down; the faint clink of cup to saucer; the little sigh of steam; and beyond, always beyond, the tavern’s blurred murmur, as if drink itself had a voice that called men away from the table where they were needed.

So she and little Mary drank their tea together, while the Captain went out and took his pleasure. She cared for nothing else but that, when her husband was away—nothing, that is, except the child’s quiet presence and the hot cup between her hands.

It was during this small, pale meal that Mr. Jack Finucane—already slightly known to us, and a townsman of Captain Shandon’s—came in. Jack always brought a sweetmeat for little Mary in his pocket; and he produced it now with the importance of a diplomat producing a treaty.

Jack thought Shandon the greatest genius on earth. He had had one or two helps from the good-natured prodigal—always a kind word, sometimes a guinea for a friend in need—and he never missed a day of seeing his patron. He ran errands, transacted money-business with publishers and newspaper editors, duns, creditors, holders of Shandon’s acceptances, gentlemen disposed to speculate in those securities; and in short was aide-de-camp to an embarrassed Irish gentleman, as naturally as a shadow follows a man in sunlight.

And as sure as there is an embarrassed Irish gentleman, there is a little troop behind him: subordinates of subordinates, all in pecuniary discomfort, all ready to march at the heels of their chief and share in the rough fortunes of his day.

“He won’t have that five-pound note very long, I bet a guinea,” Bungay had remarked as he walked away with the two young men. And Bungay judged rightly. When Mrs. Shandon came, as was her habit, to empty her husband’s pockets, she found but a couple of shillings and a few halfpence out of the morning’s remittance.

The note had melted like butter in a hot pan. A pound had gone to one follower; a leg of mutton with potatoes and beer had been sent to an acquaintance on the poor side of the prison—charity, yes, but charity with a loud thirst behind it; an outstanding tavern bill had been paid where the note was changed; there had been dinner with two friends there; and then cards, with half-crowns slipping away one by one as if they too were eager to get out of his pocket. So the night left him as poor as the morning found him.

Meanwhile, outside, the publisher and the two gentlemen talked as they walked. Warrington, in a mood of mischievous advocacy, reiterated to Bungay what he had already said to Bacon: that Pen was a high fellow of great genius, and what was more, well with the great world, and related to “no end” of the peerage. Bungay replied that he should be happy to have dealings with Mr. Pendennis, and hoped to see both gents cutting mutton with him before long; and with mutual politeness and protestations, they parted.

That night, Pen, thinking over the day as one thinks over a dish whose flavour lingers and troubles—salt and sweet together—said, “It is hard to see such a man as Shandon, of accomplishments so multifarious, and of such undoubted talent and humour, an inmate of a gaol for half his time, and a bookseller’s hanger-on when out of prison.”

“I am a bookseller’s hanger-on—you are going to try your paces as a hack,” Warrington said, laughing. “We are all hacks upon some road or other. I would rather be myself than Paley our neighbour in chambers, who has as much enjoyment of his life as a mole. A deuced deal of undeserved compassion has been thrown away upon what you call your bookseller’s drudge.”

“Much solitary pipes and ale make a cynic of you,” Pen answered. “You are a Diogenes by a beer-barrel, Warrington. No man shall tell me that a man of genius, as Shandon is, ought to be driven by such a vulgar slave-driver as yonder Mr. Bungay, who fattens on the profits of the other’s brains, and enriches himself out of his journeyman’s labour. It makes me indignant to see a gentleman the serf of such a creature—a man who can’t speak the language he lives by, who is not fit to black Shandon’s boots.”

“So you have begun already to gird at the publishers, and to take your side amongst our order. Bravo, Pen, my boy!” Warrington said, laughing still. “What have you got to say against Bungay’s relations with Shandon? Was it the publisher who sent the author to prison? Is it Bungay who is tippling away the five-pound note we saw just now—or Shandon?”

“Misfortune drives a man into bad company,” Pen said. “It is easy to cry ‘Fie!’ against a poor fellow who has no society but such as he finds in a prison; and no resource except forgetfulness and the bottle. We must deal kindly with the eccentricities of genius, and remember that the very ardour and enthusiasm of temperament which makes the author delightful often leads the man astray.”

“A fiddlestick about men of genius!” Warrington cried, suddenly severe, though severity sat on him like a borrowed coat. “I deny there are so many geniuses as people who whimper about the fate of men of letters assert. There are thousands of clever fellows who could, if they would, turn verses, write articles, read books, deliver judgments. The talk of professional critics and writers isn’t a whit more brilliant than that of any educated society. If a lawyer, soldier, or parson outruns his income and does not pay his bills, he must go to gaol; and an author must go too. If an author fuddles himself, I don’t know why he should be let off a headache the next morning; if he orders a coat from a tailor, why he shouldn’t pay for it.”

“I would give him more money to buy coats,” Pen said, smiling in spite of himself. “I suppose I should like to belong to a well-dressed profession. I protest against that wretch of a middle-man whom I see between Genius and his great landlord, the Public, and who stops more than half the labourer’s earnings and fame.”

“I am a prose labourer,” Warrington said. “You, my boy, are a poet in a small way, and so consider you are authorised to be flighty. What is it you want? A body of capitalists forced to purchase the works of all authors who present themselves, manuscript in hand? Everybody who writes his epic, every driveller who can or can’t spell and produces his novel or tragedy—are they all to find a bag of sovereigns in exchange for worthless reams of paper? Who is to settle what is good or bad, saleable or otherwise? Will you give the buyer leave, in fine, to purchase or not?

“Why, sir, when Johnson sate behind the screen at Saint John’s Gate and took his dinner apart because he was too shabby and poor to join the literary bigwigs round Mr. Cave’s best table-cloth, the tradesman was doing him no wrong. You couldn’t force the publisher to recognise genius in the young man who presented himself, ragged, gaunt, hungry. Rags are not proof of genius; whereas capital is absolute, as times go, and perforce the bargain-master. It has a right to deal with the literary inventor as with any other. If I produce a novelty in the book trade, I must do the best I can with it; but I can no more force Mr. Murray to purchase my book of travels or sermons than I can compel Mr. Tattersall to give me a hundred guineas for my horse. I may have my own ideas of the value of my Pegasus and think him the most wonderful of animals; but the dealer has a right to his opinion too, and may want a lady’s horse, or a cob for a heavy timid rider, or a sound hack for the road, and my beast won’t suit him.”

“You deal in metaphors, Warrington,” Pen said; “but you rightly say you are very prosaic. Poor Shandon! There is something about the kindness of that man, and the gentleness of that sweet creature of a wife, which touches me profoundly. I like him, I am afraid, better than a better man.”

“And so do I,” Warrington said. “Let us give him the benefit of our sympathy, and the pity that is due to his weakness: though I fear that sort of kindness would be resented as contempt by a more high-minded man. You see he takes his consolation along with his misfortune, and one generates the other or balances it, as the way of the world. He is a prisoner, but he is not unhappy.”

“His genius sings within his prison bars,” Pen said.

“Yes,” Warrington replied bitterly, “Shandon accommodates himself to a cage pretty well. He ought to be wretched, but he has Jack and Tom to drink with, and that consoles him. He might have a high place, but as he can’t, he can drink with Tom and Jack. He might be providing for his wife and children, but Thomas and John have got a bottle of brandy which they want him to taste. He might pay poor Snip the tailor the twenty pounds the poor devil wants for his landlord, but John and Thomas lay their hands upon his purse. And so he drinks whilst his tradesman goes to gaol and his family to ruin. Let us pity the misfortunes of genius—and conspire against the publishing tyrants who oppress men of letters.”

“What! are you going to have another glass of brandy-and-water?” Pen asked, with a humorous look; for this philosophy was taking place at the Black Kitchen, where hot things were brought in glasses and moral sentences cooled on the tongue.

Warrington began to laugh as usual. “Video meliora proboque—I mean, bring it me hot, with sugar, John,” he said to the waiter.

“I would have some more too, only I don’t want it,” Pen said. “It does not seem to me, Warrington, that we are much better than our neighbours.”

Warrington despatched his last glass; and the pair returned to their chambers.

Two notes waited in the letter-box, sent by their morning acquaintance, Mr. Bungay. That hospitable gentleman presented his compliments to each, and requested the pleasure of their company at dinner on an early day, to meet a few literary friends.

“We shall have a grand spread, Warrington,” Pen said. “We shall meet all Bungay’s corps.”

“All except poor Shandon,” Warrington answered.

Pen nodded good-night and went into his own little room. The day’s new faces and odd acquaintance had excited him. He lay awake thinking, while from the neighbouring apartment Warrington’s vigorous, regular snore declared that he had made his peace with the world in the simplest dialect known to man.

Captain Shandon, being urged—gently, firmly, and with that quiet domestic omnipotence which belongs to wives who “never meddle”—had made one stipulation with the new Pall Mall Gazette: that John Finucane, Esquire, of the Upper Temple, should be named sub-editor. The spirited proprietor assented; for if gratitude can ever be entered in a publisher’s ledger without being immediately crossed out as “bad debt,” it was due here.

Finucane had earned every farthing of favour by services rendered in those old romantic days when Captain Shandon, hunted by bailiffs as a hare is by hounds, used to take refuge in Fin’s chambers. So often had the Captain been “not at home” there, that at last the sheriff’s officers grew social upon the staircase, calling as regularly at the Temple as at Shandon’s own door, as if Fin’s landing had been a club and they members.

And it was to Finucane’s rooms, too, that poor Mrs. Shandon came—slipping in with her veil down, as if modesty were a disguise and sorrow a crime—bringing her griefs, her stratagems, her little child; bringing, in short, the whole kitchen of misfortune, where there is always a pot boiling and never anything to put in it. Finucane would furnish meals there—honest, hot, consolatory things: a chop that hissed on the plate like a friendly rebuke to despair; bread whose very crust seemed to say, “Courage!”; and ale that made a small brave weather in the stomach. Little Mary, installed in her crib, would say her prayers at bedtime—“God bless papa”—and Finucane, though Romish, would add an “Amen” so feeling that it might have passed for a second petition.

On the evening before all our great events, however, Fin had an appointment with Mr. Bungay upon the affairs of the new paper—an appointment which was to be discussed, as such affairs always are, over a quiet dinner; quiet, that is, until the brandy-and-water begins to speak its mind. Fin went away from Mrs. Shandon at six, but next morning he appeared at the Fleet as punctual as the turnkey’s keys, arrayed in his best bravery: cheap splendours, loud as a drum, bright as a trumpet—ornaments that did not so much glitter as announce themselves. In his pocket he carried four pounds two shillings—his week’s salary from the Daily Journal, less two shillings that had melted away, like a sacrificial offering, in the purchase of a pair of gloves on the road to the prison.

The dinner had been at Dick’s Coffee-house, with Bungay and Mr. Trotter, Bungay’s reader and literary man of business. Finucane there “cut his mutton,” as Bungay called it; and it must be owned the mutton was cut with the air of a man carving destiny. He unfolded, with a pencil that flew like a swallow, the whole anatomy of the Pall Mall Gazette: the precise type for each kind of wisdom; who should chronicle the markets and weigh butter as solemnly as empire; who should attend the turf and ring and make vice look like sport; who should report Church intelligence with suitable gravity; and who should sift fashionable chit-chat like flour, leaving nothing but the finest, whitest nonsense for the public table.

He knew the weekly earnings of every man in the Press as a cook knows the price of every joint; he was up to a thousand economical contrivances by which a spirited capitalist might save money without appearing to do so; he set down figures that danced and coupled into totals before Bungay’s slow comprehension could seize them. Bungay, dazzled and mystified in equal parts, afterwards confided to Trotter that “that Irishman seemed a clever fellow.”

Having thus roasted Bungay in admiration and basted him with wonder, Finucane worked round to the dish nearest his heart: the liberation of Captain Shandon. He knew, to a shilling, the detainers at the porter’s lodge of the Fleet; he professed to know all Shandon’s debts—an impossible claim, for no man in England, certainly not the Captain himself, was acquainted with them. Fin represented, with a tenderness which might have softened a stone—and did soften something much harder, namely a publisher—that Shandon would work better out of confinement.

“Begging your pardon,” Bungay had said, with that stubborn common-sense which is the genius of dull men, “when the Captain’s locked up we are sure to find him at home; whereas, when he’s free, you can never catch hold of him.”

But Fin played his trumps: Mrs. Shandon pining in the prison; the child sickening there; the poor lady’s life, as it were, reduced to the prison’s daily gruel—thin, grey, and always ladled out at the wrong hour. Bungay, whose soul could be reached by a proper mixture of sentiment and spirits, promised that if Mrs. Shandon would come to him in the morning he would see what could be done. And when the reckoning came—Finucane, with four guineas in his pocket, longing to discharge it in a burst of gratitude—Bungay, warmed into magnificence, struck in: “No, sir,—this is my affair, sir, if you please. James, take the bill, and eighteenpence for yourself,” and thus paid, like a man who enjoys being virtuous on other people’s opportunities.

So Fin went to bed in the Temple that night with his week’s salary intact; and on Saturday morning at the Fleet, he gave Mrs. Shandon a wink so knowing and so jubilant that it was like the pop of a cork to a thirsty heart. She, good soul, guessed the bottle held hope, and hastened for bonnet and shawl when Fin begged the honour of walking her out for a breath of fresh air.

Little Mary jumped at the word “holiday.” Finucane never came empty-handed to that child: a toy, a ticket, a promise of some London marvel—all his pockets were lined with diversions, as if he carried a sweet-shop in one waistcoat and a theatre in the other. Mrs. Shandon hesitated, looking back to the Captain.

“May I go, Charley? or shall I stay with you, for you’re poorly, dear, this morning? He’s got a headache, Mr. Finucane. He suffers from headaches, and I persuaded him to stay in bed.”

“Go along with you, and Polly. Jack, take care of ’em. Hand me over Burton’s Anatomy, and leave me to my abominable devices,” Shandon said, with perfect good-humour; and indeed he lay there mining quotations—Greek and Latin ready-dressed for print—from that wonderful repertory of learning, as a cook might pluck herbs from a well-stocked shelf.

So Fin gave his arm to Mrs. Shandon. Mary skipped down the prison passages and out through the gate into the free air, which tasted, after the Fleet, like bread fresh from the oven. Fleet Street roared as it always does—wheels, cries, the metallic clack of commerce. Yet even that din, common as a kettle’s boil to Londoners, struck Mrs. Shandon with the strange relief of honest noise: not the locked, echoing hush of stone walls and keys, but the open clamour of people living.

From Fleet Street to Paternoster Row is but a short pilgrimage. As they reached Mr. Bungay’s premises, Mrs. Bungay herself was entering by the private door, carrying a brown-paper parcel and a manuscript volume bound in red—her accounts with the butcher, set down with the seriousness of a family Bible. It was a domestic chronicle of chops and suet, of shoulders and sirloins—history written in dripping.

Mrs. Bungay’s dress flashed with shot-silk red and purple; she wore a yellow shawl, red flowers in her bonnet, and carried a parasol of brilliant light blue—colours so loud one might have expected them to make a noise of their own. Mrs. Shandon was in old black watered silk; her bonnet had known no bright prosperity, yet she could not help looking like a lady, as some women cannot help breathing. They curtseyed, each in her manner: one with the weight of property, the other with the grace of breeding.

“I hope you’re pretty well, mum?” said Mrs. Bungay.

“It’s a very fine day,” said Mrs. Shandon.

“Won’t you step in, mum?” said Mrs. Bungay—staring at little Mary with such tragic intensity that the child half fancied herself about to be weighed and priced like a goose.

“I—I came about business with Mr. Bungay—I—I hope he’s pretty well?” Mrs. Shandon faltered.

“If you go to see him in the counting-house, couldn’t you—couldn’t you leave your little gurl with me?” Mrs. Bungay asked, in a deep voice, holding out one finger towards the child as if summoning a reluctant spirit.

“I want to stay with mamma,” cried Mary, burying her face in her mother’s dress.

“Go with this lady, Mary, my dear,” said the mother, gently forcing courage into her own voice.

“I’ll show you some pretty pictures,” Mrs. Bungay said, with the tone of an ogress bribing a captive, “and some nice things besides; look here”—and she opened her parcel to reveal sweet biscuits of the choicest sort, those rich little rounds of butter and spice which Bungay loved after his wine, crisp as new paper and perfumed like a bakery door at dawn.

The biscuits worked magic. Mary, who understood the theology of sugar better than most doctors understand the human heart, followed at once; and the party entered by the private way, a side door leading into Bungay’s commercial apartments. Yet at the moment of parting from her mother, Mary’s courage failed again; she flew back to the maternal skirt. Mrs. Shandon, seeing disappointment settle on Mrs. Bungay’s face like a lid on a pot, kindly said, “If you will let me, I will come up too, and sit for a few minutes,” and so the three females ascended together. A second biscuit established full confidence; and presently Mary prattled as freely as if the house were her own.

Meanwhile, faithful Finucane found Mr. Bungay in a far severer mood than on the previous evening. Port and brandy had then warmed Bungay into that benevolence which is the tipsy cousin of virtue; but morning, that cold water thrown upon every generous impulse, had brought him back to calculation. Mrs. Bungay had rebuked him at home. He was to give no relief to Captain Shandon: a good-for-nothing fellow, whom no money would help. She disapproved of the Pall Mall Gazette altogether, and prophesied Bungay would lose money in it as they were losing “over the way” (she always called her brother’s establishment by that phrase, as if even naming it would make the loss more contagious) at the Whitehall Journal. Let Shandon stop in prison and do his work; it was the best place for him.

Finucane pleaded, promised, implored. Bungay—fresh from an hour’s domestic lecture—was inexorable.

But what Fin could not do below-stairs amid ledgers and ink, Mrs. Shandon was doing above amid biscuits and the small, soft noises of a child: the rustle of a frock, the bright click of a biscuit breaking, the quick run of Mary’s talk—little domestic sounds that, in a world of carts and printing-presses, had power to soothe. There was an artless sweetness in Mrs. Shandon’s voice, and a winning frankness of manner, that made people fond of her in spite of themselves. Taking courage from the rugged kindness with which Mrs. Bungay received her, the Captain’s wife told her story: her husband’s goodness and virtues (which she believed in as simply as she believed in bread), the child’s failing health, the misery of that place; how she had been obliged to part with two children and send them to school, because she could not keep them in that horrid prison.

Mrs. Bungay, grim as Lady Macbeth in a bonnet, melted. Domestic sorrow has its own dialect, and though Mrs. Bungay spoke in imperious monosyllables, she understood this language perfectly. “I’ll go down and speak to Bungay,” she said at last.

In that household, Mrs. Bungay’s “speaking” was command; and Bungay’s “hearing” was obedience. She descended upon her spouse with majesty, politely requested Mr. Finucane to step upstairs to his friends in her drawing-room, and when she had Bungay alone, informed him of her intentions.

“What’s in the wind now, my dear?” asked Maecenas, surprised at her altered tone. “You wouldn’t hear of my doing anything for the Captain this morning. I wonder what has been a changing of you.”

“The Capting is an Irishman,” Mrs. Bungay replied; “and those Irish I have always said I couldn’t abide. But his wife is a lady, as any one can see; and a good woman, and a clergyman’s daughter, and a West of England woman, B., which I am myself, by my mother’s side—and, O Marmaduke! didn’t you remark the little gurl?”

“Yes, Mrs. B., I saw the little girl.”

“And didn’t you see how like she was to our angel, Bessy, Mr. B.?” Mrs. Bungay’s thoughts flew back eighteen years—to the little country town where Bacon and Bungay had once been small booksellers, where hopes were cheap and love dear, and where a child named Bessy had lived only long enough to make memory a permanent ache.

“Well, well, my dear,” Bungay said, seeing his wife’s little eyes begin to twinkle and grow red; “the Captain ain’t in for much. There’s only a hundred and thirty pound against him. Half the money will take him out of the Fleet, Finucane says, and we’ll pay him half salaries till he has made the account square. When the little ’un said, ‘Why don’t you take Par out of prizn?’ I did feel it, Flora, upon my honour I did, now.”

So the two of them went upstairs together, and Bungay made a heavy, clumsy speech—like a joint badly trussed, excellent in substance but awkward in presentation—announcing that, as sixty-five pounds would set Captain Shandon free, he was ready to advance that sum, to be deducted from the Captain’s salary; and that he would give it to Mrs. Shandon on condition that she herself would settle with the creditors for her husband’s liberation.

If there is a flavour to happiness, it is not always sugar. Sometimes it is simply the warm, sudden taste of possibility. That day was the happiest Mrs. Shandon and Mr. Finucane had known for a long while.

“Bedad, Bungay, you’re a trump!” roared Fin, his brogue bursting out with his emotion. “Give us your fist, old boy: and won’t we send the Pall Mall Gazette up to ten thousand a week, that’s all!” He jumped about the room, tossed up little Mary, and performed a hundred frantic antics, as if joy were a pan on the fire and he the cook appointed to keep it from boiling over.

“If I could drive you anywhere in my carriage, Mrs. Shandon—I’m sure it’s quite at your service,” Mrs. Bungay said, glancing out at the one-horse vehicle which had just drawn up, and in which she took the air considerably, as if fresh air were a luxury to be administered by wheels.

So the two ladies drove away from Paternoster Row with little Mary between them—Mary’s tiny hand fixed fast in Mrs. Bungay’s great grasp—and Finucane on the back seat, delighted as a man carrying home a new oven and already smelling the bread. Mrs. Bungay threw triumphant glances at the opposite windows at Bacon’s, as though her charity were also a competitive advertisement.

“It won’t do the Captain any good,” Bungay thought, going back to his desk and accounts; “but Mrs. B. becomes reglar upset when she thinks about her misfortune. The child would have been of age yesterday, if she’d lived. Flora told me so;” and he wondered, with that puzzled reverence dull men sometimes feel for women, how they contrive to remember things.

Mrs. Shandon sped very successfully upon her errand. She who had so often mollified creditors with no money at all—only tears and entreaties, those thin broths of persuasion—found no difficulty now in making them relent when she could offer a bribe of ten shillings in the pound. And the next Sunday was the last, for some time at least, which Captain Shandon spent in prison.

Upon the appointed evening, Mr. Pendennis and Mr. Warrington presented themselves at Mr. Bungay’s door in Paternoster Row—not at that public mouth of the house where the booksellers’ boys, like ants out of a torn sugar-bag, streamed with sacks of Bungay’s volumes; nor where pallid aspirants hovered with manuscripts as fresh and fearful as new-laid eggs, waiting to be cracked by Sultan Bungay’s thumb. They went, instead, to the private entrance—the genteel portal by which Mrs. Bungay herself issued forth, when she rode abroad in state, settled deep among the cushions, and fired glances across at Mrs. Bacon’s windows with all the bravery of a red satin standard.

For opposite dwelt Mrs. Bacon—who was as yet a chaiseless woman; which is to say, in Flora Bungay’s lexicon, a woman without proper weapons.

On those afternoons when Flora’s splendour passed by, and jealousy in Mrs. Bacon boiled like a pot set too near the coals, Emma Bacon would fling up her drawing-room sash and appear with her four children ranged beside her like a well-fed argument. The look said, as plain as printed type: “Behold these four darlings, Flora Bungay! This is why I don’t drive. You would give a coach-and-four to have the same reason.” And thus, with those small, rosy arrows from her quiver, Emma Bacon shot at Flora, who sat in her carriage enviable and childless.

As Pen and Warrington reached Bungay’s door, a carriage and a cab drove briskly up to Bacon’s. Old Dr. Slocum descended from the first—heavily, as if he had been lowered with pulleys; his equipage was as ponderous as his style, and both made a fine sonorous impression in the Row. From the cab sprang a pair of dazzling white waistcoats, so bright they seemed to crackle.

Warrington laughed. “Bacon has his dinner-party too. That is Dr. Slocum, author of ‘Memoirs of the Poisoners.’ You would hardly have known our friend Hoolan in that gallant white waistcoat. Doolan is one of Bungay’s men—and faith, here he comes.”

Indeed Messrs. Hoolan and Doolan had travelled from the Strand in the same cab, tossing up on the way which should pay the shilling; and Mr. Doolan, alighting with the air of a man stepping out of a triumph, was in black, with large white gloves spread upon his hands like unfolded napkins. He could not help admiring them, as if they were two choice slices of something delicate laid there for his own consumption.

Within, the house porter wore an evening coat; the passage was alive with gentlemen in gloves as large as Doolan’s, but of the famous Berlin web. Hats and coats were taken away with solemnity, and names bawled up the stair as though each arrival were a dish being announced to the appetite above.

Some guests were already gathered when the three new visitors entered; but of the charming sex there was only Mrs. Bungay—in red satin, with a turban, the very image of a feast. She curtsied to each man as he came in; yet her mind was plainly elsewhere. The truth was that Mrs. Bacon’s dinner-party, next door, pricked at her like a pin through satin. No sooner had Flora received a guest than she flew back to the window embrasure to rake the opposite doorstep with her eyes and count the carriages clattering up.

When Dr. Slocum’s huge carriage, with its gaunt job-horses and its iron-jawed dignity, rolled to Bacon’s, Flora was crushed. None but hack cabs had driven to her own door that day; and a hack cab, when one is at war, is a poor flag to fly.

They were all literary gentlemen, though unknown as yet to Pen. There was Mr. Bole, the real editor of the magazine of which Mr. Wagg was the nominal chief; Mr. Trotter, who had once broken upon the world as a poet of a tragic and suicidial cast and had since subsided into Bungay’s back shops as reader; and Captain Sumph, an ex-beau reader about town, related in some indistinct manner to Literature and the Peerage. He was said to have written a book once, to have known Byron, to be connected with Lord Sumphington; and in fact the name of Byron was the perpetual seasoning of his talk, so that he could scarce speak without sprinkling his sentence with it, as one dusts a dish with pepper. “I remember poor Shelley, at school, being sent up for good for a copy of verses—every line of which I wrote, by Jove;” or “I recollect, when I was at Missolonghi with Byron, offering to bet gamba,” and so on. Pen remarked that Mrs. Bungay listened with a reverence as soft and greedy as a cat’s attention to cream; anecdotes of the aristocracy delighted her, and Captain Sumph, being a middle-aged member of that august theatre, was almost a greater man than the great Mr. Wagg himself in her eyes. Had he but arrived in his own carriage, she would have made Bungay buy any volume Captain Sumph might choose to write, even if it were nothing but his own conversation printed and bound.

Mr. Bungay went about among his guests with cordiality. “Ow are you, sir? Fine day, sir. Glad to see you ’ere, sir. Flora, my love, let me ’ave the honour of introducing Mr. Warrington to you. Mr. Warrington—Mrs. Bungay. Mr. Pendennis—Mrs. Bungay. Hope you’ve brought good appetites with you, gentlemen. You, Doolan, I know ’ave, for you’ve always ’ad a deuce of a twist.”

“Lor, Bungay!” said Mrs. Bungay.

“Faith, a man must be hard to please, Bungay, who can’t eat a good dinner in this house,” Doolan said; he winked, stroked his lean chops through his white gloves, and made appeals of friendship to Mrs. Bungay which that honest woman refused with scorn. “She couldn’t abide that Doolan,” she said afterward, with a shiver of dislike.

As they talked—Mrs. Bungay still surveying mankind from her window—there appeared a magnificent vision: an enormous grey cab-horse, advancing with the importance of a drum-major. Behind its arched neck flashed a pair of white reins held by small white gloves; above the cab-head bobbed the pale face, richly decorated with a chin-tuft, of an exiguous groom. These bright details, like garnishings on a plate, were revealed one by one to Flora’s delighted eye.

“The Honourable Percy Popjoy’s quite punctual, I declare,” she cried, and sailed to the door to be in waiting at the nobleman’s arrival.

“It’s Percy Popjoy,” Pen said, looking out and seeing an individual in extremely lacquered boots descend from the swinging cab. And it was indeed that young nobleman, Lord Falconet’s eldest son, who had come to dine with his publisher of the Row.

“He was my fag at Eton,” Warrington said. “I ought to have licked him a little more.” Pen and Popjoy had had bouts at the Oxbridge Union debates, in which Pen had had very much the better. Presently Popjoy appeared, hat under arm, with a look of indescribable good-humour and fatuity in his round, dimpled face—upon which Nature had burst out with a chin-tuft, and, exhausted by the effort, had left the rest bare.

The temporary groom of the chambers bawled, “The Honourable Percy Popjoy,” much to that gentleman’s discomposure at hearing his titles shouted like an order to the kitchen.

“What did the man want to take away my hat for, Bungay?” Popjoy asked. “Can’t do without my hat—want it to make my bow to Mrs. Bungay. How well you look, Mrs. Bungay, to-day. Haven’t seen your carriage in the Park: why haven’t you been there? I missed you; indeed, I did.”

“I’m afraid you’re a sad quiz,” said Mrs. Bungay.

“Quiz! Never made a joke in my—hullo! who’s here? How d’ye do, Pendennis? How d’ye do, Warrington? These are old friends of mine, Mrs. Bungay. I say, how the doose did you come here?”—and he turned his lacquered heels on Mrs. Bungay with a frankness which would have been less forgiven in a man without a title.

“What! do they know him?” Flora asked rapidly of Mr. Bungay, her whole manner changing, as if some new spice had been thrown into the stew of her opinion of Pen and Warrington.

“High fellers, I tell you—the young one related to all the nobility,” said Bungay; and both husband and wife ran forward smiling and bowing, to greet almost as great personages as the young lord himself—no less, indeed, than the great Mr. Wenham and the great Mr. Wagg, now announced.

Mr. Wenham entered with his usual demure look and stealthy smile, surveying the tips of his neat, shining boots, and only seldom lifting his eyes to meet those of a fellow-creature. Wagg’s white waistcoat, on the contrary, spread out with profuse brilliancy; his burly red face shone over it like a warmed joint newly basted. He liked to enter a drawing-room with a laugh, and leave it later with a joke exploding behind him. No personal calamities or distresses—of which that humourist had his share—could altogether keep his humour down; the thought of dinner rallied his great soul; and when he saw a lord, he saluted him with a pun.

Wenham went up with a smug smile and whisper to Mrs. Bungay, looked at her from under his eyes, and showed her the tips of his shoes, as if they were credentials. Wagg said she looked charming, and pushed on straight to young Popjoy, whom he called Pop, and instantly began a funny story seasoned with what the French call gros sel. He was delighted too to see Pen—shook his hand, slapped him on the back, and talked in a loud voice of Baymouth and Clavering Park and Sir Francis, and whether Pen had been to see Lady Rockminster—fine old lady, Lady Rockminster! These remarks were less for Pen than for the company, whom Wagg instructed—like a waiter reading the bill of fare—that he visited country seats and was familiar with nobility.

Wenham also shook hands with Pen; and all these scenes Mrs. Bungay marked with respectful pleasure, storing them away to be served up to Bungay afterward in the form of opinions about Mr. Pendennis’s importance—opinions from which Pen profited much more than he ever guessed.

Pen, who had read, and rather admired, some of Miss Bunion’s works, and expected to find in her a person resembling her own account of herself in the “Passion-Flower”—where she declared her youth resembled

“A violet, shrinking meanly
When blows the March wind keenly;
A timid fawn, on wild-wood lawn,
Where oak-boughs rustle greenly,”

and that her maturer beauty was something very different, but still exceedingly captivating—beheld, to his surprise and amusement, a large bony woman in a crumpled satin dress, who came creaking in with a step as heavy as a grenadier’s. Wagg instantly noted the straw clinging to the rumpled skirt and would have stooped to pick it off; but Miss Bunion disarmed criticism by seeing it herself. Setting her large foot on the straw to separate it from the dress, she stooped and picked it up, saying simply to Mrs. Bungay that she was sorry to be late, but the omnibus was very slow, and what a comfort it was to get a ride all the way from Brompton for sixpence.

Nobody laughed: the speech was uttered with such plain sincerity. The worthy woman had not the smallest notion of being ashamed of an action incidental upon her poverty.

“Is that ‘Passion-Flowers?’” Pen said to Wenham. “Why, her picture in the volume represents her as a very well-looking young woman.”

“You know passion-flowers, like all others, will run to seed,” Wenham answered. “Miss Bunion’s portrait was probably painted some years ago.”

“Well, I like her for not being ashamed of her poverty.”

“So do I,” said Mr. Wenham—who would have starved rather than have come to dinner in an omnibus—“but I don’t think she need flourish the straw about, do you, Mr. Pendennis? My dear Miss Bunion, how do you do? I was in a great lady’s drawing-room this morning, and everybody was charmed with your new volume. Those lines on the christening of Lady Fanny Fantail brought tears into the Duchess’s eyes. I said I thought I should have the pleasure of meeting you to-day, and she begged me to thank you, and say how greatly she was pleased.”

This history, told blandly, about a Duchess met that very morning, quite put poor Wagg’s dowager and baronet out of court, and placed Wenham beyond him as a man of fashion. Wenham, having thus salted the conversation to his own taste, ran on with aristocratic anecdotes, trying to draw Popjoy in—“I was telling your father this morning,” or, “I think you were present at W. house the other night when the Duke said so-and-so”—but Popjoy would not gratify him. He preferred to fall back into the window recess with Mrs. Bungay, watching the cabs at the opposite door. If he would not talk, at least he would sit where the Bacons might see that Flora had captured a nobleman for her party.

Saint Paul’s bell tolled half an hour later than the time Bungay had named; and at last the party was complete, with the exception of two guests, who now appeared—and in whom Pen was pleased to recognise Captain and Mrs. Shandon.

After making their greetings and exchanging nods of more or less recognition with most present, Pen and Warrington went up and shook hands warmly with Mrs. Shandon, who perhaps was affected to think where it was she had seen them but a few days before. Shandon was brushed up and looked pretty smart in a red velvet waistcoat and a frill, into which his wife had stuck her best brooch. In spite of Mrs. Bungay’s kindness—perhaps because of it—Mrs. Shandon felt great terror in approaching her. Indeed Flora, in red satin and bird of paradise, was more awful than ever; and it was not until she had asked, in her great voice, about the dear little gurl, that Mrs. Shandon was encouraged and ventured a reply.

“Nice-looking woman,” Popjoy whispered to Warrington. “Do introduce me to Captain Shandon, Warrington. I’m told he’s a tremendous clever fellow; and, dammy, I adore intellect, by Jove I do!” This was true: Heaven had given Popjoy little intellect of his own, but a generous faculty for admiring it in others. “And introduce me to Miss Bunion. I’m told she’s very clever too. She’s rum to look at, certainly, but that don’t matter. Dammy, I consider myself a literary man, and I wish to know all the clever fellows.”

So Mr. Popjoy and Mr. Shandon became acquainted; and the doors of the dining-room being flung open, the party entered and took their seats. Pen found himself next to Miss Bunion on one side and Mr. Wagg on the other; the truth being that Wagg fled alarmed from the vacant place by the poetess, and Pen was compelled to take it.

Miss Bunion did not talk much during dinner; but Pen remarked that she ate with a vast appetite, and never refused any supply of wine offered by the butler. Indeed, after considering Mr. Pendennis for a minute—grand airs, fashionable attire, very best chains, shirt studs, and cambric fronts—she set him down, not without reason, as a prig; and thought it better to attend to her dinner than to notice him. She told him as much later with her usual candour. “I took you for one of the little Mayfair dandies,” she said. “You looked as solemn as a little undertaker; and as I disliked, beyond measure, the odious creature on the other side of me, I thought it best to eat my dinner and hold my tongue.”

“And you did both very well, my dear Miss Bunion,” Pen answered, laughing.

“Well, so I do; but I intend to talk to you the next time a great deal: for you are neither so solemn, nor so stupid, nor so pert as you look.”

“Ah, Miss Bunion, how I pine for that next time,” Pen replied with comical gallantry—though we must return to the present dinner in Paternoster Row.

The repast was of the richest description. “What I call the florid Gothic style,” Wagg whispered to Pen in his side-wing voice. Behind the guests moved solemn men in creaking shoes and Berlin gloves, carrying on rapid undertones as they passed dishes from hand to hand, like messengers passing important papers. Doolan, attempting grandly to command one of them, cried “Waither,” and blushed when he caught his own blunder, as if he had spilt sauce on his shirt-front. Mrs. Bungay’s own footboy was lost amid those black-coated attendants, like a small sprig of parsley in a crowded tureen.

“Look at that very bow-windowed man,” Wagg said. “He’s an undertaker in Amen Corner, and attends funerals and dinners. Cold meat and hot, don’t you perceive? He’s the sham butler here; and I observe, my dear Mr. Pendennis—as you will through life—that wherever there is a sham butler at a London dinner there is sham wine. This sherry is filthy. Bungay, my boy, where did you get this delicious brown sherry?”

“I’m glad you like it, Mr. Wagg; glass with you,” said the publisher. “It’s some I got from Alderman Benning’s store, and gave a good figure for it, I can tell you. Mr. Pendennis, will you join us? Your ’ealth, gentlemen.”

“The old rogue—where does he expect to go to? It came from the public-house,” Wagg muttered. “It requires two men to carry off that sherry, ’tis so uncommonly strong. I wish I had a bottle of old Steyne’s wine here, Pendennis: your uncle and I have had many a one. He sends it about to people where he is in the habit of dining. I remember at poor Rawdon Crawley’s—Sir Pitt Crawley’s brother, Governor of Coventry Island—Steyne’s chef always came in the morning, and the butler arrived with the champagne from Gaunt House in ice-pails ready.”

“How good this is!” Popjoy said, good-naturedly, tasting everything as if it were a compliment. “You must have a cordon bleu in your kitchen.”

“O yes,” Mrs. Bungay answered, thinking he spoke of a chain, perhaps, or some noble badge she ought to have known.

“I mean a French chef,” said the polite guest.

“O yes, your lordship,” again said Flora, determined to agree, whatever the ingredient.

“Does your artist say he’s a Frenchman, Mrs. B.?” called out Wagg.

“Well, I’m sure I don’t know,” she replied.

“Because, if he does, he’s a quizzin yer,” cried Mr. Wagg; but nobody perceived the pun, and the bashful punster was disconcerted. “The dinner is from Griggs in St. Paul’s Churchyard; so is Bacon’s,” he whispered to Pen. “Bungay writes to give half-a-crown a head more than Bacon, so does Bacon. They would poison each other’s ices if they could get near them; and as for the made-dishes—they are poison. This—hum—ha—this Brimborion à la Sévigné is delicious, Mrs. B.,” he added aloud, helping himself with gusto from a dish the undertaker handed to him.

“Well, I’m glad you like it,” Mrs. Bungay answered, blushing; not knowing if the dish truly bore that name, but dimly conscious Wagg was quizzing her. Accordingly she hated Mr. Wagg with female ardour, and would have deposed him from his command over Bungay’s periodical, had not his name been great in the trade and his reputation in the land considerable.

By displacement of persons, Warrington found himself on the right of Mrs. Shandon, who sat in plain black silk with faded ornaments beside the florid publisher. The sad smile on the lady’s face moved his rough heart to pity. Nobody seemed to interest himself about her. She sat looking at her husband, who appeared abashed in the presence of some of the company. Wenham and Wagg both knew him and his circumstances. He had worked with the latter, and was immeasurably his superior in wit, genius, and acquirement; but Wagg’s star was brilliant in the world, and poor Shandon was unknown there. He could not speak against the noisy talk of the coarser and more successful man; so he drank his wine in silence—and as much of it as the people would give him.

He was under surveillance. Bungay had warned the undertaker not to fill the Captain’s glass too often or too full. It was a melancholy precaution; and the more melancholy because it was necessary. Mrs. Shandon cast alarmed glances across the table, watching that her husband did not exceed.

Abashed by the failure of his first pun—for he was impudent and easily disconcerted—Wagg kept his conversation mostly to Pen during the rest of dinner, and chiefly spoke of their neighbours. “This is one of Bungay’s grand field-days,” he said. “We are all Bungavians here. Did you read Popjoy’s novel? It was an old magazine story written by poor Buzzard years ago, forgotten until Mr. Trotter”—he nodded toward a gentleman with a large shirt-collar—“fished it out and bethought him it was applicable to the late elopement; so Bob wrote a few chapters à propos—Popjoy permitted the use of his name, and I dare say supplied a page here and there—and ‘Desperation, or the Fugitive Duchess’ made its appearance. The great fun is to examine Popjoy about his own work, of which he doesn’t know a word. I say, Popjoy, what a capital passage that is in Volume Three—where the Cardinal in disguise, after being converted by the Bishop of London, proposes marriage to the Duchess’s daughter.”

“Glad you like it,” Popjoy answered, beaming. “It’s a favourite bit of my own.”

“There’s no such thing in the whole book,” Wagg whispered to Pen. “Invented it myself. Gad! it wouldn’t be a bad plot for a high-church novel.”

“I remember poor Byron, Hobhouse, Trelawney, and myself, dining with Cardinal Mezzocaldo at Rome,” Captain Sumph began, bringing out Byron as a cook brings out the same herb for every course. “We had some Orvieto wine for dinner, which Byron liked very much. And I remember how the Cardinal regretted that he was a single man. We went to Civita Vecchia two days afterwards, where Byron’s yacht was—and, by Jove, the Cardinal died within three weeks; and Byron was very sorry, for he rather liked him.”

“A devilish interesting story, Sumph, indeed,” Wagg said.

“You should publish some of those stories, Captain Sumph, you really should. Such a volume would make our friend Bungay’s fortune,” Shandon said.

“Why don’t you ask Sumph to publish ’em in your new paper—the what-d’ye-call-’em—hay, Shandon?” bawled out Wagg.

“Why don’t you ask him to publish ’em in your old magazine, the Thingumbob?” Shandon replied.

“Is there going to be a new paper?” asked Wenham, who knew perfectly well, but was ashamed of his connection with the press, as though it were the smell of frying that clung to one’s coat.

“Bungay going to bring out a paper?” cried Popjoy, who, on the contrary, was proud of his literary reputation and acquaintances. “You must employ me. Mrs. Bungay, use your influence with him, and make him employ me. Prose or verse—what shall it be? Novels, poems, travels, or leading articles—begad. Anything or everything—only let Bungay pay me, and I’m ready—I am now, my dear Mrs. Bungay, begad now.”

“It’s to be called the Small Beer Chronicle,” growled Wagg, “and little Popjoy is to be engaged for the infantine department.”

“It is to be called the Pall Mall Gazette, sir, and we shall be very happy to have you with us,” Shandon said.

“Pall Mall Gazette—why Pall Mall Gazette?” asked Wagg.

“Because the editor was born at Dublin, the sub-editor at Cork, because the proprietor lives in Paternoster Row—and the paper is published in Catherine Street, Strand. Won’t that reason suffice you, Wagg?” Shandon said; he was getting angry now, his voice sharpening like a knife on a steel. “Everything must have a name. My dog Ponto has got a name. You’ve got a name, and a name which you deserve, more or less indeed. Why d’ye grudge the name to our paper?”

“By any other name it would smell as sweet,” said Wagg.

“I’ll have ye remember its name’s not what-d’ye-call-’em, Mr. Wagg,” Shandon said. “You know its name well enough—and—and you know mine.”

Success, like a soufflé in a draughty kitchen, rose for the Pall Mall Gazette with a confidence that made onlookers swear there must be some noble cook at the range and a whole party of grave gentlemen passing the salt in secret.

There were rumours—always the first cheap spice in London—that the journal had an influential political patronage simmering behind it; that great names were tied to the ladle and stirring the pot. Whether those names belonged there, we are not at liberty to state. But we may let fall, as one drops a clove into broth, that a weighty article on foreign policy, generally credited to a noble Lord with a very knowing acquaintance in the Foreign Office, was in truth whisked up by Captain Shandon in the parlour of the Bear and Staff public-house near Whitehall Stairs—where the air smelt of wet greatcoats, pipe-smoke, and yesterday’s porter, and where the printer’s boy, tracking him like a truffle-hound, at last found him. Mr. Bludyer, a literary ally with a temporary lodging there, sat within reach—one of those men who can live for a week on sarcasm and neat spirits, and consider both nourishing.

A whole series on finance, which the town insisted must be the work of a great Statesman of the House of Commons, was actually composed by Mr. George Warrington in the Upper Temple—among old books that rustled like dry corn in a loft, and with the steady scratch of a pen keeping time against the distant clatter of London, that endless mill-wheel of sound. If the Pall Mall Gazette had dealings with an influential party, that too was quite possible. Percy Popjoy, son of Lord Falconet and as fond of climbing stairs as of being seen doing it, was often observed mounting to Warrington’s chambers; and certain items of information appeared in the paper which had the smell of private pantries—facts that do not come from the common market-stall, but from back doors, side passages, and confidential servants.

There were poems, too—thin in thought but loud in voice—signed “P. P.”; and it must be confessed that the same initials performed a species of trumpet-service over Mr. Popjoy’s novel, praising it with a gusto so outrageous that you would have supposed the reviewers had been paid in truffles. In the political department Mr. Pen took no share; but for the literary columns he was as busy as a young cook at his first great dinner, flour on his cuffs, pride in his eye, and an appetite for applause sharper than mustard.

The Gazette’s offices were in Catherine Street, Strand. Thither Pen often hurried with manuscripts in his pocket, with a bustle and pleasure which are very like hunger—an eager, half-ashamed craving to see one’s own name served up hot in print, and to fancy, for a delicious moment, that the world is pausing to taste it. The place itself had its own soundscape: the slap of copy on desks, the snip of scissors, the soft wicked rasp of paste-brush on paper, the murmur of men manufacturing society out of scraps, and outside the street’s ceaseless grinding—omnibuses, hawkers, wheels on stone—modern London chewing and chewing.

Here Mr. Jack Finucane, sub-editor, presided with paste and scissors as if they were knife and cleaver. He watched the newspapers with the hungry vigilance of a man who has dined more on other people’s dinners than his own. With an eagle eye he scanned every paragraph that touched the world of fashion. Not a death among the aristocracy, not a dinner-party with plate enough to catch the candles, not a christening where a duke had sneezed at the font, but Jack would have it recorded. From remote provincial prints, and from Scotch and Irish papers that arrived like damp parcels of peat, he fished out astonishing intelligence regarding the upper classes—extracting them as a cook draws marrow from a bone.

It was a grand—nay, a touching—sight for a philosopher, to see Jack Finucane, in tattered trousers and dingy shirt-sleeves, dining off a plate of meat from the cookshop and washing it down with porter from the public-house, while he described the feasts of the great as if he had sat at the carving beside the host. There he was, chewing his own coarse ration, and, between bites, arranging the most brilliant fêtes in the world of fashion with the brisk neatness of a maître d’hôtel. The incongruity of the man—his poverty and his pompous paragraphs—amused Pen mightily. Since leaving his native village, where his rank had probably not been very lofty, Jack had seen little society except the tavern parlours he frequented; and yet from his writing one would have believed he lounged daily in the bow-window of White’s and took his soup among ambassadors.

Occasional errors of description did slip from his pen—like a cook calling parsley “tarragon” in the hearing of a gardener. But it was the Ballinafad Sentinel, for which he was his own correspondent, that suffered from these lapses, not the Pall Mall Gazette. In London Jack’s chiefs thought his scissors and paste were safer tools than his pen; and so he clipped other people’s grandeur into their columns with the skill of a man making a pie out of leftovers.

Pen, on his side, took pains with his reviews. He had a fair share of desultory reading, acquired early—books tasted here and there like bites taken from many loaves. He had, too, a keen sense of fun, and that quick relish which is half palate and half temper. His articles pleased his chief and the public, and he was proud to think he earned his money honestly—an honest wage being, to a young man, as sweet as warm bread when one is not yet sick of it.

We may be sure the Pall Mall Gazette was taken in regularly at Fairoaks, and read with delight by the two ladies there—each number arriving like a basket from town, full of strange herbs and sharp flavours. It was received at Clavering Park too, where there was a young lady of great literary tastes; and old Doctor Portman himself—after the widow had got her son’s articles by heart and forwarded the paper along like a family relic—signified his approval, saying the lad had spirit, taste, and fancy, and wrote, if not like a scholar, at any rate like a gentleman.

But the best dish of praise was served at the Major’s own table of vanity.

Major Pendennis, walking into one of his clubs—the Regent—found Wenham, Lord Falconet, and other gentlemen of good reputation and fashion gathered round a number of the Pall Mall Gazette, talking it over as men talk over a sauce whose piquancy pleases them. An article had appeared making bitter fun of a book recently published by the wife of a celebrated member of the opposition party: a Book of Travels in Spain and Italy, by the Countess of Muffborough. It was hard to decide which was more astonishing, the French or the English, in which her ladyship wrote indifferently—each language served half-cooked, with lumps of blunder floating to the top like suet.

The critic pounced with delightful mischief. He jumped and danced round his subject with jocularity and high spirits—showing up the Countess’s faults with mock gravity and an air of decorum so perfectly polite that it felt like being stabbed with a silver fork. Not a word was ungentlemanlike; and yet the unfortunate book was scarified and laughed at through the whole operation, as neatly as a fish may be filleted while it still seems intact.

Wenham’s bilious countenance puckered with malignant pleasure as he read. Lady Muffborough had not asked him to her parties during the last year—an omission he remembered as a man remembers a missed inheritance. Lord Falconet giggled outright; Lord Muffborough and he had been rivals ever since they began life; and these gentlemen complimented Major Pendennis. Until now the Major had scarcely noticed certain hints from Fairoaks about “dear Arthur’s constant and severe literary occupations, which I fear may undermine the poor boy’s health.” Newspaper connexions had seemed, to him, below the dignity of a Major and a gentleman—ink being, in his opinion, a substance best kept on other people’s fingers.

But now—when the oracular Wenham praised the boy’s production; when Lord Falconet, tipped off by Percy Popjoy, approved young Pen’s genius; when the great Lord Steyne himself, to whom the Major referred the article, laughed and sniggered over it, swore it was capital, and that the Muffborough would writhe under it like a whale under a harpoon—the Major’s family pride began to cook rapidly.

“By gad,” he said, “the young rascal has some stuff in him—he’ll do something. I always said he’d do something.”

And with a hand tremulous with pleasure, the old gentleman sat down to write to the widow at Fairoaks all that the great folks had said; and to the young rascal too, asking when he would come and eat a chop with his old uncle. He added that he was commissioned to take him to dinner at Gaunt House; for Lord Steyne liked anybody who could entertain him—whether by folly, wit, dulness, oddity, affectation, good spirits, or any other seasoning that made the dish go down.

Pen flung the letter across the table to Warrington. Perhaps he expected Warrington to taste the praise, smack his lips, and declare it excellent. Warrington did nothing of the kind.

Young critics have courage enough to season an elephant. They clamber up to the judgment-seat and, with scarce a hesitation, pronounce upon works intricate as a stuffed capon or profound as a cellar. Had Macaulay’s History or Herschel’s Astronomy been put before Pen at that period, he would have looked through the volumes, meditated his opinion over a cigar, and then delivered his august approval as if he were their born superior—an indulgent master and patron granting permission for genius to exist.

By the help of the Biographie Universelle or the British Museum, he could take a rapid résumé of a period, and allude to names, dates, and facts with a masterly ease that astonished his mamma at home (who wondered where her boy had got such a prodigious store of reading), and astonished Pen himself when he read his own articles two or three months later and had forgotten both subject and sources, as a man forgets yesterday’s dinner until he finds the bill in his pocket.

At that time Pen would not have hesitated, at twenty-four hours’ notice, to pass opinion upon the greatest scholars or give judgment on the Encyclopaedia. Luckily Warrington laughed at him and kept down his impertinence by a constant and wholesome ridicule—as a sensible elder might slap the hand of a child reaching for a pan too hot. For Shandon liked the dash and flippancy of his young aide-de-camp, and was better pleased with Pen’s light brilliant flashes than with the heavier metal Warrington brought. Still, though Pen might be blamed for prematurity of judgment, he was a perfectly honest critic—too candid for Mr. Bungay’s purposes, indeed, who grumbled sadly at his impartiality.

Pen and Captain Shandon disputed upon this one day.

“In the name of common-sense, Mr. Pendennis,” Shandon asked, “what have you been doing—praising one of Mr. Bacon’s books? Bungay has been with me in a fury this morning at seeing a laudatory article upon one of the works of the odious firm over the way.”

Pen’s eyes opened wide, as if someone had proposed putting soot into the soup. “Do you mean to say,” he asked, “that we are to praise no books that Bacon publishes? Or that, if the books are good, we are to say they are bad?”

“My good young friend,” said Shandon, “for what do you suppose a benevolent publisher undertakes a critical journal—to benefit his rival?”

“To benefit himself certainly,” Pen answered, “but to tell the truth too—ruat coelum—to tell the truth.”

“And my prospectus?” Shandon said, with a laugh and a sneer. “Do you consider that was a work of mathematical accuracy of statement?”

“Pardon me—that is not the question,” Pen replied; “and I don’t think you very much care to argue it. I had qualms of conscience about that prospectus, and debated the matter with my friend Warrington. We agreed, however,” Pen said, laughing, “that because the prospectus was rather declamatory and poetical, and the giant painted upon the show-board rather larger than the original who was inside the caravan, we need not be too scrupulous about this trifling inaccuracy, but might do our part of the show without loss of character or remorse. We are the fiddlers, and play our tunes only; you are the showman.”

“And leader of the van,” Shandon added.

“Well,” said Pen, with a fine sense of the dignity of his position, “we are all party men in England, and I will stick to my party like a Briton. I will be as good-natured as you like to our own side—he is a fool who quarrels with his own nest—and I will hit the enemy as hard as you like; but with fair play, Captain, if you please. One can’t tell all the truth, I suppose; but one can tell nothing but the truth. And I would rather starve, by Jove, and never earn another penny by my pen”—this redoubted instrument had now been in use for some six weeks, and he spoke of it with vast enthusiasm and respect—“than strike an opponent an unfair blow, or, if called upon to place him, rank him below his honest desert.”

“Well, Mr. Pendennis,” Shandon said with fatal good-nature, “when we want Bacon smashed, we must get some other hammer to do it.” And very likely he thought, without speaking it: “A few years hence perhaps the young gentleman won’t be so squeamish.”

The veteran condottiere himself was no longer scrupulous. He had fought and killed on so many sides for so many years that remorse had long since fled his camp. “Gad,” he said, “you’ve a tender conscience, Mr. Pendennis. It’s the luxury of novices. I may have had one once myself; but that bloom wears off with the rubbing of the world, and I’m not going to the trouble of putting on an artificial complexion like our pious friend Wenham, or our model of virtue, Wagg.”

“I don’t know,” Pen answered, “whether some people’s hypocrisy is not better than others’ cynicism.”

“It’s more profitable, at any rate,” said the Captain, biting his nails. “That Wenham is as dull a quack as ever quacked: and you saw the carriage in which he drove to dinner. Faith, it’ll be a long time before Mrs. Shandon takes a drive in her own chariot. God help her, poor thing!”

Pen went away from his chief after their dispute, drawing his own moral as a careful cook salts his own stew: “Behold this man,” he thought, “stored with genius, wit, learning, and a hundred good natural gifts—see how he has wrecked them by paltering with his honesty and forgetting to respect himself. Wilt thou remember thyself, O Pen? thou art conceited enough. Wilt thou sell thy honour for a bottle? No—by heaven’s grace—we will be honest, whatever befalls, and our mouths shall only speak the truth when they open.”

A trial was waiting for him—served up promptly, as London serves lessons, without so much as a napkin.

In the very next number of the Pall Mall Gazette, Warrington read out—between bursts of laughter—an article which did not amuse Arthur Pendennis at all. Pen himself was at work on a criticism for the coming week, when this new piece appeared, in which the Spring Annual was ferociously maltreated by some unknown writer. The poor spring flowers were pounded into a paste.

And among those most cruelly mauled was Pen himself.

His verses had not been printed in the Annual under his own name, but under an assumed signature. He had refused to review the book; and Shandon, with the easy conscience of a man who stirs all sauces with the same spoon, handed it to Mr. Bludyer, instructing him to “dispose of it.”

Bludyer disposed of it as effectually as a butcher disposes of a lamb. He was a man of considerable talent, and of a race—now, perhaps, extinct—who treated literature as something to be broken open with a mallet. He possessed a savage humour and a professional notoriety for using it. He smashed and trampled down the Spring Annual with no more mercy than a bull would show a parterre; and when he had cut up the volume to his heart’s content, he went and sold it at a bookstall, and purchased a pint of brandy with the proceeds—turning printed flowers into spirits with the brisk practicality of the age.

A few months slid by in Mr. Arthur Pendennis’s life with that smooth, unromantic sameness which makes a man feel very busy indeed, and makes his biographer feel very sleepy. We left him harnessed—like the rest of us—to his daily bread. He had become a professional writer: which is a grand name for a person who must sit down at such and such an hour, and produce wit, judgment, and genius by the column, much as a cook must send up a dinner at seven, whether the muse is hungry or the stomach inspired.

The public has a charitable notion that Pegasus, because he has wings, ought never to be put between shafts; that he should soar for pure delight, and never be made to tug at a cab over the stones. But when Pegasus has no other property than his own ribs, and a landlord who likes to be paid in coin rather than in odes, he is apt to find the collar clasped round his throat. He trots; he pants; he gets a cut of the whip; and—between ourselves—he very often deserves it. There is no more reason why a man of letters should be exempt from work, indigestion, or old age, than a butcher, a curate, or a clerk. Genius, like cookery, is a fine thing; but it is not a substitute for paying taxes.

So the Pall Mall Gazette being established, and Mr. Pendennis being found to have a light hand with a lash, he reviewed industriously each week whatever volumes tumbled into his portion of the basket; and he did it with flippancy, certainly, but with a kind of honest appetite for the truth, as a good trencherman has for a sirloin. He would carve up a solemn history—grey as yesterday’s porridge—after two mornings at the British Museum, while the author, poor old scholar, had been stewing it for five-and-twenty years like a family stock-pot. He would taste a poet’s sonnets, sniff, and declare them heavy, as though he were a judge and the bard a trembling suitor. Actors hated him too; perhaps he peppered them too freely. Yet in those days there were not many great men to be wounded. The few who received a whipping probably got something wholesome with it, as people do with bitter medicine. And if Mr. Pen ever showed a disposition to think himself the cleverest cook in the kitchen, Warrington stood at his elbow like a grim head-chef, ready to taste, grimace, and send the sauce back.

By these labours—reviews, occasional leading articles when his conscience would let him season the politics, and sundry magazine dishes—Arthur earned four pounds four shillings a week, which is not a romantic sum, but it will buy coals, candles, and chops. There were other little profits besides; and it is believed (though he never chose to confess it, any more than a person likes to name the shop where he buys his dinner) that he wrote those very brilliant London letters which appeared in the Chatteris Champion. By one way and another he made nearly four hundred a year; and on the second Christmas after his arrival he carried a hundred pounds down to his mother, as a dividend upon the money he owed Laura.

Mrs. Pendennis read every line of his printed work as though it were Scripture newly revealed; she believed him the profoundest thinker in the kingdom; she regarded the hundred pounds as a seraphic action; she trembled lest his brain should be over-boiled by labour; she rejoiced to hear of the fine people who invited him, and of the great men whose hands he shook. Whoever has seen a mother in the country listening to a son’s London triumphs knows how the smallest item becomes a feast. A brief held, a ball attended, a lord met at dinner—these are roasted, carved, and served up again and again at the family table, until the very village has had a slice.

Pen came down for a very brief space that winter and made the lonely house at Fairoaks shine. Helen had him all to herself; Laura was away visiting old Lady Rockminster; the people at Clavering Park were absent. Doctor Portman and the few old friends called, and treated Mr. Pen with marked respect—as if the ink upon his fingers had suddenly turned to blue blood. Between mother and son there was nothing but tenderness and confidence. It was the happiest fortnight of the widow’s life—perhaps of both of theirs. Then the clock struck, the coach rolled away, and London swallowed him again; and the gentle woman was left with her quiet rooms and the echoes. She sent Arthur’s money to Laura. Why Laura chose to be absent when he came, whether he was piqued or relieved by it, is one of those domestic riddles which women answer with a look, and men never translate at all.

Meanwhile Pen’s own London was growing large. His uncle’s introductions and his own pliant good-humour brought him into literary circles and into fashionable ones; and, curiously, the latter helped him with the former. A young man who is supposed to be writing for amusement is received by publishers and editors with a respect they seldom show to a hungry genius. Bacon, Bungay and Co. were proud of him; Wenham asked him to dinner; Wagg looked on him with favour. They reported how they met him in Mayfair; and Mayfair, seeing him in Mayfair, invited him because somebody else had invited him. So the young man wandered through the whole pantry and drawing-room of London—from Paternoster Row to Pimlico—and was as much at home at a nobleman’s table as in the back room of an office where proofs lay damp, ink smelt sharp, and the air buzzed with the scraping of pens.

He might breakfast at Mr. Plover’s in the company of a Peer, a Bishop, a parliamentary orator, two blue ladies, a popular preacher, the author of the last novel, and the newest imported lion; and then slip away to the newspaper office where Finucane the sub-editor had the latest whispers from the Row.
