Shandon would come in presently, nod, and begin writing his leading article at the far end of the table, flanked—like a fortress—by his pint of sherry, which the boy brought as silently and inevitably as a saucepan to a fire. In the front room Bludyer’s roaring voice would be heard as he bullied the timid publisher, impounded books upon the counter, and presently sold them at his stall; then, having dined and drunk upon the author’s value, he would call for paper and ink and “smash” the very man who had paid for his chops. Toward evening Pen would stroll to his club and take up Warrington for a walk—a constitutional, as they call it, meaning a march to blow the lungs open and invite appetite. Then dinner; then perhaps the Opera, the Eagle, a Mayfair ball, a quiet cigar with a book, or a night of talk with Warrington, or some new song bawled out at the Back Kitchen. He ran everywhere, tasted everything, listened to every sound—coach-wheels on the stones, fiddles in the gallery, laughter in taverns, the thin scratch of quills. Very likely he did not know how much he enjoyed it until later years, when the same music would sound like a barrel-organ, and pleasure itself would have the flavour of warmed-over soup.

And those times, too, have passed away. It is but a few years since—and yet most of the men are gone. Bludyer will bully no more. Shandon sleeps. Honest Doolan has been buried. The town keeps making its noise; but the voices change.

London that season was in full bloom. The fashionable papers were thick with dinners, routs, and balls; the Sovereign held levees and drawing-rooms; club bow-windows were packed with respectable red-faced gentlemen reading news as solemnly as if it were a sermon; along the Serpentine rolled endless carriages; over Rotten Row clattered squadrons of horsemen. Everybody was in town; and of course Major Arthur Pendennis, who counted himself somebody, was not absent.

On a certain morning the worthy Major sat by his fire with his head tied up in a smart bandanna, his thin frame wrapped in a brilliant Turkish dressing-gown, and his feet simmering in a bath, as though he were a pair of delicate cutlets being gently brought to tenderness. He could not face the day without his two hours’ toilet, his early tea, and his Morning Post. Nobody in the world except Morgan—not even the Major himself, perhaps—knew how feeble and ancient the old gentleman was growing, and what a thousand small comforts, like secret seasonings, were required to make him presentable.

We laugh at old ladies for their paints and perfumes and ringlets, as if time were a scandalous enemy only to women; but men are vain too, and an old buck’s toilet is as elaborate as any Belgravian Venus’s. Where does old Blushington get that constant rose tint? What conjuration makes old Blondel’s silver pass for gold? Have you ever seen Lord Hotspur dismount when he thinks nobody is looking? From behind in Rotten Row he is a young thunderbolt; on foot he totters like an umbrella in a gust. Did you ever imagine Dick Lacy—Dick for sixty years—in a natural state, without stays? These are as instructive objects as any elderly beauty; and if a parson wished, he might set such a gentleman in an armchair in the aisle and preach a whole homily upon him, to wholesome use for once. But we stray, while Major Pendennis’s feet cool in their bath and Morgan lifts them out, dries them as carefully as if they were porcelain, and proceeds to set his master upon his legs with waistband and wig, starched cravat, and boots and gloves spotless enough to eat off—though heaven forbid anybody should.

It was during these toilet hours that Morgan and his employer held their confidential conversations; for they met little at other times. The Major detested his own lodging-room as if it were a prison, and Morgan, once letters were delivered and the last curl adjusted, had leisure enough to employ as he pleased.

He employed it among the noblemen’s servants—his acquaintance—so that Morgan Pendennis (for by such compound titles gentlemen’s gentlemen recognise one another) was a frequent guest at tables where the wine was good, the joints well carved, and the talk better than either. He belonged to two influential clubs in Mayfair and Pimlico; and thus, while the town’s great people tried to keep their lives private behind glitter and etiquette, their lives were being discussed downstairs with the exactness of a kitchen inventory. Nothing is secret. Leave a manuscript open on a table, and the maid will read it; quarrel with your friend, and it will be analysed over tea in the lower regions with impartial eloquence; and if another maid drops in, her presence is no restraint—she will contribute her judgment, and carry it home next day. So it is in palaces as in parlours. A duke is no hero to his valet-de-chambre; and his Grace’s Man, at his club among other Men of equal dignity, will speak of his master’s economies, debts, intrigues, and matrimonial schemes with a candour that would shock the master upstairs. If old Pendennis was thought to know everything, and to be deliciously scandalous and discreet, it is only fair to say Morgan foraged much of that knowledge on the kitchen floor and brought it home like game.

Now there had been a drawing-room the previous day; and the Major, sipping his tea, read in the paper the presentation of Lady Clavering by Lady Rockminster, and of Miss Amory by her mother Lady Clavering; and farther down he studied the description of their dresses—those strange names and textures which future antiquaries will puzzle over as they do over dead dialects. The sight of the names carried him back to the country.

“How long have the Claverings been in London?” he asked. “Pray, Morgan, have you seen any of their people?”

“Sir Francis have sent away his foring man, sir,” Morgan replied; “and have took a friend of mine as own man, sir. Indeed he applied on my reckmendation. You may recklect Towler, sir,—tall red-aired man—but dyes his air. Was groom of the chambers in Lord Levant’s family till his Lordship broke hup. It’s a fall for Towler, sir; but pore men can’t be particklar,” said Morgan, and the very sound of his pity was like the clink of plates—melancholy, but practical.

“Devilish hard on Towler, by gad!” said the Major, amused. “And not pleasant for Lord Levant—he, he!”

“Always knew it was coming, sir,” Morgan continued, stropping the razor with a brisk rasping music that seemed part of the household’s acoustic order. “I spoke to you of it Michaelmas was four years: when her Ladyship put the diamonds in pawn. It was Towler, sir, took ’em in two cabs to Dobree’s—and a good deal of the plate went the same way. Don’t you remember seeing of it at Blackwall, with the Levant arms and coronick, and Lord Levant settn oppsit to it at the Marquis of Steyne’s dinner? Beg your pardon; did I cut you, sir?”

He had the Major’s chin in hand, and talked on as the razor went—soft, precise, and dangerous. “They’ve took a house in Grosvenor Place, and are coming out strong, sir. Her Ladyship’s going to give three parties, besides a dinner a week, sir. Her fortune won’t stand it—can’t stand it.”

“Gad, she had a devilish good cook when I was at Fairoaks,” the Major said, with the morality of a man who can feel for a soufflé more readily than for a widow.

“Marobblan was his name, sir; Marobblan’s gone away, sir,” Morgan answered; and the Major, this time with heartfelt sympathy, declared he was “devilish sorry to lose him.”

“There’s been a tremenjuous row about that Mosseer Marobblan,” Morgan went on. “At a ball at Baymouth, sir, bless his impadence, he challenged Mr. Harthur to fight a jewel, sir, which Mr. Arthur was very near knocking him down, and pitchin’ him outawinder, and serve him right; but Chevalier Strong, sir, came up and stopped the shindy—I beg pardon, the holtercation, sir—them French cooks has as much pride and hinsolence as if they was real gentlemen.”

“I heard something of that quarrel,” said the Major. “But Mirobolant was not turned off for that?”

“No, sir—that affair, sir, which Mr. Harthur forgave it him and beayved most handsome, was hushed hup: it was about Miss Hamory, sir, that he ad is dismissial. Those French fellers, they fancy everybody is in love with ’em; and he climbed up the large grape vine to her winder, sir, and was a trying to get in, when he was caught, sir; and Mr. Strong came out, and they got the garden-engine and played on him, and there was no end of a row, sir.”

“Confound his impudence! You don’t mean to say Miss Amory encouraged him?” cried the Major, startled by a particular look—one of those tiny inflections in a servant’s face which carry whole paragraphs of meaning without the risk of plain English.

Morgan became at once as blank and polished as a silver dish. “Know nothing about it, sir. Servants don’t know them kind of things the least. Most probbly there was nothing in it—so many lies is told about families—Marobblan went away, bag and baggage, saucepans, and pianna, and all—the feller ad a pianna, and wrote potry in French, and he took a lodging at Clavering, and he hankered about the primises, and it was said that Madam Fribsy, the milliner, brought letters to Miss Hamory, though I don’t believe a word about it; nor that he tried to pison hisself with charcoal, which it was all a humbug betwigst him and Madam Fribsy; and he was nearly shot by the keeper in the park.”

Thus the Major’s morning, which began with tea and a newspaper, was seasoned with scandal, like pepper shaken over a dish that was already rich enough.

And that very day, by chance, the Major took his post in the great window of Bays’s Club in St. James’s Street, at the hour when you may see half-a-score of respectable old bucks likewise ranged—heads forward, bodies comfortably withdrawn—watching the world pass as they have watched it for years. Bays’s is old-fashioned now, and its members are mostly beyond middle age; but in the Prince Regent’s time these same windows held the same sort of gentlemen, only then they were thought the finest dandies in the empire, whereas time has since altered the cut of their coats and the opinion of the public.

Major Pendennis, peering out, spied his nephew Arthur walking down the street with his friend Mr. Popjoy.

“Look!” said Popjoy to Pen as they passed, in that airy tone with which youth insults age because it has not yet been introduced to it. “Did you ever pass Bays’s at four o’clock without seeing that collection of old fogies? It’s a regular museum. They ought to be cast in wax, and set up at Madame Tussaud’s—”

“—In a chamber of old horrors by themselves,” Pen said, laughing.

“—In the chamber of horrors! Gad, doosid good!” Pop cried. “They are old rogues, most of ’em, and no mistake. There’s old Blondel; there’s my Uncle Colchicum, the most confounded old sinner in Europe; there’s—hullo! there’s somebody rapping the window and nodding at us.”

“It’s my uncle, the Major,” said Pen. “Is he an old sinner too?”

“Notorious old rogue,” Pop said, wagging his head. (“Notowious old wogue,” he pronounced it, making wickedness sound almost affectionate.) “He’s beckoning you in; he wants to speak to you.”

“Come in too,” Pen said.

“—Can’t,” replied Popjoy. “Cut uncle Col. two years ago, about Mademoiselle Frangipane—Ta, ta.” And with that the young sinner sauntered away to Blacquiere’s, where reprobates of his own age made a fresher noise; while Pen turned toward the window full of the elder criminals, and obeyed the Major’s summons.

Better people than Morgan the valet—persons with incomes, principles, and a general belief in arithmetic—were not half so accurately instructed as that gentleman regarding the true bulk and behaviour of Lady Clavering’s fortune. In London, before her Ladyship’s trunks had so much as rattled into Grosvenor Place, her money had already arrived and taken lodgings in everybody’s mouth. It was enormous; it was fabulous; it had a taste of spice, a gleam of diamond, and a rustle of bank-notes so broad that the very sound of it could have kept the mice from nibbling the wainscot.

They talked of indigo factories that dyed whole rivers blue; of opium clippers that sailed like ghosts and returned like gold mines; of banks bursting with rupees—rupees enough, it was said, to pave St. James’s Street and still leave change for Kensington. There were diamonds, too, and jewels of native princes; and interest-money—interest upon interest—paid by generations of moustached potentates who had borrowed from Lady Clavering’s father as naturally as other men borrow salt from a neighbour. Her account at her banker’s was “positively known” (as positively unknown things always are), and the sum had so many ciphers in it that the hearer’s mouth took the shape of the same letter, and remained so.

It was further whispered—whispered in clubs, in conservatories, under fans, and (most venomously) in carriage-corners—that an envoy from an Indian prince was in England at that very moment, negotiating with the Begum Clavering for the sale of a celebrated nose-ring diamond, “the light of the Dewan.” The envoy was a Colonel Altamont, the Nawaub of Lucknow’s prime favourite; an extraordinary man, who had embraced Mahometanism, or had not embraced it, or had embraced everything in turn from a creed to a card-table; and had undergone a thousand adventures, all perilous, all picturesque, and all narrated with the same oath in the middle of them.

Under the title of Begum, Lady Clavering’s fame went forward like the smell of a rich curry in a boarding-house staircase—irresistible, penetrating, and productive of immediate intimacy among persons who were strangers five minutes before. And as writers of our Constitution are forever bragging that we admit merit into our aristocracy, so might we boast—if we chose to boast honestly—that our best society admits wealth with a promptness and cordiality which merit might envy. Let a person be rich enough, and the iron gates fly back as if greased with butter. The haughtiest people are not haughty at all when there is money; they will take your hand, take your dinners, take your daughters, and (if you are lucky) allow you to take theirs; and all with a frankness so British that one almost weeps at the simplicity of it.

Now, while the town was seasoning Lady Clavering’s fortune with every spice of exaggeration, the Chevalier Strong was in the midst of actual domestic cookery of another kind—arranging, preparing, garnishing; not sauces, but salons. Having superintended the country mansion, he now gave the full benefit of his taste to the London upholsterers, and watched the town house being dressed as anxiously as if it were a roast he meant to carve himself.

Honest Strong’s soul rejoiced in hangings and cornices. He hung and re-hung pictures with the air of a man basting them. He studied the positions of sofas as a serious cook studies the placing of dishes—so that nothing should arrive cold, nothing be spilt, and every guest be tempted at the right moment. He interviewed wine merchants and purveyors; he smelt corks, he discussed binning, he spoke of claret as if it were a moral quality. At the same time, with that provident appetite which makes a gentleman’s conscience wonderfully elastic, the Baronet’s confidential friend took the opportunity of furnishing his own chambers and stocking his own snug little cellar. His friends complimented him upon the neatness of the former; and the select guests who dropped in to share Strong’s cutlet now found a bottle of excellent claret to accompany it—deep, quiet wine, that seemed to make a soft church-music in the glass when it was poured.

The Chevalier declared himself, in his own phrase, “in clover.” He had a comfortable set of rooms in Shepherd’s Inn—rooms with a certain legal smell about them, ink and dust and old parchment; but made agreeable by the human inventions of fire, food, and a tolerably clean tablecloth. He was waited on by a former Spanish Legionary and comrade, whom he had once left at a breach in a Spanish fort and afterwards found, by one of those miracles which occur daily in London, at a crossing in Tottenham Court Road. Strong elevated him to the rank of body-servant—both to himself and to the chum who at present shared his lodgings.

That chum was no other than the valiant Colonel Altamont, the Nawaub of Lucknow’s favourite, the very man whose name went about London like a dramatic flourish.

No man was less curious—or, at least, more discreet—than Ned Strong. He did not care to inquire into the mysterious connection which, soon after the meeting at Baymouth, was established between Sir Francis Clavering and the envoy of the Nawaub. The Colonel knew something—some secret, some old story, some paper, perhaps—regarding Sir Francis, which put the Baronet in his power. Strong, who knew that his patron’s youth had been irregular, and his career in India not brilliant, supposed Altamont had a hold of the kind which makes a man’s laughter short and his purse long.

Indeed, Strong had long understood Sir Francis Clavering’s character: a man utterly weak in purpose, principle, and intellect; a moral and physical trifler; a poltroon who could be coaxed, bullied, flattered, frightened—anything but led by his own will, which was not a will so much as a loose string.

Clavering and Altamont had had one or two interviews after Baymouth—conversations of which Sir Francis told Strong nothing, though he constantly sent letters to the Colonel by Strong’s hand, making the Chevalier ambassador in all sorts of affairs. On one occasion Altamont was in such an ill humour that he crushed Clavering’s letter in his fist as if it were a stale crust, and broke out with his own particular emphasis.

“A hundred, be hanged. I’ll have no more letters nor no more shilly-shally. Tell Clavering I’ll have a thousand, or by Jove I’ll split, and burst him all to atoms. Let him give me a thousand and I’ll go abroad, and I give you my honour as a gentleman, I’ll not ask him for no more for a year. Give him that message, Strong, my boy; and tell him if the money ain’t here next Friday at twelve o’clock, as sure as my name’s what it is, I’ll have a paragraph in the newspaper on Saturday; and next week I’ll blow up the whole concern.”

Strong carried the message. Its effect on Sir Francis was such that, on the day and hour appointed, the Chevalier appeared once more at Altamont’s hotel at Baymouth with the sum required. Altamont, being “a gentleman,” behaved as such: he paid his bill, spoke of honour, drank something with a snap to it, and the Baymouth paper announced his departure on a foreign tour. Strong saw him embark at Dover.

“It must be forgery at the very least,” Strong thought—“forgery, or some such handsome crime—that has put Clavering into this fellow’s power; and the Colonel has got the bill.”

But before the year was out, the happy country saw the Colonel again. A confounded run on the red had finished him at Baden-Baden, he said: no gentleman could stand against a colour coming up fourteen times. He had been obliged to draw upon Sir Francis for the means of returning home; and Clavering, though pressed for money—election expenses, country establishment, London furnishing—found means to accept the bill, though with a face as sour as unripe gooseberries. In Strong’s hearing, Sir Francis wished, with many curses, that the Colonel could have been locked up in a debtor’s gaol in Germany for life, so he might never be troubled again.

These sums Sir Francis was obliged to raise without his wife’s knowledge; for though perfectly liberal—nay sumptuous—in expenditure, Lady Clavering had inherited a tolerable aptitude for business along with Snell’s fortune. She gave her husband a handsome allowance, as she thought befitted his rank; and now and then she would make him a present or pay a gambling debt, but she always exacted a pretty accurate account of the money. Regarding subsidies to Altamont, Clavering fairly told Strong he could not speak to his wife.

Part of Strong’s business, therefore, was to procure these sums, and others. In Shepherd’s Inn many negotiations took place between gentlemen of the moneyed world and Sir Francis Clavering; and many bank-notes—crisp, scented faintly of iron and ink—and many pieces of stamped paper passed between them. When a man has been in the habit from youth of borrowing tomorrow to feed today, no good fortune can fatten him for long. A little prosperity is like a rich gravy poured upon a leaky pie; it smells comforting, but it runs out, and presently the money-lender comes back with a spoon.

Clavering found it more convenient to see these gentry at Strong’s lodgings than at his own; and such was the Chevalier’s friendship that, although he did not possess a shilling of his own, his name might be seen as drawer of almost all the bills which Sir Francis accepted. Strong drew, got them discounted in the City, parleyed when they became due, gave instalments, got time in exchange for fresh acceptances—always whisking about, as brisk as a waiter keeping a table supplied while the cook is quarrelling with the butcher in the yard.

And yet, like soldiers in a besieged garrison who act plays and dance at balls while the enemy are outside and the gallows inside, there are hundreds of gallant spirits in London who dine tolerably, laugh agreeably, and sleep comfortably, with a bailiff always somewhere near and a rope of debt round the neck. Ned Strong bore these trifling inconveniences easily. We shall meet more of Shepherd’s Inn another day; for the present, Lady Clavering and her friends have been too long left waiting on the door-steps of Grosvenor Place.

They were first ushered into the dining-room—gorgeous, solemn, and fitted up, Lady Clavering said, she couldn’t for goodness gracious tell why, in the middle-aged style “unless,” she added, laughing good-naturedly, “because me and Clavering are middle-aged people.” Here were offered the copious remains of luncheon which Lady Clavering and Blanche had just partaken.

And now the little Sylphide reappeared—no airy creature of dew and moonshine when no eyes were upon her. When company watched her at dinner, she ate about as much as those six grains of rice of Amina in the Arabian Nights; but now, when nobody was near, she was brisk with knife and fork, and fell upon the mutton cutlets with an appetite so candid and substantial that one could have respected it, had it not been masked so prettily a moment afterwards. She ate as if mutton were a secret she meant to keep; and in this piece of hypocrisy it is believed she resembled other young ladies of fashion.

Pen and his uncle declined the refection, but admired the room with fitting compliments, and pronounced it “very chaste”—that being the proper phrase, like a sauce one must pour whether one likes it or no. There were high-backed Dutch chairs of the seventeenth century that looked as if they had been built for men with shoulder-blades like shields; a carved buffet of the sixteenth; a sideboard robbed out of a church in the Low Countries, with a pious air of having known better days; a great brass cathedral lamp over the round oak table; old family portraits from Wardour Street; tapestry from France; bits of armour; double-handed swords and battle-axes made of carton-pierre and bravely pretending to have slain somebody; looking-glasses; statuettes of saints; Dresden china—nothing, in a word, could be chaster.

Behind the dining-room was the library, fitted with busts and books all of a size (as if knowledge came only by the yard), wonderful easy-chairs, and solemn bronzes in the severe classic style—cold metal gentlemen who seemed to disapprove of digestion. Guarded by double doors, it was here that Sir Francis smoked cigars, read Bell’s Life in London, and went to sleep after dinner, when he was not smoking over the billiard-table at his clubs, or punting at the gambling-houses in St. James’s.

But what could equal the chaste splendour of the drawing-rooms? The carpets were so magnificently fluffy that your foot made no more sound on them than your shadow. This silence had the unnatural hush of a room that has paid to be quiet; the air seemed padded. On the white ground bloomed roses and tulips as big as warming-pans. About were high chairs and low chairs, bandy-legged chairs, chairs so attenuated that it was a wonder any but a sylph could sit upon them without snapping an ankle of gilded wood. There were marquetry tables crowded with gimcracks, china ornaments of all ages and countries, bronzes, gilt daggers, Books of Beauty, yataghans, Turkish papooshes, and boxes of Parisian bonbons—sweetness from abroad, wrapped and perfumed as if meant to distract from any honest English apple.

Wherever you sat there were Dresden shepherds and shepherdesses convenient at your elbow; light-blue poodles in porcelain; ducks and cocks and hens, for the poultry-yard of fashion; nymphs by Boucher and shepherdesses by Greuze, all “very chaste indeed.” Muslin curtains and brocade curtains; gilt cages with parroquets and love-birds; two squealing cockatoos, each out-squealing and out-chattering the other, so that even splendour could not buy good manners from a bird. A clock sang tunes on a console-table; another boomed the hours like Great Tom on the mantelpiece. The result was a curious warfare of noises—whistles, squawks, jingles, and clangs—against that muffled carpeted hush; as if the room, afraid of the honest sound of a human step, had hired machinery and exotic throats to make a racket in its place. One couldn’t help thinking how much kinder it would have been to the nerves—and to civilisation—had somebody simply opened a window and let in the plain breathing of the street, or the far-off honest rumble of wheels that had not been trained to whisper.

Still, in a word, there was everything that comfort could desire and the most elegant taste devise. A London drawing-room fitted up without regard to expense is surely among the noblest and most curious sights of the present day. The Romans of the Lower Empire, the dear Marchionesses and Countesses of Louis XV., could scarcely have had a finer taste than our modern folks exhibit; and everybody who saw Lady Clavering’s reception-rooms was forced to confess they were most elegant, and that the prettiest rooms in London—Lady Harley Quin’s, Lady Hanway Wardour’s, or Mrs. Hodge-Podgson’s (wife of the great Railroad Croesus)—were not fitted up with a more consummate “chastity.”

Poor Lady Clavering, meanwhile, knew little regarding these things, and had a sad want of reverence for the splendours around her. “I only know they cost a precious deal of money, Major,” she said, “and I don’t advise you to try one of them gossamer gilt chairs: I came down on one the night we gave our second dinner-party. Why didn’t you come and see us before? We’d have asked you to it.”

“You would have liked to see Mamma break a chair, wouldn’t you, Mr. Pendennis?” dear Blanche said with a sneer. She was angry because Pen was talking and laughing with Mamma; because Mamma made blunders in describing the house; and for a hundred other good reasons which keep a young lady’s temper in perpetual training.

“I should like to have been by to give Lady Clavering my arm if she had need of it,” Pen answered, with a bow and a blush.

“Quel preux Chevalier!” cried the Sylphide, tossing her little head.

“I have a fellow-feeling with those who fall, remember,” Pen said. “I suffered myself very much from doing so once.”

“And you went home to Laura to console you,” said Miss Amory.

Pen winced. He did not like the remembrance of the consolation; nor was he pleased to find that his rebuff was public property—served up, as it were, cold, and handed round with a smile. Having nothing ready in reply, he became immensely interested in the furniture, praised Lady Clavering’s taste with all his might, and took refuge in “chastity” as in a screen.

“No, don’t praise me,” said honest Lady Clavering. “It’s all the upholsterer’s doings and Captain Strong’s—they did it all while we was at the Park—and—and—Lady Rockminster has been here and says the salongs are very well,” she added, with a tone of great deference, as if “salongs” were a dish whose name she had tasted but could not pronounce.

“My cousin Laura has been staying with her,” Pen said.

“It’s not the dowager: it is the Lady Rockminster,” said Lady Clavering, correcting him with awe, as if there were but one Rockminster and she sat upon a throne of calling-cards.

“Indeed!” cried Major Pendennis at that great name. “If you have her ladyship’s approval, Lady Clavering, you cannot be far wrong. No, no—you cannot be far wrong. Lady Rockminster, I should say, Arthur, is the very centre of the circle of fashion and taste.” And the Major’s voice hushed, and he surveyed the apartments respectfully, as if he had been in a church where the deity was Upholstery.

“Yes, Lady Rockminster has took us up,” said Lady Clavering.

“Taken us up, Mamma,” cried Blanche, sharp as a parrot’s beak.

“Well—taken us up, then,” Lady Clavering answered patiently; “it’s very kind of her, and I dare say we shall like it when we git used to it, only at first one don’t fancy being took—well, taken up—at all. She is going to give our balls for us; and wants to invite all our dinners. But I won’t stand that. I will have my old friends; and I won’t let her send all the cards out, and sit mum at the head of my own table. You must come to me—Arthur and Major—come, let me see, on the 14th. It ain’t one of our grand dinners, Blanche,” she said, looking at her daughter; and Blanche bit her lip and frowned, very savagely for a sylphide who had so lately been so brave with the cutlets.

The Major, smiling and bowing, said he would much rather come to a quiet meeting than to a grand dinner. He had had enough of large entertainments, and preferred the simplicity of the home circle—simplicity, delivered in a drawing-room full of squealing cockatoos and singing clocks.

“I always think a dinner’s the best the second day,” said Lady Clavering, attempting to mend her first speech, and only making it more nourishing. “On the 14th we’ll be quite a snug little party.”

At this second blunder, Miss Blanche clasped her hands in despair. “O, mamma, vous etes incorrigible.”

Major Pendennis vowed he liked snug dinners of all things in the world, and inwardly confounded Lady Clavering’s audacity for asking a man of his consequence to dine upon the second day. But being economical, and considering that he could always throw these people over if something better offered, he accepted with the blandest air. As for Pen, he was not yet a diner-out of thirty years’ standing; and the idea of a fine feast in a fine house was still welcome to him, like the smell of roast meat to a young man with an honest appetite.

When they walked away together, the Major asked, “What was that pretty little quarrel which engaged itself between your worship and Miss Amory? I thought you used to be au mieux in that quarter.”

“Used to be,” Pen answered with a dandified air, “is a vague phrase regarding a woman. Was and is are two very different terms, sir, as regards women’s hearts especially.”

“Egad, they change as we do,” cried the elder. “When we took the Cape of Good Hope, I recollect there was a lady who talked poisoning herself for your humble servant; and, begad, in three months she ran away from her husband with somebody else. Don’t get yourself entangled with that Miss Amory. She is forward, affected, and under-bred; and her character is somewhat—never mind what. But don’t think of her; ten thousand pound won’t do for you. What, my good fellow, is ten thousand pound? I would scarcely pay that girl’s milliner’s bill with the interest of the money.”

“You seem to be a connoisseur in millinery, Uncle,” Pen said.

“I was, sir, I was,” replied the senior. “And the old war-horse, you know, never hears the sound of a trumpet, but he begins to—he, he!—you understand.” And he gave a killing and somewhat superannuated leer and bow to a carriage that rolled by and entered the Park. “Lady Catherine Martingale’s carriage,” he said; “monstrous fine girls the daughters; though, gad, I remember their mother a thousand times handsomer.

“No, Arthur, my dear fellow, with your person and expectations, you ought to make a good coup in marriage some day or other; and though I wouldn’t have this repeated at Fairoaks, you rogue—ha! ha!—a reputation for a little wickedness, and for being an homme dangereux, don’t hurt a young fellow with the women. They like it, sir; they hate a milksop—young men must be young men, you know. But for marriage,” continued the veteran moralist, “that is a very different matter. Marry a woman with money. I’ve told you before it is as easy to get a rich wife as a poor one; and a doosed deal more comfortable to sit down to a well-cooked dinner, with your little entrées nicely served, than to have nothing but a damned cold leg of mutton between you and your wife. We shall have a good dinner on the 14th, when we dine with Sir Francis Clavering. Stick to that, my boy, in your relations with the family. Cultivate ’em, but keep ’em for dining. No more of your youthful follies and nonsense about love in a cottage.”

“It must be a cottage with a double coach-house, a cottage of gentility, sir,” said Pen, quoting the hackneyed ballad of the Devil’s Walk.

But his uncle did not know the poem, and went on with his remarks, pleased with the aptness of the pupil. Arthur Pendennis was a clever fellow who took his colour readily from his neighbour, and found the adaptation only too easy. Warrington, the grumbler, growled that Pen was becoming such a puppy there soon would be no bearing him; but the truth is, the young man’s success and dashing manners pleased his elder companion. The Major liked to see Pen gay and spirited, brimful of health and life and hope; as a man long past being amused by clown and harlequin still takes pleasure in watching a child at a pantomime.

Mr. Pen’s former sulkiness disappeared with his better fortune; and he bloomed as the sun began to shine upon him.

Major Pendennis, having that day engaged himself with nothing more pressing than his own importance, and Arthur, having engaged himself with an amiable vacancy of plan, arrived together at Sir Francis Clavering’s to dine; for there are houses in London where the very door-knocker seems to rap in the accent of “Society,” and the bell rings as if it had been at court.

In the drawing-room they found Sir Francis and Lady Clavering, and Captain Strong. Arthur’s face warmed at sight of the Captain, as a hearth warms at a familiar tread; but the Major’s countenance fell into that prim, pickled expression which he reserved for any man who had the misfortune to be useful for his living. A house-steward at table, thought Major Pendennis, was like a kitchen-ladle on the sideboard: necessary, no doubt, but not to be brought forward among decanters.

His spirits, however, were partly restored by the speedy appearance of Mr. Welbore Welbore, the country neighbour and brother senator; a gentleman of such solid respectability that if you had knocked on him, you might have expected to hear the ring of seven thousand a year. Welbore spoke little; he took no more part in the conversation than the footman behind his chair would have dared to do; but his dullness was ancestral and therefore comforting, and the Major always felt at ease when he could rest his eye upon landed income.

To these came the Dowager Lady Rockminster (who had her own good reasons for being pleasant to the Claverings), and Lady Agnes Foker with her son Harry, our old acquaintance, who looked as if he had been lately taken out of cotton-wool and did not yet know where to put his hands. Mr. Pynsent was detained at the House—those parliamentary duties which sit like lead on some men, and like a feather on others. Last of all, Miss Blanche Amory floated in, and instantly made the room look as if it had been dusted with moonlight.

She wore white silk—white of that insolent sort which seems to say it was born clean—and it displayed her pearly shoulders with the calm assurance of a cook who knows her sauce cannot curdle. Foker, having once whispered to Arthur that he considered her “a stunner,” proceeded to stare at her with the gratitude of a boy who has been suddenly promised pudding for life. Blanche, for her part, chose to be all cordiality and country recollection; she pressed Arthur’s hand, talked of dear Fairoaks, asked after Laura and Mrs. Pendennis, sighed prettily for fields and hedgerows, and presented herself, in short, as innocence with a good dressmaker.

Harry Foker, who ordinarily became dumb in the vicinity of petticoats, found himself miraculously gifted with speech before Blanche, as if her smile had uncorked him. By the time dinner was announced and the party moved down the broad stair, he was almost lively—indeed so much so that his mamma, watching him, looked as astonished as if her son had suddenly begun to speak Greek.

He longed, of course, to offer his arm to the fair Blanche; but she fell to Arthur’s lot, and Harry was allotted—by rank and family arithmetic—to Mrs. Welbore Welbore. He bore it as martyrs bear lesser flames, consoling himself with the hope of manoeuvring at table. Whether the move was his, or arranged by a hand more practised in such games, the event was this: Blanche sat with Arthur on one side and Harry on the other, like a dish placed artfully between two hungry gentlemen, each resolved to be the most attentive carver.

Harry, delighted to be near her, began talking with constant zeal and very little aim. “Seen Taglioni in the Sylphide, Miss Amory? Bring me that suprame of volaille again, if you please,”—this to the attendant, with the gravity of a man ordering cannon—“very good: can’t think where the suprames come from; what becomes of the legs of the fowls, I wonder?” And he fell to humming the air of that prettiest ballet, with the simple conviction that a tune is improved by being pursued and overtaken in public.

“Miss Amory is a sylph herself,” Arthur said.

“What a delightful tenor voice you have, Mr. Foker,” Blanche returned. “I am sure you have been well taught. I sing a little myself. I should like to sing with you.”

Arthur, who remembered having heard something astonishingly like that sentence before, wondered—without asking aloud—how many gentlemen had been honoured with duets since his time. Instead, he leaned on his own melancholy gallantry and said, very tenderly, that he should like to hear her sing again; he had never heard a voice he liked so well.

“I thought you liked Laura’s,” Blanche said, as innocently as a child mentioning a rival dish.

“Laura’s is a contralto,” Arthur replied; “and that voice is very often out.” He spoke bitterly, as if the contralto were a saucepan set aside and forgotten. He went on to complain, half languidly, half affectedly, of professional music—too loud, too showy—of London’s habit of making men old and blasé in a month. Like all old fellows, he said, he cared only for the songs of his youth.

“I like English music best,” Blanche cried. “I don’t care for foreign songs much.”

“Get me some saddle of mutton,” said Mr. Foker, as if he were supporting native art by native meat.

“I adore English ballads,” Blanche continued. “Sing me one of the old songs after dinner, will you?” Arthur asked, with an imploring air; and Blanche, turning to Harry, promised him an English song too—if he would come up soon—flashing him such a broadside of eyes that poor Harry felt himself struck amidships and made water instantly.

“I’ll come up after dinner, fast enough,” he said, simply. “I don’t care about much wine afterwards—I take my whack at dinner—I mean my share, you know; and when I have had as much as I want I toddle up to tea. I’m a domestic character, Miss Amory—my habits are simple—and when I’m pleased I’m generally in a good-humour, ain’t I, Pen?—that jelly, if you please—not that one, the other with the cherries inside. How the doose do they get those cherries inside the jellies?”

This last inquiry he delivered with the profound curiosity of a young food-historian confronting a lost technique. Indeed, a cherry imprisoned in clear jelly is a kind of culinary legend: the fruit lies there like a relic in amber, and you cannot help thinking of all the careful hands—hot syrup tempered, wine measured, the mould cooled just so, the cherries perhaps placed at the exact instant when the setting mass is neither fluid nor firm. Harry did not ask about the labour and timing, but his wonder was honest, and Blanche listened with inexhaustible good-humour, as if the mysteries of the kitchen were charming when explained by an earl’s grandson.

When the ladies rose, Blanche extracted solemn promises from both young men that they would quit the table early, and departed with kind glances that seemed to be rationed out with exact economy. She dropped her gloves on Harry’s side of the table and her handkerchief on Arthur’s, as if she had been feeding two tame creatures in a park and desired no biting.

Harry caught her last glance as she vanished; that bright look travelled across Strong’s broad white waistcoat and struck Harry full in the face. The door closed upon the charmer, and Harry, with a sigh, swallowed a bumper of claret, as if attempting to drown longing in Bordeaux.

The dinner, being one of the smaller sort, had been served at an hour when the day still clung to the windows. Lady Clavering—encouraged by Blanche’s impatience for her piano—made the signal early; the ladies rose while it was yet light enough for the outside world to look alive and unconcerned. From the flower-embroidered balconies above, one could see the two Parks: poor couples and children sauntering on, and equipages rolling through the arch, and horses clipping by with that neat, expensive sound of well-fed hooves.

Down below, the dining-room windows were opened; and there, like a framed picture in lamplight, sat six gentlemen in white waistcoats with decanters, fruit, and that complacent glow which wine puts on faces that have not earned it. Little boys passing would jump at the area-railings to peek, and whisper to one another about pineapple with a yearning as pure as prayer: “Hi hi, Jim, shouldn’t you like to be there and have a cut of that there pineapple?” Outside, too, the city’s soundscape shifted its gears: the clamping tread of the policeman on his beat; the rumble of wheels; the softened chatter of passers-by; then the gasman’s brief metallic business at the lamp, and the sudden little hiss and bloom of flame. Within, the butler lighted the antique chandelier, and the wax-candles made the table look like a shrine to appetite.

Jeames, with folded legs, leaned against the door-pillar and regarded the calm evening as if it were a moral lesson. He was busy attending to the quieter music of the world—the distant roll of carriages, the diminishing shrillness of boys, the polite hush that falls upon a rich street when daylight withdraws. His ear, trained by long service, could tell the footfall of a master from that of a stranger, the jangle of a cab-harness from the more shamefaced rattle of a needy cart.

While he was thus musing, an individual attached himself to the railings opposite and stared into the dining-room with the unabashed interest of a man inspecting his own supper. Policeman X, passing, gave attention to neither the moon nor the butler’s chandelier, but fixed instantly on the gawker—because the policeman’s business in life, like Mr. Strong’s in another line, was to keep certain things moving whether they wished to move or no.

The man at the railings was gorgeously attired in the vulgar splendour of one who has dressed for admiration rather than warmth. Chains, jewellery, a waistcoat that caught the lamplight like fish-scales; shiny boots; brass buttons; great white wristbands over his knuckles; whiskers dyed a Tyrian purple; and a head of black hair that looked like a borrowed thundercloud—everything about him declared “respectability” in a dialect the respectable do not speak. Yet he was grand enough that Policeman X, who had seen many sorts, took him at first for a member of Parliament or some other licensed nuisance.

He was, moreover, flushed with wine; he lurched and reeled with that unsteady gallantry which thinks itself superbly graceful. From the open window came Strong’s laughter—following on one of Strong’s own broad stories—and the stranger outside answered it with an answering snigger, slapping his thigh and winking at Jeames as much as to say, “Plush, my boy, isn’t that a good one?”

Jeames’s attention shifted, unwillingly, from the orderly heavens to this disorderly earth. He remarked later, in the servants’ hall, that a “holtercation” in the street was “never no good,” and he was not hired for any such purpose. But duty, like a kitchen timer, will not be ignored simply because it is inconvenient. So Jeames, after watching the glittering gentleman’s antics, leaned out and softly called, “Pleaceman,” and beckoned to the officer.

X marched up resolute, with one Berlin glove stuck in his belt-side; and Jeames, without another word, pointed calmly with his index finger at the laughing, reeling figure. It was a grand performance in pantomime: Jeames the silent pointer; X the moving authority; the stranger the errant note in the street’s composition.

X stepped up and said, “Now, sir, will you have the kindness to move hon?”

The stranger, being in perfect good-humour, did not seem to hear a syllable. He nodded and waggled his head toward Strong in the window, until his hat nearly toppled over the railings.

“Now, sir, move on, do you hear?” X repeated more sharply, and touched him gently with a gloved finger.

At once the ringed gentleman staggered back into what is called an attitude of self-defence, and began “squaring” at the policeman, brave as a warrior and steady as a jelly just turned from the mould.

“Hullo! keep your hands off a gentleman,” he said, with an oath which is best left to the street.

“Move on out of this,” said X, “and don’t be a blocking up the pavement, staring into gentlemen’s dining-rooms.”

“Not stare—ho, ho,—not stare—that is a good one,” cried the other, with a satiric laugh. “Who’s to prevent me from staring, looking at my friends, if I like? not you, old highlows.”

“Friends! I dessay. Move on,” answered X.

“If you touch me, I’ll pitch into you, I will,” roared the stranger. “I tell you I know ’em all—That’s Sir Francis Clavering, Baronet, M.P.—I know him, and he knows me—and that’s Strong, and that’s the young chap that made the row at the ball. I say, Strong, Strong!”

Within, Sir Francis started with a guilty look. “It’s that d—— Altamont,” he cried; and Strong, annoyed but prompt, rose and ran out.

A gentleman in a white waistcoat running bareheaded into the street; a policeman; an excited well-dressed fellow nearly coming to blows on the pavement—these things are a bell to a neighbourhood. A small crowd began to gather before Sir Francis’s door, for Londoners can resist a sermon, but not a scene.

“For God’s sake, come in,” Strong said, seizing the intruder’s arm. “Send for a cab, James, if you please,” he added under his breath; and, by main force of persuasion, he carried the excited gentleman into the hall and shut the door upon the mob, which immediately dispersed, disappointed to find that respectability, even in trouble, knows how to close its own front door.

Strong intended to usher him into Sir Francis’s private room, soothe him, and slip him away in a cab, like a hot pan removed from the fire before it scorches. But the newcomer, furious at the indignity of being asked to move on, insisted in a thick voice, “That ain’t the door—that’s the dining-room door—where the drink’s going on—and I’ll go and have some, by Jove; I’ll go and have some.”

The butler stood aghast and set himself before the dining-room door. But it opened; Sir Francis appeared, pale and anxious, as if the very house were reproaching him.

“I will have some,—by —— I will,” the intruder bellowed as Sir Francis came forward. “Hullo! Clavering, I say I’m come to have some wine with you; hay! old boy—hay, old corkscrew? Get us a bottle of the yellow seal, you old thief—the very best—a hundred rupees a dozen, and no mistake.”

Sir Francis’s eyes flickered with calculation. Only Welbore, Pendennis, and those two lads, he thought. With a forced laugh and a piteous look—like a man smiling while he hears his own crockery breaking—he said, “Well, Altamont, come in. I am very glad to see you, I’m sure.”

Colonel Altamont—for the intelligent reader will recognise in him His Excellency the Ambassador of the Nawaub of Lucknow—reeled into the dining-room with a triumphant glance at Jeames that said plainly, “There, sir: am I a gentleman or no?” and dropped into the first vacant chair.

Sir Francis timidly stammered the Colonel’s name to Welbore; and Altamont fell to drinking at once, surveying the company with alternating frowns and smiles, hiccupping praise of the liquor in the manner of a critic who has reviewed too many bottles.

“Very singular man,” Strong said gravely, his presence of mind never deserting him. “Has resided long in a native court in India. In those Indian courts they get very singular habits.”

“Very,” said Major Pendennis drily, wondering what infernal dinner-party lottery he had won.

Foker, delighted by the novelty, whispered to Arthur, “It’s the man who would sing the Malay song at the Back Kitchen.” Then, with an air of hospitality, he offered Altamont pineapple. “Try this pine, sir; it’s uncommonly fine.”

“Pines—I’ve seen ’em feed pigs on pines,” said the Colonel.

“All the Nawaub of Lucknow’s pigs are fed on pines,” Strong whispered to the Major.

“Oh, of course,” the Major replied, with a composure which suggested that pigs, pineapples, and Nawaubs were all equally part of the natural order, so long as they remained in India.

Meanwhile Sir Francis tried to explain the Colonel to Welbore, muttering that Altamont was eccentric, had Indian habits, didn’t understand English rules; to which Welbore, sipping steadily, remarked that it did indeed seem pretty clear.

Then Altamont’s attention settled on Arthur. He stared at him with such steadiness as his condition allowed, and said, “I know you, too, young fellow. I remember you. Baymouth ball, by Jingo. Wanted to fight the Frenchman. I remember you;” and he laughed, squared his fists, and acted the recollection with the enthusiasm of a man reenacting a battle in a drawing-room.

“Mr. Pendennis, you remember Colonel Altamont, at Baymouth?” Strong prompted.

Arthur bowed stiffly and said he remembered the circumstance perfectly.

“What’s his name?” cried the Colonel.

Strong repeated it.

“Pendennis!—Pendennis be hanged!” Altamont roared, thumping the table so that decanters trembled.

Major Pendennis drew himself up. “My name is Pendennis, sir,” he said, mortified beyond measure that he, Major Pendennis, should be exposed to this—this public seasoning of vulgarity. “My name is Pendennis, and I will be obliged to you not to curse it too loudly.”

Altamont turned and stared at the Major. And as he stared, something extraordinary happened: it was as if sobriety, like a cold cloth, were suddenly clapped upon his hot head. He put a hand to his forehead and displaced, in doing so, a portion of the black wig he wore; and his eyes fixed on the Major with a fierce, searching look. The Major, a resolute old campaigner in his own way, returned the stare as steadily as if they were measuring one another across a battlefield rather than a dinner-table.

After this silent inspection, Altamont began to button his brass-buttoned coat with a sudden precision, rose abruptly to the astonishment of all, reeled toward the door, and went out, followed instantly by Strong. All that Strong caught him muttering was, “Captain Beak! Captain Beak, by jingo!”

Not a quarter of an hour had passed between the Colonel’s strange entrance and his equally sudden exit. The baronet’s other guests sat blinking at the empty chair, as if the wine had conjured and dismissed a spirit. Sir Francis looked pale, agitated, and turned with almost terror toward Major Pendennis. The Major eyed his host keenly, as if tasting a sauce and detecting an ingredient that had no right to be there.

“Do you know him?” Sir Francis asked, breathless.

“I am sure I have seen the fellow,” the Major replied, puzzled. “Yes, I have it. He was a deserter from the Horse Artillery who got into the Nawaub’s service. I remember his face quite well.”

“Oh!” said Clavering, with a sigh so immense it was almost a confession; and the Major looked at him with a little twinkle, as if noting how quickly relief can rise in a man’s throat when a danger is renamed.

The cab Strong had ordered took away Strong and Colonel Altamont. Coffee was brought. The remaining gentlemen went upstairs to the ladies, and Harry Foker declared confidentially to Arthur that this was “the rummest go he ever saw,” which Arthur, laughing, said showed “great discrimination” on Mr. Foker’s part.

According to her promise, Blanche made music. Foker was enraptured, and joined in such airs as he knew; his big honest voice went blundering after the tune like a well-meaning dog. Arthur affected to talk aside with others; but Blanche drew him back to the piano by singing words of his own—verses we have met before—which she declared she had set to music herself. Whether the air was hers, or arranged for her by Signor Twankidillo, mattered little: Arthur was delighted, and turned her leaves with all the devotion of a man who believes his own syllables taste better when served in another’s voice.

“Gad! how I wish I could write verses like you, Pen,” Harry sighed later. “If I could do ’em, wouldn’t I, that’s all? But I never was a dab at writing, you see, and I’m sorry I was so idle when I was at school.”

No mention was made before the ladies of the queer scene below-stairs. Arthur was on the point of describing it to Blanche when she asked for Captain Strong to join her in a duet. Looking up, Arthur caught on Sir Francis’s ordinarily vacuous face a peculiar expression of alarm—an expression like a servant’s when a dish is in danger of being dropped. Arthur, for once discreet, held his tongue.

The evening, after the excitement, seemed rather dull. Welbore fell asleep as he always did after dinner and at music, as regularly as a clock that strikes only once and then forgets itself. Major Pendennis, who could ordinarily fill any room with anecdotes, scandal, and small poisonous bonbons of society, sat silent for the most part, listening—or pretending to listen—to Blanche, and watching her with an intentness which surprised Arthur almost as much as the compliments that presently followed.

When the hour for departure came, the Major rose and regretted aloud that so delightful an evening should have passed away so quickly. He addressed Blanche with a particularly fine compliment upon her singing. “Your daughter, Lady Clavering,” he said, “is a perfect nightingale—a perfect nightingale, begad! I have scarcely ever heard anything equal to her, and her pronunciation of every language—begad, of every language—seems to me to be perfect; and the best houses in London must open before a young lady who has such talents, and, allow an old fellow to say, Miss Amory, such a face.”

Blanche looked astonished. Arthur looked more astonished still; for the Major had lately spoken of the sylph in terms by no means so worshipful. It was as if, hearing her voice, he had heard also something else—some echo of an accent, some remembered cadence—though he said nothing of that kind, for the Major rarely translated his instincts into words.

The Major and the two young men walked home together after Harry had placed his mother in her carriage and procured a light for an enormous cigar. Harry’s company—or his tobacco—was not agreeable to Major Pendennis, who cast him several side-glances plainly meaning, “Go away, young sir, and smoke somewhere else.” But Harry hung on with the affectionate obstinacy of a man who has found a new subject and intends to wear it out in conversation.

They reached Bury Street. The Major bade the lads good night; and calling Arthur back, whispered confidentially, “Mind you make a point of calling in Grosvenor Place to-morrow. They’ve been uncommonly civil; mons’ously civil and kind.”

Arthur promised, wondering what civility had been cooked up here, and out of what ingredients. Morgan closed the door upon the Major. Harry took Arthur’s arm and walked with him some way in silence, puffing his cigar as if it were a steam-engine dragging his thoughts along the pavement. At last, near Charing Cross, Harry broke out again into his lament over poetry and his idle schooldays; and all the way along the Strand, and up to Arthur’s staircase in Lamb Court, Temple, he did not cease speaking about singing and Blanche Amory—as though her voice had lodged in his ear and would not be translated into any other language.

Since that night in Grosvenor Place—the night which had been fatal to Mr. Harry Foker’s peace and delicious to his vanity—his heart behaved with a most indecorous want of philosophy. You would have sworn, to look at him formerly, that he was one of those young gentlemen who have swallowed the world whole at nineteen, and digest it afterwards with a perpetual yawn: a person who had counselled Pendennis on love as he might have counselled him on boots; who, being blessed with money and leisure, ought by every rule of the fashionable sciences to have become daily more cynical, more satisfied with himself, and more indifferent to all created beings except Harry Foker.

And yet—this is the shameful part—he fell into the common accident, and grew uneasy about a woman; like Achilles in a helmet, Ajax in a sulk, Lord Nelson in a uniform, or Adam in a fig-leaf. Love, that ancient conqueror who has beaten better men with worse weapons, had made a prisoner of him; and the prisoner did not even clank his chains with spirit.

When he returned that night to the Back Kitchen after parting with Arthur Pendennis at the staircase-door in Lamb Court, the gin-twist was no longer a cordial but a reproach; the devilled turkey, once a thing to be toasted and championed, smelt suddenly like yesterday’s bravado. The room was in its usual uproar—pipes ticking, glasses clicking, wit sparking like poor gas in a draughty lantern—yet all the noises of it seemed muffled to him, as if somebody had put cotton in his ears and Blanche Amory in his head. Mr. Hodgen, that amiable minstrel of horrors, sang a new chant—more dreadful, more funny, more fit to make respectable hair sit upright than even “The Body Snatcher.” Harry, being a chief of the place, did his duty, smiled the proper smile, and said “Bravo, Hodgen” with the benevolence of a man awarding a prize at a cattle-show; but he never distinctly heard a syllable of “The Cat in the Cupboard,” which under that title has since gone prowling through London, alarming timid people in drawing-rooms.

Late, and worn as if he had been up roasting himself instead of turkey, he slipped to his rooms, sought his downy pillow, and found that down, which had hitherto been a faithful friend, turned traitor. The fever in him would not let him sleep; and the instant he woke—and he woke a dozen times—Miss Amory’s face sat upright at the foot of his bed like a bright ghost, saying, plainly as if she had spoken through the curtain rings, Here I am. I am your princess. You have discovered me. You shall care for nothing else.

At breakfast-time—if a gentleman may call it breakfast who eats because it is ten o’clock, and not because he is hungry—his former delights looked as stale as cold cutlets. Up to this point he had not been much accustomed to the female society of his own rank. When he spoke of those ladies he called them “modest women,” as if modesty were a kind of starch by which they were stiffened. No doubt the virtue existed; but it had not, in his opinion, made up for a want of other seasoning—pepper, lemon, a dash of daring—that he found more liberally among Mesdemoiselles of the theatre. His mother, Lady Agnes, was tender enough to baste a turkey with her own tears for him, but she did not amuse him. His cousins, the daughters of his maternal uncle, the respectable Earl of Rosherville, wearied him beyond measure. One was blue, and would talk of strata while other people were trying to swallow soup; one rode like a dragoon and smoked cigars as if the world were a barrack; one was Low Church and had views so heterodox that her own sisters shuddered; while the Highest Church sister made a little chapel of her cupboard, and fasted on Fridays with a firmness that would have made a butcher weep. Their paternal house of Drummington Harry could scarcely be got to visit. He swore he would rather go upon the treadmill than stay there; and, in truth, the inhabitants were little fonder of him than he was of them.

Lord Erith, the heir, found Harry deplorably vulgar. Harry found Erith a philanthropic nightcap; the dreariest spouter that ever tried to warm the House of Commons with cold water. Nor could the old earl, George Robert, ever forget a certain evening when he condescended to play billiards with his nephew, and the nephew—upon witnessing a stroke which did not please him—poked his lordship in the side with his cue and remarked, with friendly candour, “Well, old cock, I’ve seen many a bad stroke in my life, but I never saw such a bad one as that there.” His lordship played the game out with angelic sweetness, because Harry was a guest and also a connection; but he was nearly having a fit in the night, and kept to his own rooms afterwards until the young barbarian departed for Oxbridge. The blow was so severe that the incident was never mentioned in family conversation; the earl shunned Harry in London and in the country; and could scarcely be brought to gasp out “How d’ye do?” when compelled to meet him. But he would not break his sister Agnes’s heart by banishing her darling; nor, indeed, could he afford to quarrel with Mr. Foker, senior, between whom and his lordship there had been private transactions—cheques travelling one way, autographs travelling the other—with the letters I O U written, as it were, across the dignity of the signature.

Besides those four daughters with their various peculiarities, his lordship had a fifth girl, Lady Ann Milton; and Lady Ann, from pinafore days, had been destined like a joint in a larder—labelled, reserved, and never to be touched by any other hand. It was ordained between her parents and her aunt that when Mr. Harry Foker came to a proper age, Lady Ann should become his wife. The idea had been put into her mind as naturally as the names of months and the use of a thimble. Harry, the dirtiest of little boys, had come back with black eyes from school to Drummington or Logwood, where Ann lived much with her aunt; and the two young creatures accepted the arrangement with the placidity of children accepting porridge.

It no more entered Lady Ann’s mind to question her father’s order than it would have entered Esther’s to dispute Ahasuerus. The heir-apparent of the house of Foker was equally obedient; for when his father said, in that curt brewer’s fashion which sounds like a mallet on a barrel, “Harry, your uncle and I have agreed that when you’re of a proper age, you’ll marry Lady Ann. She won’t have any money, but she’s good blood, and a good one to look at, and I shall make you comfortable. If you refuse, you’ll have your mother’s jointure, and two hundred a year during my life”—Harry, who knew his sire was a man of few words and strict performance, acquiesced at once, and said, “Well, sir, if Ann’s agreeable, I say ditto. She’s not a bad-looking girl.”

“And she has the best blood in England, sir. Your mother’s blood, your own blood, sir,” said the Brewer with fervour, as though blood were an ale of which the family had the patent. “There’s nothing like it, sir.”

“Well, sir, as you like it,” Harry replied. “When you want me, please ring the bell. Only there’s no hurry, and I hope you’ll give us a long day. I should like to have my fling out before I marry.”

“Fling away, Harry,” answered the benevolent father. “Nobody prevents you, do they?” And so very little more was said. Harry went on with the pursuits that suited him; and in his sitting-room he hung a little picture of his cousin—a simple round face with ringlets—among the French prints, the favourite actresses and dancers, the racing and coaching pieces, the whole gallery of his heart. The little portrait made but a poor show beside Mademoiselle Petitot dancing over a rainbow, or Mademoiselle Redowa grinning in red boots and a lancer’s cap; yet it was there, like a plain biscuit on a plate of sugared confectionery, because the elders had ordered it.

Being engaged and disposed of, Lady Ann Milton did not go so much into the world as her sisters. Often she stayed at home in Gaunt Square when mamma and the other ladies went abroad. They danced with one man after another; the men came and went; the stories about them were various, like dishes at a ball-supper, tasted and discussed and forgotten. But there was only one story about Ann: she was engaged to Harry Foker; she never was to think about anybody else. It was not an amusing story; it had no savour; it was bread-and-water betrothed to champagne.

Now consider the change. The morning after Lady Clavering’s dinner, Harry woke with Blanche’s image looking at him with those clear grey eyes and that smile that seemed to taste of something bright—like a sip of cold wine when you have been drinking hot punch. Her tune, too, rang in his ears: “Yet round about the spot, ofttimes I hover, ofttimes I hover,” and poor Foker began piteously to hum it as he sat up in bed under his crimson silk coverlet.

The room was decorated, as a young gentleman’s room should be if he wishes to prove himself a connoisseur of the lighter arts. Opposite the bed a French print exhibited a Turkish lady and her Greek lover surprised by a venerable Ottoman husband—who looked as if he had been interrupted in his coffee. On the other wall a gentleman and lady rode at full gallop and kissed each other with the reckless gallantry of people who do not care what becomes of the horse. All around were more French prints—gauzy nymphs of the Opera, illustrations of novels, and here and there an English chef-d’oeuvre in which Miss Calverley of T. R. E. O. appeared in tight pantaloons as a page, or Miss Rougemont as Venus, the value of each masterpiece enhanced by a signature in exquisite facsimile: Maria Calverley, Frederica Rougemont, and so forth. Honest Harry delighted in these treasures. He was no worse than many of his neighbours: an idle, jovial, kindly fast man about town; and if his walls were rather too knowing, and his air rather too fragrant with Latakia, why, he was richer than most young men and could afford to gratify his taste. Simple Lady Agnes, when she entered his apartments, was often bewildered by the novelties—like a countrywoman in a spice-shop, sneezing and admiring and not quite understanding.

On the bed-table lay a letter from Miss Calverley, written in a very dégagé style both of spelling and handwriting, scrawling freely over filigree paper, beginning by calling him her dear Hokey-pokey-fokey; and reminding him of the dinner at the Elephant and Castle at Richmond which he had promised to stand. There was a card for a private box at Miss Rougemont’s approaching benefit. There was a bundle of tickets for “Ben Budgeon’s Night, the North Lancashire Pippin, at Martin Faunce’s, the Three-cornered Hat, in St. Martin’s Lane,” where Conkey Sam, Dick the Nailor, and Deadman (the Worcestershire Nobber) were to put on the gloves, and the lovers of the good old British sport were invited to attend. There were keys, sovereigns, cigar-cases—and a little sprig of verbena which Miss Amory had given him, dried already into a kind of aromatic accusation.

Yesterday, all these things had promised pleasure as plainly as a cook-book. This morning they were insipid. What cared he for Conkey Sam or the Worcestershire Nobber? The French prints ogled him in vain. Calverley’s bad spelling and her “Hokey-fokey”—confound her impudence! The notion of dining at Richmond with that old woman (for she was seven-and-thirty if she was a day) filled him with such disgust as a man might feel who has ordered a delicate supper and finds, at the last moment, he must dine upon cold mutton and civility.

When his fond mother saw him, she remarked on the pallor of his cheek and the general gloom of his aspect. “Why do you go on playing billiards at that wicked Spratt’s?” Lady Agnes asked. “My dearest child, those billiards will kill you, I’m sure they will.”

“It isn’t the billiards,” Harry said, gloomily.

“Then it’s the dreadful Back Kitchen,” said Lady Agnes. “I’ve often thought, d’you know, Harry, of writing to the landlady, and begging that she would have the kindness to put only very little wine in the negus which you take, and see that you have your shawl on before you get into your brougham.”

“Do, ma’am. Mrs. Cutts is a most kind motley woman,” Harry said. “But it isn’t the Back Kitchen, neither,” he added, with a sigh as deep as a soup-tureen.

Lady Agnes never denied her son anything, and fell into all his ways with the fondest acquiescence. In return she received his entire confidence. He never thought it necessary to disguise from her his haunts; on the contrary, he brought her home choice anecdotes from clubs and billiard-rooms, which the simple lady relished even if she did not understand. “My son goes to Spratt’s,” she would say to her confidential friends with maternal pride. “All the young men go to Spratt’s after their balls. It is de rigueur, my dear; and they play billiards as they used to play macao and hazard in Mr. Fox’s time. My dear father often told me they sate up always till nine o’clock next morning with Mr. Fox at Brookes’s—whom I remember at Drummington, when I was a little girl, in a buff waistcoat and black satin small-clothes. My brother Erith never played as a young man nor sate up late—he had no health for it; but my boy must do as everybody does, you know. And then he often goes to a place called the Back Kitchen, frequented by all the wits and authors whom one does not see in society, but whom it is a great privilege and pleasure for Harry to meet; and there he hears the questions of the day discussed; and my dear father always said it was our duty to encourage literature—and he had hoped to see the late Dr. Johnson at Drummington, only Dr. Johnson died. Yes, and Mr. Sheridan came over, and drank a great deal of wine—everybody drank a great deal of wine in those days—and papa’s wine-merchant’s bill was ten times as much as Erith’s is, who gets it as he wants it from Fortnum and Mason’s and doesn’t keep any stock at all.”

Harry, who wished this morning to manoeuvre his mother’s good-nature as cleverly as a cook skims a sauce to make it look clear, began artfully on yesterday’s dinner. “That was an uncommon good dinner we had yesterday, ma’am. Their clear soup’s better than ours. Moufflet will put too much tarragon into everything. The suprême de volaille was very good—uncommon—and the sweets were better than Moufflet’s sweets. Did you taste the plombière, ma’am, and the maraschino jelly? Stunningly good that maraschino jelly!”

Lady Agnes expressed agreement, as she did with most sentiments of her son. He went on. “Very handsome house, that of the Claverings. Furniture got up regardless of expense. Magnificent display of plate, ma’am.” She assented again.

“Very nice people the Claverings.”

“H’m!” said Lady Agnes, whose “h’m” could cover a multitude of moral reservations.

“I know what you mean. Lady C. ain’t distangy exactly, but she is very good-natured.”

“Oh, very,” mamma said—she being herself one of the best-natured women alive.

“And Sir Francis—he don’t talk much before ladies; but after dinner he comes out uncommon strong, ma’am—a highly agreeable, well-informed man. When will you ask them to dinner? Look out for an early day, ma’am.” And, peeping into Lady Agnes’s pocket-book as if it were a pantry list, he chose a day only a fortnight hence—an age that fortnight seemed to him—when the Claverings were to be invited to Grosvenor Street.

The obedient Lady Agnes wrote the required invitation without consulting her husband, who had his own society and habits, and left his wife to see her own friends alone. Harry looked at the card when it was done—and found fault with it in a way that would have done credit to a man detecting the absence of a favourite spice.

“You have not asked Miss—whatdyecallem—Miss Emery—Lady Clavering’s daughter.”

“Oh, that little creature!” Lady Agnes cried. “No! I think not, Harry.”

“We must ask Miss Amory,” Foker said, with an air of desperate reasonableness. “I—I want to ask Pendennis; and—and he’s very sweet upon her. Don’t you think she sings very well, ma’am?”

“I thought her rather forward, and didn’t listen to her singing. She only sang at you and Mr. Pendennis, it seemed to me. But I will ask her if you wish, Harry.” And so Miss Amory’s name was written on the card with her mother’s.

This diplomacy achieved, Harry embraced his fond parent with the utmost affection—as if she had just saved him from starvation—and retired to his own apartments, where he flung himself on his ottoman and lay brooding, sighing for the day that would bring Miss Amory under his paternal roof, and devising a hundred wild schemes for meeting her which would, doubtless, have been admirable had he not been Harry Foker.

After his grand tour, Mr. Foker, junior, had imported a polyglot valet, who took the place of Stoopid and condescended to wait at dinner attired in worked muslin shirt-fronts, gold studs, and chains enough to moor a boat. This man—of no particular country, speaking all languages indifferently ill—made himself useful in a variety of ways: read his master’s correspondence, knew his haunts and the addresses of his acquaintance, and officiated at the private dinners the young gentleman gave. As Harry lay on his sofa, robed in a wonderful dressing-gown and puffing in gloomy silence, Anatole must have perceived that something was wrong; but he did not commit the vulgarity of sympathy.

When Harry began to dress for going out, he was intolerable. Pantaloons of many different stripes, checks, and colours were tried and cursed; all the boots were villainously varnished; the shirts too “loud.” He scented his linen and person with peculiar richness this day—as if he meant to enter a room by smell before he entered it by sight; and then, after some blushing and hesitation, he said, “I say, Anatole—when I engaged you—didn’t you—hem—didn’t you say you could—hem—dress hair?”

The valet replied that yes, he could.

“Cherchy alors une paire de tongs,—et—curly moi un peu,” Mr. Foker said with an air of elegant indifference; and Anatole, wondering whether his master was in love or going masquerading, went in search of the tongs—first from the old butler who waited on Mr. Foker senior, on whose bald pate no tongs could have found enough hairs to seize; and finally from the lady who had charge of Lady Agnes’s meek auburn fronts. The tongs being procured, Monsieur Anatole twisted his young master’s locks until Harry’s head was as curly as a negro’s; after which the youth dressed himself with the utmost care and splendour and prepared to sally out.

“At what dime sall I order de drag, sir, to be to Miss Calverley’s door, sir?” the attendant whispered as his master was going forth.

“Confound her!—Put the dinner off—I can’t go!” cried Foker. Then, remembering that Poyntz and Rougemont and ever so many more were coming, and that a gentleman may be a victim without being a defaulter, he added, “No—hang it—I must go. The drag at Pelham Corner at six o’clock, Anatole.”

The drag was not one of Mr. Foker’s own equipages, but hired for festive purposes; yet he put his own carriage into requisition that morning—and for what? To drive down to Lamb Court, Temple, taking Grosvenor Place by the way, which lies in the exact direction of the Temple from Grosvenor Street, as everybody knows; where he had the pleasure of peeping up at Miss Amory’s pink window-curtains; after which feat—having looked at a set of curtains as solemnly as if they were an altar-cloth—he drove off to Pendennis’s chambers.

Why did he need to see Pen so urgently? They had parted in perfect health the night before. Pen had lived two years in London, and Foker had not paid half a dozen visits to his rooms. What sent him now in such haste?

If any young ladies read this page, they may accept the explanation without blushing: when this mishap befalls you—which now, for more than twelve hours, had befallen Harry Foker—people grow interesting to you for whom you did not care sixpence the day before; and persons of whom you fancied yourself fond become suddenly insipid and disagreeable. Eliza or Maria, to whom you wrote letters and sent locks of hair yards long, becomes as indifferent as your stupidest relation; whilst, about his relations, you begin to feel an astonishing tenderness. You will long to ingratiate yourself with his mamma; you will discover a liking for that dear kind old man his father; if he visits any house, what advances you will make to visit there too. If he has a married sister you will spend long mornings with her. You will fatigue your servant by sending notes twice or thrice a day for the most pressing occasions imaginable. You will cry if your mamma objects to your going too often to see his family. The only one of them you will dislike is perhaps his younger brother, who will persist in staying in the room when you come to see the dear new-found friend—his darling second sister.

Something like this happens; let us hope it may. You must go through the hot fits and cold fits of the pretty fever. Your mothers—if they would confess it—passed through it before you were born, your dear papa being the object of the passion, of course; who could it be but he? And as you suffer it, so will your brothers, after their kind—more selfish than you, more headstrong. They rush at their destiny when the doomed charmer appears. Or if they do not, heaven help them; for to love and win is the best thing, and to love and lose is the next best. You do not die of the complaint: very few do. The generous wounded heart suffers and survives it; and he is not a man, nor she a woman, who is not conquered by it—or who does not conquer it—in good time.

So if you ask why Henry Foker, Esquire, was in such a hurry to see Arthur Pendennis, the difficulty is none. Pen had become valuable in his eyes—not because Pen was the rose, but because he had been near the fragrant flower. Did not Pendennis go to her house in London? Did he not live near her in the country? Did he not know all about the enchantress—her very voice, the way her song hung in the air like perfume, and then was gone? What, one wonders, would Lady Ann Milton—Mr. Foker’s cousin and prétendue—have said if her ladyship had known what was going on in the bosom of that funny little gentleman?

Poor Foker’s Richmond dinner—bought with honest guineas and seasoned with melting ices—lay upon his spirits like a wet napkin on a soufflé.
