He sat at the head of his own table, amid a wreck of dessert as showy and as joyless as a sugared bride-cake left out in the rain: pineapples hacked into golden ruin; ices slumping into pale puddles; claret bottles standing about like soldiers that had done their duty and fallen where they could. Cigar-ash freckled the fruit, and the whole air had that disagreeable perfume of stale smoke and sweet stuff mixed together, as if somebody had tried to preserve a peach in a chimney.

“I wonder how the deuce I ever could have liked these people,” he said to himself, scraping his thoughts together as a cook scrapes the bottom of a pan that has caught. “Why, I can see the crow’s-feet under Rougemont’s eyes, and the paint on her cheeks is laid on as thick as Clown’s in a pantomime! Calverley’s slang is like burnt gravy—sticky, black, and everywhere. And old Colchicum—old Col—coming down here in his brougham with his coronet on it, and sitting bodkin between Mademoiselle Coralie and her mother! A peer and a horse-rider of Franconi’s! It won’t do. By Jove, it won’t do. I ain’t proud; but it will not do!”

“Twopence-halfpenny for your thoughts, Fokey!” cried Miss Rougemont, drawing at her cigar with lips as violently vermilion as if they had been dipped like a ladyfinger in cochineal. She looked him over with the connoisseurship of a dancer appraising a costume, and found him—unusually—quiet.

“Does Foker ever think?” drawled Poyntz, whose voice always sounded as though it had been trained to doze off mid-sentence, like a kettle that won’t boil. “Foker, a fair capitalist at this end of the table offers a considerable sum for the present emanations of your valuable intellect.”

“What the deuce is Poyntz a-talking about?” snapped Miss Calverley to her neighbour. “I hate him. He’s a drawlin’, sneerin’ beast.”

“What a droll of a little man is that little Fokare, my lor’,” said Mademoiselle Coralie in her sunny Gascon French, which had a twang like a guitar-string—warm, bright, and a little saucy. “He does not look to have twenty years.”

“I wish I were of his age,” sighed the venerable Colchicum, inclining his purple countenance to a great goblet of claret with the affection of an old epicure bending toward a remembered sauce.

“C’te jeunesse. Peuh! je m’en fiche,” said Madame Brack, taking a heroic pinch from my lord’s delicate gold snuff-box with fingers that looked capable of doing mischief in any dish they touched. “Je n’aime que les hommes faits, moi. Comme milor. Coralie! n’est-ce pas que tu n’aimes que les hommes faits, ma bichette?”

My lord grinned, pleased in the way of old gentlemen who like being called “fine,” even when the compliment is flung like salt. “You flatter me, Madame Brack.”

“Taisez-vous, Maman, vous n’etes qu’une bête,” Coralie cried, shrugging robustly; whereupon my lord observed, with a chuckle, that she did not flatter at any rate, and he pocketed his snuff-box as a careful housekeeper pockets the last nutmeg when a guest seems disposed to grate it all.

There is no need to ladle out the rest of that conversation for the reader, as one spares a friend the dregs at the bottom of a punch-bowl. It would not edify. Only, remember: not all ladies of the ballet are like Miss Calverley, nor all peers like the late Viscount Colchicum; though there have been such, and there have also been respectable gentlemen who objected less to the entertainment than to the noise made about it. Major Pendennis, for example, would never have said no to pleasure—provided it was served in a private room, with a proper lid on it, and a few great names to garnish the dish.

“Give the young men their pleasures,” that worthy guardian had said to Pen more than once. “I’m not one of your strait-laced moralists, but an old man of the world, begad; and I know that as long as it lasts young men will be young men.” And he had known some young men for whom he allowed a respectable seventy years as the natural season for sowing wild oats—if they were men of fashion, and the oats were sown in the right fields.

That night Foker drove his lovely guests home to Brompton in the drag; but he was as silent as a man who has eaten too much sugar and is ashamed of his stomach. The jokes behind him pattered like peas on a drum. Usually he would have answered with his own merry racket; now he sat with his shoulders a little hunched, as if the very harness of his gaiety pinched him.

When the ladies alighted and asked whether he would step in and take something to drink, he declined with such a tragical politeness that they fancied the Governor had scolded him, or that the brewery had burnt down. He said nothing of what truly ailed him. He left Mesdames Rougemont and Calverley, unheeding even the latter’s cries from her balcony—hanging over it like Jezebel at the window—bidding him give another party soon.

He sent the drag home with a groom and went on foot himself, hands in pockets, mind in the sort of stew where nothing tastes right. The stars and moon shone tranquilly overhead; London’s distant hum rose and fell like the sea heard through shutters; and the nearer sounds—the clop of late horses, the rattle of a returning carriage, a watchman’s measured call—were all so composed, so cleanly spaced, that they seemed to mock his inner clatter. In such a nightly soundscape one ought, by rights, to feel soothed; but passion is an ill-bred guest, and will not keep time with the street.

He went and gazed up at the house in Grosvenor Place, at the windows he supposed to be those of the beloved object, as if her very curtains were a holy relic. He moaned and sighed in a fashion piteous enough. Policeman X saw him, and later informed Sir Francis Clavering’s people—who were taking beer on a coach-box at a neighbouring public-house, after bringing home their lady from the French play—that there had been “another chap hanging about the premises that evening—a little chap, dressed like a swell.”

And now, with that ingenuity which belongs only to a certain passion—keen as a kitchen-boy’s nose for pies—Mr. Foker began to dodge Miss Amory through London and to appear wherever she could be met, like parsley sprinkled on every dish whether it suits or not.

If Lady Clavering went to the French play, where her ladyship had a box, Mr. Foker—whose knowledge of French was as thin as a watered consommé—appeared in a stall, straining his ears and smiling at things he did not understand. He found out where her engagements were (it is possible Anatole, his man, made acquaintance with Sir Francis Clavering’s gentleman and had a peep at her ladyship’s engagement-book), and at many evening parties Mr. Foker appeared—astonishing the world, and astonishing his mother most of all, for he ordered Lady Agnes to apply for cards to entertainments he had hitherto treated with contempt.

To the pleased and unsuspicious lady he said he went to parties because it was right to see the world. He said he went to the French play to perfect himself in the language, and that there was no lesson like a comedy or vaudeville. And when one night Lady Agnes saw him stand up and dance, and complimented his elegance and activity, the mendacious little rogue protested he had learned to dance in Paris, whereas Anatole knew perfectly well his young master used to slip off privily to an academy in Brewer Street and study steps there in the morning, as earnestly as a cook studying sauces.

The modern casino was not yet invented, or was still in its cradle; and gentlemen of Mr. Foker’s time had not the facilities for acquiring the science of dancing which our present youth enjoy, who can learn a quadrille as easily as they order an oyster—quick, loud, and fashionable.

Old Major Pendennis seldom missed church. He considered it a gentleman’s duty to patronise public worship, and that it was a correct thing to be seen on a Sunday in a pew. One day it happened he and Arthur went thither together: Pen, in high favour just now, had breakfasted with his uncle, and they walked across the Park to a church not far from Belgrave Square.

“There is a charity sermon at Saint James’s,” the Major said, having read the bills on the pillars of his parish church; and the word “charity,” like the word “discount,” could turn him as surely as a tide. “We will go across the Park; and then, begad, we will go to the Claverings’ and ask them for lunch in a friendly way. Lady Clavering likes to be asked for lunch—monstrous hospitable.”

“I met them at dinner last week at Lady Agnes Foker’s, sir,” Pen said. “The Begum was very kind indeed. She is kind everywhere. But I share your opinion about Miss Amory—one of your opinions, that is; for you were changing the last time we spoke about her.”

“And what do you think of her now?” asked the elder, turning his head as if to sniff for scandal the way a housewife sniffs for smoke.

“I think her the most confounded little flirt in London,” Pen answered, laughing. “She made a tremendous assault upon Harry Foker, who sat next to her, and to whom she gave all the talk, though I took her down.”

“Bah! Henry Foker is engaged to his cousin; all the world knows it. Not a bad coup of Lady Rosherville’s. I should say young Foker, at his father’s death—old Foker’s life’s devilish bad; you know he had a fit at Arthur’s last year—I should say young Foker won’t have less than fourteen thousand a year from the brewery, besides Logwood and Norfolk property. I’ve no pride about me, Pen. I like a man of birth, certainly; but dammy, I like a brewery that brings in fourteen thousand a year. Ha, ha! That’s the sort of man for me. Stick to fellows of that sort now you’re launched—fellows with a stake in the country, begad.”

“Foker sticks to me, sir,” Pen said. “He has been at our chambers several times lately. He has asked me to dinner. We are almost as great friends as in our youth. And his talk is about Blanche Amory from morning till night. I’m sure he’s sweet upon her.”

“I’m sure he is engaged to his cousin, and they will keep the young man to his bargain,” the Major said. “Marriages in these families are affairs of state. Lady Agnes was made to marry old Foker by the late Lord, though she was notoriously partial to her cousin killed at Albuera—saved her life out of the lake at Drummington, too. I remember Lady Agnes an exceedingly fine woman. But what did she do? Of course she married her father’s man. Foker sate for Drummington till the Reform Bill, and paid dev’lish well for his seat. And you may depend upon it, sir, Foker senior, a parvenu who loves great men as all parvenus do, has ambitious views for his son. Harry must do as his father bids him. I’ve known a hundred cases of love in young men and women: they kick, they resist, they make a riot; but they end by listening to reason, begad.”

“Blanche is a dangerous girl, sir,” Pen said. “I was smitten with her myself once, and very far gone too. But that was years ago.”

“Were you? How far did it go? Did she return it?” asked the Major, looking hard at him—so hard that Pen felt as though he were being carved like a joint.

Pen laughed and said that at one time he thought he was pretty well in Miss Amory’s good graces, but his mother did not like her, and the affair went off. He did not think fit to serve up all the particulars of that old dish again.

“A man might go farther and fare worse, Arthur,” the Major said, still looking queerly. “Her birth—her father was the mate of a ship, they say—and she has not money enough,” Pen objected, dandifying himself with the air of a man rejecting a pudding because the plate is plain.

“What’s ten thousand pound and a girl bred up like her?”

“You use my own words, and it is all very well. But I tell you in confidence—in strict honour, mind—that it’s my belief she has a devilish deal more than ten thousand. And from what I saw of her the other day, and—and have heard—I should say she’s a devilish accomplished, clever girl; would make a good wife with a sensible husband.”

“How do you know about her money?” Pen asked, smiling. “You seem to have information about everybody.”

“I do know a few things, sir, and I don’t tell all I know. Mark that.” And as if to cap the dish with a secret sauce, he added, “And as for that charming Miss Amory—charming, begad! she is—if I saw her Mrs. Arthur Pendennis, I should neither be sorry nor surprised, begad! And if you object to ten thousand, what would you say to thirty, or forty, or fifty?” The Major’s eyes glittered like a man counting coin in candlelight.

“Well, sir,” Pen said to his godfather and namesake, “make her Mrs. Arthur Pendennis. You can do it as well as I.”

“Psha! you are laughing at me, sir,” the Major replied peevishly. “And you ought not to laugh so near a church gate. Here we are at St. Benedict’s. They say Mr. Oriel is a beautiful preacher.”

The bells were tolling; the people streamed in; the carriages rolled up and discharged their pretty loads of devotees, rustling and murmuring like a flock settling. Pen, who from habitual feeling was always more than respectful in a place of worship, had a moment’s sense of the oddness of their talk—as if they had been discussing recipes at the very mouth of a fast. The Major, beside him, felt no incongruity whatever. His hat was brushed; his wig was trim; his neckcloth perfectly tied. He looked at every soul in the congregation—the bald heads and bonnets, the flowers and feathers—with a demure air, hardly lifting his eyes from his book (which he could not read without glasses).

Pen’s gravity, however, was sorely tried when, glancing toward the servants’ seats, he spied Henry Foker, Esquire, by the side of a demure gentleman in plush, having discovered this particular avenue to Heaven. Harry’s eye strayed from his book as readily as a spoon from a plate, and following its direction Pen found it fixed upon two bonnets—a yellow and a pink—perched on the heads of Lady Clavering and Blanche Amory.

If the Major was not the only man to carry worldly affairs to the church door, Harry was certainly not the only one to smuggle worldly love into the aisle.

When the congregation issued forth at the conclusion of the service, Foker was among the first out, but Pen came up with him as he lingered about the entrance, unwilling to leave until my lady’s barouche, with its bewigged coachman, had borne away mistress and daughter from their devotions.

When the two ladies emerged, they found the Pendennises—uncle and nephew—and Harry Foker, sucking the crook of his stick, standing in the sunshine as if waiting for a dinner-bell.

To see and to ask to eat were simultaneous with the good-natured Begum. She invited the three gentlemen to luncheon straightway.

Blanche was particularly gracious. “Oh, do come,” she said to Arthur, “if you are not too great a man. I want so to talk to you about—but we mustn’t say what, here, you know. What would Mr. Oriel say?” And she jumped into the carriage after her mamma. “I’ve read every word of it. It’s adorable,” she added, still addressing Pen.

“I know who is,” said Mr. Arthur, making rather a pert bow.

“What’s the row about?” asked Mr. Foker, puzzled.

“I suppose Miss Clavering means ‘Walter Lorraine,’” said the Major, nodding with the air of a man who has smelt the roast and knows what joint it is.

“I suppose so, sir. There was a famous review in the Pall Mall this morning. It was Warrington’s doing though, and I must not be too proud.”

“A review in Pall Mall? Walter Lorraine? What the doose do you mean?” Foker cried. “Walter Lorraine died of the measles, poor little beggar, when we were at Grey Friars. I remember his mother coming up.”

“You are not a literary man, Foker,” Pen said, laughing, and hooking his arm into his friend’s. “You must know I have been writing a novel, and some of the papers have spoken very well of it. Perhaps you don’t read the Sunday papers?”

“I read Bell’s Life regular, old boy,” Mr. Foker answered; at which Pen laughed again, and the three proceeded in good humour to Lady Clavering’s.

After luncheon Blanche resumed the subject of the novel, for she loved poets and men of letters—if she loved anything—with a sincerity that had at least the merit of being excited by something other than money. “Some of the passages made me cry,” she said. “Positively they did.”

Pen, with some fatuity, replied, “I am happy to think I have a part of vos larmes, Miss Blanche.” And the Major—who had not read more than six pages of Pen’s book—put on his sanctified look and said, “Yes—there are some passages quite affecting—mons’ous affecting.”

“Oh, if it makes you cry,” Lady Amory declared, “I wouldn’t read it. I wouldn’t.”

“Don’t, mamma,” Blanche said, with a French shrug; and then she fell into rhapsodies about the book: the snatches of poetry interspersed; the two heroines, Leonora and Neaera, served up like twin dishes to be compared; the two heroes, Walter Lorraine and his rival the young Duke—“and what good company you introduce us to,” she said archly. “Quel ton! How much of your life have you passed at court? Are you a prime minister’s son, Mr. Arthur?”

Pen laughed. “It is as cheap for a novelist to create a Duke as to make a Baronet. Shall I tell you a secret? I promoted all my characters at the request of the publisher. The young Duke was only a young Baron when the novel was first written; his false friend the Viscount was a simple commoner—and so on with all the story.”

“What a wicked, satirical, pert young man you have become! Comme vous voilà formé!” Blanche cried. “How different from Arthur Pendennis of the country! Ah! I think I like Arthur Pendennis of the country best, though!” And she gave him the full benefit of her eyes—first the fond, appealing glance, then the modest look down toward the carpet which showed the dark lids and long fringed lashes as a cook shows the gloss on a well-braised ham.

Pen, of course, protested he had not changed in the least. Blanche sighed tenderly; and having, as she judged, basted Arthur enough for the present—happy or miserable, whichever he chose to be—she proceeded to cajole his companion, Mr. Harry Foker, who during the literary talk had sat sucking his cane and wishing he were a clever chap like that Pen.

If the Major thought that by telling Miss Amory of Mr. Foker’s engagement to his cousin Lady Ann Milton—an item of intelligence he neatly slipped to the girl as he sat by her at luncheon—he would prevent Blanche from paying further attention to the young heir of Foker’s Entire, he was entirely mistaken. She became only the more gracious. She praised Harry, and everything belonging to him: praised his mamma; praised the pony he rode in the Park; praised the lovely breloques and gimcracks at his watch-chain; praised that dear little darling of a cane; praised those delicious monkeys’ heads with ruby eyes that ornamented his shirt and made the buttons of his waistcoat—till Harry blushed and tingled with pleasure like a boy offered extra jam.

Then, having seasoned him to her taste, she turned and took another theme.

“I am afraid Mr. Foker is a very sad young man,” she said, looking round at Pen.

“He does not look so,” Pen answered, with a sneer.

“I mean we have heard sad stories about him. Haven’t we, mamma? What was Mr. Poyntz saying here the other day, about that party at Richmond? Oh, you naughty creature!” And seeing Harry’s face turn to alarm, and Pen’s to amusement, she flashed back to Arthur: “I believe you are just as bad. I believe you would have liked to have been there—wouldn’t you? I know you would. Yes—and so should I.”

“Lor, Blanche!” cried mamma.

“Well, I would. I never saw an actress in my life. I would give anything to know one; for I adore talent. And I adore Richmond. And I adore Greenwich. And I say I should like to go there.”

“Why should not we three bachelors,” the Major broke out gallantly—to Pen’s special surprise—“beg these ladies to honour us with their company at Greenwich? Is Lady Clavering to go on forever being hospitable, and may we make no return? Speak for yourselves, young men—eh, begad! Here is my nephew with his pockets full of money—his pockets full, begad!—and Mr. Henry Foker, who, as I have heard say, is pretty well to do in the world. How is your lovely cousin, Lady Ann, Mr. Foker? Here are these two young ones—and they allow an old fellow like me to speak. Lady Clavering, will you do me the favour to be my guest? And Miss Blanche shall be Arthur’s—if she will be so good.”

“Oh, delightful!” cried Blanche.

“I like a bit of fun too,” said Lady Clavering. “And we will take some day when Sir Francis—”

“When Sir Francis dines out—yes, mamma,” Blanche finished, with the practical innocence of a girl arranging the cupboard before the cat comes in. “It will be charming.”

And a charming day it was.

The dinner was ordered at Greenwich; and if the fare was not immortal, it was at least honest—fish with the clean smell of river and salt, meat that had been properly rested, sauces not bullied by too much flour, and a bottle or two behaving better than those at Richmond. There was talk enough, and laughter enough, and—best of all for Harry—delicious opportunities of conversation with Blanche during the repast, and afterwards on the balcony of their room at the hotel, where the river moved below with a soft wash like a great spoon stirring in a basin. The very sound of it seemed to soothe the mind, until a passing steamer coughed its industrial racket into the evening, shaking the air as if modern life could not bear to let any old music play undisturbed.

They drove home in her ladyship’s barouche. Pen came down with his uncle in Sir Hugh Trumpington’s brougham, which the Major borrowed for the occasion.

“I am an old soldier, begad,” he said; “and I learned in early life to make myself comfortable.”

And being an old soldier, he allowed the two young men to pay for the dinner between them; and all the way home, in the borrowed brougham, he rallied Pen about Miss Amory’s evident partiality for him, praised her good looks, spirits, and wit, and again told him—under the strictest confidence—that she would be a devilish deal richer than people thought.

Some time ago—when Arthur Pendennis had been beaten by Oxbridge, and had retired home to nurse his pride with ink—he produced, among other smaller calamities, the larger portion of a novel. Youth, being unable to pickle itself properly, will often try preserving in German vinegar; and Pen, who had lately been learning that language, had steeped his hero in a marinade of imported misery. The result was a Walter Lorraine saturated with Byronic black pepper, Wertherian vinegar, and a Mephistophelean dash of bitter herbs, all pounded together with the hot impatience of nineteen, and served up smoking, in a dish too large for the appetite.

If the secret history of books were written—if you could see, alongside each paragraph, the author’s private weather, and what he had eaten, and what he had not eaten, and whom he had met at tea, and whom he had not—many a thin volume would suddenly acquire the richness of a stew that has simmered all night. As it was, Pen, now older and with his emotions no longer kept at a perpetual rolling boil, looked back over his pages with the odd expression of a cook who has discovered the recipe-book of his apprenticeship: here he had salted too fiercely; there he had forgotten the salt altogether; and there—yes, there was a passage he had once thought original, which now tasted undeniably of somebody else’s kitchen.

He could remember, too, the very hour and place where certain sentences had been thrown in, as one remembers where one first tasted a sharp cheese, or drank a too-sweet punch, and vowed never again. The feeling returned like a ghostly flavour on the palate—faint, undeniable, and slightly ridiculous. And what were those stains? Not ink alone. There are blots in young men’s manuscripts as there are rings on a table where hot cups have stood: signs that something once scalding was there. The spring had run, and dried.

One morning he described all this to Warrington—who sat entrenched behind a pipe and a book, making a private fog of Lamb Court, as content as any city-dweller can be who pays for air and receives coal-smoke. Pen, excited in his way, talked with hands as well as tongue; and as he brought the manuscript down on the table, the tea-things rattled, and the blue milk shivered in the jug like a small frightened lake.

He had fetched the packet the night before from a long-neglected chest crammed with relics: old shooting-jackets, old Oxbridge scribbling-books, an obsolete surplice, a cap and gown battered as if by the very logic of his examiners—mementoes that smelt of camphor, stale cloth, and the dead, sweet dust of bygone ambition. He had read the beginning in bed until he fell asleep, partly because the commencement was dull, and partly because he had returned late from a London party and the room itself seemed to yawn.

“By Jove!” he cried now, thumping the papers again, “when I think these lines were written only a few years ago, I’m ashamed of my memory. I wrote this when I believed myself eternally in love with that little coquette, Miss Amory. I used to carry down verses to her, and put them into the hollow of a tree, and dedicate them ‘Amori.’”

“That was a sweet little play upon words,” Warrington said, letting out a puff as if he were offering incense to the god of Scholarship. “Amory—Amori. It showed proof of learning. Let us hear a bit of the rubbish.”

And with the fire-tongs—just employed to coax a coal into his pipe—he reached across, seized the manuscript as if it were a joint to be carved, and began to read aloud from the title-page with an air of mock ceremony: Leaves from the Life-book of Walter Lorraine.

“‘False as thou art beautiful! heartless as thou art fair! mockery of Passion!’ Walter cried, addressing Leonora; ‘what evil spirit hath sent thee to torture me so? O Leonora—’”

“Cut that part!” Pen sprang forward, crimson. “Don’t read it out, at least. That’s about my other flame—my first—Lady Mirabel that is now. I saw her last night at Lady Whiston’s. She asked me to a party at her house and said that, as old friends, we ought to meet oftener. She’s been seeing me any time these two years in town and never thought of inviting me before; but seeing Wenham talking to me, and Monsieur Dubois—the French literary man—with a dozen orders on, like a walking pastry-shop of decorations, she condescended to remember I existed. The Claverings are to be there the same evening. Won’t it be exciting to meet one’s two flames at the same table?”

“Two flames!” Warrington said. “Two heaps of burnt-out cinders.”

“Both beauties are in the book, then?”

“Both, or something like them,” Pen admitted. “Leonora, who marries the Duke, is the Fotheringay. I drew the Duke from Magnus Charters, with whom I was at Oxford; it’s a little like him. Miss Amory is Neaera. By gad, that first woman! I thought of her walking home from Lady Whiston’s in the moonlight, and the whole early scenes came back as if they’d happened yesterday. When I got in, I pulled out the story I wrote about her and the other three years ago; and do you know, outrageous as it is, it has some good stuff in it. If Bungay won’t publish it, I think Bacon will.”

“That’s the way of poets,” Warrington said. “They fall in love; they are jilted, or jilting; they suffer; they proclaim no other mortal ever suffered so exquisitely; and when they have experienced feelings enough, they bottle them and carry the bottle to market. All poets are humbugs. All literary men are humbugs. Directly a man begins to sell his feelings for money he’s a humbug. If a poet gets a pain in his side from too good a dinner, he bellows Ai! Ai! louder than Prometheus.”

“I suppose a poet has a greater sensibility than another man,” Pen said, with spirit—rather as if defending the cook’s right to taste. “That’s what makes him a poet. He sees and feels more keenly: that’s why he speaks of what he sees and feels. You speak eagerly enough in your leading articles when you spy a false argument, or detect a quack in the House. Paley, who doesn’t care for anything else on earth, will talk for an hour about a question of law. Give another man the privilege you take yourself; let him use his faculty freely; let him be what nature has made him. Why should not a man sell his sentimental thoughts as well as you your political ideas, or Paley his legal knowledge? Each alike is experience and practice. It isn’t money that makes you perceive a fallacy or Paley argue a point; it’s aptitude. A poet sets down his thoughts and experiences on paper as a painter sets down a landscape, to the best of his ability, according to his gift. If ever I think I’ve the stuff to write an epic, by Jove I’ll try. If I only feel I’m good enough to crack a joke or tell a story, I’ll do that.”

“Not a bad speech, young one,” Warrington said, “but it does not prevent all poets from being humbugs.”

“What—Homer, Aeschylus, Shakspeare and all?”

“Their names are not to be breathed in the same sense with you pigmies,” Warrington answered. “There are men and men, sir.”

“Well, Shakspeare wrote for money, just as you and I do,” Pen said.

Warrington, who loved him, and yet could not bear his impudence without punishing it by silence, resumed his pipe and his reading.

There was no doubt that Walter Lorraine contained a great deal of Arthur Pendennis in disguise—like a ragout that pretends to be hare while every guest knows it is chiefly yesterday’s mutton. The tale would never have been cooked at all but for Pen’s private griefs, passions, and follies. As we already know those ingredients, there is no need to ladle out extracts; and besides, the narrator has a tenderness for the reader’s digestion.

Pen had kept the manuscript in his box for nearly half the length of time which a certain Horatian maxim recommends for the ripening of works of art—a maxim, by the way, which is easier to quote than to practise, and easier still to doubt. He had not laid it by because he believed it would improve in a crypt, like a great wine. He laid it by because he did not know where else to put it, and had no urgent desire to taste it again. A man who says he will hide his composition for ten years should be very sure it is a cheese meant for keeping; otherwise, when he opens it, he may find it has not grown richer, only blander.

Pen had never imagined, even in his most feverish days, that his novel was a masterpiece, or that he stood shoulder to shoulder with the giants he admired. Reading it now, he was sufficiently alive to its faults and modest enough about its merits. It was not very good; but it was, he thought, as good as most of the things that rolled through the circulating libraries like so many carriages in a fashionable street—some handsome, some rickety, all going somewhere because people paid to ride.

He had looked critically into more than one popular book of the day and thought, with the cheerful insolence of youth, that he could handle English as well as those ladies or gentlemen who were being praised for it; and as he ran over his own pages he was pleased to find here and there passages with a certain vigour—flashes, if not of genius, at least of genuine heat.

This, too, was Warrington’s verdict. After half an hour’s perusal and the consumption of two pipes, that severe critic laid the manuscript down with a yawn that seemed to open the very cellar of boredom.

“I can’t read any more of that balderdash now,” he said; “but there’s some good stuff in it, Pen, my boy. There’s a greenness and freshness in it I like. The bloom disappears off the face of poetry after you begin to shave. You can’t get up that artless rosy tint later. Your cheeks are pale now, faded by evening parties; you’re obliged to take curling-irons, and macassar, and the Lord knows what to your whiskers; they curl ambrosially, you’re very grand and genteel; but, ah, Pen, the spring-time was the best.”

“What the deuce have my whiskers to do with the subject?” Pen cried—nettled, for it was true: those whiskers were treated less like hair than like a delicate sauce, coaxed and perfumed and made to stand up as if presenting arms. “Do you think we can do anything with Walter Lorraine? Shall we take him to the publishers, or make an auto-da-fé of him?”

“I don’t see what good there is in incremation,” Warrington said, “though I’ve half a mind to put him into the fire to punish your atrocious humbug. Shall I burn him indeed? You have too great a value for him to let a hair of his head be harmed.”

“Have I? Here goes,” Pen said; and Walter Lorraine went off the table and onto the coals.

But the fire, having done its honest duty of boiling the breakfast-kettle, had given up work for the day and gone out—exactly as Pen knew. Warrington, with a scornful smile, took up the manuscript with the tongs from the harmless grey cinders.

“Oh, Pen, what a humbug you are!” he said. “And worst of all, a clumsy humbug. I saw you look to see the fire was out before you sent Walter Lorraine behind the bars. No, we won’t burn him. We’ll carry him to the Egyptians and sell him. We’ll exchange him for money—yea, for silver and gold, and for beef, and for liquors, and for tobacco, and for raiment. This youth will fetch a price in the market: he’s a comely lad though not over strong. We’ll fatten him up, give him the bath, curl his hair, and sell him for a hundred piasters to Bacon or Bungay. The rubbish is saleable enough. My advice: next time you go home for a holiday, take him in your carpet-bag, give him a more modern air, prune away—sparingly—some of the green passages, add a little comedy, cheerfulness, satire, and that sort of seasoning, and then we’ll take him to market and sell him. It’s no wonder of wonders, but it’ll do very well.”

“Do you think so, Warrington?” Pen asked, delighted; for praise from that cynical mouth was like a rare spice, expensive and therefore treasured.

“You silly young fool! I think it’s uncommonly clever,” Warrington said, in a kind voice. “So do you.”

And with the manuscript in his hand he playfully struck Pen on the cheek. That cheek turned red as ever it had done in the earliest days of blushing; Pen seized his friend’s hand and said, “Thank you, Warrington,” with all his might; and then retired with his book to his room, and spent the greater part of the day on his bed rereading and altering—adding where he could, cutting where he must, whisking in a little gaiety, a little salt of satire—until Walter Lorraine stood pretty much in the shape in which, as the respected novel-reader knows, it subsequently appeared.

While Pen was thus at his cookery, Warrington—good-natured in his fashion, and crafty as a man who has lived by noticing the appetites of the public—set to work upon the two gentlemen who “read” for Messrs. Bacon and Bungay, and inspired them with a lively curiosity regarding Walter Lorraine and the peculiar merits of its author. The time was that in which The Fashionable (that well-known dish of the season) had set all mouths going; and Warrington did not fail to insist that Pen was fashion itself: received in the houses of the greatest people, dining as easily with a Marchioness as with a mutton-chop.

Percy Popjoy, kind-hearted and simple, was brought to bear upon Mrs. Bungay, and informed that his friend Pendennis was engaged upon a work of the most exciting nature—full of wit, genius, satire, pathos, and every conceivable good quality, as if the book were a Christmas pudding containing every coin and jewel ever lost in England. Bungay knew no more of novels than he did of Hebrew or Algebra; he neither read nor understood the wares he published and paid for; but he took opinions from his advisers and from Mrs. B., and, smelling commerce, asked Pendennis and Warrington to dinner again.

Bacon, hearing that Bungay was about to treat, grew anxious—as one rival cook sniffs another’s kitchen. Was anything settled between Mr. Pendennis and that odious house “over the way”? Mr. Hack, the confidential reader, was told to inquire; and the result of that diplomatist’s inquiries was that one morning Bacon himself toiled up the stairs of Lamb Court to the door on which the names of Mr. Warrington and Mr. Pendennis were painted.

For a gentleman of fashion as poor Pen was represented to be, the chambers were not suitable—unless one admits that fashion in London consists of living near the roof and paying for soot. The carpet, long ragged, had grown only more ragged in two years. A constant odour of tobacco perfumed the sitting-room—a thick, browned atmosphere, as if the place had been smoked like a ham. Bacon tumbled over the laundress’s buckets in the passage. Warrington’s shooting-jacket was tattered at the elbows as usual. The chair offered to Bacon broke down under him with a crack that sounded like the snapping of a dry biscuit.

Warrington burst out laughing, said Bacon had got the game chair, and bawled to Pen to fetch a sound one from his bedroom. Then, seeing the publisher looking round the dingy room with profound pity and wonder, Warrington asked whether he didn’t think the apartments elegant, and whether he would like, for Mrs. Bacon’s drawing-room, any of the articles of furniture.

Mr. Bacon knew Warrington’s reputation as a humourist. “I never can make that chap out,” he was heard to say; “or tell whether he’s in earnest or only chaffing.”

It is very possible Bacon would have set the two down as impostors altogether, had there not chanced to be upon the breakfast-table certain cards of invitation brought by the morning post for Pen—bright, crisp, and aristocratic as wafers. Looking down, Bacon saw that the Marchioness of Steyne would be at home to Mr. Arthur Pendennis on a given day, and that another lady of distinction proposed dancing on a certain future evening. The vulgar noise of the Court below—doors slamming, pails clinking, the iron grind of the city’s daily mechanism—seemed for a moment checked by the hush with which Bacon regarded those cards; for in London the soundscape itself changes when a man believes he hears money.

Warrington saw him eyeing the documents.

“Ah,” Warrington said, with an air of simplicity, “Pendennis is one of the most affable young men I ever knew, Mr. Bacon. Here is a young fellow that dines with all the men in London, and yet he’ll take his mutton-chop with you and me quite contentedly. There’s nothing like the affability of the old English gentleman.”

“Oh no, nothing,” said Mr. Bacon.

“And you wonder why he should go on living up three pair of stairs with me, don’t you now? Well, it’s a queer taste. But we are fond of each other; and as I can’t afford to live in a great house, he comes and stays in these rickety old chambers with me. He’s a man that can afford to live anywhere.”

“I fancy it don’t cost him much here,” thought Bacon—who did not arrive at his fortune by fancy alone.

And the object of these praises presently entered from his adjacent sleeping-room.

Then Mr. Bacon, having tested the chair and the carpet and the general solvency of the air, began to speak on the business of his visit. He had heard Mr. Pendennis had a manuscript novel. He professed anxiety to see the work, and no doubt they could come to terms. What was Pen’s price? Would he give Bacon the refusal? He would find their house liberal; their hearts warm; their cheques—possibly warmer.

Pen, delighted, put on an air of indifference, like a cook pretending he has no need to sell his pies. He said he was already in treaty with Bungay and could give no definite answer. This piqued Bacon into liberal—though vague—offers; and Pen began to fancy Eldorado was opening to him, with a banker at the gate and a horse and cab in the yard.

The sum Mr. Pendennis finally received for the first edition of Walter Lorraine shall not be mentioned, lest other young aspirants, smelling profit, forsake their honest callings and rush fatally into romance-writing as if it were a gold-field where nuggets lie in the street. Let no young people be misled. For one book that succeeds, remember the many that fail; and, if you will venture, do so at your peril. Those who have already written novels need no warning; the ink is spilt, the cake is baked. Let them take their wares to market; let them apply to Bacon and Bungay, and all the Row; and may they be happy in their ventures. The world is wide, tastes are various, and there is always a chance: by genius, by luck, by a friend’s diplomacy. One man goes over ice that bears him, and a score who follow flounder in.

By merit then, or good fortune, or Warrington’s skilful playing off of Bungay against Bacon (a trick any amateur novelist may attempt on any two publishers), Pen’s book was sold for a sum so considerable that Pen, dizzy, began to plan like a man who has unexpectedly found a turkey in his larder. He thought of opening an account at a banker’s, keeping a cab and horse, descending from his third-floor eyrie in Lamb Court to the first floor into newly furnished rooms, or migrating to the fashionable end of town where the streets are quieter only because the noise is more expensive.

Major Pendennis advised the latter move strongly. He opened his eyes with wonder when he heard of the luck that had befallen Pen—news which the young man, full of it as a kettle of steam, hastened to pour into his uncle’s ear. The Major was almost angry that Pen should have earned so much.

“Who the doose reads this kind of thing?” he thought, hearing the bargain. “I never read your novels and rubbish. Except Paul de Kock—who certainly makes me laugh—I don’t think I’ve looked into a book of the sort these thirty years. Gad! Pen’s a lucky fellow. I should think he might write one of these in a month now,—say a month,—that’s twelve in a year. Dammy, he may go on spinning this nonsense for the next four to five years and make a fortune. In the meantime I should wish him to live properly, take respectable apartments, and keep a brougham.”

Arthur, laughing, told Warrington what his uncle’s advice had been; but he had a more reasonable counsellor than the Major in Warrington—and in his own conscience, which, speaking plainly, said: Be grateful; don’t plunge into extravagance. Pay back Laura.

So he wrote to her—tenderly, modestly—thanking her, telling her his regard, and enclosing such an instalment of his debt as nearly wiped it off. The widow and Laura might well be affected. There was no flourish, no fashionable varnish: the letter had the honest warmth of bread sent to a hungry house. Old Dr. Portman, reading a passage in which Pen, with a grateful heart, humbly thanked Heaven for his present prosperity and for sending him such dear friends to support him in ill fortune—when the Doctor came to that, his voice faltered, and his eyes twinkled behind his spectacles. And when he had finished, and taken his glasses off his nose, and folded the paper and returned it to the widow, he held Mrs. Pendennis’s hand a minute; then, by a sudden impulse more eloquent than his quotations, he drew that lady towards him and fairly kissed her.

At which salute Helen burst out crying on the Doctor’s shoulder—for her heart was too full to answer any other way. And the Doctor, blushing a great deal after his feat, led her with a bow to the sofa, seated himself by her, and mumbled in a low voice some words of a Great Poet he loved, about making “the widow’s heart to sing for joy.”

Shepherd’s Inn lay tucked away behind the sooty black gables and forgotten chimneys as a saucepan is shoved to the back of the range—still there, still warm, but out of sight of respectable eyes. You did not so much walk to it as get poured into it through narrow passages and ambiguous alleys where the sun, like a lazy scullion, simply declined to come on duty. The air smelled of damp brick and old paper; of pickled winkles and cheap gin; of singed sugar from hard-bake trays and the sour wool of secondhand bedding that promised anything except sleep.

Outside, the courts rattled and barked with a constant kitchen-clatter of life. Pattens slapped the wet flags; barrow-wheels squealed; shell-fish dealers slapped open their wares with wet, sharp sounds like fish being scaled. Ballad-singers set up their throats—deep, hoarse, and joyless—as though they’d been gargling coal-dust, and chanted songs that were half politics, half spitting. Punch’s little booth creaked and thumped; children shrieked as if being basted; women called after them with voices sharpened on worry; and now and then a husband reeled out of a gin-shop and made an entrance as noisy as a dropped tray.

Then, by one arch as sudden as a pantry door swung shut, you stepped into the quadrangle of Shepherd’s Inn itself—quiet, old-fashioned, and oddly domestic in the middle of all that din, as if London had accidentally left a small, stale biscuit of bygone time in the corner of its mouth. A mangy grass-plat sat in the centre; the statue of Shepherd rose upon it, fenced off behind iron railings from boys who would have vandalised him out of pure professional pride. The hall stood on one side, with the founder’s arms painted up high; tall, ancient chambers ran around the other sides; and an archway led through to Oldcastle Street and thence to the great roaring thoroughfare beyond.

The Inn might once have held lawyers the way a respectable larder once held good hams; but the laity had long since been admitted, and now it housed a miscellany of offices and oddities. The Polwheedle and Tredyddlum Copper Mines took one set of ground-floor rooms—mines, you might note, that were at present more acquainted with water than with copper. Another room announced itself grandly as the Registry of Patent Inventions and Union of Genius and Capital Company, a title so long it must have been paid by the letter.

And then there was the one gentleman whose name, at least, had the audacity to appear in the Law List: Mr. Campion—mustachioed, tufted, and cab-borne—who came twice or thrice a week, leaving behind him an odour of money lent at interest and hair-oil applied with confidence. In Curzon Street, Mayfair, he was Mr. Somerset Campion, and his wife entertained the nobility and gentry to whom he lent money; in Shepherd’s Inn he was Campion and Co., and the same tuft that ornamented his chin sprouted, in more economical fashion, from the under-lip of the rest of his firm.

It was a splendour—positively a culinary miracle of light—to see his cab-horse harness blazing with heraldic bearings as the vehicle stopped in that dingy place. The bit shone; the groom’s breeches were glittering white; the reins looked as if they’d been starched in pride. The horse flung froth from his nostrils, impatient as a man kept waiting for soup.

Captain Costigan had inspected that cab and horse many an afternoon with the exactness of a man assessing a roasted joint he cannot afford. He trailed about the court in carpet slippers and a dressing-gown, with his old hat cocked over one eye, and treated the quadrangle as his own little parade-ground. If the day was suitable he “sunned himself” after breakfast; and then he went to the porter’s lodge to pat children’s heads and talk to Mrs. Bolton about the “thayatres” and “me daughther Leedy Mirabel.”

Mrs. Bolton, porteress and guardian of the Inn’s gossip, had been on the stage herself in a former life—thirteenth of Mr. Serle’s forty pupils at the Wells, which is to say, not a star, but near enough to have seen where the lights were kept. Costigan lived on the third floor at No. 4, in rooms that had belonged to Mr. Podmore, whose name still clung to the door like an old label on a reused jar—indeed, somebody else’s name clung to almost every door in Shepherd’s Inn, as if the whole place were one grand exercise in secondhand identity.

When Charley Podmore—the pleasing tenor singer, T.R.D.L., and at the Back Kitchen Concert Rooms—married and went to Lambeth, he ceded his chambers to Mr. Bows and Captain Costigan, who occupied them in common. On fine days, with the windows open, you might hear Mr. Bows’s piano—patient, careful notes set out like currants on a cake—as he practised for amusement or taught one of his theatrical pupils. He had one or two, and among them was Fanny Bolton, the porteress’s daughter.

Fanny had a good voice and a pretty face and figure for the stage, and—what is rarer—an appetite for glory that was not purely imaginary. She made the beds and prepared the rooms and breakfasts for Messrs. Costigan and Bows, and in return Mr. Bows instructed her in music and singing. She heard her mother’s tales of theatrical splendour the way an eager cook hears of forgotten recipes; she longed to emulate them, and likely would, given time and the absence of catastrophe.

As for the Captain, Fanny, who supposed that all men of fashion indulged in liquor as naturally as they took their hats off indoors, thought him the finest gentleman alive. She believed all versions of all his stories with the trust of a girl tasting her first sweet wine. And she was very fond of Mr. Bows too, grateful to him; while Bows—shy, queer, old—had that fatherly fondness for her which comes of a heart that is never easy unless it loves somebody.

Costigan would have you believe that the carriages of visitors of distinction were forever stopping at his humble door, that Sir Charles and Lady Mirabel were always calling with the select nobility in tow to visit “the old man—the honest old half-pay Captain—poor old Jack Costigan,” as Cos liked to label himself, to make the pity sit better. The truth was smaller and sharper: Lady Mirabel had indeed left her husband’s card once (it had been stuck into the little looking-glass over the mantelpiece in the sitting-room at No. 4 and had stayed there like a dried bay leaf for months), and she had visited her father in person—but not lately.

When she married Sir Charles Mirabel, she had settled a little pension on her father, gravely, dutifully; and sometimes he was admitted to her table. At first, Costigan’s behaviour “in the hoight of poloit societee”—as he called Lady Mirabel’s drawing-room—was harmless if absurd. Just as he dressed his body in his best clothes, he dressed his speech in the longest words he could find, as though syllables were jewels. He adopted a solemnity that astonished everyone within range.

“Was your Leedyship in the Pork to dee?” he would ask his daughter with the gravity of a man inquiring after a duke’s health, when he meant “park,” and meant it with the whole history of Ireland hanging off the consonants. “I looked for your equipage in veen—the poor old man was not gratified by the soight of his daughther’s choriot. Sir Chorlus, I saw your neem at the Levee; many’s the Levee at the Castle at Dublin that poor old Jack Costigan has attended in his time. Did the Juke look pretty well? Bedad, I’ll call at Apsley House and lave me cyard upon ’um. I thank ye, James—a little dthrop more champeane.”

He was magnificent in courtesy—so magnificent he spent it on everyone present, including the servants, addressing them too with elaborate remarks, and the domestics had to bite their lips to keep professional faces. On his first two or three visits he maintained strict sobriety, hoarding his thirst as a man hoards an appetite for later. He would go back to the Back Kitchen afterwards and brag about his son-in-law’s claret and Burgundy until his own utterance began to fail over his sixth tumbler of whisky-punch.

But familiarity melted caution as heat melts fat. Poor Cos began to disgrace himself lamentably at Sir Charles Mirabel’s table by premature inebriation. A carriage would be called; the hospitable door would close upon him. Then, at the Back Kitchen, he would speak often and sadly of his resemblance to King Lear “in the plee,” of his thankless child, bedad; of being a “pore worn-out lonely old man,” driven to drink by ingratitude, and seeking to drown sorrows in punch—as if sorrow were a rat and punch a bucket.

It is painful to record the weaknesses of fathers; but if one is to catalogue a kitchen, one must mention the spills. When his credit was exhausted and his money gone, Costigan would beg from his daughter and season his requests with statements not altogether consistent with strict truth. One day, when a bailiff was about to lead him to prison, he wrote that unless the “—to you insignificant—sum of three pound five” could be forthcoming, his grey hairs must go to gaol. Lady Mirabel, good-natured, sent the money with a caution to be more economical.

On a second occasion he met with a “frightful accident” and broke a plate-glass window in the Strand, for which the proprietor held him liable. The money came again, carried down by Lady Mirabel’s servant to the Captain’s slipshod messenger and aide-de-camp. If the servant had followed that aide-de-camp—and in Shepherd’s Inn, secrets travel by foot if at all—he would have seen the fellow call a cab and rattle down to the Roscius Head in Harlequin Yard, Drury Lane, where the Captain was “indeed in pawn,” and where several glasses of rum-and-water or other spirituous refreshment were employed in celebrating Lady Mirabel’s dutiful remittance.

For, observe, an Irish gentleman, however poor, always has a poorer Irish gentleman to run his errands and transact his pecuniary affairs; it is one of the few institutions that survives everything.

On a third melancholy occasion the Captain wrote that he was attacked by illness and wanted money to pay the physician he was compelled to call in. This time Lady Mirabel, alarmed—perhaps also reproaching herself that she had lately lost sight of her father—called for her carriage and drove to Shepherd’s Inn. She alighted at the gate, found her way to No. 4, third floor, “name of Podmore over the door,” as the porteress said with many curtsies; and mounted the dingy stair with the resolution of a woman going to view a pot that has long been boiling unattended.

Alas. The Podmore door was opened not upon some pale invalid with a hot-water bottle, but upon poor Cos in his shirt-sleeves, cheerful and flushed, preparing with a gridiron to receive the mutton-chops Mrs. Bolton had gone to purchase. Whatever illness he had was of the sort that improves wonderfully at the smell of frying fat.

Nor was it pleasant for Sir Charles Mirabel to have letters constantly addressed to him at Brookes’s, with the information that Captain Costigan was in the hall waiting for an answer; or, when Sir Charles went to play his rubber at the Travellers’, to be obliged to shoot out of his brougham and run up the steps rapidly lest his father-in-law should seize upon him; or to think, while he read his paper or played his whist, that the Captain was walking on the opposite side of Pall Mall with that dreadful cocked hat and the eye beneath it fixed steadily upon the club windows—watching, listening for the particular tone of his son-in-law’s footfall, as though the man’s very gait were a language he meant to translate into money.

Sir Charles was weak; he was old and infirm. He cried about his father-in-law to his wife, whom he adored with senile infatuation. He swore he must go abroad, go to the country—he would die, or have another fit, if he saw that man again; he knew he should. It was only by paying a second visit to Captain Costigan and representing to him that if he plagued Sir Charles by letters, accosted him in the street, or made further applications for loans, his allowance would be withdrawn altogether, that Lady Mirabel managed to keep her papa in order and restore tranquillity to her husband.

On that visit she rebuked Mr. Bows sternly for not keeping better watch over the Captain; ordered that he should not be allowed to drink in that shameful way; and that the people at the horrid taverns he frequented should be told, on no account, to give him credit. “Papa’s conduct is bringing me to the grave,” she said—though she looked perfectly healthy—“and you, as an old man, Mr. Bows, and one that pretended to have a regard for us, ought to be ashamed of abetting him in it.”

Those were the thanks honest Bows got for his friendship and his life’s devotion. He bore them as a man bears an over-salted dish: not because it is pleasant, but because it is on the table and he has no other dinner. And perhaps he was no worse off than many.

In the next house, at No. 3, on the second floor, lived two other acquaintances: Colonel Altamont, agent to the Nawaub of Lucknow, and Captain Chevalier Edward Strong. There was no name over their door. Strong did not choose to let all the world know where he lived; his cards bore the address of a Jermyn Street hotel. As for the Colonel—Ambassador Plenipotentiary of an Indian potentate—he was an envoy accredited neither to St. James’s nor to Leadenhall Street, but here on a confidential mission quite independent of the East India Company or the Board of Control.

“In fact,” Strong said, with that air men adopt when explaining why they must be mysterious, “Colonel Altamont’s object being financial, and to effectuate a sale of some of the principal diamonds and rubies of the Lucknow crown, his wish is not to report himself at the India House or in Cannon Row, but rather to negotiate with private capitalists—with whom he has had important transactions both in this country and on the Continent.”

Their chambers had become very comfortable since the arrival of Sir Francis Clavering in London; and Strong could boast, with reason, that few retired Captains were more snugly quartered than he in his “crib” at Shepherd’s Inn. There were three rooms below: an office where Strong transacted his business—whatever that might be—still fitted with the desk and railings left by departed clerks; Strong’s own bedroom; and his sitting-room. A private stair led out of the office to two upper apartments: one for Colonel Altamont, and one that served as kitchen and as bedroom for Mr. Grady, their attendant.

These upper rooms sat level with Bows’s and Costigan’s next door at No. 4; and by leaning over the communicating leads, Grady could command the mignonette-box blooming in Bows’s window. From Grady’s kitchen casement came odours more fragrant than mignonette—honest, edible perfumes, the true incense of the poor. You might smell onions softened patiently until their sharpness turned sweet; pepper waking up in hot fat with a sneeze; rice steaming, clean and nutty; a whiff of coriander and toasted cumin like dry leaves crackling; and sometimes the rich, dark promise of a curry reduced to its proper thickness, as careful as a historian reducing a sauce until nothing remains but concentrated truth.

The three old soldiers of No. 3 were all skilled in the culinary art, and took to it as veterans take to storytelling—because it uses what you have left: time, fire, and memory. Grady was great at an Irish stew: he could turn a few scrag ends of mutton, a fist of potatoes, and an onion into something that made a man forgive the rain. The Colonel was famous for pillaus and curries, and treated spice the way other men treat medals—arranged, displayed, and bragged of. And as for Strong, he could cook anything. He made French dishes and Spanish dishes, stews, fricassees, omelettes to perfection; and when his purse was full, or his credit good, there was no man in England more hospitable. At those happy periods he could give a friend, as he said, a good dinner, a good glass of wine, and a good song afterwards.

Poor Cos, sitting next door, often heard with envy the roar of Strong’s choruses—big, masculine noises rolling out like barrels—and the musical clinking of glasses, and the rise and fall of laughter, and the scrape of a chair, and the brief hush that comes when something particularly savoury hits the tongue. Shepherd’s Inn, that day, could be read by its sounds: gin’s harsh shout outside, and inside the quadrangle, the gentler music of friends eating and talking. Yet it was not expedient to invite Mr. Costigan always: his inebriation was lamentable; and he bored Strong’s guests with his stories when sober and with his tears when drunk. His voice, too, had the habit of drowning out others—like a cheap ballad sung too loud in a small room—until nobody could remember what anyone else had said.

A strange and motley set were these friends of the Chevalier. Major Pendennis would not have relished them; Arthur and Warrington liked them not a little; and Pen found them as amusing as the society of the finest gentlemen in the finest houses he had the honour to frequent. There was a history about every man, and most of their histories came with a smell: stale tobacco in one man’s coat, sea-salt in another’s beard, brandy in a third’s breath, foreign spices in a fourth’s speech. They all seemed to have ridden tides of luck and bad fortune; they all carried schemes in their pockets the way old women carry peppermints, and promised rapid extraordinary fortunes with the ease of men promising a second helping.

Jack Holt had been in Don Carlos’s army when Ned Strong fought on the other side; now he was organising a scheme for smuggling tobacco into London that must bring thirty thousand a year to any man who would advance fifteen hundred—just to bribe the last Excise officer who held out and had wind of the plan. Tom Diver, late of the Mexican navy, knew of a specie-ship sunk in the first year of the war with three hundred and eighty thousand dollars on board and a hundred and eighty thousand pounds in bars and doubloons. “Give me eighteen hundred,” Tom said, “and I’m off tomorrow. I take out four men, and a diving-bell; and I return in ten months to take my seat in Parliament, by Jove! and to buy back my family estate.” Keightley, manager of the waterlogged copper mines, sang as good a second as any professional man and also had a Smyrna Sponge Company and a little quicksilver operation in view which would set him straight with the world yet. Filby had been everything: corporal of dragoons, field-preacher, missionary-agent for converting the Irish; actor at a Greenwich fair-booth, where his father’s attorney found him when the old gentleman died and left him a famous property from which he got no rents and whose very situation nobody exactly knew—as if the land itself had forgotten the language in which it was supposed to pay.

Added to these was Sir Francis Clavering, Bart., who liked their society though he did not add much to its amusement by his convivial powers. Yet he was made much of now on account of his wealth and place in the world. He told his little story and sang his little song or two with affability; and he, too, had a history before his accession to good fortune, having seen the inside of more prisons than one and written his name on many a stamped paper.

When Altamont first returned from Paris—after he had communicated with Sir Francis Clavering from the hotel where he had taken up his quarters, which he had reached in a very denuded state considering the diamonds and rubies entrusted to him—Strong was sent by the Baronet to his patron, paid the little bill at the inn, and invited Altamont to come and sleep for a night or two at the chambers, where he subsequently took up residence.

To negotiate with such a man was one thing; to have him settled in one’s rooms and to be constantly burdened with such society was another. It did not suit the Chevalier’s taste, and he grumbled to his principal with the freedom of a cook asked to share his kitchen with a bear.

“I wish you would put this bear into somebody else’s cage,” he said to Clavering. “The fellow’s no gentleman. I don’t like walking with him. He dresses himself like a nigger on a holiday. I took him to the play the other night; and, by Jove, sir, he abused the actor who was doing the part of villain, and swore at him so that the people in the boxes wanted to turn him out. The after-piece was the ‘Brigand,’ where Wallack comes in wounded, you know, and dies. When he died, Altamont began to cry like a child, and said it was a d——d shame, and cried and swore so that there was another row, and everybody laughing. Then I had to take him away because he wanted to take his coat off to one fellow who laughed at him; and bellowed to him to stand up like a man.

“Who is he? Where the deuce does he come from? You had best tell me the whole story. Frank; you must one day. You and he have robbed a church together, that’s my belief. You had better get it off your mind at once, Clavering, and tell me what this Altamont is, and what hold he has over you.”

“Hang him! I wish he was dead!” was the Baronet’s only reply; and his face grew so gloomy, so abruptly shut—like an oven-door slammed on a flare-up—that Strong did not press him further then. But he resolved, if need were, to discover for himself what secret tie bound Altamont to Clavering, and why one man’s name could make the other’s cheer go out as suddenly as a song smothered by the roar of the street.

Early next morning—at that hour when the milk-carts are still politely whispering over the stones and the city has not yet worked itself up into its customary iron clatter—Colonel Altamont came rolling out of his room in Shepherd’s Inn as if he had been fired from a cannon and was now seeking somewhere soft to land. He wandered into Captain Strong’s sitting-room, where the Chevalier sat planted in an easy-chair with the newspaper, a cigar, and the serene air of a man who could make a bivouac feel like a breakfast-parlour.

Strong had already performed, with the gravity of a priest at an altar, the morning rite of fried eggs and broiled rashers—Mr. Grady having executed them secundum artem, the fat in the pan singing a small crisp hymn, the bacon snapping like applause, the eggs set tender as custard at the centre and just kissed into colour at the edges. The smell had soaked into the room—salt, pepper, browned meat, coffee—and even the old floorboards seemed to creak more contentedly under it. Whatever the world did to Captain Strong—camp, Fleet, prison, battle, bankruptcy—it never managed to get at his digestion; and his digestion, like a good regiment, kept him in order. He had, the night before, seen Altamont safely bedded with a friendliness that cost him nothing, removed the candle like a nurse confiscating a child’s fireworks, discovered a spirit-bottle empty upon which he had been counting, and consoled himself with water and his pipe as placidly as if Providence had expressly brewed it.

Altamont’s first act was not to notice the eggs, the bacon, or any other blessing of the table; he bellowed for a pint of pale ale. Grady brought it. The Colonel poured it into a pewter flagon, and from the flagon into himself. He set the tankard down empty with the air of a man who had just rescued his own life at sea, drew a mighty breath, and wiped his mouth with his dressing-gown. (Strong, who had a soldier’s eye for uniforms and a man’s eye for other men, could not help observing—as he had long observed—that Altamont’s dyed whiskers and the honest colour of his beard were not on speaking terms; and that under the black wig lurked hair of a different story. But Strong, who was tidy in manners as in camp, made no remark.)

“Nothing like that beer,” said Altamont, revived into loquacity. “When the coppers are hot. Many a day I’ve drunk a dozen of Bass at Calcutta, and—and—”

“And at Lucknow, I suppose,” Strong put in, laughing, and flicking ash with military neatness. “I got the beer for you on purpose. Knew you’d want it after last night.”

Altamont beat his great hand against his head as if he would knock the sense back into it by force. “I can’t help myself. I’m a madman when I get the liquor on board me; and ain’t fit to be trusted with a spirit-bottle. Once I begin, I can’t stop till I’ve emptied it; and when I’ve swallowed it, Lord knows what I say or what I don’t say. I dined at home here quiet. Grady gave me just my two tumblers. I meant to pass the evening at the Black and Red as sober as a parson. Why did you leave that confounded sample-bottle of Hollands out of the cupboard, Strong? Grady must go out too, and leave me the kettle a-boiling for tea. It was no use. I couldn’t keep away from it. Washed it all down, sir—by Jove. And it’s my belief I had some more afterwards at that infernal little thieves’ den.”

“What, were you there too?” Strong asked. “Before you came to Grosvenor Place? That was beginning betimes.”

“Early hours to be drunk and cleared out before nine, eh? But so it was. Yes—like a great big fool—I must go there; and I found ’em dining—Blackland, young Moss, and two or three more of the thieves. If we’d gone to Rouge et Noir, I must have won. But we didn’t try the black and red. No—hang ’em—they know’d I’d have beat ’em at that. I must have beat ’em. I can’t help beating ’em, I tell you. But they was too cunnin for me. That rascal Blackland got the bones out, and we played hazard on the dining-table. And I dropped all the money I had from you in the morning—be hanged to my luck.”

He spoke with the wounded splendour of a man who thinks Providence has cheated him at dice.

“That set me wild,” he went on. “I suppose I must have been very hot about the head, for I went off thinking to get some more money from Clavering, I recollect; and then—and then I don’t much remember what happened till I woke this morning and heard old Bows at No. 4 playing on his pianner.”

Strong paused to light his cigar from a coal, and listened a moment—because in a lodging-house you never have silence, you only have the next room’s opinion of music. Somewhere below, Mr. Bows was indeed worrying his instrument in a manner that suggested the keys had personally offended him. The notes, half-stifled by boards and plaster, came up like distant carpentry.

“I should like to know,” Strong said at last, in that tone of mild curiosity he used for asking about cannon as well as consciences, “how you always draw money from Clavering, Colonel.”

Altamont burst out laughing. “Ha, ha! He owes it me.”

“I don’t know that that’s a reason with Frank for paying,” Strong answered, without moving his eyes. “He owes plenty besides you.”

“He gives it me because he is so fond of me,” Altamont said, with a grin that had something sharp in it. “He loves me like a brother; you know he does, Captain.—No?—He don’t?—Well, perhaps he don’t; and if you ask me no questions, perhaps I’ll tell you no lies, Captain Strong—put that in your pipe and smoke it, my boy.”

Then, as if the confession of knavery had made him virtuous by reaction: “But I’ll give up that confounded brandy-bottle. I must give it up, or it’ll be the ruin of me.”

“It makes you say queer things,” Strong said, looking full at him. “Remember what you said last night, at Clavering’s table.”

Altamont’s face changed so quickly it was as if the wig had slipped and shown the bare skull of fear. “Say? What did I say? Did I split anything? Dammy, Strong—did I split anything?”

“Ask me no questions, and I will tell you no lies,” Strong replied, paying him back his own coin with a smile that didn’t ring. He remembered well enough the Colonel’s sudden blanching and hurried retreat the moment he had recognised Major Pendennis—“Captain Beak,” as Altamont had called him, with that drunken instinct for the sore point. But Strong, who could march all night and hold his tongue all day, did not choose to jog Altamont’s memory into sharper mischief.

“No,” he said aloud. “You didn’t split, as you call it. It was only a trap of mine to see if I could make you speak; but you didn’t say a word that anybody could comprehend—you were too far gone for that.”

So much the better, thought Altamont; and he heaved a great sigh, like a man reprieved from hanging because the hangman couldn’t find the rope.

Strong noted the relief—filed it away, as he filed away everything useful—and took no notice. Altamont, now that his neck felt safe for the moment, expanded into narrative again.

“Yes, I own to my faults,” he said, with the grand candour of a sinner who expects admiration for not denying the obvious. “There is some things I can’t, do what I will, resist: a bottle of brandy, a box of dice, and a beautiful woman. No man of pluck and spirit—no man as was worth his salt—ever could, as I know of. There’s hardly p’raps a country in the world in which them three ain’t got me into trouble.”

“Indeed?” said Strong.

“Yes. From the age of fifteen—when I ran away from home, and went cabin-boy aboard an Indiaman—till now, when I’m fifty year old, pretty nigh—them women have always been my ruin. Why, it was one of ’em—with such black eyes, and jewels on her neck, and battens and ermine like a duchess—it was one of ’em at Paris that swept off the best part of the thousand pound as I went off with.”

And so, with the gusto of a man who can taste his own disasters, he began to dish up Paris.

At first, he said, he had lived like a gentleman—Colonel Altamont at Meurice’s, public tables only, cautious as a cook measuring pepper. He described the smart world as if it were a supper: white kid gloves, tufted chins, names with hyphens like skewers. There was a certain Bloundell-Bloundell; there was Madame the Countess de Foljambe—“such an eye, Strong! such a hand at the pianner.” She played and sang, he swore, until she “warbled your soul out of your body a’most,” and he made it sound as if the music were a syrup poured warm down a man’s throat, sweet at first and then cloying and finally poisonous. She had him every Tuesday; he had opera-boxes and dinners at the restaurateur’s—champagne with its bright biting fizz, and afterwards that “confounded brandy,” which, in his telling, always entered like a villain in a melodrama.

It was not the dinners and opera-boxes that took the money, he maintained, but “another way”: one night at the Countess’s supper—Bloundell-Bloundell, the Honourable Deuceace, the Marquis de la Tour de Force, “all tip-top nobs”—champagne, punch mixed by the Countess herself, cards, drink, and then his memory went the way of a candle in a draught. He woke to a headache and visitors.

First came Deuceace—easy, smiling, with that air of a gentleman who can borrow money as if he were doing you a favour. Deuceace told him he had borrowed thirty louis at vingt-et-un, given an I.O.U., and that Altamont had pocketed it. Altamont found the paper in the card-case the Countess had “worked” for him—sure enough. Deuceace paid him in gold on the bed-table—chink, chink, chink—each coin sounding like a small insult.

Then came Bloundell-Bloundell and the Marquis—“the Marky,” as Altamont called him, twiddling moustachios at the chimney-glass and making lunges like a man fencing with his own reflection. They insisted on “affairs.” They produced notes of hand: three hundred and forty louis to the Marquis; two hundred and ten to Bloundell. Altamont sprang out of bed roaring, swore he owed nothing, called them names, and was met with threats—exposure, chastisement, honour, all the theatre of it. Bloundell, being larger and heavier, was not a man to be flung out of windows as easily as a marquis.

Then a fourth gentleman arrived—Altamont’s Boulogne friend, the one who hadn’t played, and who had warned him. This witness, as witnesses will, was inconvenient. He declared Altamont had insisted on the high stakes; the Countess had begged him to stop; the others had offered repeatedly to leave off. And then, with the relish of a man delivering the worst news with the greatest delicacy, he told Altamont the Marquis would shoot him “as sure as”—as sure as his name was whatever it was. He added that he had left the Countess crying, nearly hysterical, terrified there’d be a quarrel and a bullet, and that he believed—indeed he was certain—that she was distractedly in love with Altamont.

“Do you think so?” said Altamont, who could swallow danger more easily than vanity.

His friend described the Countess on her knees—“Save Colonel Altamont!”

“As soon as I was dressed,” Altamont continued, “I went and called upon that lovely woman. She gave a shriek and pretty near fainted. She called me Ferdinand—I'm blest if she didn’t.”

“I thought your name was Jack,” Strong said, laughing.

Altamont blushed—an odd dull red showing through the dye and bravado. “A man may have more names than one, mayn’t he, Strong? When I’m with a lady, I like to take a good one. She called me by my Christian name. She cried fit to break your heart. I can’t stand seeing a woman cry—never could—not whilst I’m fond of her. She said she couldn’t bear to think of my losing so much money in her house. Wouldn’t I take her diamonds and necklaces, and pay part?”

He swore he refused—wouldn’t touch a farthing’s worth. “But what can a woman do more than give you her all? That’s the sort I like.”

She warned him they would shoot him—kill her Ferdinand.

“They’ll kill my Jack wouldn’t have sounded well in French,” Strong said, and laughed again at the absurdity of names changing with borders as if identity were a coin that needed different stamping for different markets.

“Never mind about names,” Altamont said, sulkily. “A man of honour may take any name he chooses, I suppose.”

He went on: he had refused the duel—“field of honour be hanged”—and the Countess, shocked as if he’d spilt sauce on her altar-cloth, had drawn back and questioned whether a British officer could refuse. Her father had been a General of the Grand Army; a soldier should pay “debts of honour.”

“What could I do?” Altamont cried, spreading his hands as if fate itself had shuffled the deck. “Everybody was against me. Caroline said I had lost the money; though I didn’t remember a syllable about the business. Every one of these chaps was a man of fashion and honour; and the Marky and the Countess of the first families in France. And—by Jove, sir—rather than offend her, I paid the money up—five hundred and sixty gold Napoleons, by Jove: besides three hundred which I lost when I had my revenge.”

He sat musing, as if trying to taste in memory whether the thing had been robbery or romance. “And I can’t tell you at this minute whether I was done or not,” he ended. “Sometimes I think I was: but then Caroline was so fond of me. That woman would never have seen me done: never, I’m sure she wouldn’t: at least, if she would, I’m deceived in woman.”

Strong might have let him go on—there was no end to a man’s past when the bottle had edited it—but their door was knocked at. Grady opened it, and in came Sir Francis Clavering.

“The Governor, by Jove,” Strong exclaimed, surprised; while Altamont scowled from under his heavy eyebrows. “It’s no good, I warrant.”

Indeed, good very seldom carried Sir Francis anywhere. Money carried him—as regularly and as ignobly as a sedan-chair. When he entered Shepherd’s Inn, one could almost hear the rustle of protested bills behind him like dead leaves dragged on a boot. He came pale with irritation, his face set in that pinched expression of a man who has spent his life dodging creditors and still fancies himself pursued by injustice rather than arithmetic.

He began at once, addressing Altamont: “So, sir—you’ve been at your old tricks.”

“Which of ’um?” Altamont asked, with a sneer as broad as his shoulders.

“You have been at the Rouge et Noir. You were there last night,” Clavering cried.

“How do you know—were you there?” Altamont said. “I was at the Club, but it wasn’t on the colours I played—ask the Captain—I’ve been telling him. It was with the bones. It was at hazard, Sir Francis, upon my word and honour it was.” And he looked at the Baronet with a mock humility so knowing that it was like being bowed to by a pickpocket.
