“What the deuce do I care,” shrieked Clavering, “how a man like you loses his money—whether at hazard or roulette? What I will not have is that you should use my name, or couple it with yours. Damn him, Strong—why don’t you keep him in better order? I tell you he has gone and used my name again—drawn a bill upon me—and lost the money on the table—I can’t stand it—I won’t stand it. Flesh and blood won’t bear it. Do you know how much I have paid for you, sir?”

“This was only a very little ’un, Sir Francis,” Altamont said, with the easy cheerfulness of a man asking forgiveness for setting fire to a curtain. “Only fifteen pound. Captain Strong, they wouldn’t stand another. And it oughtn’t to anger you, Governor. Why, it’s so trifling I did not even mention it to Strong—did I now, Captain? I protest it had quite slipped my memory—and all on account of that confounded liquor I took.”

“Liquor or no liquor, sir, it is no business of mine,” Clavering snapped. “I don’t care what you drink or where you drink it—only it shan’t be in my house. And I will not have you breaking into my house of a night, and a fellow like you intruding himself on my company. How dared you show yourself in Grosvenor Place last night, sir—and—and what do you suppose my friends must think of me when they see a man of your sort walking into my dining-room uninvited, and drunk, and calling for liquor as if you were the master of the house?”

“They’ll think you know some very queer sort of people, I dare say,” Altamont returned, impenetrably good-humoured. “Look here, Baronet, I apologise; on my honour I do. Ain’t an apology enough between two gentlemen? It was a strong measure, I own—walking into your cuddy and calling for drink as if I was the Captain. But I had had too much before, you see—that’s why I wanted some more; nothing can be more simple. And it was because they wouldn’t give me no more money upon your name at the Black and Red, that I thought I would come down and speak to you about it. To refuse me was nothing; but to refuse a bill drawn on you that have been such a friend to the shop, and are a baronet and a member of parliament, and a gentleman and no mistake—damme, it’s ungrateful.”

Clavering’s temper, always thin as watered wine, boiled over. “By heavens, if ever you do it again—if ever you dare to show yourself in my house; or give my name at a gambling-house or any other house—by Jove, at any other house—or give any reference at all to me, or speak to me in the street, by God, or anywhere else until I speak to you—I disclaim you altogether—I won’t give you another shilling.”

“Governor, don’t be provoking,” Altamont said, his good humour thickening into sullenness. “Don’t talk to me about daring to do this thing or t’other, or when my dander is up it’s the very thing to urge me on. I oughtn’t to have come last night, I know I oughtn’t. But I told you I was drunk, and that ought to be sufficient between gentleman and gentleman.”

“You a gentleman! dammy, sir,” cried Clavering, the words flying out as if they’d been waiting years to escape. “How dares a fellow like you call himself a gentleman?”

After the little junketings at Grosvenor Place and Greenwich—where Major Pendennis had eaten, bowed, and smiled with a conscientiousness that amounted to labour—his friendship for the Claverings ripened with the speed of a peach in a hothouse. He called daily; he hovered; he suggested, with the air of a man casually mentioning the weather, that Lady Clavering’s proper element was precisely those drawing-rooms where a great deal of money was admired in silence and a great deal of pedigree was discussed in whispers.

Would her ladyship not grace Gaunt House? There was to be a grand entertainment. Would she not condescend to a breakfast-ball at Viscount Marrowfat’s at Fulham, where “everybody” was expected—by which the Major meant the precise set who could make “everybody” feel like nobody? There was to be a Watteau quadrille, too; and Miss Amory, in such a piece of painted pastoral, would look—so the Major vowed—like a shepherdess with an income. He offered to conduct, to escort, to fetch, to carry, to be useful; and when a man has reached the age at which usefulness becomes his chief surviving romance, he is very ardent about it.

Sir Francis Clavering, in spite of his title and his present house and his present impudent air of belonging to them, was still received by the world with that cautious politeness which is only a shade warmer than the door being shut. Suspicious rumours clung to him as kitchen-smells cling to a coat—one may air it for an hour, but the faint savour remains and every one pretends not to notice it while taking care to stand a little aside. He was blackballed at two clubs running. In the House he attached himself with a kind of fatal instinct to the very men whom decent people avoid in a street at noon. The gentleman called Mr. Hotspur—who, in his professional capacity, could be civil to a chimney-sweep if the sweep held a vote—confessed to a loathing for Sir Francis which no necessity could sweeten.

“If that man’s wanted for a division,” Hotspur said, “ten to one he’s to be found in a hell. He was educated in the Fleet, and he hasn’t heard the end of Newgate yet. He’ll muddle away the Begum’s fortune at thimble-rig, be caught picking pockets, and finish aboard the hulks.”

Now if Hotspur, with such opinions, could still smile and shake hands for votes, why should not Major Pendennis have reasons of his own for smiling and shaking hands for dinners?

“He has a very good cellar and a very good cook,” the Major remarked with the calm of a philosopher who measures virtue by the state of a sauce. “As long as he’s silent he isn’t offensive, and he very seldom speaks. If he chooses to lose his money to blacklegs, what’s that to me? Don’t look too curiously into any man’s affairs, Pen, my boy. Every fellow has some cupboard in his house he wouldn’t like you and me to peep into. Why should we try, when the rest of the house is open to us? And a devilish good house too, as you and I know. If the man isn’t all one could wish, the women are excellent. The Begum is not over-refined, but as kind a woman as ever lived—and devilish clever too. And as for little Blanche—you rogue—you know my opinion. My belief is she’s sweet upon you, and would have you for the asking. But you’re growing such a great man I suppose you won’t be content under a Duke’s daughter. Hey, sir? Ask one of ’em. Try.”

Pen, who had lately found the world very obliging to him, allowed the notion to glitter for a moment—Miss Amory, clever and bright as a knife, might indeed be disposed to renew the old, brisk flirtation that had once skimmed along the banks of the Brawl like a dragonfly above water. Yet he was not disposed to be pinned down. He said so, with that fashionable fatigue young men cultivate as they do their whiskers.

“You are very happy, sir,” he told the Major, “and you get on very well alone, and so do I. With a wife at my side, I should lose my place in society. I don’t much fancy retiring into the country with a Mrs. Pendennis; or taking my wife into lodgings to be waited on by the servant-of-all-work. The period of my little illusions is over. You cured me of my first love—who certainly was a fool, and would have had a fool for her husband, and a sulky discontented husband too. We young fellows live fast, sir; and I feel as old at five-and-twenty as many of the old—” (here he caught the Major’s eye and amended himself) “as many of the old bachelors whom I see in the bow-window at Bays’s. Don’t look offended; I only mean I’m blasé about love matters, and I could no more fan myself into a flame for Miss Amory now than I could adore Lady Mirabel over again. I rather like old Mirabel for his infatuation, and think his passion the most respectable part of his life.”

“Sir Charles Mirabel was always a theatrical man, sir,” the Major said, bristling as if Pen had spoken lightly of the Ark of the Covenant. “He acted at Carlton House when he was page to the Prince. He has been mixed up with that sort of thing. He can afford to marry whom he chooses. And Lady Mirabel is a most respectable woman, received everywhere—everywhere, mind. The Duchess of Connaught receives her. Lady Rockminster receives her. It doesn’t become young fellows to speak lightly of people in that station. There’s not a more respectable woman in England than Lady Mirabel—and the old fogies, as you call ’em, at Bays’s are some of the first gentlemen in England, of whom you youngsters had best learn a little manners, a little breeding, and a little modesty.”

The Major began to suspect that Pen was getting pert; and as the Major’s own entire system depended on everybody else being properly respectful to everybody above them, Pen’s impertinence was, in a manner, a revolutionary pamphlet.

Pen, on his part, was amused. He studied his uncle as one tastes an old wine—finding odd flavours in it, and being entertained by the solemn way it insists upon its own importance.

“I am a youngster of fifteen years’ standing, sir,” he said, “and if you think we are disrespectful, you should see those of the present generation. A protégé of yours came to breakfast with me the other day. You told me to ask him, and I did it to please you. We had a day’s sights together, dined at the club, went to the play. He said the wine at the Polyanthus was not so good as Ellis’s at Richmond, smoked Warrington’s cavendish after breakfast, and when I gave him a sovereign as a farewell token, said he had plenty of them, but would take it to show he wasn’t proud.”

“Did he?—did you ask young Clavering?” the Major cried, appeased as if a key had turned in his temper. “Fine boy—rather wild—but a fine boy. Parents like that sort of attention, and you can’t do better than pay it to our worthy friends at Grosvenor Place. So you took him to the play and tipped him? That was right, sir—that was right.” And the Major, having had his doctrine honoured, departed in peace, thinking the world not quite lost and Pen still salvageable.

Young Frank Clavering, in the meantime, grew in years, stature, and obstinacy until he was too large for a governess and too noisy for a mother’s patience. With his father he was silent and sulky, keeping out of Sir Francis’s way as if the Baronet’s very glance smelt of stale cigars and worse debts. With his mother he roared and fought whenever appetite or whim was opposed; and in disputes with his governess over his book, he kicked that mild creature’s shins so fiercely that education was obliged to retire. He attempted once or twice to treat his sister Blanche in the same manner; but Miss Amory possessed the sort of spirit that does not argue—it acts. She boxed his ears so soundly that Master Frank learned, for the first time, the meaning of a boundary.

When the family came to London Sir Francis declared, with an oath of paternal wisdom, that “the little beggar had best be sent to school.” So the young heir of Clavering was packed off to the Reverend Otto Rose’s establishment at Twickenham—one of those preparatory temples where boys are introduced to Latin by means of comfort.

We will not follow Master Clavering through scholarship; it would be like watching a fat duck waddle towards water. The path to learning, for him, was smoothed like a well-buttered muffin. He advanced towards the fane in a carriage-and-four, so to speak, and might halt for refreshment whenever he pleased. Varnished boots shone on him at an age when other boys still suffered from honest leather; cambric handkerchiefs fluttered; lemon-coloured kid gloves were drawn on hands scarcely old enough to be ashamed of ink. At Mr. Rose’s they dressed for dinner; there were shawl dressing-gowns, fires in bedrooms, occasional horse-and-carriage exercise, and oil for the hair—so that even their heads were marinated in gentility. Corporal punishment was abolished: moral discipline was to do everything; and the boys were advanced so rapidly in many branches of learning that they acquired the art of drinking spirits and smoking cigars before they were old enough to be publicly ashamed of it. Young Frank stole his father’s Havannahs and conveyed them to school, or smoked them in the stables with astonishing precocity; and at ten years old he drank champagne as sturdily as any whiskered cornet of dragoons, with the additional accomplishment of making a face like a judge passing sentence on a lemon.

When the interesting youth came home for vacations, Major Pendennis was as civil to him as to the ladies, though the boy privately held “old Wigsby” in contempt; mimicked him behind his back as the polite Major bowed and smirked; and drew rude caricatures in which the Major’s wig, nose, and tie were represented with artless ferocity. Still, the Major was untiring. He urged Pen to take notice of the boy; to invite him to chambers; to give him a dinner at the club; to take him to Madame Tussaud’s, the Tower, the play; and to tip him at the end of the day, as if sovereigns were the natural dessert to amusements.

Arthur, good-natured and fond of children, went through the ceremonies one day. The boy breakfasted in the Temple, and made the most contemptuous remarks on the furniture, the crockery, and the tattered state of Warrington’s dressing-gown—observations delivered with the serene certainty of a young gentleman who has never had to pay for a chair, a plate, or a gown. He smoked a short pipe and recounted the history of a fight between Tuffy and Long Biggings at Rose’s, to the high entertainment of his hosts, who listened as men listen to a foreign language—catching a word here and there and pretending the rest is very fine.

As the Major predicted, Lady Clavering was deeply grateful for Arthur’s attention to the boy—more grateful than the boy himself, who took attentions as he took food: as a matter of course, and with an opinion on the quality. He very likely carried more sovereigns in his pocket than poor Pen, who nevertheless gave him one out of his slender stock.

The Major’s eyes—sharp by nature and sharpened by age—watched the boy and the family with a discretion which looked like delicacy and was really calculation. Without appearing rudely curious, he contrived, as an old neighbour and family friend, to discover Lady Clavering’s means, the disposition of her capital, and what the boy was to inherit. He set to work as diligently as if fortune were a sauce requiring exact reduction; and soon possessed a tolerably accurate knowledge of the Begum’s affairs. The daughter, it appeared, would have a slender provision. The bulk of the property would go to the son. Sir Francis cared for nobody, least of all his heir; the mother was dotingly fond of the child of her later days; the sister disliked him. Such, in round numbers, was the result of Major Pendennis’s gentle enquiries.

“Ah, my dear madam,” he would say, patting the boy’s head with a hand that had patted many a circumstance into a convenient shape, “this boy may wear a baron’s coronet one day at a coronation—if matters are managed rightly, and if Sir Francis would but play his cards well.”

At this the widow Amory heaved a deep sigh. “He plays only too much of his cards, Major, I’m afraid,” she said.

The Major admitted, with sympathetic gravity, that he had heard of Sir Francis’s unfortunate propensity. He pitied her—he seemed to pity her with such sense, such seasoned tenderness, that Lady Clavering, who had long been obliged to keep her troubles shut up like preserves, found herself eager to take down the jar and show him. Major Pendennis became her confidant, her house-friend; and as a mother, a wife, and—most tender of all offices—a capitalist, she consulted him.

He let her understand, with respectful commiseration, that he knew something of her first unlucky marriage, and even of her late husband’s person—having remembered him in Calcutta, in those days when she lived in seclusion with her father. The poor lady, with tears in her eyes—tears of shame more than sorrow—told her version.

Sent back as a child to India after two years at a European school, she had met Amory and, with the heedless courage of a girl whose head had been filled with novels and whose ears were unused to men’s voices, she had married him. She spoke of the calm nights on the passage out; of his wild stories and adventures; of how beautifully he talked in the dark, when the sea made that steady whispering sound against the ship’s side that persuades young hearts they are in a poem. Then the domestic truth arrived—loud, coarse, and persistent as a street-organ beneath a sick-room window.

“Oh, you don’t know how miserable that man made me,” she said, “or what a life I passed betwixt him and my father. Before I saw him I had never seen a man except my father’s clerks and native servants. You know we didn’t go into society in India on account of—” (here she stopped, and the Major bowed as if that single pause contained a whole suppressed language) “I was a wild romantic child—my head full of books. I listened to him. Well, I married him, and I was wretched from that day—wretched with my father—whose character you know, Major Pendennis, and I won’t speak of: but he wasn’t a good man, sir—neither to my poor mother nor to me—except that he left me his money—nor to no one else that I ever heard of. And as for Amory, he was almost worse. He was a spendthrift when my father was close. He drank dreadful, and was furious when in that way. He wasn’t a good or faithful husband to me, Major Pendennis, and if he’d died in the gaol before that trial, instead of afterwards, he’d have saved me a deal of shame and unhappiness since, sir.”

Then she confessed, with a candour that made the Major’s eyebrows lift slightly as if acknowledging an inconvenient truth: perhaps she would never have married again had she not been so anxious to change the horrid name. And her second marriage—she supposed he knew—had not made her happy.

“Ah, Major Pendennis,” she said, “I’ve got money, to be sure, and I’m a lady, and people fancy I’m very happy, but I ain’t. We all have our cares and griefs and troubles. Many’s the day I sit down to one of my grand dinners with an aching heart; and many a night I lay awake on my fine bed more unhappy than the maid that makes it. I’m not happy in my husband; I’m not in my daughter. She ain’t a good girl like that dear Laura Bell at Fairoaks. She’s cost me many a tear, though you don’t see ’em; and she sneers at her mother because I haven’t had learning and that. How should I? I was brought up amongst natives till I was twelve, and went back to India when I was fourteen. Ah, Major, I should have been a good woman if I’d had a good husband.”

Her voice broke; and she added that she must go upstairs and wipe her eyes, for they were red with crying, and Lady Rockminster was coming to drive in the Park. And when Lady Rockminster did arrive, there was not a trace of tears left—only Lady Clavering’s buoyant good humour and her lively assaults upon the king’s English, which she murdered with as much spirit as if it had insulted her first.

“Begad, she is not such a bad woman,” the Major thought. “Not refined, certainly, and calls Apollo ‘Apoller;’ but she has some heart, and I like that sort of thing—and a devilish deal of money too. Three stars in India Stock to her name. Which that young cub is to have—is he?” And he reflected, with a pious wishfulness, how pleasant it would be if some of those stars might be induced to shine in Miss Blanche’s name; and better still, in Mr. Arthur Pendennis’s.

Still pursuing his schemes—whatever they might presently declare themselves to be—the old negotiator used the privilege of age and intimacy to talk kindly, fatherly, and confidentially with Miss Blanche when he found her alone. He came so often at luncheon-time, and became so domesticated among them, that the ladies did not even hesitate to quarrel in his presence; and Lady Clavering’s loud tongue and brusque temper had many a battle with the Sylphide while the family friend sat by, serene as a cat near a dairy.

Blanche’s wit seldom failed to master these skirmishes; her words went in like little skewers, neat and stinging, and drove her mother, in a rage, from the field. “I am an old fellow,” the Major would say, “and I’ve nothing to do in life. I have my eyes open. I keep good counsel. I’m the friend of both of you; and if you choose to quarrel before me, I shan’t tell any one. But you are two good people, and I intend to make it up between you. I have between lots of people—husbands and wives, fathers and sons, daughters and mammas—before this. I like it. I’ve nothing else to do.”

One day he entered Lady Clavering’s drawing-room just as her ladyship quitted it in a towering indignation and swept past him up the stairs to her own apartments. She could not speak to him now, she said; she was too angry with that—that—that little, wicked—Anger choked the rest and carried it out of hearing.

“My dear, good Miss Amory,” the Major said, advancing into the drawing-room, “I see what is happening. You and mamma have been disagreeing. Mothers and daughters disagree in the best families. It was but last week I healed up a quarrel between Lady Clapperton and Lady Claudia. Lady Lear and her eldest daughter have not spoken for fourteen years. Kinder and more worthy people I never knew—admirable to everybody but each other. They can’t live together; they oughtn’t to live together; and I wish with all my soul, my dear creature, I could see you with an establishment of your own—for there is no woman in London who could conduct one better—with your own establishment, making your own home happy.”

“I am not very happy in this one,” said the Sylphide; “and the stupidity of mamma is enough to provoke a saint.”

“Precisely so. You are not suited. Your mother committed one fault in early life—or was it Nature, my dear, in your case?—she ought not to have educated you. You ought not to have been bred to become the refined and intellectual being you are, surrounded by those who have not your genius or refinement. Your place would be to lead in the most brilliant circles, not to follow. I have watched you, Miss Amory: you are ambitious; and your proper sphere is command. You ought to shine—and you never can in this house. I hope I shall see you in another and happier one some day, and the mistress of it.”

The Sylphide shrugged her lily shoulders with scornful grace. “Where is the Prince, and where is the palace, Major Pendennis? I am ready. But there is no romance in the world now—no real affection.”

“No, indeed,” said the Major, with a face so simple and sentimental that it deserved to be framed.

“Not that I know anything about it,” Blanche added, casting down her eyes, “except what I have read in novels.”

“Of course not,” the Major cried. “How should you, my dear young lady? And novels ain’t true, as you remark admirably, and there is no romance left in the world. Begad, I wish I was a young fellow like my nephew.”

“And what,” continued Miss Amory, musing, “what are the men we see at balls every night—dancing guardsmen, penniless Treasury clerks—boobies! If I had my brother’s fortune, I might have such an establishment as you promise me. But with my name and my little means, what am I to look to? A country parson; or a barrister in a street near Russell Square; or a captain in a dragoon regiment who will take lodgings for me, and come home from mess tipsy and smelling of smoke like Sir Francis Clavering. That is how we girls are destined to end life. O Major Pendennis, I am sick of London, and of balls, and of young dandies with their chin-tips, and of insolent great ladies who know us one day and cut us the next—and of the world altogether. I should like to leave it and go into a convent. I shall never find anybody to understand me. And I live here as much alone in my family and in the world as if I were in a cell locked up for ever. I wish there were Sisters of Charity here, and that I could be one and catch the plague and die of it. I wish to quit the world. I’m not very old; but I am tired—I have suffered so much—I’ve been so disillusionated—I’m weary, I’m weary—O that the Angel of Death would come and beckon me away!”

Translated into plain domestic prose, this meant: a few nights earlier, Lady Flamingo had cut Miss Amory and Lady Clavering; Miss Blanche had not been invited to Lady Drum’s ball; it was the end of the season and nobody had proposed; she had made no sensation at all—she, who was cleverer than any girl of the year. Dora with five thousand pounds, Flora with nothing, and Leonora with red hair were to be married, and nobody had come for Blanche.

“You judge wisely about the world and your position, my dear Miss Blanche,” the Major said. “Princes don’t marry nowadays, as you say—unless the Princess has a doosid deal of money in the funds, or is a lady of his own rank. The young folks of the great families marry into the great families; if they haven’t fortune, they have each other’s shoulders to push on in the world, which is pretty nearly as good. A girl with your fortune can scarcely hope for a great match—but a girl with your genius, your admirable tact, and fine manners, with a clever husband by her side, may make any place for herself. We are grown doosid republican. Talent ranks with birth and wealth now, begad; and a clever man with a clever wife may take any place they please.”

The noble Henry Foker—whom we had the impoliteness to mislay for a little—had, in the interval, been doing what steady men do with a steady passion: feeding it, tending it, turning it on the spit, basting it hourly with hope, and then burning his fingers when it spluttered.

If a few of my youthful readers, who dabble in that cookery, would but keep accounts for a week, they would discover love to be one of the dearest articles in the market. It begins by robbing you of sleep, which is the first of household provisions. You lie awake, listening to the whole night—coach-wheels grumbling in the street like distant thunder, a drunken voice spoiling a tune that once belonged to somebody’s village, a watchman’s call going by like a melancholy refrain—until you come down to breakfast when the toast is cold and the family has long since gone to work. Then, when at last you sit to your occupation, you stir it without looking, like a man who spoils a sauce because his nose is elsewhere. The day’s labour is slurred over, friends neglected, home becomes insipid, and the honest dinner, which your poor mother has contrived with affectionate skill—cutlets properly turned, gravy reduced to the right gloss, a pudding that should have made any Christian grateful—is sent away untasted. The whole table of life has no flavour, except one single dish; and even that one you are forever forbidden to eat in peace.

Such is the condition of ill-regulated youth; and such, precisely, was Mr. H. Foker’s. Having been reared in the comfortable belief that whatever his fancy asked for was a thing Providence meant him to have, he gave himself to this longing with his usual good-natured selfishness. Nor let any man of the world be astonished that one who had preached prudence to Arthur Pendennis should himself become a captive. Who among us has not been a solemn food-historian at another man’s table—explaining, with learned gravity, the virtues of moderation—only to go home and devour the very pie he condemned? You, madam, perhaps, are a creature of perfect digestion and perfect virtue; you, sir, so strong-minded that no foolish appetite ever interrupts your attendance at ’Change. We will not trouble such lofty persons with sympathy. We keep ours for the fallible, who burn their hands, taste again, and carry on cooking with the rest of mankind. Angels are very admirable, but intolerable companions; they sit above us, pristine as untouched sugar, and we cannot reach up to talk to them over the pot.

There are no perfect characters here—save perhaps one little one, and she, poor soul, does not know it, but suspects herself of being as wicked as need be. At present, however, she is not in London; and it is by no means for the like of her that Harry’s heart was simmering and boiling over.

Besides, what does a few failings matter to worship? Need we be saints to be treated like them? The world’s taste is a mighty miscellany. There is no aged booby, no pompous offender, no stupid tyrant, no figure cut from the coarsest joint, that may not, some day, find himself preferred to virtue—hugged, clung to, defended, as though sin were a family recipe and repentance an exotic condiment. History and the newspapers can furnish love-stories between persons as unpromising as yesterday’s bones and beer; yet the passion has been as grand, to the sufferers, as Cleopatra’s banquets.

So Henry Foker longed after his love and cursed the fate that kept him from her. When Lord Gravesend’s family retired to the country—his lordship leaving his proxy behind with the venerable Lord Bagwig—Harry still lingered in London, not to the smallest sorrow of Lady Ann, his affianced cousin, who missed him no more than she would miss an extra footman at dinner. Wherever Miss Clavering went, the infatuated youth contrived to hover. But because his engagement to Lady Ann was known, he was forced to keep his fever under his coat; and so it raged inwardly, like a pot too tightly covered, until one wondered it did not blow him up and scatter him, lid and all, into the street.

A grand entertainment took place at Gaunt House one beautiful June evening; and next day the journals printed, in close-set columns, two yards of nobility and gentry who had been honoured with invitations. Among the guests were Sir Francis and Lady Clavering and Miss Amory—whom the indefatigable Major Pendennis had thrust, by patient engineering, into the blaze of fashion—together with our two young friends, Arthur and Harry. Each danced a great deal with Miss Blanche.

As for the worthy Major, he assumed the charge of Lady Clavering, and, knowing her ladyship’s brightest talent lay not in conversation but in consumption, conducted her into the refreshment-room: that sacred chapel of cold chicken and hot flattery, where, under Titians and Giorgiones, beneath Vandyke’s cavaliers and Reynolds’s ladies, and amongst gold and silver salvers that might have served a regiment, supper went on all night with the reckless splendour of people who never paid for it. There were creams that trembled like pale custard clouds, jellies shining as if a ruby had learned to wobble, white soups exhaling pepper and marrow, salads crisp with that sharp green scent that wakes the tongue, peaches that seemed to have stolen their bloom from dawn, grapes that burst with a faint crack like tiny drums. Tea steamed in bright urns; champagne whispered and hissed, like fashionable applause.

Of how many of these articles Lady Clavering partook does not become us to say. The Major followed her with admirable patience, signalling to solemn footmen and lovely servant-maids, bringing plate after plate to the Begum, ministering to her palate as though it were the public service. What he suffered—what heroic pangs in boots, what rheumatism politely ignored, what silent prayer for bed—no man can compute. He never confessed; he only smiled.

Mr. Wagg, who was present, counted Lady Clavering’s dishes as long as arithmetic remained possible; but as he himself drank champagne with the zeal of a patriot, his calculations grew untrustworthy. Still, he recommended Lady Steyne’s medical man, Mr. Honeyman, to look carefully after the Begum, and to call next day for tidings of her health—as one might inquire after a ship that had taken in too much cargo.

Sir Francis Clavering showed himself too; he lurked about the magnificent rooms with the air of a man who has strayed into church by mistake. The splendour and the company were not to the Baronet’s taste; after tossing off a tumbler of wine or two at the buffet, he escaped to the region of Jermyn Street, where his true worship awaited him: Loder, Punter, little Moss Abramns, Captain Skewball, and the familiar green table. There, in the rattle of the box and the agreeable din of gaming talk—coins clinking, oaths popping like corks, the harsh music of London pleasure—Sir Francis’s spirits rose to their accustomed pitch of feeble hilarity.

Meanwhile in the dancing-room Mr. Pynsent, having engaged Miss Amory, came up to claim her hand. But scowls of recognition had already passed between him and Arthur Pendennis; and Arthur, rising abruptly, claimed Miss Amory for the present dance. Mr. Pynsent, biting his lips, scowled yet more savagely, bowed profoundly, and withdrew, saying he gave up his claim. There are certain men whom life keeps throwing across one’s path as persistently as a bad tune in the street. Pynsent and Pen had that fate with each other; and each judged the other accordingly.

“What a confounded conceited provincial fool!” thought the one. “Because he has written a twopenny novel, his head’s turned. A kicking would cure him.”

“What an impertinent idiot!” thought the other, and said aloud to his partner, “His soul is in Downing Street; his neckcloth is foolscap; his hair is sand; his legs are rulers; his vitals are tape and sealing-wax. He was a prig in his cradle and has only laughed three times—always at the same joke of his chief. I have the same liking for that man, Miss Amory, that I have for cold boiled veal.”

Blanche, of course, pronounced him wicked—méchant—perfectly abominable; and wondered, with charming malice, what he would say when her back was turned.

“Say?” cried Pen. “Say you have the most beautiful figure and the slimmest waist in the world, Blanche—Miss Amory, I mean. I beg your pardon. Another turn: this music would make an alderman dance.”

“And you have left off tumbling when you waltz now?” she asked, looking up at him with that little air of mock concern which is more provoking than scorn.

“One falls and one gets up again in life, Blanche,” he said. “I used to call you so in old times—and it is the prettiest name in the world. Besides, I have practised since then.”

“And with a great number of partners, I’m afraid,” she sighed—sham sigh—and shrugged her shoulders. And indeed Mr. Pen had practised a good deal in this life and had become a better dancer.

If Pendennis was impertinent, Foker—usually bland and talkative—became wholly mum and melancholy when he danced with Miss Amory. To clasp her slender waist was rapture, to whirl with her was delirium; but to speak—what could he say worth the hearing of such a queen? His tongue, which could discourse at length upon horses, coats, bets, and the private history of half the club, now stuck like dough that will not rise.

Blanche did the talking. She asked after that dear little pony; she thanked him with a tender kindness and regret, and refused the dear little pony with a sigh so delicately administered it might have been whipped syllabub.

“I have nobody to ride with in London,” she said. “Mamma is timid, and her figure is not pretty on horseback. Sir Francis never goes out with me. He loves me like—like a stepdaughter. Oh, how delightful it must be to have a father—a father, Mr. Foker!”

“Oh—uncommon,” said Mr. Harry, who enjoyed that blessing with calmness. At which—forgetting her sentiment in a flash—Blanche’s grey eyes twinkled so archly that both burst out laughing; and Harry, enchanted and suddenly at ease, began to chatter with a rush of innocent prattle—kind, simple Foker talk—seasoned with expressions not to be found in dictionaries, and full of little personal histories of himself and horses, with artless freedom about people passing in the ballroom, whose looks and motives he sketched with a humorous ease that would have made him, in a different world, an excellent kitchen gossip.

When his modesty returned and the talk flagged, Blanche knew how to stir the sauce again. She asked of Logwood: Was it pretty? Was he a hunting man? Did he like women to hunt?—in which case she was prepared to adore hunting. But Mr. Foker, expressing his dislike of sporting females, pointed out Lady Bullfinch passing by—whom he had seen at cover with a cigar in her face. Immediately Blanche too detested field sports, and declared it made her shudder to think of a dear sweet little fox being killed; on which Harry laughed and waltzed with renewed vigour.

At the end of the waltz—the last they danced together that night—Blanche questioned him about Drummington: was it a fine house? His cousins, she heard, were accomplished. Lord Erith she had met; which cousin was his favourite? Was it not Lady Ann? Yes—she was sure it was she—sure by his looks and blushes. She was tired; it was very late; she must go to mamma; and, without another word, she sprang away from Harry’s arm and seized upon Pen’s, who was swaggering about the room, and cried, “Mamma, mamma!—take me to mamma, dear Mr. Pendennis!”—shooting Harry through with a Parthian glance as she fled.

Lord Steyne, with garter and ribbon, bald head and shining eyes, and that collar of red whiskers about his face, looked grand upon an occasion of state; and he made a prodigious impression on Lady Clavering when he introduced himself at the request of the obsequious Major. With his own white and royal hand he gave her a glass of wine; said he had heard of her charming daughter; begged to be presented; and at that instant Arthur Pendennis came up with Blanche upon his arm.

The peer bowed profoundly; Blanche made the deepest curtsy ever executed by young person with a tired foot. His lordship gave Arthur his hand; said he had read his book—very wicked and clever—asked Miss Blanche if she had read it; at which Pen blushed and winced, because Blanche, in black ringlets and a little altered, was one of his heroines. She had read it. Her eyes did the praising with rapture enough to make an author feel at once crowned and ashamed. The little scene played off, the Marquis made two more bows to mother and daughter and moved on through his guests, spreading grandeur as a stove spreads heat.

Mamma and daughter were loud in their admiration of the noble Marquis the moment his broad back was turned. “He said they make a very nice couple,” whispered Major Pendennis to Lady Clavering. Did he, indeed? Mamma thought they would. Mamma was so flustered—by the honour, by the lights, by the compliments, by the supper, by all the sweet froth of the night—that her good-humour overflowed like punch in a crowded bowl. She laughed; she winked; she nodded knowingly at Pen; she tapped him with her fan; she tapped Blanche; she tapped the Major. Her contentment was boundless, and she expressed it upon everything within reach.

When the party at last went down the great staircase of Gaunt House, morning had risen stark and clear over the black trees of the square. The sky was tinged with pink, like the inside of a shell. The faces of some of the dancers—ah, how ghastly they looked in that honest light!—were like dishes that have stood out too long. And the admirable Major above all—who had for hours been by Lady Clavering’s side, feeding her body with everything nice and her ear with everything flattering—what an object he was now! The rings round his eyes were the colour of bistre; those orbs themselves resembled the plovers’ eggs of which Lady Clavering and Blanche had tasted; the wrinkles in his old face were cut deeper than usual; and a silver stubble, like chilly dew, glittered on his chin beside the dyed whiskers now limp and out of curl.

There he stood, enduring without complaint a silent agony; knowing everybody could see his collapse (as he could see theirs), longing for bed for hours, aware that suppers disagreed with him, yet having eaten a little to keep Lady Clavering in good-humour; with twinges in back and knees; with weary feet burning in varnished boots. If the gods admire fortitude, surely that Power in whose chapels Major Pendennis worshipped must have looked approvingly upon this martyrdom. There are sufferers in this cause as in the other; priests have gashed themselves for their idols, and men will torture themselves to please what they take for divinity. Smash the idols if you can—but don’t be too savage upon the idolaters; they adore the best thing they know.

The elder and younger Pendennis waited with Lady Clavering and her daughter until her carriage was announced; and then the Major’s martyrdom ended, for the good-natured Begum insisted upon leaving him at his door in Bury Street. So he took the back seat after a feeble bow or two and a speech of thanks—polite to the last, resolute in duty. The Begum waved her dumpy hand in farewell to Arthur and Foker; Blanche smiled languidly at the young men and wondered whether she looked wan and green under her rose-coloured hood, and whether it was the mirrors at Gaunt House or the fatigue and fever in her eyes that made her seem so pale.

Arthur, perhaps, saw well enough how yellow Blanche looked, and did not attribute it to glass or fancy. Our young man of the world could use his eyes keenly and saw Blanche’s face pretty much as nature and late hours had made it. But poor Foker—dazzled and blinded—found no more fault in it than in the sun now flaring over the rooftops.

Among the wicked London habits Pen had acquired, the moralist may observe he kept abominable hours, and often went to bed when sober country people were thinking of getting up. Men grow used to any hour: editors, Covent Garden folk, night cabmen and coffee-sellers, chimney-sweeps, and the ladies and gentlemen of fashion who frequent balls are often lively at three or four in the morning when honest mortals are snoring. Pen, as we have shown, was brisk at this period, inclined to smoke his cigar and speak freely.

So Foker and Pen walked away from Gaunt House indulging in both amusements—or rather, Pen talked and smoked, and Foker looked as if he wanted to say something and couldn’t find the words. Pen, after being amongst great folks, grew sarcastic and dandified; he imitated their tones without knowing, and, having a lively imagination, mistook himself for a person of importance with extraordinary ease. He rattled on, attacking this person and that; sneering at Lady John Turnbull’s bad French—introduced into all conversation in spite of everybody’s groans—at Mrs. Slack Roper’s extraordinary costume and sham jewels; at old dandies and young ones; at whom didn’t he sneer?

“You fire at everybody, Pen—you’re grown awful, that you are,” Foker said. “Now you’ve pulled about Blondel’s yellow wig, and Colchicum’s black one, why don’t you have a shy at a brown one—hay? you know whose I mean. It got into Lady Clavering’s carriage.”

“Under my uncle’s hat? My uncle is a martyr, Foker, my boy,” Pen cried. “My uncle has been doing excruciating duties all night. He likes to go to bed early. He gets a dreadful headache if he sits up and touches supper. He has the gout if he walks or stands much at a ball. He has been sitting up, and standing up, and supping—and he has gone home to the gout and the headache for my sake. Shall I make fun of the old boy? No—not for Venice!”

“How do you mean—for your sake?” Foker asked, stopping short with a look as if someone had suddenly clapped a cold plate into his hands.

“Boy! canst thou keep a secret if I impart it to thee?” Pen cried, in high spirits. “Art thou of good counsel? Wilt thou swear? Wilt thou be mum, or wilt thou preach? Wilt thou be silent and hear—or wilt thou speak and die?” And as he flung himself into a ridiculous theatrical attitude, the cabmen at the stand in Piccadilly looked up from their dozing and grinned at the antics of the two young swells, while the city’s morning noises—wheels, hoofs, a hawker’s cry—began their daily overture.

“What the doose are you driving at?” Foker asked, very much agitated.

Pen, scarcely noting the agitation, kept his bantering, excited tone. “Henry, friend of my youth,” he declaimed, “and witness of my early follies—though dull at thy books, yet thou art not altogether deprived of sense—nay, blush not, Henrico; thou hast a good portion of that, and of courage and kindness too, at the service of thy friends. Were I in a strait of poverty, I would come to my Foker’s purse. Were I in grief, I would discharge my grief upon his sympathising bosom—”

“Gammon, Pen—go on,” Foker muttered, uneasy as a man who hears his own name called in a kitchen where creditors are waiting.

“I would, Henrico, upon thy studs, and upon thy cambric worked by the hands of beauty to adorn the breast of valour! Know then, friend of my boyhood’s days, that Arthur Pendennis of the Upper Temple, student-at-law, feels he is growing lonely and old. Care is furrowing his temples, and Baldness is busy with his crown. Shall we stop and have a drop of coffee at this stall? it looks very hot and nice. Look how that cabman is blowing at his saucer. No, you won’t? Aristocrat! I resume my tale. I am getting on in life. I have got devilish little money. I want some. I am thinking of getting some, and settling in life. I’m thinking of settling. I’m thinking of marrying, old boy. I’m thinking of becoming a moral man; a steady port-and-sherry character: with a good reputation in my quartier, and a moderate establishment of two maids and a man—with an occasional brougham to drive out Mrs. Pendennis, and a house near the Parks for the accommodation of the children. Ha! what sayest thou? Answer thy friend, thou worthy child of beer. Speak, I adjure thee by all thy vats.”

“But you ain’t got any money, Pen,” said the other, still looking alarmed.

Major Pendennis, having fought that last campaign at Gaunt House as if it had been Waterloo and his liver the enemy, discovered next morning that heroism is admirable but very trying to the joints. So, as soon as it was medically decent to stir him, he bundled his groaning dignity into a chaise and went off to Buxton to be steeped like an old tea-leaf in healing waters. Parliament shut its mouth; the Claverings shut their house; London, having made its noise for the season, took itself away as completely as a dinner-party after the last glass.

The lawyers flew off to their circuits, the fine people to the Continent, the healthy to Scotland, the unhealthy to spas, and the idle—being the most perishable article—dispersed to wherever idleness is best preserved. Pall Mall looked as if it had been laid out to dry. The clubs’ bow-windows, usually full of heads considering nothing with immense importance, displayed only emptiness contemplating itself. The red jackets vanished from the Palace gates. Tradesmen who had spent the year bowing now went abroad to practise walking upright. Tailors, who had been hemming other men’s manners, grew moustachios and floated up the Rhine. Bootmakers met their customers at Ems and blushed to see that their handiwork was still attached to its owner. The Sunday sermons in St. James’s were preached to half a congregation, and not a sinner of distinction among them—a dreadful discouragement to the clergy. Even the band in Kensington Gardens put its brass and silver to bed; only a couple of old chaises crept along the Serpentine like insects looking for summer.

Clarence Bulbul, chained by Treasury duty, rode in Rotten Row and declared it as vast and lonely as the Arabian desert; which was a very loud comparison for so silent a place, and proved, if anything proves it, that man can import noise into a hush as easily as a barrel-organ can invade a meadow. Warrington, who knew the value of silence the way some men know the value of port, packed a gross of Cavendish tobacco and retired to his brother’s in Norfolk. Pen was left alone in chambers for a while; he could not quit the metropolis at his own pleasure, being kept there by the small tyranny of his newspaper, the Pall Mall Gazette, for which he acted as editor and charge d’affaires while Captain Shandon, that great general of leading articles when compelled at bayonet-point, took his ease with his family at Boulogne.

Now, although Mr. Arthur Pendennis had for years been protesting that he was blasé, scorched-out, and generally done for, the fact remained that he was a young man of excellent digestion and a conscience elastic enough to stretch over almost any dinner. He ate at least once a day with true feeling; and if he could not secure a good dinner, he seated himself before a bad one with perfect serenity, as if to say to Providence, “You do your worst: I can swallow it.” And though he talked of misanthropy, he had a perpetual appetite for faces, voices, and the agreeable clatter of mankind. If he could not have wit, rank, or beauty, he took what he could get—tavern-parlours, Greenwich steamboats, jaunts to Hampstead with Finucane his colleague, the little theatres across the river, and especially Vauxhall, where the lamps burned like captive stars and where the air was always seasoned with fried fish, hot sausages, wilted bouquets, damp gravel, cigar smoke, and that peculiar London perfume compounded of river-breeze and humanity.

Pen would stroll there and watch the grimaces of comic singers and the graces of equestrians, and, with a satiric humour that still had a crumb of kindness in it, he could look as pleasantly at the lookers-on as at the show—at the roystering youths drinking their fun straight as gin; at the honest parents feeding their delighted children on cake, awe, and sticky fingers; at the poor girls laughing too loud, as if loudness could drown care. Pen boasted of this sympathy with “all conditions of men,” called it anthropology, and said he hoped to keep it to the last; which is a handsome hope, and easy enough while one’s own boots are tight, varnished, and not pinching.

Indeed he had lately been talking in his impetuous manner to Warrington about having burned out romance like a kitchen fire that has eaten its own fuel. If ever he married, he said, it would be a marriage of reason—good temper, good looks, a little money: something to cushion the carriage through life. Romance, he declared, was done.

“Stuff!” growled Warrington. “You fancied you were getting bald the other day, and bragged of it; and then you began rubbing bear’s-grease on your head the minute the hairdresser hinted at it. You smell like a barber’s shop.”

“You are Diogenes,” Pen answered, blushing as philosophers should not blush. “You want every man to live in a tub like you. Violets smell better than stale tobacco, you grizzly cynic.” And then he went on with the air of a weary pilgrim who takes immense pains to look well on the road.

It happened, then, in this dull season—on a shining autumn Friday night—that Pen, having written at the office a brilliant leading article (one of those pieces which Captain Shandon might have written had the Captain been in good humour and inclined to work, which he never was unless a necessity stood over him with a cudgel), reviewed his wet proof with satisfaction, and determined to cross the water and regale himself with Vauxhall’s fireworks.

He slipped into his pocket the order that admitted “Editor of Pall Mall Gazette and friend,” paid honest coin to get over Waterloo Bridge, and walked through the clear night. Above, the stars shone quietly—lamps of a better management than Vauxhall’s—and below, the river made that dark, thick London sound which is half water, half city, and wholly unlike any country stream. There was none of the grinding industrial uproar here that turns music into mere rivalry; only the soft, continuous hush and lap, with distant wheels murmuring like a bad conscience far away.

Before you enter Vauxhall’s blaze, you must pass that black, dreary passage and its wickets, like a throat you swallow through to reach the feast. In the wall are two bright holes, and in each hole sits a gentleman at a desk, ready to take your money or your ticket; and while the lamps inside promise fairyland, the little box at the gate has the tone of a counting-house, which is a useful reminder that even enchantment must balance its books.

Pen stepped forward to show his order; but at the aperture before him a gentleman and two ladies were already in noisy parley. The gentleman’s hat was slanted rakishly, his cloak was shabby but worn with a boldness that tried to make shabbiness a fashion; and he was crying out in a voice Pen knew as one knows a tune that has been played too often in one’s rooms.

“Bedad, sir, if ye doubt me honour, will ye obleege me by stipping out of that box, and——”

“Lor, Capting!” cried the elder lady.

“Don’t bother me,” said the man in the box, sulkily, with the air of a person whose chief pleasure in life is refusing people.

“And ask Mr. Hodgen himself,” the gentleman continued, “who’s in the gyardens, to let these leedies pass. Don’t be froightened, me dear madam; I’m not going to quarl with this gintleman—at anyreet not before leedies. Will ye go, sir, and desoire Mr. Hodgen, with Captain Costigan’s compliments, to stip out and let in the leedies—for meself, sir, I’ve seen Vauxhall, and I scawrun any interfayrance on moi account: but for these leedies—one of them has never been there—sure ye’d not take advantage of me misfartune in losing the ticket, to deproive her of her pleasure?”

“It ain’t no use, Captain. I can’t go about your business,” the check-taker answered.

The Captain swore; the elder lady echoed him in a milder dialect. The younger, who had been bearing up bravely, looked up at the Captain and said, “Never mind, Captain Costigan, I’m sure I don’t want to go at all. Come away, mamma.” Which, being the speech of disappointment, ended as such speeches often end: her mouth quivered, her courage broke, and she began to cry.

“Me poor child!” cried Costigan, instantly turning paternal and tragic. “Can ye see that, sir, and will ye not let this innocent creature in?”

“It ain’t my business,” said the doorkeeper, peevishly; and at that moment Pen came up, recognised the Captain, and spoke.

“Don’t you know me, Captain? Pendennis!”

“My dear boy! Me dear friend!” cried Costigan, stretching out his hand as if he would clasp all mankind when he was in trouble. He poured out the tale of “a most unluckee conthratong.” He had had an order from Mr. Hodgen—who was within, and would sing “The Body Snatcher,” “The Death of General Wolfe,” “The Banner of Blood,” and other tender domestic songs—admitting two. Captain Costigan, by a natural extension of arithmetic, had concluded that “two” might be made to include “three,” and had brought two ladies accordingly. Worse: the order was lost upon the road; the paper had vanished; and here were the leedies, to be turned away like last year’s fashions.

Pen’s good nature, always ready like a knife at supper, flew out at once. He had seen the girl’s appealing face and the sudden helpless tears; and though he had talked of being used up, the sight of a young creature cheated of a pleasure by a slip of paper touched him more than all his own rhetoric. If it had been his last guinea, he would have paid it to dry those eyes. The girl turned her face away when she saw a stranger looking at her grief, and dabbed at her cheeks with a little handkerchief.

Arthur stood there very handsome and kind—hat off, blushing, bowing, generous, a gentleman. “Who are they?” he asked himself; and he fancied he had seen the elder woman somewhere in his daily comings and goings.

“If I can be of any service, Captain Costigan,” Pen said, “I hope you will command me. Is there any difficulty about taking these ladies in? Will you kindly make use of my purse? And—and I have a ticket myself that will admit two—I hope, ma’am, you will permit me?”

His first instinct was to pay for the whole party and throw away his own order in some gallant manner; but the elder woman’s look—and a certain sensible air about both of them—warned him that they would rather not be patronised with too grand a flourish. So he handed his purse to Costigan, produced his ticket with a laugh, and offered his arm to the elder lady with the politeness he could afford to anybody in a petticoat, the humbler the wearer, the more ceremonial his civility.

“Fanny, take the gentleman’s arm,” said the elder. “Since you will be so very kind. I’ve seen you often come in at our gate, sir, and go in to Captain Strong’s at No. 3.”

Fanny made a curtsey and slipped her hand under Arthur’s arm. The glove was shabby, but the hand itself was small and pretty, with that soft, warmed life in it that makes a young man suddenly aware he is not a statue. She was not a child, but scarcely a woman yet; her tears dried quickly, as young tears do, and her cheeks took on a blush as if pleasure, once admitted, rushed to the face like a guilty secret. She looked up with gratitude and delight.

Arthur, in a protecting way, laid his other hand lightly over hers as it rested on his sleeve. “Fanny’s a pretty name,” he said. “And you know me, do you?”

“We keep the lodge, sir, at Shepherd’s Inn,” Fanny answered, curtseying again. “And I’ve never been at Vauxhall, sir, and Papa didn’t like me to go—and—and—O—O—law, how beautiful!”

For the Gardens burst upon her all at once—an eruption of lamps, avenues strewn with light, domes and arches and gilded nonsense set shining against the night. The air seemed to change flavour at the threshold: outside, river damp and soot; inside, sugar, smoke, roasted meat, spilled ale, crushed herbs underfoot, and a faint metallic tang from the fireworks’ promised chemistry. The crowd’s voices rose and fell like surf; and threaded through it all were the birdlike calls of vendors, the clink of glasses, a distant fiddle, and that steady human roar which is London’s true national anthem.

Fanny shrank back in wonder and then leaned closer, as if the brightness might carry her off unless a gentleman anchored her. Pen was pleased with her pleasure and pressed her little hand gently to his sleeve. “What would I not give for a little of this pleasure?” thought the blasé young man, who suddenly discovered his blasé-ness had been mislaid like Costigan’s ticket.

Behind them came Captain Costigan’s voice, rich with triumph. “Your purse, Pendennis, me dear boy—will ye count it? it’s all roight—no—ye thrust in old Jack Costigan—he thrusts me, ye see, madam. Ye’ve been me preserver, Pen—I’ve known um since choildhood, Mrs. Bolton; he’s the proproietor of Fairoaks Castle, and many’s the cooper of clart I’ve dthrunk there with the first nobilitee of his neetive countee—Mr. Pendennis, ye’ve been me preserver, and me daughtther will thank ye—Mr. Simpson, your humble servant, sir.”

If Pen was magnificent in courtesy to the women, what was Costigan’s splendour? He bowed to lamps, to singers, to passers-by, to the idea of Vauxhall itself; he cried bravo before anyone began; he took the very air as an applause due to him.

A man descended, like Costigan, from a long line of Hibernian kings, chieftains, and other magistrates of imagination, had of course too much dignity to walk arm-in-arm with a lady who occasionally swept his room and fried his mutton-chops. On the way from Shepherd’s Inn he had marched beside Mrs. Bolton and Miss Fanny in a patronising manner, pointing out buildings, discoursing upon foreign parts he had visited (at least in narrative), and dropping names of people of rank as if they were raisins in a pudding. And now, within the illuminated property, he could not be expected to relax his grandeur and lend an arm to a woman who was, in truth, little better than a housekeeper or charwoman.

Pen, for his part, had no such scruples. Miss Fanny Bolton did not make his bed nor sweep his chambers; and, besides, he was not inclined to let go a pretty companion whose astonishment made his own evening seem fresher. As for Fanny, her colour heightened; her eyes shone; and she looked at other ladies strolling under other gentlemen’s protection and decided, with that quick, sweet injustice of youth, that her gentleman was handsomer than any in the Gardens.

There were votaries of pleasure of every sort—rakish young surgeons, fast young clerks, commercial gentry bent on wasting their week’s conscience, a stray dandy of the Guards—while at a supper-box you might see a fine lady nibbling an ice as if it were a sin, and in a darker walk a poor girl laughing as if laughter were her only gown. Old Lord Colchicum was there in attendance upon Mademoiselle Caracoline, the equestrian celebrity from the ring, who spoke her native French very loud and used idioms of remarkable strength, as if she were cracking whips even in conversation.

Colchicum leaned upon Caracoline; and little Tom Tufthunt leaned upon Colchicum. There is never a Don Juan without a Leporello to hold the ladder, and Tom was delighted with his post. He would carve the fowl, make the salad, run errands, admire everything, and feel himself in the very centre of fashionable vice.

When Pen, with Fanny on his arm, crossed near that party, Lord Colchicum gave Arthur only a passing leer of recognition; his lordship’s eyes travelled at once from Pen’s face to the bonnet that sheltered Pen’s companion, as a connoisseur’s eye leaves the frame to examine the picture. Tom Tufthunt, however, nodded with genial impudence. “How are you, old boy?” he said, with a knowing look at the historian of these matters.

“That is the great rider at Astley’s; I have seen her there,” Miss Bolton whispered, looking after Mademoiselle Caracoline. “And who is that old man? Is it not the gentleman in the ring?”

“That is Lord Viscount Colchicum, Miss Fanny,” said Pen, with an air of protection, meaning no harm, and even enjoying that she should be impressed and that a noble Don Juan should have seen her leaning on his arm.

Fanny was very pretty: dark brilliant eyes, teeth like little pearls, a mouth fresh and red—not painted scarlet like Caracoline’s vermilion, but naturally coloured as if it had just tasted raspberry. And what a difference between the girl’s voice and the woman’s; between the girl’s laugh, which rang clear as a spoon against a glass, and the woman’s, which was all practised sparkle! Only lately, indeed, had Fanny—dusting the little glass over the Bows-Costigan mantelpiece—begun to suspect she might be a beauty. A year ago she had been a gawky schoolgirl, sneered at by her father and overlooked by the girls at Miss Minifer’s day-school in Newcastle Street; and it was in the porter’s dim lodge at Shepherd’s Inn, unnoticed as a herb growing in shade, that she bloomed.

So she hung upon Mr. Pen’s arm, and they paced the Gardens. Empty as London was, there were still two million people left behind; and among them were one or two of Arthur’s acquaintances.

Among these, silent and alone, pale, hands in pockets, passed Henry Foker, Esq., giving Pen a rueful nod. Young Henry wandered from place to place, from light to light, trying to shake off thought; but Blanche sat on his heart like a stone in a pocket. He thought of her in the dark walks; he thought of her in the lamp devices. He even consulted a fortune-teller and was disappointed when the gipsy told him he loved a dark lady who would make him happy—a prophecy as impertinent as it was inaccurate. At the concert, though Mr. Momus sang his most stunning comic songs and asked his most astonishing riddles, no smile came to visit Foker’s lips. In fact, he never heard Mr. Momus at all; the loudest joke cannot compete with a quiet grief.

Pen and Miss Bolton stood near listening to the same concert; she noticed Foker’s woebegone face, and Pen laughed at it.

“What makes that odd-looking little man so dismal?” Fanny asked.

“I think he is crossed in love,” Pen said. “Isn’t that enough to make any man dismal, Fanny?” And he looked down at her with that grand protecting air he liked to practise—like a hero in a play who is sure the audience admires his tenderness.

“Crossed in love is he? poor gentleman,” said Fanny, with a sigh; and her eyes went kindly towards Harry with a pity so honest it would have startled him—had he seen it. But he did not.

“How dy do, Mr. Pendennis!” broke in a voice; and there stood a young man in a large white coat and red neckcloth, with a dingy shirt-collar turned down to display a dubious neck. A big pin of bullion or something pretending to be bullion glittered on him; his waistcoat was imaginative with glass buttons; his trousers cried aloud, “Come look at me and see how cheap and tawdry I am; my master, what a dirty buck!” He had a little stick in one pocket and a lady in pink satin on the other arm.

“How dy do—Forget me, I dare say? Huxter,—Clavering.”

“How do you do, Mr. Huxter?” said Pen, with his most princely manner. “I hope you are very well.”

“Pretty bobbish, thanky,” said Mr. Huxter, wagging his head. “I say, Pendennis, you’ve been coming it uncommon strong since we had the row at Wapshot’s, don’t you remember. Great author, hay? Go about with the swells. Saw your name in the Morning Post. I suppose you’re too much of a swell to come and have a bit of supper with an old friend? Charterhouse Lane to-morrow night,—some devilish good fellows from Bartholomew’s, and some stunning gin-punch. Here’s my card.”

And Mr. Huxter, releasing his hand from the pocket where his cane lived, pulled off the top of his card-case with his teeth and produced a visiting-ticket, which he offered to Arthur with the generosity of a man who believes he bestows distinction.

“You are exceedingly kind, I am sure,” Pen said, taking it with a lofty courtesy; “but I regret that I have an engagement which will take me out of town to-morrow night.” And he slipped the card into his waistcoat pocket, wondering how such a creature could have the audacity to distribute his pasteboard to anybody. Mr. Huxter’s father, after all, was a surgeon and apothecary at Clavering, as Pen’s had been at Bath; but the impudence of some men—especially when helped by bad company and worse punch—defies arithmetic.

“Well, old fellow, never mind,” said Mr. Huxter, always frank and now, from vinous excitement, more familiar than ever. “If ever you are passing, look up our place, I’m mostly at home Saturdays; and there’s generally a cheese cupboard. Ta, ta.—There’s the bell for the fireworks ringing. Come along, Mary.”

He ran off with the crowd towards the fireworks.

When he was out of sight, Pen too began to run with his little companion, drawn forward by the promise of rockets and by the delicious way Fanny’s hand clung to his arm as if he were her safeguard in the bright bewilderment. Mrs. Bolton followed, calling and hurrying; and at her side marched Captain Costigan, too majestic to run for friend or enemy, preserving his jaunty swagger as if dignity were a uniform not to be disordered even by fireworks—so that, in a moment, he and his companion were left behind, and Pen and Miss Fanny were carried onward into the noisy, scented, glittering heart of Vauxhall.

Costigan did not come thundering at Arthur Pendennis’s door with a challenge, nor did Mr. Huxter fling any hostile billet-doux over the area-railings. So when Pen woke, he did what very few London men wake to do: he woke without immediately swallowing a mouthful of care, like cold gruel one must bolt before breakfast.

The City gentleman, the instant his eyes open, hears—in his mind, if not through the sash—the clink of coin and the rasp of ledgers; the lawyer sits up already entangled in somebody else’s quarrel, and can taste the ink before he has even rinsed his mouth. Most of us, when sleep drops the curtain, find Anxiety waiting in the front row at matinée, tapping its cane for the play to begin. Sleep, that honest cook of Providence, sends us out again with our spirits re-seasoned; but Pen’s day’s work was not of the kind to make him leap up greedy for it. Literature, when you are paid by the column and must trot daily like a hired horse, loses its froth and sparkle; Pegasus, once harnessed to a stage-coach, begins to look about as romantic as a cab-hack, and requires either the whip or the corn, and generally both.

So Arthur did his pieces for the Pall Mall Gazette—now with a novelist’s name and a somewhat better salary—and sometimes the dish came out crisp, sometimes heavy; but always made, always sent in, with the professional air of a man stirring sauce because the kitchen expects it, not because the smell intoxicates him.

Society did not feed him either. He bragged of it; he yawned over it. He was too young to get the best of women’s talk (which, like certain old wines, can only be tasted properly when you have stopped admiring your own glass); too young to be an equal among men who had made their mark; and, by a cruel trick of time, too old for the riotous boys of his own age. Too much of a pleasure-man for the business tribe, too much of a business-man (in appearances) for the pleasure tribe—destined to sit a good deal alone, like a guest who has arrived between the fish and the roast. He bore it well enough, but talked of it as if it were martyrdom—because complaining, with Pen, was a kind of after-dinner habit.

And yet, this morning, the first thing he thought of—before his boots, before his columns, before his own face in the glass—was a girl’s voice.

“What a nice little artless creature that was,” he said to himself, while the memory of Vauxhall still hung about him like the faint scent of crushed mint on fingers. “So much pleasanter than the practiced simpers in ball-rooms. Who would have guessed a rose could grow in a porter’s lodge? And in Shepherd’s Inn too—that old flower-pot of a place. She sings, does she? Taught by old Bows. If her singing is half as sweet as her speaking—those low veiled voices—why, it must go to the heart. ‘What would you like me to call you?’ Poor little Fanny! It hurt me to put on the grand air and bid her call me ‘Sir’—but no nonsense, no Faust-and-Margaret cookery for me.”

Then, as his thoughts always did, his mind turned from the young to the old, from the fresh bread to the seasoned stew.

“That old Bows! He’s a dear old fellow—a gentleman in those ancient clothes, a philosopher with a kind heart. How good he was in the Fotheringay business. He has had his griefs, too. I must cultivate old Bows. One ought to know people of every sort. I’m tired of the fine world. Besides, there’s nobody in town. I’ll go and see Bows—and Costigan too. What a character! I’ll study him and put him in a book.”

Thus spoke Mr. Arthur, anthropologist of London, who liked to fancy he went among his fellows as a naturalist in search of specimens, while his heart, like everybody else’s, went on its own errands. It was Saturday—the Gazette had appeared, the ink-bottle might be corked, and contributors could take their brains for a walk like dogs. Pen resolved upon Shepherd’s Inn at once—of course to see old Bows.

The truth (which is always more mischievous than the intentions we proclaim) was that if Arthur had been the most determined deceiver who ever polished a smile to ruin a girl, he could hardly have chosen better tactics than those he had used the night before. His dandified protecting manner, his conceit dressed up as good-humour, his generosity, and—worse than all for poor Fanny—his very honesty in checking the timid little flutter of her sensibility, had combined like spice, sugar, and flame to make a dish irresistible. A man’s scruple is sometimes the most seductive thing he can offer.

If we could peep into Fanny Bolton’s bed (a cupboard-bed, where she lay wedged with two small sisters like loaves in a too-tight tin), we should find the poor maid tossing, thereby disturbing those innocent sleepers, and living over again every glance, every word, every laugh of that delicious night. She had read novels—three-volume romances passed from hand to hand, volumes greasy at the corners as if they had been buttered by a hundred secret thumbs. Penny papers had not yet grown into their later trade of selling sixteen pages of murder and aristocratic perfidy for a copper; but Miss Minifer’s circulating library (tacked, as it were, onto a school and a small brandy-ball and millinery business) had furnished Fanny with plenty of heroines and heroes. Arthur walked into her imagination as the embodied Prince of all those battered books.

And Pen, who was, as we know, particular in linen and haberdashery—as a chef is particular with his knives—had appeared to her in all the splendour of fine shirt-front, glittering studs, cambric handkerchief, white gloves, and boots whose polish looked almost edible, like black currant jelly. The Prince had taken possession of the handmaid. His voice, his blue eyes, that look half love, half pity (the most dangerous seasoning in a gentleman’s pantry), the manly smile, the frank laugh—all rang in her head as plainly as the fiddles of Vauxhall. She could still feel his arm about her, and see him, grand as a steward, filling the champagne-glass—bubbles rising like little bright promises.

Then she thought of the girls who sneered at her—Emma Baker, mighty because she was engaged to a cheesemonger in a white apron; Betsy Rodgers, who made a whole ceremony of an attorney’s clerk that carried a bag. And thus, when, about two in the afternoon, after the Bolton family had finished dinner (and Mr. Bolton—porter of the Inn and occasional assistant to Messrs. Tressler, undertakers of the Strand—being out in the country with the Countess of Estrich’s hearse), a gentleman in a white hat and white trousers appeared under the archway and halted at the porter’s wicket, Fanny was not surprised. She was only delighted—only happy—blushing as if the very air had turned hot.

She knew it could be no other than He.

“Mamma, mamma!” she cried up to the upper room, and flew to the wicket, shoving the children aside with the careless authority of a girl whose whole world has suddenly narrowed to one pair of boots.

How she blushed as she gave him her hand! How affably he lifted his white hat as he stepped in, while the children stared up as if a royal carriage had driven into the court. He asked Mrs. Bolton whether she had slept well after the fatigues of the night, hoped she had no headache, and said that as he was passing he could not go by without asking after his little partner.

Mrs. Bolton, at first, was shy—suspicious, too, as a mother ought to be when a handsome young gentleman comes calling where there is no silver on the sideboard. But Pen’s good-humour was like a kettle kept perpetually on the boil. He could not imagine himself unwelcome. He looked about for a chair; but one bore a dish-cover, another a workbox, and every place that might have received him seemed already occupied by domestic industry. So he took a child’s chair and perched himself upon that puny throne, his knees up like a stork’s.

The children giggled. Fanny laughed louder than all, not because it was so witty, but because it was so magnificent—His Royal Highness on a nursery chair! Many a time afterwards she would look at that chair as at a relic. Haven’t we all some bit of furniture—an old seat, a corner by the hearth—where memory sets dear figures down again, and we hear voices that perhaps will never speak to us more?

Pen sat and talked away to Mrs. Bolton with volubility, as if words were coins he was scattering to make his path pleasant. He asked about the undertaking business—how many mutes had gone down with Lady Estrich; about the Inn and who lived there; about Mr. Campion’s cab and horse (he had met Mr. Campion in “society,” he said, with the air of a man who can season any conversation with that expensive word). He thought he should like shares in the Polwheedle and Tredyddlum. Were there chambers to let? It was better than the Temple; he should like to come and live in Shepherd’s Inn.

“As for Captain Strong—and—Colonel Altamont—was that his name?” Pen said, as though he merely happened to remember them while stirring the pot. He was deeply interested in those gentlemen too. The Captain was an old friend at home. He had dined with him in chambers here, before the Colonel came to live with him. What sort of man was the Colonel? Wasn’t he stout, with a quantity of jewellery—rings enough to stock a pawnbroker’s tray—and a wig and large black whiskers—very black?

Here Pen grew immensely waggish, and, to show his powers of culinary description, insisted the whiskers were not merely black but blue-black—indeed a rich greenish-purple—like something overcooked and varnished. The ladies shrieked with delight, that hysteric giggle which is laughter whipped too long.

“That was the man,” said Mrs. Bolton eagerly. “You’ve met him too, at Sir Fr—— in society.”

“Oh, we know,” said the ladies—meaning they knew, as lodges do, everything that enters or leaves an archway. “Sir F—— is Sir F. Clavering; he’s often here—two or three times a week with the Captain. My little boy has been out for bill-stamps for him. O Lor! I beg pardon—I shouldn’t have mentioned no secrets,” Mrs. Bolton added, suddenly remembering that secrecy is a virtue when one has already committed the sin. But Pen had talked her, by this time, into that broad good-nature which makes people feel safe while they are being pumped.

“But we know you to be a gentleman, Mr. Pendennis,” she went on, “for I’m sure you’ve shown you can beayve as such. Hasn’t Mr. Pendennis, Fanny?”

Fanny loved her mother for that. She lifted her dark eyes to the low ceiling—where the smoke and cooking smells of many dinners seemed to cling like old stories—and said, with a voice full of feeling, “Oh, that he has, I’m sure, Ma.”

Pen, at the mention of bill-stamps, pricked up his curiosity, and began, with considerable adroitness, to inquire about the transactions in Captain Strong’s chambers. When Altamont came and joined the Chevalier, was he too sending out for stamps? Who came to see them? Did many people go up and down? And so forth—questions shaped like polite small-talk, but meant to fish out Sir Francis Clavering’s doings for reasons of Pen’s own. Mrs. Bolton, who had neither the instincts of a diplomat nor the learning of a food-historian, answered artlessly to the very limit of her knowledge—which, like the contents of a small larder, was soon exhausted.

Pen found himself at a loss for fresh topics; but luckily he remembered his grand privilege as a man of the Press—like a cook who, when conversation flags, produces a pudding. He asked the ladies whether they would like any orders for the play.

The theatre was their delight, as it almost always is with those who live near its smell and glitter, and count its names as other people count the saints. When Bolton was away “professionally” (and it appeared the porter of Shepherd’s Inn, of late, had taken a serious turn—drank a good deal, and made himself otherwise unpleasant at home), Mrs. Bolton and Fanny would like of all things to slip out to a theatre, leaving little Barney to keep the lodge. Mr. Pendennis’s offer—most generous, most genteel—was received as if he had promised them a share in paradise.

Fanny clapped her hands; her face shone; she looked and nodded and laughed at her mamma, who nodded and laughed in return. Mrs. Bolton was not, in her own opinion, too old for admiration; and very likely Pen, with that easy art which costs men nothing and women much, had dropped compliments into his talk as lightly as pepper. She had begun by mistrusting him. She was now his partisan, and almost as enthusiastic as her daughter. When two women set to liking a man, they warm one another at the same fire, and each pushes the other closer to the blaze.
