Only one small cloud crossed the sunshine: one of the younger children, hearing “Astley’s” named, came forward and declared she would like very much to go too; on which Fanny said, rather sharply, “Don’t bother!” and mamma followed with, “Git-long, Betsy-Jane, do now, and play in the court.”

So Betsy-Jane and Ameliar-Ann, in clean pinafores, were sent away to disport on the smooth gravel round about the statue of Shepherd the Great, and no doubt contributed their small shrieks and patter to the Inn’s soundscape—the innocent, living music of a place not yet entirely conquered by the iron roar and commercial clamour that, in other streets, drowns all tenderness out of human ears.

And there, while those small feet went tap-tap over the stones, and Pen’s voice went on, rich and civil, within the lodge, an old gentleman passed under the archway from the Inn-square and came and looked in at the door.

He made a blank, rueful face when he saw Mr. Arthur perched like Macheath upon his child’s chair, in easy discourse with Mrs. Bolton and her daughter.

“What! Mr. Bows? How d’you do, Bows?” cried Pen, in a cheery, loud voice. “I was coming to see you, and was asking your address of these ladies.”

“You were coming to see me, were you, sir?” Mr. Bows said; and he came in with a sad face and shook hands with Arthur.

“Plague on that old man!” somebody thought in the room; and perhaps somebody else besides her.

Our friend Pen, spying Mr. Bows, cried out “How d’ye do, Mr. Bows?” with such a brave, tavern-bell cheeriness that you would have thought he meant to pay for everybody’s dinner and whistle the band besides. Yet, for all that trumpet of a greeting, there was a blush on Arthur’s face—one of those sudden kitchen-fires that flare up in a man who has been playing with matches. Fanny, in the porter’s lodge, answered it at once: her cheek flew the same little red signal, as quick as if her blood had been taught to curtsy.

Bows and Arthur shook hands. Bows, with that mild, funereal irony of his, accepted Pen’s airy assertion that he was “just going up to Captain Costigan’s,” as though the captain’s chambers were a chapel and Pen was a punctual parishioner. Then fell a silence—gloomy, guilty, and thick as yesterday’s gravy. Pen tried to whisk it away by making a great rattling noise, as if sound could be stirred like soup and made wholesome by sheer clatter. The silence, of course, broke; but the gloom stayed—indeed it deepened, the way a cellar looks darker when you bring down one candle and discover, by its very light, how much is still black.

Pendennis began, in a jocular style, to tell over last night’s transactions, and attempted an imitation of Costigan wrangling with the check-taker at Vauxhall. It was not good. Who can counterfeit that perfection? Nobody laughed. Mrs. Bolton stared as if he were describing a recipe in Greek—couldn’t tell whether he was the check-taker or the captain being carved up. Fanny tried a timid giggle, like a spoon tapping the rim of a cup—little sound, no comfort in it. Old Bows looked as glum as when he used to saw out mournful music in an orchestra, or hammer a difficult piece on the old piano in the Back Kitchen, with all the mirth of a man chopping onions for a funeral pie.

Pen felt his story fail in his mouth; his voice sank, dwindled, flickered, and went out. And it was dark again. You could hear the ticket-porter under the archway, lolling along the flags; the clink of his boot-heels rang through the court like a metronome keeping time to everybody’s embarrassment. In such places, sound is a tyrant: a heel on stone, a latch clicked, a cough—each one sets the mind to listening for what it dreads.

“You were coming to see me, sir,” Mr. Bows said at last. “Won’t you have the kindness to walk up to my chambers with me? You do them a great honour, I am sure. They are rather high up; but—”

“Oh! I live in a garret myself, and Shepherd’s Inn is twice as cheerful as Lamb Court,” Pen broke in quickly, as though he could salt the conversation into palatableness.

“I knew that you had third-floor apartments,” Mr. Bows said, “and was going to say—you will please not take my remark as discourteous—that the air up three pair of stairs is wholesomer for gentlemen, than the air of a porter’s lodge.”

“Sir!” cried Pen, and his temper—like a candle in a draught—flared up the instant it was touched. Men are quarrelsome when they’re wrong, as cooks are touchy when the sauce has broken. “Will you permit me to choose my society without—?”

“You were so polite as to say that you were about to honour my umble domicile with a visit,” Bows went on, with the same patient sorrow in his voice, and the same old stage-door dignity in his words. “Shall I show you the way? Mr. Pendennis and I are old friends, Mrs. Bolton—very old acquaintances; and at the earliest dawn of his life we crossed each other.”

He pointed to the door with a trembling finger, hat in the other hand, a little theatrical in attitude—his vocabulary forever smelling faintly of footlights and paint. But he was not acting; Pen knew it, though he was minded to sneer at the old fellow’s melodramatic manner, as young gentlemen will sneer at an old knife that still cuts.

“Come along, sir,” Arthur said, with a poor sort of swagger, “as you are so very pressing. Mrs. Bolton, I wish you a good day. Good-bye, Miss Fanny; I shall always think of our night at Vauxhall with pleasure; and be sure I will remember the theatre tickets.”

He took her hand; he pressed it; it pressed him back—warm, quick, like a small loaf just pulled from the oven—and then he was gone.

“What a nice young man, to be sure!” cried Mrs. Bolton, delighted, as women will be delighted by a fine coat and civil words, as if politeness were a new kind of tea.

“D’you think so, ma?” said Fanny; but the question sounded less like doubt than like a child asking if she may have another slice.

“I was a-thinkin who he was like. When I was at the Wells with Mrs. Serle,” Mrs. Bolton continued, peeping through the curtain as if looking after a roast in a street-stall, “there was a young gentleman from the city, that used to come in a tilbry, in a white at, the very image of him, only his whiskers was black, and Mr. P.’s is red.”

“Law, ma! they are a most beautiful hawburn,” Fanny said; and you could have heard, under the words, the sighing little hiss of vanity, like fat meeting a hot pan.

“He used to come for Emly Budd, who danced Columbine in ‘Arleykin Ornpipe, or the Battle of Navarino,’ when Miss De la Bosky was took ill—a pretty dancer, and a fine stage figure of a woman—and he was a great sugar-baker in the city, with a country ouse at Omerton; and he used to drive her in the tilbry down Goswell Street Road; and one day they drove and was married at St. Bartholomew’s Church, Smithfield, where they had their bands read quite private; and she now keeps her carriage, and I sor her name in the paper as patroness of the Manshing-House Ball for the Washywomen’s Asylum. And look at Lady Mirabel—capting Costigan’s daughter—she was profeshnl, as all very well know.”

Thus, and more to the same pastry of romance, Mrs. Bolton talked—now peeping through the curtain, now cleaning mugs and plates, stacking them in the corner cupboard with the tidy pride of a woman who believes order is almost a virtue. She finished as she and Fanny shook out the dinner-cloth between them—snapping it so that the air smelt faintly of stale beer, damp linen, and yesterday’s cabbage—and folded it with solemn care into its drawer.

Costigan had once been made to understand Pen’s means and expectations pretty exactly; but the Captain had either forgotten what he learned years ago at Chatteris, or his natural enthusiasm had risen like yeast in warm weather and swelled the young man’s fortune to a splendid, imaginary loaf. Last night, strolling with Mrs. Bolton while Pen was on his little escapade with Fanny, the Captain had described Fairoaks Park as if it were the Garden of Eden with a title-deed; had dilated on the enormous wealth of Pen’s famous uncle the Major; and talked of funded and landed property with the intimacy of a man who has never had to pay for it.

Very likely, in the night, Mrs. Bolton had seasoned and stewed these statements in her own wise head, and gone to sleep tasting, in fancy, the rich gravy of them—visions of Fanny driving in her carriage, like that old comrade Columbine who had danced out of poverty and into patronage.

At the last fold of the cloth, mother and daughter, of necessity, came close together. As Fanny gave it the final crease, Mrs. Bolton put a finger under the girl’s chin and kissed her. Again that red signal flew out and fluttered on Fanny’s cheek. It was not alarm now. It was pleasure—warm, shamefaced, and delicious as the first spoonful of sweetened cream when you’ve been living on dry bread.

Poor little Fanny! Is love a sin, that it begins so pleasant and ends so bitter?

After the kiss, Mrs. Bolton declared she was going out upon business, and that Fanny must keep the lodge; which Fanny, after the faintest of objections—no more than the protest a hungry child makes before taking the second bun—consented to do.

So Mrs. Bolton took her bonnet and market-basket and departed; and the instant the door had closed and her footfall was swallowed by the court’s echoing stone, Fanny ran to the window that commanded Bows’s door and sat there, never once taking her eyes away. Betsy-Jane and Amelia-Ann buzzed in a corner, pretending to read a picture-book held topsy-turvy—a dreadful tract out of Mr. Bolton’s collection, full of moral skeletons and admonitions. They chattered like sparrows in a pantry; Fanny heard nothing. Her ears were full of the court’s little noises: a distant cart in the Strand grumbling like thunder; the court’s own small echoes; the whisper of her needlework bag; the occasional metallic click of a latch. All of it was only the accompaniment to one expected sound—the opening of Bows’s door.

At last she gave a little shake, and her eyes lighted up. He had come out. He would pass the door again. But her poor little countenance fell in an instant, as quickly as a soufflé collapses when the oven’s opened too soon. Pendennis, indeed, came out—but Bows followed him.

They passed under the archway together. Pen only took off his hat and bowed as he looked in. He did not stop to speak. And then, in three or four minutes—Fanny did not know how long; her sense of time had been boiled down to mere minutes and heartbeats—Bows returned alone and entered the porter’s room.

“Where’s your Ma, dear?” he asked Fanny.

“I don’t know,” Fanny said, with an angry toss, as if she were flinging salt at him. “I don’t follow Ma’s steps wherever she goes, I suppose, Mr. Bows.”

“Am I my mother’s keeper?” Bows said, with his usual melancholy bitterness; and then, changing to a gentler voice, called, “Come here, Betsy-Jane and Amelia-Ann; I’ve brought a cake for the one who can read her letters best, and a cake for the other who can read them the next best.”

He examined the young ladies with a patience he did not spend on grown people; and rewarded them with gingerbread medals, which they carried off into the court, crunching their triumph and making the very stones sound sweeter. Meanwhile Fanny drew out some work and pretended to be busy, plying her needle with great industry, as if she could stitch down her vexation. But her mind was in a ferment—anger, mortification, desire; all whipping together like eggs that refuse to be quiet.

Bows sat so that he could command the entrance from the lodge to the street; his pale eyes kept watch, as if he listened not only with his ears but with his very bones, for the footfall he feared. Yet the person he perhaps expected never returned. Mrs. Bolton came in from market at last, rustling parcels, the basket smelling of greens and onions and a bit of cheap fish—and found Mr. Bows in the lodge instead of the person she had expected. The reader may guess his name.

The interview between Bows and his guest, when they climbed to the apartment occupied by Bows in common with the descendant of the Milesian kings, was not particularly satisfactory to either. Pen was sulky. If Bows had anything to say, he did not care to say it before Captain Costigan—who stayed in the room the whole time of Pen’s visit, having quitted his bedchamber only a few minutes before Pendennis arrived.

We have already been admitted to the deshabille of Major Pendennis: will any man wish to be valet-de-chambre to our other hero? It appeared that the Captain, before issuing, had scented himself with otto-of-whisky. A rich odour of that delicious perfume breathed from him—sweet, sharp, and sorrowful; a spirituous cologne fit to preserve a man in pickle. The hand he held out in cordiality shook woefully; it was a wonder how it ever held the razor with which he daily operated on his chin.

Bows’s room, on the other hand, was as neat as Costigan’s was disorderly. His humble wardrobe hung behind a curtain. Books and manuscript music were trimly arranged on shelves. Over the old gentleman’s bed hung a lithographed portrait of Miss Fotheringay as Mrs. Haller, the actress’s sprawling signature in the corner like a flourish made by a woman in a hurry to be admired. Lady Mirabel, Bows reflected, wrote much better: her ladyship had laboured at penmanship since her marriage, and in common notes acquitted herself very genteelly. Bows loved the old handwriting best, though—the earlier manner, the first language of her hand before it had been disciplined into respectable shapes. He had but one specimen of the newer style, a note in reply to a song he had composed and dedicated to Lady Mirabel, by her most humble servant Robert Bows; and that precious scrap lay in his desk among his state papers, like a dried herb pressed between pages to keep a scent alive.

He was teaching Fanny Bolton now to sing and to write, as he had taught Emily in former days. It was in the nature of the man to attach himself to something. When Emily was torn away, he took a substitute—as a man looks out for a crutch when he loses a leg; or lashes himself to a raft after shipwreck. Some men give their hearts to a woman in youth, and end, in age, by being made miserable over a poodle’s cough. It was hard upon Bows—hard upon his pride as a man and his sentiment as a lover of old airs—that he should find Pendennis again upon his track, and in pursuit of this little Fanny, who was learning to shape letters as if each one might spell rescue.

Costigan, meanwhile, had not the least idea that his company could be anything but welcome to Messrs. Pendennis and Bows; and imagined Pen’s visit intended for himself. He expressed himself vastly pleased by the mark of poloightness, and promised in his own mind to repay the obligation—at least that obligation, which was far from the only debt he owed in this world—by several visits to his young friend.

He entertained Pen affably with news of the day, or rather of ten days previous; for Pen, being a journalist, remembered having seen some of the Captain’s opinions already printed in the Sporting and Theatrical Newspaper, Costigan’s oracle, from which he took his politics, his morals, and his weather. The Captain announced that Sir Charles and Lady Mirabel were gone to Baden-Baden, and were most pressing that he should join them.

Pen replied gravely that he had heard Baden was very pleasant, and the Grand Duke exceedingly hospitable to English.

Costigan answered that the laws of hospitalitee bekeam a Grand Juke; that he sariously would think of paying him a visit; and presently launched into remarks upon the splendid festivities at Dublin Castle, when his Excellency the Earl of Portansherry held the viceraygal coort there—festivities which, if they had ever occurred outside Costigan’s head, must have happened in some mythic Ireland where every glass is full and every story true. He spoke with relish, like a man tasting an old tale as if it were a stew re-warmed; and Pen, listening to these oft-told legends, recollected the time when he had half believed them, and had felt a certain respect for the Captain.

Emily and first love, and the little room at Chatteris, and the kind talk with Bows on the bridge, came back to him. He grew kindly disposed towards the two old friends; and when he rose to go, he shook the hands of both of them cordially. While the Captain talked, Pen had quite forgotten little Fanny Bolton; he had been absorbed in other selfish meditations, as men are apt to be when they stand near their own histories.

He only remembered her again as Bows came hobbling down the stairs after him—plainly bent upon following him out of Shepherd’s Inn, as though guarding a pantry from a cat.

That precaution was not lucky. The wrath of Mr. Arthur Pendennis rose at the poor old fellow’s feeble persecution. Confound him—what does he mean by dogging me? thought Pen; and once he was in the Strand and alone, he burst out laughing at the elder’s stratagem.

It was not an honest laugh, Arthur Pendennis. Perhaps the thought struck him as it struck you; for he blushed, ashamed of his own sense of humour, as if he had found himself chuckling over a burnt dinner he himself had spoiled.

He went off to banish the thoughts that occupied him, whatever those thoughts might be, and tried various places of amusement with indifferent success. He struggled up the highest stairs of the Panorama; but when he arrived, panting at the eminence, Care had climbed up too and stood at his elbow—quiet, faithful, and intolerable as a dripping tap in the night. He went to the Club and wrote a long letter home, exceedingly witty and sarcastic; and if he said not a single word about Vauxhall and Fanny Bolton, it was because he judged that subject—however pungent to him—would not be interesting to his mother and Laura, who preferred their correspondence without the flavour of such sauce.

Nor could the novels or the library-table fix his attention; nor the grave and respectable Jawkins (the only man in town), who wished to engage him in conversation; nor any of the amusements he tried after flying from Jawkins. He passed a Comic Theatre on his way home and saw “Stunning Farce,” “Roars of Laughter,” “Good Old English Fun and Frolic” blazing in vermilion letters on the gate—loud promises shouted in paint, as modern places shout everything, as if noise could be sold for merriment.

He went into the pit and saw the lovely Mrs. Leary, as usual, in a man’s attire; and that eminent buffo actor Tom Horseman dressed as a woman. Horseman’s travesty seemed to him a horrid, hideous degradation; Mrs. Leary’s glances and ankles had not the least effect. He laughed again—bitterly, to himself—as he remembered the effect she had produced on him the first night of his arrival in London, a short time—what a long, long time ago.

Fashion, like a spoiled housecat, had long ago turned its back on the Temple Garden, found something noisier to sit on, and pretended not to hear when you called it. The place was still green enough to soothe a respectable eye; still cut into neat beds and walks, still offering a view of the Thames that could make even a lawyer momentarily ashamed of his own existence. But the famous roses—those historical, war-starting roses that York and Lancaster once plucked with such fatal leisure—had given up the attempt. The air was too smoky, the soot too confident. A rose, like a language, needs room to breathe; and London, in those parts, preferred to speak in coal.

Most of the present tenants of the surrounding buildings neither knew nor cared whether a bud ever dared show itself. Their Sundays were for digestion and debts. Attorneys’ clerks did not rush through the gate with posies under their arms (their bags were already heavy enough with briefs and other desolations), and the few barristers who walked for “constitution” marched as if their feet were cross-examining the gravel. Only antiquarians and literary idlers came to look with any tenderness—imagining Addison’s thin face passing, or Goldsmith in the summer-house, counting the day’s disappointments against tomorrow’s suit from Mr. Filby the tailor. If you listened with a proper ear—an ear that cared about the world’s breathing—you could almost hear those old footsteps: the genteel rasp of shoe-leather, the careful tap of a cane, the soft hush of a page turned. Then, over it all, the modern sound: the impatient city, forever grinding its own teeth.

Arthur Pendennis, being much more devoted to such phantoms than to the law, chose the Temple Gardens that evening for exercise and meditation, as one chooses a quiet pantry to think in—away from the clang of pots, away from eyes. It was vacation-time. The chambers were mostly empty; the great men were dining at distances measured in claret; the lesser men were dining at distances measured in half-pints; and the Temple itself held its breath in that Sunday calm when even the river seems to run more politely.

Pen had dined alone at a tavern nearby—one of those meals that fills a stomach without ever speaking to it. No attentive butter, no grateful herb; nothing that could make a man feel rooted to the earth by taste. Perhaps that was why, as he returned toward his chambers, he drifted through the old gate and into the gardens as if seeking a better kind of sustenance.

The evening was bright and still. Across the water the warehouses looked as rosy and clean as if, for once, they had washed for the holiday. Steamers hurried by, packed with holiday passengers whose laughter came in gusts and then vanished, like a tune played past an open window. From the city, church bells rang for evening prayers—a whole multitude of metallic throats calling in different dialects of devotion. The sound lay over the garden like a cloth, smoothing the mind. It carried Pen back, not by argument but by rhythm, to the terrace at home: his mother beside him, the old familiar village noises—elm leaves whispering, the church tower holding its steady note against the sunset.

Was it that memory, or only the sun sinking behind some imagined Clavering elms, that made him colour? He sat in one of the summer-houses and drummed time on the bench to the bells outside. Then—startled at himself, as people are when they catch their own heart in the act—he brushed dust from his shining boots, rose abruptly, stamped once as if to crush a thought, and said aloud, “No, by Jove, I’ll go home.”

He stepped out—and nearly collided with two very small persons trotting along the gravel, their long blue shadows slanting eastward like little banners.

One child cried “Oh!” from sheer surprise; the other, who possessed a more worldly philosophy, began to laugh and said, with a knowing infant chuckle, “Missa Pendennis!”

Arthur looked down—and there they were again: Mesdemoiselles Ameliar-Ann and Betsy-Jane, his acquaintances of the previous day, as recognisable as if they had been served again on the same plate. He blushed—more than a grown man has any right to blush at two children—and, seizing the one he had almost upset, he lifted her into the air and kissed her with the suddenness of a man who has been thinking too long and needs an interruption.

Ameliar-Ann, being unprepared for aerial embraces, burst into frightened tears.

That cry brought up their attendants at once, as efficiently as the clatter of a dropped ladle summons a cook: Mrs. Bolton in a rich scarlet Caledonian cashmere shawl over a black silk dress, and Miss F. Bolton with a yellow scarf, a sweet sprigged muslin, and a parasol held like a badge of gentility. Fanny said not a single word; but her eyes spoke with an inconvenient brilliance, flashing welcome as brightly as any window in Paper Buildings.

Mrs. Bolton, after admonishing Betsy-Jane with a maternal “Now then,” exclaimed, “Lor, sir—how very odd that we should meet you ’ere! I ope you ave your ealth well, sir.—Ain’t it odd, Fanny, that we should meet Mr. Pendennis?”

Odd? People snigger at such “coincidences” when they occur below stairs, and call them “romance” when they happen in shrubberies. But why should accident be restricted to country-houses? When a young Croesus strolls at a Hall, have you never found yourself, by singular chance, walking your own Fanny along the same path? When a band plays at Brighton, do Captain Padmore and young De Boots not also, by miracle, clink down the pier at precisely the moment you are listening? Providence has a wide service, and does not confine its little ironies to the wealthy.

In truth, Pen had only said the previous day—artlessly enough—that though some Temple courts were gloomy, parts were cheerful, especially the chambers by the river and around the gardens, and that the gardens made a pleasant Sunday walk and were frequented by many people. Here, by the merest chance, were these people.

Arthur, as if to defend himself with starch and linen, was unusually smart. White duck trousers and a white hat; a many-coloured neckcloth; a light waistcoat; gold chains and shirt-studs—he looked, if not exactly like a prince, then certainly like a prince’s tailor’s daydream. The splendour suited him; and worse, his blushes suited him too.

The children had been so struck with him yesterday that, after he left, they had played at being him. Ameliar-Ann, sticking her chubby fingers into the arm-holes of her pinafore in imitation of Pen’s favourite waistcoat-attitude, had declared, “Now, Bessy-Jane, I’ll be Missa Pendennis.” Fanny had laughed till she cried and smothered her sister with kisses for the performance. And now, seeing Arthur embrace the child, she looked as if she had been given a feast after a famine.

Yet, close as she stood, Fanny herself seemed worn and pale—her face having the look of someone who has lived all night by lamplight and longing.

Arthur remarked it, and asked why she looked so fatigued.

“I was awake all night,” said Fanny, and began to blush a little, as if the night had been a secret she could taste again.

“I put out her candle,” Mrs. Bolton broke in, proud of discipline, “and hordered her to go to sleep and leave off readin.”

“You were reading? And what was it that interested you so?” Arthur asked, amused.

“Oh, it’s so beautiful!” Fanny breathed.

“What?”

“‘Walter Lorraine,’” she sighed out, as though the title itself were perfume. “How I do hate that Neaera—Neaera—I don’t know the pronunciation. And I love Leonora, and Walter—oh, how dear he is!”

Now, how had she come by ‘Walter Lorraine’? And how had she discovered that the author was Arthur Pendennis? The little person had stored every word he spoke the night before, as carefully as a thrifty cook saves drippings. He wrote in books and newspapers, he had said. What books? Her curiosity had been so hungry that it nearly drove her to be civil to old Mr. Bows again—Mr. Bows, who was currently suffering under her displeasure—but she had decided first to question Captain Costigan.

She began by coaxing the Captain and smiling upon him with her most winning air, while she set his humble apartment in order and fussed over his dinner. She announced, with the authority of a domestic monarch, that his linen wanted mending—an opinion in which the Captain’s linen-closet, containing specimens of flax and cotton that looked as if they had survived a battle, meekly concurred. She would mend his shirts—all his shirts. What horrid holes, what funny holes! She put her little face through one of them and laughed at the old warrior, as if turning ruin into a game.

Then she removed his dinner things daintily, tripping about the room as she had seen dancers do at the play—light-footed enough to make the very floorboards sound less shabby. She danced to the cupboard, produced the whisky-bottle, mixed him a tumbler, insisted on tasting a drop herself—a little drop—and the Captain must sing her one of his songs, his dear songs, and teach it to her. So the room filled with the quavering richness of an Irish melody, Costigan believing himself the enchanter, while Fanny, in truth, listened only until her appetite could be served.

And then, at the proper moment—like a cook slipping in the crucial question while the guest’s mouth is busy—she asked about Mr. Pendennis and his novel. Having got her answer, she cared for nothing else. She left the Captain at the piano, about to sing again; left the dinner-tray in the passage; left the shirts on the chair; and ran downstairs, her pace quickening with triumph.

Costigan, as he would have said, was not a litherary cyarkter and had not yet found time to peruse his young friend’s ellygant perfaurumance, though he intended to teak an early opporchunitee of purchasing a cawpee. But he knew the name because Messrs. Finucane, Bludyer, and the other frequenters of the Back Kitchen spoke of Mr. Pendennis—often unkindly, Bludyer calling him a confounded coxcomb, and Hoolan wondering why Doolan didn’t kick him—by the sobriquet of Walter Lorraine.

“And she went and ast for it at the libery,” Mrs. Bolton explained now, “—several liberies—and some ad it and it was hout, and some adn’t it. And one of the liberies as ad it wouldn’t let ’er ave it without a sovering: and she adn’t one, and she came back a-cryin to me—didn’t you, Fanny?—and I gave her a sovering.”

“And, oh,” Fanny added, cheeks and eyes glowing as if she had swallowed a bit of sunlight, “I was in such a fright lest any one should have come to the libery and took it while I was away. And, oh, I do like it so!”

Arthur, vain as he was, could not help being touched by sympathy so naïve and so fiercely felt. It flattered him—no review had ever tasted so sweet. For a moment he wanted to feed it: to bring her the book, to give her more words, more pages, to see her light up again. His heart made a foolish little leap—like a boy reaching for jam.

“Do you like it?” he said. “If you will come up to my chambers I will—No, I will bring you one—no, I will send you one. Good night. Thank you, Fanny. God bless you. I mustn’t stay with you. Good-bye, good-bye.”

And pressing her hand once—one brief pressure, like a hand on a hot stove—he nodded to Mrs. Bolton and the children and strode out of the gardens.

He quickened his pace as he went, as if the sound of the bells behind him were chasing him forward. He ran out at the gate talking to himself, passers-by turning to look at the smart young man with the hunted face.

“Dear, dear little thing,” he said. “Darling little Fanny! You are worth them all. I wish to heaven Shandon was back. I’d go home to my mother. I mustn’t see her. I won’t. I won’t, so help me—”

As he was speaking thus, and running, he ran against a little old man.

Mr. Bows.

“Your very umble servant, sir,” said Mr. Bows, making a sarcastic bow and lifting his old hat.

“I wish you a good day,” Arthur answered, sulkily. “Don’t let me detain you, or give you the trouble to follow me again. I am in a hurry, sir. Good evening.”

Bows’s face sharpened with suspicion. “Where are they?” he cried. “You know whom I mean. They’re not in your rooms, sir, are they? They told Bolton they were going to church at the Temple, they weren’t there. They are in your chambers: they mustn’t stay in your chambers, Mr. Pendennis.”

“Damn it, sir!” Arthur cried, stopping short with fury. “Come and see if they are in my chambers: here’s the court and the door—come in and see.”

And Bows, taking off his hat and bowing first—as if politeness were armour—followed him up.

The chambers, as we know, contained no women and no children. They contained only the poor masculine disorder of a man trying to look prosperous on credit: Warrington’s old bookcase and battered library; Pen’s writing-table littered with papers; the air of a room that had never known the smell of bread baking, or onions softening in a pan, or any of the homely sounds that make four walls into a life. Outside, the city’s murmur crept in; inside, the quiet felt almost accusatory.

“Will you like to look in the bedrooms, Mr. Bows,” Arthur said bitterly, “and see if my victims are there? Or whether I have made away with the little girls, and hid them in the coal-hole?”

“Your word is sufficient, Mr. Pendennis,” Bows answered in his sad tone. “You say they are not here, and I know they are not. And I hope they never have been here, and never will come.”

“Upon my word, sir,” Arthur said haughtily, “you are very good, to choose my acquaintances for me; and to suppose that anybody would be the worse for my society. I remember you, and owe you kindness from old times, Mr. Bows; or I should speak more angrily than I do, about a very intolerable sort of persecution to which you seem inclined to subject me. You followed me out of your Inn yesterday, as if you wanted to watch that I shouldn’t steal something.”

He stammered and turned red the instant the words were out. He had given the other man his opening, and Bows took it like a lawyer with a grievance.

“I do think you came to steal something, as you say the words, sir,” Bows replied. “Do you mean to say that you came to pay a visit to poor old Bows, the fiddler; or to Mrs. Bolton, at the porter’s lodge? O fie! Such a fine gentleman as Arthur Pendennis, Esquire, doesn’t condescend to walk up to my garret, or to sit in a laundress’s kitchen, but for reasons of his own. And my belief is that you came to steal a pretty girl’s heart away, and to ruin it, and to spurn it afterwards, Mr. Arthur Pendennis.”

He went on—heated, indignant, full of those large denunciations that come easily to the wronged and do not always hit the right target. He spoke of “you young dandies,” of “aristocrats” trampling upon the people, of sport and shame, of toys flung into the street when the rich grow bored. His voice rang in Pen’s bare rooms, and the words sounded doubly loud because there was so little else in the place: no crackle of fire, no clink of spoon, no domestic music to soften anger. Even outside, the bells were fading; the city’s own harsher noises waited to take their place.

Bows was speaking beside the immediate point, and Pen—being no saint, and very glad to dodge—took advantage of it.

Arthur broke out with a laugh, and then, because he was not altogether hard, begged pardon for laughing.

“Yes, I am an aristocrat,” he said. “In a palace up three pair of stairs, with a carpet nearly as handsome as yours, Mr. Bows. My life is passed in grinding the people, is it? In ruining virgins and robbing the poor? My good sir, this is very well in a comedy, where Job Thornberry slaps his breast and asks my Lord how dare he trample on an honest man and poke out an Englishman’s fireside; but in real life—to a man who has to work for his bread as much as you do—how can you talk about aristocrats tyrannising over the people? Have I ever done you a wrong? Or assumed airs of superiority over you? Did you not have an early regard for me—in days when we were both romantic young fellows, Mr. Bows? Come, don’t be angry with me now, and let us be as good friends as we were before.”

“Those days were very different,” Bows answered. “And Mr. Arthur Pendennis was an honest, impetuous young fellow then; rather selfish and conceited, perhaps, but honest. He liked you then, because you were ready to ruin yourself for a woman.”

“And now, sir?” Arthur asked, the question coming out sharper than he intended.

“And now times are changed, and you want a woman to ruin herself for you,” Bows said.

Then the old man’s anger shifted into something more personal and more grievous. He spoke of Fanny as a child with a heated brain—warmed and warped by novels until love and lovers were her whole diet, and she scarcely noticed that she trod on a kitchen floor. He admitted her talents, her winning ways. He confessed his own fondness: a lonely old man among boon companions who left him melancholy; a life he did not like; this girl the only creature he cared for. And as he spoke, his voice broke.

“Have pity upon me,” he said, “and don’t take her away from me, Mr. Pendennis—don’t take her away.”

That crack in the voice did more than all his threats. Pen felt it like a hand laid suddenly on a sore place.

“Indeed,” Arthur said kindly, “you do me a wrong if you fancy I intend one to poor little Fanny. I never saw her till Friday night. It was the merest chance that our friend Costigan threw her into my way. I have no intentions regarding her—that is—”

“That is, you know very well that she is a foolish girl, and her mother a foolish woman,—that is, you meet her in the Temple Gardens, and of course without previous concert,—that is, that when I found her yesterday reading the book you’ve wrote, she scorned me,” Bows said, bitterness returning like an aftertaste. “What am I good for but to be laughed at? A deformed old fellow like me; an old fiddler, that wears a threadbare coat, and gets his bread by playing tunes at an ale-house? You are a fine gentleman, you are. You wear scent in your handkerchief, and a ring on your finger. You go to dine with great people. Who ever gives a crust to old Bows?”

He plunged then into his own history—ambition once, plays, poems, music, no hearing, women laughing at him, all hopes failing, and now old age alone. The words tumbled out with the desperation of someone trying to keep hold of the last scraps of himself before the world sweeps them away. Identity, like a dialect, can be rubbed down until it seems fit only for jokes; and Bows had lived too long in a world that translated him into “fiddler” and “oddity” and forgot the rest.

“Don’t take this girl from me,” he said again. “Leave her with me a little longer. She was like a child to me till yesterday. Why did you step in, and made her to mock my deformity and old age?”

“I am guiltless of that, at least,” Arthur said, with a sigh that surprised him by being sincere. “Upon my word of honour, I wish I had never seen the girl. My calling is not seduction, Mr. Bows. I did not imagine that I had made an impression on poor Fanny, until—until to-night. And then, sir, I was sorry, and was flying from my temptation, as you came upon me.”

He paused. The room had gone dim; the day’s last light was slipping away, and with it that easy confidence which daylight lends to people who live by appearances. When he spoke again, his voice shook.

“And I do not mind telling you, sir,” he said, “that on this Sabbath evening, as the church bells were ringing, I thought of my own home, and of women angelically pure and good, who dwell there; and I was running hither as I met you, that I might avoid the danger which beset me, and ask strength of God Almighty to do my duty.”

After that, there was silence. The city’s noises seemed louder by contrast: a distant cart, a shout, some harsh metallic scrape—modern life insisting, always, on its own accent. When Bows spoke again, his tone was gentler, as if Pen’s words had translated him back into “old friend” rather than “enemy.”

He stayed only a little longer. On taking leave, he asked permission to shake hands. There was warmth and affection in the grasp on both sides, and Bows, with a humility that cost him something, apologised for having mistaken Arthur. He even paid Pen compliments that made the young man squeeze his hand again, hard, as if clinging to reconciliation.

At the door, Arthur said, “I have given a promise, and I hope and trust that you may rely on it?”

“Amen to that prayer,” said Mr. Bows; and he went slowly down the stairs, his steps fading one by one into the Temple’s listening hush.

Clavering, after its own manner, was once more happy.

It was never a place to set a poet singing at the window. The town had few surprises, and those mostly of the poultry-yard: a hen stolen, a pig returned in triumph, the wind in the elm-tops sounding like a sermon being torn up and re-read. Still, it had its circles—little rings of gentility and tea and opinion—turning steadily as a kitchen-spit. And when one spoke of Clavering, one was sooner or later forced to speak of the Huxters; for Mrs. Huxter’s parlour was a kind of inland harbour where every vessel, however leaky with gossip, came in for repairs.

Mr. Samuel Huxter—Mr. Sam at Bartholomew’s, “Huxter” wherever young gentlemen laughed loudest—was one of the town’s chief exports. He returned in vacations with London in his coat-pocket: a theatre joke here, a club anecdote there, and always a little superior air, as if he had been personally presented to the Prince and had prescribed him rhubarb. In Clavering, his mother’s tea-table adored him; and in the surgery he had been known, even as a schoolboy, to find his way to the tamarind-pots with the unerring instinct of a truffle-hound. There were rose-water bottles too, and he could scent his pocket-handkerchief with a care that would have done credit to an apothecary compounding a love-philtre.

About this time of his earlier importance he had assisted, unintentionally and with much self-applause, at a romance: Mr. Hobnell—yes, the very young gentleman whom Pen had once thrashed for the Fotheringay quarrel—had been made welcome at Mrs. Huxter’s, had grown familiar with the sweetmeats and the surgical luxuries, and had taken a liking to Miss Sophy Huxter, which ripened, in proper rural fashion, into marriage. When Hobnell’s father died, the son carried Sophy home to the Warren—a few miles off, a place that had been farmed by Hobnells for years, honest yeomen first, then a little whiter and grander each generation, as if the very limewash were hereditary.

Old Hobnell had pulled down the plain farmhouse (which had had, no doubt, a perfectly respectable smell of hearth-smoke, bacon, and damp earth), and had put up a flaring new whitewashed mansion with capacious stables and a piano in the drawing-room—because nothing says “county” like a piano that nobody plays. He had kept a pack of harriers, and he had assumed the title of Squire Hobnell, as if “Squire” were a crop you sowed in spring and reaped at Michaelmas. When he died, his son reigned in his stead; and the family, by common consent and a little furniture, was now to be counted gentry.

Sam, in London, did not forget to boast of it. The Warren, the hounds, the horses, the hospitality—he handed them round Bartholomew’s like a dish at table, and watched his comrades take second helpings with envy. And indeed Hobnell did his part in supporting the legend. Every year, commonly at the very season when Mrs. Hobnell could not leave the nursery without the nursery coming after her, Squire Hobnell came up to town “for a lark,” took rooms at the Tavistock, and he and Sam went at pleasure to Ascot, theatres, Vauxhall, and the taverns about Covent Garden where the very air was seasoned with tobacco, spilled ale, and the clang of song. Hobnell always said that when he was in London he liked to do as London does, and to “go it a bit,” which meant, in practice, eating later, drinking more, and laughing louder than in the country; and when he went back west he carried home, as tribute, a new bonnet and shawl to Mrs. Hobnell, and returned to hunting, farming, and respectability for eleven months—like a man putting on his best coat for an evening and then hanging it carefully away.

Sam and his brother-in-law kept up a correspondence: metropolitan “news” went down in Sam’s letters; baskets came up from the Warren in exchange—hares, partridges, clouted cream packed like a treasure in cool sweetness. The Warren folk had the notion, too, that Sam was a youth more brilliant than any they knew. When he appeared among them, the house roared. He sang songs; he told stories; he filled the rooms with that particular music a family makes when it feels amused and safe. He had once saved their eldest darling’s life by taking a fish-bone out of her throat; and this surgical heroism, added to his London polish, made him a sort of domestic demigod. In a place where dinners were remembered longer than deaths, such feats endure.

It was therefore, as ill-luck would have it, that Pen fell in with Mr. Huxter again—only three days after the night at Vauxhall.

Pen had kept his vow. He had not been to see little Fanny. He was trying to drive her from his mind by sheer occupation, as a cook might try to overpower one sharp spice by throwing in a whole handful of another. He worked in his rooms, though not too profitably; and as critic for the Pall Mall Gazette he made savage war upon a poem and a romance that had the misfortune to come under his knife. He cut them up, carved them, served them out cold, and did not find his appetite improved.

After that he went to dine alone at the Polyanthus, that lonely club where the very silence seems upholstered, and the vast rooms have the chill of empty plates. Those solitudes frightened him and made him more moody. He tried theatres for relaxation. The whole house roared with laughter and applause; he saw only a farce so ignoble it made him sadder, as if the gaiety were a badly tuned instrument scraping his nerves. It would have damped the spirits of the buffoon on the stage to have looked down and seen Pen’s dismal face, set like a man tasting vinegar when everyone else has pudding. Scene and dialogue passed before him like a feverish dream.

He thought then of the Back Kitchen—his old haunt with Warrington. He was not sleepy. The day before he had walked twenty miles over Hampstead Common and through Hendon lanes in search of rest, and had found none. He would go to the Back Kitchen: at least, he told himself, he should see Bows; and even in misery a man clings to his small consolations as to a crust.

Bows was there—very calm, presiding at the old piano as if it were a stove he kept steadily hot for other people’s mirth. Tremendous comic songs were sung: the room cracked with laughter, the tables thumped, glasses rang, voices rose and fell in choruses that shook the ceiling. How strange it all seemed to Pen, whose mind was elsewhere! He could only see Bows, and the way light caught her hair, and the quick familiar movements of her hands. In an extinct volcano, as he had boasted his breast to be, it was wonderful how a mere two days’ indulgence had kindled a flame; how two days’ abstinence had set it burning in fury. He sat musing, drinking one glass after another—whisky-and-water going down with that soft, treacherous warmth that persuades a man the world has grown kinder, when it has only grown blurred.

And then ill-luck—faithful as ever—brought in Mr. Huxter.

Huxter had been to the theatre too, and entered with two or three comrades, fresh, noisy, and perfectly pleased with himself. Pen saw him whisper to his friends, and the whispering—small as it was, a mere thread of sound among so many—snagged on Pen’s ear. A man in pain hears particular noises: the scrape of a chair, the laugh that seems aimed, the whisper that makes a dagger of itself. Arthur felt certain the other was talking about him.

Huxter worked through the room and planted himself opposite Pen, nodding familiarly, holding out a dirty hand to shake—as if old acquaintance were a privilege he bestowed. Pen shook it. He remembered, suddenly, that he had perhaps been needlessly savage the last time; and Huxter, being perfectly good-humoured with himself and the world, never once considered that he could be disagreeable to anybody. The dispute at Vauxhall—“chaff,” as he called it—was nothing to him, a fly brushed away.

He called for “four stouts,” with the air of a man ordering medicine for the company, and then cast about for the most amusing topic. By a happy malignity of chance he hit upon the precise one that was most painful.

“Jolly night at Vauxhall—wasn’t it?” he said, and winked in a very knowing way.

“I’m glad you liked it,” poor Pen answered, groaning inwardly.

“I was dev’lish cut—uncommon—been dining with some chaps at Greenwich. That was a pretty bit of muslin hanging on your arm—who was she?” asked the fascinating student, with the coarse curiosity of a man who thinks impertinence is intimacy.

That question—lightly tossed, like a dirty towel across a clean table—was too much. Pen felt his cheeks burn.

“Have I asked you any questions about yourself, Mr. Huxter?” he said.

“I didn’t mean any offence—beg pardon—hang it, you cut up quite savage,” Huxter replied, staring, honestly surprised that another man’s feelings should exist.

“Do you remember what took place between us the other night?” Pen asked, wrath gathering, slow and dark.

“You forget? Very probably. You were tipsy, as you observed just now, and very rude.”

“Hang it, sir, I asked your pardon,” Huxter said, turning red now, with that injured look of a person accused of stepping on a toe when he has trodden on a heart.

“You did certainly, and it was granted with all my heart. I am sure. But if you recollect, I begged that you would have the goodness to omit me from the list of your acquaintance for the future; and when we met in public, that you would not take the trouble to recognise me. Will you please to remember this, hereafter? and as the song is beginning, permit me to leave you to the unrestrained enjoyment of the music.”

With that, Pen took his hat, bowed, and left Huxter staring, amazed; while Huxter’s comrades, after a pause, set up such a roar of laughter at him that it brought the president down upon them. The man bawled, “Silence, gentlemen; do have silence for the Body Snatcher!” and the popular song began as Pen went out into the street, where the night air felt thin and sharp after the room’s steam of beer, sweat, smoke, and merriment.

Pen flattered himself he had commanded his temper perfectly. He rather wished Huxter had been pugnacious. He would have liked to fight him—or somebody—anything to give his misery a shape and a target. He went home. The day’s work, the lonely dinner, the theatre, the whisky-and-water, the quarrel—nothing soothed him. He slept no better than the night before.

A few days later, Mr. Sam Huxter sat down in London and wrote a letter to Mr. Hobnell in the country—one of those communications which begins with moral indignation and ends with thanks for rabbits. Mr. Arthur Pendennis formed the principal subject. Sam described Arthur’s pursuits in town and his confounded insolence to old friends from home. He called him an abandoned criminal, a regular Don Juan; a fellow who, if he ever came into the country again, ought to be kept out of honest people’s houses. He reported that he had seen him at Vauxhall dancing with an innocent girl in the lower ranks of life—of whom he was making a victim. He had found out, from an Irish gentleman formerly in the army who frequented a club of which Huxter was a member, who the girl was upon whom this conceited humbug was practising his infernal arts; and he thought he should warn her father, and so forth, and so forth. Then, with the easy conscience of a man who has done his virtuous duty, he touched on general news, conveyed his thanks for the last parcel and the rabbits, and hinted with great delicacy his readiness for further favours.

Now, about once a year at the Warren—as regularly as harvest, as steadily as the pantry’s demand—there was occasion for a christening. It happened that the ceremony took place a day after Hobnell received Sam’s letter. The infant, a darling little girl, was christened Myra Lucretia, after its two godmothers, Miss Portman and Mrs. Pybus of Clavering; and Hobnell, having communicated Sam’s letter to his wife, Mrs. Hobnell imparted its horrid contents to her two gossips.

A pretty story it was; and, like a rich gravy, it ran everywhere.

Myra—Miss Portman—did not speak of it to her mamma; she was too much shocked, and carried her indignation like a covered dish, hot but held in. Mrs. Pybus had no such reserve. She talked it over with Mrs. Portman; with Mr. and the Honourable Mrs. Simcoe; with Mrs. Glanders (ordering her daughters out of the room to make the scandal safer and more delicious); with Madame Fribsby; and, in a word, with the whole of Clavering society. The tale, warmed by each retelling, acquired new seasonings: a sigh here, a lifted eyebrow there, a bit of Scripture sprinkled on top, as if wickedness were improved by quotation.

Madame Fribsby, looking furtively up at her picture of the dragoon and inward into her own wounded memory, said men would be men, and as long as they were men would be deceivers; and she quoted lines from Marmion, asking with mournful relish where deceiving lovers should rest. Mrs. Pybus could find no words of hatred, horror, contempt strong enough for a villain capable of conduct so base. This was what came of early indulgence, insolence, extravagance, aristocratic airs (it was quite true Pen had refused to drink tea with Mrs. Pybus), and attending corrupt parties in the dreadful modern Babylon. Mrs. Portman was afraid she must acknowledge that the mother’s fatal partiality had spoiled the boy; that his literary successes had turned his head; and his horrid passions had made him forget the principles Doctor Portman instilled in early life.

When the atrocious Captain of Dragoons, Mr. Glanders, heard it from Mrs. Glanders, he whistled and made jocular allusions at dinner. Mrs. Glanders called him a brute and ordered the girls out again, while the horrid Captain laughed. Mr. Simcoe received the intelligence calmly, even with a certain smug pleasure: it only confirmed what he had always thought of that wretched young man—though he knew nothing about him, had not read one line of his dangerous and poisonous works (Heaven forbid he should!), but really what could be expected from such a youth and such lamentable want of seriousness?

Pen, absent and ignorant in London, became present everywhere in Clavering. He formed the subject for a second sermon at the chapel-of-ease, where the dangers of London and the crime of reading or writing novels were pointed out on a Sunday evening to a large and warm congregation. They did not wait to hear whether he was guilty. They took his wickedness for granted; and among these admirable moralists it became a kind of pious competition—who should fling the stone with the most righteous arm.

The next day Mrs. Pendennis, alone and almost fainting with emotion and fatigue, walked—ran rather—to Doctor Portman’s house to consult him. She had received an anonymous letter: some Christian had thought it his or her duty to stab a good soul who had never done mortal wrong. The letter, edged with references to Scripture as if holy words were knives meant for private use, gave a detailed account of Pen’s “crime” and pointed out the doom of such sinners. Two or three hours of this pain had aged her already; her face bore it as a kitchen bears smoke—stained at once and helplessly.

In her first agitation she had dropped the letter, and Laura had read it. Laura blushed—not with shame, but anger; her whole frame trembled as if the very paper had insulted her.

“The cowards,” she said. “It isn’t true. No, mother, it isn’t true.”

“It is true, and you’ve done it, Laura!” cried Helen fiercely, in that delirium of grief which snatches at the nearest throat to choke. “Why did you refuse him when he asked you? Why did you break my heart and refuse him? It is you who led him into crime. It is you who flung him into the arms of this—this woman. Don’t speak to me. Don’t answer me. I will never forgive you, never. Martha, bring me my bonnet and shawl. I’ll go out. I won’t have you come with me. Go away. Leave me, cruel girl; why have you brought this shame on me?”

And bidding her daughter and the servants keep away, she hurried down the road to Clavering as if speed itself could outrun disgrace.

Doctor Portman, glancing over the letter, thought he knew the handwriting; and of course he had already heard the charge. Against his own conscience perhaps—for the worthy Doctor, like most of us, had a natural aptitude for receiving any report unfavourable to neighbours—he strove to console Helen. An anonymous slander, he said, must be the work of a rascal; the charge might not be true—was not true most likely; at least Pen must be heard before condemned; the son of such a mother was not likely to commit such a crime; and so on, and so on, in that tone of official comfort which tries the lock while it pretends the door is bolted.

Helen saw through the feint at once.

“You think he has done it,” she cried. “You know you think he has done it. Oh, why did I ever leave him, Doctor Portman, or suffer him away from me? But he can’t be dishonest—pray God, not dishonest—you don’t think that, do you? Remember his conduct about that other—person—how madly he was attached to her. He was an honest boy then—he is now. And I thank God—yes, I fall down on my knees and thank God he paid Laura. You said he was good—you did yourself. And now—if this woman loves him—and you know they must—if he has taken her from her home, or she tempted him, which is most likely—why still, she must be his wife and my daughter. And he must leave the dreadful world and come back to me—to his mother, Doctor Portman. Let us go away and bring him back—yes—bring him back—and there shall be joy for the—the sinner that repenteth. Let us go now, directly, dear friend—this very—”

She could say no more. The words broke; her strength went with them. She fell back and fainted.

They carried her to a bed in the Doctor’s house; the surgeon was called; and she lay all night in an alarming state. Laura came—came to the rectory rather—for Helen would not see her. Doctor Portman, still beseeching tranquillity, and growing bolder and more confident of Arthur’s innocence as he witnessed the terrible grief of the poor mother, wrote to Pen warning him of the rumours against him and earnestly praying that he would break off and repent of a connexion so fatal to his best interests and his soul’s welfare.

And Laura—was her heart not wrung? Was it not bitter, to think that by one stroke she should lose all the love she cared for in the world; to feel that the very language of home—mother, brother, trust—had been turned, by other people’s tongues, into weapons she could not parry, and accusations she could not translate into anything but pain?

Doctor Portman’s letter went off to London with all the solemnity of a parish procession: sealed, directed, stamped, and entrusted to that iron-hearted creature the post, which will carry a love-letter and a dun alike, without any flutter of compassion. The worthy clergyman, having thus discharged ink and conscience together, set himself to the more delicate business of calming Mrs. Pendennis—who, being a gentlewoman of strong feelings, did not find it in the least calming to be told, every quarter of an hour, that she ought to be calm.

For a day or two, too, there was no question of her rushing up to town like an injured prophetess and confronting her son amid his sins and his lodging-house furniture. The apothecary, that domestic tyrant with a pill-box for sceptre, forbade her to stir so much as to Fairoaks. And so, on the following morning, there she was again installed upon her sofa at home, with Laura by her side—faithful as a shadow, and almost as silent.

Unluckily—for him, for her, for everybody who had any stake in Arthur Pendennis’s skin and soul—Pen never read the Doctor’s homily until weeks after it had been written. The letter, poor thing, travelled punctually enough: it was posted; it was delivered into the Lamb Court box; it was carried upstairs with the rest of “his lordship’s correspondence;” it was laid on his writing-table by Mrs. Flanagan the laundress (the same domestic minister whose zeal for spirits we have had occasion to observe). But letters, like dinners, require a consumer; and Pen, who could be induced to swallow a tumbler of punch at an hour’s notice, had a singular inability to take in advice.

Day after day the widow waited for a reply—some word, any word—while her illness fed upon each unanswered post. Laura had to carry, not only her own anxiety, but Helen’s suffering; and then, as if that were not enough, to endure that cold estrangement which pain will sometimes set up between hearts that most need to cling. She did it as she did everything: without parade, without clatter—like good cooking, which is never the dish itself, but makes the dish possible. Her strength came, not with trumpet and testimonial, but in the quiet of her own chamber; and therefore we must speak of it lightly, as one speaks of a fragrance that would be spoiled by being pointed at. Only this: a good woman is a rare herb; she seasons the whole household, and yet sits modestly at the back of the cupboard.

Meanwhile Pen’s chief enemy—whom many of us know and harbour and pamper—was not a rival editor, nor a malicious aunt, nor an underbred porter with a grievance. It was Mr. Pen himself. He had indulgenced that gentleman all his life; and, like every spoiled servant, the fellow had grown insolent. The moment anyone proposed a little wholesome self-denial, Mr. Self stamped and swore, upset the tray, and declared he would not be controlled.

Pen had resolved—resolved magnificently—that he would not see Fanny; and he didn’t. He tried to banish her by all the recognised recipes for banishing a thought: by work, by exercise, by society, by dissipation, by walking and riding until his very bones had opinions; by eating, drinking, and smoking as if he meant to cure his heart by pickling it. The cigars smoked; the punch went down with a friendly gurgle; the streets of London rang with wheels and footsteps; the very chimneys had their soot-stifled cough. Yet, in all that city clatter—the constant rasp of urban life that never lets the mind hear its own birds—little Fanny’s image stayed, as a tune stays, and will not be drowned. At the end of a week of this heroic discipline, our young gentleman’s triumph was complete: he achieved a fever, and took to bed in Lamb Court.

Let any philanthropist who values matrimony as a public institution employ Cruikshank or Leech, and have illustrated for the nation, in a series of plates, “The Horrors of a Bachelor’s Chambers.” Begin with the lonely breakfast: the black kettle sulking on a fire that is either indecently hot in midsummer or offensively dead at Christmas; the room smelling of yesterday’s smoke and to-day’s damp; the master shivering while he plays housemaid—hunting coals, coaxing flame, and discovering that Mrs. Flanagan is absent without leave. Proceed to the bachelor’s shirt—wanted at dinner-time, found with buttons missing like teeth in a drunkard. Add the bachelor’s return after a merry country Christmas: he lights his dismal candle at the sputtering stair-lamp, enters the blank familiar room, and finds that the only things waiting to greet him, as if they had affection, are the Christmas bills spread out on his table like cards in a hand. Crown the whole with “The Bachelor Ill”—and the Temple will be depopulated, and the rents will fall, and young men will fly into respectable domesticity as into a refuge.

To be well in chambers is lonely enough; but to be ill there is to discover how thin a civilisation is when it comes to a glass of water at two in the morning. Long nights, hot pillow, ticking watch, medicine administered by one’s own feverish hand; no kindly foot on the stair, no familiar voice, no soft household rustle—nothing but the city’s distant grinding and rattling, like a great machine that does not care whether you live or die so long as it turns. We will not dwell on the tragedy. We will only pity those who endure it, and in particular Mr. Arthur Pendennis when his hour came.

He went to bed one night ill, and woke the next morning worse. Besides Mrs. Flanagan and her moral support (which chiefly consisted of moistened sympathy), his only visitor was the Printer’s Devil from the Pall Mall Gazette, to be fed—like a young raven—with copy. Pen struggled to satisfy him; and each effort at political wisdom and leading-article fire only blew upon his fever. Shandon was away; Warrington was not in town; and the Gazette’s columns looked as blank as a larder when the cook has fainted.

Mr. Finucane, warm-hearted Irishman, rushed up, found Pen in a state unfit for either party politics or human company, and—like a man who will put his shoulder to the cart even when it is laden with other people’s nonsense—set about doing what he could. The paper next day blossomed (if that be the word) with pieces in which Ireland rose like yeast through every paragraph. The genius and virtue of that injured country bubbled magnificently from his pen; and Shandon, enjoying himself at Boulogne-sur-Mer, recognised the hand at once, and laughed as he tossed the sheet to his wife. “Look here, Mary, my dear—here is Jack at work again.”

Indeed Jack had a faithful habit of remembering, whatever the subject, that Rafferty was the greatest painter in Europe; that the Academy’s refusal to make him an R.A. was petty jealousy; that Mr. Rooney, M.P., was “generally reported in the West End” to be appointed Governor of Barataria; and that any political crisis could be improved by a compliment to the Round Towers or the Giant’s Causeway. Besides doing Pen’s work, he offered—good fellow—to spend his Saturday and Sunday nursing Arthur; but Pen, who could still be proud when he could no longer be well, insisted the other should take his holiday, and declared (with that brave selfishness sick people often call independence) that he could bear it best alone.

Finucane, taking his supper at the Back Kitchen on Friday night after the paper had been got through, mentioned Pen’s illness to Captain Costigan. The Captain remembered it two days later, and on Sunday afternoon marched to Lamb Court to pay his visit.

He found Mrs. Flanagan in tears in the sitting-room, and extracted from her, between sob and sniff, a report as gloomy as her gin-bottle was cheerful. Pen had alarmed her; and she, to enable herself to bear the shock of his sufferings, had been obliged to have recourse to brandy. Then, hanging about the bed, trying to “minister,” she had become intolerable to the invalid, who begged her peevishly to keep away. Hence her tears, and the redoubled grief, and the renewed application to the bottle which she used as an anodyne. Captain Costigan rated her soundly for her intemperance, and foretold the fatal consequences which must ensue if she persisted—addressing her as if he were a temperance lecturer and she the whole gin-trade.

Pen, fevered as he was, was genuinely pleased at the Captain’s coming. He heard the well-known voice in the outer room, and called eagerly, and thanked him as if he had been brought a banquet. Costigan felt the pulse with great gravity—his own tremulous, clammy hand growing steady for the instant with the importance of the touch. The pulse was racing; the face haggard and hot; the eyes bloodshot and gloomy; and his “bird” (the Captain afterwards pronounced the word with much relish) had not been shaved for nearly a week. Pen made him sit down, and, tossing in that comfortless bed, tried to talk gaily about the Back Kitchen, about Vauxhall and when they should go again—and then, as inevitably as a hungry man comes round to food, he came round to Fanny.

How was little Fanny?

How, indeed. We know how she went home, very sad, the previous Sunday evening—after seeing Arthur light his lamp in his chambers, while he had that interview with Bows. Bows returned presently to his own rooms, and as he passed the lodge looked in upon Mrs. Bolton’s, as was his habit; but with a face so melancholy you might have thought he had been practising adagios on his own heart.

Fanny had a weary night. Restless, she woke the little bedfellows more than once. She dared not read further in Walter Lorraine: her father was at home and would allow no light; so she kept the book under her pillow, feeling for it in the dark as if it were a talisman. She had only just drifted into sleep when the children began to stir with the morning almost as early as the birds—those real birds outside, whose small clean songs were the only music in that quarter not paid for, not advertised, and not banged out to sell somebody’s pleasure.

Though she was angry with Bows, she went to his room at her accustomed hour; and there the good-hearted musician began to talk.

“I saw Mr. Pendennis last night, Fanny,” he said.

“Did you? I thought you did,” she answered, looking fiercely at the melancholy old gentleman.

“I’ve been fond of you ever since we came to live in this place,” he continued. “You were a child when I came; and you used to like me, Fanny, until three or four days ago—until you saw this gentleman.”

“And now, I suppose, you are going to say ill of him,” said Fanny. “Do, Mr. Bows—that will make me like you better.”

“Indeed I shall do no such thing,” Bows answered. “I think he is a very good and honest young man.”

“Indeed! you know that if you said a word against him, I would never speak a word to you again—never!” cried Miss Fanny, clenching her little hand and pacing. Bows watched her—admiring and sorrowful. Her cheeks flushed; her frame trembled; her eyes shone love, anger, defiance all in one beam. “You would like to speak ill of him,” she said; “but you daren’t—you know you daren’t!”

“I knew him many years since,” Bows went on, “when he was almost as young as you are, and he had a romantic attachment for our friend the Captain’s daughter—Lady Mirabel that is now.”

Fanny laughed. “I suppose there was other people, too, that had romantic attachments for Miss Costigan,” she said. “I don’t want to hear about ’em.”

“He wanted to marry her; but their ages were quite disproportionate—and their rank in life. She would not have him because he had no money. She acted very wisely in refusing him; for the two would have been very unhappy, and she wasn’t a fit person to go and live with his family, or to make his home comfortable. Mr. Pendennis has his way to make in the world, and must marry a lady of his own rank. A woman who loves a man will not ruin his prospects, cause him to quarrel with his family, and lead him into poverty and misery for her gratification. An honest girl won’t do that—for her own sake, or for the man’s.”

At that, Fanny’s defiance collapsed into dismay, and dismay into pleading. “What do I know about marrying, Bows?” she cried. “When was there any talk of it? What has there been between this young gentleman and me that’s to make people speak so cruel? It was not my doing; nor Arthur’s—Mr. Pendennis’s—that I met him at Vauxhall. It was the Captain took me and Ma there. We never thought of nothing wrong, I’m sure. He came and rescued us, and he was so very kind. Then he came to call and ask after us; and very, very good it was of such a grand gentleman to be so polite to humble folks like us! And yesterday Ma and me just went to walk in the Temple Gardens, and—and—”

Here she broke out into that unanswerable feminine argument which has silenced more philosophers than logic ever did: she cried. “Oh! I wish I was dead! I wish I was laid in my grave; and had never, never seen him!”

“He said as much himself, Fanny,” Bows said; and she asked through sobs why, why should he wish that? Had she harmed him? She would perish rather than harm him. Whereupon the musician told her of the conversation of the day before, and showed her—gently, painfully—that Pen could not and must not think of her as a wife, and that she, if she valued her honest name, must try to forget him. She promised to avoid the danger; and yet, being convinced in mind and unconvinced in heart (as most of us are, when convinced at all), she went back to the lodge and told her mother everything.

She spoke of her love with that artless extravagance which is half poetry, half hunger. She bewailed the inequality that raised barriers between them; and straightway, as girls do, she borrowed language from the stage to dress feelings which had no words of their own. “There’s the Lady of Lyons,” she said. “Oh, Ma! how I did love Mr. Macready when I saw him do it; and Pauline, for being faithful to poor Claude, and always thinking of him; and he coming back to her, an officer, through all his dangers! And if everybody admires Pauline—and I’m sure everybody does—for being so true to a poor man—why should a gentleman be ashamed of loving a poor girl? Not that Mr. Arthur loves me—oh no, no! I ain’t worthy of him; only a princess is worthy of such a gentleman as him. Such a poet! writing so beautifully, and looking so grand! I am sure he’s a nobleman, and of ancient family, and kep’ out of his estate. Perhaps his uncle has it. Ah, if I might—oh, how I’d serve him, and work for him, and slave for him! I wouldn’t ask for more than that, Ma—just to be allowed to see him of a morning; and sometimes he’d say ‘How d’you, Fanny?’ or ‘God bless you, Fanny!’ as he said on Sunday. And I’d work, and work; and I’d sit up all night, and read, and learn, and make myself worthy of him. The Captain says his mother lives in the country, and is a grand lady there. Oh, how I wish I might go and be her servant, Ma! I can do plenty of things, and work very neat; and—and sometimes he’d come home, and I should see him!”

Her head dropped on her mother’s shoulder, and she cried as if tears were the only language left her. The matron joined in, because mothers will weep with a daughter even while they are laying plans for her. “You mustn’t think no more of him, Fanny,” she said. “If he don’t come to you, he’s a horrid, wicked man.”

“Don’t call him so, Mother,” Fanny pleaded. “He’s the best of men, the best and the kindest. Bows says he thinks he is unhappy at leaving poor little Fanny. It wasn’t his fault, was it, that we met?—and it ain’t his that I mustn’t see him again. He says I mustn’t—and I mustn’t, Mother. He’ll forget me, but I shall never forget him. No! I’ll pray for him, and love him always—until I die—and I shall die, I know I shall—and then my spirit will always go and be with him.”

“You forget your poor mother, Fanny,” Mrs. Bolton said, “and you’ll break my heart by goin on so. Perhaps you will see him. I’m sure you’ll see him. I’m sure he’ll come to-day. If ever I saw a man in love, that man is him. When Emily Budd’s young man first came about her, he was sent away by old Budd—a most respectable man, and violoncello in the orchestra at the Wells—and his own family wouldn’t hear of it neither. But he came back. We all knew he would. Emily always said so; and he married her; and this one will come back too; and you mark a mother’s words and see if he don’t, dear.”

At that point Mr. Bolton entered for his evening meal; and instantly all romance was snuffed like a candle. Mrs. Bolton turned to coaxing and clatter. “Lor, Mr. B., who’d have thought to see you away from the Club of a Saturday night. Fanny, dear, get your pa some supper. What will you have, B.? The poor gurl’s got a gathering in her eye, or somethink in it—I was lookin at it just now as you came in.” She squeezed her daughter’s hand as a signal for prudence and secrecy. Fanny’s tears dried as if she had been paid to dry them. By that wondrous hypocrisy—call it self-defence, call it training—which women practise and nature arms them with, every trace of emotion vanished; she took her work and sat demure in the corner, so that the careless male parent never suspected a thing beyond the mysterious “gathering.”

Thus, as if fate were determined to keep the poor child’s passion at a full boil, everything about her helped to stir it. Her mother applauded it; and the very words Bows used to quench the flame only fanned it. Pen was not wicked: he was high-minded in staying away. Pen loved her: the magnificent youth with the gold chains and the scented auburn hair! And perhaps he did—perhaps he would have five years earlier, before the world hardened the reckless boy; before he learned that society forgives much except being found out; before he grew ashamed of foolish tenderness and throttled it, not as a crime, but as a scandal.

Any respectable person will say he was right not to marry an ill-educated girl of low degree, with relations a gentleman could not acknowledge and manners that would sit oddly in his new station. Any philosopher will add that passions are like summer flies, and should be brushed away; that nobody dies about a woman (or a man) except in novels; that, being disappointed in one object, we must choose another and digest our mortification. And yet—there is sometimes something in the other side too. Bows, perhaps, was right to admire the blind heat which would stake everything; perhaps if self-sacrifice be a virtue, worldly prudence is not the noblest imitation of it. Let each moralist settle it in his own dialect, and quarrel with his neighbours about the words.

This is certain: with the experience Mr. Pen now had, he would have laughed at and scouted the idea of marrying a penniless girl out of a kitchen. That point fixed, he was doing the honest thing, in his own view, by crushing any fondness he felt.

So Fanny waited—waited as only the young can wait, believing time is a servant and must come when called. She waited a whole week. And it was at the end of that time that she heard, from Captain Costigan, of the illness under which Arthur was suffering.

It chanced—on that very evening after Costigan had visited Pen—that Arthur’s uncle, the excellent Major, arrived in town from Buxton, where his health had been mended. He sent his valet, Morgan, to inquire for Arthur and to request that gentleman would breakfast with the Major next morning. The Major was merely passing through London on his way to the Marquis of Steyne’s place, Stillbrook, where he was engaged to shoot partridges.

Morgan came back with a very long face. He had seen Mr. Arthur. Mr. Arthur was very bad indeed. Mr. Arthur was in bed with a fever. A doctor ought to be sent; and Morgan thought the case most alarming.

Gracious goodness! Here was a pretty breakfast invitation. The Major had hoped Arthur might come down to Stillbrook; he had arranged it; he had obtained an invitation from Lord Steyne. He must go himself—he couldn’t throw Lord Steyne over. The fever might be catching. It might be measles. He had never himself had measles; and measles were dangerous at his age. Was anybody with Mr. Arthur?

Morgan said there was somebody a-nussing of Mr. Arthur.

Had Mr. Pendennis taken any advice?

Morgan said he had asked that question, and had been told that Mr. Pendennis had had no doctor.

Fanny had no need of introductions. The moment she saw the two ladies—one older, one younger—entering the passage with faces set as if carved for a monument, she knew, by a flash of likeness in the elder’s worn eyes, whose presence chilled the air. Those were the same eyes Arthur had borrowed when fever had tossed him—only steadier now, and far less forgiving.

Mrs. Pendennis looked at Fanny as a housekeeper looks at a suspicious stain. Laura looked past her, as if the poor girl were a chair that had been put in the wrong place.

“I—I wrote to you yesterday, if you please, ma’am,” Fanny stammered, every syllable shaking out of her like a spoonful of water from trembling hands. “To tell you how he was.”

“Did you, madam?” Mrs. Pendennis said. Her voice had the smooth, cold edge of a knife freshly honed. “I suppose I may now relieve you from nursing my son. I am his mother, you understand.”

“Yes, ma’am. This way to his room—Oh! wait—” Fanny caught her breath as if she had swallowed smoke. “I must prepare you for his—”
