For a second the widow’s hard composure slipped. A gasp—quick, frightened—broke out of her, and she crushed it down again at once, as though even pity must not be allowed to make a noise in respectable society.

“He’s been so since yesterday,” Fanny whispered, teeth chattering.

From the open door of Pen’s room came a burst of sound: not a groan, but a horrible shout of laughter, as if some cruel tavern jest had been cracked at the foot of his bed. Then more yells—then, incongruously, a college drinking-song, bellowed in a cracked, triumphant voice; and between verses the thump of his fist on the paneling, like a man rapping for more wine.

“He does not know me, ma’am,” Fanny said, with the helpless exactness of a cook admitting the soufflé has fallen.

“Indeed. Perhaps he will know his mother. Let me pass, if you please.” And with that Mrs. Pendennis swept by her—through the narrow, dark passage, into the sitting-room beyond, where the sick man’s life and death were making such a racket. Laura followed, silent, sailing past without so much as a glance. Major Pendennis came last, his eyelids lowered, peeping from under them with a furtive, uneasy shame.

Fanny sank onto the bench in the passage—the same bench where Pen’s printer’s devil used to perch for hours, ink-stained and hungry—and she cried and prayed as well as she could, with that desperate, salt prayer that is less religion than drowning. She would have given her own blood to cool his fever. They gave her nothing—not even the smallest crumb of thanks; not even the courtesy you offer a maid who has kept the broth from burning.

Time went strange: a draught in the passage, the muffled commotion inside, the taste of tears, and that smell which clings to illness—stale linen, spilled physic, hot breath, and the faint metallic tang that foretells worse.

At last Doctor Goodenough came, brisk and benevolent, like a man who has seen too many sickrooms to be frightened of them, and too many grieving faces to be careless.

“What, nurse?” he asked, with his kind professional cheer. “How’s your patient? Has he had any rest?”

“Go and ask them. They’re inside,” Fanny said.

“Who? his mother?”

She nodded, dumb as a scullery-girl caught in a lie—though she had done nothing but tell the truth with her whole life.

“You must go to bed yourself, my poor little maid,” said the Doctor. “You’ll be ill too, if you don’t.”

“Oh, mayn’t I come and see him—mayn’t I come and see him!” She clasped his hand, falling on her knees with such honest anguish that it fogged the kind man’s spectacles and made him blink hard behind them. “I—I love him so.”

“Pooh, pooh! Nonsense!” he said—because doctors must scold where they would rather weep. He set her back on the bench, tapped her pale cheek with a finger that had steadied many a pulse, and bustled into the room.

Mrs. Pendennis had established herself at the bedside like a general in possession of an enemy fort. A great chair was her throne; her watch lay on the table among the bottles and papers; her bonnet and cloak were set aside with the tidy certainty of a woman who could arrange a drawing-room even in a crisis. Her Bible—always travelling with her like a moral umbrella—rested in her lap.

Her first act, on entering, had been small and speaking: she had taken Fanny’s shawl and bonnet—poor little things that smelt of rain and cheap lavender—and carried them out as if they were soiled cloths, dropping them on the study-table with a motion that said, wordlessly, Out. She had closed the door on Major Pendennis and Laura too, keeping even family at a distance while she claimed her son.

She had feared—silently, fiercely—that Arthur would not know her. Fever makes strange foreigners of our dearest. But that pang was spared her in part: Pen did know his mother, and smiled and nodded with a familiar, childish friendliness. In the instant she came in, his mind transported them home to Fairoaks; he began talking in wild loops and leaps, laughing, chattering, making nonsense of memory. Outside the door Laura heard that laughter, and it stung her like smoke in the eyes. To her, every shout sounded like confession: it was true then—he had been guilty, and with that creature—and she had loved him—and now he might die, raving, unrepentant, and merry as a man at a supper-table.

Major Pendennis offered, now and then, a humming little sentence meant for comfort. Laura scarcely heard him. Grief has its own deafness.

It was a dismal sitting for all. When Goodenough came in he seemed, by mere contrast, an angel—an angel with pills and a practical manner.

A doctor does not visit only the sick man: he is summoned by the terror and longing of everybody who loves the sick man. The sound of his wheels in the street, the knock at the door, the stir on the stairs—how it lifts and drops whole households. We read his face like a menu when we are starving for hope: will he bring nourishment, or only the polite refusal of it? Mothers search his eyes for the word he may not dare say. Wives watch his fingers on the pulse as if he were Fate in a neckcloth. Children, hushed and puzzled, feel the whole house listening—listening not just to voices but to the very acoustic weather of the room: the hiss of breath, the clink of a spoon in a glass, the heavy tread of an anxious foot. In such hours, even the silence has a sound, and it can be crueler than any factory din.

Goodenough made short work of introductions, for there are moments when ceremony is an impertinence. He examined Pen and saw at once what there was to see: high fever, no ambiguity, no politeness possible. Strong antiphlogistic measures were needed. He offered Mrs. Pendennis what comfort he honestly could—youth, constitution, hope—and then drew Major Pendennis aside into Warrington’s empty room to consult.

The case was critical. If they did not stop the fever, it might carry the young fellow off. He must be bled at once. The mother must be told. And why—Goodenough asked, with that grim irritation doctors feel at foolish additions to a sickroom—why had the other young lady been brought? She was out of place there.

“And there was another woman still—be hanged to it!” the Major said, rubbing his hands as if guilt were grease. “The—the little person who opened the door.” He had seen the bonnet and shawl flung out upon the study-table. Did the Doctor know anything about the—the little person? “I just caught a glimpse of her as we passed in,” the Major added, and even now, with death in the next room, could not help a worldly aside: “begad she was uncommonly nice-looking.”

Goodenough looked at him in a queer way and—yes—smiled. In the gravest minutes, the smallest absurdity will pop up and grin at us, like a cork forced to the surface of black water. The smile did not lessen the gloom; it sharpened it.

“I have it,” the Doctor said at last.

He went into the study, wrote two notes rapidly, sealed one, then took up Fanny’s little shawl and bonnet—as if to give the rejected things an errand, a dignity—and carried them with the notes into the passage where Fanny sat.

“Quick, nurse,” he said. “You must carry this to the surgeon and bid him come instantly. Then go to my house and ask for my servant Harbottle; give him this prescription and tell him to get it prepared and wait until I—until it is ready. It may take a little time.”

So off went poor Fanny, sent from the doorway like a turnspit from the kitchen, only her task was not gravy but life. She trudged to the apothecary hard by in the Strand; he came straightway with his lancet—small, bright, efficient as modern commerce—ready to operate. Then she made for the Doctor’s house in Hanover Square.

Goodenough was back at the chambers before the mixture was finished—Harbottle taking an age to compound whatever dark draughts science then ladled out with such confidence. And during the rest of Arthur’s illness Fanny never again appeared as nurse in his rooms. Yet for that day and the next, a little figure could be seen hovering on Pen’s staircase: a face made tragically older by love and sleeplessness, watching, questioning with her eyes the apothecary, his boy, the laundress, the Doctor himself—anyone who came down from the sickroom carrying news, or the smell of it.

On the third day Doctor Goodenough’s carriage stopped at Shepherd’s Inn. The good man went into the porter’s lodge—because kindness, like a well-made broth, belongs where it is needed most, not where it is most admired—and tended a little patient of his there. For the best medicine he could give her was the moment he was able to tell Fanny Bolton that the crisis was over, and that there was at length every hope for Arthur Pendennis.

J. Costigan, Esquire, late of Her Majesty’s service, happened to see the Doctor’s carriage and did what he always did with any spectacle: reviewed it.

“Green liveries, bedad!” the General said. “And as foin a pair of high-stepping bee horses as ever a gentleman need sit behoind—let alone a docthor. There’s no ind to the proide and ar’gance of them docthors nowadays—” Then, with that swift Irish turn that can abuse and bless in one breath: “Not but that is a good one—and a scoientific cyarkter—and a roight good fellow, bedad; and he’s brought the poor little girl well troo her faver, Bows, me boy.”

From that day, whenever Costigan met Goodenough’s carriage, he saluted it with such magnificent ceremony as if the physician were the Lord Lieutenant himself and the General were back in his own glory at Phoenix Park.

Mrs. Pendennis’s gratitude to the Doctor knew no bounds—or at least no bounds except those set by pride. The kind gentleman laughed at the notion of taking a fee from a literary man, or from the widow of a brother practitioner. Mrs. Pendennis determined that on returning to Fairoaks she would send him the silver-gilt vase—the jewel of the house, wrapped reverently in green baize—presented long ago to the late John Pendennis at Bath by Lady Elizabeth Firebrace, after the recovery of her son, the late Sir Anthony, from scarlet fever. Hippocrates, Hygeia, King Bladud, and a wreath of serpents crowned it still; Messrs. Abednego of Milsom Street had executed it at their best, and Mr. Birch, tutor to the young baronet, had supplied the inscription. It was a trophy of old cures and old gratitude—an heirloom of medicine and memory, shining with the kind of splendour that tries to make suffering look genteel.

That priceless cup she would gladly give. There was scarcely any other favour her thankfulness would not have granted him—except the one he desired most: that she should think kindly of poor Fanny.

Goodenough had learned something of the artless, sad story in his brief interviews with the girl, and he was disposed to be gentle with her—and not too admiring of Pen in the affair, or not knowing precisely what Pen’s conduct had been. He knew enough to understand that the poor, infatuated child was without stain as yet; that her watch in Pen’s room had been, in her mind, a vigil by a deathbed; that Arthur scarcely knew she was there; and that her grief, whether he lived or died, had the pitiful depth of love that has no language for itself—no respectable dialect, no sanctioned vocabulary. It could only speak in sobs, and those were considered vulgar.

But when Goodenough once or twice alluded to Fanny, Mrs. Pendennis’s countenance—commonly soft and gentle—hardened into something cruel and inexorable, as if her very features had taken up a dominant lexicon in which mercy had no word. The Doctor saw it was useless. He stopped asking for justice; he ceased pleading for pity. There is an affliction, the poets tell us, no poppy or mandragora can soothe; and when it appears in ladies, no later discovery—neither homoeopathy, nor hydropathy, nor mesmerism, nor the newest fashionable doctor—can cure it. Call it not jealousy, if you like. Call it rivalry, emulation: it bites just the same.

Now, certain prosaic persons—those who count cupboards in novels, and measure rooms as if the heart were a piece of furniture—may ask how, in a set of chambers in the Temple consisting of three rooms, two cupboards, a passage, and a coal-box, all these souls could be packed: Arthur sick; Helen his mother; Laura her adopted daughter; Martha their country attendant; Mrs. Wheezer, a nurse from St. Bartholomew’s; Mrs. Flanagan, an Irish laundress; Major Pendennis; Morgan his valet; Pidgeon, Pen’s boy; and the rest. The answer is simple: almost everybody in the Temple was out of town, and the house in Lamb Court was nearly empty except for those drawn, like moths to a dangerous flame, to the bedside of a fevered young gentleman.

We will not linger over the fever’s long, ugly details, nor enlarge much on the happier theme of recovery. But the house filled, as households do in such times, with an odd domestic mythology: the whisper that meant danger, the footstep that meant hope, the clatter of a tray that sounded like salvation. And above all, the city’s own roar beyond the windows—the cart-wheels, calls, and bells—kept up its indifferent, industrial chorus, as if London could not bear to lower its voice even when a single human life asked for quiet.

Of course such a fashionable man as young Mr. Sibwright, who occupied chambers on the second floor in Pen’s staircase, could not be supposed to remain in London. Mrs. Flanagan, Pen’s laundress, knew Mrs. Rouncy who did for Mr. Sibwright; and so that gentleman’s bedroom was put in order for Miss Bell, or for Mrs. Pendennis, when she should be persuaded to leave her son’s room and seek a little rest.

If Percy Sibwright—flower of Baker Street—could have known who was sleeping in his bed, he would have been proud enough to compose odes to his own sheets. He wrote poems (some printed in annuals, some lingering in manuscript albums of the noble), had been a Camford man, and was said to have narrowly missed the English Prize Poem. Sibwright, however, was absent, and his pretty little brass bed, with chintz curtains lined in pink, was surrendered to Laura.

It was, truly, the daintiest bower. In the window stood a mignonette-box, breathing out a clean, peppery sweetness that seemed almost indecent beside the sour medicinal smells next door. Shiny boots were arranged in trim rows over the wardrobe like a little exhibition of vanity at a fair. There was a museum of scent, pomatum, and bear’s-grease pots—each with its own oily, perfumed history—curious enough for any food-historian of the toilette. Portraits of women—always melancholy, often disguised or half undressed—glittered round the neat walls: Medora with her hair down, strumming sorrow over Conrad; Fleur-de-Marie peeping mournfully through convent bars; Dorothea washing her eternal feet. It was an elegant gallery for a gallant lover of the sex.

In Sibwright’s sitting-room there was an infant law-library in fresh calf-skin—books dressed for court, though perhaps never speaking there—and a tolerably large collection of classics he could not read, along with English and French poetry and fiction he read much too well. Invitation-cards from the past season still decorated his looking-glass; and scarcely anything betrayed the lawyer except the wig-box beside the Venus on the middle shelf, with “P. Sibwright, Esquire” gilded on it.

With Sibwright in chambers was Mr. Bangham, a sporting man married to a rich widow, who had no practice, came to chambers thrice in a term, and went circuit for those mysterious reasons which make men go circuit. Their rooms have nothing to do with our history and will likely never appear again; but we glance through their open doors as we pass, because in life, too, we cannot help peeping into shops on the Strand, or counting our neighbour’s dinner, or noticing the faces under bonnets in the next pew—especially when our own hearts are too full to look straight ahead.

Many years after these events, Laura—older, and with humour softened by happiness—confessed with a blush and a laugh that she had once read a French novel then much in vogue; and when her husband asked where on earth she had procured such a volume, she owned it was in the Temple, when she lived in Percy Sibwright’s chambers.

“And also,” she said, “I never confessed—on that same occasion—what I must now own: that I opened the japanned box, and took out that strange-looking wig inside it, and put it on and looked at myself in the glass.”

Suppose Sibwright had entered at that moment—enraptured rogue! What would all his pictures of disguised beauties have been beside that living one?

But when Laura played that prank, Pen could not have been dangerously ill upstairs; for had he been, common feeling and decorum would have prevented tricks and disguises. Besides, a great and delightful alteration had taken place. Goodenough’s blisters, potions, and lancet had subdued the fever. It had retreated, returning only in feeble fits. The wandering had settled into exhausted sense.

Pen had been able—weak, hollow-eyed, bearded with illness—to kiss and bless his mother for coming; to call for Laura and his uncle; to press their hands and thank them with an affection that startled them, each according to temperament. Then, after his affectionate nurse had turned them out, he had sunk into a sleep so deep and long it seemed like a rehearsal for death—sixteen hours, they said—until he woke and called out, in a voice half cracked and wholly human:

He was hungry.

If it is hard to be ill and loathe food, how sweet it is to be getting well and to feel hunger return—honest, bodily hunger, like a homely bell calling you back to the world. With age that joy thins, as other joys do; and then comes the illness for which there is no convalescence at all.

On the day of this happy sign another arrival came to Lamb Court, introduced not by ceremony but by large puffs of tobacco-smoke. The puffs were followed by an individual with a cigar in his mouth and a carpet-bag under his arm: Warrington, come back from Norfolk the moment he heard. Mr. Bows had thoughtfully written to inform him; Warrington had been away from home when the letter reached his brother’s house; the Eastern Counties had no railway then (for we only commit anachronisms when we choose, and only violate natural laws when some great moral truth requires it); and so he appeared, as luck would have it, on the lucky day when Pen’s convalescence might be said to have begun.

Warrington let himself in with his pass-key. His surprise was not great to find the chambers occupied and Major Pendennis seated demurely in an easy-chair, listening—or pretending to listen—to a young lady reading Shakespeare in a low, sweet voice, the cadence of it falling on the room like soft rain after street-noise.

At the apparition of the tall traveller with cigar and carpet-bag, the lady stopped, started, and laid down the book. Warrington, suddenly shy as a boy, flung the cigar into the passage, took off his hat, dropped that too, and went straight up to the Major, seizing his hand.

“How is Arthur?” he cried.

The Major answered in a tremulous, cheery voice—emotion had curiously aged him in an instant—and, returning Warrington’s pressure with a shaking hand, told him of the happy crisis, of the mother’s arrival—with her young charge—with Miss—

“You need not tell me her name,” Warrington said quickly, eyes bright with relief and feeling. “You need not tell me your name. I knew at once it was Laura.”

He held out his hand and took hers. Beneath his rough brows, immense tenderness shone; it shook his voice as he looked at her. His face seemed to say, And this is Laura. Her heart answered, And this is Warrington—Arthur’s hero—the brave and kind—who has come hundreds of miles when he heard his friend was struck down.

“Thank you, Mr. Warrington,” was all she said. She returned his pressure, and blushed so hotly that she was glad the lamp was behind her and could hide her face.

As they stood thus, the door of Pen’s bedchamber opened stealthily—as his mother was wont to open it—and Warrington saw another lady appear. She looked at him once; then, turning toward the bed, she said softly, urgently, “Hsh!” and lifted her hand.

It is one of those facts which a biographer records with the modesty of a cook confessing he once burnt a sauce: disgraceful to the hero, mortifying to the narrator, but indispensable to truth. Arthur Pendennis, having taken to his bed with fever and a sentimental inflammation besides, was duly submitted to the whole pharmacopoeia—bled, blistered, shaved, lectured, and dosed—until, when the bodily furnace at last cooled, the other heat went out too; and the passion which had made him talk poetry over a porter’s daughter departed as briskly as steam when the kettle is taken off the fire.

He lay on his pillow, and actually laughed—softly, for invalids must not split stitches, even when their hearts have been mended. He could not for the life of him remember what particular spice had seemed so intoxicating in Fanny Bolton. Not her wit, not her breeding, not her beauty—London could show prettier faces at any greengrocer’s stall, and better manners at any respectable dinner-table. The change, he perceived with the calm of a food-historian dissecting yesterday’s pie, was not in the dish but in the appetite. She was as she had been; only the palate that had raved over her was altered. It is a humiliating comfort to find you are cured.

Yet he was grateful too—grateful in that selfish way young men have of being thankful chiefly that they have escaped consequences. He reviewed, from the safe high ground of convalescence, the precipice he might have fallen down. At least—so he told himself—he had not tumbled. He had resisted when he was weakest; and whatever foolishness had been simmering in his head, he had not let it boil over into open shame.

Meanwhile, the quiet presence at his bedside was like warm broth after a long illness: Mrs. Pendennis’s tenderness, her watchfulness, her readiness to execute any caprice as though it were an order from the Privy Council, filled him with a peace he had not felt since childhood. Her love wrapped him round as a shawl wraps an invalid who fancies every draught a hurricane.

As for the early days of the fever—those hours in which Fanny had indeed been near him—he had only dim misty scraps, like half-remembered tunes heard through a wall. Delirium had muddled them. He could not separate what had actually happened from what his heated brain had invented. And because he had never spoken of Fanny to his mother when he was well, he could not suddenly begin to confide in her now. Silence on both sides—such an excellent precaution, and such a fatal one—kept each ignorant of what the other suffered.

For Mrs. Pendennis, seeing Miss Bolton installed as nurse, had made up her mind—without the tiresome ceremony of inquiry—that the worst stories of Arthur were true. There are tales against a man which the women who love him most are sometimes the keenest to believe; jealous affection has a sharp nose, and sniffs scandal like smoke. That pure and tender creature sat by her boy, smiling when she could, and feeling within her, under the forced calm, a horror far worse than the fever she watched—believing him stained by a sin she dared not name, and compelled to nurse him while nursing her suspicion too.

While Lamb Court kept its sick-room hush, Boulogne went on clinking glasses. Captain Shandon, reading the Pall Mall Gazette there, observed to Mrs. Shandon that Jack Finucane’s hand no longer showed in the leading articles, and that Warrington must have taken the whip again.

“I know his cut,” Shandon said, with that affectionate brutality of journalists. “Jack Bludyer hacks like a butcher. Mr. Warrington lays on neat, straight, scientific lashes—draws blood in every line.”

“Law, Charles!” cried Mrs. Shandon. “How can you talk so? Mr. Warrington always seemed a kind gentleman. I’m sure he was most kind to the children.”

“He’s kind to the children,” Shandon conceded, “and savage to the men. But never mind. Mix another tumbler, my dear. There’s little good comes of newspapers. Better here—wine plenty, brandy two francs. ‘Cras ingens iterabimus aequor’—bad luck to it.”

In truth, Warrington did Pen’s portion of the Gazette with all his might and malice. He wrote criticism, he attended theatres and concerts, and treated them as if they were political enemies. His hand was too heavy for light trifles; yet he took a grim pleasure in telling Mrs. Pendennis and Major Pendennis and Laura that Arthur’s pen was the most graceful and elegant in the whole fraternity.

“These people don’t know what style is, ma’am,” he would say. “If they did, they’d see our young one’s merit. I call him ours, for I bred him. And, bating a little wilfulness, a little selfishness, a little dandification—he’s as loyal and gentle a creature as lives. His pen can be wicked, but he would not harm a fly.”

Helen—who carried her own secret ache—sighed deep at this; and Laura, wounded as she was, felt grateful nevertheless, and loved Warrington the more for loving Pen. Major Pendennis, for his part, grew enthusiastic—almost indecently so, for him.

“He is a gentleman,” the Major told Helen, swelling like a man reciting a recipe from memory and improving it as he goes. “Every inch. The Suffolk Warringtons—Charles the First’s baronets. What could he be but a gentleman? Sir Miles—friend of the Prince of Wales—very known in London—beg your pardon, Miss Bell. Talents, accomplishments—sure to get on if he had but the motive.”

Laura blushed, partly because the Major praised so loudly, and partly because Warrington’s face—manly, worn, with those dark melancholy eyes—had set her fancy working. She had already decided, with the confidence of youth and romance, that he must have been the victim of some unhappy attachment. Catching herself at the thought, she blushed again.

Warrington took chambers close by—Grenier’s in Flag Court—and after hammering out copy in the mornings, came in the afternoons to sit in the sick-room company during those mild, sunny autumn evenings. More than once he had the honour of giving Miss Bell his arm for a turn in the Temple Gardens. When Laura asked Helen’s leave, the Major burst in, eager as a beadle for propriety.

“Yes, yes, begad—of course. It’s like the country. Everybody walks with everybody in the Gardens. There are beadles, you know—perfectly safe.”

If the Major, that self-appointed inspector of morals, saw no danger, Helen could hardly object; and besides, she was glad her girl should breathe air off the river and return with a little colour, as if the Thames—muddy old fellow—could still do a kindness now and then.

For Helen and Laura, in these days, had come to an explanation. When news arrived of Pen’s alarming illness, Laura had insisted on travelling to London with the terrified mother. Helen, still angry, refused; Laura refused the refusal. And when it seemed the poor lad might die, and when it was known that his conduct made any union hopeless, Laura—through tears that came as naturally as breath—confessed what every attentive spectator had long guessed: how fondly, truly, entirely she had loved him. She could not marry him now; must she be denied even the poor consolation of owning her love? Their tears mingled; their grief shared itself; and the journey’s terrors were softened by companionship.

Now consider poor Fanny Bolton’s case. What could she expect when dragged, as it were, into court before two such judges—mother and sweetheart? She could expect nothing but condemnation, sentence, and expulsion. Women, in such matters, are critics without mercy; and we, being Turkish in our hearts (the present narrator declares himself turbaned and bearded, and ready—Bismillah!—for the sack), applaud their severity—provided only they execute the right culprit. Let the barge be ready, by all means; only do not clap the wrong Fatima into the sack and pop her into the Bosphorus merely because you are in a hurry to get back to supper. That is all one pleads—no more, by the Prophet’s whiskers.

So the Major, far from objecting, encouraged Warrington’s intimacy with Laura as if it were an exhibition to be visited with proper tickets. Any sight in town? Warrington should escort her. Vauxhall itself? The Major would probably have said, “Perfectly harmless—beadles everywhere.” And in truth there was no harm between two honourable creatures: Warrington, who for the first time found himself in close companionship with a woman pure, artless, and high-minded; and Laura, who for the first time was thrown daily with a gentleman of strong natural gifts, varied acquirements, enthusiasm, simplicity, and humour—so different from Pen’s languid, dandified sovereignty.

In Warrington’s very roughness there was a kind of refinement. His energy, his hearty laughter, his desire to please, his respect—how unlike Sultan Pen, yawning graciously over the homage women had piled upon him until it cloyed him like too much sugar on a child’s tongue. At home he had been a despot because the women had spoiled him—fed him too continually on sweet attentions, until he grew weary of the very sweetness. Abroad, like many men, he had found his appetite sharpened by change. Does any reader dare interpret that as advice to revolt? Never! The narrator, still Turkish, still turbaned, still sentimental about slavery—would sooner cut off all heads in Christendom or Turkeydom than be henpecked. There: the domestic constitution is saved.

And yet—Pen being what he was—why had Laura loved him so? Why had she talked of him all the way from Fairoaks to London in that post-chaise, as if his childhood toothaches and bird’s-nests were epics?

Because she had seen scarcely anybody else. Because Helen praised Arthur constantly. Because he was gentlemanlike, good-looking enough, witty. And because it is in a girl’s nature to attach herself to Somebody. She does not, like an Arabian princess, fall in love with a dream; she does not usually plight her heart to a portrait in an exhibition or an engraving in a newspaper. She meets Somebody. She hears Somebody praised. She walks, rides, waltzes, talks, sits in the same church pew with Somebody. Again, again—and then “marriages are made in Heaven,” mamma says, pinning on orange-flowers, and there is a wedding breakfast. Or else the affair breaks, and poor heart—why then it twines itself round Somebody Else. We love partly for the beloved, and partly because we have within us that hunger to love. Do you suppose you would eat if you were not hungry?

So Laura had nursed Pen’s image through long solitudes, clasped it, brooded over it; and when she came to London, and Mr. George Warrington appeared daily—odd, original, powerful, amusing—what was to prevent her from finding him agreeable?

Long afterwards—when Fate, with its clumsy hand, had put each of these people into their appointed place—some of them perhaps looked back and thought those Lamb Court days strangely happy: their evening talks, their little walks, their simple recreations round Pen’s convalescent sofa. Major Pendennis ever after spoke of September in London as “doosid pleasant, begad,” and would go home to Bury Street wondering how the evening had slipped away. He climbed the Temple stairs daily with a benevolent perseverance, and—being a man to whom feeding was a species of virtue—he made interest with the chef at Bays’s to prepare little jellies, clear soups, aspics, and dainty invalid trifles, as carefully clarified as a good consommé and almost as consoling.

Doctor Goodenough allowed Pen a glass or two of pure sherry; whereupon the Major, with tears almost in his eyes, related how his noble friend the Marquis of Steyne, passing through London, had ordered any quantity of his precious Amontillado—gift of King Ferdinand himself—to be placed at Mr. Arthur Pendennis’s disposal. The widow and Laura tasted it with reverence (and disliked its bitterness, as good women often do strong wine), but Pen declared himself invigorated, Warrington pronounced it superb, and on the first day it appeared, made a mock after-dinner speech proposing the Major’s health—and Lord Steyne’s—and the aristocracy in general.

Major Pendennis returned thanks with the gravity of a man addressing the House, and used the phrase “the present occasion” the proper number of times. Pen cheered faintly from his armchair. Warrington taught Laura to cry “Hear! hear!” and rap the table with her knuckles. Pidgeon the attendant grinned, and Doctor Goodenough, arriving for his faithful gratuitous visit, found them merry as if sherry were medicine and laughter part of the prescription.

Warrington knew Sibwright, who lived below; and Sibwright, informed that his chambers had been lent for the ladies’ use, replied with a letter so polite and flowery that one might have thought the very carpet had bowed. His bed was at their disposal, his rooms at their service. Kindness gathered round the sick man like neighbours bringing broth to a cottage door. Pen’s heart melted at it; and his mother’s too, we may be sure.

In Sibwright’s chambers stood a piano—an instrument upon which that gallant lover of the arts performed himself, and excellently ill, and to which a song had been dedicated (words by Sibwright, air by his devoted friend Leopoldo Twankidillo). At this “music-box,” as Warrington called it, Laura, at first trembling and blushing—very prettily—would play and sing of an evening, simple airs and old home-songs. Her voice was a rich contralto, warm as brown bread. Warrington, who could scarcely tell one tune from another and whose whole repertoire consisted of a discordant bray of “God save the King,” sat rapt as if she were feeding him with invisible loaves. He could follow the rhythm if not the harmony; and day by day his enthusiasm grew for the pure, tender creature who made the music.

And I wonder—how did that poor pale girl in the black bonnet, who sometimes stood by the lamp-post in Lamb Court looking up at the open windows, like a hungry child outside a baker’s—how did she like to hear it?

When Pen’s bedtime came, the songs were hushed. Lights moved in the upper room—his room—whither the widow helped him. Then the Major and Warrington, and sometimes Laura, would play écarté or backgammon; or she would sit working at a pair of slippers in worsted—gentleman’s slippers. They might have been intended for Arthur, or for George, or for Major Pendennis; any one of the three would have given a great deal for those slippers, and not merely for the warmth of wool.

While this snug business went on within, the shabby old gentleman—Fanny’s father—would appear and lead away the pale girl in the black bonnet, who had no right to be out in the night air. The Temple porters, a laundress or two, and other amateurs who had listened to the concert, would drift off as well; the evening’s little domestic theatre closed, the audience dispersed into darkness and damp.

Just before ten came another musical performance: the chimes of St. Clement’s in the Strand, which played a clear cheerful psalm before striking its ten fatal strokes. As they rang, Laura folded up the slippers. Martha from Fairoaks appeared with a bed-candle and a constant smile. The Major started as if time were a surprise invented to insult him.

“God bless my soul! is it so late?”

Warrington and the Major rose, left their unfinished game, and shook hands with Miss Bell. Martha lighted them through the passage and down the stairs; and as they descended they heard her bolt and lock “the sporting door” after them upon her young mistress and herself. If there had been danger, grinning Martha said, she’d have fetched “that thar hooky soord as hung up in gantleman’s room”—meaning the Damascus scimitar with the Prophet’s names engraved upon the blade and a red velvet scabbard, which Percy Sibwright had brought from the Levant along with an Albanian dress, and had worn with such effect at Lady Mullingar’s fancy ball—where it entangled itself in Miss Kewsey’s train (she appearing in the dress in which she had been presented to their Sovereign), and led to events which have nothing to do with this history. Is not Miss Kewsey now Mrs. Sibwright? Has not Sibwright a county court?—Good night, Laura, and good night, Fairoaks Martha. Sleep well and wake happy, pure and gentle lady.

Since Arthur’s illness had brought him to that helpless state in which a man is grateful for a glass of water and yet incapable of finding his own other boot, Mrs. Pendennis had taken entire possession of him—of his pillows, his pulses, his draughts, his temperature, his conscience, and (what is far more intimate than a pulse) his drawers and closets. There was nothing in those domestic repositories which her motherly hand did not rearrange with a kind of tender ferocity: shirts had their buttons restored as if to moral respectability; stockings were darned with the solemnity of little funerals; collars were re-folded until they looked like the very emblem of propriety.

And then—among these humble and fragrant linens, where soap and lavender ought to have reigned alone—there lay letters.

It is astonishing how many sorts of paper can breed in a young gentleman’s chamber. There are the quiet, well-meaning envelopes from tradesmen, which smell faintly of leather and ledger: bootmakers with their beseeching “next Saturday” and hatters with their firm belief that a man’s head may be covered on credit, but his conscience must be settled in cash. Pen, being free-handed and careless, had a little colony of such missives; not enough to ruin him, but quite enough to ruin his mother’s digestion.

So she did what a vigilant commander does in a beleaguered city: she seized the gates. The brass knocker on the inner door—the postman’s cheerful instrument of terror—was actually unscrewed, lest the startling rat-tat should disturb her patient’s sleep. The very sound of a letter arriving is a kind of kitchen-knife to an uneasy conscience. Blessed, indeed, is the man who can hear the postman and think of nothing but affection. The good are made brisk by that knock; the guilty feel as if the world itself were tapping them on the shoulder.

Mrs. Pendennis intercepted everything. She paid some of the accounts out of her own small hoard—those savings pinched from ribbons and trifles, stored up by a simplicity that had the look of parsimony, though it came of love. If a young man’s correspondence is ever to be surrendered to parental hands, it is usually at the price of having one’s debts quietly slain and buried.

But what she wanted most was not a bill.

She wanted the key to the dreadful Fanny Bolton mystery—an anxiety she had never once confessed to Arthur, and yet which lay in her mind like an undigested crust: always there, always scratching. She opened other letters only to get at that one—like a cook lifting pot-lids in a panic, not because she expects a stew, but because she smells smoke.

And now, out at Richmond, with the river murmuring its mild domestic music beyond the windows, and the terrace outside full of summer light, she could bear herself no longer. She drew Major Pendennis into consultation, like a nervous housewife dragging the family lawyer into the pantry and whispering over the jam.

Pen and Warrington were on the terrace in the sunshine, talking and laughing like men who have never had a letter to dread; and Helen, holding her terrors as one holds a hot dish one is afraid to drop, addressed her brother-in-law.

When she asked what she ought to do—whether he knew anything—Major Pendennis puckered his face so that it was impossible to tell whether he was about to pronounce wisdom or enjoy himself. His little eyes gave her one queer glance, then dropped demurely.

“My dear, good creature,” he said, “I don’t know anything about it; and I don’t wish to know anything about it; and, as you ask my opinion, I think you had best know nothing about it too. Young men will be young men; begad, and if you think our boy is a Jo—”

“Pray, spare me this!” Helen cut in, growing suddenly stately, as if virtue itself had stiffened her spine.

“My dear creature, I did not commence the conversation,” the Major returned, with a bow that looked as if it had been ironed.

“I can’t bear to hear such a sin—such a dreadful sin—spoken of in such a way,” she cried; tears started, not only from sorrow but from sheer vexation. “I can’t bear to think that my boy should commit such a crime. I wish he had died, almost, before he had done it. It is breaking my heart, Major Pendennis, to think that his father’s son—my child—whom I remember so good—oh, so good, and full of honour!—should be fallen so dreadfully low, as to—as to—”

“As to flirt with a little grisette, my dear creature?” said the Major. “Egad, if all the mothers in England broke their hearts because—Nay, nay. Don’t cry. I can’t bear tears—I never could. But how do we know that anything serious has happened? Has Arthur said anything?”

“His silence confirms it,” sobbed Mrs. Pendennis, behind her pocket-handkerchief, as if the cambric were a confessional grille.

“Not at all,” said the Major, slipping in a little worldly truth as delicately as a cook slips anchovy into a sauce. “There are subjects, my dear, about which a young fellow cannot surely talk to his mamma.”

“She has written to him,” Helen blurted.

“What, before he was ill? Nothing more likely.”

“No, since,” gasped the lady. “Not before; that is, I don’t think so—that is, I—”

“Only since; and you have—yes, I understand,” said the Major, with the quick comprehension of a man who has seen many cupboards opened in his time. “I suppose when he was too ill to read his own correspondence, you took charge of it?”

“I am the most unhappy mother in the world,” she cried.

“The most unhappy mother in the world, because your son is a man and not a hermit!” the Major said, almost briskly. “Have a care, my dear sister. If you have suppressed any letters to him, you may have done yourself a great injury; and if I know anything of Arthur’s spirit, you may cause a difference between him and you which you’ll rue all your life—a difference a dev’lish deal more important, my good madam, than the little—little—trumpery cause which originated it.”

“There was only one letter,” Helen burst out—“only a very little one—only a few words. Here it is. Oh—how can you, how can you speak so?”

When she said “only a very little one,” Major Pendennis had to exercise all the discipline of old campaigners not to laugh outright; for the smallest letter can contain enough to set a whole household clattering like an overturned tray. But he composed his features into gravity.

“I recommend you,” he said, “if you can, to seal it up—those letters ain’t unfrequently sealed with wafers—and to put it amongst Pen’s other letters, and let him have them when he calls for them. Or if we can’t seal it, we mistook it for a bill.”

“I can’t tell my son a lie,” said the widow, in the tone of one who would rather be executed than equivocal.

The truth was, that the little paper had poisoned her bag for two days. Martha had brought it; Helen had never seen Fanny Bolton’s handwriting, but the instant the letter lay in her palm she knew its author—as surely as a cook knows the smell of an onion the moment the skin is nicked. She had been watching for it daily, her nerves pricked to attention by every footstep on the stair. She had opened other letters simply as one opens cupboards in search of a single forbidden jar.

Now she held the thing out to the Major.

He read only the address in the timid, sprawling hand—“Arther Pendennis, Esq.”—and his lip curled, not so much at the girl as at the whole human comedy.

“No, my dear,” he said, “I won’t read any more. But you who have read it may tell me what it contains—only prayers for his health in bad spelling, and a desire to see him? Well, there’s no harm in that. And as you ask me—” Here he grew demure, as if about to confess to a pastry-theft. “—I don’t mind telling you that Morgan, my man, has made some inquiries; and my friend Doctor Goodenough looked into it; and it appears this person was greatly smitten with Arthur; that he paid for her and took her to Vauxhall Gardens, as Morgan heard from an old acquaintance of ours—an Irish gentleman, who was very nearly once having the honour of being the—from an Irishman, in fact. The girl’s father, a violent man of intoxicated habits, has beaten her mother; the mother persists in declaring the daughter entirely innocent to her husband, while telling Goodenough that Arthur has acted like a brute to the child. So you see the story remains a mystery. Will you have it cleared up? I have but to ask Pen, and he will tell me at once—he is as honourable a man as ever lived.”

“Honourable!” Helen repeated, with a bitterness that made the word taste like burnt sugar. “Oh, brother, what is this you call honour? If my boy has been guilty, he must marry her. I would go down on my knees and pray him to do so.”

“Good God! are you mad?” Major Pendennis cried, loud enough to startle the very upholstery. And then—because old memories and old fears can move faster than any carriage—he saw in a flash what such a prayer might do. Arthur was obstinate enough, wild enough, and chivalrous enough (in the dangerous way) to commit any folly where a woman was concerned.

“My dear sister,” he continued, after a pause in which his mind had galloped, “have you lost your senses? What right have we to suppose that anything has passed between this girl and him? Let’s see the letter.”

He took it then, and let his eye run over it quickly—over the misspellings that offended Helen as if they were stains, over the little broken phrases that betrayed a heart without education but not without feeling.

“Her heart is breaking; pray, pray, write to me—home unhappy—unkind father—your nurse—poor little Fanny,” he muttered, half-mocking the orthography and half acknowledging the pathos. “But, good heavens! what is there in this? Only that the little devil is making love to him still. Why, she didn’t come into his chambers until he was so delirious he didn’t know her. What-d’you-call-’em—Flanagan, the laundress—told Morgan so. She came in company of an old fellow, old Mr. Bows, who came most kindly down to Stillbrook and brought me away—by the way, I left him in the cab and never paid the fare; dev’lish kind it was of him. No, there’s nothing in the story.”

“Do you think so? Thank Heaven—thank God!” Helen cried, a laugh and a sob tumbling into one another. “I’ll take the letter to Arthur and ask him now. Look at him there—on the terrace with Mr. Warrington—talking to some children. My boy was always fond of children. He’s innocent, thank God—thank God! Let me go to him.”

Old Pendennis had his own opinion—an opinion he kept as neatly folded as a dress-shirt. He had argued “not guilty” briskly enough; but he judged Arthur by what Arthur’s uncle would have done with a pretty girl, a summer evening, and a ticket to Vauxhall. If Helen went to Arthur and Arthur spoke truth (as rascals will, when cornered), it would spoil everything. So the old diplomatist tried once more, turning persuasion as deftly as one turns an omelette—without letting the tender part break.

“My dear, good soul,” he said, taking her hand and kissing it, “as your son has not acquainted you with this affair, think if you have any right to examine it. As you believe him to be a man of honour, what right have you to doubt his honour in this instance? Who is his accuser? An anonymous scoundrel who brings no specific charge. If there were any such, wouldn’t the girl’s parents have come forward? He is not called upon to rebut, nor you to entertain, an anonymous accusation; and as for believing him guilty because a girl of that rank happened to be in his rooms acting as nurse—begad you might as well insist upon his marrying that dem’d old Irish gin-drinking laundress, Mrs. Flanagan.”

Mrs. Pendennis burst out laughing through her tears—so sudden and helpless a laugh that it seemed as if the very idea of Mrs. Flanagan in bridal white had driven out the devil for the moment.

“Marry Mrs. Flanagan, by Ged!” the Major continued, tapping her slender hand as if sealing the treaty. “No. The boy has told you nothing, and you know nothing. The boy is innocent—of course. And what is the course for us to pursue? Suppose he is attached to this girl—don’t look sad again, it’s merely a supposition—and begad a young fellow may have an attachment, mayn’t he? Directly he gets well he will be at her again.”

“He must come home! We must go off directly to Fairoaks,” Helen cried, snatching at the safety of old rooms and familiar fields as if they were a shawl.

“My good creature, he’ll bore himself to death at Fairoaks,” said the Major. “He’ll have nothing to do but think about his passion there. There’s no place in the world for making a little passion into a big one like a lonely country-house where there’s nothing to do. We must occupy him: amuse him: take him abroad. He’s never been abroad except to Paris for a lark. We must travel a little. He must have a nurse with him—Goodenough says he had a dev’lish narrow squeak of it (don’t look frightened)—and so you must come and watch; and I suppose you’ll take Miss Bell; and I should like to ask Warrington to come. Arthur’s dev’lish fond of Warrington. He can’t do without Warrington. Warrington’s family is one of the oldest in England, and he’s one of the best young fellows I ever met. I like him exceedingly.”

“Does Mr. Warrington know anything about this—this affair?” Helen asked. “He had been away, I know, two months before it happened; Pen wrote me so.”

“Not a word—not a word,” the Major cried, with a touch too much eagerness, as if he were slamming a cupboard door on a rattling pan. “I’ve asked him. I’ve pumped him. He never heard of the transaction—never. I pledge you my word. And I think you had much best not talk to him about it—much best not—of course not. The subject is delicate and painful.”

The widow pressed her brother’s hand with all the gratitude of a woman who has been starving on worry and suddenly gets a morsel of comfort.

“Thank you, brother,” she said. “You have been very, very kind. You have given me a great deal of comfort. I’ll go to my room and think of what you have said. This illness and these—these emotions—have agitated me a great deal; and I’m not very strong, you know. But I’ll go and thank God that my boy is innocent. He is innocent. Isn’t he, sir?”

“Yes, my dearest creature, yes,” said the old fellow, kissing her affectionately, softened in spite of himself—moved by her tenderness, and yet seasoning it with a private, worldly scorn. When she was gone he looked after her and murmured, “Innocent! I’d swear till I was black in the face he was innocent, rather than give that good soul pain.”

Then, having won his little battle, the fatigued warrior threw himself on the sofa, laid his yellow silk pocket-handkerchief over his face like a curtain at the end of a play, and took a snug nap, snoring with a refreshing regularity—an amiable domestic bass note against the lighter treble of the summer day.

Outside, the terrace was full of sun. Pen and Warrington dawdled away the hours, very happy, and Pen (at least) very talkative. He unfolded to George an immense plan for a new novel and a new tragedy; and when Warrington laughed at the idea of his writing tragedy, Pen swore by Jove he would show he could, and began to spout lines, as if Richmond were Drury Lane and the sparrows his audience.

The Major’s solo—performed, as it were, upon the instrument of his own nose—was interrupted by Miss Bell’s entrance. She had been visiting her old friend Lady Rockminster, who had taken a summer villa nearby; and the great lady, hearing of Arthur’s illness and Helen’s arrival, had called—bringing, for the benefit of the invalid she did not like, grapes, partridges, and other attentions that smelt deliciously of condescension and the larder. For Laura, however, Lady Rockminster had a real fondness, and longed to carry her off; but Laura would not leave Mrs. Pendennis now, for Helen, worn by watching and worry, had fallen into a frailty of her own, so that Doctor Goodenough prescribed for mother and son alike.

Major Pendennis started up at once—his slumbers were light, as if he suspected even his own dreams of plotting. He made Miss Bell a gallant speech; he had been full of gallantry toward her of late. Where had she been gathering the roses that bloomed upon her cheeks? How happy he was to be disturbed from visions by so charming a reality!

Laura, who had humour and honesty in good supply, possessed also something like contempt for the old gentleman; it amused her to draw out his worldliness and hear his club-wisdom on great people and morals. But now she was not satirical. She had brought home game for Pen and flowers for mamma; and she looked grave—grave enough to make the room seem quieter.

She had just been with Mrs. Pendennis. Helen was very worn; she feared she was very, very ill. Laura’s large eyes filled with sympathy that was as simple and nourishing as broth. Could not that good dear Doctor Goodenough cure her?

“Arthur’s illness,” Major Pendennis said slowly, “and other mental anxiety, no doubt, have shaken Helen.”

A burning blush came on Laura’s face; she understood his allusion at once. She looked him full in the face and made no reply, but thought, fiercely and silently, He might have spared me that. What is he aiming at by recalling that shame?

He was aiming at something, likely enough; the Major seldom opened his mouth without meaning to put something inside someone else’s. He went on: Goodenough had spoken of their dear friend’s health. She wanted rest and change of scene—yes, change. Painful circumstances must be forgotten and never alluded to. He begged pardon for even hinting at them; he never should do so again—nor, he was sure, would she. Everything must be done to soothe and comfort Helen; and his proposal was that they should go abroad for the autumn, to a watering-place in the Rhine neighbourhood, where Helen might rally her exhausted spirits and Arthur try to become a new man. Of course Miss Bell would not forsake her mother?

Of course not. It was Helen—Helen only (and Arthur for Helen’s sake)—that Laura cared about now. She would go abroad or anywhere with Helen.

And Helen herself, after an hour alone in her room, had grown as eager for the tour as a schoolboy made sea-mad by a book of voyages. Whither should they go? The farther the better—somewhere so remote that even recollection could not follow them; somewhere so delightful that Arthur should never wish to leave; anywhere, so that he could be happy.

She opened her desk with trembling fingers, took out her banker’s book, counted her little savings as if each figure were a prayer, and thought, If more is wanted, there is the diamond cross. I will borrow from Laura again. Let us go—let us go—directly he can bear the journey. Come, kind Doctor Goodenough; come quick, and give us leave to quit England.

The good Doctor drove over to dine with them that very day, and found her in a state of flutter that made even her breathing seem overworked.

“If you agitate yourself so,” he told her, “and if your heart beats so, and if you persist in being so anxious about a young gentleman who is getting well as fast as he can, we shall have you laid up, and Miss Laura to watch you; and then it will be her turn to be ill; and I should like to know how the deuce a doctor is to live who is obliged to come and attend you all for nothing? Mrs. Goodenough is already jealous of you, and says—quite justly—that I fall in love with my patients. And you must please to get out of the country as soon as ever you can, that I may have a little peace in my family.”

When the plan was proposed to Arthur, it was received with the greatest alacrity. He longed to be off that instant. He began to let his moustachios grow from the very moment—perhaps to put his mouth into training for French and German—only to become seriously disquieted when those moustachios, arriving with slow importance, proved to be of a decidedly red colour. He had looked forward to an autumn at Fairoaks; and perhaps the prospect of two or three months there did not delight him.

“There is not a soul to speak to in the place,” he said to Warrington. “I can’t stand old Portman’s sermons and pompous after-dinner conversation. I know all old Glanders’s stories about the Peninsular war. The Claverings are the only Christian people in the neighbourhood, and they’re not to be at home before Christmas, my uncle says; besides, Warrington, I want to get out of the country. Whilst you were away—confound it—I had a temptation, from which I’m very thankful to have escaped, and which I count that even my illness came very luckily to put an end to.”

And here he narrated to his friend the whole Vauxhall affair.

Warrington listened gravely. Putting moral delinquency aside, he was very glad Arthur had escaped a danger that might have made his whole life wretched—and which certainly would have occasioned the wretchedness and ruin of the other party.

“And your mother,” Warrington added, “and—and your friends—what pain it would have been to them!”

“Not a word to my mother!” Arthur cried, alarmed as if he heard, not the postman, but the judge. “She would never get over it. An esclandre of that sort would kill her, I do believe. And the best way—when a danger of that sort menaces—is not to face it, but to turn one’s back on it and run.”

“And were you very much smitten?” Warrington asked.

“Hm!” said Arthur, with the knowing air of a young man who would like to be thought a veteran in affairs of the heart. “She dropped her h’s, but she was a dear little girl.”

Poor Clarissas of the world—poor little girls with their unguarded hearts and their unguarded spelling—if you could but hear how the Lovelaces speak of you when you are not present; if you could but see your tender little letters pulled from a case like cigars and handed round for amusement, you would be less eager to write, and far less eager to believe. There is a sort of baseness that is not complete unless it boasts; and the man who betrays your honour is, nine times out of ten, eager to betray your secret too.

“It’s hard to fight, and it’s easy to fall,” Warrington said gloomily. “And as you say, Pendennis, when danger like this is imminent, the best way is to turn your back on it and run.”

After this discourse—upon which Arthur would have been eloquent enough a month earlier—the talk returned to travel. Arthur pressed Warrington to come with them. Warrington was part of the family now—part of the cure. Arthur declared he should not have half the pleasure without him.

But George said no. He could not go. He must stay and take Arthur’s place at home.

“That’s needless,” Arthur urged; “Shandon’s back in London. I’m entitled to a holiday.”

“Don’t press me,” Warrington said. “I can’t go. I’ve particular engagements. I’m best at home. I’ve not got the money to travel—that’s the long and short of it—for travelling costs money, you know.”

This little obstacle fell on Arthur like a wet cloth. He mentioned it to his mother. Mrs. Pendennis was very sorry; Mr. Warrington had been exceedingly kind; but she supposed he knew best about his affairs. And then, no doubt, she reproached herself—quietly, as women do—for the selfish wish to carry her boy away and have him wholly to herself.

Could Helen have guessed that recovery is a kind of witchcraft—one which not only knits flesh back to bone, but stitches up old follies and sets them walking again? As Arthur’s pulse steadied and his appetite came creeping back (a spoonful of broth one day, a decent slice of toast the next, and presently that dangerous return of opinion about what the cook “ought” to have done), his unfortunate tenderness for little Fanny began to stir too, like yeast warming in a bowl.

Mrs. Pendennis never once pronounced the girl’s name. If you had offered her “Fanny” as a word upon a platter, she would have pushed it away as if it smelt of garlic in a drawing-room. Yet she watched her son with a vigilance that would have shamed a barnyard goose guarding her goslings: always looking down into her teacup, always turning a page, always somehow aware—by motherly instinct, by fear, by that quiet domestic clairvoyance—of every letter that came to the table.

Arthur, who had been forbidden (on the plea of “health,” which in families is the grand despotism) to fatigue himself with correspondence, still could not help that twitch of the heart which accompanies the sound of paper slid from an envelope. Each post brought a little tremor with it, like the first tap of a cook’s knife on the chopping-board before the onions begin to weep. He expected, daily, to see a small hand—one he would have known without ever having seen it—lying there among the bills and invitations. He half dreaded it; he half desired it; he could not have told you which. When it did not come, day after day, he was relieved in a way that vexed him, and vexed in a way that shamed him.

For there is a particular sort of pride in sentimental bankruptcy. A man does not like to shut up his shop with no announcement, no decent inventory of ruins. We loiter before we pull down the shutters; we hold mournful meetings of partners; we pawn a jewel—an excuse, a reminiscence, a last little lie—to keep the concern going another week. On the whole, Arthur was almost angry with Fanny for making the separation so clean. What! could she go down in that little storm of hers without even stretching out a hand and crying, “Help, Arthur?” Why, one expects a drowning person to splash and clutch: it flatters one’s sense of importance. Yet not everybody who ventures upon that voyage sinks; many are only ducked, and, sputtering, crawl ashore. The reader, who has observed Mr. Arthur Pendennis’s habits of self-preservation, may form an opinion as to which of these he was most likely to prove.

He was still too weak to walk far; he was treated like a choice soufflé that might collapse if the door were slammed. A drive alone was forbidden. But Helen could not keep watch on Mr. Warrington as well, nor had she authority over that gentleman’s legs when they chose to carry him to London.

Indeed, when business called him to town, she could not say “stay,” though a secret, selfish part of her may have wished him gone and kept gone. She checked the wish as soon as she recognised it (her conscience was a creature that never slept), and she received Warrington with the same melancholy kindness she gave to all who served her boy. Yet on the morning he set off, she divined—by some domestic omen, perhaps by the pitch of his voice, perhaps by the way he fastened his glove—that he was going to learn news of Fanny for Arthur.

Arthur himself had spoken with George. He had told him, more gravely than he meant, how the business began, how it ended, how it had frightened him. He was thankful—he said so—he had escaped. Warrington heartily said “Amen” to that, as a man says it over any hot pan he has not spilled into his lap. Arthur had no great wrong, he believed, to reproach himself with; yet if they parted (and part they must), he wished, at least, to breathe a God bless her, and hope she might remember him kindly.

He spoke with so much feeling that George—who had been the stern preacher of separation—began to suspect his friend’s cure was not as complete as his boasts. If the two met again, all the temptation would have to be fought over—like a sauce which separates the moment you turn your back, and must be coaxed together again at the very edge of boiling.

“It is hard to struggle, Arthur,” Warrington said, “and easy to fall. The best courage for us poor wretches is to run away from danger. I would not have been what I am now, had I practised what I preach.”

“And what did you practise, George?” Arthur cried, eager as a child prying into the locked spice-box. “I knew there was something. Tell us.”

“There was something that can’t be mended,” Warrington answered, and his voice, which could jest so readily, went dull. “It broke my fortunes early. I said I’d tell you some day—and I will—but not now. Take the moral without the fable, Pen. If you want to see a man wrecked against a rock he struck when a boy—look at me. So I warn you.”

While this sober counsel was being given in a quiet house, another kind of counsel—wetter, noisier, and delivered in brandy-and-water—was being taken nightly in London at a place with the amiable name of the Back Kitchen.

Mr. Huxter, the young surgeon from Saint Bartholomew’s, had written home to Clavering with vast importance about a fashionable club he attended, and about an Irish officer of distinction he met there, who had told him—among other news—the intelligence regarding Pendennis that Huxter had forwarded with such patriotic speed. The Back Kitchen, indeed, was one of those haunts where youth supposes it is tasting Life, chiefly by swallowing it in half-pints.

There, Captain Costigan—General Costigan, if you asked himself—was a standing dish. His brogue, his stories, his readiness to be drawn out, were the very oysters on which the young gentlemen fattened their mirth. Huxter, who possessed a natural genius for mimicking everything—actors, animals, corkscrews, and any human creature who offered a weakness to the stage—took especial delight in studying the honest old fellow. Sixpennyworth of brandy-and-water was the bait; Costigan swallowed it with the trusting simplicity of a trout; and then, under its warming influence, who so happy as he to sing his own triumphs? He could be produced, as if on command, fighting a jewel in the Phaynix; bowing to the Juke of York; feasting at his son-in-law’s teeble with the nobilitee; or—best of all, to the cruel audience—crying drunk, confidentially lamenting his daughter’s ingratichewd, and explaining how his grey hairs were hastening to a praymachure greeve. The landlord pardoned many foibles, seeing they brought many customers; and though it is not the proudest station for an old man, it must be recorded that Costigan had no notion his station was low. In his whiskied blood there was no black drop of malice, nor in his muddled brains any bitter resentment. Even his “cruel Emily” he would have forgiven with tears, if she would only have come. And what more can one say of a man’s charity than that he is ready to forgive the person who has done him every kindness—when he himself has been wrong the whole time?

Among the Back Kitchen wags there was a legend that Costigan made a mystery of his lodgings—either to escape duns or to cultivate romance. The landlord, being a gentleman of principle where other people’s privacy was concerned, refused to answer impertinent curiosity, saying he knew gentlemen only in his room, and once they paid their scores and walked out, his acquaintance with them ceased.

Costigan too, when “confidential,” was astonishingly evasive. Not because there was any grand secret—we, who have been more than once admitted to his apartments, know better—but because in the vicissitudes of his life he had often lodged in places where privacy was a comfort, and certain visitors would have been pain. Hence the legends multiplied. He slept in a watch-box, in a cab, in the Duke of York’s Column—Huxter inventing the wildest with the joyful cruelty of an imaginative young man.

One fine September morning—pink light on chimney-pots, shutters still asleep, Covent Garden smelling of damp vegetables and yesterday’s crushed herbs—Huxter, with the sticky palate of a night’s dancing at Vauxhall, stood at a coffee-stall, treating himself to a cup that was more soot than Mocha. He had paid his twopence—indeed, he had only eightpence left, or he would have ridden home in a cab like a gentleman of fortune—and as he sipped, he spied the General reeling down Henrietta Street, with a troop of hooting boys at his heels.

These were the city’s early birds: creatures who had slept under arches and rose betimes for breakfast and mischief. Cabmen and watermen at the stand knew the old man and made their comments; policemen looked after him with scorn and pity, warning off the boys. But scorn and pity are poor missiles against a skull lined with whisky. Costigan reeled along with glazed eyes, with just sense enough to know his beat homewards. How often had he gone to bed not knowing how he reached it? He woke and found himself there and asked no questions, as if each day’s disgrace were a dish cleared away before morning.

Huxter’s curiosity leapt like flame under fat. He followed.

Costigan dived down the alleys by Drury Lane Theatre, where gin-shops and oyster-shops and theatrical wardrobes lurk—places that in daylight look like kitchens after a feast, littered with the crumbs of glamour. The shopkeepers were asleep behind shutters; the dawn made a mockery of their chimneys. Through courts and passages Huxter tracked his prey, until they reached Oldcastle Street, where the gate of Shepherd’s Inn stands like a patient, ancient jaw waiting to swallow the needy.

Just as Costigan was within sight of home, a slice of orange-peel—London’s own little banana-skin comedy, though less genteel—slid beneath his heel. The General went down backwards with a thump that seemed to ring on the morning air, and for a moment even the street had the good manners to pause.

Huxter ran up, and while the old veteran gathered what dizzy sense he could from the pavement and the whisky, the young surgeon lifted him, examined him with that professional hand which is so brisk and so coldly kind, and offered to conduct him home.

Costigan refused at first, thickly insisting his lodgings were “hard by,” that he could reach them without difficulty. He shook off Huxter’s arm and made a rush, like a ship trying to tack alone. But he lurched so wildly that Huxter insisted, soothed him with cheerful doctorly lies, and got the old man’s dirty hand under what he called his “fin,” and guided him across the street.

At the ancient gate, decorated with the armorial bearings of the venerable Shepherd, Costigan stopped.

“Here ’tis,” he said, and tugged the bell. Old Mr. Bolton the porter came out scowling, grumbling as he did each morning when it was his turn to let in that disreputable early bird.

Costigan attempted a moment of genteel conversation. Bolton would not be baited.

“Don’t bother me,” said he. “Go to your hown bed, Capting, and don’t keep honest men out of theirs.”

So the Captain tacked across the square and reached his staircase, Huxter close behind like a conscientious shadow. Costigan had a key; Huxter, being steadier, inserted it; and there was no need to wake little Mr. Bows—the old musician—who had only lately fallen asleep.

Huxter helped disrobe the tipsy patient, ascertained no bones were broken, and got him to bed. He applied compresses and water to the knee and shin that had suffered; and with the trousers, which had encased the limbs, the General had torn himself pretty badly. At that age, with that habit of body, such wounds do not heal briskly. Inflammation followed; pain and fever sat down like unpleasant guests who would not be turned out. For some days Costigan lay ill.

Mr. Huxter undertook the case with tremendous confidence—the kind young men always have when the world has not yet punished them for it—and treated it with becoming skill. He came day after day; he consoled the old fellow with lively rattle and conversation for the lack of society without which Costigan withered. And he gave special instructions to the nurse about the quantity of whisky the patient was to take—instructions which, as the poor man could not reach the bottle himself, could not easily be broken.

At the bedside waited Bows; waited Mrs. Bolton; and when she was able, waited little Fanny. They made the old warrior as comfortable as their narrow means and broader good nature could manage.

Thus Huxter—whose affable manners made him quickly familiar wherever he fell, and whose “refinement” was not of that sort which shrinks from garrets—became intimate in Shepherd’s Inn with the garrets and the porter’s lodge alike. He thought he had seen Fanny somewhere; he felt sure he had; but it is no wonder he could not place her. The poor little thing never chose to tell him where they had met; and he had seen her at a time when his own judgment of faces and morals was clouded with drink and music. Besides, Fanny was altered. Three weeks of fever, agitation, passion, and despair had worn her as a knife wears down a wooden spoon. Her head was bowed now; her face pale and wan; and many a time those sad eyes had searched the postman’s as he came into the Inn, while her heart sank as he passed away.

When her father’s accident happened, she was almost glad—yes, glad—to have something to do besides ache. Duty is a kind of gruel for sorrow: thin fare, perhaps, but it keeps one alive. She stirred her father’s gruel, and if a tear dropped in, she stirred again and swallowed it down as part of the portion. Courage, little Fanny: if everybody died outright of that complaint, undertakers would have the merriest year of all.

Whether from compassion or from delight in Costigan’s talk, Huxter now found occasion to visit two or three times a day at least. And if none of the porter’s lodge family were at the bedside, the young doctor always had “particular directions” to deliver at their own door. He was kind in that bustling, boyish way: he brought toys for the children; apples and brandy-balls; he brought a mask and frightened them, until even pale Fanny smiled for a moment. He called Mrs. Bolton “Mrs. B.” and was so familiar, facetious, and impudent with her that she liked him the better for it—quite different, she declared, from that “aughty, artless beast,” Mr. Pendennis, whom she now vowed she never could abear.

It was from Mrs. Bolton, who was free with her opinions as with her tongue, that Huxter soon learned what illness was preying upon little Fan, and what Mr. Pendennis had done. Her account, it may be imagined, was not entirely impartial. From her story, one would think Arthur had used the most persevering and flagitious artifices, made solemn promises by the dozen like a pastrycook turning out pies, and then broken them all with the ease of snapping a biscuit.

Huxter, already sore under Arthur’s contempt, was quite ready to believe everything unfavourable. Yet—oddly—he did not write home to Clavering as he had before, with this delicious scandal. He announced in a letter to his brother-in-law that that “nice young man,” Mr. Pendennis, had nearly died of fever and would no doubt delight Clavering by recovering. He mentioned an “interesting case of compound fracture”—an officer of distinction—that kept him in town. But as for Fanny Bolton, he wrote not a word. No more than Pendennis himself had written a word.

O mothers at home, with your quiet parlours and your belief in the wholesome candour of your boys—how much do you think you know?

With Bows, however, Huxter had no reason to keep silent; and a short time after talking with Mrs. Bolton, he spoke his mind to the musician. He described Pendennis as a confounded conceited blackguard, and declared he would punch his impudent head the moment the fellow was well enough to stand like a man.

Then Bows, on his side, told his version: how the meeting of Arthur and Fanny had been no contrivance of Arthur’s but a blunder of the old Irishman now in bed with a broken shin; how Pendennis had acted with manliness and self-control; how Mrs. Bolton was an idiot; and he repeated the conversation he himself had had with Arthur, and the sentiments the young man had uttered.

Perhaps this narrative pricked Huxter with a twinge of conscience. He owned frankly he had been wrong in his judgment, and withdrew his project of punching Mr. Pendennis’s head—an act of mercy, no doubt, to Pendennis, but also to Huxter’s own knuckles.

Yet the cessation of hostility did not diminish Huxter’s attentions to Fanny; and here unlucky Mr. Bows began to mark them with his habitual jealousy and bitterness.

“I have but to like anybody,” he thought, “and somebody is sure to come and be preferred to me. It has been so since I was a lad—until now, that I am sixty. What can such a man expect but to be laughed at? It is for the young to succeed and be happy, not for old fools like me. I’ve played second fiddle through life,” he said, with a bitter laugh. “How can I suppose the luck is to change after it has gone against me so long?”

Few would have seen reason for jealousy in that pale, grief-stricken child; she received Huxter’s good-natured efforts kindly enough, laughed now and again at his antics with her little sisters, then sank back quickly into her dejection—a dejection that ought to have proved to Bows there was no room in her heart for any new preference, had he been able to see clearly.

But he could not. Fanny, by a miserable twist of pain, attributed Pendennis’s silence to Bows’s interference. She hated him for it. She treated him with constant cruelty and injustice; turned from him when he spoke; loathed his clumsy consolations. A hard life had Mr. Bows—hard, and with a cruel return for his regard.

When Warrington came to Shepherd’s Inn as Arthur’s ambassador, he asked for Mr. Bows’s apartments—as if the matter had been arranged beforehand between principal and agent in this delicate negotiation. He did not even catch sight of Miss Fanny when he stopped at the gate and made his inquiry. Directed upstairs, he found Bows tending the patient; the musician came out from the sick-room to receive him. They had known one another previously, and shook hands with sufficient cordiality.

After some preliminary talk, Warrington said he had come from Arthur Pendennis and his family to thank Bows for his attendance at the beginning of Arthur’s illness, and for his kindness in hastening into the country to fetch the Major.

Bows answered it was his duty; he had scarcely expected to see the young gentleman alive again when he went; he was glad Mr. Pendennis had recovered and had his friends around him.

“Lucky are they who have friends, Mr. Warrington,” said he. “I might be up in this garret and nobody would care for me—nobody mind whether I was alive or dead.”

“What! not the General, Mr. Bows?” Warrington asked.

“The General likes his whisky-bottle more than anything in life,” Bows replied. “We live together from habit and convenience; and he cares for me no more than you do. What is it you want to ask me, Mr. Warrington? You ain’t come to visit me, I know. Nobody comes to visit me. It is about Fanny, the porter’s daughter, you are come—I see that—very well. Is Mr. Pendennis, now he has got well, anxious to see her again? Does his lordship the Sultan propose to throw his ’andkerchief to her?

“She has been very ill, sir, ever since the day when Mrs. Pendennis turned her out of doors—kind of a lady, wasn’t it? The poor girl and myself found the young gentleman raving in a fever, knowing nobody, with nobody to tend him but his drunken laundress. She watched day and night by him. I set off to fetch his uncle. Mamma comes and turns Fanny to the right-about. Uncle comes and leaves me to pay the cab. Carry my compliments to the ladies and gentleman, and say we are both very thankful—very.
