“Why, a countess couldn’t have behaved better. And for an apothecary’s lady, as I’m given to understand Mrs. Pendennis was—I’m sure her behaviour is most uncommon aristocratic and genteel. She ought to have a double-gilt pestle and mortar to her coach.”

Major Pendennis, being a man who could keep a promise as neatly as he kept a crease, contrived to satisfy his own conscience and, what was harder work, to soothe poor Helen’s. He let her understand—by nods, hems, and the kind of sentences that end before they begin—that all connexion between Arthur and the odious little gatekeeper had been clipped off as clean as parsley with a sharp knife. Helen might sleep, then, without fearing that her son would be carried off by imprudence, or—worse in her creed—by a degrading marriage.

Arthur’s mind, too, after the first smart to his vanity (that tender part of a gentleman which bruises easiest), recovered its ease in a very comfortable reflection: Miss Fanny was not going to die of love for him; the world would not be scandalized by any tragic sequel; no inconvenient child, no lawsuit, no melodrama would pop out from behind the scenes. The luckless little episode, like an overdone cutlet, might be forgotten, and the family might travel.

So they went; and Pen, now styled by himself a “rentier,” and by his passport a personage of weight and height, set forth “voyageant avec Madame Pendennis and Mademoiselle Bell,” with George Warrington, “particulier, age de 32 ans, taille 6 pieds (Anglais),” and other marks by which men are reduced at frontiers to hair-colour and inches. They procured passports at Dover; crossed to Ostend; and made their way with that leisurely gravity which English people assume on the Continent as if time were a waiter they had hired—through Bruges and Ghent to Brussels and the Rhine.

It is not our business to paint every gable and canal; but it would have been worth any man’s while to observe how the very air altered to Helen Pendennis. In those old cities it was not only the bells that were strange, but the silences between the bells; the hush in a beguinage court where a woman’s step seemed an impertinence; the sudden roar of an organ that shook the ribs like thunder in a kitchen-flue; the muttering of prayers in a tongue that was not her own, and therefore sounded to her like conspiracies. The Catholic ceremonies, with their black veils and outstretched arms, their candles and incense, their crowned images bowing to crowned images, pressed on her mind as heavily as a hot lid on a boiling pot. Barefooted friars padding along the stones; confessionals like dark cupboards; theatres open on Sundays; dancers scraping merrily while her conscience sat rigid as a pew—all these novelties bewildered the simple country lady more than any foreign grammar.

At their lodgings, when the young men came back from drive or promenade, they found always the same domestic little altar of habit: Helen’s books of devotion laid open on the table; Laura reading softly, and breaking off as they entered, as if their footfall had startled the very words. The late troubles connected with Arthur had shaken Helen cruelly. Laura, tender as bread fresh from the oven and as watchful, too, observed every change in her friend’s face—those faint blanchings and flushes which tell you, if you have any eyes, that the heart is being pinched somewhere out of sight. Pen, for his part, was constant in the outward duties; he waited upon his mother with affectionate punctuality. Yet between them a cloud hung always, as if a curtain had been drawn across a familiar room. Helen’s love yearned towards him; and yet there was a secret—an anguish, almost a rage—at finding recesses in her son’s heart which she dared not enter. She sickened thinking of the sacred boyish days when Arthur had poured into her lap his triumphs and childish griefs as naturally as a child pours milk into a bowl; when home had been his nest; before selfishness, nature, fate—call the cook by what name you please—had sent him forth to range, to sing his own song, to seek his own mate.

Once Laura, with that honest feminine logic which goes straight to the wound, said, “If Pen had loved me as you wished, I should have gained him; but I should have lost you, mamma—I know I should. And I like you to love me best. Men do not know what it is to love as we do, I think.” Helen sighed, and agreed to the last part, protesting against the first; and perhaps Miss Laura was right in both. Love with a man is too often an hour snatched between taxes and tailors; with a woman it is breakfast, dinner, supper, and the long night between—the continual simmering of the heart, which never is taken off the fire.

Old Major Pendennis had only escorted them to the water’s edge, placed them aboard as one stows away valuables in a carriage, and handed over the chief charge of the expedition to Warrington. The Major himself was bound for a brief visit to the house of a great man—an establishment where pheasants were still plentiful though the best partridges had been thinned off, and where the guests were of that rich variety which makes a man feel important for having eaten the soup in their presence. At Stillbrook, where the Marquis of Steyne entertained dukes, foreigners of note, and illustrious statesmen, the Major disported with comfort and deserved complacency. It warmed his heart to see his own name peeping in the Morning Post among the distinguished company, as modestly as a truffle among mushrooms.

He was invaluable in such a house: full of anecdotes that young men laughed at, and with, in the smoking-room; obsequious with the ladies in the morning as if each were a duchess and he her waiting-maid; a guide who could point out the best view of the lake, the place where the old road went before the new bridge, the very patch in the wood where old Lord Lynx discovered Sir Phelim O’Neal on his knees before her ladyship—etcetera, etcetera. He knew lodge-keepers and gardeners by name, the number of domestics who sat down in the housekeeper’s room, and how many ate in the servants’ hall; he had a word for everybody and a little against everybody. A country-house is a great kitchen of talk: the Major was an excellent cook at the dish.

Nor was he ill-pleased, perhaps, at having shifted the Continental command to Warrington, thus keeping that stiff gentleman in the service of the ladies—a servitude George undertook willingly for his friend’s sake, and for the sake of a society that daily grew more delightful. Warrington, being a good German scholar, gave Miss Laura lessons; she drank in new words as eagerly as she would have sipped a new sauce. Pen, for his part, was too weak or lazy to resume his own studies, preferring the more practical education of sleep and meals.

Warrington acted as courier and interpreter; saw baggage in and out of inns and boats; managed money matters; marshalled the little troop. He found the English church, and, if Mrs. Pendennis and Miss Laura were inclined that way, walked with proper decorum beside them. He walked by Mrs. Pendennis’s donkey when she took her evening excursions, as gravely as if she rode in state; he procured ‘Galignani’; he invented comfortable seats under lime-trees where the bath guests paraded after dinner while the Kursaal band played—music floating and settling in the leaves, making the air itself seem to have a tune.

Many a fine-whiskered Prussian or French dandy, in town for Trente-et-quarante, cast longing glances at the fresh-coloured English girl beside the pale widow, and would have liked to whirl her at a galop or waltz. But Laura seldom appeared in the ballroom, except once or twice when Pen vouchsafed to walk with her; and Warrington, that rough diamond, had not been polished by any dancing-master, and did not know how to waltz—though he would have liked to learn, if the partner had been Laura. Such a partner! Psha—what had a stiff bachelor to do with partners? What was he about, drinking in pleasure with the risk of lonely longing to follow? Yet he stayed on.

You might have taken him for the widow’s son from his constant care; or for an adventurer sniffing after fortune—though the truth is most people, generously or meanly, are occupied about Number One. Warrington devoted himself to Helen; Helen devoted herself to Pen; and Pen, at this present period, devoted himself chiefly to himself—except for a real disquiet about his mother’s health. They sat together often; they did not talk much; the cloud stood between them.

Every day Laura looked for Warrington and welcomed him with frank eagerness. He found himself talking to her as he had not known he could. He performed small gallantries and afterwards stared at himself as if surprised to find his own hands had done them. He began to look blankly in the glass at the crow’s-feet round his eyes, at the streaks of white in his hair, at the intrusive silver bristles in his grim blue beard. He looked at the young bucks—the tight-waisted Germans, the capering Frenchmen with lacquered moustaches, the English dandies, Pen among them, calm and insolent in their languor—and envied each some excellence of youth. And every night, when he quitted the little circle, he went away with greater reluctance, and felt his own lodging emptier than before.

The widow could not help seeing his attachment. She understood now why Major Pendennis (always a tacit enemy of her darling project) had been so eager Warrington should be of their party. Laura frankly owned her enthusiastic regard for him; and Arthur made no movement. He did not choose to see; or did not care to prevent; or actually encouraged it. Helen remembered his saying he could not understand how a man proposed to a woman twice. She was in torture—at secret feud with her own son—averse to Warrington, who was good and generous, and yet threatened her schemes; in doubt about Laura in a way she dared not name. No wonder the healing waters of Rosenbad did her little good, and that Doctor von Glauber found the poor lady made no progress.

Meanwhile Pen recovered rapidly; slept with immense perseverance twelve hours out of the twenty-four; ate huge meals with the steady application of a man repaying the body for its late inconvenience; and by the end of a couple of months had almost regained his former strength and weight.

After they had passed about fifteen days at Rosenbad, a letter came from Major Pendennis announcing his speedy arrival; and soon after, the Major himself appeared, accompanied by Morgan—faithful valet and indispensable apparatus. The old gentleman travelled in a jaunty, juvenile costume; from the back you might have taken him for one of those slim youths whom Warrington was beginning to envy. Only when he moved did you see that Time had weakened his knees, and unkindly interfered with the action of the natty varnished boots which still pinched his toes.

Rosenbad that autumn was full of magnates. The Major read the strangers’ list with gratification on the night of his arrival, delighted to find acquaintances among the great folks, and promised himself the honour of presenting his nephew to a German Grand Duchess, a Russian Princess, and an English Marquis. Pen was not averse: he liked polite life and its splendours. That very evening the Major, leaning on Arthur’s arm, made his appearance in the Kursaal and lost or won a napoleon or two at Trente-et-quarante. He did not play to lose or win, he said; he played because other folks played; and betted his napoleon with an air of virtue.

He pointed out Russians and Spaniards gambling for heaps of gold, denouncing their eagerness as sordid and barbarous. An English gentleman should play where the fashion is to play, but should not elate or depress himself at the sport. He told of seeing his friend the Marquis of Steyne, when Lord Gaunt, lose eighteen thousand at a sitting and break the bank three nights running at Paris without ever showing emotion. “That’s what I call being an English gentleman, Pen, my dear boy,” the old man said, warming as he prattled—“the great manner only remains with us and with a few families in France.”

And as Russian Princesses passed whose reputations had long ceased to be doubtful, and damaged English ladies with their faithful attendant for the time being, the Major, with mischievous relish, poured into Pen’s ear wonderful particulars, seasoning the evening with scandal as cooks pepper a stew. Egad, he felt young again, he said, as Princess Obstropski—rouged, grinning, her enormous chasseur behind her carrying her shawl—smiled, recognized, and accosted him. He remembered her in ’14, when she was an actress on the Boulevard; and how Obstropski, the Emperor Alexander’s aide-de-camp (a man of talents, who knew a great deal about the Emperor Paul’s death, and was a devil to play), married her. The Major asked leave to call upon her, and to present his nephew, Mr. Arthur Pendennis; and pointed out half a dozen other famous personages whose histories were, to his mind, equally “satisfying.”

What would poor Helen have thought, had she heard those tales, or known to what sort of people her brother-in-law was presenting her son? She had passed once through the room where the green tables were prepared, and the croaking croupiers called their fatal Rouge gagne and Couleur perd. She had shrunk out as from a kitchen full of smoke and knives, imploring Pen, extorting a promise on his word of honour that he would never play. The pandemonium that stifled her amused the worldly old veteran and made him younger. Her right was not his right; his food was her poison. Men breathe different airs and call them health.

To Pen’s credit, he kept his promise honestly, and stoutly told his uncle he would abide by it.

Yet the Major’s arrival cast a damp upon at least three in the little party: upon Laura, who had anything but respect for him; upon Warrington, whose manner showed involuntary haughtiness and contempt; and upon timid Helen, who dreaded his interference with her desperate projects. Indeed, the Major, unknown to himself, was the bearer of tidings that would bring about a catastrophe in their affairs.

Pen and the two ladies had apartments in the town; Warrington lodged hard by; the Major, as befitted his dignity, took quarters at one of the great hotels—the Roman Emperor or the Four Seasons—where two or three hundred gamblers, pleasure-seekers, and invalids sat down daily and over-ate themselves at an enormous table-d’hôte, as if trying to drown their maladies in gravy.

On the morning after the Major’s arrival, Pen went dutifully to pay respects. He found his uncle’s sitting-room set out by Morgan with the precision of a well-ordered pantry: hats brushed, coats laid out; despatch-boxes, umbrella-cases, guidebooks, passports, maps—all trim as if still in Jermyn Street. Even the medicine bottle was fresh filled from the pharmacien’s; and the old fellow’s prayer-book lay ready, for he made a point of appearing at the English church in every place he honoured with a stay. “Everybody did it,” he said; “every English gentleman did it,” and he would as soon have omitted the national worship as he would have failed to call upon an ambassador.

The Major had gone to take one of Rosenbad’s famous baths and was not yet finished with his toilette when Pen arrived. The elder called out cheerily from the inner room. Presently Morgan came in bearing a little packet addressed to Pen—Mr. Arthur’s letters and papers, brought from his chambers in London. Chiefly numbers of the Pall Mall Gazette, which Mr. Finucane, in his benevolent tyranny, thought his collaborateur would like to see. The papers were tied together; the letters lay in an envelope in Finucane’s handwriting.

Among them was a little note addressed, as a former one had been, to “Arther Pendennis, Esquire.” Arthur opened it with a start and a blush, and read with a keen pang of interest, sorrow, and regard. Fanny Bolton wrote that she had come to his house and found he was gone—gone away to Germany without leaving a word for her, or an answer to her last letter, in which she prayed but for one word of kindness—or the books he had promised her in happier times, before he was ill, which she would like to keep in remembrance. She would not reproach those who had found her at his bedside in the fever, when he knew nobody, and who had turned the poor girl away without a word. She thought she should have died of that; but Doctor Goodenough had kindly tended her and kept her life, though perhaps the keeping of it was of no good. She forgave everybody; and as for Arthur, she would pray for him forever. When they cut off his hair, she had made so free as to keep one little lock for herself, and that she owned; and might she still keep it, or would his mamma order that that should be given up too? She was willing to obey him in all things, and could not but remember that once he was so kind—oh, so good and kind—to his poor Fanny.

When Major Pendennis came out fresh and smirking from his toilette, he found Arthur with the note before him and a savage anger on his face. The elder gentleman started, surprised.

“What news from London, my boy?” he asked rather faintly. “Are the duns at you, that you look so glum?”

“Do you know anything about this letter, sir?” Arthur asked.

“What letter, my good sir?” said the other, dry at once, and perceiving what had happened.

“You know what I mean—about, about Miss—about Fanny Bolton—the poor dear little girl,” Arthur broke out. “When she was in my room—was she there when I was delirious? I fancied she was—was she? Who sent her out of my chambers? who intercepted her letters to me? Who dared to do it? Did you do it, uncle?”

“It’s not my practice to tamper with gentlemen’s letters, or to answer damned impertinent questions,” Major Pendennis cried, trembling with indignation. “There was a girl in your rooms when I came up at great personal inconvenience, daymy—and to meet with a return of this kind for my affection to you is not pleasant, by Gad, sir—not at all pleasant.”

“That’s not the question, sir,” Arthur said hotly—“and I beg your pardon, uncle. You were, you always have been, most kind to me: but I say again, did you say anything harsh to this poor girl? Did you send her away from me?”

“I never spoke a word to the girl,” the uncle said. “I never sent her away from you, and know no more about her, and wish to know no more about her, than about the man in the moon.”

“Then it’s my mother that did it,” Arthur broke out. “Did my mother send that poor child away?”

“I repeat I know nothing about it, sir,” the elder said testily. “Let’s change the subject, if you please.”

“I’ll never forgive the person who did it,” said Arthur, bouncing up and seizing his hat.

The Major cried, “Stop, Arthur, for God’s sake, stop;” but before the words were well out Arthur had rushed from the room. The next minute the Major saw him striding rapidly down the street towards home.

“Get breakfast,” said the old fellow to Morgan; and he wagged his head and sighed as he looked from the window. “Poor Helen—poor soul! There’ll be a row. I knew there would: and begad all the fat’s in the fire.”

When Pen reached home he found only Warrington in the ladies’ drawing-room, waiting their arrival to conduct them to the room where the little English colony held their Sunday church. Helen and Laura had not appeared yet; Helen was ailing, and her daughter was with her. Pen’s wrath was too hot to stand over like porridge; it must boil over at once.

He flung Fanny’s letter across the table to his friend. “Look there, Warrington,” he said. “She tended me in my illness; she rescued me out of the jaws of death; and this is the way they have treated the dear little creature. They have kept her letters from me; they have treated me like a child, and her like a dog, poor thing! My mother has done this.”

“If she has,” Warrington said quietly, “you must remember it is your mother.”

“It only makes the crime the greater, because it is she who has done it,” Pen answered. “She ought to have been the poor girl’s defender, not her enemy: she ought to go down on her knees and ask pardon of her. I ought! I will! I am shocked at the cruelty which has been shown her. What? She gave me her all, and this is her return! She sacrifices everything for me, and they spurn her.”

“Hush!” said Warrington. “They can hear you from the next room.”

Our poor widow—who had been turned into a sort of saintly house-ghost long before she had any official right to the character—had ordered, with Martha of Fairoaks for minister and laughing heresy-monger, a little feast in honour of Major Pendennis’s arrival. Martha, who could roast a joint as if she were settling a lawsuit, and who considered German domestic economy a kind of Protestant witchcraft, had marched through the simple household with that air of a woman who knows where the nutmeg is kept and therefore fears no man.

The table was laid with modest bravery: a fowl browned to the exact shade of respectable hypocrisy, potatoes that broke open with a soft steam-sigh, and a jug of ale that sang—if you listened closely—more faithfully than many a hired violin. The house itself had its own music: the tick of the clock in the passage, the faint crackle of coals, the wind nosing at the panes, and, under all, the country silence—so different from London’s iron coughing and cart-rattle, where even a sparrow must shout to be heard. If peace were a broth, Fairoaks had been simmering it all day.

Only the Major and his two younger friends sat down to it; for Helen sent word that she was too unwell to dine at their table, and Laura stayed with her. The Major did nearly all the eating with his tongue, and, being a man who could carve conversation as neatly as he carved poultry, did not perceive—or did not choose to perceive—the gloom that sat between Pen and Warrington like an extra guest who had not been invited but would not go away.

It was evening before Helen and Laura came into the sitting-room. Helen entered leaning upon Laura, keeping her back to the waning light, so that Arthur could not at first see how pale and worn she was. Her step had that careful, floating uncertainty which belongs to people who are not quite sure whether they are walking on a floor or on a prayer. She went straight to Pen—whom she had not seen during the day—put her arms about his shoulders, and kissed him with a tenderness that was all the more piercing because it was almost wordless. Laura, as if she had handed over a fragile dish, withdrew to the other side of the room.

Pen felt, rather than saw, how his mother trembled. Her hand, when she lifted it to his forehead, was clammy and cold, like a cloth dipped in water and wrung out too soon. She clung to him piteously. And this very spectacle of misery—Heaven help the young, who are so often cruelest when they are most wounded—only sharpened something sour and fiery in him. He scarcely returned her kiss. The look with which he met the appeal of her eyes was hard.

“She persecutes me,” he thought, “and now she comes to me with the air of a martyr.”

“You look very ill, my child,” she said. “I don’t like to see you look in that way.” And she tottered to the sofa, still holding one of his passive hands in her thin, cold fingers, as a drowning creature holds a plank.

“I have had much to annoy me, mother,” Pen said, his breast throbbing.

At the sound of his voice, Helen’s heart began to beat with such terror that she sat almost dead and speechless. Warrington, Laura, and the Major all remained breathless; each knew by the stillness—by that hush that has its own terrible acoustics—that the storm was about to break.

“I have had letters from London,” Arthur continued; “and one that has given me more pain than I ever had in my life. It tells me that former letters of mine have been intercepted and purloined away from me;—that—that a young creature who has shown the greatest love and care for me, has been most cruelly used by—by you, mother.”

“For God’s sake stop,” cried Warrington. “She’s ill—don’t you see she is ill?”

“Let him go on,” said the widow faintly, and would not look away from her son’s face, as though truth—even when it is a knife—were better than ignorance.

“Let him go on and kill her,” Laura cried, springing to Helen’s side. “Speak on, sir, and see her die.”

“It is you who are cruel,” Pen broke out, more savage because his heart—soft at the core—revolted at the injustice of the suffering he seemed to inflict. “It is you who are cruel, who attribute all this pain to me: it is you who are cruel with your wicked reproaches, your wicked doubts of me, your wicked persecutions of those who love me,—yes, those who love me, and who brave everything for me, and whom you despise and trample upon because they are of lower degree than you. Shall I tell you what I will do,—what I am resolved to do, now that I know what your conduct has been?—I will go back to this poor girl whom you turned out of my doors, and ask her to come back and share my home with me. I’ll defy the pride which persecutes her, and the pitiless suspicion which insults her and me.”

“Do you mean, Pen, that you—” Helen began, with eager eyes and outstretched hands, as if she would catch at the sentence and pull it into a different meaning; but Laura, like a nurse stopping a patient from rising, whispered fiercely, “Silence—hush, dear mother,” and Helen hushed. Savagely as Pen spoke, she was only too eager to hear what more he would say. “Go on, Arthur—go on, Arthur,” she murmured, almost swooning as she spoke.

“By Gad, I say he shan’t go on, or I won’t hear him, by Gad,” the Major thundered, trembling with wrath. “If you choose, sir, after all we’ve done for you—after all I’ve done for you myself—to insult your mother and disgrace your name by allying yourself with a low-born kitchen-girl, go and do it, by Gad,—but let us, ma’am, have no more to do with him. I wash my hands of you, sir—I wash my hands of you. I’m an old fellow—I ain’t long for this world. I come of as ancient and honourable a family as any in England, by Gad, and I did hope, before I went off the hooks, by Gad, that the fellow that I’d liked, and brought up, and nursed through life, by Jove, would do something to show me that our name—yes, the name of Pendennis, by Gad, was left undishonoured behind us; but if he won’t, dammy, I say, amen. By G—, both my father and my brother Jack were the proudest men in England, and I never would have thought that there would come this disgrace to my name,—never—and—and I’m ashamed that it’s Arthur Pendennis.”

Here the old fellow’s voice broke into a sob—rough as a rasp on mahogany—yet more moving for its very awkwardness; it was the second time Arthur had drawn tears from those wrinkled lids.

That sound—like a cracked bell in the dusk—stopped Pen’s anger as if a hand had been laid upon his shoulder. He ceased pacing. Laura remained at Helen’s sofa. Warrington, who had watched like a man standing by a kitchen fire that threatens to flare up into the curtains, spoke at last; and his deep voice, tremulous in the twilight, carried an emotion that silenced the room more effectually than the Major’s oaths.

“Will you let me tell you something about myself, my kind friends?” he said. “You have been so good to me, ma’am—so kind to me, Laura—I hope I may call you so sometimes—my dear Pen and I have been such friends that I have long wanted to tell you my story, such as it is, and would have told it earlier but that it is a sad one and contains another’s secret. However, it may do good for Arthur to know it—it is right that every one here should. It will divert you from thinking about a subject which, out of a fatal misconception, has caused a great deal of pain to all of you. May I please tell you, Mrs. Pendennis?”

“Pray speak,” was all Helen said; and indeed she scarcely heeded him at first, her mind clutching at Pen’s words with a terrified hope that his threatened act might mean what she wished it to mean.

Warrington poured himself a bumper of wine—its rich, dark scent rising like a memory of better hours—and drank it off, as if fortifying himself for a confession.

“You all of you know how you see me,” he began, “a man without a desire to make an advance in the world: careless about reputation; living in a garret and from hand to mouth, though I have friends and a name, and, I daresay, capabilities of my own that would serve me if I had a mind. But mind I have none. I shall die in that garret most likely, and alone. I nailed myself to that doom in early life.

“Shall I tell you what it was that interested me about Arthur years ago, and made me inclined towards him when first I saw him? The men from our college at Oxbridge brought up accounts of that early affair with the Chatteris actress—about whom Pen has talked to me since—and who, but for the Major’s generalship, might have been your daughter-in-law, ma’am. I can’t see Pen in the dark, but he blushes, I’m sure; and I dare say Miss Bell does; and my friend Major Pendennis, I dare say, laughs as he ought to do—for he won. What would have been Arthur’s lot now had he been tied at nineteen to an illiterate woman older than himself, with no qualities in common between them to make one a companion for the other—no equality, no confidence, and no love speedily? What could he have been but most miserable? And when he spoke just now and threatened a similar union, be sure it was but a threat occasioned by anger.”

He paused, and in that pause the room’s small sounds returned: coal settling in the grate; the clock continuing its indifferent work; outside, a bird’s late note—thin and solitary—cutting through the domestic hush like a needle through cloth.

“You must give me leave to say, ma’am,” he went on, “that the anger was very natural on his part. For after a generous and manly conduct—let me say, who know the circumstances well—most generous and manly and self-denying (which is rare with him), he has met from some friends of his with a most unkind suspicion, and has had to complain of the unfair treatment of another innocent person, towards whom he and you all are under much obligation.”

Helen tried to rise; Warrington, seeing it, asked gently, “Do I tire you, ma’am?”

“Oh no—go on—go on,” she said, with a sudden brightness, delighted, and he continued.

“I liked him, you see, because of that early history of his… and because I like a man—if you will pardon me for saying so, Miss Laura—who shows that he can have a great unreasonable attachment for a woman. That was why we became friends—and are all friends here—for always, aren’t we?” he added in a lower voice, leaning toward her, “and Pen has been a great comfort and companion to a lonely and unfortunate man.

“I am not complaining of my lot. Up in my garret, where you left the flowers, and with my old books and my pipe for a wife, I am pretty contented, and only occasionally envy other men whose careers are more brilliant, or who can solace their ill fortune by what Fate and my own fault have deprived me of—the affection of a woman or a child.”

A sigh came from somewhere near him in the dark; a hand moved out toward Warrington as if drawn by instinctive human kindness—and was withdrawn at once. For our excellent female world, trained to blush at its own natural heart, will often snatch back its tenderness as though it had accidentally shown an ankle. Modesty, having slapped friendship on the knuckles, retreated again, and Warrington resumed.

“My fate is such as I made it, and not lucky for me or for others involved in it.

“I, too, had an adventure before I went to college; and there was no one to save me as Major Pendennis saved Pen. Pardon me, Miss Laura, if I tell this story before you. It is as well that you all should hear my confession. Before I went to college, as a boy of eighteen, I was at a private tutor’s, and there, like Arthur, I became attached—or fancied I was attached—to a woman of a much lower degree and a greater age than my own. You shrink from me—”

“No, I don’t,” Laura said; and this time the hand went out resolutely and laid itself in Warrington’s, as one lays a steadying palm on a man who is about to carry a hot pan.

“She was a yeoman’s daughter in the neighbourhood,” Warrington said, his voice faltering. “I fancied—what all young men fancy. Her parents knew who my father was, and encouraged me with all sorts of coarse artifices and scoundrel flatteries about their house. To do her justice, I own she never cared for me, but was forced into what happened by the threats and compulsion of her family. Would to God that I had not been deceived: but in these matters we are deceived because we wish to be so, and I thought I loved that poor woman.

“What could come of such a marriage? I found, before long, that I was married to a boor. She could not comprehend one subject that interested me. Her dulness palled upon me till I grew to loathe it. And after some time of a wretched, furtive union—I must tell you all—I found letters somewhere (and such letters they were!) which showed me that her heart, such as it was, had never been mine, but had always belonged to a person of her own degree.

“At my father’s death, I paid what debts I had contracted at college, and settled every shilling that remained to me in an annuity upon—upon those who bore my name, on condition that they should hide themselves away, and not assume it. They have kept that condition, as they would break it, for more money. If I had earned fame or reputation, that woman would have come to claim it: if I had made a name for myself, those who had no right to it would have borne it; and I entered life at twenty, God help me—hopeless and ruined beyond remission. I was the boyish victim of vulgar cheats; and perhaps it is only of late I have found out how hard—ah, how hard—it is to forgive them.”

He drew breath, as if he had come up from under water.

“I told you the moral before, Pen; and now I have told you the fable. Beware how you marry out of your degree. I was made for a better lot than this, I think: but God has awarded me this one—and so, you see, it is for me to look on and see others successful and others happy, with a heart that shall be as little bitter as possible.”

“By Gad, sir,” cried the Major, suddenly in high good-humour, as if glad to find himself again on ground where he could be jocular without bleeding, “I intended you to marry Miss Laura here.”

“And, by Gad, Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pound,” Warrington returned.

“How d’ye mean a thousand? it was only a pony, sir,” replied the Major simply, at which Warrington laughed; and even in that dark room laughter sounded like a lamp being lit.

Helen, meanwhile, was so delighted—so seized by the relief of discovering that her terrible suspicion had been wrong—that she started up and cried, “God bless you—God for ever bless you, Mr. Warrington,” kissed both his hands, and ran to Pen and fell into his arms.

“Yes, dearest mother,” he said, holding her, and in a noble rush of tenderness—so late, so needed—embraced and forgave her. “I am innocent, and my dear, dear mother has done me a wrong.”

“Oh yes, my child, I have wronged you—thank God, I have wronged you!” Helen whispered. “Come away, Arthur—not here—I want to ask my child to forgive me—and—and my God, to forgive me; and to bless you, and love you, my son.”

He led her, tottering, into her room and closed the door, while the three spectators—Laura with tears, Warrington with a quiet, stricken look, and the Major with his face turned away as if it had suddenly begun to rain indoors—stood in pleased silence at the reconciliation.

Ever after, ever after, Arthur remembered the accents of that voice faltering sweetly in his ear; the sacred eyes beaming with affection unutterable; the quiver of the fond lips smiling mournfully. In his best moments, and in his trials, and in success or in sorrow, that mother’s face would return to him like a light remembered—not a light of noise and show, but of pity and purity—as he saw it that night, when she yet lingered with him, and seemed, ere she quite left him, an angel transfigured and glorified with love.

The moon had risen; Arthur recollected afterwards how it struck along the floor and found his mother’s sweet pale face, as if Heaven had sent a last lamp into the room. Their talk—his, chiefly, for she scarcely could speak—was more tender and confidential than it had been for years. He became again the frank boy of her early days. He told her the story that had caused her such pain: his struggle to fly from temptation; his gratitude that he had overcome it. He never would do the girl wrong—never—or wound his own honour, or his mother’s pure heart. That threat, to return, had been uttered in a moment of exasperation; he repented it. He never would see Fanny Bolton again.

But Helen—so quickly humbled, so quickly loving—said yes, he should. It was she who had been proud and culpable. She wished to give Fanny something. She begged her dear boy’s pardon for opening the letter. She would write to the girl—if—if she had time. Was it not natural, she asked, that she should love her Arthur? And again she kissed him and blessed him.

As they were talking, the clock struck nine. Helen reminded him how, when he was a little boy, she used to go up to his bedroom at that hour and hear him say Our Father. And once more—oh, once more—the young man fell down at his mother’s knees and sobbed out the prayer which has gone, in so many dialects and broken voices, through so many centuries; each mouth shaping the same words, yet no two hearts tasting them alike. As he spoke the last petition, Helen’s head sank down upon his, and her arms closed round him, and together they repeated “for ever and ever” and “Amen.”

A little time after—perhaps a quarter of an hour—Laura heard Arthur’s voice call from within, “Laura! Laura!” She rushed in instantly and found him still on his knees, holding his mother’s hand. Helen’s head had sunk back; her face was quite pale in the moonlit room. Pen looked round, scared with a ghastly terror.

“Help, Laura, help!” he cried. “She’s fainted—she’s—”

Laura screamed and fell by Helen’s side. The shriek brought Warrington and Major Pendennis and the servants running. The sainted woman was dead. The last emotion of her soul had been joy—joy to be henceforth unchequered and eternal. The tender heart beat no more; it was to have no more pangs, no more doubts, no more griefs. Its last throb was love; and her last breath a benediction.

The melancholy party bent their way speedily homewards. Helen was laid by her husband’s side at Clavering, in the old church where she had prayed so often. For a while Laura went to stay with Dr. Portman, who read the service over his dear departed sister amidst his own sobs and those of the little congregation gathered round her tomb.

There were not many who cared for her, or spoke of her when she was gone. People had known of her scarcely more than they know of a nun in a cloister. A few words ran among the cottagers whom her bounty had fed as quietly as a daily loaf; a little talk moved from house to house at Clavering—one saying she died of a complaint in the heart; another wondering what property she left; a third debating whether Arthur would let Fairoaks or live in it, and expecting he would not be long getting through his money. By the next market-day the village noise—always hungry, always clattering—had rolled on to fresher gossip, and her name, like a soft word spoken in a fading dialect, was in danger of vanishing from common speech.

But if the world forgets, the few remember. The great blank she left was in Laura’s heart, to whom her love had been everything. “I am glad that she gave me her blessing before she went away,” Warrington said to Pen. And Arthur—humbled, astonished at so much affection—hardly dared ask Heaven to make him worthy of it, though he felt as if a saint were interceding for him.

All Helen’s affairs were found in perfect order, her little property ready for transmission to her son, in trust for whom she held it. Papers in her desk showed she had long been aware of her complaint—one of the heart—and knew it would suddenly remove her; and there was a prayer in her handwriting asking that her end might be, as it was, in the arms of her son.

Laura and Arthur talked over her sayings. Laura remembered them with a devotion that was like keeping a family recipe safe when the language it was written in has begun to die; Arthur, to his shame, thought how much greater Helen’s love had been for Laura than his own attentions ever were. He referred himself entirely to Laura to know what Helen would have wished: which poor persons she would have liked to relieve, what remembrances to send.

They packed up the vase which Helen, in her gratitude, had destined to Dr. Goodenough, and duly sent it to that kind physician; a silver coffee-pot she used was sent to Portman; a diamond ring, with her hair, was given, with affectionate greeting, to Warrington.

It was a hard day for Laura when she went over to Fairoaks first, to the little room she had occupied and which was hers no more; and then to the widow’s own blank chamber where those two had passed so many beloved hours. There were the clothes in the wardrobe; the cushion where she prayed; the chair at the toilette; the glass that would no more reflect that dear sad face. The house had changed its music: the silence was no longer restful, but hollow—like a kitchen after the fire has been raked out, when you can still smell yesterday’s broth yet cannot warm your hands.

After she had been there a while Pen knocked, led her downstairs to the parlour, made her drink a little wine, and said, “God bless you,” as she touched the glass. “Nothing shall ever be changed in your room,” he said. “It is always your room—it is always my sister’s room. Shall it not be so, Laura?” And Laura said, “Yes.”

Among Helen’s papers was found a packet marked, in her own hand, “Letters from Laura’s father,” and Arthur gave it to her. They were the old letters that had passed between the cousins in those early days before either married. The ink was faded; the tears dried out; the grief healed now whose bitterness they recorded; the friends doubtless united whose parting on earth had cost such cruel pangs. Laura learned, for the first time fully, what tie had bound her so tenderly to Helen: how faithfully her more-than-mother had cherished her father’s memory, how truly she had loved him, how meekly resigned him.

There was one legacy of Helen’s that Laura could not know of: her wish to make some present to Fanny Bolton. Pen remembered it, and wrote to Fanny, putting his letter under an envelope to Mr. Bows and requesting that gentleman to read it before he delivered it—an arrangement by which propriety, like a sour but vigilant housekeeper, insisted on tasting the message before the girl received it.

“Dear Fanny,” Pen wrote, “I have to acknowledge two letters from you, one of which was delayed in my illness”—(he found the first in his mother’s desk after her death, and it gave him a strange pang to read it then)—“and to thank you, my kind nurse and friend, who watched me so tenderly during my fever. And I have to tell you that the last words of my dear mother, who is no more, were words of goodwill and gratitude to you for nursing me: and she said she would have written to you, had she had time—that she would like to ask your pardon if she had harshly treated you—and that she would beg you to show your forgiveness by accepting some token of friendship and regard from her.”

He ended by saying that his friend George Warrington, Esq., of Lamb Court, Temple, was trustee of a little sum, the interest of which would be paid to her until she became of age, or changed her name; and that she would always be remembered by her grateful friend, A. Pendennis.

The sum was small enough, though enough to make a little heiress of Fanny Bolton. Her parents were appeased. Her father said Mr. P. had acted quite as the gentleman—though Bows growled that to plaster a wounded heart with a banknote was an easy kind of sympathy. And poor Fanny—whatever her father’s calculations, whatever Mr. Bows’s cynicism—felt only too clearly what the letter was in truth: not a gift, but a farewell.

London had taken its annual holiday on Epsom Downs—the great sacrament of English idleness, where dukes, draymen, debutantes, debtors, and dogs all agree, for one day, to breathe the same chalky air and call it liberty. The very turf seemed to hum, not with pastoral bees, but with the multitudinous racket of civilisation at play: wheels crunching gravel, whips cracking like pistol-shots, brass bands braying, hawkers yelping, corks popping, and a perpetual storm of “Hullo!” that battered the ear as factory-hammers do—only here the noise was considered “fine sport,” and paid for accordingly.

In a handsome open carriage—well horsed, well varnished, and well conscious of it—sat Mrs. Bungay of Paternoster Row, blazing in ribbons and new silk like an altar dressed for a feast-day. Beside her, modest Mrs. Shandon wore that air of patient gentility which can endure both sun and patronage without melting. Bungay, having fortified himself with a luncheon that might have served a small parish, was at that moment madly attacking the “Sticks” hard by—shying, pitching, and perspiring until his bald crown shone as if it had been glazed for publication. Shandon wandered among the beer-stands and gipsies with that shambling gait which seems always to be looking for a friend and finding a creditor. Finucane hovered about the ladies like a lively mosquito that had learned manners.

Up came Mr. Archer, bowing with the air of a man who had known everybody famous since Adam first took briefs.

“Yonder’s the Prime Minister,” Archer said, arranging the course with his finger as if Epsom were a map he had corrected. “His lordship just advised me to back Borax; but I confess I like Munmeer’s action better. And there—look in the Grand Stand—there sits the Chinese Ambassador with the Mandarins of his suite. Fou-choo-foo—my most intimate friend—brought me letters from the Governor-General of India. I was very kind to him for some time. His chopsticks were laid at my table whenever he chose to dine.”

Mrs. Bungay’s eyes grew large as sovereigns.

“But, would you believe it,” Archer continued, dropping his voice with the relish of a man opening a tureen, “he brought his own cook; and one day, when I was out, and the Ambassador was with Mrs. Archer in our garden eating gooseberries—of which the Chinese are passionately fond—the beast of a cook, seeing my wife’s dear little Blenheim spaniel (a present from the Duke of Marlborough himself—whose ancestor’s life Mrs. Archer’s great-great-grandfather saved at Malplaquet), seized the poor little devil, cut his throat, skinned him, and served him up—stuffed with forced-meat—in the second course.”

“Law!” said Mrs. Bungay, as if the syllable were a lid hastily clapped on a saucepan of horror.

“You may fancy my wife’s agony!” Archer cried, warming to his kitchen-tragedy. “The cook came screaming upstairs and told us she’d found poor Fido’s skin in the area—just after we’d all tasted the dish. Mrs. Archer never would speak to the Ambassador again—never; and upon my word he has never been to dine with us since. The Lord Mayor, who did me the honour to dine, liked the dish very much; and, eaten with green peas, it tastes rather like duck.”

“You don’t say so, now!” exclaimed Mrs. Bungay, who loved a scandal as much as she loved a sauce—provided both were rich.

“And observe that lady in blue seated by his Excellency,” Archer went on. “That is Lady Flamingo. They say she is going to marry him and return to Pekin. She is squeezing her feet down on purpose. But she’ll only cripple herself. My wife has the smallest foot in England—wears a child’s shoe; but what is that to a Chinese lady’s foot, Mrs. Bungay?”

At this moment Mrs. Bungay, whose curiosity moved swiftly from ambassadors to annuities, leaned forward.

“Who is that carriage as Mr. Pendennis is with, Mr. Archer? He and Mr. Warrington was here jest now. He’s ’aughty in his manners, that Mr. Pendennis, and well he may be, for I’m told he keeps tip-top company. ’As he ’ad a large fortune left him, Mr. Archer? He’s in black still, I see.”

“Eighteen hundred a year in land,” Archer said promptly, as if reading from a ledger in his head, “and twenty-two thousand five hundred in the Three-and-a-half per Cents. That’s about it.”

“Law! why, you know everything, Mr. A.!”

“I happen to know, because I was called in about poor Mrs. Pendennis’s will,” Archer replied. “Pendennis’s uncle, the Major, seldom does anything without me; and as he is likely to be extravagant, we’ve tied up the property, so that he can’t make ducks and drakes with it.—How do you do, my lord?—Do you know that gentleman, ladies? You have read his speeches in the House; it is Lord Rochester.”

“Lord Fiddlestick,” sang out Finucane from the box. “Sure it’s Tom Staples of the Morning Advertiser, Archer.”

“Is it?” Archer said, simply. “Well, I’m very short-sighted, and upon my word I thought it was Rochester.”

Then he nodded at a man with a double opera-glass, and at another tall figure, distributing titles as a cook ladles gravy: “That’s Lord John; and the tall man—don’t you know him?—is Sir James.”

“You know ’em because you see ’em in the House,” growled Finucane.

“I know them because they are kind enough to allow me to call them my most intimate friends,” Archer returned, without a blush. “Look at the Duke of Hampshire—pattern of a fine old English gentleman! Never misses the Derby. ‘Archer,’ he said to me only yesterday, ‘I have been at sixty-five Derbies! first appeared on the field on a piebald pony when I was seven, with my father, the Prince of Wales, and Colonel Hanger; missing only two—one with the measles at Eton, and one in the Waterloo year, when I was with my friend Wellington in Flanders.’”

“And who is that yellow carriage with the pink and yallow parasols, that Mr. Pendennis is talking to, and ever so many gentlemen?” asked Mrs. Bungay, scenting fresh history as a cat scents cream.

“That is Lady Clavering of Clavering Park—next estate to my friend Pendennis. That’s the young son and heir on the box; he’s awfully tipsy, the little scamp! And the young lady is Miss Amory—Lady Clavering’s daughter by a first marriage—uncommonly sweet upon my friend Pendennis; but I’ve reason to think he has his heart fixed elsewhere. You have heard of young Mr. Foker—the great brewer, Foker, you know—he was going to hang himself for Miss Amory who refused him, but was cut down just in time by his valet, and is now abroad under a keeper.”

“How happy that young fellow is!” sighed Mrs. Bungay, who always thought tragedy improved a gentleman’s position. “Who’d have thought, when he came so quiet and demure to dine with us, three or four years ago, he would turn out such a grand character! Why, I saw his name at Court t’other day, and presented by the Marquis of Steyne and all; and in every party of the nobility his name’s down as sure as a gun.”

“I introduced him a good deal when he first came up to town,” Archer said, “and his uncle, Major Pendennis, did the rest. Hallo! There’s Cobden here, of all men in the world! I must go and speak to him. Good-bye, Mrs. Bungay. Good morning, Mrs. Shandon.”

And off he went, leaving behind him a faint scent of self-importance, as of truffles shaved over nothing.

An hour earlier, in another quarter of the Downs, a different England was shouting itself hoarse from the battered roof of an old stage-coach—Wheeler’s drag from the Harlequin’s Head—where shabby raffs stamped and hallooed as the Derby swept by like a gust of living colour. The air there was thick with dust, beer-fumes, hot bread, cheap cigar smoke, and that peculiar metallic tang which always rises from a crowd that has been yelling.

As the horses flashed, each “choice spirit” bellowed what he hoped to be the winner, for hope is a beverage Englishmen drink more greedily than ale.

“The Cornet!”
“It’s Muffineer!”
“Blue sleeves!”
“Yallow cap! yallow cap! yallow cap!”

Then the signal fluttered out; Podasokus had won; and one gentleman on the roof sprang up as if winged by fortune.

“Hurray, hurray!” he roared, coming down again so heavily that the boards cracked under his joy. “Podasokus is the horse! Supper for ten, Wheeler, my boy. Ask you all round, of course, and damn the expense.”

“Thank you—congratulate you, Colonel—sup with you with pleasure,” cried the others, smiling like knives; and whispered with affectionate vigilance, “The Colonel stands to win fifteen hundred, and he got the odds from a good man too.”

Immediately each began to eye his neighbour as if friendship were a kind of pickpocketing; for a man who has won money at Epsom must be guarded like a pie cooling on a windowsill—everyone passing feels entitled to a slice.

At yet another part of the course—more modest, and in truth more shabby, though with a certain domestic bravery about it—stood cab No. 2002, lately hired from the Strand. A gentleman and two ladies had established themselves on and about it, turning the cab into a little travelling parlour with luncheon. The younger lady, perched on the box, looked so fresh, so rosy, and so prettily alive that dandies strolling from the grand carriages drifted toward her as moths drift toward a candle—only these moths were scented, and the candle wore a straw bonnet with a pink ribbon.

The party’s meal was a very English poem written in grease and foam: lobster salad—its vinegar and pepper pricking the nose; pale bitter ale, rising in a froth that smelled of warmed grain; and for the elder lady, brandy-and-water that deepened her complexion to match the very shell of the lobster she cracked and devoured with cheerful resolution. Every bite had its sound: the snap of shell, the crunch of a pickle, the gurgle of ale poured and swallowed, the ceaseless surrounding roar of the Downs like surf against a sea-wall.

Their escort—Mr. Sam—had been inexhaustible from the very start, flinging “chaff” from the moving cab as if it were confetti. He had shouted jokes into drags full of solemn guardsmen; he had saluted donkey-chaises and dustmen; he had peppered the roadside with volleys of wit into school windows, maidservants’ casements, nurses’ arms, babies’ faces, dissenting maiden ladies’ disapproving noses. The cab had filled with spoils from the Sticks: pincushions, wooden apples, backy-boxes, Jack-in-the-boxes, little soldiers—small, cheap objects that nonetheless clinked with the music of a holiday won.

He had even hauled up a gipsy with a tawny child to tell fortunes; and the only cloud over the party’s sunshine came when the gipsy informed the young lady that she must beware a fair man false to her; that she had had a bad illness; and that she would find a man who would prove true. The words, no doubt, had been ladled out to a hundred carriages like the same thin soup; yet they fell into this cab with a particular plop.

The girl coloured; her mother and Mr. Sam exchanged looks of quick intelligence, like cooks who know a flavour before the taster speaks.

Now, making his way alone through the crush—observing, as was his habit, the human kitchen of Epsom, where vanity and appetite were stirred in the same pot—Arthur Pendennis came suddenly upon cab No. 2002 and the little group around it.

The moment the young lady on the box saw him, she started and turned pale. Her mother reddened as if the brandy had leapt straight to her cheeks. The gay Mr. Sam, so late triumphant, took on a fierce suspicious look, and his eyes travelled savagely from Fanny Bolton—yes, it was she—to Pendennis advancing.

Arthur, too, looked dark upon perceiving Mr. Samuel Huxter in company with his old acquaintances. His suspicion was that kind of morality which is half alarm and half self-importance; like a person who, hearing a strange noise in the pantry, imagines at once a thief—and feels virtuously awake for having heard it.

Fanny’s heart began to patter. Huxter’s fists, sunk in the pockets of his paletot, clenched themselves as if they were tools ready for surgery of a coarser kind. Mrs. Bolton began to talk with all her might, and with that wondrous volubility which can plaster over any crack in the wall.

“Lor! I’m so ’appy to see you, Mr. Pendennis! and how well you do look! and we was talking of you only jest before, wasn’t we, Fanny? And if this is the famous Epsom races they make such a talk about, I don’t care, for my part, if I never sees ’em again. And how is Major Pendennis? and that kind Mr. Warrington, as brought your kindness to Fanny? I never shall forget it—never. And Mr. Warrington is so tall, he almost broke his ’ead against our lodge door. You recollect him a-knocking of his head—don’t you, Fanny?”

While her mother chattered, what a whole pantry of memories must have burst open in Fanny’s mind: dear times and dreary ones; sad struggles; lonely griefs; and then those shy consolations that come after shame, like cold tea offered when dinner is spoiled. There stood the man she had been ready to die for ten months before—dandified now, supercilious, in mourning black as if grief were a fashion he wore correctly: black crape on his white hat, jet buttons in his shirt-front, a pink in his coat (given, no doubt, by some other hand), lavender gloves sewn with black, the neatest cane, the shiniest boot. And there was Sam Huxter beside him—no gloves, great Blucher boots, tobacco on his breath, and the general air of a fellow who had met both the road and the cigar too intimately. How could the eye not measure? How could the heart not compare?

Fanny, after taking Pendennis’s offered hand with a little twittering pressure, managed at last to say, in a voice that shook like a spoon in a cup:

“This is Mr. Samuel Huxter whom you knew formerly, I believe, sir; Mr. Samuel, you know you knew Mr. Pendennis formerly—and—and, will you take a little refreshment?”

Those few tremulous words did more than all Mrs. Bolton’s speeches: they told Arthur, plainly enough, that there was nothing secret here to fear—no guilty ambush, no melodrama of betrayal. A load slid from his mind; perhaps another from his heart. The frown melted off his face, and his good-nature came out like sunshine after a passing shower.

“I am very thirsty,” he said, “and I will be glad to drink your health, Fanny; and I hope Mr. Huxter will pardon me for having been very rude the last time we met—when I was so ill and out of spirits that indeed I scarcely knew what I said.”

And he held out the lavender-coloured glove in amity.

The dirty fist in Huxter’s pocket had to unarm itself and come forth. The young surgeon felt, as he laid it in Pendennis’s hand, how hot and how black his own was; it left marks upon the glove—he saw them. A part of him longed to snatch his hand back, to clench it, to dash it into that easy smiling face, and see—here, on the Downs, with Fanny and all England looking on—which man was the better. But the moment passed; manners, those invisible policemen of society, blew their whistle.

Arthur took a glass—content to drink after the ladies—filled it with frothing lukewarm beer, and declared it delicious. He drank cordially to the health of the party, as if the bitter, warmed by sun and crowd, were a nectar of reconciliation.

While he spoke on in an engaging way, a young lady in a shot dove-coloured dress passed by him, leaning on the arm of a stalwart gentleman with a military moustache. Her parasol was white lined with pink; her boots the prettiest dove-colour that ever stepped over dust. She clenched a tiny fist and gave Pendennis a mischievous side-look as she went; her moustachioed companion burst into a jolly laugh, and lifted his hat to the ladies on the cab.

You should have seen Fanny Bolton’s eyes follow that dove-coloured figure—as if she were tasting a new dish and trying to guess every ingredient.

“What a beautiful creature!” Fanny said. “What a lovely dress! Did you remark, Mr. Sam, such little, little hands?”

“It was Capting Strong,” said Mrs. Bolton, craning. “And who was the young woman, I wonder?”

“A neighbour of mine in the country—Miss Amory,” Arthur said. “Lady Clavering’s daughter. You’ve seen Sir Francis often in Shepherd’s Inn, Mrs. Bolton.”

And with that small information, Fanny’s mind—quick as a cook improvising a feast out of scraps—built a whole romance in three volumes: love, faithlessness, splendid marriage at St. George’s, Hanover Square, broken-hearted maid; and Mr. Sam Huxter was not the hero of it—poor Sam, who by now had produced an exceedingly rank Cuba cigar and was smoking it under Fanny’s little nose, as if tobacco could fog away a rival.

After that “confounded prig Pendennis” (as Sam named him in the silent court of his own jealousy) joined and left the party, the day altered. The sun seemed less bright, the sky less blue; the Sticks had no attraction; the bitter beer turned hot and undrinkable. The world had changed its seasoning. Sam had peas and a tin pea-shooter in his pocket for the homeward route, but forgot them until another wag on the return fired a volley into Sam’s sad face; upon which salute, after a few oaths of surprised profanity, he burst into a savage and sardonic laugh.

Fanny, meanwhile, was charming all the way home. She coaxed, and snuggled, and smiled; she laughed pretty laughs and admired everything. She took out the darling little Jack-in-the-boxes and was so obliged to Sam—turning the cheap toys into treasures by sheer warmth of manner, as some people can make even a crust seem like cake.

When they reached home, and Mr. Huxter, still dark of brow, was taking a frigid leave, she burst into tears and called him a naughty unkind thing.

Then jealousy, which had hardened him, melted in a moment. He caught her in his arms, swore she was an angel and he a jealous brute; owned he was unworthy of her and had no right to hate Pendennis; and asked her—implored her—to say once more that she—

That she what? The end of the question and Fanny’s answer were spoken by lips so near together that no bystander could catch the words. Mrs. Bolton only said, brisk as a matron breaking up a scullery flirtation, “Come, come, Mr. H.—no nonsense, if you please; and I think you’ve acted like a wicked wretch, and been most uncommon cruel to Fanny, that I do.”

When Arthur left cab No. 2002, he went up the hill to pay his respects to the yellow carriage with the pink and yellow parasols—where the dove-coloured author of Mes Larmes had returned to her mamma’s side. There sat Lady Clavering, taking in homage as naturally as she took in air. Indefatigable old Major Pendennis waited upon her, installed in the back seat as if born to be an appendage to quality. The box was in possession of young Hopeful—Lady Clavering’s heir—under the care of Captain Strong, who looked as if he could manage at once a horse, a boy, and a dozen fools.

Around the carriage clustered a knot of dandies and men of a certain fashion—military bucks, young rakes of public offices, fellows who prided themselves on being “men’s men” rather than ladies’—and they offered Miss Amory bets, banter, and that species of knowing talk which calls itself wit and is often only insolence. They pointed out “who was on the course,” and the “who” was not always a name a young lady should be invited to taste.

Pen had to push his way through these gentlemen to come near Miss Blanche Amory, who beckoned him with little signals as pretty and commanding as the flick of a fan.

“Je l’ai vue,” she said. “Elle a de bien beaux yeux; vous êtes un monstre!”

“Why monster?” Pen laughed. “Honi soit qui mal y pense. My young friend yonder is as well protected as any young lady in Christendom. She has her mamma on one side, her prétendu on the other. Could any harm happen to a girl between those two?”

“One does not know what may or may not arrive,” Miss Blanche said lightly, in French, “when a girl has the mind, and when she is pursued by a wicked monster like you. Figure to yourself, Major, that I come to find Monsieur, your nephew, near to a cab, by two ladies, and a man—oh, such a man!—and who ate lobsters, and who laughed, who laughed!”

“It did not strike me that the man laughed,” Pen said; “and as for lobsters, I thought he would have liked to eat me after the lobsters. He shook hands with me and gripped me so that he bruised my glove black-and-blue. He is a young surgeon. He comes from Clavering. Don’t you remember the gilt pestle and mortar in High Street?”

“If he attends you when you are sick,” Miss Amory continued, “he will kill you. He will serve you right; for you are a monster.”

The perpetual recurrence of the word jarred upon Pen as a too-sweet syrup cloys the palate. She spoke of such matters too lightly. If he had been the monster she named, she would have received him just the same—with the same pretty laughter, the same careless flourish of words borrowed from another tongue, as if French made mischief less mischief by giving it a foreign label. His face fell.

“This is not,” he thought, “the way an English lady should speak or think. Laura would not speak in that way, thank God.”

“Of what are you thinking? Are you going to bouder me at present?” Blanche asked. “Major, scold your méchant nephew. He does not amuse me at all. He is as bête as Captain Crackenbury.”

“What are you saying about me, Miss Amory?” grinned Captain Crackenbury, a guardsman with the confidence of a man who has never been quiet a moment in his life. “If it’s anything good, say it in English, for I don’t understand French when it’s spoke so devilish quick.”

“It ain’t anything good, Crack,” said Crackenbury’s companion, Captain Clinker. “Let’s come away, and don’t spoil sport. They say Pendennis is sweet upon her.”

“I’m told he’s a devilish clever fellow,” sighed Crackenbury, with honest envy. “Lady Violet Lebas says he’s a devilish clever fellow. He wrote a work, or a poem, or something; and he writes those devilish clever things in the—in the papers, you know. Dammy, I wish I was a clever fellow, Clinker.”

“That’s past wishing for, Crack, my boy,” Clinker said. “I can’t write a good book, but I think I can make a pretty good one on the Derby. What a flat Clavering is! And the Begum! I like that old Begum. She’s worth ten of her daughter. How pleased the old girl was at winning the lottery!”

“Clavering’s safe to pay up, ain’t he?” asked Crackenbury.

“I hope so,” said his friend; and the two drifted off into the roaring, clinking, shouting tide toward the Sticks—where men spent money like water, and made water of their memories by the bucketful of beer.

Nearly a year—one of those years that look thin on a calendar and fat in recollection—had slid by since the little incident mentioned some pages ago; and Arthur Pendennis, like a man who has been simmering gently and is suddenly clapped into brisker boil, found himself altered in a number of particulars, external and internal.

For one thing, his mourning had done its duty and was dismissed. The black coat, which had hung about him like a public notice of private sorrow, was on the point of being exchanged for a blue one—blue cloth, bright facings, a tightness about the chest that obliges a gentleman to breathe shallowly and speak with decision. For another, he had flung off his wig, as a cook flings off an ill-fitting lid that keeps the steam from rising as it should. His own hair—thinner, certainly, like a sauce reduced beyond its first lavish promise—returned to public view; and there is no denying that the world likes a dish the better for believing it has not been warmed up.

And Arthur had the honour—an honour much insisted on by his uncle—of appearing at Court in the uniform of a Cornet of the Clavering troop of the ——shire Yeomanry Cavalry, being presented to the Sovereign by the Marquis of Steyne. It was one of those solemnities which are served with so much garnish that the meat beneath seems less important than the parsley. The Major would not hear of a year passing before this ceremony of gentlemanhood was gone through. “A young man,” implied the old gentleman, “must be trussed and browned in the proper fashion, and set before society with the right sauce, or the guests will turn to something else.”

He would have had his nephew belong to some club a shade more select than the Megatherium; and he announced everywhere his disappointment that the young man’s property had not turned out by any means so handsomely as he could have hoped, and was under fifteen hundred a year. Under fifteen hundred! The Major spoke of it as a butcher might speak of a joint that weighed less than promised: not inedible, certainly, but a disappointment to the eye and the appetite.

Yet in the world—where respect is measured with a merchant’s scales and often smells faintly of new money—that sum had a perfume of its own. Arthur’s publishers began to respect him much more than formerly; and even mammas—those keen-nosed providers who can detect a competence through a wall—were by no means uncivil. For if the pretty daughters were, naturally, to marry people of very different expectations, still Mr. Pendennis would be eligible for the plain ones. If the brilliant and fascinating Myra was to hook an earl, then poor little Beatrice, who had one shoulder higher than the other, must hang on to some boor through life; and why should not Mr. Pendennis be her support, her prop, her convenient literary ornament?

Accordingly, in the very first winter after his accession to his mother’s fortune, Mrs. Hawxby, at a country-house, caused her Beatrice to learn billiards from Mr. Pendennis, and would be driven by nobody but him in the pony-carriage—because he was literary, and her Beatrice was literary too; and then, with the brisk inconsistency of a hostess who offers you sweetmeats and afterwards calls you greedy, declared that the young man, under the instigation of his horrid old uncle, had behaved most infamously in trifling with Beatrice’s feelings.

The truth was less romantic, and therefore more true. The old gentleman, who knew Mrs. Hawxby’s character, and how desperately that lady would practise upon unwary young men—like a cook who will try to use yesterday’s scraps to make to-day’s grand entrée—had come to the country-house in question and carried Arthur out of the danger of her immediate claws, though not out of reach of her tongue. (Mrs. Hawxby’s tongue, once set clattering, was like a badly-oiled factory belt: it slapped, it whirred, it made noise enough for a whole parish, and did no useful work.)

The elder Pendennis would have had his nephew pass part of Christmas at Clavering, whither the family had returned; but Arthur had not the heart for that. Clavering was too near poor old Fairoaks; and Fairoaks was too full of sad recollections—rooms where silence fell as heavily as a wet cloth laid over a dish to keep it warm, and where the very floorboards seemed to remember footfalls in a dialect grief speaks best: the creak, the hush, the pause.

We have lost sight of the Claverings too, until their reappearance upon the Epsom race-ground, and must give a brief account of them in the interval. During the past year, the world had not treated any member of the Clavering family very kindly; and Lady Clavering—one of the best-natured women that ever enjoyed a good dinner, or made a slip in grammar—had had her appetite and good-nature sadly tried by constant family grievances. These are disputes of the sort that make the efforts of the best French cook unpalatable, and the most delicately-stuffed sofa-cushion hard to lie on. A man may sit before a pineapple, Muscatel grapes, and a bird that has been coaxed into tenderness by all the arts of the kitchen; but if the dining-room air is thick with murmurs and accusation, if knives scrape too sharply, if voices strike the ear like tin spoons against a pan, the very sweetness turns stale on the tongue.

“I’d rather have a turnip, Strong, for dessert, than that pineapple, and all them Muscatel grapes, from Clavering,” said poor Lady Clavering one day, looking at her dinner-table and confiding her grief to her faithful friend, “if I could but have a little quiet to eat it with. Oh, how much happier I was when I was a widow and before all this money fell in to me!”

The Clavering family had indeed made a false start in life, and had got neither conduct, nor position, nor thanks for the hospitalities which they administered; nor a return of kindness from the people whom they entertained. The success of their first London season was doubtful, and their failure afterwards notorious. Human patience, it was said, was not great enough to put up with Sir Francis Clavering. He was too hopelessly low, dull, and disreputable. You could not say what, but there was a taint about the house and its entourages—as though some sour jar had been kept too long in the pantry, and however one scoured the shelves the smell would cling.

Who was the Begum, with her money and without her h’s, and where did she come from? (In London, a dropped consonant is treated like a dropped fork: proof, apparently, that a person was never properly trained at table.) What an extraordinary little piece of conceit the daughter was, with her Gallicised graces and daring affectations, not fit for well-bred English girls to associate with! What strange people were those they assembled round about them! Sir Francis was a gambler, living notoriously in the society of blacklegs and profligates. Hely Clinker, who was in his regiment, said he not only cheated at cards, but showed the white feather.

What could Lady Rockminster have meant by taking her up? And after the first season, indeed, Lady Rockminster, who had taken up Lady Clavering, put her down. The great ladies would not take their daughters to her parties; the young men who attended behaved with the most odious freedom and scornful familiarity; and poor Lady Clavering avowed that she was obliged to take what she called “the canal” into her parlour, because the tip-tops wouldn’t come.

She had not the slightest ill-will towards “the canal”—the poor dear lady—nor any pride about herself, nor idea that she was better than her neighbour. She had taken, implicitly, the orders which her social godmother had given: she had been willing to know whom they knew, and ask whom they asked. The “canal,” in truth, was much pleasanter than what is called “society.” There was less shriek of varnished laughter, fewer metallic compliments that rang like coin dropped on a counter, less of that incessant fashionable din which is not sound but racket: a kind of moral steam-hammering that flattens thought. But, as was said, to leave a mistress is easy; to be left by her is cruel. One may give up society with relief—like stepping out of a room where the pianoforte is being murdered; but severe are the mortifications and pains if society gives up you.

One young man of fashion at least might have been expected to remain faithful amongst the faithless: Harry Foker, Esq. And indeed he was faithful; but he had not managed his fidelity with prudence. The unhappy passion at first confided to Pen became notorious and ridiculous to the town—rolled about in talk as a dried pea in a drum. It reached the ears of his weak and fond mother; and finally came under the cognisance of the bald-headed and inflexible Foker senior, who, when once roused, had the steady, grinding persistence of a mill driven by water: no persuasion could make it stop.

When Mr. Foker learned the news, there took place between him and his son a violent and painful scene, which ended in the poor little gentleman’s banishment from England for a year, with a positive order to return at the expiration of that time and complete his marriage with his cousin; or retire into private life and three hundred a year altogether, and never see parent or brewery more. So Mr. Henry Foker went away, carrying with him that grief and care which passes free at the strictest Custom-houses, and which proverbially accompanies the exile; and with this crape over his eyes, even the Parisian Boulevard looked melancholy to him, and the sky of Italy black. The songs of street-sellers—those small bright calls that ought to be as cheerful as the clink of plates in a warm kitchen—came to him muffled and distant, as though the world’s soundscape itself had turned its back.

To Sir Francis Clavering, that year was a most unfortunate one; and the events described in the last chapter came to complete the ruin of it. It was that year of grace in which—our sporting readers will remember—Lord Harrowhill’s horse (the young nobleman was classical, and named his stud out of the Iliad) when Podasokus won the Derby, to the dismay of the knowing ones who pronounced the winning horse’s name in various extraordinary ways, and who backed Borax, who was nowhere in the race.

Sir Francis, intimate with some of the most rascally characters of the turf and therefore always in possession of “valuable information,” had laid heavy odds against the winning horse, and backed the favourite freely; and the result of his dealings was, as his son stated to poor Lady Clavering, a loss of seven thousand pounds.

It was a cruel blow upon the lady, who had discharged her husband’s debts many times over; who had received as many times his oaths and promises of amendment; who had paid his money-lenders and horse-dealers; who had furnished his town and country houses; and who was called upon now instantly to meet this enormous sum—the penalty of her husband’s cowardly extravagance. If you have ever kept a household where the same leak returns each season—patched, sworn at, and patched again—you know that the weariness is not only in the purse, but in the ear: the drip, drip of the same excuse; the same clatter of fresh demands; the same harsh scraping sound when a creditor’s voice is dragged across the table like a knife across bone.

It has been described in former pages how the elder Pendennis had become the adviser of the Clavering family; and, in his quality of intimate friend of the house, had gone over every room of it, and even seen that ugly closet which we all of us have, and in which, according to the proverb, the family skeleton is locked up. About the Baronet’s pecuniary matters, if the Major did not know, it was because Clavering himself did not know them; and hid them from himself and others in such a hopeless entanglement of lies that it was impossible for adviser or attorney or principal to get an accurate knowledge of his affairs.

But concerning Lady Clavering, the Major was much better informed; and when the unlucky mishap of the Derby arose, he took upon himself to become completely and thoroughly acquainted with all her means, whatsoever they were. He was now accurately informed of the vast and repeated sacrifices which the widow Amory had made on behalf of her present husband. He did not conceal—and he had won no small favour from Miss Blanche by avowing it—his opinion that Lady Clavering’s daughter had been hardly treated, at the expense of her son, by her second marriage; and in his conversations with Lady Clavering he had fairly hinted that he thought Miss Blanche ought to have a better provision.
