We have said already that he had given the widow to understand he knew all the particulars of her early and unfortunate history—having been in India at the time when the painful circumstances occurred which ended in her parting from her first husband. He could tell her where to find the Calcutta newspaper containing the account of Amory’s trial; and he showed—she was not a little grateful for his forbearance—how, being aware all along of this mishap, he had kept all knowledge of it to himself, and been constantly the friend of her family. It is a curious power, that of holding a story in reserve: like possessing a spice so strong that a pinch could ruin a whole dish. The Major, who understood power-dynamics as neatly as a master-cook understands heat, never flung the spice in; he merely let the other person know it existed.

“Interested motives, my dear Lady Clavering,” he said, “of course I may have had. We all have interested motives; and mine, I don’t conceal from you, was to make a marriage between my nephew and your daughter.”

To which Lady Clavering—perhaps with some surprise that the Major should choose her family for an alliance with his—said she was quite willing to consent. But he, frank as a tradesman who will tell you your joint is small, continued: “My dear lady, my boy has but five hundred a year, and a wife with ten thousand pounds to her fortune would scarcely better him. We could do better for him than that, permit me to say; and he is a shrewd, cautious young fellow who has sown his wild oats now—who has very good parts and plenty of ambition—and whose object in marrying is to better himself.

“If you and Sir Francis chose—and Sir Francis, take my word for it, will refuse you nothing—you could put Arthur in a way to advance very considerably in the world, and show the stuff which he has in him. Of what use is that seat in Parliament to Clavering, who scarcely ever shows his face in the House, or speaks a word there? I’m told by gentlemen who heard my boy at Oxbridge, that he was famous as an orator, begad!—and once put his foot into the stirrup and mount him, I’ve no doubt he won’t be the last of the field, ma’am. I’ve tested the chap, and know him pretty well, I think. He is much too lazy, and careless, and flighty a fellow, to make a jog-trot journey and arrive, as your lawyers do, at the end of their lives; but give him a start and good friends and an opportunity, and take my word for it he’ll make himself a name that his sons shall be proud of.

“I don’t see any way for a fellow like him to parvenir, but by making a prudent marriage—not with a beggarly heiress—to sit down for life upon a miserable fifteen hundred a year—but with somebody whom he can help, and who can help him forward in the world, and whom he can give a good name and a station in the country, begad, in return for the advantages which she brings him. It would be better for you to have a distinguished son-in-law, than to keep your husband on in Parliament, who’s of no good to himself or to anybody else there; and that’s why I’ve been interested about you, and offer you what I think a good bargain for both.”

“You know I look upon Arthur as one of the family almost now,” said the good-natured Begum. “He comes and goes when he likes; and the more I think of his dear mother, the more I see there’s few people so good—none so good to me. And I’m sure I cried when I heard of her death, and would have gone into mourning for her myself, only black don’t become me. And I know who his mother wanted him to marry—Laura, I mean—whom old Lady Rockminster has taken such a fancy to, and no wonder. She’s a better girl than my girl. I know both. And my Betsy—Blanche, I mean—ain’t been a comfort to me, Major. It’s Laura Pen ought to marry.”

“Marry on five hundred a year! My dear good soul, you are mad!” Major Pendennis said—bringing down that verdict with the brisk finality of a man who has tasted the broth and knows it lacks salt. “Think over what I have said to you. Do nothing in your affairs with that unhappy husband of yours without consulting me; and remember that old Pendennis is always your friend.”

For some time previous, Pen’s uncle had held similar language to Miss Amory. He had pointed out to her the convenience of the match he had at heart, and was bound to say that mutual convenience was, of all things, the very best in the world to marry upon—the only thing.

“Look at your love-marriages, my dear young creature,” the Major would say, with that air of seasoned certainty which makes youth feel raw and underdone. “The love-match people are the most notorious of all for quarrelling afterwards; and a girl who runs away with Jack to Gretna Green constantly runs away with Tom to Switzerland afterwards. The great point in marriage is for people to agree to be useful to one another. The lady brings the means, and the gentleman avails himself of them. My boy’s wife brings the horse, and begad Pen goes in and wins the plate. That’s what I call a sensible union. A couple like that have something to talk to each other about when they come together. If you had Cupid himself to talk to—if Blanche and Pen were Cupid and Psyche, begad—they’d begin to yawn after a few evenings if they had nothing but sentiment to speak on.”

As for Miss Amory, she was contented enough with Pen as long as there was nobody better. How many other young ladies are like her? And how many love-marriages carry on well to the last? How many sentimental firms do not finish in bankruptcy? How many heroic passions do not dwindle down into despicable indifference, or end in shameful defeat?

These views of life and philosophy the Major was constantly inculcating to Pen, whose mind was such that he could see the right on both sides of many questions. He could comprehend the sentimental life—which was quite out of the reach of the honest Major’s intelligence—and could understand the practical life too; and he accommodated himself, or thought he could accommodate himself, to it. Thus it came to pass that during the spring succeeding his mother’s death he became a good deal under the influence of his uncle’s advice, and domesticated in Lady Clavering’s house; and in a measure was accepted by Miss Amory without being a suitor, and received without being engaged.

The young people were extremely familiar, without being particularly sentimental, and met and parted with each other in perfect good-humour—like guests who have dined together often, know each other’s habits, and neither expect nor offer surprises. “And I,” thought Pendennis, “am the fellow who eight years ago had a Grand passion, and last year was raging in a fever about Briseis!” Yes, it was the same Pendennis; and time had brought to him, as to the rest of us, its ordinary consequences—consolations, developments.

We alter very little. When we talk of this man or that woman being no longer the same person whom we remember in youth, and remark (of course to deplore) changes in our friends, we do not perhaps calculate that circumstance only brings out the latent defect or quality, and does not create it. The selfish languor and indifference of to-day’s possession is the consequence of the selfish ardour of yesterday’s pursuit; the scorn and weariness which cries vanitas vanitatum is but the lassitude of the sick appetite palled with pleasure; the insolence of the successful parvenu is only the continuance of the career of the needy struggler.

Our mental changes are like our grey hairs or our wrinkles—fulfilments of the plan of mortal growth and decay. That which is snow-white now was glossy black once; that which is sluggish obesity to-day was boisterous rosy health a few years back; that calm weariness, benevolent, resigned, disappointed, was ambition, fierce and violent, but a few years since, and has only settled into submissive repose after many a battle and defeat.

Lucky he who can bear his failure generously, and give up his broken sword to Fate the Conqueror with a manly and humble heart.

Are you not awestricken, friendly reader, who, taking the page up for a moment’s light reading, may lay it down perchance for a graver reflection—to think how you, who have consummated your success or your disaster, may be holding marked station or a hopeless and nameless place in the crowd; who have passed through how many struggles of defeat, success, crime, remorse, to yourself only known; who may have loved and grown cold, wept and laughed again, how often; to think how you are the same You, whom in childhood you remember, before the voyage of life began?

It has been prosperous, and you are riding into port, the people huzzaing and the guns saluting—and the lucky captain bows from the ship’s side, and there is a care under the star on his breast which nobody knows of; or you are wrecked, and lashed, hopeless, to a solitary spar out at sea: the sinking man and the successful one are thinking each about home, very likely, and remembering the time when they were children—alone on the hopeless spar, drowning out of sight; alone in the midst of the crowd applauding you.

Lady Clavering—our Begum, whose good heart had been stretched and stitched and stretched again like an old kitchen apron—began by declaring she would tie no more knots in the leaking money-bag of her husband’s honour. The last Derby business, that famous harvest of ruin, had brought home to her, as plainly as a scorched taste in the mouth, what manner of man Sir Francis was: not merely weak, but cunningly weak; not merely foolish, but industriously so. She vowed she would separate; she would keep what little of her fortune remained from being skimmed off like fat by a pack of gentlemen who lived on wagers and wine.

Sir Francis, after that fatal day’s transactions, was in the condition of a man who has swallowed an oyster-shell and insists it was a bonbon. He avoided everybody—his turf friends, because he owed them; his wife, because she had eyes and could count. When Lady Clavering asked next morning if he was in the house, the answer came back like a cold plate: he had not returned. He had sent a messenger to his valet, ordering clothes and letters to be forwarded.

Captain Strong—Chevalier Strong, as they called him, as if a title could season a character—knew the pattern of his principal’s cowardice. Sir Francis, when fortune tapped him on the shoulder, always began by bolting out the back door and hiding in the nearest hole that would take an “Mr. Francis.” And sure enough, a note arrived: Strong was implored to call at Short Hotel, Blackfriars, and ask for Mr. Francis there.

But London, like a well-trained kitchen, runs on whispers and the clatter of small errands. The boots at Mr. Short’s carried the message to Grosvenor Place and returned with a carpet-bag; the boots knew at once whose bag it was, in the same way a cook knows whose appetite has been in the pantry. He told the footman; the footman told the servants’ hall; the servants’ hall told Mrs. Bonner; and Mrs. Bonner told my lady. Thus, before dinner, every soul under that roof knew that Sir Francis Clavering, Baronet, was skulking at an inn on the Blackfriars Road, under a name as thin as watered broth. Sir Francis’s coachman, with that particular delight coachmen have in other men’s disasters, carried the news outward; it travelled by stables and street-corners to other households, and to Tattersall’s, where they began already to pack him off in conversation to the Levant, as if disgrace were a steamship.

Meanwhile the hall-table at Grosvenor Place, that altar of genteel correspondence, received offerings. Letters arrived in shoals, like fish drawn by a smell. Bills, too: the French cook’s account (which, had it been paid, might have perfumed a dozen dinners); tradesmen’s statements for meats and wines, and those other necessities of existence called ribbons and trimmings—Messrs. Finer and Gimcrack, and Madame Crinoline, who could make a bonnet look like a moral ruin. And in the same basket, like a private spice among public provisions, came Miss Amory’s personal little reckonings—no small pinch, those, but a liberal handful.

The afternoon after the Derby, Strong—having first visited his distracted friend at Short’s and found him performing tears into curacoa, like a child sweetening medicine—went, as was his custom, to Grosvenor Place to transact business. In Sir Francis’s study he found the documents laid out in rows: little white napkins of paper each covering some morsel of debt. Strong opened and examined them with a face fit for bad news and thin soup.

Mrs. Bonner descended upon him in the midst of it—Mrs. Bonner, her ladyship’s housekeeper and confidential maid, a fixture of the household like the tea-urn, and as necessary to her mistress as Strong was to Sir Francis. She was, by duty, even angrier than Lady Clavering; a servant’s indignation is often the family’s indignation boiled down to a sharper gravy.

“She won’t pay, if she takes my advice,” Mrs. Bonner said, with the decision of one who has salted many a joint and knows when enough is enough. “You’ll please to go back to Sir Francis, Captain—and he lurking about in a low public-house and don’t dare to face his wife like a man!—and say that we won’t pay his debts no longer. We made a man of him, we took him out of gaol (and other folks too perhaps), we’ve paid his debts over and over again—we set him up in Parliament and gave him a house in town and country, and where he don’t dare show his face, the shabby sneak! We’ve given him the horse he rides and the dinner he eats and the very clothes he has on his back; and we will give him no more. Our fortune, such as is left of it, is left to ourselves, and we won’t waste any more of it on this ungrateful man. We’ll give him enough to live upon and leave him, that’s what we’ll do: and that’s what you may tell him from Susan Bonner.”

As she spoke, you could almost hear the house itself agreeing: the muffled hush of carpets, the far clink of china, the restrained cough of a clock. A great London house is an instrument; when the master plays false, every room knows the discord.

Lady Clavering, hearing Strong had arrived, sent for him at this moment. The Chevalier went up with a faint hope—he had often coaxed her good nature back into service, as one coaxes a sauce that has begun to separate, warming and stirring and promising it will come together again. He tried once more. He painted in dismal colours the condition in which he had found Sir Francis: crying, drinking, despairing; and he would not answer for consequences if means could not be found to meet the engagements.

“Kill hisself,” laughed Mrs. Bonner, as if the notion were a joke told badly. “Kill hisself, will he? Dying’s the best thing he could do.”

Strong swore he had found razors on the table. At that, Lady Clavering laughed too—bitterly, as if she tasted something burnt and would not spit it out.

“He’ll do himself no harm, as long as there’s a shilling left of which he can rob a poor woman. His life’s quite safe, Captain: you may depend upon that. Ah! it was a bad day that ever I set eyes on him.”

“He’s worse than the first man,” cried Mrs. Bonner, remembering some older misery like an old recipe gone wrong but still remembered by the tongue. “He was a man, he was—a wild devil, but he had the courage of a man—whereas this fellow—what’s the use of my lady paying his bills, and selling her diamonds, and forgiving him? He’ll be as bad again next year. The very next chance he has he’ll be a-cheating of her, and robbing of her; and her money will go to keep a pack of rogues and swindlers—I don’t mean you, Captain—you’ve been a good friend to us enough, bating we wish we’d never set eyes on you.”

That slip—diamonds—fell into Strong’s ear like the faint chink of a key. He saw that Lady Clavering’s heart, bruised though it was, still retained its terrible elasticity. She was disposed to relent, at least once more; and where there is relenting, there is money.

He leaned in with real sympathy—he could feel for her, and admire her, even while serving her husband’s squalid interests. “Upon my word, ma’am,” he said, “anything you say against Clavering, or Mrs. Bonner here cries out against me, is no better than we deserve, both of us; and it was an unlucky day for you when you saw either. He has behaved cruelly to you; and if you were not the most generous and forgiving woman in the world, I know there would be no chance for him. But you can’t let the father of your son be a disgraced man, and send little Frank into the world with such a stain upon him. Tie him down; bind him by any promises you like: I vouch for him that he will subscribe them.”

“And break ’em,” said Mrs. Bonner, as promptly as she would have said “and scorch it” of a careless cook.

“And keep ’em this time,” Strong insisted, with a heat that sounded like sincerity and was partly made of it. “He must keep them. If you could have seen how he wept, ma’am! ‘Oh, Strong,’ he said to me, ‘it’s not for myself I feel now: it’s for my boy—it’s for the best woman in England, whom I have treated basely—I know I have.’ He didn’t intend to bet upon this race, ma’am—indeed he didn’t. He was cheated into it: all the ring was taken in. He thought he might make the bet quite safely, without the least risk. And it will be a lesson to him for all his life long. To see a man cry—oh, it’s dreadful.”

“He don’t think much of making my dear missus cry,” said Mrs. Bonner—“poor dear soul!—look if he does, Captain.”

When Strong carried the result of this kitchen-council of war back to his principal, he spoke more plainly than he had upstairs.

“If you’ve the soul of a man, Clavering,” he said, “you’ll keep your promise this time: and, so help me Heaven! if you break word with her, I’ll turn against you, and tell all.”

“What all?” cried Mr. Francis, at Short’s Hotel, where Strong found him again in the same posture of anguish—tears and curacoa, like sugar on sorrow.

“Psha! Do you suppose I am a fool?” Strong broke out. “Do you suppose I could have lived so long in the world, Frank Clavering, without having my eyes about me? You know I have but to speak and you are a beggar to-morrow. And I am not the only man who knows your secret.”

“Who else does?” gasped Clavering, turning a colour which in another man might have been shame, but in him was merely fear.

“Old Pendennis does, or I am very much mistaken. He recognised the man the first night he saw him, when he came drunk into your house.”

“He knows it, does he?” shrieked Clavering, the sound sharp enough to crack a glass. “Damn him—kill him.”

“You’d like to kill us all, wouldn’t you, old boy?” Strong said, sneering, and puffing his cigar as if moral reproof were best delivered through smoke.

Sir Francis flung his weak hand to his forehead. Perhaps the other had translated him too accurately. “Oh, Strong!” he cried, “if I dared, I’d put an end to myself, for I’m the d——est miserable dog in all England. It’s that that makes me so wild and reckless. It’s that which makes me take to drink”—and he drank, trembling, a bumper of his fortifier—“and to live about with these thieves. I know they’re thieves, every one of ’em, d——d thieves. And—and how can I help it?—and I didn’t know it, you know—and, by Gad, I’m innocent—and until I saw the d——d scoundrel first, I knew no more about it than the dead—and I’ll fly, and I’ll go abroad out of the reach of the confounded hells, and I’ll bury myself in a forest, by Gad! and hang myself up to a tree—and, oh—I’m the most miserable beggar in all England!”

And so he went on, seasoning his repentance with blasphemy, and his despair with oath after oath, like a cook who cannot leave off peppering a dish already ruined.

Yet the proverb held: an ill wind blows good to somebody. The day Sir Francis’s debts were settled, another tenant of Strong’s chambers in Shepherd’s Inn found himself, by lucky accident, “good” in a wager. Colonel Altamont had taken thirty to one in fifties against the winning horse; and when Captain Clinker paid Sir Francis’s creditors—Lady Clavering, by Major Pendennis’s advice, refusing to let the Baronet touch the business with his own fingers—Altamont received his odds with a satisfaction as audible as the snap of bank-notes.

Altamont’s friends swarmed round him at once, like flies round a fresh tart. His set, and the gentlemen of the convivial Wheeler at the Harlequin’s Head, came to congratulate and, with hearty generosity, to propose how they might spend his luck on their behalf. Tom Driver said now was the time to raise that specie ship sunk in the Gulf of Mexico with its three hundred and eighty thousand dollars and bars and doubloons. Mr. Keightley insinuated the Tredyddlums were low—never such a chance to buy shares for an old song. Jack Holt pressed a tobacco-smuggling scheme whose sheer audacity tickled the Colonel more than any sober honesty could have done. Then the Harlequin’s Head boys: Jack Rackstraw recommended a pair of horses; Tom Fleet begged two hundred pounds to float his satirical paper, The Swell, which would be worth a thousand a year to any man “with such a power and influence, Colonel, you rogue, and the entree of the green-rooms in London.” Little Moss Abrams, in a tone of injured virtue, implored him not to listen to these absurd fellows but to invest in some good bills that Moss could procure, returning fifty per cent “as safe as the Bank of England.”

They all made their pitches with the eager rhythm of a bad orchestra—voices overlapping, the scrape of chairs, the thump of hands on tables. It is one of the worst noises in the world: the sound of men hearing money and mistaking it for music.

But Altamont had courage enough to resist. He buttoned up his notes in his coat-pocket, went home to Strong, and “sported” the outer door. Strong had advised him about his acquaintances; and though, when pressed, he did not mind frankly taking twenty pounds himself out of the Colonel’s winnings, he was too upright to let the rest of the pack get their teeth in.

Altamont, in good fortune, was not an unkind fellow. He ordered a smart livery for Grady; he made poor old Costigan’s gratitude bubble up and spill over into tears that dried almost as soon as they came, by giving him a five-pound note after a snug dinner at the Back Kitchen—Irish stew thick with onions and pepper, a steam that clung to the clothes and made even poverty smell briefly like home. He bought a green shawl for Mrs. Bolton, and a yellow one for Fanny—two bright “sacrifices” from a Regent Street haberdasher’s window, as gaudy as sweetmeats in a jar.

Not long after, on Miss Amory’s birthday in June, a parcel arrived from “a friend”: an enormous brass-inlaid writing-desk, and in it a set of amethysts—great staring stones like the most hideous eyes ever looked upon—a musical snuff-box, and two Keepsakes of the year before last, and gown pieces of colours so astounding that the Sylphide laughed and wondered immoderately. It was known that about this time Altamont had bought cigars and French silks from some duffers in Fleet Street; and Strong found him in the open Auction Room in Cheapside investing in two desks, several pairs of richly plated candlesticks, a dinner epergne, and a bagatelle-board. The epergne remained at chambers and figured at their banquets, glittering in candlelight until Jack Holt said it looked as if it had been taken “in a bill.” Jack Holt knew.

The dinners at Shepherd’s Inn became pretty frequent, and Sir Francis Clavering condescended to partake of them constantly. His own house was shut up; the successor of Mirobolant, who had sent his bill in with such unseasonable promptitude, was dismissed by the indignant Lady Clavering; the luxuriance of the establishment was pruned as ruthlessly as an overgrown herb bed. One of the large footmen was cashiered; the other gave warning, not liking to serve without his mate, or in a family where “on’y one footman was kep’.” Economical reforms were practised with a severity that would have done credit to a hard winter. The Major as friend, Strong as advocate for the culprit, her lawyer, and the honest Begum herself executed them briskly.

After paying the Baronet’s debts—the settlement occasioning scandal enough to make the very street sound different under one’s boots—Lady Clavering quitted London for Tunbridge Wells in high dudgeon, refusing to see the reprobate husband whom nobody pitied. Clavering remained in London, patient enough, not eager to meet her just indignation. He sneaked in and out of the House of Commons, and from thence he and Captain Raff and Mr. Marker would go to billiards and cigars and sporting public-houses; or he might be seen lurking about Lincoln’s Inn and his lawyers’ offices, kept waiting for hours while clerks winked at each other over his bowed head.

No wonder he relished Shepherd’s Inn. There he was nowhere scorned; there he was chief guest—“Yes, Sir Francis,” “No, Sir Francis”—there he told his wretched jokes; there he quavered his dreary little French song after Strong had sung his jovial chorus and Costigan had piped Irish ditties. Such a jolly menage as Strong’s, with Grady’s Irish stew bubbling like a small domestic myth in the saucepan, and the Chevalier’s punch after dinner—hot lemon, sugar melting, the sharp fragrant sting of spirits rising with the steam—would have been welcome to many a better man than Clavering. The solitude of his own great house frightened him; there, attended only by an old woman and a valet who sneered, he heard too plainly the hollow sound of his life.

“Yes, dammit,” he said at Shepherd’s Inn, “that fellow of mine, I must turn him away, only I owe him two years’ wages, curse him, and can’t ask my lady. He brings me my tea cold of a morning, with a dem’d leaden teaspoon, and he says my lady’s sent all the plate to the banker’s because it ain’t safe.—Now ain’t it hard that she won’t trust me with a single teaspoon; ain’t it ungentlemanlike, Altamont? You know my lady’s of low birth—that is—I beg your pardon—hem—that is, it’s most cruel of her not to show more confidence in me. And the very servants begin to laugh—the damn scoundrels! I’ll break every bone in their great hulking bodies, curse ’em, I will.—They don’t answer my bell: and—and my man was at Vauxhall last night with one of my dress-shirts and my velvet waistcoat on, I know it was mine—the confounded impudent blackguard—and he went on dancing before my eyes confound him! I’m sure he’ll live to be hanged—he deserves to be hanged—all those infernal rascals of valets.”

Now he was very kind to Altamont. He listened to the Colonel’s loud stories—how he had worked his way home from New Zealand after a whaling expedition and had to slink on board at night to escape from their wives, by Jove; and how the poor devils paddled after the ship in canoes when she sailed; how he had been lost in the bush three months in New South Wales on a trading speculation; how he had seen Boney at Saint Helena and been presented to him with the rest of the officers of an Indiaman. Over cups Altamont told many such tales, and lied and bragged a great deal; Sir Francis listened with hungry attention, drinking wine with him and treating him with distinction.

“Leave him alone, I know what he’s a-coming to,” Altamont said, laughing to Strong, when Strong remonstrated. “And leave me alone; I know what I’m a-telling, very well. I was officer on board an Indiaman, so I was; I traded to New South Wales, so I did, in a ship of my own, and lost her. I became officer to the Nawaub, so I did; only me and my royal master have had a difference, Strong—that’s it. Who’s the better or the worse for what I tell? or knows anything about me? The other chap is dead—shot in the bush, and his body reckonised at Sydney. If I thought anybody would split, do you think I wouldn’t wring his neck? I’ve done as good before now, Strong—I told you how I did for the overseer before I took leave—but in fair fight, I mean—in fair fight; or, rayther, he had the best of it. He had his gun and bay’net, and I had only an axe. Fifty of ’em saw it—ay, and cheered me when I did it—and I’d do it again,—him, wouldn’t I? I ain’t afraid of anybody; and I’d have the life of the man who split upon me. That’s my maxim, and pass me the liquor.—You wouldn’t turn on a man. I know you. You’re an honest feller, and will stand by a feller, and have looked death in the face like a man. But as for that lily-livered sneak—that poor lyin’ swindlin’ cringin’ cur of a Clavering—who stands in my shoes—stands in my shoes, hang him! I’ll make him pull my boots off and clean ’em, I will. Ha, ha!”

He burst into a wild laugh. Strong rose and put away the brandy-bottle as if shutting a door against noise.

“You’re right, old boy,” Altamont said, still good-humoured. “You always keep your head cool, you do—and when I begin to talk too much—I say, when I begin to pitch, I authorise you, and order you, and command you, to put away the rum-bottle.”

“Take my counsel, Altamont,” Strong said gravely, “and mind how you deal with that man. Don’t make it too much his interest to get rid of you; or who knows what he may do?”

The very event Altamont had been awaiting with cynical relish came quickly. One day, Strong being absent on an errand for his principal, Sir Francis appeared at the chambers and found the envoy of the Nawaub alone. He began by abusing the world for being heartless; then his wife for being ungenerous; then Strong for being ungrateful. Hundreds of pounds, he said, had he given Ned Strong—been his friend for life and kept him out of gaol, by Jove—and now Ned was taking her ladyship’s side and abetting her infernal unkindness.

“They’ve entered into a conspiracy to keep me penniless, Altamont,” he whined. “They don’t give me as much pocket money as Frank has at school.”

“Why don’t you go down to Richmond and borrow of him, Clavering?” Altamont broke in with a savage laugh. “He wouldn’t see his poor old beggar of a father without pocket-money, would he?”

“I tell you, I’ve been obliged to humiliate myself cruelly,” Clavering said; and he produced pawn-tickets, as if they were a menu of shame. “Look here, sir—look here, at these pawn-tickets! Fancy a Member of Parliament and an old English Baronet, by Gad! obliged to put a drawing-room clock and a buhl inkstand up the spout; and a gold duck’s-head paper-holder, that I dare say cost my wife five pound, for which they’d only give me fifteen-and-six! Oh, it’s a humiliating thing, sir, poverty to a man of my habits; and it’s made me shed tears, sir,—tears; and that d——d valet of mine—curse him, I wish he was hanged!—he had the confounded impudence to threaten to tell my lady: as the things in my own house weren’t my own, to sell or to keep, or fling out of window if I chose—by Gad! the confounded scoundrel.”

“Cry a little; don’t mind cryin’ before me—it’ll relieve you, Clavering,” Altamont said. “Why, I say, old feller, what a happy feller I once thought you, and what a miserable son of a gun you really are!”

“It’s a shame that they treat me so, ain’t it?” Clavering went on—for though ordinarily silent and apathetic, about his own griefs he could whine like a kettle that will not boil. “And—and, by Gad, sir, I haven’t got the money to pay the very cab that’s waiting for me at the door; and the porteress, that Mrs. Bolton, lent me three shillin’s, and I don’t like to ask her for any more: and I asked that d——d old Costigan, the confounded old penniless Irish miscreant, and he hadn’t got a shillin’, the beggar; and Campion’s out of town, or else he’d do a little bill for me, I know he would.”

“I thought you swore on your honour to your wife that you wouldn’t put your name to paper,” Altamont said, puffing at his cigar.

“Why does she leave me without pocket-money, then? Damme, I must have money,” cried the Baronet. “Oh, Am——, oh, Altamont, I’m the most miserable beggar alive.”

“You’d like a chap to lend you a twenty-pound note, wouldn’t you now?” Altamont asked.

“If you would, I’d be grateful to you for ever—for ever, my dearest friend,” Clavering cried, leaning forward as if gratitude could be used as collateral.

“How much would you give? Will you give a fifty-pound bill, at six months, for half down and half in plate?” Altamont asked, with a grin that had more edge than mercy.

“Yes, I would, so help me——, and pay it on the day,” screamed Clavering. “I’ll make it payable at my banker’s: I’ll do anything you like.”

“Well, I was only chaffing you,” Altamont said. “I’ll give you twenty pound.”

“You said a pony,” Clavering interposed, greedy even in correction; “my dear fellow, you said a pony, and I’ll be eternally obliged to you; and I’ll not take it as a gift—only as a loan, and pay you back in six months. I take my oath, I will.”

A little while after that piece of luck which overtook Colonel Altamont at Epsom—luck being, in his case, a kind of accidental gravy that would insist on settling upon him whether he deserved it or not—the Colonel at last set off upon his promised foreign tour. The chronicler of the polite world (that indefatigable fellow who seems to live on piers and platforms, and to take his meat standing, so long as it is seasoned with titles) went down to London Bridge to wave farewell to Fashion as she fled the island; and duly reported that the Soho to Antwerp had on board “Sir Robert, Lady, and the Misses Hodge; Mr. Serjeant Kewsy, and Mrs. and Miss Kewsy; Colonel Altamont, Major Coddy, etc.”

Altamont travelled as became a gentleman: in rich travelling gear; in a brave temper; and with a constitution that took brandy-and-water as if it were a national beverage and not a moral episode. While other passengers were turning pale and pious, he stayed pleasantly red and profane. He had, too, his body-servant with him—the faithful Irish legionary who, for some time, had divided his allegiance between the Colonel and Captain Strong in their chambers in Shepherd’s Inn, and who now, with the air of a man changing kitchens, changed his master.

Before the embarkation, the Chevalier (for so Captain Strong still liked to be titled by himself, as a cook likes to be called “Chef” when he is only minding a chop) dined with his departing friend at Blackwall. There was a copious meal—one of those dinners where the very table seems to groan like a bass-viol under the weight of beef and bottles; where oysters whisper, ham sings, and punch goes roaring down the throat with the cheerful sound of a small cataract. Altamont paid; others praised; and several healths were drunk with that sincerity which always attends a free-handed host at his own expense.

“Strong, old boy,” said the Colonel, in the comfortable pause after a mouthful and before a sentiment—“if you want a little money, now’s your time. I’m your man. You’ve been a good feller to me; and a twenty-pound note, more or less, will make no odds to me.”

But Strong—who could carve a joint, or a difficulty, with equal neatness—said No. He didn’t want any money; he was flush, quite flush—“that is, not flush enough to pay you back your last loan, Altamont, but quite able to carry on for some time to come.” So they parted, not uncordially; and the Colonel, buoyant with good fortune and spirits, went off to the Continent like a bottle of champagne that has just been uncorked and means to go everywhere.

And now, when the noise of the Colonel’s boots had died upon the stairs, Strong stood a moment listening to the altered acoustics of his life. A room has its own music, and a companion is often the chief instrument in it. Altamont had been a loud one—brassy, perhaps; occasionally out of tune; but still something that made the place less silent. Without him, Shepherd’s Inn sounded like a pantry after the servants have all gone to supper: the ticking of a clock becomes impertinent; the scrape of a chair is an event; and a man’s own cough seems to declare him a solitary.

Had money made Altamont more honest and amiable than he had hitherto been? Or did it only season him in Strong’s eyes, as butter seasons a loaf which yesterday was too dry to notice? Perhaps the Colonel truly was better. Perhaps Strong only respected the beauty of wealth—the bright crust that makes any man look more wholesome. But Strong argued within himself, turning over his thoughts as one turns over a steak to keep it from scorching on one side only.

“This poor devil—this unlucky outcast of a returned convict—is ten times as good a fellow as my friend Sir Francis Clavering, Bart. He has pluck and honesty, in his way. He’ll stick to a friend, and face an enemy. The other never had courage to do either. And what is it that has put the poor devil under a cloud? He was only a little wild, and signed his father-in-law’s name. Many a man has done worse, and come to no wrong, and holds his head up. Clavering does. No, he don’t hold his head up: he never did in his best days.”

So, perhaps, Strong repented of the small lie he had told—that he did not want money. It was a lie on the side of honesty; and there are falsehoods which a man’s stomach (even if his conscience is willing) cannot digest. He could not bring himself to borrow a second time from his outlawed friend. Besides, he could get on. Sir Francis had promised him some supply: not that Clavering’s promises were to be relied on, any more than a poor family’s Sunday pudding is to be relied on when the cat has been left alone in the kitchen; but Strong was of a hopeful turn, and trusted in a number of chances of catching his patron, waylaying a remittance, and securing those stray sovereigns and notes—provisions, as it were—for the lean larder of the Chevalier. In the procuring of these supplies for his principal lay now Mr. Strong’s chief business in life; and it was conducted with as much watchfulness and stratagem as a thrifty housekeeper employs in obtaining a bargain at market.

He had grumbled about Altamont’s companionship in the Shepherd’s Inn chambers; yet he found the lodgings more glum now without his partner than with him. Solitude is a thin soup for a social soul. He had, too, fallen into extravagant and luxurious habits; for a time he had had a servant to run his errands, to arrange his toilets, and to cook his meal. And it was a grand and touching sight now—truly fit for an epic in saucepans—to see the portly, handsome gentleman painting his own boots, and broiling his own mutton chop.

The chop, too, had its commentary. It hissed upon the gridiron with an honest, homely sound—a sound which seemed to say, “Here is work, here is life, here is a man who must turn himself, and not wait to be turned.” The fat sputtered like small, impatient applause; the coals gave out their steady breath; and the smell, warm and animal and familiar, rose in the room and made memory stir. He had once had a wife—a Spanish lady of Vittoria—who, after a few months’ union with the Captain, broke his head with a dish and went back to her friends. There are women whose domestic education includes missiles. He began to wonder whether he should not go and see his Juanita again; for in moments of depression a man’s heart runs back, as the tongue does, to an old flavour. The Chevalier was “down on his luck,” as he called it—picturesquely, as if Fortune were a horse and he had slid off into the mud. Such intervals occur constantly in the lives of heroes: Marius at Minturnæ, Charles Edward in the Highlands, Napoleon before Elba—and Captain Strong before a solitary chop. What great man has not been called upon to face evil fortune and weak tea?

From Clavering no supplies were to be had for some time. The five-and-twenty pounds—the “pony”—which the exemplary Baronet had received from Mr. Altamont, had bolted out of Clavering’s keeping as quickly as many previous ponies. Indeed, Sir Francis treated money as some people treat a hot potato: he could not keep it in his hands without a dance and a yelp.

He had been down the river with a choice party of sporting gents, who dodged the police and landed in Essex, where they put up Billy Bluck to fight Dick the cabman—whom the Baronet backed, and who had it all his own way for thirteen rounds, when, by an unlucky blow in the windpipe, Billy killed him. Thus, in one instant, pleasure turned to horror; the shouting turned to a strange hush; and then came the low, frightened talk that follows any violent interruption of sport—like the sudden stopping of a fiddler in a public-house when a constable looks in at the door. Sir Francis’s account of it, delivered afterwards to Strong, had the tone of a man who complains that Providence will not play fair with his betting-book.

“It’s always my luck, Strong,” he said; “the betting was three to one on the cabman, and I thought myself as sure of thirty pound, as if I had it in my pocket. And dammy, I owe my man Lightfoot fourteen pound now which he’s lent and paid for me: and he duns me—the confounded impudent blackguard. And I wish to Heaven I knew any way of getting a bill done, or of screwing a little out of my lady! I’ll give you half, Ned, upon my soul and honour, I’ll give you half if you can get anybody to do us a little fifty.”

But Ned—who, though he could turn a chop, would not turn a trick—said sternly that he had given his word of honour, as a gentleman, that he would be no party to any future bill-transactions in which her husband might engage (who had given his word of honour too, after his fashion). The Chevalier said that he, at least, would keep his word, and would black his own boots all his life rather than break his promise. And what is more, he vowed he would advise Lady Clavering that Sir Francis was about to break faith towards her upon the very first hint he could get that such was Clavering’s intention.

Upon this information Sir Francis, according to his custom, cried and cursed very volubly. He spoke of death as his only resource; he besought and implored his dear Strong, his best friend, his dear old Ned, not to throw him over; and when he quitted his dearest Ned, and went down the stairs of Shepherd’s Inn, he swore and blasphemed at Ned as the most infernal villain, traitor, blackguard, and coward under the sun, wished Ned in his grave and in a worse place, only would like the confounded ruffian to live until Frank Clavering had had his revenge out of him. Sir Francis’s emotions, like his meals, came in courses: entreaty, rage, despair—each served hot, and each forgotten as soon as the next was on the table.

In Strong’s chambers, as the Baronet was passing out in this agreeable frame of mind, he met a gentleman whose visits were now very frequent in Shepherd’s Inn—Mr. Samuel Huxter, of Clavering. That young fellow—who had poached walnuts in Clavering Park in his youth, and had seen the Baronet drive through the street at home with four horses, and prance up to church with powdered footmen—had an immense respect for his Member, and a prodigious delight in making his acquaintance. He introduced himself with much blushing and trepidation: a Clavering man; son of Mr. Huxter, of the market-place; father attended Sir Francis’s keeper, Coxwood, when his gun burst and took off three fingers; proud to make Sir Francis’s acquaintance.

All of which Sir Francis received affably; for the Baronet could be as gracious as a landlord when he expects the rent. And honest Huxter went and talked about Sir Francis to the chaps at Bartholomew’s, and told Fanny in the lodge that, after all, there was nothing like a thoroughbred ’un, a regular good old English gentleman, one of the olden time!

To which Fanny replied that she thought Sir Francis was an ojous creature—she didn’t know why—but she couldn’t abear him—she was sure he was wicked, and low, and mean—she knew he was.

And when Sam replied that Sir Francis was very affable, and had borrowed half a sovereign of him quite kindly, Fanny burst into a laugh, pulled Sam’s long hair (which was not yet of irreproachable cleanliness), patted his chin, and called him a stoopid, stoopid, old foolish stoopid; and said Sir Francis was always borrering money of everybody, and that Mar had actially refused him twice, and had had to wait three months to get seven shillings which he had borrowed of ’er.

“Don’t say ’er but her, borrer but borrow, actially but actually, Fanny,” Mr. Huxter replied—not to a fault in her argument, but to the grammatical errors in her statement. He corrected her as a cook corrects a sauce—adding a pinch here, thinning there—without altering the substance.

“Well then, her, and borrow, and hactually—there then, you stoopid,” said the other; and the scholar made such a pretty face, with such a triumph of wrongness, that the grammar-master was quickly appeased, and would have willingly given her a hundred more lessons on the spot at the price which he took for that one.

Of course Mrs. Bolton was by; and one may suppose that Fanny and Dr. Sam were on exceedingly familiar and confidential terms by this time, and that time had brought to the former certain consolations, and soothed certain regrets—which are deucedly bitter when they occur, but which are, like tooth-pulling or any other pang, not eternal. The house had its little domestic sounds—kettle singing, fire settling, footsteps on the stair, Fanny’s laugh—small honest noises that make a poor room rich; and, if you will listen rightly, they are the very opposite of that metallic roar of modern life which sells itself as pleasure and gives itself out as pain.

As you sit, surrounded by respect and affection—happy, honoured, and flattered in your old age; your foibles gently indulged; your least words kindly cherished; your garrulous old stories received for the hundredth time with dutiful forbearance and never-failing hypocritical smiles; the women of your house constant in their flatteries; the young men hushed and attentive when you begin to speak; the servants awestricken; the tenants cap in hand and ready to act in the place of your worship’s horses when your honour takes a drive—it has often struck you, O thoughtful Dives, that this respect and these glories are for the main part transferred, with your fee simple, to your successor: that the servants will bow and the tenants shout for your son as for you; that the butler will fetch him the wine (improved by a little keeping) that’s now in your cellar; and that when your night is come, and the light of your life is gone down, as sure as the morning rises after you and without you, the sun of prosperity and flattery shines on your heir.

Men come and bask in the halo of consols and acres that beams round about him. The reverence is transferred with the estate; of which, with all its advantages, pleasures, respect, and good-will, he in turn becomes the life-tenant. How long do you wish or expect your people will regret you? How much time does a man devote to grief before he begins to enjoy? A great man must keep his heir at his feast like a living memento mori. If he holds very much by life, the presence of the other must be a constant sting and warning. “Make ready to go,” says the successor to your honour; “I am waiting: and I could hold it as well as you.”

What has this reference to the possible reader to do with any of the characters of this history? Do we wish to apologise for Pen because he has got a white hat, and because his mourning for his mother is fainter? All the lapse of years, all the career of fortune, all the events of life—however strongly they may move or eagerly excite him—never can remove that sainted image from his heart, or banish that blessed love from its sanctuary. If he yields to wrong, the dear eyes will look sadly upon him when he dares to meet them; if he does well, endures pain, or conquers temptation, the ever-present love will greet him, he knows, with approval and pity; if he falls, plead for him; if he suffers, cheer him—be with him and accompany him always until death is past; and sorrow and sin are no more.

Is this mere dreaming, or, on the part of an idle story-teller, useless moralising? May not the man of the world take his moment, too, to be grave and thoughtful? Ask of your own hearts and memories, brother and sister, if we do not live in the dead; and (to speak reverently) prove God by love?

Of these matters Pen and Warrington often spoke in many a solemn and friendly converse in after-days; and Pendennis’s mother was worshipped in his memory, and canonised there, as such a saint ought to be. Lucky he in life who knows a few such women! A kind provision of Heaven it was, that sent us such; and gave us to admire that touching and wonderful spectacle of innocence, and love, and beauty.

But as it is certain that if, in the course of these sentimental conversations, any outer stranger—Major Pendennis, for instance—had walked into Pen’s chambers, Arthur and Warrington would have stopped their talk and chosen another subject, and discoursed about the Opera, or the last debate in Parliament, or Miss Jones’s marriage with Captain Smith, or what not,—so let us imagine that the public steps in at this juncture, and stops the confidential talk between author and reader, and begs us to resume our remarks about this world, with which both are certainly better acquainted than with that other one into which we have just been peeping.

On coming into his property, Arthur Pendennis at first comported himself with a modesty and equanimity which obtained his friend Warrington’s praises—though Arthur’s uncle was a little inclined to quarrel with his nephew’s meanness of spirit for not assuming greater state and pretensions now that he had entered on the enjoyment of his kingdom. The Major would have had Arthur installed in handsome quarters, riding on showy park-hacks or in well-built cabriolets every day.

“I am too absent,” Arthur said, laughing, “to drive a cab in London; the omnibus would cut me in two, or I should send my horse’s head into the ladies’ carriage-windows. And you wouldn’t have me driven about by my servant like an apothecary, uncle?”

No; Major Pendennis would on no account have his nephew appear like an apothecary. The august representative of the house of Pendennis must not so demean himself. And when Arthur, pursuing his banter, said, “And yet, I dare say, sir, my father was proud enough when he first set up his gig,” the old Major hemmed and ha’d; his wrinkled face reddened with a blush as he answered, “You know what Buonaparte said, sir, ‘Il faut laver son linge sale en famille.’ There is no need, sir, for you to brag that your father was a—a medical man. He came of a most ancient but fallen house, and was obliged to reconstruct the family fortunes as many a man of good family has done before him. You are like the fellow in Sterne, sir—the Marquis who came to demand his sword again. Your father got back yours for you. You are a man of landed estate, by Gad, sir, and a gentleman—never forget you are a gentleman.”

Then Arthur slyly turned upon his uncle an argument he had heard the old gentleman often use regarding himself.

“In the society which I have the honour of frequenting through your introduction, who cares to ask about my paltry means or my humble gentility, uncle?” he said. “It would be absurd of me to attempt to compete with the great folks; and all that they can ask from us is, that we should have a decent address and good manners.”

“But for all that, sir, I should belong to a better club or two,” the uncle answered. “I should give an occasional dinner, and select my society well; and I should come out of that horrible garret in the Temple, sir.”

And so Arthur compromised by descending to the second floor in Lamb Court—Warrington still occupying his old quarters, and the two friends being determined not to part one from the other. Cultivate kindly, reader, those friendships of your youth: it is only in that generous time that they are formed. How different the intimacies of after-days are; and how much weaker the grasp of your own hand after it has been shaken about in twenty years’ commerce with the world, and has squeezed and dropped a thousand equally careless palms! As you can seldom fashion your tongue to speak a new language after twenty, the heart refuses to receive friendship pretty soon: it gets too hard to yield to the impression. A dialect once unlearned is not easily recovered; and the words that were natural to the young mouth become stiff in the older. There are affections, too, that cannot be translated back.

So Pen had many acquaintances, and being of a jovial and easy turn got more daily; but no friend like Warrington. The two men continued to live almost as much in common as the Knights of the Temple—riding upon one horse (for Pen’s was at Warrington’s service), and having their chambers and their servitor in common.

Mr. Warrington had made the acquaintance of Pen’s friends of Grosvenor Place during their last unlucky season in London, and had expressed himself no better satisfied with Sir Francis and Lady Clavering and her ladyship’s daughter than was the public in general.

“The world is right,” George said, “about those people. The young men laugh and talk freely before those ladies, and about them. The girl sees people whom she has no right to know, and talks to men with whom no girl should have an intimacy. Did you see those two reprobates leaning over Lady Clavering’s carriage in the Park the other day, and leering under Miss Blanche’s bonnet? No good mother would let her daughter know those men, or admit them within her doors.”

“The Begum is the most innocent and good-natured soul alive,” interposed Pen. “She never heard any harm of Captain Blackball, or read that trial in which Charley Lovelace figures. Do you suppose honest ladies read and remember the Chronique Scandaleuse as well as you, you old grumbler?”

“Would you like Laura Bell to know those fellows?” Warrington asked; and his face turned rather red, as if some inward fire had found air. “Would you let any woman you loved be contaminated by their company? I have no doubt the poor Begum is ignorant of their histories. It seems to me she is ignorant of a great number of better things. It seems to me your honest Begum is not a lady, Pen. It is not her fault, doubtless, that she has not had the education, or learned the refinements of a lady.”

“She is as moral as Lady Portsea, who has all the world at her balls; and as refined as Mrs. Bull, who breaks the King’s English, and has half a dozen dukes at her table,” Pen answered, rather sulkily. “Why should you and I be more squeamish than the rest of the world? Why are we to visit the sins of her father on this harmless kind creature? She never did anything but kindness to you or any mortal soul. As far as she knows she does her best. She does not set up to be more than she is. She gives you the best dinners she can buy, and the best company she can get. She pays the debts of that scamp of a husband of hers. She spoils her boy like the most virtuous mother in England. Her opinion about literary matters, to be sure, is not much; and I daresay she never read a line of Wordsworth, or heard of Tennyson in her life.”

“No more has Mrs. Flanagan the laundress,” growled out Pen’s Mentor; “no more has Betty the housemaid; and I have no word of blame against them. But a high-souled man doesn’t make friends of these. A gentleman doesn’t choose these for his companions, or bitterly rues it afterwards if he do. Are you, who are setting up to be a man of the world and a philosopher, to tell me that the aim of life is to guttle three courses and dine off silver? Do you dare to own to yourself that your ambition in life is good claret; and that you’ll dine with any, provided you get a stalled ox to feed on? You call me a Cynic—why, what a monstrous Cynicism it is, which you and the rest of you men of the world admit! I’d rather live upon raw turnips and sleep in a hollow tree—or turn backwoodsman or savage—than degrade myself to this civilisation, and own that a French cook was the thing in life best worth living for.”

“Because you like a raw beefsteak and a pipe afterwards,” broke out Pen, “you give yourself airs of superiority over people whose tastes are more dainty, and are not ashamed of the world they live in. Who goes about professing particular admiration, or esteem, or friendship, or gratitude even, for the people one meets every day? If A. asks me to his house, and gives me his best, I take his good things for what they are worth and no more. I do not profess to pay him back in friendship, but in the conventional money of society. When we part, we part without any grief. When we meet, we are tolerably glad to see one another. If I were only to live with my friends, your black muzzle, old George, is the only face I should see.”

“You are your uncle’s pupil,” said Warrington, rather sadly; “and you speak like a worldling.”

“And why not?” asked Pendennis. “Why not acknowledge the world I stand upon, and submit to the conditions of the society which we live in and live by? I am older than you, George, in spite of your grizzled whiskers, and have seen much more of the world than you have in your garret here, shut up with your books and your reveries and your ideas of one-and-twenty. I say, I take the world as it is; and being of it, will not be ashamed of it. If the time is out of joint, have I any calling or strength to set it right?”

“Indeed, I don’t think you have much of either,” growled Pen’s interlocutor.

“If I doubt whether I am better than my neighbour,” Arthur continued, “if I concede that I am no better,—I also doubt whether he is better than I. I see men who begin with ideas of universal reform, and who, before their beards are grown, propound their loud plans for the regeneration of mankind; give up their schemes after a few years of bootless talking and vainglorious attempts to lead their fellows; and after they have found that men will no longer bear them, as indeed they never were in the least worthy to be heard, sink quietly into the ranks-and-file,—acknowledging their aims impracticable, or thankful that they were never put into practice. The fiercest reformers grow calm, and are fain to put up with things as they are: the loudest Radical orators become dumb, quiescent placemen; the most fervent Liberals when out of power become humdrum Conservatives, or downright tyrants or despots in office. Look at the Thiers; look at Guizot, in opposition and in place! Look at the Whigs appealing to the country, and the Whigs in power! Would you say the conduct of these men is an act of treason, as the Radicals bawl—who would give way in their turn, were their turn ever to come? No: only that they submit to circumstances which are stronger than they; march as the world marches towards reform, but at the world’s pace (and the movements of the vast body of mankind must needs be slow); forgo this scheme as impracticable, on account of opposition; that as immature, because against the sense of the majority; are forced to calculate drawbacks and difficulties, as well as to think of reforms and advances; and compelled finally to submit, and to wait, and to compromise.”

“The Right Honourable Arthur Pendennis could not speak better, or be more satisfied with himself,” Warrington said, “if he was First Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer.”

The intelligence Major Pendennis had gathered touching the Claverings—partly from Strong’s blundering honesty, partly from his own seasoned habit of listening with one ear and laying traps with the other—was enough to make even that old calculator pause over any scheme in which his nephew might be asked to stake his comfort.

A wife, to be sure, was an excellent thing in the abstract, like a well-roasted capon or a well-ripened Stilton; but the Major had never yet met with an abstract wife, and he knew that the bird came with its stuffing. In Miss Amory’s case, the stuffing was two fathers-in-law: one a bankrupt baronet with a talent for signing his own ruin; the other an invisible gentleman who, if he ever became visible within reach of British law, would have the kindness to save everybody trouble by swinging at the end of a rope. A guardian may have nerves; he may have digestion; he may have a tender regard for the family name and the family liver. Why should he season a young man’s marriage-broth with such ingredients?

Nor, even if the Begum (that magnificent Eastern saucepan of gold) were to pour money into Clavering’s empty pot, would the dish ever come wholesome. The Baronet would ladle it out to every rogue in London who brought a stamped paper and an oily grin; the treasury would be scraped to the bottom; and the young lady, instead of bringing income and influence, would bring—what? Her beauty, her gentle breeding, and a pedigree which at its last male name carried, as it were, a black little note in the margin—like the smell of something burnt that no amount of rose-water quite gets rid of.

The Major, revolving these matters, felt that another line of manoeuvre remained. He did not like to show his cards; he liked still less to lose the game. But before we arrive at that, the reader must submit to a small domestic circumstance of London life: how a gentleman under money troubles becomes as hard to catch as a trout, and much more slippery to hold when caught.

When a man in embarrassments drops out of his usual flock—ceases to wheel round Pall Mall and perch at Clubs—it is astonishing in what queer back-yards he will reappear, chirping, after dusk. He has a house, but never inhabits it; an address, but only the innocent ever go there. His friends are those who know where he takes breath—over bad brandy, worse tobacco, and the consolations of other people’s cash.

So Sir Francis Clavering, after his squabbles with his wife and after Strong had been moralising at him till morals became unbearable, was not to be found “at home” for love or money—especially money, which has so strange an attraction for a man who is running away from it. The tradesmen might call; the lawyers might write; the family friends might knock; the Baronet was always “out,” and his very knocker looked as if it had been bribed to lie.

Major Pendennis, having an object that required speech—not a note, not a message, not a third person’s version—set himself to trap this shy bird. It cost him time, patience, and (what was harder) meals.

One day he wrote with honeyed innocence and invited Sir Francis to Greenwich—whitebait, a few friends, pleasant air, the river making pretty noises against the boat, and no business on earth. Sir Francis accepted, suspected, and stayed away; leaving the Major, who had meant to be “the few friends” in his own person, to eat the whitebait alone, with the sound of other parties laughing round him like knives on plates. Another day the Major begged ten minutes’ talk. Sir Francis replied instantly, named four o’clock next day at “Bays’s precisely,” and underlined “precisely” as though punctuality were a virtue which could be manufactured by ink. Four o’clock came—faithful as a boiling kettle—and no Baronet appeared. To look for Sir Francis in daylight, with conscience and accounts in the air, was like looking for a mouse on a drum.

Yet that same day—while Strong’s patron had been blessing him to his face and cursing him behind his back, in the wholesome old fashion of the world—Sir Francis, who had sworn on a Bible (and very likely kissed it) that he would draw or accept no more bills, had actually set his respectable name to a piece of stamped paper. His friend Mr. Moss Abrams carried it off, promising to have it “done” by some accommodating personage. And Strong heard of this performance from the best possible witness: the landlord of the little back-parlour where it had been cooked.

It was at Mr. Santiago’s cigar-shop—an establishment where the air was always thick with Havana, and conversation always had something smouldering in it. Strong, who haunted the place in the evenings, received the news as a man receives a whiff of scorching when his roast has caught.

“He is at his old work again,” said Santiago, with the calm of one who has seen many reputations burnt to ashes and swept up next morning. “He and Moss Abrams were in my parlour. Moss sent out my boy for a stamp. It must have been a bill for fifty pound. I heard the Baronet tell Moss to date it two months back. He will pretend it is an old bill, and that he forgot it when he settled with my Lady. They will squeeze a little more out of her now he is clear.”

To have the habit of signing promises to pay is at least to have the satisfaction of knowing that one’s signature is passed round London like a questionable sausage at a cheap ordinary—everybody handles it, nobody knows what is in it, and the smell follows the owner.

Mr. Santiago’s shop stood near St. James’s Street, close to Major Pendennis’s lodgings in Bury Street. The Major, stepping delicately along as if his boots were afraid to make a sound on the pavement, met Strong striding toward him with wrath in his eye and Havana on his breath.

“Confound these young men,” thought the Major, sniffing as though smoke were an indecency like garlic at a duchess’s luncheon. “How they poison everything. Mustachios and cigars—low fellows. Oh! it’s Mr. Strong.”

He bowed with dignity, produced his polished key, and was about to slip into his own door and away from trouble, when Strong stopped him and held out a frank hand. The Major offered two reluctant fingers, as though charity were contagious.

“What is your good news?” the Major asked, in that tone by which he could make the commonest remark sound like a favour. “Still in town, Mr. Strong? I hope I see you well.”

“My news is bad news, sir,” Strong said, blunt as a cleaver. “It concerns our friends at Tunbridge Wells, and I should like to talk to you about it. Clavering is at his old tricks again, Major Pendennis.”

“Indeed! Pray come into my lodging,” cried the Major, suddenly hospitable; for nothing opens a prudent man’s door like a secret that may be useful.

Within the drawing-room, Strong poured out his indignation as one might empty a saucepan that has boiled over. He spoke of the Baronet’s recklessness and treachery, of oaths made on bended knees and broken standing up, of the Bible fetched to sanctify a lie, and the bell rung for Heaven’s witness to a fraud.

“No promises will bind him, sir,” Strong said. “You remember how he wanted to swear perdition on his soul if he ever gave another bill. He has been signing one this very day, sir. He will sign as many more as you please for ready money. He will deceive anybody—his wife, his child, his old friend who has backed him a hundred times. Why, there’s a bill of his and mine due next week.”

“I thought we had paid all,” the Major said, with a slight tightening of the mouth.

“Not that one,” Strong answered, colouring. “He asked me not to mention it, and—and—I had half the money for that, Major. They will be down on me. But I don’t care; I’m used to it. It’s Lady Clavering that riles me. It’s a shame that that good-natured woman—who has paid him out of gaol a score of times—should be ruined by his heartlessness. A parcel of bill-stealers, boxers—any rascals—get his money; and he don’t scruple to throw an honest fellow over. Would you believe it, sir—he took money of Altamont—you know whom I mean.”

“Indeed? of that singular man,” said Major Pendennis, whose face could have been carved in mahogany, “who I think came tipsy once to Sir Francis’s house? Who is Altamont, Mr. Strong?”

Strong stared, half astonished, half suspicious, as if the Major had asked what salt was. “I am sure I don’t know, if you don’t know,” he said.

“To tell you frankly,” the Major went on smoothly, “I have my suspicions—I suppose—mind, I only suppose—that in our friend Clavering’s life (who, between you and me, Captain Strong, is about as loose a fish as any in my acquaintance) there are some queer secrets and stories which he would not like to have known. None of us would. And very likely this fellow Altamont knows something against him, and has some hold, and gets money out of him. I know men of the best families in England paying through the nose in that way. But their private affairs are no business of mine, Mr. Strong. I do not pry. I am interested for Lady Clavering’s sake, and her daughter’s. When her ladyship asked me, I looked into her affairs, and tried to set them straight. I shall do so again if called upon—if called upon. And by the way—this Mr. Altamont—how is he? I believe you are acquainted with him. Is he in town?”

“I don’t know that I am called upon to know where he is, Major Pendennis,” Strong said, rising and taking up his hat with the offended stiffness of a man whose honesty has been patted on the head like a lap-dog.

The Major’s tone changed at once; his hauteur melted into a knowing good-humour, as a lump of sugar disappears in hot tea.

“Ah, Captain Strong, you are cautious too,” he said, smiling. “Quite right, my good sir—quite right. We don’t know what ears walls may have. There is no use throwing away your fire. You may have your ideas, I may put two and two together and have mine. But there are things that many a man had better not know until he has reason for knowing them—and that I believe is your maxim too. With regard to our friend the Baronet, I agree with you: it would be advisable he should be checked. I reprehend any man’s departure from his word, or any conduct giving pain to his family. That is my full and frank opinion, and I am sure it is yours.”

“Certainly,” said Strong, drily, as one says “certainly” when the weather is obviously wet.

“I am delighted to hear it,” the Major replied, as though unanimity were an elegant sauce. “Delighted. And I am exceedingly glad of this lucky meeting. Good evening. Thank you. Morgan, show the door to Captain Strong.”

Thus dismissed, Strong went out more puzzled than appeased, and Morgan, who had floated about the room as silently as smoke itself, was puzzled too—for he had caught fragments, names, hints, and the sharp clink of money behind them, as a man hears knives at table without seeing the dish.

“Who is that Altamont? Know anything about him and Strong?” Morgan asked Mr. Lightfoot at the Club, upon the first occasion when a valet could talk like a gentleman behind gentlemen’s backs.

“Strong’s his man of business,” Lightfoot answered. “Draws the Governor’s bills, indorses ’em, does his odd jobs. I suppose Altamont’s in it too. That kite-flying always takes two or three to set the paper going. Altamont put the pot on at the Derby and won a good bit. I wish the Governor could get some somewhere, and I could get my book paid up.”

“Do you think my Lady would pay his debts again?” Morgan asked, with a softness that was all arithmetic. “Find out that for me, Lightfoot, and I’ll make it worth your while.”

Major Pendennis had often said laughingly that Morgan was richer than himself. The joke had a bone in it. Morgan, with that valet’s genius for knowing everything without seeming to listen, had been gathering money as squirrels gather nuts—quietly, persistently, and always in other people’s woods. He had made acquaintance with valets of distinction, had learned their masters’ weaknesses as a cook learns where the joint is tender, and had turned knowledge into profit without ever appearing to have an opinion.

When Arthur came into his little property, Morgan had approached him with an air of meek domesticity and offered, with the simplicity of a man offering salt at dinner, to lend him money if ever he wanted it—a little sum, fifty or a hundred pounds, which Morgan wished to “lay out.” Would Mr. Arthur, who lived among lawyers and papers in the Temple, kindly advise an investment?

Arthur laughed, declined, and told his uncle; and the Major, amused and a little nettled, observed that Morgan had been getting devilish rich for a devilish long time—had even bought the house in Bury Street where his master lodged—and had done it, in part, by buying up Clavering paper on the sly, because he knew the Begum would pay.

On the day of Strong’s visit, that recollection came back to the Major like the aftertaste of some pungent relish. He bethought him: if anyone could find Sir Francis, it would be a man who tracked money by smell. So he sent for Morgan and rallied him with that free insolence which a certain class of gentleman practises as naturally as breathing.

“I hear you have got some money to invest, Morgan,” said the Major.

“It’s Mr. Arthur has been telling, hang him,” thought Morgan, keeping his face demure.

“I’m glad my place is such a good one.”

“Thank you, sir. I’ve no reason to complain of my place, nor of my master,” said Morgan.

“You’re a good fellow. I believe you are attached to me. I hope you’ll be prudent and not be taking a public-house or that kind of thing.”

A public-house! thought Morgan, with inward scorn. Me in a public-house! The old fool! If I was ten years younger, dammy, I’d sit in Parliament before I died. Aloud he said, “No, thank you kindly, sir. I don’t think of the public line, sir. And I’ve got my little savings pretty well put out, sir.”

“You do a little in the discounting way, eh, Morgan?” the Major asked, as if speaking of a harmless hobby like fishing.

“Yes, sir, a very little. I—I beg your pardon, sir—might I be so free as to ask a question—”

“Speak on, my good fellow,” said the Major, gracious as a man granting alms.

“About Sir Francis Clavering’s paper, sir. Do you think he’s any longer any good, sir? Will my Lady pay on ’em any more, sir?”

“What, you’ve done something in that business already?” the Major cried.

“Yes, sir, a little,” replied Morgan, lowering his eyes like a saint confessing to a sin that has paid interest. “And I don’t mind owning, sir—and I hope I may take the liberty of saying, sir—that a little more would make me very comfortable, if it turned out as well as the last.”

“Why, how much have you netted by him, in Gad’s name?” demanded the Major, half shocked, half impressed—as one might be on discovering that the quiet footman makes better sauces than the chef.

“I’ve done a good bit, sir, at it: that I own, sir. Having some information, and made acquaintance with the fam’ly through your kindness, I put on the pot, sir.”

“You did what?”

“I laid my money on, sir—I got all I could, and borrowed, and bought Sir Francis’s bills. Many of ’em had his name, and the gentleman’s as is just gone out, Edward Strong, Esquire, sir. And of course I know of the blow-hup and shindy as took place in Grosvenor Place, sir. And as I may as well make my money as another, I’d be very much obleeged to you if you’d tell me whether my Lady will come down any more.”

Major Pendennis was as astonished as if Morgan had suddenly produced a coronet from his pocket. To be sure, he was indignant too—indignant that a fellow in livery should grow rich under his nose, should handle sums and secrets, should have a private fortune like a gentleman and yet continue to answer a bell like a shadow. But the Major, who admired money as sincerely as he despised smoke, felt an involuntary respect creep into him; and, what was worse, a slight fear—such as men feel when they discover that the person they have been patronising has teeth.

“Well, Morgan,” he said at last, “I mustn’t ask how rich you are; and the richer the better for your sake, I’m sure. If I could give you information to serve you, I would. But frankly—if Lady Clavering asks me whether she shall pay any more of Sir Francis’s debts, I shall advise— and I hope she won’t—though I fear she will. That is all I know. And so you are aware Sir Francis is beginning again in his—eh—reckless course?”

“At his old games, sir—can’t prevent that gentleman. He will do it,” Morgan replied, with the calm of a man discussing the weather.

“Mr. Strong was saying that a Mr. Moss Abrams holds one of Sir Francis Clavering’s notes. Do you know anything of this Mr. Abrams—or the amount of the bill?”

“Don’t know the bill, know Abrams quite well, sir.”

“I wish you would find out about it for me,” the Major said; and then, lowering his voice with the relish of a man ordering a delicate dish, “I wish you would find out where I can see Sir Francis Clavering, Morgan.”

“Thank you, sir—yes, sir—I will, sir,” said Morgan, and glided away as noiselessly as he had entered, leaving the Major to sit and digest the new fact that his servant had been frying, turning, and serving a whole little financial stew under his very eyes.

Next morning Morgan returned with the promptness of a well-trained kitchen-boy bringing the dish when it must be hot. He had seen Mr. Abrams; he knew the amount of the bill that gentleman wished to “negotiate;” and he knew where Sir Francis would be found that very day at one o’clock.

“In the back-parlour of the Wheel of Fortune Tavern, sir,” Morgan said.

At one o’clock, sure enough, Sir Francis Clavering sat in that parlour—a descendant of an ancient line set down among spittoons and Windsor chairs, cheerful prints of boxers, trotting horses and pedestrians, and the stale tobacco-fumes of last night hanging about the room like a dirty curtain. Before him lay an old copy of Bell’s Life in London, blotched with beer, as if even the news had been drinking.

Into this temple of aristocratic retirement walked Major Pendennis, neat as a pin, scented as propriety, and looking as much out of place as a silver fork in a greasy chop-house.

“So it’s you, old boy?” cried Sir Francis, brightening for a moment, taking him—naturally—for money in person, and thinking Mr. Moss Abrams had arrived in human shape with the cash.

“How do you do, Sir Francis Clavering? I wanted to see you, and followed you here,” said the Major.

At the sight of him, the Baronet’s face fell—like a soufflé that hears footsteps.

Now that he had his man, the Major meant to strike quickly and not allow time for slinking out of the back door. He went into action with a sharpness that would have done credit to a cook catching a thief with his hand in the larder.

“I know,” he said, “who is the exceedingly disreputable person for whom you took me, Clavering; and the errand which brought you here.”

“It ain’t your business, is it?” Sir Francis answered, sulky and frightened at once, like a boy caught with jam on his fingers. “Why are you following me about and taking the command, and meddling in my affairs, Major Pendennis? I’ve never done you any harm, have I? I’ve never had your money. And I don’t choose to be dodged about in this way, and domineered over. I don’t choose it, and I won’t have it. If Lady Clavering has any proposal to make to me, let it be done in the regular way, and through the lawyers. I’d rather not have you.”

On a bit of well-behaved common near Tunbridge Wells—where the grass seems to have been trained in a genteel seminary—Lady Clavering discovered a villa exactly suited to a lady who has lately quarrelled with her husband and now desires Nature to take her part. Thither she retired after the unlucky season in London, dragging behind her, as inevitably as a snail its shell, Miss Amory; and Master Clavering came down for the holidays, bringing with him that tender spirit of domestic concord which shows itself, in boys of his years, by perpetual skirmishes with his sister.

Frank’s chief occupation at home was to fight Blanche; but this was merely an indoor game, and he liked his outdoor games better. Tunbridge offered cricket and horses and that choicest delicacy of boyhood—plenty of other boys to make a riot with.
