The Begum’s house presently swarmed with young gentlemen of thirteen, who came in gusty flocks, ate as if they were paid by the mouthful, and drank as if champagne were lemonade and lemonade a moral weakness. There were tarts—great shining, sticky, jammy tarts—vanishing in wedges; there were crusts shattered like battlements; there were buttery crumbs marched into carpets; there were bottles popped with a sound like a pistol-shot in a drawing-room—and all this juvenile feasting was garnished with lawn-races on horseback, cigars furtively nibbled and then heroically swallowed, and a general air of small men trying to be big men and only succeeding in being ill.

The dining-room, in consequence, became unbearable to Miss Blanche. She did not like the society of young gentlemen of thirteen; their talk was noisy, their laughter cracked, their forks clattered like ironmongery, and the very act of their eating seemed conducted with a species of percussion. To be sure Blanche could endure almost anything—if it was a change. For a week she would have liked poverty and a cottage and bread-and-cheese; and for a night she might have entertained a dungeon and bread-and-water; the point was not the fare, but the novelty. Tunbridge, therefore, was welcome. She wandered in woods and sketched trees and farmhouses; she read French novels as regularly as a person takes physic; she drove into Tunbridge Wells whenever there was the faintest promise of a play, a ball, a conjurer, or any musician likely to be applauded on credit. She slept a great deal. She quarrelled with Mamma and Frank before luncheon. She found the village school and attended it—first petting the girls and thwarting the mistress with smiles, then scolding the girls and laughing at the teacher with the same smiles sharpened. She was constant at church, of course.

It was a pretty little church—one of those ancient bijous which look as if they had been built in the reign of King Somebody, repaired in the reign of King Anybody, and redecorated last week by a committee. There were painted windows that threw red and blue patches on the prayer-books like spilled wine; carved saints’ heads peeped down as if listening; gilt texts shone with a hard metallic piety; and the pews were open, so that no one could hide from the eyes of neighbours or Heaven. Blanche began at once a most correct High-Church altar-cover, stitching little crosses with the patience of a seraph and the temper—well, with the temper of Blanche. For a while she passed for a saint with the clergyman, whom she took in with consummate art; coaxed him, wheedled him, fondled him—an entire liturgy of flattery—so that poor Mrs. Smirke, who had at first been charmed, then borne, then become chilly, at last grew almost mad with jealousy.

Mrs. Smirke was the wife of our old acquaintance Smirke—Pen’s former tutor and poor Helen’s former suitor. When Helen refused him, he had consoled himself (under maternal direction) with a young lady from Clapham. When his mamma died, his opinions, like his hair, began to grow. Every day they developed—his views in church matters, his locks down his back. He cut off his coat-collar as if it were a snare of the Evil One; he gave up the curl on his forehead (once as dear to him as doctrine); he gave up the neckcloth tie, and at last gave up any tie at all, as though the smallest knot were a compromise with Rome. On Fridays he went without dinner; he read the Roman Hours; he intimated, gently but distinctly, that he was ready to receive confessions in the vestry, as if the parish were full of secret Borgias. The most harmless creature alive, he was denounced as a black and dangerous Jesuit by Muffin of the Dissenting chapel and Mr. Simeon Knight at the old church—men who could smell Popery in a candlestick at twenty paces.

Mr. Smirke had built his chapel-of-ease with the money left him by his mother at Clapham. Lord! what would that excellent lady have said could she have heard a table called an altar!—seen candlesticks on it!—received letters dated on the Feast of Saint So-and-so or the Vigil of Saint What’s-his-name! Yet all these things the Clapham boy practised with conscientious simplicity, and his faithful wife followed him, step by step, as if holiness consisted chiefly in keeping pace.

But when Blanche held a conference of near two hours in the vestry with Mr. Smirke, Belinda paced up and down on the grass among the two little gravestones already there, wishing—oh, with what fervour—that there were a third, only so it need not be hers. She fancied her husband, in his long hair and loose collar, offered up—himself—to that creature who had infatuated him in a fortnight. She pictured the convent, the veil, the renunciation, and all the rest of the melodrama; and her neighbours, meanwhile, pictured Smirke in direct correspondence with the Bishop of Rome, and Belinda bewailing errors to her even more odious than death. Yet Smirke meant no earthly harm. The post never brought him any letters from the Pope. He thought Blanche, at first, the most pious, gifted, right-thinking, fascinating person he had ever met; her manner of singing the chants delighted him into open-mouthed rapture—tea-less and bread-and-butter-less, as inspiration commonly is.

He had heard that the opera was fascinating, but had only once attended any exhibition of that kind—an event he mentioned with a blush and a sigh, as though he had been caught in a tambourine. It was on the day he had accompanied Helen and her son to the play at Chatteris. He could not conceive anything more delicious—more celestial, he had almost said—than Miss Amory’s music. She had a precious soul; remarkable talents; to all outward seeming the most heavenly disposition—etcetera, etcetera. Such was the kind of talk with which, being at the height of his own fever and bewitchment, Smirke discoursed to Arthur Pendennis when Arthur came down to pass a few days at Tunbridge Wells with the Begum.

The meeting of the old acquaintances was cordial. Arthur loved anybody who loved his mother; and Smirke could speak on that theme with real feeling, in a tone at once kind and melancholy, with his eyelids lowered and his fair head bowed slightly as if to a perpetual hymn. They told each other a hundred things—those little biographies we hand round like family recipes, each man seasoning his own with what he can bear to taste. Smirke observed, with modest emphasis, that Arthur would perceive his—his views on Church matters had developed since their former acquaintance. Mrs. Smirke, exemplary in everything, seconded these views with all her endeavours, as if opinions were joints to be basted.

Arthur was immensely amused—at Smirke’s airs, follies, and simplicity; at the blank stock, the long hair; at the real goodness and friendliness that made the whole absurdity innocent. And Smirke’s praises of Blanche both pleased and surprised him, and made him regard her with eyes of particular favour.

The truth is, Blanche was very glad to see Arthur; as one is glad, in the country, to see a man who brings down the last London news like a hamper of delicate provisions. He could talk better than most country-folks; at least he could talk that darling London jargon—so dear to London people, so indispensable to them, and so little understood by persons “out of the world,” who have the misfortune to speak plainly.

The first day Pen came down he kept Blanche laughing for hours after dinner. She sang with redoubled spirit. She did not scold her mother; she fondled and kissed her, to the Begum’s honest surprise, as though affection were a new dish she had just learned to dress. When bedtime came she said “Déjà!” with the prettiest regret in the world, and squeezed Arthur’s hand quite fondly. Arthur, who was of that turn that eyes very moderately bright can dazzle, gave her little palm a cordial pressure in return.

Later, standing at his window, he looked out into the night and took his thoughts, as men do, with their smoke. The air had the clean coolness that makes a cigar taste more itself; the summer hush was broken only by far-off hoofs on a road and the soft, living stir of leaves—an honest soundscape, not the clanking, brazen, coach-and-cry racket of London. The little Saxon church lay in the moonlight, white and tidy, as if Heaven kept it under glass.

“She is very much improved,” thought Pen. “Very much. I suppose the Begum won’t mind my smoking with the window open. She’s a jolly good old woman, and Blanche is immensely improved. I liked her manner with her mother to-night. I liked her laughing way with that stupid young cub of a boy, whom they oughtn’t to allow to get tipsy. She sang those little verses very prettily; they were devilish pretty verses too, though I say it who shouldn’t say it.”

And he hummed the tune Blanche had put to some verses of his own.

“Ah! what a fine night! How jolly a cigar is at night! What a comfort it is to hear nothing but the world breathing, instead of London grinding its teeth! I wonder what old Warrington’s doing? Yes, she’s a dayvlish nice little thing, as my uncle says.”

“Oh, heavenly!” broke out a voice from a clematis-covered casement near by—a girl’s voice: the voice of the author of “Mes Larmes.”

Pen burst into a laugh, and leaned out. “Don’t tell about my smoking,” he said.

“Oh! go on! I adore it,” cried the lady of “Mes Larmes,” with the same lavish enthusiasm that made her distribute adjectives as if they were comfits. “Heavenly night! heavenly, heavenly moon! but I must shut my window, and not talk to you on account of les moeurs. How droll they are, les moeurs! Adieu.”

And Pen began to sing the goodnight to Don Basilio, as if the moon were an audience and the village hedges a row of boxes.

Next day they walked in the fields together, laughing and chattering—the gayest pair of friends. They talked about the days of their youth, and Blanche became prettily sentimental, as if she were tasting an old sauce and finding it agreeably sharp. They talked about Laura—dearest Laura. Blanche had loved her as a sister. Was she happy with that odd Lady Rockminster? Wouldn’t she come and stay with them at Tunbridge? Oh, what walks they would take together! what songs they would sing—the old, old songs! Laura’s voice was splendid. Did Arthur—she must call him Arthur—remember the songs they sang in the happy old days, now he was grown such a great man and had such a succès?

And the day after, enlivened by a ramble through woods to Penshurst, with a sight of that pleasant park and hall—where the rooks’ cawing and the distant thud of an axe in timber seemed to belong to the place as naturally as the scent of bruised fern—came that conversation with the curate which has been narrated, and which set Arthur thinking more and more.

“Is she all this perfection?” he asked himself. “Has she become serious and religious? Does she tend schools and visit the poor? Is she kind to her mother and brother? Yes, I am sure of that; I have seen her.”

And walking with his old tutor over the little parish, and going to see the school, it was with inexpressible delight that Pen found Blanche seated instructing the children—her voice lowered into an industrious softness, her fingers busy with slates and spelling-books; and he fancied how patient she must be, how good-natured, how ingenuous, how really simple in her tastes, and unspoiled by the world.

“And do you really like the country?” he asked, as they walked together.

“I should like never to see that odious city again,” Blanche cried. “O Arthur—that is, Mr.—well, Arthur then—one’s good thoughts grow up in these sweet woods and calm solitudes, like those flowers which won’t bloom in London, you know. The gardener comes and changes our balconies once a week. I don’t think I shall bear to look London in the face again—its odious, smoky, brazen face! But—heigho!”

“Why that sigh, Blanche?”

“Never mind why.”

“Yes, I do mind why. Tell me—tell me everything.”

“I wish you hadn’t come down;” and out came a second edition of “Mes Soupirs,” freshly printed and very damp.

“You don’t want me, Blanche?”

“I don’t want you to go away. I don’t think this house will be very happy without you, and that’s why I wish you never had come.”

Here “Mes Soupirs” were laid aside and “Mes Larmes” began in good earnest. Ah! what answer is given to those in the eyes of a young woman? What is the method employed for drying them? What took place?

O ringdoves and roses, O dews and wildflowers, O waving greenwoods and balmy airs of summer! Here were two battered London rakes, for a moment taking themselves in, and fancying they were in love with each other like Phyllis and Corydon. When one thinks of country houses and country walks, and the way a quiet field can muffle the world’s harsh noises until a sigh sounds like fate, one wonders that any man is left unmarried.

Easy as Arthur Pendennis was with Warrington—easy as a man can be who will tell you, over a chop, the entire history of his hat—how did it come to pass that he could not tell George the trifling occurrences at that villa near Tunbridge Wells? He spoke freely enough of meeting old Smirke again (as a man tells of stumbling on a forgotten spice in the back of a cupboard), and of Mrs. Smirke, and of the church with its Anglo-Norman arches that looked, to his fancy, like ribs of some stone beast; he told of the plan of leaving Clapham, and of Rome, and of pictures, and of all manner of things that could be talked of without committing the soul. But when Warrington, with that quiet drawl of his, let Blanche’s name fall—just so, as you might drop a bay-leaf into a pot to see whether it floats—Pen’s answers became thin broth. He said she was good-natured and clever; that, rightly guided, she might make no such bad wife after all; that for the present he had no intention of marrying; that his romance was done; that he was content with his lot; and the like—phrases that fill the mouth and starve the meaning.

Yet to Lamb Court in the Temple there came, now and again, little satin envelopes, pretty enough to be sugared almonds, superscribed in the neatest hand, and sealed with one of those admirable ciphers which say, “This is nobody’s business,” and thereby proclaim it to all the world. Had Warrington been curious enough to watch his friend’s correspondence (which he was not), or had the cipher been made for human eyesight, it might have told him that Mr. Arthur was writing to a young lady whose initials were B. A. Pen answered these dainty missives in his best manner: news of the town, little jokes, small points of wit, and, no doubt, little verses; for Blanche had a Muse who wrote “Mes Larmes,” and a man of Pen’s ingenuity will never refuse a rhyme any more than a cook refuses a truffle. Blanche, you perceive, offers “branch,” “stanch,” “launch,” and other convenient syllables—like a well-stocked larder. Indeed, it was about this time, we incline to believe, that those love-verses of Mr. Pen’s appeared which afterwards made such a pleasing figure in the “Roseleaves,” that charming annual edited by Lady Violet Lebas, and decorated with portraits of female nobility by Mr. Pinkney; and that the lines, before they were pinned like paper roses into print, were first sent, warm from the pen, to Blanche by post—cornets, as it were, blown before Pinkney’s garland.

“Verses are all very well,” said Major Pendennis, finding Pen one day scratching down an artless effusion at the Club while he waited for his dinner—an hour sacred, in a well-ordered life, to the contemplation of sauces. “And letter-writing, if mamma allows it, and between such old country friends there may be a correspondence, and that sort of thing. But mind, Pen—don’t commit yourself, my boy. For who knows what the doose may happen? Make your letters safe. I never wrote a letter in all my life that would commit me; and demmy, sir, I have had some experience of women.”

And the Major—growing more confidential with age, and as fond of a cautionary tale as of a well-hung venison—told instances out of “Society” which, to his mind, proved that ardour is a fine thing in a cutlet and a bad thing in a note. Young Spoony, for example, having addressed the widow Naylor in poetical language, found himself honoured by a remonstrance from her brother Colonel Flint, and compelled into matrimony with a lady old enough to have been his nurse. Miss Louisa Salter, again, having at last secured young Sir John Bird, Hopwood of the Blues, was undone by some letters of her own which Hopwood produced: Sir John withdrew, and afterwards married Miss Stickney of Lyme Regis. The Major might not read much, but he observed; and out of the great world-book—thumbed, dog-eared, and stained with club-gravy—he could quote a multitude of modern instances.

Pen laughed, blushed a little, and promised to be cautious. He blushed, perhaps, because he already was cautious; because, in his letters to Miss Blanche, he had from instinct—or honesty, if you choose—refrained from any avowals that might compromise him. “Don’t you remember the lesson I had in Lady Mirabel’s—Miss Fotheringay’s affair?” he said, with mock humility. “I’m not to be caught again, uncle.” Old Pendennis congratulated himself on the prudence of his nephew, and was pleased to see Arthur taking his place as a man of the world.

Had Warrington been consulted, his opinion would likely have seasoned the dish with other spices. He might have said that a foolish, open letter is more honest than an adroit compliment with a back-door; that only a knave or a coward goes wooing with a retreat prepared. But Pen said nothing to Warrington of Blanche; for he knew pretty well that he was not innocent, and that George’s verdict would have been sharp as vinegar.

While Pen was thus cooking little gallantries for the post, fate began roasting another man at a slow fire. Colonel Altamont had been absent some weeks on his foreign tour, and Sir Francis Clavering had retired into the country, according to his compact with Major Pendennis; when ill-luck fell heavily on the sole remaining partner of the little firm in Shepherd’s Inn. When Strong had refused Altamont’s loan at parting—out of conscience and delicacy—he made a sacrifice which afterwards pinched him like a too-tight boot. Why should a fellow in want refuse a kind offer kindly made? Why should a thirsty man decline a pitcher because the outside of it is a little soiled? Strong’s conscience smote him for having been so scrupulous about money the other had fairly come by and generously proffered; and now, when it was too late, he thought ruefully that Altamont’s cash would have been as well in his pocket as in that of a gaming-house proprietor at Baden or Ems, where his Excellency would be sure to leave his Derby winnings.

It was whispered among tradesmen, bill-discounters, and other gentlefolk of commerce, that Strong and the baronet had parted company, and that the Captain’s “paper” was now no better than pastry—very fine to look at, and eaten in a mouthful. The same tradesmen, who had hitherto put a wonderful confidence in Strong—who could resist his jolly face and honest manner?—now poured in their bills with a unanimity as cowardly as it was punctual. Knocks at the chamber-door were constant. Tailors, bootmakers, pastrycooks who had furnished dinners (and had been praised for their gravies in better days), in their own persons or by their boys, held levees on Strong’s stairs. To these clamorous folk were added a quieter species, more dangerous because less noisy—lawyers’ clerks—who lurked about the Inn, or concerted with Mr. Campion’s young man hard by, carrying dismal pocketbooks in which lay copies of writs to be served on Edward Strong, requiring him to appear, etc. etc.

Strong, with not a guinea in his pocket, had of course no refuge but the Englishman’s castle. Into it he retired, shutting outer and inner door upon the enemy, and not quitting his stronghold till after nightfall. Against that barrier the foe would knock and curse in vain, while the Chevalier peeped from behind the little curtain he had hung over the letter-box orifice, and had the miserable satisfaction of seeing the furious faces of clerk and dun dash up to the door and retreat. But as they could not always keep watch—any more than one can keep a kettle singing forever without coals—the enemies of the Chevalier sometimes left him free.

When pressed, Strong was not quite alone. He had allies, and, like a man besieged, he established signals. His friends kept the garrison from starving by bringing in supplies and by bringing, too, what is more nourishing than bread—cheerfulness. Two faithful allies were Huxter and Miss Fanny Bolton. When hostile visitors prowled about the Inn, Fanny’s little sisters were taught a particular cry or jodel, which they whooped innocently in the court; when Fanny and Huxter came to visit Strong, they sang the same note at his door; the barrier would open, the honest garrison come out smiling, provisions and a pot of porter would be carried in, and the beleaguered one passed a comfortable night. There are men who could not live under this excitement. Strong had seen service. He could stand a siege and keep his temper sweet, as a good cook keeps a stew sweet—by patience, and by not letting it boil over.

Besides allies, Strong had secured—under difficulties—that still more necessary aid, a retreat. It has been mentioned how Messrs. Costigan and Bows lived next door to Captain Strong, and how the window of one of their rooms stood not far from the kitchen-window in the upper story of Strong’s chambers. A leaden water-pipe and gutter served both; and Strong, looking out one day, saw he could spring easily to his neighbour’s sill and clamber by the pipe. He had laughingly shown this refuge to his chum Altamont, and they agreed it would be best not to mention it to Captain Costigan, whose own duns were numerous, and who would be constantly flying down the pipe into Strong’s rooms if he knew of such a roadway.

But now the evil days were come, Strong made use of the passage; and one afternoon burst in upon Bows and Costigan with his jolly face, explaining that the enemy was waiting on his staircase and that he had taken this means of slipping them. So while Mr. Marks’s aides-de-camp were in attendance in the passage of No. 3, Strong walked down the steps of No. 4, dined at the Albion, went to the play, and returned home at midnight—to the astonishment of Mrs. Bolton and Fanny, who had not seen him quit his chambers and could not conceive how he had passed the line of sentries.

He bore this siege for some weeks with admirable spirit; as only an old soldier can, for the pains and privations were enough to depress a man of ordinary courage. What vexed and riled him—his own phrase—was the infernal indifference and cowardly ingratitude of Clavering. Strong wrote letter after letter; the baronet never acknowledged them by a single word, nor sent the smallest remittance; though “a five-pound note,” Strong said, “would have been a fortune.”

Better days, however, were in store for the Chevalier. In the midst of his despondency came a welcome aid.

“Yes—if it hadn’t been for this good fellow here,” Strong said afterwards—“for a good fellow you are, Altamont, my boy, and hang me if I don’t stand by you as long as I live—I think, Pendennis, it would have been all up with Ned Strong. I was the fifth week of being kept a prisoner—couldn’t always be risking my neck across that water-pipe and taking my walks abroad through poor old Cos’s window—and my spirit was quite broken, sir. Dammy, quite beat. I was thinking of putting an end to myself, and should have done it in another week, when who should drop down from heaven but Altamont!”

“Heaven ain’t exactly the place, Ned,” said Altamont. “I came from Baden-Baden; and I’d had a deuced lucky month there, that’s all.”

“Well, sir,” Strong cried, “he took up Marks’s bill, and he paid the other fellows that were upon me, like a man—sir, that he did!”

“And I shall be very happy to stand a bottle of claret for this company,” said Mr. Altamont, blushing, “and as many more as the company chooses. Hallo, waiter! bring us a magnum of the right sort, d’ye hear? We’ll drink our healths all round—may every good fellow like Strong find another good fellow to stand by him at a pinch. That’s my sentiment, Mr. Pendennis, though I don’t like your name.”

“No? And why?” asked Arthur.

Strong pressed the Colonel’s foot under the table here; and Altamont, rather excited, filled another bumper, nodded to Pen, drank, and said that Pen was a gentleman, and that was sufficient, and they were all gentlemen.

This meeting of “all gentlemen” took place at Richmond, whither Pendennis had gone to dinner, and where he found the Chevalier and his friend at table in the coffee-room. Both were hilariously talkative and excited by wine; and Strong, an admirable story-teller, told his siege, his escapes, and his adventures with great liveliness and humour—describing the talk of the sheriff’s officers at his door, the pretty signals of Fanny, the grotesque exclamations of Costigan when the Chevalier burst in at his window, and his final rescue by Altamont—so graphically that his hearers could almost hear the Inn itself: the court’s hollow echo, the stair’s creak, the muffled thud of a dun’s impatient boot, and that childish jodel—bright as a bird-note against the thick, dirty city hum.

“As for me, it’s nothing,” Altamont said. “When a ship’s paid off, a chap spends his money, you know. And it’s the fellers at the black and red at Baden-Baden that did it. I won a good bit of money there, and intend to win a good bit more—don’t I, Strong? I’m going to take him with me. I’ve got a system. I’ll make his fortune, I tell you. I’ll make your fortune, if you like—dammy, everybody’s fortune. But what I’ll do, and no mistake, boys, I promise you: I’ll put in for that little Fanny. Dammy, sir, what d’ye think she did? She had two pound, and I’m blest if she didn’t go and lend it to Ned Strong! Didn’t she, Ned? Let’s drink her health.”

“With all my heart,” said Arthur, and pledged the toast cordially.

Mr. Altamont then began, with extraordinary volubility, to describe his system—how it was infallible if played coolly; how he had it from a chap at Baden who had lost by it, true, but only for want of capital; if he could have stood one more turn of the wheel he would have had all his money back; how he and several more chaps were going to make a bank and try it; how he would put in every shilling he was worth; how he had come back to England expressly to fetch his money and Captain Strong; how Strong should play for him; how he could trust Strong’s temper better than his own, and better than Bloundell-Bloundell or the Italian that “stood in.” As he emptied his bottle he unfolded plans and prospects to Pen, who listened with interest to the daring lawless good-humour of the man, and to the queer music of his talk—half sea-oath, half nursery generosity—beating time, as it were, to the clink of glasses and the scrape of chairs.

“I met that queer fellow Altamont the other day,” Pen said to his uncle, a day or two later.

“Altamont? What Altamont? There’s Lord Westport’s son,” said the Major.

“No, no; the fellow who came tipsy into Clavering’s dining-room when we were there,” said the nephew, laughing. “He said he didn’t like the name of Pendennis, though he did me the honour to think me a good fellow.”

“I don’t know any man of the name of Altamont—I give you my honour,” said the impenetrable Major; “and as for your acquaintance, I think the less you have to do with him the better, Arthur.”

Arthur laughed again. “He’s going to quit the country and make his fortune by a gambling system. He and my amiable college acquaintance, Bloundell, are partners; the Colonel takes out Strong as aide-de-camp. What is it that binds the Chevalier and Clavering, I wonder?”

“I should think,” said the Major, “mind you, Pen—I should think, but of course I have only the idea—that there has been something in Clavering’s previous life which gives these fellows, and some others, a certain power over him. And if there should be no such secret, which affair of ours, my boy—dammy, I say—ought to be a lesson to a man to keep himself straight in life, and not give any man a chance over him.”

“Why, I think you have some means of persuasion over Clavering, uncle, or why should he give me that seat in Parliament?”

“Clavering thinks he ain’t fit for Parliament,” the Major answered. “No more he is. What’s to prevent him putting you or anybody else into his place if he likes? Do you think Government or Opposition would make any bones about accepting the seat if he offered it? Why should you be more squeamish than the first men, and the most honourable men, and men of the highest birth and position—begad?” The Major had an answer of this sort to most of Pen’s objections; and Pen accepted them—not because he believed them, but because he wished to believe them. We do a thing—who of us has not?—not because everybody does it, but because we like it; and our acquiescence proves not that everybody is right, but that we and the world are poor creatures alike.

On his next visit to Tunbridge, Mr. Pen did not forget to amuse Miss Blanche with the history he had learned at Richmond: the Chevalier’s imprisonment, and Altamont’s gallant rescue. And after he had told it in his usual satirical way, he spoke with praise and a certain emotion of little Fanny’s generous behaviour—those two pounds lent out of a small purse, like the last loaf shared in a hard winter—and of Altamont’s enthusiasm on her behalf.

Miss Blanche was somewhat jealous, and a good deal piqued and curious about this Fanny. Among the many confidential little communications which Arthur made to Miss Amory in the course of their delightful rural drives and their sweet evening walks—where the hedges smelled of leaf-mould and last year’s apples, and the gravel underfoot gave that crisp, domestic whisper which is the very opposite of London’s iron roar—he would not omit a story so likely to interest her as that of the poor little Ariadne of Shepherd’s Inn. His own part in the drama he described, to do him justice, with becoming modesty; the moral he wished to draw being one in his satirical key: that women get over their first loves quite as easily as men do; that number one withdrawn, they transfer themselves to number two without much difficulty. And little Fanny was offered as an instance to prove it.

What griefs she had endured and surmounted, what bitter pangs of hopeless attachment she had borne, what time it had taken to heal the wounds of that tender little heart—Pen did not know, or perhaps did not choose to know. For he was at once modest and doubtful about his own power as a conqueror, and averse to believe he had made any dangerous ravage in that particular place. And yet his own argument told against him; for if, as he said, Miss Fanny was by this time in love with her surgical adorer—who had neither good looks, nor good manners, nor wit, nor anything but ardour and fidelity—must she not, in her first sickness of the love-complaint, have had a serious attack indeed, and suffered keenly for a man who certainly had more of the showy qualities that Mr. Huxter wanted?

“You wicked odious creature,” Miss Blanche said, “I believe you are enraged with Fanny for being so impudent as to forget you, and that you are actually jealous of Mr. Huxter.”

Perhaps Miss Amory was right; for a blush came, in spite of him, and tingled on Pen’s cheek—one of those slaps with which vanity keeps a man awake. Superseded! And by such a rival! By such a fellow as that—without any conceivable good quality! O Mr. Pendennis! If Nature had not made that provision for each sex in the credulity of the other—which sees good qualities where none exist, beauty in donkey’s ears, wit in their numskulls, and music in their bray—there would not be near so much marrying and giving in marriage as now obtains, and as is necessary for the continuance of the noble race.

“Jealous or not,” Pen said, “and, Blanche, I don’t say no, I should have liked Fanny to have come to a better end than that. I don’t like histories that end in that cynical way; and when we arrive at the conclusion of a pretty girl’s passion, to find such a figure as Huxter’s at the last page. Is life a compromise, my lady fair, and the end of the battle of love an ignoble surrender? Is the search for the Cupid which my poor little Psyche pursued in the darkness—the god of her soul’s longing—the god of the blooming cheek and rainbow pinions—to result in Huxter smelling of tobacco and gallypots? I wish—though I don’t see it in life—that people could be like Jenny and Jessamy, or my Lord and Lady Clementina in the story-books, and at once under the ceremony, and as it were at the parson’s benediction, become perfectly handsome and good and happy ever after.”

“And don’t you intend to be good and happy, pray, Monsieur le Misanthrope,” asked the author of “Mes Larmes,” with a charming moue, “and are you very discontented with your lot? and will your marriage be a compromise—and is your Psyche an odious vulgar wretch? You wicked satirical creature, I can’t abide you! You take the hearts of young things, play with them, and fling them away with scorn. You ask for love and trample on it. You—you make me cry, that you do, Arthur—and—and don’t—and I won’t be consoled in that way—and I think Fanny was quite right in leaving such a heartless creature.”

“Again, I don’t say no,” said Pen, looking gloomily at Blanche, and not offering to repeat the attempt at consolation which had drawn from her that sweet monosyllable “don’t.” “I don’t think I have much of what people call heart; but I don’t profess it. I made my venture when I was eighteen; I lighted my lamp and went in search of Cupid. And what was my discovery of love?—a vulgar dancing-woman. I failed, as everybody does—almost everybody; only it is luckier to fail before marriage than after.”

“Merci du choix, Monsieur,” said the Sylphide, making him a curtsey.

“Look, my little Blanche,” said Pen, taking her hand, his voice in that sad good-humour which is half confession and half performance; “at least I stoop to no flatteries.”

“Quite the contrary,” said Miss Blanche.

“And tell you no foolish lies, as vulgar men do. Why should you and I, with our experience, ape romance and dissemble passion? I do not believe Miss Blanche Amory to be peerless among the beautiful, nor the greatest poetess, nor the most surpassing musician, any more than I believe you to be the tallest woman in the whole world—like the giantess whose picture we saw as we rode through the fair yesterday. But if I don’t set you up as a heroine, neither do I offer you your very humble servant as a hero. But I think you are—well, there, I think you are very sufficiently good-looking.”

“Merci,” Miss Blanche said, with another curtsey.

“I think you sing charmingly. I’m sure you’re clever. I hope and believe you are good-natured—and that you will be companionable.”

Clavering Park had once known a gloom so complete that the very shutters seemed to have gone into mourning; when its master fled abroad, the house mourned after him like a deserted soup-tureen—huge, silver, and useless without a hand to stir it. Yet Sir Francis, returning to his own walls, did not bring spring with him. He inhabited only a few ground-floor rooms, as a man camps in the ruins of his own magnificence; and the rest of the mansion—passages, saloons, long galleries made for laughter—was closed up, silent, and cold, like an overbuilt larder in a hard winter.

His housekeeper and a helper from the lodge-gate attended him with that dutiful briskness which is half pity and half professional habit, and cooked a portion of the game he spent his dreary mornings in shooting. Even that comfort had a melancholy savor: the birds were roasted, yes, but without triumph—no bustling household to applaud the carving, no bright table-talk to make the gravy seem richer. The crack of the gun, the thud of a falling pheasant, the thin music of knives on plates in a half-empty dining-room: such were the domestic acoustics of Clavering Park now, where once the voices of guests had rolled through the corridors like a generous chorus.

Lightfoot, Sir Francis’s man, had slipped over to my Lady’s service; and (as Pen learned by letter from Mr. Smirke, who performed the ceremony) had carried out his prudent intention of marrying Mrs. Bonner, my Lady’s woman. Mrs. Bonner—mature, saving, and resolute—had long kept her feelings in a tidy drawer, like good napery; but at last, being struck by the charms of youth, she brought them out with her bank-book and her person, and bestowed both upon Lightfoot. Their joint ambition was to be landlord and landlady of the Clavering Arms; and it was agreed they should remain in Lady Clavering’s service until quarter-day, then take possession of their inn and its beer, its beds, its bar, its unavoidable quarrels, and its perpetual clatter of arriving boots.

Pen promised graciously that when Sir Francis vacated his seat in Parliament in the young man’s favor, he would give his election dinner at that very Clavering Arms. And as Pen’s uncle had arranged it—Clavering seeming able to refuse him nothing—Arthur came down in September to Clavering Park. The Baronet was very glad of a companion: solitude makes a man listen too hard to his own thoughts, and Sir Francis preferred other people’s purses and laughter. Within a couple of days, Pen provided him with the small ready money he desired; and no sooner did these modest funds warm Sir Francis’s pocket than his health and spirits, in the most miraculous manner, demanded business at Chatteris and the neighboring watering-places, of which the county boasts many—chiefly when there are race-grounds and billiard-rooms to transact it in. Off he went to “see to his affairs,” leaving Arthur master of the great silent house and its echoing respectability.

Arthur could live alone well enough. He had the uncommon talent of being able to dine with his own company and find it tolerable—especially when he had books, paper, and a cigar. He could walk with the gamekeeper of a morning and read of an evening; and if the Park’s emptiness had a sound, it was not a human one but a natural one—the wind in the trees, the distant caw, the soft, satisfied sigh of a fire settling down after it has done its duty.

In truth, Pen found the society of Sir Francis perfectly intolerable within two or three days; and with a mischievous satisfaction he had offered the pecuniary aid which the other solicited, providing him at once with the means of fleeing his own house. Besides, our ingenious friend had work to do: he must ingratiate himself with the townspeople of Clavering and the voters of the borough he hoped to represent. He set himself to it with the more eagerness because he remembered how unpopular he had been there before—and because his sense of humor made him relish the whole performance.

Naturally rather reserved and silent in public, he became all at once as frank, easy, and jovial as Captain Strong. He laughed with anybody who would exchange a laugh; shook hands right and left with a cordiality that deserved a patent; appeared at market-day and the farmers’ ordinary; and in fine behaved like a consummate hypocrite, which is to say, like a gentleman of spotless integrity bent on gaining a seat and willing to pay for it in smiles.

The town accepted him with that practical appetite with which it accepted everything: as one takes a free sample from a shop, knowing perfectly well it is meant to tempt you into buying a whole pound. A glib tongue costs the distributor nothing; the receiver likes to taste it. Pen went about laboriously simple, adroitly pleased, a wholly different being from the scornful young dandy the inhabitants remembered ten years ago. He had the air of a man who not only asked after your wife but could imagine her making decent broth; who not only admired your harvest but could smell the wheat. It was astonishing how much more human a candidate becomes when he pretends to possess a palate.

The Rectory was shut up. Doctor Portman was off to Harrogate with his gout and his family—an absence Pen deplored in a letter in which, in a few kind words, he expressed regret at missing his old friend, whose advice he wanted and whose aid he might one day require. But Pen consoled himself by making acquaintance with Mr. Simcoe, the opposition preacher; with the two partners of the cloth-factory at Chatteris; and with the Independent preacher there—all of whom he met at the Clavering Athenaeum, which the Liberal party had set up in the “advanced spirit of the age,” and perhaps in opposition to the aristocratic old reading-room where the Edinburgh Review had once scarcely been admitted and where no tradesmen were allowed an entrance, as if print itself became contagious when handled by a man with a shop.

Pen propitiated the younger cloth partner by inviting him to dine at the Park; he complimented the Honourable Mrs. Simcoe with hares and partridges from the same quarter, along with a request to read her husband’s last sermon. And being a little unwell one day, the rascal took advantage of the circumstance to show his tongue to Mr. Huxter, who sent medicines and called the next morning. Old Pendennis would have been delighted with his pupil’s dexterity. Pen himself was amused with the sport, and his success put him in a wicked good-humor, as of a man who has found the secret spice by which plain fare is made palatable to any company.

Yet when, at night, he walked out of Clavering after presiding at an Athenaeum meeting or enduring an evening with Mrs. Simcoe (who, with her husband, was properly awed by the young Londoner’s reputation), other thoughts came on him. There are places that do not let you be merely a politician; they make you a son.

Crossing the old familiar bridge over the rushing Brawl, he heard the water’s ceaseless talk—an ancient, honest sound that no committee had ever voted into being and no fashionable doctrine could silence. And there among the trees stood his cottage of Fairoaks, its dark outline clear against a starlit sky. In the window of the room he remembered best, there was still a light.

It seemed to pursue him with a wan reproach, as though it were his mother’s spirit watching and warning. The night was very clear; the stars shone keen as newly-whetted knives; the river ran on, tireless. The old home trees whispered and moved gently over the cottage roof. In the faint glimmer lay the terrace where, as a boy, he had walked on summer evenings—ardent, trustful, unspotted, untried, sheltered as yet from the world’s contamination in the pure and anxious bosom of love. The clock of the near town struck midnight with a clang that broke his reverie like a dropped dish in a hushed room; and he went onwards through the lodge into the Clavering avenue and under the dark arcades of rustling limes.

When next he saw the cottage, it was smiling in sunset. The bedroom windows were open where the light had burned the night before. Captain Stokes of the Bombay Artillery—Pen’s tenant (whose mother, old Mrs. Stokes, lived in Clavering)—received his landlord with cordiality; showed him over the grounds and the new pond he had made in the back garden from the stables; talked confidentially of roof and chimneys; and begged Mr. Pendennis to name a day when he would do himself and Mrs. Stokes the pleasure to, etc.

Pen, who had been a fortnight in the country, excused himself for not calling sooner by frankly owning he had not had the heart to do it.

“I understand you, sir,” the Captain said; and Mrs. Stokes, who had slipped away at the bell (how odd it seemed to Pen to ring the bell!), presently came down in her best gown, surrounded by her children. The young ones clambered about Stokes; the boy jumped into an arm-chair.

It was Pen’s father’s arm-chair. Arthur remembered the days when he would as soon have thought of mounting the King’s throne as of seating himself in that chair. He asked if Miss Stokes—who was the very image of her mamma—could play: he should like to hear a tune on that piano.

She played. The old piano sounded again—enfeebled by age, its notes thinned and tremulous, as if the instrument itself had grown old in remembering. He did not listen to the player. He listened to Laura singing as in the days of their youth; he saw his mother bending and beating time over the girl’s shoulder. Memory has its own dialect, perfectly understood by the heart and perfectly untranslatable to any other listener in the room. No dictionary in the world can render it.

The dinner at Fairoaks, given in Pen’s honor by his tenant, was very stupid and melancholy for Pen at first. Old Mrs. Stokes was there; Captain Glanders; Squire Hobnel; and the clergyman and his lady from Tinckleton. The talk went round and round like a dish passed too often—polite, lukewarm, and growing duller at each circuit—until a waiter from Clavering arrived to assist the captain’s stable-boy and Mrs. Stokes’s butler. Pen remembered the fellow as a street boy; he was now barber in the place, and, as if to prove that advancement does not at once improve one’s grip, he dropped a plate over Pen’s shoulder.

“I suppose, Hodson, your hands are slippery with bear’s-grease,” Mr. Hobnell remarked (who also employed him). “He’s always dropping the crockery about, that Hodson is—haw, haw!”

Hodson blushed and looked so disconcerted that Pen burst out laughing; and by that lucky crack of china, good-humor and hilarity were the order of the evening. For the second course there was a hare and partridges top and bottom; and when, after the withdrawal of the servants, Pen said to the Vicar of Tinckleton, “I think, Mr. Stooks, you should have asked Hodson to cut the hare,” the joke was taken instantly by the clergyman, then by Captains Stokes and Glanders, and then by Mr. Hobnell—who arrived rather late in the laughter, but with an immense guffaw, as men do who like mirth best when it has been chewed for them.

While Mr. Pen was in the country practicing his agreeable hypocrisies, the lady of his choice—if not of his affections—came up to London from the Tunbridge villa bound upon shopping expeditions and important business. She was accompanied by old Mrs. Bonner, her mother’s maid: a woman who had lived with Blanche since infancy, quarrelled with her at every stage of growth, and loved her at all of them; and who, being about to quit Lady Clavering’s service for the hymeneal state, was anxious—like a good soul—to bestow some token of respectful kindness upon her old and young mistress before she left them altogether, to take up her post as the wife of Lightfoot and landlady of the Clavering Arms.

Mrs. Bonner took advantage of Miss Blanche’s taste to make the purchase she intended for her ladyship. She requested Blanche to choose something for herself, something that should be to her liking and remind her of her old nurse who had attended her through wakeful nights, teething, childish fever, and all the small tragedies by which babies educate their elders in fatigue. The purchases were made; and as the nurse insisted on buying an immense Bible for Blanche, the young lady suggested that Bonner should purchase a large Johnson’s Dictionary for her mamma. Each of the two women might certainly profit by the present; and Blanche, who liked to do mischief under the guise of moral improvement, enjoyed the thought.

Then Mrs. Bonner invested money in bargains in linen-drapery that might be useful at the Clavering Arms, and bought a red-and-yellow neck-handkerchief which Blanche recognized at once as intended for Mr. Lightfoot. Younger than herself by at least five-and-twenty years, Mrs. Bonner regarded that youth with a fondness at once parental and conjugal and loved to lavish ornaments on his person, which already glittered with pins, rings, studs, chains, and seals purchased at the good creature’s expense. One could almost hear the little metallic jingle of those vanities, as if Lightfoot had been fitted with a harness of courtship.

It was in the Strand that Mrs. Bonner made her purchases, aided by Blanche, who liked the fun very well. And when the old lady had bought everything she desired and was leaving the shop, Blanche—with a smiling face and a sweet bow to one of the shopmen—said, “Pray, sir, will you have the kindness to show us the way to Shepherd’s Inn?”

Shepherd’s Inn was but a few score yards off; Old Castle Street was close by. The elegant young shopman pointed out the turning. Blanche and her companion walked off.

“Shepherd’s Inn!” Bonner inquired. “What can you want in Shepherd’s Inn, Miss Blanche? Mr. Strong lives there. Do you want to go and see the Captain?”

“I should like to see the Captain very well. I like the Captain; but it is not him I want. I want to see a dear little good girl, who was very kind to—to Mr. Arthur when he was so ill last year, and saved his life almost; and I want to thank her and ask her if she would like anything. I looked out several of my dresses on purpose this morning, Bonner!”

And she looked at Bonner as though virtue were a ribbon and she had tied it on herself with uncommon skill. Blanche was very fond of sugar-plums; she would have fed the poor on them when she had had enough, and given a country girl a ball-dress when she had worn it and tired of it.

“Pretty girl—pretty young woman!” mumbled Mrs. Bonner. “I know I want no pretty young women to come about Lightfoot.” And in imagination she peopled the Clavering Arms with a harem of the most hideous chambermaids and barmaids, all elbows and freckles, none with a tempting mouth.

Blanche, in pink and blue with feathers, flowers, and trinkets—no chatelaine existed yet, or she would surely have worn one like a portable shop—entered Shepherd’s Inn like a radiant proclamation of fashion. Her shot-silk dress whispered as she moved; her mantle fell with studied grace; her parasol made a little private rustle against the city’s harsher noises. She bewildered Mrs. Bolton, who was scrubbing the lodge-floor and whose ears were full of the wet slap of brush on stone and the sour hiss of brown-soap water. Betsy-Jane and Ameliar-Ann looked at Blanche with delight, as children look at iced cakes behind glass.

Blanche smiled upon them with ineffable sweetness and protection; like Rowena going to see Rebecca; like Marie Antoinette visiting the poor in a famine; like the Marchioness of Carabas alighting from her carriage-and-four at a pauper-tenant’s door and taking from John No. II the packet of Epsom salts for the invalid’s benefit, carrying it with her own imperial hand into the sick-room. Blanche felt a queen stepping down from her throne to visit a subject and enjoyed all the bland consciousness of doing a good action.

“My good woman! I want to see Fanny—Fanny Bolton; is she here?”

Mrs. Bolton, seeing such splendor in such a place, suspected at once it must be a play-actor or something worse.

“What do you want with Fanny, pray?” she asked.

“I am Lady Clavering’s daughter—you have heard of Sir Francis Clavering? And I wish very much indeed to see Fanny Bolton.”

“Pray step in, miss. Betsy-Jane, where’s Fanny?”

Betsy-Jane said Fanny had gone into No. 3 staircase, on which Mrs. Bolton said she was probably in Strong’s rooms and bade the child go and see.

“In Captain Strong’s rooms! Oh, let us go to Captain Strong’s rooms,” cried Miss Blanche. “I know him very well. You dearest little girl, show us the way to Captain Strong!” For the lodge-floor reeked of scrubbing, and the goddess did not like the smell of brown-soap; it offended her as industrial odors offend poets—by reminding them that cleanliness has a price and a sound.

And as they passed up the stairs, a gentleman by the name of Costigan, who happened to be swaggering about the court and gave a very knowing look with his “oi” under Blanche’s bonnet, remarked to himself, “That’s a devilish foine gyurll, bedad, goan up to Sthrong and Altamont: they’re always having foine gyurlls up their stairs.”

“Hallo—hwhat’s that?” he presently said, looking up at the windows. From them issued piercing shrieks.

At the sound of a distressed female voice, the intrepid Cos rushed up the stairs as fast as his old legs would carry him, nearly overthrown by Strong’s servant descending. Costigan found the outer door of Strong’s chambers open and began to thunder at the knocker. After many fierce knocks, the inner door was partially unclosed and Strong’s head appeared.

“It’s oi, me boy. Hwhat’s that noise, Sthrong?” asked Costigan.

“Go to the d——!” was the only answer, and the door was shut on Cos’s venerable red nose. He went downstairs muttering threats, vowing he would have satisfaction for the indignity—though indignities, like cheap spirits, were a commodity he had taken in often and seldom paid for.

Meanwhile, the reader, more fortunate than Captain Costigan, may be made acquainted with the secret withheld from that officer.

It has been said how generous Mr. Altamont could be; and when well supplied with funds, how liberally he spent them. Of a hospitable turn, he had no greater pleasure than drinking in company; so there was no man more welcome at Greenwich and Richmond than the Emissary of the Nawaub of Lucknow. Now it chanced that on the very day when Blanche and Mrs. Bonner climbed to Strong’s room in Shepherd’s Inn, the Colonel had invited Miss Delaval of the ——— Theatre Royal and her mother, Mrs. Hodge, to a little party down the river; it had been agreed they were to meet at chambers and then walk down to a landing in the Strand to take water.

So when Mrs. Bonner and Mes Larmes came to the door, where Grady, Altamont’s servant, stood, the domestic said, “Walk in, ladies,” with the utmost affability, and led them into a room arranged as if they had been expected. Indeed, two bouquets from Covent Garden—Altamont’s tender gallantry—waited upon the table.

Blanche smelt at a bouquet and put her dainty nose into it; she tripped about, peeped behind curtains, examined books and prints, and noticed—among these bachelor curiosities—the plan of the Clavering estate hanging on the wall like a recipe for property. She asked after Captain Strong and almost forgot him in the pleasure of the adventure: the odd, delightful, droll little notion of being in bachelor chambers in a queer old City place! The whole inn had its own soundscape—doors thudding, distant kettles singing, feet and voices muffled by stairwells—but here there was perfume in the air, as if flowers had been used to translate the room into a more fashionable language.

Grady, meanwhile, having produced a pair of ample varnished boots, disappeared into his master’s room. Blanche had hardly leisure to remark how big the boots were and how unlike Mr. Strong’s.

“The women’s come,” said Grady, helping his master into them.

“Did you ask ’em if they would take a glass of anything?” asked Altamont.

Grady came out. “He says, will you take anything to drink?” the domestic asked.

Blanche, amused with the artless question, broke into a pretty little laugh and asked Mrs. Bonner, “Shall we take anything to drink?”

“Well, you may take it or lave it,” said Mr. Grady, who thought his offer slighted and did not like the contemptuous manners of the newcomers, and so left them.

“Will we take anything to drink?” Blanche asked again, and laughed again—her laughter, in that confined space, sounding too bright for the dingy staircase beyond, like a silver spoon clinking in a cracked mug.

“Grady!” bawled a voice from within—a voice that made Mrs. Bonner start.

Grady did not answer. His song was heard far off from the kitchen, his upper room, where he was singing at his work.

“Grady, my coat!” roared the voice again.

“Why, that is not Mr. Strong’s voice,” said the Sylphide, still half laughing. “Grady, my coat! Bonner, who is Grady, my coat? We ought to go away.”

Bonner still looked puzzled at the sound—puzzled, and then frightened, as if a forgotten word from a dead dialect had suddenly been spoken aloud.

The bedroom door opened, and the individual who had called for his coat appeared without it. He nodded to the women and walked across the room.

“I beg your pardon, ladies. Grady, bring my coat down, sir! Well, my dears, it’s a fine day, and we’ll have a jolly lark at—”

He said no more, for here Mrs. Bonner—staring at him with scared eyes—suddenly shrieked, “Amory! Amory!” and fell back screaming and fainting in her chair.

The man, so apostrophised, looked at her an instant; then rushed up to Blanche, seized her, and kissed her.

“Yes, Betsy,” he said, “by G—it is me. Mary Bonner knew me. What a fine gal we’ve grown! But it’s a secret, mind. I’m dead, though I’m your father. Your poor mother don’t know it. What a pretty gal we’ve grown! Kiss me—kiss me close, my Betsy? D—— it, I love you: I’m your old father.”

Betsy—or Blanche—looked quite bewildered and began to scream too: once, twice, thrice. It was those piercing shrieks Captain Costigan had heard from the court below.

At the sound, the perplexed parent clasped his hands—his wristbands open, and on one brawny arm letters tattooed in blue—and rushed to his room. He came back with an eau-de-Cologne bottle from a grand silver dressing-case, and began liberally sprinkling Bonner and Blanche, as though a flood of scent could wash away shock, as though fragrance were an absolution. The room, already perfumed by flowers, became a cloud of sharp, spirituous sweetness; the air stung the nose and caught at the throat—too much elegance at once, like too much seasoning flung into a stew to disguise doubtful meat.

The screams brought in the other occupants: Grady from the kitchen, and Strong from his apartment in the upper story. Strong, one glance at the women’s faces, saw what had occurred.

“Grady,” he said, “go and wait in the court; and if anybody comes—you understand me.”

“Is it the play-actress and her mother?” said Grady.

“Yes—confound you—say there’s nobody in chambers, and the party’s off for to-day.”

“Shall I say that, sir? and after I bought them bokays?” asked Grady.

“Yes,” said Amory with a stamp of his foot.

And Strong, going to the door too, reached it just in time to prevent Captain Costigan’s entrance, as that officer mounted the stair with his dignity inflamed and his curiosity galloping.

The ladies from the theatre did not have their treat to Greenwich. Nor did Blanche pay her visit to Fanny Bolton that day. And Cos, taking occasion majestically to inquire of Grady what the mischief was and who was crying, received for answer that ’twas a woman—another of them—and that they were, in Grady’s opinion, the cause of ’most all the mischief in the world.

While Pen was in his own county laying out his little campaign as carefully as a man lays out sandwiches for a picnic—counting slices, saving the best for himself, and calling it “public spirit”—a message came that Lady Rockminster had reached Baymouth, and had brought with her Laura.

At the name of Laura, his sister, so near at hand, Pen’s fine plans began to taste in his mouth like a spoonful of ink. He had wanted—more than he owned—to stand high in her esteem. She was, as it were, his mother’s bequest, wrapped up in brown paper and sealed with duty: to be protected, guided, provided for; and he, the handsome gentleman with his political prospects and practised smiles, suddenly felt like a boy caught with jam on his fingers.

How should he speak to her of Blanche? How should he explain the respectable trade he was driving—honour for money, affection for advancement, conscience for a seat? He fancied Laura’s quiet clear eyes as a sort of daylight that shows dust you didn’t know was there. He wrote at once to Baymouth a letter full of polished phrases, affectionate protestations, and that easy raillery with which he always tried to make seriousness seem like a joke; but between the lines he felt a panic, and had the disagreeable sense that he was dressing up a lie and calling it good society.

It was absurd, to be sure, that a simple country girl should be able to frighten a man who could talk down half a club and smile through any awkwardness. Yet his worldly diplomacy—so fit for committees and drawing-rooms—could not stand her plain truth. He rode from Clavering to Baymouth with the guilty feeling of a schoolboy who knows he has not learned his lesson and hears, in imagination, the master’s step in the corridor. Truth, after all, is a master who always has the book.

In the year since Helen’s death, Laura had lived under the charge of Lady Rockminster—kind, tyrannical, capricious, and absolute, like an old cook who loves you but will still rap your knuckles if you touch the sauce. Laura had seen the world, learned its little graces, picked up accomplishments as one picks up foreign words and ribbons; and she had endured what a tender home-bred girl must endure when she is suddenly set down among people who do not think it their chief business to be gentle.

Helen’s love had been so watchful that the poor widow seemed to hover about Laura like a warm shawl: if Laura’s head ached, the whole house must know it; if she sighed, the very clock was expected to go softly. That anxious heart had stopped; and Laura, deprived at once of her mother and her mother’s perpetual protection, had had to stand alone among strangers who were not bound to care whether she felt hurt or not.

She was not quite the equal, in rank, of her patroness and that patroness’s friends. Some slighted her; some were cold; servants, accustomed to Lady Rockminster’s way of speaking as though the world were a set of drawers to be banged, could be rude in imitation. Lady Rockminster herself was often sharp enough to cut a loaf without a knife. Laura found herself sometimes in family gatherings where the intimacy paused, as if a door had been opened upon company not meant to be admitted; and her sensitive mind suffered from the fear that her presence was an intrusion.

Yet, with a cheerful philosophy that had the good sense of a woman who can make dinner out of very little, she compared her lot with that of governesses and dependent girls who must sell their time and their dignity by the hour; and she said to herself that she, at least, was among people who were, in their fashion, kind. So she adapted herself, and went forward with a trusting smile—as if Fortune were a neighbour met on the road, to be greeted civilly instead of suspected.

Fortune, like many a human creature, has a weakness for those who do not cringe and do not bargain. Laura had that rare gift—more precious than jewels, and harder to counterfeit than lace—of liking people and making people like her. She carried it with her as quietly as she carried the little cross Pen had given her; and it served her better than any diamond, lighting dark corners and softening sour tempers.

Before she had been a year in Lady Rockminster’s household, there was scarcely a soul in it that did not belong to her. The old lady’s woman—who had endured forty years of scolding, clawing, and daily criticism, as some kettles endure the fire and come out black—had begun, as usual, by being angry with the new companion, as she had been with the fifteen before. But when Laura fell ill in Paris, that same sour veteran nursed her in defiance of her mistress (who feared fever as she feared bad French cookery), and fought with Martha from Fairoaks—now promoted to be Miss Laura’s maid—for the right to administer medicines.

And in the midst of this domestic campaign rose Grandjean, the chef, who behaved as if Laura’s recovery were a matter of national importance and depended entirely on his saucepans. He would have killed her, if affection could do it, with delicacies: broths clarified till they looked like amber; little birds and cutlets, dressed as tenderly as if they were infants; jellies trembling with too much zeal. When she ate her first slice of chicken, the man actually wept, as though the fowl had been a lost relative restored.

The Swiss major-domo celebrated her praises in every language he spoke—none of them correctly, but all of them earnestly. The coachman was proud to drive her. The page cried when she was ill. Calverley and Coldstream, those two huge footmen who usually looked as if nothing short of an earthquake could stir them, became hilariously unsteady with joy at the news of her convalescence, and celebrated it by getting the page drunk in a wine-shop, to do honour to Miss Bell’s health.

Even Lady Diana Pynsent—Mr. Pynsent having married her by this time—who had once nursed a considerable dislike to Laura, condescended to declare Miss Bell “very agreeable,” and grandmamma’s “trouvaille.” Laura had won all this, not by arts and flattery, but by that simple good-nature which is like good bread: everybody is better tempered after they’ve had a slice.

Pen, remembering Lady Rockminster’s former brusqueries to himself, arrived at Baymouth expecting to find Laura a humble dependent, cowed and overlooked. Instead, when she heard he was come, she ran down the stairs; and if she did not embrace him in the presence of Calverley and Coldstream, it was only because the laws of gravity and decorum happened to be passing through the hall. Those two giants would have watched any event—embrace or beheading—with equal serenity, without so much as disturbing a grain of powder on their heads.

Laura looked so well that Pen was struck into admiration. Health had brightened her frank eyes; colour had come back to her cheek; and when she kissed him, the blush was as fresh as a rose in a country hedge. He had never thought her so beautiful. Why had he not thought of her beauty before? Why did the thought come now, with a tenderness that made him uncomfortable? He took her hand and kissed it with a fondness that surprised himself, and read in her clear gaze that unguarded welcome he had always been sure to find there. Her innocence smote him; he felt it as one feels the first cold splash of water on a guilty face.

“How good you are to me, Laura—sister,” he said. “I don’t deserve—that you should be so kind.”

“Mamma left you to me,” she answered, bending and brushing his forehead with her lips quickly. “You know our compact last year, before we parted: you were to come to me when you were in trouble, or to tell me when you were very happy. Which is it now? Are you very happy, or are you in trouble?” She looked at him with a bright arch kindness. “Do you like going into Parliament? Do you mean to distinguish yourself? How I shall tremble for your first speech!”

“Do you know about that plan, then?” Pen asked.

“Know? Everybody knows,” Laura said. “Lady Rockminster’s doctor talked of it to-day. I daresay it will be in the Chatteris paper to-morrow. It’s all over the county that Sir Francis Clavering is going to retire in favour of Mr. Arthur Pendennis of Fairoaks, and that the young and beautiful Miss Blanche Amory is—”

“What! that too?” Pen cried.

“That too, dear Arthur. Tout se sait,” said Laura, with a little Parisian air she had learned without losing her own. “I mean to be very fond of her. She must be clever and pretty. She has written me such a kind letter. She speaks so warmly of you! I hope—I know—she feels what she writes. When is it to be? Why didn’t you tell me? I may come and live with you then, mayn’t I?”

“My home is yours, dear Laura, and all I have,” Pen said, swallowing. “If I didn’t tell you, it was because—because nothing is decided yet. No words have passed.” Then, for want of honest words, he fell back on the sort of arrangement which a prudent man makes with furniture. “But you think Blanche could be happy with me—don’t you? Not a romantic fondness, you know. I don’t think I have a heart. I’ve told her so. Only a sober attachment—and I want my wife on one side of the fire and my sister on the other; Parliament in the session and Fairoaks in the holidays; and my Laura never to leave me—until somebody who has a right comes to take her away.”

Somebody with a right. Somebody with a right! As he said it slowly, looking at her, an absurd anger rose in him against this invisible claimant. A minute ago he had been anxious how she would take the news of Blanche; now he was hurt that she took it so easily, as though his happiness were an ordinary appointment in the diary.

“Until somebody comes,” Laura said, laughing, “I’ll stay at home and be Aunt Laura, and take care of the children when Blanche is in the world. I have arranged it all. I’m an excellent housekeeper. Do you know I’ve been to market in Paris with Mrs. Beck, and taken lessons from M. Grandjean? He showed me how to choose a fowl by the look of the skin and the feel of the breast; how to make a stock that smells like sunshine on bones; how to skim it till it’s clear as conscience ought to be. And I’ve had singing lessons too—out of the money you sent me, you kind boy—and I sing much better now. I’ve learned to dance—though not so well as Blanche. And when you become a minister of state, Blanche shall present me!” And, with provoking good humour, she made him the latest Parisian curtsey, as if in a drawing-room rather than in Lady Rockminster’s house at Baymouth.

Lady Rockminster entered at the exact moment of this curtsey, and gave Pen one finger to shake, which he took and bowed over as if it were a relic, though clumsily enough.

“So you are going to be married, sir,” said the old lady.

“Scold him for not telling us,” Laura cried, retreating; whereupon Lady Rockminster began instantly, as if scolding were the first course of dinner and she had an appetite.

“So you are going to marry, and go into Parliament instead of that good-for-nothing Sir Francis Clavering. I wanted him to give my grandson his seat. Why didn’t he give my grandson his seat? I hope you are to have a great deal of money with Miss Amory. I wouldn’t take her without a great deal.”

“Sir Francis is tired of Parliament,” Pen said, wincing, “and I—wish to attempt that career. The rest is—premature.”

“I wonder, when you had Laura at home, you could take up with such an affected little creature as that,” the dowager continued.

“I am sorry Miss Amory does not please your ladyship,” said Pen, smiling as men do when they are pinched.

“You mean it’s no affair of mine, and I’m not going to marry her. Well, I’m not, and I’m glad I’m not—odious little thing. When I think a man can prefer her to my Laura, I’ve no patience. And so I tell you, Mr. Arthur Pendennis.”

“I’m very glad you see Laura so favourably,” Pen said.

“You are very glad and very sorry. What does it matter? A young man who prefers Miss Amory to Miss Bell has no business to be glad or sorry. A young man who takes up with such a crooked lump of affectation—because she is crooked, I tell you she is—after seeing my Laura, has no right to hold up his head. Where is your friend Bluebeard? That tall young man—Warrington. Why doesn’t he come down and marry Laura? What do young men mean by not marrying such a girl? They all marry for money now. You are selfish and cowards. We ran away and made foolish matches in my time. I’ve no patience with you! In Paris this winter I asked the three attaches at the Embassy why they didn’t fall in love with Miss Bell. They laughed. They said they wanted money. You are all selfish. You are all cowards.”

“I hope, before you offered Miss Bell to the attaches,” Pen said, growing hot, “you did her the favour to consult her?”

“Miss Bell has only a little money. Miss Bell must marry soon. Somebody must make a match for her; and a girl can’t offer herself,” said the dowager, with the air of pronouncing a law of nature. Then, raising her voice: “Laura, my dear, I’ve been telling your cousin all young men are selfish, and there isn’t a pennyworth of romance left. He is as bad as the rest.”

Laura came back, smiling, but with a brightness that looked as if it had been carefully put on. She took Pen’s hand.

“Have you been asking Arthur why he won’t marry me?” she said. “He is going to marry somebody else; and I intend to be very fond of her, and to go and live with them—provided then he doesn’t ask every bachelor who comes to his house why he doesn’t marry me.”

Pen’s conscience, having expected reproaches and received none, settled down again like a timid creature that finds the lash is not lifted. His duty, and still more his inclination, led him constantly to Baymouth; where Lady Rockminster declared a place was always kept for him at her table.

“And I recommend you come often,” she said, “for Grandjean is an excellent cook; and being with Laura and me will do your manners good. It’s easy to see you are always thinking about yourself. Don’t blush and stammer. Almost all young men always think about themselves. My sons and grandsons did, until I cured them. Come here and learn to behave. You shan’t have to carve—that’s done at the side-table. Hecker will give you as much wine as is good for you; and when you are very good and amusing you shall have champagne. Hecker, mind: Mr. Pendennis is Miss Laura’s brother. Make him comfortable. See he doesn’t drink too much. And don’t let him disturb me while I take my nap after dinner. You are selfish, young man. I intend to cure you. Dine here when you have no other engagements; and if it rains, you’d better put up at the hotel.”

So long as she could command, she was not hard to please. All her little court trembled, and yet loved her; for there is something oddly comforting in a tyrant who is at least consistent.

Her society was not numerous or brilliant. The doctor was always there, faithful as his own pill-box. The vicar came; the curate; on public days the vicar’s wife and daughters and a few visitors were received. Generally it was a small table: good plate, better cookery, and conversation that went round in a narrower circle than the soup tureen.

After dinner Lady Rockminster retired to her doze, and Laura played and sang her to sleep; and Pen drank his wine alone, hearing the soft drift of music through the house, like a scented vapour—lavender and bergamot translated into sound. In that quiet domestic music there was no advertisement, no harshness; it did not clang like the new brass bands of public life. It was made for one tired old woman, in one room, in one house; and the very modesty of it seemed to protest against the world’s vulgar noise.

“If my music can give her a nap,” Laura said, “ought I not to be glad it can do so much good? Lady Rockminster sleeps very little at night. I used to read to her till I fell ill in Paris; since then she won’t hear of my sitting up.”

“Why didn’t you write to me when you were ill?” Pen asked, colouring.

“What good could you do me?” she said simply. “I had Martha to nurse me, and the doctor every day. You are too busy to write to women or think about them. You have your books, your newspapers, your politics, your railroads. I wrote when I was well.”

And Pen blushed again, remembering that while she had been ill—while Grandjean had been weeping over chicken and footmen were toasting her recovery—he had never written, and had scarcely thought of her at all.

Because she was his cousin and, in this household, his acknowledged belonging, Pen could walk and ride with her freely; and in those walks and rides he learned her again. In their mother’s lifetime she had never spoken so openly to him; Helen’s eager wish to unite her children had thrown a reserve over Laura’s manner, a modest guard against hopes she dared not encourage. Now there was no need. He was bound—so the county said—to another woman; and Laura became at once his sister: cheerful, dutiful, determined to hope for his prosperity, determined to do everything affection could do to make her mother’s darling happy.

They spoke often of their dead mother, and from a hundred little stories Laura told—how Helen had saved some trifle for him, how she had excused him, how she had prayed over him, how she had watched his letters and his silences—Pen came to understand what that devotion had been: constant, absorbing, silent, like a lamp kept burning in a window for a traveller who may never come home. It had ended only with Helen’s last breath.

One day the people at Clavering saw a lad holding two horses at the churchyard gate, and it was told through the place that Pen and Laura had gone together to Helen’s grave. Pen had been there once or twice since he came into the country; but alone, the sight of the stone had brought him no consolation. What right had he, he thought, to stand in that holy ground—he, a man bartering faith and honour for a fortune and a career; a speculator in life, making his bargain with open eyes? The quiet of the place only seemed to make his inner noise more jarring.

They rode by the gates of Fairoaks. Pen shook hands with his tenant’s children playing on the lawn and terrace. Laura looked steadily at the cottage wall, at the creeper on the porch, at the magnolia rising toward her old window. Later one of the boys told his mother: “Mr. Pendennis rode by to-day with a lady. He stopped and talked to us, and asked for a bit of honeysuckle off the porch and gave it her. I couldn’t see if she was pretty; she had her veil down. She was on one of Cramp’s horses, out of Baymouth.”

Across the downs between Baymouth and home they rode very close together, but Pen spoke little. He was thinking how men refuse happiness when it is offered, or, having it, kick it away; how they barter it, eyes open, for beggarly honours and worthless money. And then, with that sour cleverness which was his refuge, he told himself: what does it matter? The best and purest lives are consumed in desire and end in disappointment—like Helen’s, who had longed and planned, and died baulked. The stone covers hopes and memories. Our place knows us no more.

“Other people’s children are playing on the grass,” he said suddenly, in a hard voice, “where you and I used to play. And look how the magnolia we planted has grown. I went round to one or two cottages where my mother used to visit. It’s scarcely a year since she’s gone, and the people she benefited care no more for her death than for Queen Anne’s. We are all selfish. The world is selfish. There are a few exceptions—like you—to shine like good deeds in a naughty world, and only make the blackness more dismal.”

“I wish you would not speak so, Arthur,” Laura said, looking down, her fingers touching the honeysuckle on her breast as if its scent were a comfort she could hold. “When you told the little boy to give me this, you were not selfish.”

“A pretty sacrifice,” Pen said, with his bitter laugh, “to get it for you.”

“But your heart was kind when you did it,” she persisted. “One cannot ask for more than love and kindness; and if you think humbly of yourself, are they diminished? I often thought our dearest mother spoiled you at home by worshipping you; and that if you are—how I hate the word—what you say, her too great fondness helped to make you so. And as for the world—when men go into it, perhaps they cannot help being selfish. You have to fight, and get on, and make a name. Mamma and your uncle encouraged you in that ambition. If it is vain, why pursue it? I suppose such a clever man as you means to do good to the country by going into Parliament, or you would not wish to be there. What are you going to do in the House of Commons?”
