“Women don’t understand politics, my dear,” Pen said; and even as he said it he sneered at himself for the cheapness of the answer.

“Then why don’t you make us understand?” Laura returned. “I could never tell why Mr. Pynsent should like it so much. He is not clever.”

“He certainly is not a genius,” Pen said.

“Lady Diana says he attends committees all day, then is at the House all night; that he always votes as he is told; that he never speaks; that he will never rise beyond a subordinate place; and his grandmother tells him he is choked with red-tape. Is that what you mean to do, Arthur? What is there so brilliant that you should be eager for it? I would rather you stayed at home and wrote books—good books, kind books, with gentle kind thoughts such as you have, dear Arthur, such as might do people good to read. And if you do not win fame, what then? You own it is vanity; you can live happily without it. I must not pretend to advise—but you speak so bitterly of the world, and say it is wicked and tires you. Why don’t you leave it?”

“And what would you have me do?” Pen asked.

“I would have you bring your wife to Fairoaks,” Laura said softly, “and live there, and study, and do good round about you. I would like to see your own children playing on the lawn, Arthur; and that we might pray in our mother’s church once more, dear brother. If the world is a temptation—are we not taught to pray that we may not be led into it?”

There are three rooms on the ground floor of the Wheel of Fortune, besides the bar where the landlady reigns like a general behind her fortifications. One is the common parlour, where any mortal with a thirst and a shilling may sit and grow wise over ale; another is the livery-room, where gentlemen’s gentlemen gather to compare cuffs and calamities; and the third is the sacred chamber with PRIVATE painted on the door in uncompromising capitals—the hired den of “The Confidentials,” Messrs. Morgan and Lightfoot and their brethren, who spoke of the world as if they owned it, and of their masters as if they merely let it out on a short lease.

Mr. James Morgan—Major Pendennis’s valet, noiseless as a cat and nearly as affectionate—had that day listened in at his master’s lodgings while Mr. Strong and the Major spoke together; and he had carried away from that conversation certain fat morsels of knowledge which, like a rich gravy, would thicken any man’s future. A desire for more sauce led him to follow the Major when Pendennis went to the Wheel of Fortune; and while the Major and Sir Francis Clavering sat in the parlour with their tempers rising like overworked yeast, Morgan took his seat in the Confidential room, in the particular corner from which Providence (or the builder) had arranged that one could hear nearly everything in the next apartment.

They were speaking loud—gentlemen always do, when they are trying to appear reasonable—and so Morgan had the pleasure of overhearing almost the whole.

Sir Francis had known Altamont at once in Sydney. Sir Francis wasn’t married to Lady Clavering. Altamont was the man. Altamont was a convict. Young Arthur would get into Parliament, and the Governor promised not to split—oh, what a sly old rogue, that Governor, thought Morgan. No wonder he was so anxious to clap Blanche and Arthur together: Blanche would have a hundred thousand if she had a penny, and carry a seat in Parliament to her husband as neatly as a well-trussed capon is carried to table.

If you had been a physiognomist, you would have asked to see Morgan’s face at that moment, the way a food-historian begs to smell an ancient spice jar. His mind was sniffing, tasting, cataloguing. Nobody saw it; but Morgan, going later to a looking-glass, surveyed himself with the gravity of a man examining a joint before carving.

“But for my hage,” he reflected, touching his own chin as if it were the offending ingredient in the dish of his life, “and the confounded preudices of society—dammy, James Morgan, you might marry her yourself.”

Since he could not marry Miss Blanche and her fortune, he could, at least, do what many a gentleman does with a fortune he cannot eat: trade upon it. The secret touched a number of people, and most of them would rather swallow hot tallow than have it spoken aloud.

Sir Francis’s fortune depended on keeping it quiet. Colonel Altamont’s neck depended on keeping it quiet. And that young upstart beast, Mr. Harthur, who was to get into Parliament on the strength of it, and strutted as if he were a duke with half a million a year—he, Morgan was sure, would pay anything sooner than have the world say he had married a convict’s daughter, and bought his seat with silence.

As for Lady Clavering, Morgan’s mind served up two sauces. If she was tired of Clavering and wanted rid of him, she’d pay. If she was frightened for her son and fond of the little beggar, she’d pay all the same. And Miss Blanche would “come down handsome” to the man who put her into her rights—rights she had been defrauded of, no mistake.

“Dammy,” Morgan concluded, dealing himself these splendid cards as if it were whist and he had looked under the table, “with such a hand, James Morgan, you are a made man. It may be a reg’lar enewity. Every one of ’em must susscribe. And with what I’ve made already, I may cut business, give my old Gov’nor warning, turn gentleman, and have a servant of my own—begad.”

This kind of arithmetic is apt to make a man’s pulse beat; yet Morgan, who had the self-command of a cook who can smell a roast burning and still smile at the guests, kept his face as smooth as his master’s freshly stropped razor. Until the proper day came, Major Pendennis’s boots were varnished, his hair was curled, his early cup of tea carried to his bedside, and his oaths, rebukes, and senile satire endured with a silence so respectful you would have taken it for devotion.

Who would have supposed, seeing Morgan packing and shouldering trunks, waiting at table in country-houses, or standing behind chairs while people praised a saddle of mutton as if they had invented sheep, that he was richer than his employer and knew secrets that could season or poison half the county? Among the brotherhood of valets he was admired for wealth and wisdom; the younger gentlemen’s gentlemen voted him “stoopid,” a feller of no idears, a fogey; but even they would have said amen to the serious-minded prayer uttered at supper-tables: “When I die, may I cut up as well as Morgan Pendennis!”

Major Pendennis, being a man of fashion, passed the autumn from house to house. If the Duke was abroad and the Marquis was in Scotland, he condescended to stay with Sir John or even the plain squire; but truth compels us to own that his reputation was somewhat on the wane. Many of the men of his time had died out; and their heirs, sitting in the old halls and wearing the old titles as if they were new-made coats, did not know Major Pendennis and cared little for his stories of “the wild Prince and Poins,” and the heroes of the world that had been.

It must have pinched him, walking by London doors that had once swung open at his knock, to see how seldom they opened now—and how often he used to rap there, and step through to banquets and welcomes twenty years before. He began to feel, in a dim, damp way, like a gentleman returning to a familiar kitchen and discovering the hearth replaced by a new-fangled range and the old cook dismissed. The young men laughed at him. The serious youths pitied him. He was rather simple; his examination of moral questions had never been deep. Until lately, it had hardly struck him that he was not, in all respects, a most respectable and rather fortunate man.

“The old grand manner is gone,” he told himself, with the regularity of an old recipe repeated until it loses its taste. He compared the old Castlewood processions—four post-chaises, sixteen horses, and the whole North Road turning out to gape—with the present lord sneaking away from a railway station, smoking a cigar in a brougham among bagmen. The late lord filled Castlewood with company drinking claret till midnight; the present buries himself in a hut on a Scotch mountain or in two or three closets in an entresol at Paris, where his amusements are a dinner at a café and a box at a little theatre. His Lady Lorraine of the Regent’s days—gorgeous in diamonds and velvets, daring in rouge—was in his mind like a rich dish no modern palate dared attempt; to-day’s Lady Lorraine, in black silk like a governess, talked astronomy, labouring classes, emigration, and the deuce knows what, and crept to church at eight o’clock in the morning.

Abbots-Lorraine, once the noblest house in the county, was turned into a monastery—a regular La Trappe. They drank hardly two glasses of wine after dinner, and every other man at table was a curate in a white neckcloth, discoursing of Polly Higson’s progress at school or Widow Watkins’s lumbago. The young men sprawled over sofas and billiard-tables, stole off to smoke pipes in each other’s bedrooms, revered nothing—“not even an old gentleman who has known their fathers and their betters, not even a pretty woman.” They poisoned the very turnips and stubble-fields with tobacco. The breed was gone, thought the Major; replaced by cotton-spinners, utilitarians, and young sprigs of parsons with their hair combed down their barks.

He was not entirely wrong. His time was over; the new time had begun to reign. And after a rather unsuccessful autumn—during which Mr. Morgan followed him faithfully, as a shadow follows a fat man on a sunny wall—the Major came back to London at the dismal end of October, when the fogs and the lawyers return together, like twin pests.

Who has not watched the loaded cabs at that season, piled with boxes and children, rattling through the dun evenings, stopping at dark houses to discharge nurse and infant, girls, matron, and father, their holidays over? Yesterday it was France and sunshine, or Broadstairs and liberty; to-day it is work and a yellow fog; and there—ye gods!—what a heap of bills lies in master’s study. In half an hour the printer’s boy will be in the passage; Mr. Smith with that little account will call at ten; and duty, difficulty, struggle, stand in the doorway with their hats on, ready to enter. Even the city’s sound seems to change: the holiday’s easy shuffle becomes the sharp clack of wheels on stone, the cough of clerks, the metallic cry of commerce. London hums like an over-wound instrument—too many harsh notes, too much din—and the ear, like the heart, feels poorer for it.

Old Pendennis had no special labours or bills to encounter, having no affection at home to soothe him. He always had money in his desk for his wants; and being by nature and habit tolerably indifferent to the wants of other people, he was seldom disturbed by theirs. But even a gentleman who owes nothing may be out of temper; selfishness itself cannot always keep a man warm.

He had had two or three twinges of gout in the country-house where he had been staying; the birds were wild and shy; walking over ploughed fields fatigued him deucedly; the young men had laughed at him; he had been peevish at table; he could not get his whist of an evening; and so he was glad to come away. In all his dealings with Morgan he had been sulky and discontented—swearing and abusing him for days. He scalded his mouth with bad soup at Swindon. He left his umbrella in the railway carriage; at which forgetfulness he flew into such a rage that he cursed Morgan more freely than ever. Both chimneys smoked furiously in his lodgings; he had the windows flung open; and he swore so acrimoniously that Morgan, hearing it, felt inclined to fling him out of one of those opened casements in return. The valet swore after his master as the Major went down the street to the Club.

Bays’s was not pleasant. The house had been newly painted and smelt of varnish and turpentine; and a large streak of white paint inflicted itself on the back of the old boy’s fur-collared surtout, as if the building wished to mark him for a victim. The dinner was not good—thin soup, dispirited fish, and a joint that had been carved with less tenderness than it had been cooked. The three most odious men in London pursued him there: old Hawkshaw, whose cough came with such accompaniments as to make a man feel he was dining with a churchyard; old Colonel Gripley, who seized all the newspapers as if they were property; and irreclaimable Jawkins, who placed himself at the next table and described every inn-bill of his foreign tour with the exactitude of a man translating a dead language into one still more dead. The Club waiter trod on Pendennis’s toe while bringing coffee. Never alone appear the Immortals: the Furies hunt in company. They pursued Pendennis from home to the Club, and from the Club home.

While the Major was absent, Morgan sat in the landlady’s parlour, drinking hot brandy-and-water and pouring into Mrs. Brixham’s ear some of the abuse his master had poured down upon him upstairs. Mrs. Brixham was Mr. Morgan’s slave. He was, in effect, his landlady’s landlord. He had bought the lease of the house she rented; he had got her name and her son’s to acceptances; he had a bill of sale which made him master of the poor widow’s furniture. Young Brixham was a clerk in an insurance office, and Morgan could put him, as he called it, into quod any day. Mrs. Brixham was a clergyman’s widow; and Morgan, after performing his duties on the first floor, took a pleasure in making her fetch his bootjack and slippers as if she were his scullery-maid. The little black profiles of her son and daughter, the very picture of Tiddlecot Church where she had been married and where her poor dear Brixham lived and died—these hung over the mantelpiece like relics; and even these, in Morgan’s eyes, were now his property.

He sat in the ex-curate’s old horsehair study-chair, made Mrs. Brixham bring supper, and fill his glass again and again. The liquor was bought with the poor woman’s own coin—so Morgan indulged only the more freely; and he had eaten his supper and was drinking a third tumbler when Major Pendennis returned, and went upstairs to his rooms.

Morgan swore savagely at the bell when he heard it, finished his tumbler before answering the summons, and went up with his temper steaming like the kettle Mrs. Brixham dared not call her own.

He received the Major’s abuse in silence. Pendennis’s foot-bath was at the fire; his gown and slippers waited. Morgan knelt to take off his boots with due subordination; and as the Major scolded from above, Morgan kept a low growl of maledictions below at his feet. So when Pendennis cried, “Confound you, sir, mind that strap—curse you, don’t wrench my foot off,” Morgan, under his breath, expressed a wish to strangle him, drown him, and punch his head off.

The boots removed, Morgan had to take off the Major’s coat, and for that must approach near—near enough that Pendennis could not but perceive what occupation had lately warmed the valet’s spirits. The Major, with that simple and forcible phraseology which gentlemen sometimes employ toward servants, informed Morgan that he was a drunken beast, and smelt of brandy.

At this the man broke out. Patience, like a stock-pot left too long on the fire, had reduced to a bitter essence.

“I’m drunk, am I? I’m a beast, am I? I’m d——d, am I? you infernal old miscreant!” Morgan cried, flinging up subordination as if it were a soiled apron. “Shall I wring your old head off, and drownd yer in that pail of water? Do you think I’m a-goin’ to bear your confounded old harrogance, you old Wigsby! Chatter your old hivories at me, do you, you grinning old baboon! Come on, if you are a man, and can stand to a man. Ha! you coward—knives, knives!”

“If you advance a step, I’ll send it into you,” said the Major, snatching a knife from the table. His hand shook, but his voice tried hard not to. “Go downstairs, you drunken brute, and leave the house; send for your book and your wages in the morning, and never let me see your insolent face again. This d——d impertinence of yours has been growing for months past. You have been growing too rich. You are not fit for service. Get out of it, and out of the house.”

“And where would you wish me to go, pray, out of the ’ouse?” Morgan asked, with a sudden mocking bow, as if they were on a stage and the audience expected a flourish. “And won’t it be equal convenient to-morrow mornin’?—tootyfay mame shose, sivvaplay, munseer?”

“Silence, you beast, and go!” cried the Major.

Morgan began to laugh—a laugh with a clang in it, as if it carried a key. He seated himself deliberately.

“Look yere, Pendennis,” he said. “Since I’ve been in this room you’ve called me beast, brute, dog—and d——d me, haven’t you? How do you suppose one man likes that sort of talk from another? How many years have I waited on you? How many damns and cusses have you given me along with my wages? Do you think a man’s a dog, that you can talk to him so?

“If I choose to drink a little, why shouldn’t I? I’ve seen many a gentleman drunk form’ly, and peraps have the abit from them. I ain’t a-goin’ to leave this house, old feller—and shall I tell you why? The house is my house. Every stick of furnitur’ in it is mine—excep’ your old traps, and your shower-bath, and your wigbox. I’ve bought the place with my own industry and perseverance. I can show a hundred pound where you can show a fifty, or your damned supersellious nephew either.

“I’ve served you honourable, done everythink for you these dozen years—and I’m a dog, am I? I’m a beast, am I? That’s the language for gentlemen, not for our rank. But I’ll bear it no more. I throw up your service. I’m tired on it. I’ve combed your old wig and buckled your old girths and waistbands long enough. Don’t look savage at me—I’m sitting in my own chair, in my own room, a-telling the truth to you. I’ll be your beast, and your brute, and your dog no more, Major Pendennis Alf Pay.”

The Major’s fury, met with this abrupt revolt, was checked as if a cold shower had been dashed over him—appropriately enough, for his shower-bath stood ready like a silent witness to domestic humiliation. The shock cooled his anger; and when anger is cooled, curiosity often begins to simmer. Morgan’s courage interested him. The Major almost respected the fellow, as in the fencing-room he might have admired an adversary who hit him neatly.

“You are no longer my servant,” the Major said at last, with a stiff dignity that tried to cover a very human dismay. “And the house may be yours; but the lodgings are mine, and you will have the goodness to leave them. To-morrow morning, when we have settled our accounts, I shall remove into other quarters. In the meantime, I desire to go to bed, and have not the slightest wish for your further company.”

“We’ll have a settlement, don’t you be afraid,” Morgan said, getting up. “I ain’t done with you yet; nor with your family, nor with the Clavering family, Major Pendennis—and that you shall know.”

“Have the goodness to leave the room, sir—I’m tired,” said the Major.

“Hah! you’ll be more tired of me afore you’ve done,” Morgan answered with a sneer, and walked out, leaving the Major alone with the fire, the foot-bath, the knife on the table, and a silence that seemed suddenly loud—London’s muffled roar beyond the windows, the distant rattle of wheels, the ever-present cough of the city. Even in solitude, the soundscape would not grant him dignity.

He sat and mused by the fireside over the impudence and ingratitude of servants. He thought how he should get a new man; how devilish unpleasant it was, at his age and with his habits, to part with a fellow to whom he had been accustomed. He remembered, with an odd tenderness, Morgan’s receipt for boot-varnish—better and more comfortable to the feet than any he had ever tried; how well Morgan made mutton-broth, skimming it patiently, keeping it clear, coaxing savour out of bone and time; how neatly he had tended him when he was unwell.

“Gad, it’s a hard thing to lose a fellow of that sort,” thought the Major, in the tone of a man who has broken his best carving-knife and suddenly feels the inadequacy of all substitutes. “But he must go. He has grown rich, and impudent since he has grown rich. He was horribly tipsy and abusive to-night. We must part, and I must go out of the lodgings. Dammy, I like the lodgings. I’m used to ’em. It’s very unpleasant, at my time of life, to change quarters.”

His testiness was gone; the umbrella, the paint-smell at Bays’s, the cough of Hawkshaw, the newspapers of Gripley, the inn-bills of Jawkins—all were forgotten under this superior disturbance. “Confound the insolent villain!” he thought. “He understood my wants to a nicety. He was the best servant in England.”

He thought about Morgan as a man thinks of a horse that has carried him long and well, and is safe no longer. How the deuce to replace him? Where find such another animal?

He had donned his dressing-gown and replaced his head of hair—Mr. Truefitt had lately introduced a little grey into the coiffure, which gave the Major’s head an artless and respectable appearance; and now, having taken off his wig and put on his night-handkerchief, he sat absorbed when a feeble knock came at the door.

It opened, and Mrs. Brixham stood there.

“God bless my soul, Mrs. Brixham!” cried the Major, startled that a lady should behold him in the plain apparatus of his night-toilet. “It—it’s very late, Mrs. Brixham.”

“I wish I might speak to you, sir,” said the landlady piteously.

“About Morgan, I suppose? He has cooled himself at the pump. Can’t take him back, Mrs. Brixham. Impossible. I’d determined to part with him before, when I heard of his dealings in the discount business—I suppose you’ve heard of them, Mrs. Brixham? My servant’s a capitalist, begad.”

“Oh, sir,” Mrs. Brixham said, and her voice was like a cracked teacup that still tries to be useful, “I know it to my cost. I borrowed from him a little money five years ago; and though I have paid him many times over, I am entirely in his power. I am ruined by him, sir. Everything I had is his. He’s a dreadful man.”

“Eh, Mrs. Brixham?” said the Major, with that shrugging philosophy which sits so easily on the comfortable. “Tout pis—dev’lish sorry for you; and that I must quit your house after lodging here so long: there’s no help for it. I must go.”

Morning in Bury Street arrived with its usual city chorus: a cart’s iron rim grumbling over cobbles, a milkman’s call pitched like a cracked bugle, and—under it all—the steady, nerve-sawing hiss of London, as if the town were forever frying something it oughtn’t. Morgan opened Mr. Pendennis’s shutters as though unveiling a portrait, solemn as a beadle at a funeral, and marched in with the old gentleman’s clothes, water-cans, and that glittering little arsenal of toilet gear—silver cases, brushes like officers’ moustaches, and a razor strapped and shining with as much ceremony as a sword.

“It’s you, is it?” growled Major Pendennis from the depths of his tent-bed. “I shan’t take you back again, you understand.”

“I ’ave not the least wish to be took back agin, Major Pendennis,” Morgan returned, as grave as a judge and twice as offended. “Nor to serve you nor hany man. But as I wish you to be comftable as long as you stay in my house, I came up to do what’s nessary.”

And so, with the air of a man laying out sacramental vessels rather than a dressing-case, Morgan performed his last devotions: set the silver top open, placed the bottles and pomades in rank, and snapped the razor’s strap as if it were a military salute. Then he drew himself up, enjoying—almost tasting—the sound of his own voice the way certain persons savour rich gravy.

“Thinkin’ you would most likely be in want of a respectable pusson,” he said, “until you suited yourself, I spoke to a young man last night, who is ’ere.”

“Indeed,” said the Major, who could make one syllable sound like a whole paragraph of contempt.

“He ave lived in the fust famlies, and I can wouch for his respectability.”

“You are monstrous polite,” grinned the old man; and there was that in the grin which made Morgan feel he was being handled—like a fish on a hook—without any visible line.

Yet Morgan had, in fact, been to his club at the Wheel of Fortune the night before, and there, between the clink of glasses and the noisy thud of modern London conviviality (that aggressive sort of merriment which seems to exist chiefly to drown out thought), he had recruited a substitute: Frosch, courier and valet, lately returned from foreign travel with young Lord Cubley, and for the moment as disposable as yesterday’s newspaper.

“The man have awaited on you before, sir,” Morgan continued. “Lord De la Pole, sir, gave him to his nephew young Lord Cubley, and he have been with him on his foring tour; and not wishin’ to go to Fitzurse Castle—which Frosch’s chest is delicate, and he cannot bear the cold in Scotland—he is free to serve you or not, as you choose.”

“I repeat, sir, that you are exceedingly polite,” said the Major, as if repeating it might make it true in some dangerous sense. “Come in, Frosch—you will do very well—Mr. Morgan, will you have the great kindness to—”

“I shall show him what is nessary, sir, and what is customry for you to wish to ave done,” Morgan said, with the dignity of a man resigning a ministry. “Will you please to take breakfast ’ere or at the Club, Major Pendennis?”

“With your kind permission, I will breakfast here,” said the Major, “and afterwards we will make our little arrangements.”

“If you please, sir.”

“And will you now oblige me by leaving the room?”

Morgan withdrew, stiff-backed, insulted not by abuse—he could bear that—but by politeness sharpened to a point.

While the Major made his mysterious toilet, we may as decently turn away; and besides, the sounds of the house below are more instructive: the scrape of a broom, the clatter of a pail, the thin footfalls of Betty—known as “Betty” to her mistress and “Slavey” to Morgan—moving like a frightened mouse through a lion’s den.

After breakfast, Major Pendennis and his new aide-de-camp set about departure. The Major’s domestic empire was of that marching kind which packs like a campaign: no superfluous wardrobe, no sentimental hoards. His library and gallery were a soldier’s shrine: a Bible (his mother’s, the one relic he handled with gentleness), a road-book, Pen’s novel bound calf elegant, the Duke of Wellington’s Despatches, and a few prints, maps, and portraits of that illustrious General, of sundry sovereigns and their consorts, and of the Indian commander under whom the Major had served. He lived as if always listening for the drumbeat to strike up again.

The very cases in which he had moved into those lodgings fifteen years earlier still waited in the loft, ready as old comrades. Down they came under Betty’s arms and Mrs. Brixham’s anxious eye, while Morgan hovered like a dark weather cloud, guarded and silent, his face set in that solemnity which, in certain men, is only anger in its Sunday clothes. Mrs. Brixham—poor widow—had not been told her fate; she merely felt it, the way one feels a change in the air before a storm, and trembled accordingly.

Old Pendennis, cane in hand, superintended as if inspecting troops. Frosch packed with brisk foreign neatness. Betty burned such papers as the Major wished to leave behind, and flung open cupboards until they gaped empty as a picked bone. At last all boxes were shut except the Major’s desk, which waited—open-mouthed—for Morgan’s final accounts.

Then Morgan appeared with his books.

“As I wish to speak to you in privick,” he said, “peraps you will ave the kindness to request Frosch to step downstairs.”

“Bring a couple of cabs, Frosch, if you please,” said the Major, “and wait downstairs until I ring for you.”

Morgan watched Frosch go, the way a cat watches a door close, then produced his accounts: simple enough; the sums settled quickly. The Major wrote a cheque. Morgan pocketed it, signed with a flourish, and then—like a man who has swallowed a hot coal and is glad of the burn—leaned in.

“And now, sir,” he said, “now that accounts is closed between us, sir, I porpose to speak to you as one man to another. And I must tell you, that I’m in possession of certing infamation.”

“And may I inquire of what nature, pray?” asked the Major, all majesty—an old war-horse lifting its head.

“It’s valuble information, Major Pendennis, as you know very well. I know of a marriage as is no marriage—of a honourable Baronet as is no more married than I am; and which his wife is married to somebody else—as you know too, sir.”

The Major understood in a flash; the secret’s name did not need to be spoken aloud. His eyes hardened.

“Ha! this accounts for your behaviour,” he said. “You have been listening at the door, sir, I suppose. I forgot to look at the keyhole when I went to that public-house, or I might have suspected what sort of a person was behind it.”

“I may have my schemes as you may have yours,” Morgan answered, drawing himself up. “I may get my information, and I may act on that information, and I may find that information valuble as anybody else may. A poor servant may have a bit of luck as well as a gentleman, mayn’t he? Don’t you be putting on your aughty looks, sir, and comin’ the aristocrat over me. That’s all gammon with me. I’m an Englishman, I am, and as good as you.”

“To what the devil does this tend, sir?” the Major asked. “And how does the secret which you have surprised concern me, I should like to know?”

“How does it concern me, indeed!” Morgan cried, tasting each syllable like strong spirits. “How does it concern my nephew, I wonder? How does it concern my nephew’s seat in Parlyment—and to subornation of bigamy? How does it concern that? What, are you to be the only man to have a secret, and to trade on it? Why shouldn’t I go halves, Major Pendennis? I’ve found it out too. Look here! I ain’t goin’ to be unreasonable with you. Make it worth my while, and I’ll keep the thing close. Let Mr. Arthur take his seat, and his rich wife, if you like—I don’t want to marry her. But I will have my share, as sure as my name’s James Morgan. And if I don’t—”

“And if you don’t, sir—what?” said the Major, deadly quiet.

“If I don’t, I split, and tell all. I smash Clavering, and have him and his wife up for bigamy—so help me, I will! I smash young Hopeful’s marriage, and I show up you and him as makin’ use of this secret, in order to squeeze a seat in Parlyment out of Sir Francis, and a fortune out of his wife.”

“Mr. Pendennis knows no more of this business than the babe unborn, sir,” cried the Major, genuinely shaken. “No more than Lady Clavering—than Miss Amory does.”

“Tell that to the marines, Major,” Morgan sneered. “That cock won’t fight with me.”

“Do you doubt my word, you villain?”

“No bad language,” Morgan said, with the insolence of a man who thinks himself armoured by knowledge. “I don’t care one twopence’a’p’ny whether your word’s true or not. I tell you, I intend this to be a nice little annuity to me, Major: for I have every one of you; and I ain’t such a fool as to let you go. I should say you might make it five hundred a year to me among you, easy. Pay me down the first quarter now and I’m as mum as a mouse. Just give a note for one twenty-five. There’s your cheque-book on your desk.”

“And there’s this too, you villain,” cried the Major.

From the open desk he snatched a little double-barrelled pistol—an old campaign companion that had belonged to his former commander-in-chief in India. The Major’s fury flared like gunpowder catching; his hands—old, but steady—held the weapon as though it had never been anything but loaded.

“One more word, you scoundrel, and I’ll shoot you like a mad dog. Stop—by Jove, I’ll do it now. You’ll assault me, will you? You’ll strike at an old man, will you, you lying coward? Kneel down and say your prayers, sir—for by the Lord you shall die.”

Morgan blanched, then—in a fit of theatrical terror—let out a shriek of “Murder!” and sprang to the open window, bawling down into the street where a policeman happened to be pacing his beat.

“Murder! Police!”

But to Morgan’s astonishment, the Major did not fire. Instead, he wheeled the table aside with surprising strength, strode to the other open window, and beckoned the constable up with the authority of a man who has commanded troops and never forgotten the tone.

“Come up here, policeman,” he said, and placed himself against the door so Morgan could not bolt.

“You miserable sneak,” he added, turning on his valet. “The pistol hasn’t been loaded these fifteen years, as you would have known very well, if you had not been such a coward. That policeman is coming, and I will have him up, and have your trunks searched; I have reason to believe that you are a thief, sir. I know you are. I’ll swear to the things.”

“You gave ’em to me—you gave ’em to me!” Morgan blustered, but the words came out like a man trying to whistle while drowning.

The Major laughed—short, dry, victorious.

“We’ll see,” he said.

Morgan’s mind flashed, not to honour, but to inventory: fine lawn-fronted shirts; a gold-headed cane; an opera-glass he had “forgotten” to bring down; and sundry garments the Major neither wore nor missed. The thought of those articles being displayed in public made Morgan’s throat tighten as if he had swallowed a pin.

Policeman X entered, followed by Mrs. Brixham, white-faced, and Betty behind her, half-curious, half-terrified. The door had scarcely closed before the noise from the street—the eager amateur audience of London—pressed itself against it like a second crowd.

The Major began at once, speaking with the calmness of a man who has rehearsed the truth into a weapon.

“I have had occasion to discharge this drunken scoundrel,” he said. “Both last night and this morning he insulted and assaulted me. I am an old man and took up a pistol. You see it is not loaded, and this coward cried out before he was hurt. I am glad you are come. I was charging him with taking my property, and desired to examine his trunks and his room.”

“The velvet cloak you ain’t worn these three years, nor the weskits,” Morgan burst out, “and I thought I might take the shirts, and I—I take my hoath I intended to put back the hopera-glass!” He roared it in a mixture of rage and fear, as if volume might turn theft into virtue.

“The man acknowledges that he is a thief,” said the Major, serenely. “He has been in my service for years, and I have treated him with every kindness and confidence. We will go upstairs and examine his trunks.”

Now, in those trunks were things Morgan would have given good money to keep invisible. For Mr. Morgan, besides being a valet and (newly) a landlord, was a gentleman of commerce in the darker pantry of London: he discounted bills, yes—but also supplied certain young gentlemen with “goods” along with money. Snuff-boxes and pins; jewels and pictures; cigars whose pedigree would not bear investigation. The notion of such a hoard being turned out at a police-office—like spoiled meat on a slab—was enough to make even Morgan’s robust impudence wilt.

He looked piteous in his terror; and the Major, who had been ready to crush him utterly, hesitated. He glanced at Mrs. Brixham—thin, harried, living by the scant economies of a kettle and a broom—and he thought how a desperate man, once caged, might sing very loudly indeed; and some songs are best not loosed upon the air, where they can be taken up, misheard, repeated, and turned into weapons by any passing tongue.

“Stop,” said the Major. “Policeman. I’ll speak with this man by himself.”

“Do you give Mr. Morgan in charge?” asked X.

“I have brought no charge as yet,” said the Major, and gave Morgan a look with more meaning than any affidavit.

“Thank you, sir,” Morgan breathed, scarcely audible.

“Go outside the door and wait there, policeman, if you please.”

The constable withdrew. Mrs. Brixham and Betty hovered, then were waved back too, leaving the two men alone with the desk, the smell of smoke, and the city’s muffled roar seeping through the windows like an ill-tuned organ.

Morgan began to recover his nerve. The Major did not allow the recovery to ripen.

“Now, Morgan,” he said, “you have played one game with me, and you have not had the best of it, my good man. No, begad, you’ve not had the best of it, though you had the best hand; and you’ve got to pay, too, now, you scoundrel.”

“Yes, sir,” said Morgan, who had discovered that “sir” costs less than courage.

“I’ve only found out, within the last week, the game which you have been driving, you villain. Young De Boots, of the Blues, recognised you as the man who came to barracks, and did business one-third in money, one-third in eau-de-Cologne, and one-third in French prints—you confounded demure old sinner! I didn’t miss anything, or care a straw what you’d taken, you booby; but I took the shot, and it hit—hit the bull’s-eye, begad. Dammy, six, I’m an old campaigner.”

“What do you want with me, sir?” Morgan asked, sourly, like a cook caught watering the soup.

“I’ll tell you. Your bills, I suppose, you keep about you in that dem’d great leather pocket-book, don’t you? You’ll burn Mrs. Brixham’s bill?”

“Sir, I ain’t a-goin’ to part with my property,” Morgan growled.

“You lent her sixty pounds five years ago,” the Major went on, “and she and that poor devil of an insurance clerk, her son, have paid you fifty pounds a year ever since; and you have got a bill of sale of her furniture, and her note of hand for a hundred and fifty pounds. She told me so last night. By Jove, sir, you’ve bled that poor woman enough.”

“I won’t give it up,” said Morgan. “If I do I’m—”

“Policeman!” cried the Major, turning his head sharply toward the door.

“You shall have the bill,” Morgan snapped, beaten by the mere sound of authority. “You’re not going to take money of me, and you a gentleman?”

“I shall want you directly,” the Major called, and X appeared, then withdrew again at a sign.

“No, my good sir,” the Major continued, “I have not any desire to have further pecuniary transactions with you; but we will draw out a little paper, which you will have the kindness to sign. No, stop—you shall write it. You have improved immensely in writing of late, and have now a very good hand.”

That was one of those polite thrusts that leave a bruise exactly where the pride lives.

“You shall sit down and write, if you please—there, at that table—so—let me see—we may as well have the date. Write ‘Bury Street, St. James’s, October 21, 18—.’”

Morgan wrote, the scratching of the pen loud in the room’s sudden hush—hush only on the inside; outside, London kept clattering and calling, as if a city’s noise were determined to prevent any human being from hearing their own conscience.

The Major dictated slowly, tasting each clause like a cook tasting a sauce—adjusting, correcting, making it bite.

“‘I, James Morgan, having come in extreme poverty into the service of Arthur Pendennis, Esquire, of Bury Street, St. James’s, a Major in her Majesty’s service, acknowledge that I received liberal wages and board wages from my employer, during fifteen years.’ You can’t object to that, I am sure.”

Morgan wrote: “during fifteen years,” and his jaw clenched.

“‘In which time, by my own care and prudence, I have managed to amass sufficient money to purchase the house in which my master resides, and, besides, to effect other savings. Amongst other persons from whom I have had money, I may mention my present tenant, Mrs. Brixham, who, in consideration of sixty pounds advanced by me five years since, has paid back to me the sum of two hundred and fifty pounds sterling, besides giving me a note of hand for one hundred and twenty pounds, which I restore to her at the desire of my late master, Major Arthur Pendennis, and therewith free her furniture, of which I had a bill of sale.’ Have you written?”

“I think if this pistol was loaded, I’d blow your brains out,” Morgan muttered.

“No, you wouldn’t,” said the Major, cool as ever. “You have too great a respect for your valuable life, my good man. Let us go on and begin a new sentence.

“‘And having, in return for my master’s kindness, stolen his property from him, which I acknowledge to be now upstairs in my trunks; and having uttered falsehoods regarding his and other honourable families, I do hereby, in consideration of his clemency to me, express my regret for uttering these falsehoods, and for stealing his property; and declare that I am not worthy of belief, and that I hope—yes, begad—that I hope to amend for the future. Signed, James Morgan.’”

“I’m d——d if I sign it,” said Morgan.

“My good man, it will happen to you, whether you sign or no, begad,” said the Major, chuckling at his own grim joke. “There. I shall not use this, you understand, unless—unless I am compelled to do so.”

He rang; Mrs. Brixham came in, hands twisting in her apron, eyes pleading without words. Policeman X returned too, obedient to the bell as if it were a drum.

“Mrs. Brixham, and our friend the policeman, will witness it, I dare say, without reading it,” said the Major. “And I will give the old lady back her note of hand, and say—which you will confirm—that she and you are quits. I see there is Frosch come back with the cab for my trunks; I shall go to an hotel.—You may come in now, policeman; Mr. Morgan and I have arranged our little dispute. If Mrs. Brixham will sign this paper, and you, policeman, will do so, I shall be very much obliged to you both. Mrs. Brixham, you and your worthy landlord, Mr. Morgan, are quits. I wish you joy of him. Let Frosch come and pack the rest of the things.”

The paper was signed. The note of hand returned. Mrs. Brixham looked as if someone had lifted a sack of stones from her shoulders, and she tried to speak—blessings and gratitude bubbling up like a pot finally allowed to boil. But Major Pendennis offered her a finger to shake, briskly, as a man might give a crumb to a sparrow, and cut her speech short before tears could make a puddle.

Frosch, aided by Betty, carried the Major’s boxes down to the waiting cabs, while Morgan stood by with a composure so stiff it might have been starched. Outside, the street’s racket surged and fell: boots, wheels, voices; and above it, now and then, the sharp cry of a seller hawking wares as if noise itself were the commodity. One might have wished for the quiet of a farmyard at dusk, when you can hear the last hen settle and the wind comb through straw. But London gives you no such mercy: it drowns every private drama in a public din, and then sells you the echo.

Major Pendennis walked out, cane in hand, to the hotel in Jermyn Street—only a few steps away, as if he were merely changing rooms in the same noisy inn called life. Morgan, watching from the parlour-window, delivered anything but blessings after him; yet the stout old Major could afford not to be frightened. He flung his late servant one look—half contempt, half humour—and strutted away as though marching off a parade ground.

It was not many hours later that Morgan, now enjoying his otium with great dignity, sat upon the door-steps smoking a cigar—smoking, that is, in flagrant rebellion against the late master who would have treated tobacco like treason. Evening fog had come down, thick and greasy, swallowing the street-lamps and turning each sound into something muffled and sour. The city’s noise persisted, but differently: less bright clatter, more distant rumble, as if London had put a lid on its own pot and let it simmer.

Then Arthur Pendennis appeared at the familiar door.

“My uncle out, I suppose, Morgan?” he asked, with the easy tone of a man who knows the answer and enjoys the asking—especially knowing that a cigar in Morgan’s mouth would have been a court-martial offence in the Major’s presence.

“Major Pendennis is hout, sir,” Morgan said, bowing gravely, but not touching the elegant cap he wore—an omission that declared, as plainly as a shouted insult, that the old regime was over. “Major Pendennis have left this ouse to-day, sir, and I have no longer the honour of being in his service, sir.”

“Indeed, and where is he?”

“I believe he ave taken tempory lodgings at Cox’s otel, in Jummin Street,” Morgan answered. Then, after a pause that was almost a tasting of the moment, he added, “Are you in town for some time, pray, sir? Are you in Chambers? I should like to have the honour of waiting on you there—and would be thankful if you would favour me with a quarter of an hour.”

“Do you want my uncle to take you back?” Arthur asked, insolent and good-natured.

“I want no such thing; I’d see him—” Morgan began, and for one instant the old glare returned; then he swallowed it, as a man swallows a mouthful too hot, and forced a softer voice. “No, sir, thank you. It’s only with you that I wish to speak, on some business which concerns you; and perhaps you would favour me by walking into my house.”

“If it is but for a minute or two, I will listen to you, Morgan,” Arthur said, thinking, with amused indifference, that the fellow probably wanted patronage.

He stepped inside.

In the front window, already, a card announced that apartments were to be let—language made into a little signboard, the way modern London turns everything into advertisement. Morgan led him into the dining-room, offered a chair, took one opposite, and, with the careful relish of a man about to serve a dish long simmered in secrecy, began to convey information to Arthur Pendennis—information which we, being already in possession of it, can taste in advance.

Arthur Pendennis reached London as a man might reach a kitchen door in a sudden rain—only for a moment, only to fetch what he needed, and then out again to whatever obligation was simmering next. He had convoyed a couple of west-country fellow-travellers to their hotel, seen them safely stowed like parcels in a porter’s hands, and then made for Lamb Court, where the Temple’s old brick baked in such sunshine as cared to stoop into that narrow place.

The chambers looked dreary, but not unkindly. There is a sort of domestic hearth-warmth in a set of rooms where a man is free—freer than he ever is under a parental roof or a wife’s vigilant housekeeping—though he may have nothing hotter than a grudging coal and the distant clatter of other men’s boots on the stairs. In Lamb Court the air held its usual chorus: the scrape of quills, the cough of ancient clerks, the thin shout of boys in the passage, and, above all, the steady industrious mutter of London itself—cart-wheels, cab-bells, hammering somewhere beyond the walls, like a bad drummer who has never learned to stop. It was not music. It was what the city took in place of birds.

Pen’s man informed him that Warrington was in chambers too; and Arthur, as naturally as if he were following the scent of dinner, ran straight to his friend’s room. He found it as of old—perfumed, not with any fashionable distillation, but with pipe-smoke: that thick honest incense which clings to curtains and books, and makes even yesterday’s newspaper seem seasoned. Warrington sat among reviews and journals as if they were cold dishes set round him; his pipe in his mouth; his face grave and a little saturnine; his blue beard already beginning to abrade the linen at his throat, as if even cloth could not keep its dignity near him long.

They greeted each other with the rough cordiality of Englishmen—no embraces, no shrieks of affection, no scented kisses distributed upon moustachios; only that brief exchange which means, in their dialect, everything.

“Well, young one!” said Warrington, taking the pipe from his lips.

“How are you, old boy?” said Pen, holding out his hand.

And thus two friends who would have lent each other their last shilling, or stood by each other in the teeth of any hazard, made acquaintance again after months with the economy of men who hoard warmth as if it were fuel and fear it will be wasted in talk.

“Been in Switzerland?” Pen asked.

“Yes,” said Warrington.

“And the Alps? the glaciers? the—”

“Couldn’t find a bit of tobacco fit to smoke till we came to Strasburg,” Warrington replied, gloomily satisfied to have named at least one summit he could praise—“where I got some caporal.”

Thus do certain Englishmen conceal their raptures as a cook might hide his best spice and pretend he has made the soup with nothing but water. Warrington’s enthusiasm, if it rose at all, rose under cover; it would come out later, perhaps, in some line he wrote at midnight, when nobody watched him feel.

He gave, in that shy sulky voice of his—half as if he were ashamed of having seen anything beautiful, half as if beauty had insulted him—a rapid itinerary: Switzerland, North Italy, the Tyrol; home by Vienna, Dresden, and the Rhine. The names fell like stones into a well.

Then Pen began upon his own adventures: he had been in the country; he had been bored; canvassing was uncommonly slow; he was in London only for a day or two; then on to the neighbourhood of Tunbridge Wells, to friends who would, he supposed, be uncommonly slow too. How hard it is to make an Englishman confess he has been happy, even when he has been eating the world’s best cherries out of season.

“And the seat in Parliament, Pen?” Warrington asked. “Have you made it all right?”

“All right—as soon as Parliament meets and a new writ can be issued. Clavering retires, and I step into his shoes.”

“And under which king does Bezonian speak or die?” Warrington said. “Do we come out as Liberal Conservative, or Government man, or on our own hook?”

Pen shrugged. “There are no politics now; every man’s politics are pretty much the same. I haven’t acres enough to make me a Protectionist; and I don’t think I could be one if I owned the whole county. I shall go pretty much with Government, and in advance of them on some social questions—don’t grin, you old cynic; I have been getting up Blue Books, and intend to come out rather strong on the Sanitary and Colonisation questions.”

Warrington’s mouth twitched. “We reserve the liberty of voting against Government though generally friendly. We are friends of the people avant tout. We give lectures at the Clavering Institute and shake hands with the intelligent mechanics. We enlarge the franchise considerably, and meanwhile remain at perfect liberty to accept office some day, when the House has heard a few crack speeches and the Administration perceives our merit.”

Pen’s smile faded into his usual touch of melancholy, as if some draught had cooled the room. “I’m not Moses. I have no laws from Heaven to bring down. I don’t belong to the mountain at all, or pretend to lead mankind. My faith isn’t strong enough—nor my vanity, nor my hypocrisy. I’ll tell no lies, George, that I promise you; and do no more than coincide in those which are necessary and pass current, and can’t be got in without recalling the whole circulation. If I find a good thing to say in the House, I’ll say it; a good measure, I’ll support it; a fair place, I’ll take it, and be glad of my luck. But I’d no more flatter a great man than a mob; and now you know as much of my politics as I do. What call have I to be a Whig? Whiggism isn’t a divine institution. Why not vote with the Liberal Conservatives? They’ve done for the nation what the Whigs would never have done without them. Who converted both?—the Radicals and the country outside. I think the Morning Post is often right, and Punch is often wrong. I don’t profess a call, but take advantage of a chance. Parlons d’autre chose.”

Warrington, who loved to prick a man’s vanity as a cook pricks a sausage—partly to stop it bursting, partly because it amuses him—let politics drop, and reached for what he thought was Pen’s next hottest dish.

“The next thing at your heart, after ambition, is love, I suppose? How have our young loves prospered? Are we going to change our condition and give up our chambers? Are you going to divorce me, Arthur, and take unto yourself a wife?”

“I suppose so,” Pen said. His voice had the careful steadiness of a man slicing thin. “She’s very good-natured and lively. She sings, and she don’t mind smoking. She’ll have a fair fortune—I don’t know how much—but my uncle augurs everything from the Begum’s generosity, and says she’ll come down handsomely. And I think Blanche is dev’lish fond of me.”

Warrington nodded, as if tasting and recognising the ingredient. “That means we accept her caresses and her money.”

“Haven’t we said before life was a transaction?” Pen answered. “I don’t pretend to break my heart about her. I’ve told her pretty fairly what my feelings are—and—and have engaged myself to her. And since I saw her last—these last two months especially, while I’ve been in the country—I think she’s been growing fonder and fonder of me. Her letters to me, and especially to Laura, show it. Mine have been simple enough—no raptures, no vows—looking on the thing as an affaire faite; not desirous to hasten or defer the completion.”

“And Laura?” Warrington asked, plainly.

Pen looked at him hard, as if he would cut through the smoke and see what lay beneath it. “Laura, George—by heaven, Laura is the best, and noblest, and dearest girl the sun ever shone upon.”

His own voice sank; the words came as if each cost him. He stretched out his hand. Warrington took it, and only nodded—an English benediction.

“Have you only found out that now, young un?” Warrington said, after a pause.

“Who has not learned things too late?” Pen burst out, heat rising in him as if some old kettle had begun to boil again. “Whose life is not a disappointment? Who carries his heart entire to the grave without a mutilation? I never knew anybody quite happy; or who hasn’t had to ransom himself out of Fate’s hands by paying some dearest treasure. Lucky if we are left alone after we’ve paid our fine, and the tyrant visits us no more. Suppose I’ve found out I’ve lost the greatest prize in the world now that it can’t be mine—that for years I had an angel under my tent and let her go—am I the only one?—ah, dear old boy, am I the only one? And do you think my lot is easier because I own I deserve it? She’s gone from us. God’s blessing be with her! She might have stayed, and I lost her. It’s like Undine: isn’t it, George?”

“She was in this room once,” Warrington said.

That was all; but the room filled at once with what was not there. The past came back with the simplest relics: a glass that had held a nosegay—empty now, yet still seeming to remember its perfume; a Bible with Helen’s handwriting. Warrington heard again, in his mind’s ear, that sweet low voice—so different from the Temple’s perpetual din, so unlike the city’s grinding accompaniment. It is a poor exchange we make: skylarks for street-cries; the hush of fields for the clank of commerce. And when a voice like hers is lost, the very noise of London seems louder, more insolent, as if modern life could not endure being reminded there are tones it cannot counterfeit or sell.

They sat silent a while, each aware of the other’s thoughts, as men are aware of a neighbour’s fire through a wall—feeling the heat, not naming it.

Pen rose first. He said he must go and seek his uncle and report progress. The Major had written in a very bad humour; the Major was getting old.

“I should like to see you in Parliament,” the old gentleman had scrawled, “and snugly settled with a comfortable house and an heir to the name before I make my bow. Show me these, and then let old Arthur Pendennis make room for younger fellows; he has walked the Pall Mall pave long enough.”

“There’s a kindness about the old heathen,” Warrington said. “He cares for somebody besides himself—at least for some other part of himself besides that which is buttoned into his own coat—for you and your race. He’d like to see the progeny of the Pendennises multiplying and increasing, and hopes they may inherit the land. The old patriarch blesses you from the Club window of Bays’s, and is carried off and buried under the flags of St. James’s Church, in sight of Piccadilly, the cabstand, and the carriages going to the levee. It is an edifying ending.”

“The new blood I bring into the family,” Pen mused, “is rather tainted. If I had chosen, I think my father-in-law Amory would not have been the progenitor I should have desired for my race; nor my grandfather-in-law Snell; nor our Oriental ancestors. By the way, who was Amory? Lieutenant of an Indiaman. Blanche wrote some verses about him—storm, mountain wave, seaman’s grave, gallant father, and that sort of thing. Amory was drowned commanding a country ship between Calcutta and Sydney. Amory and the Begum weren’t happy together. She’s been unlucky in her selection of husbands, the good old lady; for, between ourselves, a more despicable creature than Sir Francis Clavering of Clavering Park, Baronet, never—”

“Never legislated for his country,” Warrington broke in; at which Pen coloured, despite himself.

“By the way,” Warrington continued, as if turning over an afterthought like a slice of bread to see if it had browned, “at Baden I found our friend the Chevalier Strong in great state, wearing his orders. He told me he had quarrelled with Clavering—of whom he seemed to have almost as bad an opinion as you have; and in fact, though I won’t be certain, he pretty much confided to me that Clavering was an utter scoundrel. That fellow Bloundell—who taught you card-playing at Oxbridge—was with Strong; and time, I think, has brought out his valuable qualities, and rendered him a more accomplished rascal than he was during your undergraduateship. But the king of the place was the famous Colonel Altamont—carrying all before him, giving flies to the whole society, and breaking the bank, it was said.”

“My uncle knows something about that fellow—Clavering knows something about him,” Pen replied. “There’s something louche regarding him. But come! I must go to Bury Street, like a dutiful nephew.”

He took up his hat. Warrington rose too. “I will walk,” he said.

They went down together, and stopped at Pen’s rooms—which now were on the lower story. Here Arthur began to sprinkle himself with eau-de-Cologne and to scent his hair and whiskers with a minuteness usually reserved for chefs with truffles: dab, pat, smooth—an anxious little ritual, as if he meant to season himself before presenting to company.

“What is the matter?” Warrington growled. “You’ve not been smoking. Is it my pipe that has poisoned you?”

“I am going to call upon some women,” Pen said, still arranging his neckcloth as carefully as if he were folding napkins for a grand dinner. “I’m—I’m going to dine with ’em. They are passing through town, and are at an hotel in Jermyn Street.”

Warrington watched with good-natured interest as the young fellow completed his transformation into a polished dish for society’s table: gorgeous shirt-front and neckcloth, fresh gloves, boots that caught light as if they had been glazed like pastry. Warrington himself had thick high-lows; his old shirt was torn about the breast and ragged at the collar, where his beard had worried it like a file.

“Well, young un,” he said simply, “I like you to be a buck, somehow. When I walk about with you, it is as if I had a rose in my button-hole. And you are still affable. I don’t think there is any young fellow in the Temple turns out like you; and I don’t believe you were ever ashamed of walking with me yet.”

“Don’t laugh at me, George,” Pen said.

“I say, Pen,” Warrington added, and there was a sudden awkward tenderness in the way he handled the words, as if they were too hot, “if you write—if you write to Laura, I wish you would say ‘God bless her’ from me.”

Pen blushed; then looked at him; and then—his composure giving way with the comic relief of a man who has been holding in steam too long—burst into an uncontrollable fit of laughing.

“I’m going to dine with her,” he said. “I brought her and Lady Rockminster up from the country to-day—made two days of it—slept last night at Bath. I say, George, come and dine too. I may ask any one I please, and the old lady is constantly talking about you.”

Warrington refused. Warrington had an article to write. Warrington hesitated; and—strange to say—at last he agreed. Perhaps the thought of Laura’s voice, set against the Temple’s grim acoustics, was too tempting; perhaps he wanted to sit near that sound again, as a man in a city craves a mouthful of clean country air.

So it was agreed they should go and call upon the ladies; and they marched away in high spirits to the hotel in Jermyn Street, where London’s roar was softened by carpets and curtains into a respectable purr, like a great animal taught to behave indoors.

Once more the dear face shone upon Warrington; once more the sweet voice spoke; once more the tender hand pressed a welcome. There still wanted half an hour to dinner—half an hour in which hearts, like sauces, thicken of their own accord if you only keep them warm and do not stir them too much.

“You will go and see your uncle now, Mr. Pendennis,” old Lady Rockminster said, with the airy despotism of a woman who expects the men to obey and is amused when they do. “You will not bring him to dinner—no. His old stories are intolerable; and I want to talk to Mr. Warrington; I daresay he will amuse us. I think we have heard all your stories. We have been together for two whole days, and I think we are getting tired of each other.”

So, obedient to her ladyship’s command, Arthur went downstairs and walked to his uncle’s lodgings.

Dinner had been waiting with that patient, simmering resentment which roast fowls acquire when they are kept too long from their proper destiny. Arthur came in at last, not with the victorious air of a man who has conquered time, but with the look of one who has been pursued by it, and nearly taken. His face, usually as ready with a smile as a well-trained waiter with the sauce-boat, was pale and startled, as if some unseen hand had clapped a cold dish over his heart.

Lady Rockminster, who regarded punctuality as a moral virtue and other people’s punctuality as her personal property, opened fire at once.

“So! We condescend to dine with us at last!”

Laura, however, had the quick eye of a woman who can tell by the colour of a cheek whether the soup is too hot or the news too dreadful. She cut across her patroness’s cannonade with a softness that still carried authority, like a spoon laid firmly upon a rattling teacup.

“Arthur—what has happened? Are you ill?”

Arthur, who looked as if a single word might shatter him, said nothing for a moment, but seized a great glass of sherry and drank it as a man swallows courage—fast, without tasting, as though afraid it might escape him. The sherry, at least, did its honest work: it gave him a little colour, though not composure.

“I have heard the most extraordinary news,” he said, glancing at the servants, who were very respectfully deaf in the way servants are when a family secret is whispering at the table. “I will tell you afterwards.”

He was nervous all through the meal; his foot kept up a miserable little tattoo under the cloth, as if trying to drum the truth out of hiding.

“Don’t tramp and beat so with your feet under the table,” cried Lady Rockminster, whose ear for domestic sound was sharp when the sound annoyed her. “You have trodden on Fido, and upset his saucer. You see Mr. Warrington keeps his boots quiet.”

Mr. Warrington did keep his boots quiet; but the quiet had a pressure in it, like a closed oven-door with something dangerous inside.

At last dessert came—late, languid, interminable; the poor fruit looked as if it had been peeled with melancholy. Lady Rockminster surveyed the company as a general reviews a defeated army.

“This dinner has been exceedingly stupid,” she announced. “I suppose something has happened, and that you want to speak to Laura. I will go and have my nap. I am not sure that I shall have any tea—no. Good night, Mr. Warrington. You must come again, and when there is no business to talk about.”

With that she tossed up her head and swept out, dignity crackling around her like starched linen.

The gentlemen rose. Warrington was already shaping his farewell—his “Good night” had nearly reached his lips—when Arthur, with sudden urgency, held him.

“Pray, stay, George. You should hear my news too, and give me your counsel in this case. I hardly know how to act in it.”

Laura’s heart, which had been beating the whole dinner like a covered kettle, gave a little scalding leap.

“It’s something about Blanche, Arthur,” she said; and the blush that rose in her cheek startled herself, as if some long-silent dialect of feeling had spoken suddenly without permission.

“Yes—and the most extraordinary story,” Arthur answered. “When I left you to go to my uncle’s lodgings, I found his servant, Morgan—who has been with him so long—at the door. He said he and his master had parted that morning; that my uncle had quitted the house, and had gone to an hotel—this hotel. I asked for him when I came in; but he was gone out to dinner. Morgan then said he had something of the most important nature to communicate to me, and begged me to step into the house—his house it is now. It appears the scoundrel has saved money in my uncle’s service, and is now a capitalist, a millionaire, for what I know.”

Arthur’s lip curled as if the word “millionaire” had an aftertaste.

“Well, I went into the house; and what do you think he told me? This must be a secret between us all—at least if we can keep it, now that it is in possession of that villain. Blanche’s father is not dead. He has come to life again. The marriage between Clavering and the Begum is no marriage.”

The words fell, one after another, like knives dropped upon a plate.

“And Blanche, I suppose, is her grandfather’s heir,” Warrington said quietly, as if arranging the facts on a board for carving.

“Perhaps: but the child of what a father!” Arthur broke out. “Amory is an escaped convict—Clavering knows it; my uncle knows it—and it was with this piece of information held over Clavering in terrorem that the wretched old man got him to give up his borough to me.”

Laura’s hands clenched and unclenched in her lap, as if kneading an invisible dough of terror into something bearable.

“Blanche doesn’t know it,” she said, almost whispering. “Nor poor Lady Clavering?”

“No,” Arthur answered. “Blanche does not even know the history of her father. She knew that he and her mother had separated; and had heard as a child, from Bonner, her nurse, that Mr. Amory was drowned in New South Wales. He was there as a convict, not as a ship’s-captain, as the poor girl thought. Lady Clavering told me they were not happy, and that her husband was a bad character. She would tell me all, she said, some day; and I remember her saying, with tears in her eyes, that it was hard for a woman to be forced to own she was glad to hear her husband was dead: and that twice in her life she should have chosen so badly.”

He paused, the picture of those women—innocent, domestic, sitting with their needlework and their small daily noises—set against this brutal revelation, making the air in the room feel suddenly coarse, like flour cut with grit.

“What is to be done now?” he asked. “The man can’t show and claim his wife: death is probably over him if he discovers himself—return to transportation certainly. But the rascal has held the threat of discovery over Clavering for some time past, and has extorted money from him time after time.”

“It is our friend Colonel Altamont, of course,” Warrington said. “I see all now.”

Arthur went on, anger growing as naturally as yeast.

“If the rascal comes back, Morgan—who knows his secret—will use it over him; and having it in his possession, proposes to extort money from us all. The d——d rascal supposed I was cognisant of it,” Arthur cried, white with rage; “asked me if I would give him an annuity to keep it quiet; threatened me—me—as if I was trafficking with this wretched old Begum’s misfortune, and would extort a seat in Parliament out of that miserable Clavering. Good heavens! was my uncle mad, to tamper in such a conspiracy? Fancy our mother’s son, Laura, trading on such a treason!”

“I can’t fancy it, dear Arthur,” Laura said, and caught his hand and kissed it—as if the gesture could wipe off the very thought. Her touch was like bread broken and shared: simple, sustaining, unmistakably meant.

“No!” Warrington’s deep voice broke out; there was a tremor in it like a low note heard under a loud room. He looked at them—those two, so honest in their affection—then spoke, forcing himself into practicality as a cook forces a boil into order.

“No. Our boy can’t meddle with such a wretched intrigue as that. Arthur Pendennis can’t marry a convict’s daughter; and sit in Parliament as member for the hulks. You must wash your hands of the whole affair, Pen. You must break off. You must give no explanations of why and wherefore, but state that family reasons render a match impossible. It is better those poor women should fancy you false to your word than that they should know the truth. Besides, you can get from that dog Clavering— I can fetch that for you easily enough—an acknowledgment that the reasons you have given to him as head of the family are amply sufficient for breaking off the union. Don’t you think with me, Laura?”

He scarcely dared to look at her. A man can make brave noises in a noisy room; it is harder when the room is quiet enough to hear the shame in one’s own throat.

Arthur had started up, staring at him, eager, almost pleading to be told what to do. Warrington turned his head away. Laura rose too, went to Arthur, and once again took his hand and kissed it.

“She thinks so too—God bless her!” Warrington said, with a sound in his voice that was half gratitude, half loss.

But Laura did not think so. She grew very pale, and began speaking quickly, as if afraid that if she paused the courage would cool.

“Her father’s shame is not Blanche’s fault, dear Arthur, is it? Suppose you had been married—would you desert her because she had done no wrong? Are you not pledged to her? Would you leave her because she is in misfortune? And if she is unhappy, wouldn’t you console her? Our mother would, had she been here.”

And as she spoke she put her arms round Arthur, and hid her face on his breast, as if to shut out the brutal vocabulary the world had thrust into their gentle lives. Whatever language the scandal used—convict, hulks, bribery—hers rejected it and spoke only the old words that needed no translation: promise, pity, duty.

“Our mother is an angel with God,” Arthur sobbed. “And you are the dearest and best of women—the dearest, the dearest and the best. Teach me my duty. Pray for me that I may do it—pure heart. God bless you—God bless you, my sister!”

“Amen,” Warrington groaned, and covered his face with his hands. “She is right,” he murmured to himself. “She can’t do any wrong, I think—that girl.”

Laura looked up then, and smiled—radiant and quiet. Warrington would see that smile long afterwards, as one hears again in memory a particular sound in a particular room: the soft hush before the kettle sings, the familiar foot on a stair. It was domestic, and therefore holy.

She leaned her little fair hand on the table a moment, playing on it, as if the scene could be brought back to ordinary life by some simple household motion.

“And now, and now,” she said, looking between the two men—

“And what now?” Warrington asked.

“And now we will have some tea,” Laura said, with her smile.

It was the most English attempt at magic: to drown tragedy in a cup.

But before the kettle could even be imagined, a servant came with the message that Major Pendennis had returned to the hotel and was waiting to see his nephew.

Laura’s face changed. She gave Arthur one of those looks that manage to be both command and prayer—Behave yourself well; hold to the right; do your duty; be gentle, but firm—and then she withdrew to her room.

Warrington, who cared little for tea at any time, found himself grudging that cup with quite unreasonable bitterness. Why could not old Pendennis have arrived an hour later? Yet what is an hour, earlier or later, when the inevitable is already on the stair? The hour strikes all the same; the door shuts all the same; and when the brief warmth is gone you are alone with the cold.

Warrington went out. In the street, the hotel windows looked alike, each pane reflecting the same indifferent night.

“In which of those many windows does her light beam?” a man might ask himself, and then hate himself for asking it.

He strode to a neighbouring club and took refuge in the smoking-room, where men were talking loud—politics, opera-girls, horse-racing, the atrocious tyranny of committees. They made noise as if noise were a virtue; the air was thick with smoke and laughter, that commercialized counterfeit of feeling which men buy with brandy and approval. Warrington, carrying his private truth like a stone under his coat, entered the brawl, and even joined it; for it is one of the oddest things in life that we can be shouting a joke while some quieter self sits apart within, listening to another sound entirely—the small, honest sound of a girl’s voice saying, “And now we will have some tea.”

Arthur, walking through the hotel passages toward his uncle, felt anger rouse within him step by step. He was indignant to think that the old gentleman—whom he was about to see—had made him a tool and puppet, and had compromised his honour and good name. The corridor had its usual hotel noises—distant doors, a clink of tray, a cough—but in Arthur’s ears they seemed to accuse, like coins dropped upon a counter.

He found the Major by the fire, shrunken into his dressing-gown, peevish as an old man whose comforts have been mislaid by Providence.

The Major’s hand, when Arthur took it, was cold and shaky. He was coughing; he was grumbling; Frosch could not bring his dressing-gown or arrange his papers as that d——d impudent scoundrel of a Morgan.

“The confounded impudent scoundrel!” the Major cried, bemoaning himself with an injured pathos that had, as usual, one eye on his own inconvenience. “He was drunk last night and challenged me to fight him, Pen; and begad, at one time I was so excited I thought I should have driven a knife into him; and the infernal rascal has made ten thousand pound, I believe—and deserves to be hanged, and will be; but curse him, I wish he could have lasted out my time. He knew all my ways; and dammy, when I rang the bell, the confounded thief brought the thing I wanted—not like that stupid German lout.”

He shifted, coughed, and looked toward Arthur with the affectionate inspection of a man counting his own investments.

“And what sort of time have you had in the country? Been a good deal with Lady Rockminster? You can’t do better. She is one of the old school—vieille ecole, bonne ecole, hey? Dammy, they don’t make gentlemen and ladies now; and in fifty years you’ll hardly know one man from another. But they’ll last my time. I ain’t long for this business: I am getting very old, Pen, my boy; and gad, I was thinking to-day, as I was packing up my little library, there’s a bible amongst the books that belonged to my poor mother; I would like you to keep that, Pen. I was thinking, sir, that you would most likely open the box when it was your property, and the old fellow was laid under the sod, sir.”

He wagged his head over the fire and coughed again.

The sight of his age—his genuine fondness—did what it always did: it softened Arthur’s wrath into something more complicated. Compunction crept in, unwelcome and heavy. Arthur knew the announcement he must make would smash the Major’s favourite air-castle, that pretty, profitable fantasy the old man had been baking for years.

“Hey—hey—I’m off, sir,” the Major nodded, half joking, half trembling. “But I’d like to read a speech of yours in the Times before I go—‘Mr. Pendennis said, Unaccustomed as I am to public speaking’—hey, sir? hey, Arthur? Begad, you look dev’lish well and healthy, sir. I always said my brother Jack would bring the family right. You must go down into the west, and buy the old estate, sir. Nec tenui penna, hey? We’ll rise again, sir—rise again on the wing—and begad, I shouldn’t be surprised that you will be a Baronet before you die.”

The words smote Arthur like a hymn heard in a place where one is about to commit a sin.

“And it is I,” he thought, “that am going to fling down the poor old fellow’s air-castle. Well, it must be. Here goes.”

Aloud, slowly: “I—I went into your lodgings at Bury Street, though I did not find you—and I talked with Morgan, uncle.”

“Indeed!” The old gentleman’s cheek flushed despite himself. He muttered, “The cat’s out of the bag now, begad!”

“He told me a story, sir, which gave me the deepest surprise and pain,” Arthur said.

The Major tried to look unconcerned, and failed with the particular failure of old men who have been managing other people’s morals too long.

“What—that story about—about—What-d’-you-call-’em, hey?”

“About Miss Amory’s father—about Lady Clavering’s first husband, and who he is, and what.”

“Hem—a dev’lish awkward affair!” the Major said, rubbing his nose. “I—I’ve been aware of that—eh—confounded circumstance for some time.”

“He is all safe,” the Senior thought, relieved. “Gad! I should have liked to keep it from you altogether—and from those two poor women, who are as innocent as unborn babes in the transaction.”

“I wish I had known it sooner, or not at all,” Arthur said gloomily.

“Gad! I should have liked to keep it from you altogether,” the Major repeated aloud, a little too quickly; “and from those two poor women—”

“You are right. There is no reason why the two women should hear it; and I shall never tell them—though that villain, Morgan, perhaps may,” Arthur said. “He seems disposed to trade upon his secret, and has already proposed terms of ransom to me. I wish I had known of the matter earlier, sir. It is not a very pleasant thought to me that I am engaged to a convict’s daughter.”

“The very reason why I kept it from you—my dear boy. But Miss Amory is not a convict’s daughter, don’t you see?” the Major cried, eager now, warming to his own argument as if it were a glass of hot negus. “Miss Amory is the daughter of Lady Clavering, with fifty or sixty thousand pounds for a fortune; and her father-in-law, a Baronet and country gentleman, of high reputation, approves of the match, and gives up his seat in Parliament to his son-in-law. What can be more simple?”

“Is it true, sir?” Arthur asked.

“Begad, yes, it is true, of course it’s true. Amory’s dead. I tell you he is dead. The first sign of life he shows, he is dead. He can’t appear. We have him at a deadlock, like the fellow in the play—the ‘Critic,’ hey?—dev’lish amusing play, that ‘Critic.’ Monstrous witty man, Sheridan; and so was his son. By Gad, sir, when I was at the Cape, I remember—”

His voice wandered, as if he would lead Arthur away from the subject into safer colonial reminiscence, where convict-fathers were merely anecdotes and not daggers.

Arthur cut in sharply.

“If you had told me this tale sooner, I believe you would have spared me and yourself a great deal of pain and disappointment; and I should not have found myself tied to an engagement from which I can’t, in honour, recede.”
