“No, begad, we’ve fixed you—and a man who’s fixed to a seat in Parliament, and a pretty girl, with a couple of thousand a year, is fixed to no bad thing, let me tell you,” the Major said, with that brisk, businesslike cheerfulness which, in some men, passes for conscience.

“Great Heavens, sir!” Arthur cried. “Are you blind? Can’t you see?”

“See what, young gentleman?” the other snapped.

“See, that rather than trade upon this secret of Amory’s,” Arthur cried out, “I would go and join my father-in-law at the hulks! See, that rather than take a seat in Parliament as a bribe from Clavering for silence, I would take the spoons off the table! See, that you have given me a felon’s daughter for a wife; doomed me to poverty and shame; cursed my career when it might have been—when it might have been so different but for you! Don’t you see that we have been playing a guilty game, and have been overreached;—that in offering to marry this poor girl, for the sake of her money, and the advancement she would bring, I was degrading myself, and prostituting my honour?”

“What in Heaven’s name do you mean, sir?” the Major cried, shocked less at the morality than at the disruption of his plan.

“I mean to say that there is a measure of baseness which I can’t pass,” Arthur said. “I have no other words for it, and am sorry if they hurt you. I have felt, for months past, that my conduct in this affair has been wicked, sordid, and worldly. I am rightly punished by the event; and having sold myself for money and a seat in Parliament, by losing both.”

“How do you mean that you lose either?” shrieked the old gentleman. “Who the devil’s to take your fortune or your seat away from you? By G—, Clavering shall give ’em to you. You shall have every shilling of eighty thousand pounds.”

“I’ll keep my promise to Miss Amory, sir,” Arthur said.

“And, begad, her parents shall keep theirs to you.”

“Not so, please God,” Arthur answered. “I have sinned, but Heaven help me, I will sin no more. I will let Clavering off from that bargain which was made without my knowledge. I will take no money with Blanche but that which was originally settled upon her; and I will try to make her happy. You have done it. You have brought this on me, sir. But you knew no better: and I forgive—”

The Major, at that, broke as suddenly as a hard crust cracked to show it was only air inside. All his toughness ran out of him.

“Arthur—in God’s name—in your father’s, who, by Heavens, was the proudest man alive, and had the honour of the family always at heart—in mine—for the sake of a poor broken-down old fellow, who has always been dev’lish fond of you—don’t fling this chance away—I pray you, I beg you, I implore you, my dear, dear boy, don’t fling this chance away. It’s the making of you. You’re sure to get on. You’ll be a Baronet; it’s three thousand a year: dammy, on my knees, there, I beg of you, don’t do this.”

And the old man actually sank on his knees, seized Arthur’s hand, and looked up piteously. It was dreadful to see: the shaking fingers, the wrinkled, quivering face, the watery eyes winking and spilling, the broken voice—this proud manager of other people reduced to begging like a discharged servant.

“Ah, sir,” Arthur groaned, “you have brought pain enough on me—spare me this. You have wished me to marry Blanche. I marry her. For God’s sake, sir, rise! I can’t bear it.”

“You—you mean to say that you will take her as a beggar, and be one yourself?” the Major said, rising with a cough that sounded like anger choking on its own fumes.

“I look at her as a person to whom a great calamity has befallen, and to whom I am promised,” Arthur answered. “She cannot help the misfortune; and as she had my word when she was prosperous, I shall not withdraw it now she is poor. I will not take Clavering’s seat, unless afterwards it should be given of his free will. I will not have a shilling more than her original fortune.”

The Major stared at him as if Arthur had begun speaking in some foreign provincial tongue—honour, duty, pity—words which, to the old man, had always required translation into income.

“Have the kindness to ring the bell,” he said at last, with a sudden coldness. “I have done my best, and said my say; and I’m a dev’lish old fellow. And—and—it don’t matter. And—and Shakspeare was right—and Cardinal Wolsey—begad—‘and had I but served my God as I’ve served you’—yes, on my knees, by Jove, to my own nephew—I mightn’t have been—Good night, sir. You needn’t trouble yourself to call again.”

Arthur took his hand. The Major left it in his grasp without pressure—passive, clammy, like something already withdrawing from life. His face looked older in the firelight, as if the fight and the loss had aged him in an hour.

The next day the Major kept his bed, and refused to see his nephew.

Pen, in that loose, domestic costume which makes even a philosopher look like a culprit—his dressing-gown—went up, as regularly as if it were morning prayers, to Warrington’s chambers, meaning to pour out the whole history of last night’s campaign with the Major, and to get from George, as usual, counsel, consolation, contradiction, or laughter.

Instead of George he found Mrs. Flanagan, laundress, empress, and sole surviving inhabitant of those beloved rooms; and she stood there with her arms folded, as if to say that linen, not literature, was now the reigning power.

“Gone, is it?” Pen cried.

“Gone, sir,” said Mrs. Flanagan; and there was in her voice that particular melancholy with which a good woman speaks of a gentleman who has not only paid his washing, but also behaved like one. “I found him at the table, when I came, the dear gentleman—writing at his papers, and one of the candles burned out; and hard as his bed is, he wasn’t in it all night, sir.”

On the table lay the evidence of his trade—packets directed to the newspaper and the review; proofs and scribbled sheets; books tugged from the shelves and left open like mouths caught mid-remark; a litter of torn manuscript, like peelings from some harsh fruit he had been obliged to pare in haste; pens, ink, a blotting-paper scored with half-visible lines; and a bit of sealing-wax twisted, bitten, and broken, as if it had been some tough piece of toffee gnawed in angry thought. If you could have heard the room you might have known him too: no talk, no fiddle, no companionable tread—only the faint after-rustle of paper, the imaginary scratch of a pen, and that city hush which is never truly quiet, but merely waiting to clang again.

George had come home from the Club when the brawl there grew too coarse even for a satirist to endure; and instead of drinking and shouting with the rest, he had set himself down to his work with that savage steadiness by which men try to master what they cannot otherwise bear. He bent all his strength upon the labour; and the night wore away—one candle consumed, the other guttering—until the tardy November dawn, grey as dishwater, looked in at the windows and found him still there, solitary at his desk, finishing what the public would presently read over breakfast as though it had been baked for them in the night like a batch of rolls.

In the next day’s paper, or the quarter’s review, many a comfortable gentleman would admire the fierce vigour of his satire, the depth of his reason, the variety of his illustration—taking it, as people do take their meals, without guessing the kitchen’s heat. There was no hint in the writing of the other thoughts that sat always beside him, like a silent second at the table. Those who knew his name and flavour might have detected, perhaps, an extra bitterness; a melancholy note behind the laughter, as if a bell had been muffled. For the face behind the mask is often grave; and the man who lives by the pen knows nights of labour when the room is full of invisible company—care, sickness, dread, grief—while the hand goes on, because ink must be earned, and the world’s appetite does not wait.

Pen flung himself into George’s empty chair and stared about him, noting things according to his habit, or in spite of it. In the bookcase there was a gap, next to the old College Plato with the Boniface Arms; and that gap hit him like a hand on the heart.

Helen’s Bible had been there.

“He has taken that with him,” Pen thought; and he knew—without any need of Mrs. Flanagan’s commentary—why his friend was gone. The room seemed suddenly to have lost not merely a tenant but a tone, as when a familiar instrument is removed from an orchestra and the air misses its particular string.

Dear, dear old George! Pen rubbed his hand over his eyes, and the thought went through him with a humility that was almost rage. How much wiser, better, nobler he is than I! Where shall I ever hear that frank voice and kind laughter again? Where shall I see such a true gentleman? No wonder she loved him. What was I compared to him? What could she do else but love him? And then, with that queer loyal imagination by which men console themselves when they have been beaten fairly, he vowed that to the end of their days they would be her brothers—knights even—waiting on her, and when old, telling one another how they had loved her.

Coming down to his own chambers, he saw, at last, the little letter that had been slipped into his letter-box—addressed to A. P., Esq., in George’s unmistakable hand. He broke it with an impatience that was almost fear.

“Dear Pen,—I shall be half-way home when you breakfast, and intend to stay over Christmas, in Norfolk, or elsewhere.

“I have my own opinion of the issue of matters about which we talked in J——— St. yesterday; and think my presence de trop.

“Vale. G. W.”

“Give my very best regards and adieux to your cousin.”

So George was gone; and Mrs. Flanagan reigned over the empty chambers as over an abandoned province.

Pen, of course, had to go dutifully and present himself at his uncle’s door the day after their colloquy. Not being admitted—Major Pendennis, when he was offended, could barricade himself as grandly as a fortress—Arthur did what he always did when turned out of one room: he went to another where he was sure of kindness, and presented himself in Lady Rockminster’s apartments.

The old lady instantly asked for Bluebeard and insisted he should come to dinner.

“Bluebeard is gone,” Pen said; and he took out George’s scrap of paper and handed it to Laura.

Laura looked at it—did not look at Pen in return—gave it back, and walked away, as if the small square of writing had been a coal and her fingers scorched.

Pen, who could not bear a silence, rushed into an eloquent eulogium of his dear old George for Lady Rockminster’s benefit; the dowager stared at him in honest amazement. She had never heard him so warm in praise of anybody, and told him, with her usual frankness, that she didn’t think it had been in his nature to care so much about any other person.

Not long after, as Arthur was passing through Waterloo Place in one of his many walks to the hotel where Laura lived—and whither his daily duty to his uncle carried him—he saw issuing from Messrs. Gimcrack’s celebrated shop an old acquaintance, followed to a brougham by an obsequious shopman bearing parcels.

The gentleman was in the deepest mourning: the brougham, the driver, and the horse were in mourning. Grief, when it can afford the comfortablest springs and cushions, has a way of looking properly upholstered; and the whole equipage seemed to say, “Affliction is very distressing, but please observe we have ordered it with the best appointments.”

“What, Foker! Hail, Foker!” cried Pen; and indeed it was his old schoolfellow, the heir of the late John Henry Foker, Esq., master of Logwood and other houses, principal partner in the great brewery of Foker and Co.—the greater portion of Foker’s Entire, now solemnly transferred into the care of a son who looked as if he had been bred to sip rather than to govern vats.

A little hand, gloved in the blackest possible ebony and set off by three inches of snowy wristband, came forth to meet Arthur’s. The other little hand held a morocco case, which, no doubt, contained something precious newly acquired under Gimcrack’s persuasive lights.

Pen’s sharp eyes and satiric instinct took in the errand at once, and thought of Horace and heirs, of gathered wine from a father’s vats; and how human nature keeps its recipes unchanged whether it be in the Via Sacra or Regent Street.

“Le Roi est mort. Vive le Roi!” said Arthur.

“Ah!” said the other, and that “Ah!” contained condolence, embarrassment, and a desire to get away before any moral observation could be served with the handshake. “Yes. Thank you—very much obliged. How do you do, Pen?—very busy—good-bye!” And he jumped into the black brougham and sate like a little black Care behind the black coachman.

He had blushed at seeing Pen—signs of guilt and perturbation which Arthur, in his sardonic way, set down partly to the novelty of being a monarch in mourning, partly to the knowledge that Gimcrack’s is not the natural retreat of a broken heart.

“Yes: so wags the world,” Pen thought as he walked on. “The stone closes over Harry the Fourth, and Harry the Fifth reigns in his stead. The old ministers at the brewery come and kneel before him with their books; the draymen fling up their red caps and shout. What grave deference and sympathy the bankers and lawyers show!” And then, because his mind would always knead bitterness into whatever loaf of thought was rising, he reflected that when one man keeps another out of twenty thousand a year, the younger is apt to hanker after the crown; and the wish is father to the thought of possession. “Thank Heaven,” he concluded, “there was no thought of money between me and our dear mother, Laura.”

“There never could have been. You would have spurned it!” cried Laura when he said as much to her later. “Why make yourself more selfish than you are, Pen?—and allow your mind to own for an instant that it would have entertained such—such dreadful meanness? You make me blush for you, Arthur: you make me—” Her eyes finished the sentence, and her handkerchief followed.

“There are some truths women will never acknowledge,” Pen said, “and from which your modesty always turns away. I do not say I ever knew the feeling—only that I am glad I had not the temptation. Is there any harm in that confession of weakness?”

“We are all taught to ask to be delivered from evil, Arthur,” said Laura in a low voice. “I am glad if you were spared from that great crime; and only sorry to think you could by any possibility have been led into it. But you never could; and you don’t think you could. Your acts are generous and kind: you disdain mean actions. You take Blanche without money, and without a bribe. Yes, thanks be to Heaven, dear brother. You could not have sold yourself away; I knew you could not when it came to the day, and you did not. Praise be—be where praise is due. Why does this horrid scepticism pursue you, my Arthur? Why doubt and sneer at your own heart—at every one’s? Oh, if you knew the pain you give me—how I lie awake and think of those hard sentences, dear brother, and wish them unspoken, unthought!”

“Do I cause you many thoughts and many tears, Laura?” asked Arthur.

The fulness of innocent love answered him more plainly than words: a smile pure as fresh milk, a glance of unutterable tenderness and sympathy shone in her face—those indications of love and goodness which he could only worship, as one watches them in a child, as one fancies one might regard them in an angel.

“I—I don’t know what I have done,” he said simply, “to have merited such regard from two such women. It is like undeserved praise—or too much good fortune, which frightens one—or a great post, when a man feels he is not fit for it. Ah, sister, how weak and wicked we are; how spotless, and full of love and truth, Heaven made you! I think for some of you there has been no fall,” he added, looking at her with an almost paternal admiration. “You can’t help having sweet thoughts, and doing good actions. Dear creature! they are the flowers which you bear.”

“And what else, sir?” asked Laura, quick as a bird to hear the change in his breathing. “I see a sneer coming over your face. What is it? Why does it come to drive all the good thoughts away?”

“A sneer, is there? I was thinking, my dear, that nature in making you so good and loving did very well: but—”

“But what? What is that wicked but? and why are you always calling it up?”

“But will come in spite of us. But is reflection. But is the sceptic’s familiar, with whom he has made a compact; and if he forgets it and indulges in happy day-dreams—or listens to sweet music, let us say, or to the bells ringing to church—But taps at the door and says, Master, I am here. You are my master; but I am yours. Go where you will, you can’t travel without me. I will whisper to you when you are on your knees at church. I will be at your marriage pillow. I will sit down at your table with your children. I will be behind your deathbed curtain. That is what But is.”

“Pen, you frighten me,” cried Laura.

“Do you know what But came and said to me just now, when I was looking at you? But said, If that girl had reason as well as love, she would love you no more. If she knew you as you are—the sullied, selfish being which you know—she must part from you, and could give you no love and no sympathy.” And then, softening, as he always did when he saw her pained: “Didn’t I say some of you seem exempt from the fall? Love you know; but the knowledge of evil is kept from you.”

“What is this you young folks are talking about?” asked Lady Rockminster, sweeping in at this moment, having performed, in the mystic retirement of her apartments and under the hands of her attendant, those elaborate rites without which she never presented herself to the public. “Mr. Pendennis, you are always coming here.”

“It is very pleasant to be here,” Arthur said; “and we were talking, when you came in, about my friend Foker, whom I met just now; and who, as your ladyship knows, has succeeded to his father’s kingdom.”

“He has a very fine property, he has fifteen thousand a year. He is my cousin. He is a very worthy young man. He must come and see me,” said Lady Rockminster, with a look at Laura that was as plain as a command.

“He has been engaged for many years past to his cousin, Lady—”

“Lady Ann is a foolish little chit,” Lady Rockminster cut in, with immense dignity; “and I have no patience with her. She has outraged every feeling of society. She has broken her father’s heart, and thrown away fifteen thousand a year.”

“Thrown away? What has happened?” asked Pen.

“It will be the talk of the town in a day or two; and there is no need I should keep the secret any longer,” said her ladyship, who had already written and received a dozen letters on the subject, and enjoyed the catastrophe as some people enjoy a new sauce. “I had a letter yesterday from my daughter, who was staying at Drummington until all the world was obliged to go away on account of the frightful catastrophe which happened there. When Mr. Foker came home from Nice, and after the funeral, Lady Ann went down on her knees to her father, said she never could marry her cousin, that she had contracted another attachment, and that she must die rather than fulfil her contract. Poor Lord Rosherville, who is dreadfully embarrassed, showed his daughter what the state of his affairs was, and that it was necessary the arrangements should take place; and in fine we all supposed she had listened to reason, and intended to comply with the desires of her family. But what has happened? Last Thursday she went out after breakfast with her maid, and was married in the very church in Drummington Park to Mr. Hobson, her father’s own chaplain and her brother’s tutor; a red-haired widower with two children.

“Poor dear Rosherville is in a dreadful way: he wishes Henry Foker should marry Alice or Barbara; but Alice is marked with the small-pox, and Barbara is ten years older than he is. And of course now the young man is his own master, he will think of choosing for himself. The blow on Lady Agnes is very cruel. She is inconsolable. She has the house in Grosvenor Street for her life, and her settlement, which was very handsome. Have you not met her? Yes, she dined one day at Lady Clavering’s—the first day I saw you, and a very disagreeable young man I thought you were. But I have formed you. We have formed him, haven’t we, Laura? Where is Bluebeard? Let him come. That horrid Grindley, the dentist, will keep me in town another week.”

To the latter part of this speech Arthur gave no ear. His mind—perverse in its curiosities—had run back to Gimcrack’s parcels. For whom could Foker be buying those trinkets? Why had Harry looked so eager to escape? Could he be still faithful to that attachment which had once agitated him so much and sent him abroad eighteen months back?

Psha! The bracelets and fine things were for some old acquaintance of the Opera or the French theatre. Rumours from Naples and Paris—those airy, greasy whispers borne into club smoking-rooms—had announced that the young man had found distractions; or, precluded from his virtuous attachment, had flung himself back upon old companions and amusements: not the only man (or woman) whom society forces into evil, or debars from good; not the only victim of the world’s selfish laws. Even the city seemed complicit: it clattered, hissed, and rolled—wheels, hoofs, voices—like a huge indifferent kitchen, forever turning out noise, and caring little what hearts were being chopped beneath it.

Meanwhile Laura, with the zeal of a person who thinks happiness must be served piping hot or it will spoil, pressed Pen’s marriage on with a feverish anxiety. Pen, who could afford to let the matter simmer, would have waited; but Laura would hear of no delay. She wrote, implored, urged, hurried. It seemed as if she could have no rest until Arthur’s happiness was complete, as if she were trying by speed to outrun some sound she dreaded hearing behind her.

She offered herself to Blanche—dearest Blanche—to come and stay at Tunbridge when Lady Rockminster should go on her intended visit to the reigning house of Rockminster; and though the old dowager scolded, ordered, commanded, Laura was deaf and disobedient. The dowager might nurse her rheumatism, might read herself to sleep if she would not hear her maid (whose voice croaked and made sad work of sentimental passages); but Laura must go—would go—and be with her new sister. She who ordinarily had no will of her own, and complied smilingly with anybody’s whim, showed, in this one instance, what the world calls selfishness and what love calls necessity.

Thus began a correspondence—No. 1, No. 2, No. 3—so full of “dearests” that the very paper might have turned sugary.

Laura wrote, proposing, with many loves and regards to Lady Clavering, to pass some time with dearest Blanche.

Blanche answered instantly to dearest Laura’s No. 1: with what extreme delight she should welcome her sister; how charming it would be to practise their old duets together, to wander o’er the grassy sward and amidst the yellowing woods of Penshurst and Southborough. Blanche counted the hours till she should embrace her dearest friend.

Laura’s No. 2 expressed delight at this affectionate reply. She hoped their friendship would never diminish; that their confidence would grow in after years; that they should have no secrets from each other; that the aim of the life of each would be to make one person happy.

Blanche’s No. 2 came two days later with a grievance: how provoking! Their house was very small, the two spare bedrooms were occupied by that horrid Mrs. Planter and her daughter, who had thought proper to fall ill (she always fell ill in country-houses), and she could not or would not be moved for some days.

Laura’s No. 3: it was indeed provoking. She had hoped to hear one of dearest Blanche’s dear songs on Friday; but she was consoled to wait, because Lady Rockminster was not very well and liked to be nursed by her. Poor Major Pendennis was very unwell too, in the same hotel—too unwell even to see Arthur, who was constant in his calls on his uncle. Arthur’s heart was full of tenderness and affection. She had known Arthur all her life. She would answer—yes, even in italics she would answer—for his kindness, his goodness, and his gentleness.

And then Blanche’s No. 3 arrived like a plate dashed suddenly down in the middle of a gentle meal:

“What is this most surprising, most extraordinary letter from A. P.? What does dearest Laura know about it? What has happened? What, what mystery is enveloped under his frightful reserve?”

Blanche required an explanation; and it could not be better given than in the surprising and mysterious letter of Arthur Pendennis.

Arthur wrote to Blanche as a man writes who has just heard the tureen-lid crack in the very moment of triumph, and sees all his promised gravy running away into the table-cloth.

“My dear Blanche,” he said, “you have been reading and dreaming your pretty dramas, where the heroine sweeps into her father’s palace as if into a well-warmed dining-room, and says to the astonished company, ‘All this is mine and thine,’ and the servants bring in the great silver covers with a flourish, and everybody’s portion is large and certain. Will you be prepared—only for once—to act the other part? Not the princess with the bridal cake and the trumpets; but the unlucky lady who discovers that the grand entertainment was all a bill of fare, and the dinner itself a crust eaten by the kitchen-fire.

“You remember Alnaschar with his tray of porcelain? He kicked it down, and with it went all his castles of tea-cups and saucers, all his hopes, all his glittering future. I am not sure he had even so much as a wife to help him pick up the pieces; but the moral is the same. Something has happened within the last few hours—something I cannot tell you now, and perhaps never need tell, if God is merciful—which has overset my tray as neatly as if a malicious foot had been waiting for it.

“You have known my little property, and you have known your own little fortune. It will be no Belgravia feast; it will be plain fare. There will be days when we shall dine off the steady, honest joint of our own industry, and be proud of it; and days when the joint will be small, and the carving a little anxious. There will be no stars and epaulettes for the hero; I shall not be a duke with a garter at his knee, nor a bishop on the bench, nor a member of Parliament for Clavering—at least not now. I have written to Sir Francis Clavering that I cannot accept the seat he offered me until after my marriage; and in like manner I cannot and will not accept any larger fortune with you than that which has always been yours since your grandfather’s death and the birth of your half-brother.

“Do you understand what it is to live decently on what we can honestly earn? We may take a cab sometimes, and not be too proud to take an omnibus when we are tired; we shall have friends, books, laughter, and the humble comforts which come like the smell of bread from a neighbour’s oven—common, and yet cheering. I may buy back the Pall Mall Gazette, since the publishers are weary of it after poor Shandon’s death, and will sell it for a small sum. Warrington will be my right hand. You shall have your share of the paper’s little vanities—opera-boxes if we can afford them, fashionable intelligence if you like it, and the poet’s corner if it must be. We can live over the office: four good rooms, a kitchen, and a garret for Laura, in Catherine Street in the Strand. Or a house in the Waterloo Road—pleasant enough, except for that halfpenny toll at the Bridge, which is the sort of tax Fate delights to lay on romance. The boys may go to King’s College, may they not?

“Does this read like a joke? It is none. Our fine day-dreams are gone—whisked away like Cinderella’s coach at midnight, only with less punctuality and more malice. If you can say, ‘Yes, Arthur, I will follow your fate, and be a loyal and loving wife to aid and cheer you,’ then come to me, dear Blanche, and may God help me to do my duty by you. If not—if you look to a higher station—I must not bar your fortune. I will stand in the crowd and see your ladyship go to Court when you are presented, and you shall give me a smile from your chariot window. Lady Mirabel went to the drawing-room last season, all flowers and glitter: her happy husband beside her blazing with stars and cordons, the coachman’s bosom a garden. Will you have the chariot, or walk on foot and mend your husband’s stockings?

“My uncle is very unwell, and takes my refusal of the seat in Parliament in sad dudgeon; the scheme was his, and he naturally bemoans its failure. But Warrington, Laura, and I have held a council of war: they know this dreadful secret, and back me in my decision. You must love George as you love what is generous and upright and noble; and Laura—she must be our sister, Blanche, our saint, our good angel. With two such friends at home, what need we care for the world without?”

To this came back Blanche’s letter—addressed to Laura—and another to Arthur, written with all the clearness of her neat hand, and perfumed so that the paper seemed to have been laid in a drawer of rose-leaves and sighs.

“You are spoiled by the world,” she wrote, “you do not love your poor Blanche as she would be loved, or you would not offer thus lightly to take her or to leave her. No, Arthur, you love me not. A man of the world, you have given me your plighted troth, and are ready to redeem it; but that entire affection, that love whole and abiding—where is it? I am but a pastime of your life, and I would be its all. I would have our two hearts one; but ah, my Arthur, how lonely yours is! how little you give me of it! You speak of our parting with a smile on your lip; of our meeting, and you care not to hasten it! I have wept—I have prayed—I have passed sleepless hours—bitter, bitter tears over your letter! I bring you the gushing poesy of my being—the yearnings of the soul that longs to be loved—love, love, love, beyond all!—and you are cold. You accept my soul’s treasure as though ’twere dross. You treat me like a slave, and bid me bow to my master! Is this the guerdon of a free maiden—is this the price of a life’s passion? Foolish girl that I was! One by one the flowers of my young life have faded away; and this, the last, the sweetest—where is it? But no more. Bless you, bless you always, Arthur!

“I will write more when I am more collected. My racking brain renders thought almost impossible. I long to see Laura! She will come to us directly we return from the country, will she not? And you, cold one!

“B.”

The words were plain enough, each letter set as carefully as if she had been decorating a cake; yet the meaning puzzled Arthur. Did she refuse him because he was cold? or accept him because she was tragic? Her phrases turned like a spit before two opposite fires. He sat twiddling the gilt-edged, musky riddle between finger and thumb, and laughed—sardonically, because laughter was easier than tasting the bitterness that rose in his mouth. Fortune had jilted him; and, like many a jilted gentleman, he found a kind of humour in examining the very shoe-print on his heart.

He was so employed, grimly amused, when his servant entered with a card.

“A gentleman wishes to speak to you very particularly, sir.”

“Show him in,” said Arthur; and if he had stepped into the passage he would have seen, sucking his stick, rolling his eyes, and wearing anxiety as ill as a borrowed coat, his old acquaintance Mr. Samuel Huxter.

Huxter came in, a young man with the air of one who has swallowed a pill without water.

“Pray take a chair, Mr. Huxter,” Arthur said, in his most superb manner. “In what way can I be of service to you?”

“I’d rather not speak before the flunk—before the man, Mr. Pendennis,” said Huxter; and Arthur’s attendant withdrew.

“I’m in a fix,” said the young surgeon, gloomily.

“Indeed.”

“She sent me to you.”

“Fanny? Is she well? I was coming to see her; but I have had a great deal of business since my return to London.”

“I heard of you through my governor and Jack Hobnell,” Huxter blurted. “I wish you joy, Mr. Pendennis—both of the borough and the lady, sir. Fanny wishes you joy, too,” he added, colouring a little in spite of himself.

“There’s many a slip between the cup and the lip,” Arthur said. “Who knows who will sit for Clavering next session?”

“You can do anything with my governor,” Huxter went on. “You got him Clavering Park. The old boy was mighty pleased at your calling him in. Hobnell wrote me. Do you think you could speak to him for me, Mr. Pendennis?”

“And tell him what?”

Huxter gave Arthur a look which tried to be daring and succeeded only in being miserable.

“I’ve gone and done it, sir.”

Arthur started up as if he had heard a plate crash. “You—you don’t mean to say you have—done any wrong to that dear little creature?”

“I hope not,” said Huxter, with a hangdog face. “But I’ve married her. And there’ll be an awful shindy at home. It was agreed I was to be taken into partnership when I’d passed the College—Huxter and Son. But I would have it—confound it. It’s all over now; and the old boy’s wrote that he’s coming up to town for drugs. He’ll be here to-morrow, and then it must all come out.”

“And when did this event happen?” Arthur asked, not over pleased—perhaps because a lady who had once taken a place in his own little court had now crowned another man.

“Last Thursday was five weeks,” Huxter answered. “Two days after Miss Amory came to Shepherd’s Inn.”

Arthur remembered Blanche mentioning that visit; and a cold little pain ran under his ribs.

“I was called in,” Huxter continued. “I was in the Inn, looking after old Cos’s leg—and about something else too, likely enough—and I met Strong, who told me there was a woman taken ill in chambers. I went up to give my professional services. It was the old lady that attends Miss Amory—housekeeper, or something. Taken with strong hysterics. I found her kicking and screaming like a good one—in Strong’s chambers—Strong and Colonel Altamont there, Miss Amory crying and pale as a sheet, and Altamont fuming about—regular kick-up. They were two hours in chambers; and the old woman went whooping off in a cab. She was much worse than the young one.

“I called next day at Grosvenor Place to see if I could be of use; but they were gone without so much as thanking me. And the day after—I had business of my own. Bad business too,” Huxter said, and looked down as though the floor reproached him. “But it’s done, and can’t be undone; and we must make the best of it.”

She has known the story for a month, Arthur thought—this accounts for her letter. She will not implicate her father. She wishes to let me off, and finds a pretext—the generous girl! The thought brought a pang of grief, and a gloomy kind of gratitude.

“Do you know who Altamont is, sir?” Huxter asked after a pause. “Fanny and I have talked him over; and we can’t help fancying it’s Mrs. Lightfoot’s first husband come to life again—and she that’s just married a second. Perhaps Lightfoot won’t be very sorry for it,” he added, with a savage sigh; for jealousy still gnawed him, and now, married as he was, he fancied Fanny’s heart had been packed away for Arthur Pendennis like contraband.

“Let us talk about your affairs,” Arthur said. “Show me how I can serve you. Let me congratulate you on your marriage. I am thankful that Fanny—so good, so fascinating, so kind—has found an honest man, and a gentleman who will make her happy. Tell me what I can do.”

“She thinks you can,” Huxter said, taking Arthur’s offered hand. “And I’m very much obliged. If you’d talk over my father and break it to him—and my mother, that always has her back up about being a clergyman’s daughter. Fanny ain’t of a good family, I know, and not up to us in breeding—but she’s a Huxter now.”

“The wife takes the husband’s rank,” Arthur said.

“And with a little practice in society,” Huxter went on, biting his stick, “she’ll be as good as any girl in Clavering. You should hear her sing and play. Old Bows taught her. And she’ll do on the stage if the governor throws me over—though I’d rather not have her there. She can’t help being a coquette, Mr. Pendennis—can’t help it. Dammy, sir, I’ll be bound two or three of the Bartholomew chaps I’ve brought into my place are sitting with her now. Even Jack Linton—took him down as my best man—is as bad as the rest; and she’ll go on singing and making eyes at him. Bows says if there were twenty men in a room and one not taking notice of her, she wouldn’t be satisfied till the twentieth was at her elbow.”

“You should have her mother with her,” Arthur said, laughing.

“She must keep the lodge,” Huxter said, drawing himself up with the dignity of a man in a dirty collar. “She can’t see so much of her family as she used. I can’t, you know, go on with that lot. Consider my rank in life.”

“Au fait,” said Arthur, who was infinitely amused—though, as happens with amused men, the joke bit himself somewhere.

In the midst of this, there came another knock; and the servant announced Mr. Bows.

The old man entered slowly, pale, blushing as if ashamed of being seen, his hand trembling a little as he took Arthur’s. He coughed, wiped his face with a checked cotton handkerchief, sat down with hands on knees, the sunlight shining frankly on his bald head. Arthur looked at him with a sudden kindness. Here, too, was a man who had brought his heart like a dish to a woman’s table, and had had it pushed aside.

“So we have lost, Mr. Bows,” Arthur said, “and here is the lucky winner.”

“Here is the lucky winner,” Bows answered, dryly.

“I suppose you have come from my place?” Huxter said; and having winked at Bows with one eye, he now favoured Arthur with a wink of the other—a wink which tried to say, “Infatuated old boy—head and ears—poor old fool,” and succeeded only in making him look like a man with grit in his eyelash.

“Yes,” Bows said. “I have been there ever since you went away. It was Mrs. Sam sent me after you—said she thought you might be doing something stupid—something like yourself, Huxter.”

“There’s as big fools as I am,” growled the young surgeon.

“A few, p’raps,” Bows returned. “Not many, let us trust. She sent me after you for fear you should offend Mr. Pendennis; and because she thought you wouldn’t give her message, and beg him to go and see her; and she knew I would take her errand. Did he tell you that, sir?”

Huxter blushed scarlet, and tried to cover it with an oath. Arthur laughed, because the scene suited his bitter humour.

“I have no doubt Mr. Huxter was going to tell me,” Arthur said. “And very much flattered I shall be to pay my respects to his wife.”

“It’s in Charterhouse Lane, over the baker’s, on the right-hand side as you go from St. John’s Street,” Bows continued, with pitiless exactness. “You know Smithfield, Mr. Pendennis? Doctor Johnson’s been down that street many a time with ragged shoes and a bundle of penny-a-lining for the Gent’s Magazine. You literary gents are better off now—ride in cabs, wear yellow kid gloves.”

“I have known so many brave men fail, and so many quacks succeed,” Arthur said, more sadly than before, “that you mistake me if you think I am puffed up by my own good luck. Do you think the prizes of life are carried by the most deserving? You must feel you are as good as I. I have never questioned it. It is you that are peevish against the freaks of fortune, and grudge what befalls others. It is not the first time you have unjustly accused me, Bows.”

“Perhaps you’re not far wrong,” the old fellow said, wiping his forehead. “A man grumbles when he thinks of himself. Here’s the fellow got the prize; here’s the fortunate youth.”

“I don’t know what you are driving at,” Huxter said, bewildered by talk which seemed to him to have nothing to do with drugs, marriage, or rank.

“Perhaps not,” Bows said. “Mrs. H. sent me here to look after you, and see you gave that message you didn’t give. Women always are right; they have always a reason. Why, sir,” he added, turning to Arthur with a sour twist, “she had a reason even for sending me. I was sitting with her after you left us—quiet and comfortable—talking away, and she mending your shirts—when your two young friends Jack Linton and Bob Blades looked in from Bartholomew’s; and then she found out she had this message. You needn’t hurry; she don’t want you back again. They’ll stay two hours, I daresay.”

At this, Huxter sprang up as if the chair had pricked him. He plunged his stick into his paletot pocket, seized his hat.

“You’ll come and see us, sir, won’t you?” he said to Arthur. “You’ll talk over the governor, won’t you, if I can get out of this place and down to Clavering?”

“You will promise to attend me gratis if ever I fall ill at Fairoaks,” Arthur said, good-humouredly. “I will do anything I can. I will come and see Mrs. Huxter immediately, and we will conspire together.”

“I thought that would send him out,” Bows said, settling back into his chair as the young surgeon bolted. “And it’s all true—every word. She wants you back again, and sends her husband after you. She cajoles everybody, the little devil. She tries it on you, on me, on poor Costigan, on the young chaps from Bartholomew’s. She’s got a little court already. And if there’s nobody, she practises on the old German baker downstairs, or coaxes the black sweeper at the crossing.”

“Is she fond of that fellow?” Arthur asked.

“There’s no accounting for likes and dislikes,” Bows said.

“Yes—she’s fond of him; and having took it into her head, she wouldn’t rest till she married him. Banns at St. Clement’s; nobody heard, nobody objected. One day she slips out of the porter’s lodge, gets the business done, goes off to Gravesend with Lothario, and leaves a note for me to go and explain to her Ma. Bless you—the old woman knew as well as I did, though she pretended not. And so she goes, and I’m alone again. I miss her, sir—tripping along that court, coming for her singing lesson. I’ve no heart to look into the lodge now; it looks empty without her. And I go and sit and dangle about her lodgings like an old fool. She makes ’em very trim, though; gets up all Huxter’s shirts and clothes; cooks his little dinner; sings at her work like a lark. What’s the use of being angry? I lent ’em three pound to go on with; for they haven’t got a shilling till the reconciliation, and Pa comes down.”

When Bows had gone, Arthur carried Blanche’s letter, and the news which had just come to him, to his usual adviser, Laura. It was curious how this gentleman—who commonly took his own way, and called it fate—now wanted another person’s counsel upon everything; as if his mind, having had one great dish snatched away, must needs ask leave before it tasted even bread and butter.

He produced Blanche’s letter and asked Laura to interpret it. Laura read, grew agitated, puzzled, and very grave.

“It seems to me,” she said, “as if Blanche is acting very artfully.”

“And wishes so to place matters that she may take me or leave me?” Arthur asked. “Is it not so?”

“It is, I am afraid, a kind of duplicity which does not augur well for your happiness,” Laura said; “and it is a bad reply to your candour and honesty. Do you know—I think—I scarcely like to say what I think.” She blushed deeply; but under Arthur’s persuasion the shy confession came. “It looks to me, Arthur, as if there might be—there might be somebody else.”

“And if there is,” Arthur broke out, “and if I am free once again, will the best and dearest of all women—”

“You are not free, dear brother,” Laura said, calmly. “You belong to another; of whom I own it grieves me to think ill. But I can’t do otherwise. It is very odd that in this letter she does not urge you to tell her the reason why you have broken arrangements so advantageous to you; and avoids speaking of it. She somehow writes as if she knows her father’s secret.”

The train whisked Arthur Pendennis down to Tunbridge with the brisk, unfeeling punctuality of a kitchen spit turned by machinery: click, click, and your joint is done whether your conscience is cooked through or raw at the bone. He sat with his carpet-bag at his feet like a modest hamper of provisions, and in the brief miles between stations contrived to season his whole youth with remorse, tasting it as a too-sensitive diner tastes a sauce and finds the salt his own hand shook in.

“Here,” thought he, as the wheels sang their iron song over the rails—clack-clack, clack-clack, a kind of harsh minstrelry that drowned the small human voice within—“here is the end of my romances and airs. Whether I am obstinate or yielding, I blunder into the same dish at last: disappointment served hot.”

He went over it all as a careful food-historian might turn the pages of an old household book, seeing how one poor substitution in a receipt changes the entire flavour of a family. If he had married Laura because his mother implored, would Laura have been the angel his mother saw? No; angels, like truffles, can’t be forced upon a man’s palate by another’s enthusiasm. He had refused one woman’s fortune on scruple, accepted another’s on guarantee; and now Fate, that capricious cook, had whipped away the dowry and left him with the wife—like taking away the sugar after the pudding is baked and bidding you call it a delicacy.

His uncle, honest old man, could swallow any provenance so long as it was coined and clinked; could not even comprehend the nausea Arthur felt at the thought of dining off money with a taint upon it. And Arthur, by insisting on clean bread, contrived only to starve everybody’s comfort. He dissatisfied all, and worst of all himself. What prospect was there for that poor little frivolous girl who was to take his obscure name and share his uncertain fortune? He had not even ambition to keep him warm—no stout stew of self-esteem to sustain him when affection ran thin.

He looked at his fellow-travellers, as one looks round a noisy taproom in which the talk is hearty but the air heavy. Opposite sat a foreign priest, head bent over his breviary as over a cherished family recipe written in a language that refuses to be made common—eyes never lifting except when darkness in a tunnel made reading impossible. Beside him an old gentleman glowered over his newspaper with the fixed rancour of a man whose breakfast has been spoiled daily for thirty years by the same disagreeable cook. Their faiths, their hates, their certainties—each sounded, in the carriage’s small acoustic world, like a different instrument: the priest’s hush; the newspaper’s crackle; the old man’s snort.

“Would you like to look at the paper, sir?” asked a stout gentleman—thrusting it out with a zeal that suggested he was serving a dish he found delicious and assumed must delight the whole table. The journal blazed with an attack upon the “black-coated order” across from them, and Arthur, who could as soon have judged a delicate consommé while a brass band practised in the dining-room, took it politely and read nothing.

“And yet,” he thought, letting the print swim before him unheard, “would I take either of those men’s creed, with all its consequences? They have no doubts. They march on with their loads of logic like mules with panniers. But I—” The clatter of the carriage seemed to argue with him. “Ah me! a man must bear his own burden, cook his own faith, and eat it whether it agrees with him or not. To what mortal ear could I tell all—even if I wished? Who could taste another’s bitterness and call it by the right name? There are flavours no language holds: a lost dialect on the tongue, an old nursery word for comfort that no polished lexicon can translate.”

He felt, in that moment, how much of life is altered by accidents as small as a grain of sand in the mill-stone, or a pebble flung in a stream. A chance word in youth; a terror; a mischance; some remembered tone of a parent’s voice that governs a man thereafter as surely as a kitchen bell. Who can weigh the circumstances and temptations that season our good and evil account—save One?

“Here it ends,” he told himself; “this day or to-morrow winds up the account of my youth.” And his head fell, not in theatrical despair, but in a tired humility; the heart in him prostrated itself before that Throne where wisdom sits with pity. The train’s noise, for once, seemed less an insult than a penance—industrial din that could not drown prayer, only force it inward.

“What matter fame or poverty,” he thought. “If I marry the woman I have chosen, may I have strength to be true to her and make her happy. If I have children—God teach me to speak truth among them, and leave them an honest name.” He saw, with a sudden clearness, that there were no splendours for his marriage; and perhaps none were deserved. Let the feast be plain if it be wholesome.

At Tunbridge the train stopped with a jerk; the newspaper went back to its owner; the priest still bowed to his book; and Arthur, carpet-bag in hand, stepped down as briskly as a man can who carries a whole larder of doubts inside him. He resolved to face his fortune as a cook faces a new kitchen: tie the apron, sharpen the knives, and do the work.

A fly took him to Lady Clavering’s house. The streets had their own small soundscape: hooves on hard road, wheels hissing over gravel, distant voices, a dog’s bark—domestic noises that soothed by their very ordinariness, like hearing one’s own kettle sing at home after too much railway clamor. In the jolting ride Arthur composed the little speech he meant for Blanche—an honest, plain, best-meaning dish.

“Blanche,” it ran, “I cannot understand your last letter. If my proposal is acceptable, I am ready. I forgo worldly advantages I cannot take without dishonour. If you doubt my affection, here I am: send for Smirke; let us be married at once; and with all my heart I purpose to keep my vow, cherish you through life, be true and loving.”

With this moral roulade prepared, he sprang from the fly to the hall-door. A servant met him whom he did not know, and stared at the carpet-bag as if it were a suspicious parcel from a dubious market-stall.

“Her Ladyship’s not at home, sir,” the man said, making no move to relieve Arthur of his burden.

“I am Mr. Pendennis,” Arthur answered. “Where is Lightfoot?”

“Lightfoot is gone,” said the man. “My Lady is out, and my orders was—”

Arthur, whose ear caught what his eye had not yet seen, heard Miss Amory’s voice in the drawing-room—warbling like a caged bird convinced of its own nightingale-hood. “Take the bag to a dressing-room,” he said; and, passing the porter as if passing an underling at a kitchen door, he walked straight toward the sound.

The door opened on music—melodious, passionate, melancholy, well-sauced, a little too richly spiced for the midday. Blanche sat at the piano singing with all her might and fascinations, the notes curling out into the room like steam from a pot meant to intoxicate. Master Clavering lay asleep on the sofa, as indifferent to that expensive noise as a well-fed cat to poetry. But near Blanche sat a gentleman utterly enraptured, as if each note were a syllable in the only language he truly understood.

As Arthur entered, the gentleman started up with a “Hullo!” Blanche stopped with a little shriek, and Frank Clavering woke as if an unexpected dish had been clapped under his nose. Arthur advanced and said, with the calm incredulity of a man who has already tasted betrayal and finds it now in a new flavour, “What, Foker! How do you do, Foker?”

There, by Miss Amory’s side, was a purple-leather box—twin to the one Arthur had seen in Harry’s hand three days before at a jeweller’s in Waterloo Place. It was open; and on its white satin cushion lay a bracelet—a magnificent serpentine thing, ruby-headed and diamond-tailed, glittering like a sweetmeat too bright to be wholesome.

“How de-do, Pendennis?” said Foker, with the air of a boy caught stealing jam and uncertain whether to blush or fight.

Blanche made agitated movements—shoulders, hands, eyes all fluttering like napkins in a draught. She whipped her handkerchief over the bracelet as if it were a scandalous pâté, and came forward with a trembling hand to greet Arthur.

“How is dearest Laura?” she asked; and there was something in the question like vinegar dashed into milk.

Foker, in his profound mourning for the lost possibility of Blanche-and-Pendennis, looked at Arthur with a piteous bewilderment which no pen need paint; and Frank Clavering, after one glance at the tableau, had time only to cry, “Here’s a jolly go!” before he vanished sniggering—like a boy escaping the pantry after seeing the cook with her hands in the pie.

Arthur had held himself in so far; but the sight of that bracelet, that box, that devout, blushing Harry—these things mixed into a draught too absurdly potent. He burst into laughter—wild, loud, irrepressible—so that Blanche, who could face tragedy like a practiced actress, was frightened by comedy, which is less manageable.

“And this was the secret, was it?” he cried. “Don’t blush and turn away, Foker, my boy. Why, man, you are a pattern of fidelity. Could I stand between Blanche and such constancy—could I stand between Miss Amory and fifteen thousand a year?”

“It is not that, Mr. Pendennis,” Blanche said, drawing herself up with a dignity that smelt faintly of pomade and performance. “It is not money, it is not rank, it is not gold that moves me; but it is constancy, it is fidelity, it is a whole trustful loving heart offered to me, that I treasure—yes, that I treasure!”

She reached again for her handkerchief, recollecting what lay beneath it, and checked herself with a little start, like a hostess who remembers she has hidden the best dish for later company and must not reveal it too soon.

“I do not disown—I do not disguise—my life is above disguise—that I once thought I loved you; yes, thought I was beloved by you, I own. How I clung to that faith! How I strove, I prayed, I longed to believe it! But your conduct always—your own words so cold, so heartless, so unkind—have undeceived me. You trifled with the heart of the poor maiden! You flung me back with scorn the troth which I had plighted! I have explained all—all to Mr. Foker.”

“That you have,” said Foker, with a devotion that would have basted a roast.

“What, all?” Arthur asked, and looked at Blanche with a meaning glance—as if sniffing a sauce and detecting an ingredient not named.

“It is I am in fault, is it?” Arthur continued. “Well, well, Blanche, be it so. I won’t appeal against your sentence. I came down looking to very different things, Heaven knows, and with a heart truly and kindly disposed towards you. I hope you may be happy with another, as it was my wish to make you so; and I hope my honest old friend here will have a wife worthy of his loyalty, constancy, and affection. Indeed they deserve the regard of any woman—even Miss Blanche Amory. Shake hands, Harry; don’t look askance at me. Has anybody told you that I was false and heartless?”

“I think you’re a—” Foker began, swelling like a kettle about to boil over.

“Henry, not a word!” Blanche interposed, with saintly command. “I pray you let there be forgiveness!”

“You’re an angel, by Jove, you’re an angel!” cried Foker; whereupon Blanche lifted her eyes seraphically toward the chandelier, as if light itself owed her applause.

“In spite of what has passed,” she continued, “for the sake of what has passed, I must always regard Arthur as a brother. We have known each other years; we have trodden the same fields and plucked the same flowers together. Arthur! Henry! I beseech you, take hands and be friends! Forgive you!—I forgive you, Arthur, with my heart I do. Should I not do so for making me so happy?”

“There is only one person of us three whom I pity, Blanche,” Arthur said gravely; and there was no laughter left in his voice now. “And I say again, I hope you will make this good fellow—this honest and loyal creature—happy.”

“Happy! O Heavens!” cried Harry. He could not speak; his happiness broke out at his eyes like broth boiling over. “She don’t know—she can’t know how fond I am of her; and—and who am I? a poor little beggar, and she takes me up and says she’ll try and I—I—love me. I ain’t worthy of so much happiness. Give us your hand, old boy. Since she forgives you after your heartless conduct, and says she loves you, I’ll make you welcome. I tell you I’ll love everybody who loves her. By—, if she tells me to kiss the ground I’ll kiss it. Tell me to kiss the ground! I say, tell me. I love you so. You see I love you so.”

Blanche looked upward again, her gentle bosom heaving with the exact rhythm of a practiced aria. She held out one hand as if to bless Harry, and then royally permitted him to kiss it. With the other she took up the handkerchief and hid her own eyes, as if modesty were a garnish she must add at the last moment.

“I swear that is a villain who deceives such a loving creature as that,” Arthur said.

Blanche laid down the handkerchief and rested her second hand softly on Foker’s head—his head bent down kissing and weeping over hand number one.

“Foolish boy?” she murmured. “It shall be loved as it deserves. Who could help loving such a silly creature!”

At that moment Frank Clavering broke in briskly, like a waiter tired of sentiment when there’s a bill to settle.

“I say, Pendennis!”

“Well, Frank!”

“The man wants to be paid and go back. He’s had some beer.”

“I’ll go back with him,” Arthur said, seizing the excuse as one seizes a door out of a stifling room. “Good-bye, Blanche. God bless you, Foker, old friend. You know neither of you want me here.”

He longed to be off that instant; but Blanche stopped him with a quiet authority.

“Stay—I must say one word to you. One word in private, if you please. You can trust us together, can’t you, Henry?”

The way she said “Henry”—as if the name were a sweet she placed on his tongue—ravished him.

“Trust you!” cried Foker. “Oh, who wouldn’t trust you! Come along, Franky, my boy.”

“Let’s have a cigar,” said Frank as they went into the hall.

“She don’t like it,” Harry murmured.

“Law bless you—she don’t mind. Pendennis used to smoke regular,” Frank returned, with the candour of youth.

Left alone, Blanche’s face settled into a calm so complete it was almost a different complexion.

“It was but a short word I had to say,” she began. “You never loved me, Mr. Pendennis.”

“I told you how much,” Arthur answered. “I never deceived you.”

“I suppose you will go back and marry Laura,” Blanche continued.

“Was that what you had to say?” Arthur asked.

“You are going to her this very night. There is no denying it. You never cared for me.”

“And you?” Arthur said, and waited.

“Et vous?” she answered, and then with a small shrug, as if confession were only another costume: “Et moi, c’est different. I have been spoilt early. I cannot live out of the world—out of excitement. I could have done so, but it is too late. If I cannot have emotions, I must have the world. You would offer me neither one nor the other. You are blasé in everything—even in ambition. You had a career before you, and you would not take it. You give it up!—for what? for une bêtise, for an absurd scruple. Why would you not have that seat, and be such a puritain? Why should you refuse what is mine by right—by right, entendez-vous?”

“You know all, then?” Arthur asked.

“Only within a month. But I have suspected ever since Baymouth—n’importe since when. It is not too late. He is as if he had never been; and there is a position in the world before you yet. Why not sit in Parliament, exert your talent, and give a place in the world to yourself—to your wife? I take celui-là. Il est bon. Il est riche. Il est—vous le connaissez autant que moi enfin. Think you that I would not prefer un homme qui fera parler de moi? If the secret appears I am rich a millions. How does it affect me? It is not my fault. It will never appear.”

“You will tell Harry everything, won’t you?” Arthur said.

“Je comprends. Vous refusez,” Blanche answered, and for a flash the calm cracked, showing a savage edge beneath—like a spoon scraping the bottom of a pan. “I will tell Harry at my own time—when we are married. You will not betray me, will you? You, having a defenceless girl’s secret, will not turn upon her and use it? S’il me plaît de le cacher, mon secret—pourquoi le donnerai-je? Je l’aime, mon pauvre père, voyez-vous? I would rather live with that man than with you fades intriguers of the world. I must have emotions—il m’en donne. Il m’écrit. Il écrit très-bien, voyez-vous—comme un pirate—comme un Bohémien—comme un homme. But for this I would have said to my mother—Ma mère! quittons ce lâche mari, cette lâche société—retournons à mon père.”

“The pirate would have wearied you like the rest,” Arthur said, with a sadness that had no heat in it.

“Eh! Il me faut des émotions,” Blanche returned, as if the phrase were her only native word—her true dialect amid all the borrowed flourishes.

Arthur, in that brief private colloquy, knew more of Blanche than he had learned in years—though he also imagined more than existed. For she could not carry any feeling to its full honest end: her enthusiasms were like show-dishes—glittering, ingeniously arranged, flaring for an instant under the dining-room lamps, and then cooling into something tasteless the moment the next course arrived. Her love, her grief, her hatred, her taste—all were a kind of theatrical cookery, made to look and sound delicious rather than to nourish anyone at the table.

Pen fretted upon the Tunbridge platform as if the very rails had been laid to torment him. The place had its own little orchestra: the gulls quarrelling over crusts, the porters’ boots keeping time on the boards, the iron-stiff cough of a luggage-truck, and—over all—those modern whistles that split a man’s thought in two like a cleaver through gristle. Half an hour of that was six hours to a heart that had been simmering all day.

At last the evening train came up snorting and panting like a great black kitchen-stove that had eaten too much coal. Pen flung himself into it, and away they went, with the steady clack-clack of wheels that can sound like comfort to the hopeful and like a mortuary bell to the miserable. London received him with its usual stew: damp stone, horse-sweat, fried fish, stale porter, and that thin metallic tang which seems distilled from perpetual motion. Some gentleman forgot his carpet-bag, rushed at a cab, and cried, “Drive as hard as you can go to Jermyn Street.” The cabman—though a hansom-man, and therefore by nature suspicious of promises—said “Thank you” for the coin put in his hand; and Pen, who could have out-run the horse had despair been a spur, bounded up the hotel stairs to Lady Rockminster’s rooms.

Laura was alone in the drawing-room, pale by the lamplight, a book open before her which she was not reading so much as staring through—like a cook who has set a sauce to thicken and, hearing a footstep, forgets whether she has salted it. She looked up. The great moments of life, which poets paint with thunder, come as quietly as the click of a latch; your doom is spoken in two hurried sentences, and the world, with all its plates and puddings and ledgers, goes on as before.

Pen did not wait for greetings. He crossed the room, seized the hand she had half risen to give him—warm, trembling, honest—and dropped to his knees as if the floor had drawn him down.

“I have seen her,” he said quickly. “She has engaged herself to Harry Foker—and—and now, Laura?”

Her fingers answered first; the pressure was a whole vocabulary, a native dialect of the heart which no fashionable language can translate. Her eyes shone; her lips quivered with words that could not get themselves made. Pen’s head sank into her lap, and he sobbed out like a boy who has been starved and suddenly set before bread, “Come and bless us, dear mother.”

And indeed, in that instant, it was as though Helen’s presence—soft as the smell of clean linen warmed by the fire—folded him. Laura’s arms went round him, tender as any mother’s, and the room, a moment before so cold with suspense, seemed filled with a domestic sunshine that did not come from the lamp.

Of course, just then, in came Lady Rockminster, who had been taking her after-dinner nap—like any sensible person who knows the value of resting between courses. She entered her sitting-room and, seeing the tableau, delivered herself of her first remark, which was as much a knock on the head as a remark can be.

“Upon my word, young people!” she cried; and her attendant, Beck, made great wondering eyes over her shoulder, as if she had discovered a new recipe for scandal.

“Beck! leave the room,” Lady Rockminster snapped. “What do you want poking your nose in here?”

Pen sprang up, triumphant, still holding Laura’s hand as if it were the title-deed of his future.

“She is consoling me for my misfortune, ma’am,” he said.

“What do you mean by kissing her hand? I don’t know what you will be next doing.”

Pen, to show that his audacities were evenly distributed, kissed her Ladyship’s hand too. “I have been to Tunbridge,” he said, “and seen Miss Amory; and find on my arrival that—that a villain has transplanted me in her affections.”

“Is that all? Is that what you were whimpering on your knees about?” the old lady cried, her indignation rising like milk in a neglected saucepan. “You might have kept the news till to-morrow.”

“Yes—another has superseded me,” Pen went on, with the air of a tragedian who has been hired for the part of Hamlet and finds himself asked to play a footman. “But why call him villain? He is brave, he is constant, he is young, he is wealthy, he is beautiful.”

“What stuff are you talking, sir? What has happened?”

“Miss Amory has jilted me, and accepted Henry Foker, Esq. I found her warbling ditties to him as he lay at her feet; presents had been accepted, vows exchanged, these ten days. Harry was old Mrs. Planter’s rheumatism, which kept dearest Laura out of the house. He is the most constant and generous of men. He has promised the living of Logwood to Lady Ann’s husband, and given her a splendid present on her marriage; and he rushed to fling himself at Blanche’s feet the instant he found he was free.”

“And so, as you can’t get Blanche, you put up with Laura; is that it, sir?” asked Lady Rockminster, who could cut you a slice of truth thinner than any cook can shave truffle.

“He acted nobly,” Laura said, lifting her head with that gentle firmness which is more terrible than a scold.

“I acted as she bade me,” said Pen.

“Never mind how, Lady Rockminster,” he continued, warming now, “but to the best of my knowledge and power. And if you mean that I am not worthy of Laura, I know it, and pray Heaven to better me; and if the love and company of the best and purest creature in the world can do so, at least I shall have these to help me.”

“Hmm,” said the old lady, looking at them with an air that had softened a shade—as hard butter yields if you only keep it long enough near the fire. “It is all very well; but I should have preferred Bluebeard.”

Pen, to turn the knife from a place where it might cut too deep, bethought him suddenly of his morning’s meeting with Huxter and of Fanny Bolton’s whirlwind of a destiny—matters he had let slip under the immediate boil and bubble of his own emotions. So he told his tale, and told it with that particular relish a man has when he is both happy and anxious to prove himself innocent. He described how Huxter had elevated Fanny to the rank of wife, and how he shook at the thought of his father’s arrival; and Pen, who could season a story as neatly as any sauce, dwelt especially on Fanny’s coquetry, her irrepressible appetite for admiration, her way of tossing her little nets over the whole male species—meaning, without saying: You see, Laura, it wasn’t I that went fishing; I was the fish that escaped.

Laura understood, as women do, the meaning behind the words and the pleading behind the humour.

“If you did any wrong, you repented, dear Pen,” she said; and then, with eyes and blushes that confessed as much as any speech, she added, “and you know that I have no right to reproach you.”

“Hm!” grumbled Lady Rockminster. “I should have preferred Bluebeard.”

“The past is broken away. The morrow is before us,” Pen said. “I will do my best to make your morrow happy, dear Laura.”

He spoke bravely; but his heart was humbled by the nearness of his happiness, awestricken as a poor man is when first he sits down in a great house and is afraid of spoiling the napery. And she—she was shining with that strange, quiet radiance which comes when a long hunger ends, and the soul at last is fed. It seemed to her almost as if Helen stood there indeed, unseen but real: as one smells, in a new kitchen, the faint ghost of the herbs that have been chopped there for years. Laura moved with a different step; she bloomed with a beauty that was not paint nor fashion but something deeper, like bread risen properly—by patience and warmth.

Arthur saw the change. Lady Rockminster saw it too, because old women, if they have any honesty in them, are better historians of young hearts than young hearts are of themselves. Leaning near, she whispered to Laura while Pen was laughing over Huxter’s panic—

“What a sly demure little wretch you have been! And how you have kept your secret!”

“How are we to help the young couple?” Laura asked aloud then; for generous lovers are like generous cooks—they can’t be content with their own full table, but must be planning dinners for other people.

“We must go and see them,” said Pen.

“Of course we must go and see them,” said Laura. “I intend to be very fond of Fanny. Let us go this instant. Lady Rockminster, may I have the carriage?”

“Go now!” cried the old lady. “Why, you stupid creature, it is eleven o’clock at night. Mr. and Mrs. Huxter have got their nightcaps on, I dare say. And it is time for you to go now. Good night, Mr. Pendennis.”

They begged for ten minutes more, as if time could be begged like sugar.

“We will go to-morrow morning, then,” Pen said. “I will come and fetch you with Martha.”

“An earl’s coronet,” Pen added, pleased as a boy with a new toy, “will have a great effect in Lamb Court and Smithfield. Stay—Lady Rockminster, will you join us in a little conspiracy?”

“How do you mean conspiracy, young man?”

“Will you please to be a little ill to-morrow; and when old Mr. Huxter arrives, will you let me call him in? If he is put into a good humour at the notion of attending a baronet in the country, what influence won’t a countess have on him? When he is softened—when he is quite ripe, we will break the secret upon him; bring in the young people, extort the paternal benediction, and finish the comedy.”

“A parcel of stuff,” said Lady Rockminster. “Take your hat, sir. Come away, miss. There—my head is turned another way. Good night, young people.”

And who knows but, nodding and humming to herself as she went away on Laura’s arm, she tasted—like some old country dish remembered for a moment—the flavour of her own earlier days?

With the early morning came Laura and Martha according to appointment; and the desired sensation, let us hope, was produced in Lamb Court—where sensation is not usually on the bill. From thence the three proceeded to Charterhouse Lane, to wait upon Mr. and Mrs. Samuel Huxter.

There was a small domestic hush in Fanny’s lodging—a neatness with pretensions, like a tart set out with more pride than fruit. The sounds were intimate: a kettle’s faint complaint in the grate; a cat padding as silently as a thief; the distant grind of carts in the lane like the sea heard through walls. Laura and Fanny looked at each other with great interest, and with no little emotion on Fanny’s part. She had not seen her “guardian”—as she liked to call Pen in consequence of his bequest—since the event which had united her to Mr. Huxter.

“Samuel told me how kind you had been,” she said. “You were always very kind, Mr. Pendennis. And—and I hope your friend is better, who was took ill in Shepherd’s Inn, ma’am.”

“My name is Laura,” Laura said, blushing. “I am—that is, I was—that is, I am Arthur’s sister; and we shall always love you for being so good to him when he was ill. And when we live in the country, I hope we shall see each other. And I shall be always happy to hear of your happiness, Fanny.”

“We are going to do what you and Huxter have done, Fanny,” Pen cried, unable to keep his joy from skipping. “Where is Huxter? What nice, snug lodgings you’ve got! What a pretty cat!”

While Fanny fluttered answers—half curtsies, half confessions—Laura, in her own mind, was doing what women do best: tasting, judging, revising.

“Well, now really! is this the creature about whom we were all so frightened? What could he see in her? She’s a homely little thing, but such manners! Well, she was very kind to him,—bless her for that.”

Mr. Samuel had gone out to meet his Pa. Mrs. Huxter said the old gentleman was to arrive that day at the Somerset Coffee-house in the Strand; and Fanny confessed she was in a sad tremor about the meeting.

“If his parent casts him off, what are we to do?” she cried. “I shall never pardon myself for bringing ruing on my ’usband’s ’ead. You must intercede for us, Mr. Arthur. If mortal man can, you can bend and influence Mr. Huxter senior.”

Fanny still regarded Pen as a superior being; and Pen, seeing her little tragedy-airs and trepidations, her vanity kneaded with genuine terror, could not help remembering the past—how easily a life may be altered by a few wrong ingredients and a too-hasty heat.

As soon as the interview was over, in came Messrs. Linton and Blades, of course to visit Huxter, bringing with them a fine fragrance of tobacco, like two walking chimneys. They had watched the carriage at the baker’s door and remarked the coronet with awe; and they asked Fanny who that uncommonly heavy swell was who had just driven off. They pronounced the countess “of the right sort.” Then, hearing it was Mr. Pendennis and his sister, they remarked—because envy always keeps its own little dictionary—that Pen’s father was only a sawbones, and that he gave himself confounded airs; they had been in Huxter’s company on the night of his little altercation with Pen in the Back Kitchen, and never forgot a grudge any more than they forgot their pipes.

Returning home through Fleet Street, and as Laura—very prettily and conscientiously—was explaining to Pen’s infinite amusement that Fanny was very well, but that really there was no beauty in her (there might be, but she could not see it), they were delayed near Temple Bar by the usual roar and jostle: wheel against wheel, voices hawking, bells, oaths, the eternal iron clatter of London chewing its own cud.

There they saw young Huxter hurrying back to his bride.

“The governor has arrived,” he panted. “He’s at the Somerset Coffee-house. He’s in tolerable good-humour—something about the railway. But I’ve been afraid to speak about—about that business. Would Mr. Pendennis try it on?”

Pen said he would go at that moment and call upon Mr. Huxter, and see what might be done. Huxter junior would lurk outside while that awful interview took place. The coronet on the carriage inspired his soul also with wonder.

And old Mr. Huxter himself beheld that coronet with delight from the coffee-house window, as he looked down the Strand—always a treat to him, like a grand market-street to a man from a village, full of sights and sounds to carry home and recount.

“And I can afford to give myself a lark, sir,” said Mr. Huxter, shaking Pen’s hand with cordiality. “Of course you know the news? We have got our bill, sir. We shall have our branch line—our shares are up, sir—and we buy your three fields along the Brawl, and put a pretty penny into your pocket, Mr. Pendennis.”

“Indeed!—that is good news,” Pen said; remembering suddenly a letter from Mr. Tatham which had been waiting at Chambers these three days—unopened, because a man in love can let money lie as carelessly as a cook lets the roast drip when the kitchen is on fire.

“I hope you don’t intend to grow rich, and give up practice,” Pen added. “We can’t lose you at Clavering, Mr. Huxter; though I hear very good accounts of your son. My friend, Dr. Goodenough, speaks most highly of his talents. It is hard that a man of your eminence should be kept in a country town.”

“The metropolis would have been my sphere of action, sir,” Mr. Huxter said, surveying the Strand as if the very paving-stones were patients waiting for him. “But a man takes his business where he finds it; and I succeeded to that of my father.”

“It was my father’s, too,” said Pen. “I sometimes wish I had followed it.”

“You, sir, have taken a more lofty career,” said the old gentleman. “You aspire to the senate, and to literary honours. You wield the poet’s pen, sir, and move in the circles of fashion. We keep an eye upon you at Clavering. We read your name in the lists of the select parties of the nobility. Why, it was only the other day that my wife was remarking how odd it was that at a party at the Earl of Kidderminster’s your name was not mentioned. To what member of the aristocracy may I ask does that equipage belong from which I saw you descend? The Countess Dowager of Rockminster? How is her Ladyship?”

“Her Ladyship is not very well,” Pen said; “and when I heard that you were coming to town, I strongly urged her to see you, Mr. Huxter.”

Old Huxter felt that if he had a hundred votes for Clavering he would give them all to Pen on the spot. The machinery of flattery is simple and very old: you oil a man’s vanity, and he runs without squeaking.

“There is an old friend of yours in the carriage—a Clavering lady too—will you come out and speak to her?” Pen asked.

The old surgeon was delighted, and ran out bowing and smiling to the coroneted carriage in the midst of the full Strand, where the sound of fashion is as loud as the sound of wheels. Huxter junior, dodging about like a guilty mouse, saw his father meet Laura; saw her put out her hand; and presently, after a little colloquy with Pen, saw his father actually jump into the carriage and drive away with Miss Bell.

There was no room for Arthur. He came back laughing to the young surgeon and told him where his parent was bound.

During the whole journey Laura coaxed and wheedled and cajoled the old gentleman with an art so domestic and so perfect that one might have called it cookery: she seasoned praise just so, she let the conversation simmer where his pride might soften, she never once let it boil over into offence. And Lady Rockminster, who affected to despise conspiracies and yet could conduct one as if she had invented the trade, achieved the final victory by complimenting him on his skill and professing anxiety to consult him.

What were her Ladyship’s symptoms? Should he meet her Ladyship’s usual medical attendant? Mr. Jones was called out of town? He should be delighted—delighted—to devote his very best energies and experience to her Ladyship’s service. He was so charmed with his noble patient that he wrote home about her to his wife and family, and talked of nothing but Lady Rockminster to Samuel when that youth came in the evening to partake of beefsteak and oyster-sauce and accompany his parent to the play.
